# Super Mario World (SNES) Game Genie codes

## Free-roaming debug mode (L+A)

**Code:** `EDA6-DFD7`
**Raw form:** `00CC84:F0` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 16:20:00

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** Press L+A to cycle a debug mode through 3 states
(`DebugFreeRoam` = 0/1/2). In states 1 and 2, Mario is invincible
(`IFrameTimer` is set to `$FF`). The d-pad moves him freely around the
screen, and normal physics do not apply. The code that changes the state
always runs in the retail game. Only the code that uses the state is
unreachable:

```
ResetAni:
if ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)                         ;\=================== J, U, & SS ================
    LDA.B axlr0000Hold                        ;!
    AND.B #$20                                ;!
    BEQ +                                     ;!
    LDA.B axlr0000Frame                       ;!
    CMP.B #$80                                ;!
    BNE +                                     ;!
    INC.W DebugFreeRoam                       ;!
    LDA.W DebugFreeRoam                       ;!
    CMP.B #$03                                ;!
    BCC +                                     ;!
    STZ.W DebugFreeRoam                       ;!
  + LDA.W DebugFreeRoam                       ;!
    BRA CODE_00CCBB                           ;! Change to BEQ to enable debug code below
                                              ;!
    LSR A                                     ;! \ Unreachable
    BEQ ADDR_00CCB3                           ;! | Debug: Free roaming mode
    LDA.B #$FF                                ;! |
    STA.W IFrameTimer                         ;! |
    LDA.B byetudlrHold                        ;! |
    ...
endif
```

`axlr0000Hold AND #$20` tests if L is held. `axlr0000Frame CMP #$80`
tests if A was pressed on this frame (A is `$80` in the `axlr0000`
layout). So the input is: hold L, then press A. This increments
`DebugFreeRoam` in the order 0->1->2->0. The code changes the `BRA`
opcode (`$80`) to `BEQ` (`$F0`). A still holds `DebugFreeRoam`. In state 0,
`BEQ` branches to `CODE_00CCBB` (the normal animation reset). In states 1
and 2 the value is not zero, so the branch is not taken and the free-roam
code runs.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00CC84` in `ResetAni` (`bank_00.asm`). This is the
opcode byte of `BRA CODE_00CCBB`. Its comment says "Change to BEQ to enable
debug code below". Checked against the disassembly source and the built ROM.
In the ROM, `$00CC84` holds `$80`, as the source predicts.

**Caveats:** **NTSC-only block** (`if ver_is_ntsc`): present in J/U/SS,
not present in E0/E1.

## Boss cutscene select (L+R)

**Code:** `7DBD-04AF`
**Raw form:** `00950B:30` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 16:20:00

**Mechanism:** During a castle boss-defeat cutscene, hold L+R. The scene
reloads and a debug menu (`DebugCutsceneSelect`) opens. In this menu,
Up+Select moves to the next boss cutscene (Iggy through Bowser, then the
credits). This is the best-documented debug leftover in the game. The source
comment gives the exact fix:

```
GM1BCutscene:                                 ; Game Mode 1B - Credits / Castle Cutscene
    JSL OAMResetRoutine                       ; Clear OAM.
    LDA.W CutsceneID                          ;\ 
    CMP.B #!Cutscene_Credits                  ;| Branch down if specifically running the credits.
    BEQ ProccessCredits                       ;/
    LDA.B axlr0000Hold                        ;\ 
    AND.B #0                                  ;|] DEBUG: Change #%00000000 to #%00110000 to enable the boss cutscene select.
    CMP.B #!ButL|!ButR                        ;| Pressing L + R will then reload the cutscene.
    BNE ProcessCastleCutscene                 ;/

DebugCutsceneSelect:                          ;# DEBUG: Boss cutscene select.
    LDA.B byetudlrHold                        ;#\ 
    AND.B #!DpadUp                            ;#|
    BEQ ++                                    ;#|
    LDA.W CutsceneID                          ;#| If up is also being held,
    INC A                                     ;#|  advance to the next boss cutscene.
    CMP.B #!Cutscene_Credits+1                ;#|
    BCC +                                     ;#|
    LDA.B #!Cutscene_Iggy                     ;#|
  + STA.W CutsceneID                          ;#/
 ++ LDA.B #!GameMode_FadeToCutscene           ;#\ Reload the scene.
    STA.W GameMode                            ;#/
    RTS                                       ;#

ProcessCastleCutscene:                        ; Debug code skipped; boss beaten cutscene continues.
```

The code changes the operand of `AND.B #0`. With a mask of `$00`, `A` is
always `0`. So `CMP.B #!ButL|!ButR` (`$30`) never matches, and
`BNE ProcessCastleCutscene` always goes to the normal cutscene code.
`DebugCutsceneSelect` never runs. With the operand set to `$30`, the `AND`
keeps the L and R bits of `axlr0000Hold`. Now, if L and R are both held, the
compare matches and the debug menu runs. In the menu, hold Up and press
Select to increment `CutsceneID`. After the last boss it goes back to the
first. The cutscene then reloads through `GameMode_FadeToCutscene`.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00950B` in `GM1BCutscene` (`bank_00.asm`). This is
the immediate operand of `AND.B #0`. Its comment gives the exact fix ("Change
#%00000000 to #%00110000 to enable the boss cutscene select"). Checked
against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$00950B`
holds `$00`, as the source predicts.

**Caveats:** Works only in game mode `1B` (while a castle boss-defeat
cutscene plays).

## Slow motion (player 2 controller, while paused)

**Code:** `EDC0-6FAD`
**Raw form:** `00A247:F0` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 16:20:00

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** Pause the game with Start (Player 1). While the game is
paused, hold **B on controller 2**. The game advances one frame about every
16 frames (~3.75 fps), so it runs in slow motion. Press **Y on controller 2**
to advance exactly one frame for each press. Holding Y does not repeat.
This code needs a second controller. Without one, it does nothing and pause
works normally.

```
CODE_00A242:
    LDA.W PauseFlag
    BEQ CODE_00A28A
    BRA CODE_00A25B

    BIT.W byetudlrP2Frame                     ; \ Unreachable
    BVS ADDR_00A259                           ; | Debug: Slow motion
    LDA.W byetudlrP2Hold                      ; |
    BPL CODE_00A25B                           ; |
    LDA.B TrueFrame                           ; |
    AND.B #$0F                                ; |
    BNE CODE_00A25B                           ; |
ADDR_00A259:
    BRA CODE_00A28A                           ; /

CODE_00A25B:
    ; ... paused-frame handling, ends in RTS without touching the screen ...
```

`CODE_00A25B` is the "stay paused" path. It does the paused-frame work and
returns. It does not do the normal screen and sprite update that
`CODE_00A28A` does. Normally, when `PauseFlag != 0`, `BRA CODE_00A25B`
always jumps over the debug code to the paused path on every frame.

The code changes that `BRA` ($80) to `BEQ` ($F0). The result is a branch
that is **never taken**. The last instruction that set the flags is
`LDA.W PauseFlag`. The `BEQ CODE_00A28A` after it was not taken, so
`PauseFlag != 0` (Z=0). No instruction between that point and the patched
byte changes Z. So the new `BEQ CODE_00A25B` is never taken, and the
unreachable code runs:

- `BIT byetudlrP2Frame` / `BVS ADDR_00A259`: if Y on controller 2 was
  pressed on this frame (bit `$40`), go to `ADDR_00A259` →
  `BRA CODE_00A28A`. This runs one normal frame, which is a single
  frame step.
- If not, `LDA byetudlrP2Hold` / `BPL CODE_00A25B`: if B on controller 2 is
  not held (bit `$80`), take the normal paused path. Pause works as before.
- If B *is* held, `LDA TrueFrame / AND #$0F / BNE CODE_00A25B` branches away
  on 15 of every 16 frames. On the 16th frame it does **not** branch, so it
  continues to `ADDR_00A259` → `CODE_00A28A` and runs one normal frame. This
  gives the slow-motion effect.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00A247` in `CODE_00A242` (`bank_00.asm`). This is
the opcode byte of `BRA CODE_00A25B`, just above the label `CODE_00A25B`.
Checked against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM,
`$00A247` holds `$80`, as the source predicts. No other code reads this.
This is the only place that decides, on each paused frame, whether to stay
paused or advance.

**Caveats:** **Needs a second controller.** Without one,
`byetudlrP2Frame`/`byetudlrP2Hold` read as "nothing pressed" and the
code does nothing.

## Beat level with Start+Select (while paused)

**Codes:** `EDC5-6D6D` + `DDC1-64DD` (use both)
**Raw form:** `00A272:F0` (orig `$80`) + `00A268:00` (orig `$20`)
(address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 16:20:00 (second code added 2026-11-01)

Tags: `utility` `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** Pause the game with Start. Then hold **Select** (Player 1)
while paused. In the retail game, this exits the level with no reward,
and only on a level you have already beaten. With this code, the level is marked complete and the overworld
opens the next path, the same as when you reach the goal. Hold **B** with
Select (Select+B) to get the *secret* exit instead of the normal exit.

`CODE_00A25B`/`CODE_00A270` runs only while the game is paused (see the Slow
Motion code above). It also needs `byetudlrHold AND #$20` (Select held),
and the current level's `OWLevelTileSettings` entry must be negative.
Bit 7 is set by `CODE_048F5F` when the level's path opens, so negative
means the level is already beaten:

```
CODE_00A25B:
if ver_is_console(!_VER)
    LDA.B byetudlrHold
    AND.B #$20
    BEQ Return00A289
    LDY.W TranslevelNo
    LDA.W OWLevelTileSettings,Y
    BPL Return00A289
    LDA.W OWLevelExitMode
    BEQ CODE_00A270
    BPL Return00A289
CODE_00A270:
    LDA.B #$80
    BRA CODE_00A27E                           ;!

    LDA.B #$01                                ;! \ Unreachable
    BIT.B byetudlrHold                        ;! | Debug: Beat level with Start+Select
    BPL +                                     ;! |
    INC A                                     ;! /
  + STA.W MidwayFlag                          ;!
CODE_00A27E:
    STA.W OWLevelExitMode
    INC.W CreditsScreenNumber
    LDA.B #$0B
    STA.W GameMode
endif
Return00A289:
    RTS
```

This code (Select while paused, with the conditions above) **already runs**
in the retail game. `LDA #$80` / `BRA CODE_00A27E` always runs. It writes
`$80` to `OWLevelExitMode` and sets `GameMode $0B` (exit level and return
to the overworld). It never writes `MidwayFlag`. `MarioDeathAni`
(`bank_00.asm:9396`) writes the same `$80` to `OWLevelExitMode` when Mario
dies. `MidwayFlag` stays `0`, and this is important. The overworld code that
opens new paths (`bank_04.asm:1437`) starts with `LDA MidwayFlag / BEQ`,
which skips everything when the flag is zero. So in the retail game,
pause+Select only returns you to the map. Nothing opens. It is the same as
quitting the level.

The code changes the `BRA` ($80) to `BEQ` ($F0). This changes what runs
*before* `CODE_00A27E`. `LDA.B #$80` two lines above always sets Z=0
(`$80 != 0`), so the new `BEQ` is never taken. The unreachable code runs
instead:

```
LDA.B #$01
BIT.B byetudlrHold      ; test bit 7 ($80, the B button) of held buttons
BPL +
INC A                   ; A = 2 if B is also held, else 1
+ STA.W MidwayFlag
```

Execution then continues into `CODE_00A27E`. It writes the *same* `1` or
`2` to `OWLevelExitMode` (not `$80`), and also to `MidwayFlag`.

**What 1, 2 and $80 mean**, based on the code that reads them:

- `bank_04.asm:1437-1443` (`LDA MidwayFlag / BEQ skip`, then `LDA
  OWLevelExitMode / BEQ skip / BPL CODE_048F5F`, else continue). Now
  `MidwayFlag` is not zero. `OWLevelExitMode = 1` or `2` is positive, so the
  `BPL` branch goes to `CODE_048F5F`. That code does
  `LDA OWLevelTileSettings,X / ORA #$0080 / AND #$FFBF / STA ... / INC
  OverworldProcess`. It sets bit 7 (path open) and clears bit 6, **and**
  increments `OverworldProcess` to play the path-opening animation.
  `OWLevelExitMode = $80` is negative and takes a different branch. That
  branch only sets bit 6 and does not increment `OverworldProcess`.
- `bank_04.asm:1842` (`LDX OWLevelExitMode / BEQ OWPU_NotAutoWalk / DEX / LDA
  DATA_049060,X`). This routine makes Mario walk away from the level icon
  automatically. `X = OWLevelExitMode - 1` is an index into `DATA_049060`
  (`db $05,$03,$01,$00`). It gives **`$05` for value 1** and **`$03` for
  value 2**. These are two different shift counts for the level tile's
  `OWLayer2Directions` nibble. This value selects which of up to four
  connected paths Mario walks along. So `1` and `2` can make Mario walk in
  different directions. The difference is not only visual.
- The game itself uses the same `1`/`2` values. The goal-tape handler
  (`bank_00.asm:8532-8551`) calculates them with
  `LDA SecretGoalTape / INC A`, then continues to the shared exit code at
  `CODE_00C9FE`. A **normal** goal-tape finish gives `1`. The game's
  "secret goal tape" case gives `2`, but that case is never used in
  practice. Select+B copies this secret-exit value on purpose.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00A272` in `CODE_00A270` (`bank_00.asm`). This is
the opcode byte of `BRA CODE_00A27E`, just above the label `CODE_00A27E`.
Checked against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM,
`$00A272` holds `$80`, as the source predicts.

**Caveats:** Every reader we found checks only whether `MidwayFlag` is zero
or not zero, and whether `OWLevelExitMode` is zero, positive or negative.
None of them uses `CMP` to compare against `1` or `2`. The *only* place
where the number matters is the `DATA_049060` walk-direction index above.
We did not find any other place that handles `1` and `2` differently. So do
not think of these as two fully different debug modes. The only difference
is that one direction table. **Console-only block** (`if ver_is_console`):
present in J/U/E0/E1, not present in SS. **The game must be paused.**

**Second code (`DDC1-64DD`):** with only the first code, the debug block
runs only on levels that are already beaten. On a new level, `LDA.W
OWLevelTileSettings,Y / BPL Return00A289` (`$00A267`: `10 20`) returns
before it reaches `CODE_00A270`. The second code sets that branch offset
to `$00`, so the branch goes to the next instruction either way, and the
clear works on any level. Then pause + Select always clears the level, so
it can no longer be used just to leave a level. The second code was made
from `comparison_U.smc` and is for U only. The bytes around it are
different in J, E0 and E1, and codes for them were not made.

- Tested on 2026-11-01 (both codes, U ROM, in Mesen2): the level is
  cleared.

## Change Yoshi colour (Select, overworld)

**Code:** `ED60-642D`
**Raw form:** `04824B:F0` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 16:20:00

Tags: `demo-ready` `utility`

**Mechanism:** On the overworld, press **Select** (either player). This
moves that player's saved Yoshi colour forward by two steps. After the last
valid colour, it goes back to the first.

```
GameMode_0E_Prim:
    PHB
    PHK
    PLB
    LDX.B #$01                                ; \ If player 1 pushes select...
CODE_048246:
    LDA.W byetudlrP1Frame,X                   ; |
    AND.B #$20                                ; | ...disabled by BRA
    BRA CODE_048261                           ; / Change to BEQ to enable debug code below

    LDA.W SavedPlayerYoshi,X                  ; \ Unreachable
    INC A                                     ; | Debug: Change Yoshi color
    INC A                                     ; |
    CMP.B #$04                                ; |
    BCS +                                     ; |
    LDA.B #$04                                ; |
  + CMP.B #$0B                                ; |
    BCC +                                     ; |
    LDA.B #$00                                ; |
  + STA.W SavedPlayerYoshi,X                  ; /
CODE_048261:
    DEX
    BPL CODE_048246
    JSR CODE_0485A7
```

The loop runs for `X = 1` and then `X = 0`, so it handles both players. It
reads `byetudlrP1Frame,X`. The name says P1, but `X` makes it read both
players. The code changes the `BRA` opcode to `BEQ`. Now the branch to
`CODE_048261` (skip) is taken only when Select was **not** pressed on this
frame (`AND #$20` gives zero). When Select **was** pressed, the `BEQ` is not
taken and the unreachable code runs. It increments `SavedPlayerYoshi,X`
two times. Then it limits the value: a result below `$04` becomes `$04`, and
a result of `$0B` or more becomes `$00`. After several presses, the
possible values are `$00, $04-$0A`.

**Evidence:** Patches `$04824B` in `CODE_048246` (`bank_04.asm`), just below
`GameMode_0E_Prim`. This is the opcode byte of `BRA CODE_048261`. Checked
against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$04824B`
holds `$80`, as the source predicts. Shared reader: one loop handles both
player slots (`X=1,0`) with one patched instruction. So it works the same
for a Select press from either player.

**Caveats:** None, other than the shared loop described above.

## Score value per point-sprite type (200-point stomp awards 2000)

**Code:** `A6C5-0768`
**Raw form:** `02AD7E:C8` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:40:49

**Mechanism:** `PointMultiplierLo` (`bank_02.asm`) is a table with 17
entries. It has one byte for each score-sprite type. Each byte is the score
**divided by 10**. `CODE_02ACEF` documents the index values: `1=10 2=20 3=40 4=80 5=100
6=200 7=400 8=800 9=1000 A=2000 B=4000 C=8000 D=1up`. Entry `+6` (score-sprite
type 6, the "200 points" reward for a stomp or shell hit) is `$14` (20 ->
200 points). Entry `+A` (type 10, "2000 points") is `$C8` (200 -> 2000
points). `CODE_02AE12` adds the score. It does a 24-bit add from the table
to the player's score:

```
CODE_02AE12:
    LDA.W PlayerTurnLvl
    ASL A
    ADC.W PlayerTurnLvl
    TAX
    LDA.W PlayerScore,X
    CLC
    ADC.W PointMultiplierLo,Y
    STA.W PlayerScore,X
    LDA.W PlayerScore+1,X
    ADC.W PointMultiplierHi,Y
    STA.W PlayerScore+1,X
    LDA.W PlayerScore+2,X
    ADC.B #$00
    STA.W PlayerScore+2,X
```

On entry, `Y` is `ScoreSpriteNumber,X`. This is the score-sprite type that
was saved when the point sprite was created. This path is used for any type
`< $0D` (all normal point values, types 1-C). Types `$0D`-`$10` are the
extra-life types and use a different branch. The code copies the `A` entry
of `PointMultiplierLo` (`$C8`) into the `+6` entry. After this, every
"200 points" award (a Koopa or Goomba stomp, most shell kills and block
hits) gives the "2000 points" value. `PointMultiplierHi+6` does not change,
so the high byte stays `$00`. This is the same as `PointMultiplierHi+A`,
which is also `$00`.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02AD7E` in the `PointMultiplierLo` table
(`bank_02.asm`), the byte at offset `+6`. Checked against the disassembly
source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$02AD7E` holds `$14`, as the source
predicts (original value `$14` = 20, which is 200 points because the table
uses ×10). This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in
play.

**Caveats:** **Shared reader.** `CODE_02AE12` does a 24-bit
`ADC PointMultiplierLo,Y` / `ADC PointMultiplierHi,Y` pair. So this one byte
is used for every award of score-sprite type 6. You cannot change the
"200 points" of only one enemy or object. The code changes only the low byte,
and `PointMultiplierHi+6` stays `$00`. So the result is exactly the same as
the existing `A` (2000-point) entry. It does not make an incorrect value.

## Level timer values (200 -> 900 starting time)

**Code:** `DB62-D4F9`
**Raw form:** `0584D8:09` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:42:42

**Mechanism:** `TimerTable` (`bank_05.asm`) is a table with 4 entries, `db
$00,$02,$03,$04`. Each entry is the hundreds digit of the level's start
time. The index is the 2-bit time setting in the level header. Entry `+1`
(time setting `1`, "200") is `$02`. The game reads the table once when a
level starts. A check makes sure it is used only in the first room of a
level with several rooms:

```
    LDA.W SublevelCount                       ; |
    BNE +                                     ; |
    LDA.L TimerTable,X                        ; |
    STA.W InGameTimerHundreds                 ; |
    STZ.W InGameTimerTens                     ; |
    STZ.W InGameTimerOnes                     ; /
```

The code changes `TimerTable+1` from `$02` to `$09`. Every level whose
header uses time setting `1` now starts with `900` on the timer, not `200`.
The same code always sets the tens and ones digits to zero. So the start
time is always `<byte>00`.

**Evidence:** Patches `$0584D8` in the `TimerTable` table (`bank_05.asm`),
the byte at offset `+1`. Checked against the disassembly source and the
built ROM. In the ROM, `$0584D8` holds `$02`, as the source predicts. This
effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Depends on `SublevelCount`.** The game reads the table only
when `SublevelCount` is zero, which is in the first room of a level. When
Mario enters a later room of the same level, the timer is not loaded from
this table again. So the effect applies only when the level starts. Only
levels with time setting `1` in their header change. The other three
entries (`+0`, `+2`, `+3`) do not change.

## Level music (overworld-music levels play the boss theme)

**Code:** `D962-D429`
**Raw form:** `0584DB:05` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:42:42

**Mechanism:** `LevelMusicTable` (`bank_05.asm`) is a table with 8 entries.
Each entry is a `!BGM_*` constant. The header comment says "A level can
choose between 8 tracks. This table contains the tracks to choose from."
Entry `+0` is `!BGM_OVERWORLD` (`$02`). Entry `+6` is `!BGM_BOSSFIGHT`
(`$05`). The game reads the table once when a level loads. The index is
bits 4-6 of the third byte of the level header:

```
    AND.B #$07                                ; |
    TAX                                       ; |Get music
    LDA.L LevelMusicTable,X                    ; |
    LDX.W MusicBackup                         ; | \
    BPL +                                     ; |  |
    ORA.B #$80                                ; |  |Related to not restarting music if the new track
  + CMP.W MusicBackup                         ; |  |is the same as the old one?
    BNE +                                     ; |  |
    ORA.B #$40                                ; | /
  + STA.W MusicBackup                         ; /
```

The code changes `LevelMusicTable+0` from `$02` (`!BGM_OVERWORLD`) to `$05`
(`!BGM_BOSSFIGHT`). Every level whose header uses music slot `0` now plays
the boss-fight music, not the overworld-style music. The value still goes
through the `MusicBackup` same-track check just after the load. So if a
level reloads while that track is already playing, the music restarts
correctly with no glitch.

**Evidence:** Patches `$0584DB` in the `LevelMusicTable` table
(`bank_05.asm`), the first byte of the table (offset `+0`). Checked against
the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$0584DB` holds `$02`,
as the source predicts. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** Changes every level whose header uses music slot `0`, not only
one level. It changes the whole table entry. The value goes through the
`MusicBackup` same-track check, so there is no glitch when a level reloads
or restarts. The other seven `LevelMusicTable` entries do not change.

## Pipe travel speed (vertical pipes suck Mario down 4x faster)

**Code:** `0D2B-0D6D`
**Raw form:** `00D192:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:42:42

**Mechanism:** `PipeSpeed` (`bank_00.asm`) is a table of signed 8-bit pipe
speeds, with entries for each direction. Each row has a comment: `+0/+1` horizontal pipe
X speed, `+2/+3` horizontal pipe Y / vertical pipe X speed, `+4/+5` vertical
pipe Y speed. The vertical Y row is inside a block that depends on the game
version:

```
PipeSpeed:
    db $F8,$08                                ; horizontal pipe X speed
    db $00,$00                                ; horizontal pipe Y speed, vertical pipe X speed
if ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)                         ;\================== J, U, & SS =================
    db $F0,$10                                ;! vertical pipe Y speed
else                                          ;<=================== E0 & E1 ===================
    db $F2,$0E                                ;! vertical pipe Y speed
endif                                         ;/===============================================
```

`+5` (`$10` = +16, down) is the second byte of the NTSC vertical Y pair.
It is the speed that pulls Mario down into a vertical pipe when he enters
it from above. The game reads it during the pipe-entry animation:

```
    LDA.B PlayerPipeAction
    LSR A
    TAY
    INY
    LDA.W DATA_00D193-1,Y
```

The code changes `PipeSpeed+5` from `$10` to `$40` (+64). This makes the
downward speed 4 times larger, so Mario goes down vertical pipes about 4x
faster than normal.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00D192` in the `PipeSpeed` table (`bank_00.asm`),
the second byte of the NTSC vertical Y speed pair. Checked against the
disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$00D192` holds `$10`, as
the source predicts. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** **U-only address.** This row is inside an `if
ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)` block. The E0/E1 (PAL) builds use the `else` row
(`$F2,$0E`) at a *different* address, so this code does not work on those
versions. It changes only the speed for entering a vertical pipe going
down. Horizontal pipe travel and the other three `PipeSpeed` bytes do not
change.

## Always die on contact (one-hit-death mode)

**Code:** `6DE2-0FAF`
**Raw form:** `00F5D7:80` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:40:49

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** Every hit from an enemy or hazard goes through `HurtMario`
(`bank_00.asm`). First it checks the animation and invincibility state.
Then it loads `Powerup`. If the value is zero (Small Mario), it branches
to `KillMario`:

```
HurtMario:
    LDA.B PlayerAnimation                     ; \ Return if animation sequence activated
    BNE Return00F628                          ; /
    LDA.W IFrameTimer                         ; \ If flashing...
    ORA.W InvinsibilityTimer                  ; | ...or have star...
    ORA.W EndLevelTimer                       ; | ...or level ending...
    BNE Return00F628                          ; / ...return
    STZ.W GameCloudCoinCount
    LDA.W WallrunningType
    BEQ +
    ...
  + LDA.B Powerup                             ; \ If Mario is small, kill him
    BEQ KillMario                             ; /
    CMP.B #$02                                ; \ Branch if not Caped Mario
    BNE PowerDown                             ; /
```

The code changes the `BEQ KillMario` opcode from `$F0` (`BEQ`) to `$80`
(`BRA`). The branch is now always taken. For every value of `Powerup`
(including Big, Caped and Fire Mario), execution goes to `KillMario`. It
skips the `CMP #$02` cape check and the `PowerDown` path. Any hit that
reaches `HurtMario` now kills Mario, the same as for Small Mario.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00F5D7` in `HurtMario` (`bank_00.asm`). This is the
opcode byte of `BEQ
KillMario`. Checked against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In
the ROM, `$00F5D7` holds `$F0`, as the source predicts. This effect comes
from the disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Used by all damage.** Every source of player damage in the
game (enemy contact, hazards, and others) goes to `HurtMario`. So this is a
true one-hit-death mode for the whole game, not for one enemy type. The
checks above the patched line (star power, the hurt-flash timer, level end)
still run first. So Mario is still safe in those states.

## In-game-second length (level timer burns as slowly as possible)

**Code:** `EE64-6767`
**Raw form:** `008E2E:FF` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:51:37

**Mechanism:** `UpdateStatusBar` (`bank_00.asm`) reloads the frame counter
of the level timer each time it goes below zero. It uses the constant
`!FramesInOneIGT-1`. This is `con(41,41,41,35,35)` for each version, minus
one. For the U version it is `$28` (40):

```
UpdateStatusBar:                              ; Routine to update the status bar.
    LDA.W EndLevelTimer                       ;\ 
    ORA.B SpriteLock                          ;| Don't decrement the timer if:
    BNE UpdateTime                            ;|  - Ending a level
    LDA.W IRQNMICommand                       ;|  - Game frozen
    CMP.B #!IRQNMI_Bowser                     ;|  - In Bowser
    BEQ UpdateTime                            ;|  - A second hasn't passed
    DEC.W InGameTimerFrames                   ;|
    BPL UpdateTime                            ;/

    LDA.B #!FramesInOneIGT-1                  ;
    STA.W InGameTimerFrames                   ;
    LDA.W InGameTimerHundreds                 ;\ 
    ...
```

`InGameTimerFrames` decrements once per game frame. When it goes below
zero, this code loads `!FramesInOneIGT-1` into it again and subtracts one
from the timer digits on screen (hundreds, tens, ones). Normally the value
is `$28` (40 frames = ~0.67s at 60fps). So one in-game "second" is about
2/3 of a real second. The code changes it to `$FF` (255, the largest value
one byte can hold). Now each timer digit counts down as slowly as possible:
about 4.25s for each in-game "second", about 6.4x slower than normal. This
is the longest level time that a one-byte patch can give. When the digits
reach `000`, the same routine calls `JSL
KillMario` a few lines below.

**Evidence:** Patches `$008E2E` in `UpdateStatusBar` (`bank_00.asm`). This
is the immediate operand of `LDA.B #!FramesInOneIGT-1` (opcode `$A9` is at
`$008E2D`). Checked against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In
the ROM, `$008E2E` holds `$28` (40), as the source predicts. This matches
`!FramesInOneIGT` = `con(41,41,41,35,35)` for the U version (index 1),
minus one. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in
play.

**Caveats:** **A second site is not patched.** The same immediate value
(`LDA.B #!FramesInOneIGT-1` -> `STA.W InGameTimerFrames`) is also in the
level start code at `$008D8B`. It also holds `$28`, with the same opcode and
operand layout. That site sets the first value of the counter when a level
starts. This code patches only the `UpdateStatusBar` reload site. So the
*first* in-game second after a level starts is still the normal ~40
frames. Every reload after that (after the timer first goes below zero)
uses the new 255-frame period. Patching both sites needs a 2-byte code.
This code does not do that, to keep it a single-byte patch. This follows
the backlog note to use only the `:1571` site.

## Maximum lives cap (lives clamped to 5)

**Code:** `D060-AD07` + `D060-AF07` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `008F41:04` + `008F45:04` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:52:02

**Mechanism:** `HandleLives` (`bank_00.asm`) runs on every frame before
the game draws the life count on the status bar. It limits `PlayerLives` to
a maximum value:

```
HandleLives:                                  ; Handle the current player's lives and write them to the status bar.
    LDA.W PlayerLives                         ;\ If Mario has a negative number of lives (i.e. game over), don't max out the life count.
    BMI +                                     ;/
    CMP.B #!MaximumLives-1                    ;\ Maximum number of lives the player can have.
    BCC +                                     ;|
    LDA.B #!MaximumLives-1                    ;| Amount of lives to use if the maximum life limit is reached.
    STA.W PlayerLives                         ;/
  + LDA.W PlayerLives                         ;\ 
    INC A                                     ;|
    JSR HexToDec                              ;| Write the life count to the status bar.
```

`!MaximumLives-1` is `$62` (98). The compare value and the limit value are
the *same* constant, and both are 98. The `BMI` check above skips this code
when `PlayerLives` is negative. A negative value means "game over". So a
limit here can never change the game-over path. The screen shows
`PlayerLives + 1` (the `INC A` below). So a stored limit of `$04` shows as
"5".

The code sets both operand bytes to `$04`. This keeps the compare value
and the limit value the same, as in the original code. `CMP.B #$04` / `BCC`
skips when `PlayerLives < 4`. If not, `LDA.B #$04` / `STA PlayerLives` sets
it back to 4. If you change only one of the two bytes, the code breaks. For
example, if you lower only the compare and keep the limit at `$62`,
`PlayerLives` jumps *up* to 98 when it reaches 4. That is the opposite of a
limit. So both sites get the same value, the same way the game already uses
this constant.

**Evidence:** Patches `$008F41` (the `CMP.B #!MaximumLives-1` operand,
opcode `$C9` is at `$008F40`) and `$008F45` (the `LDA.B
#!MaximumLives-1` operand, opcode `$A9` is at `$008F44`). Both are in
`HandleLives` (`bank_00.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source and
the built ROM. In the ROM, both addresses hold `$62` (98), as the source
predicts. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in
play.

**Caveats:** **Two sites, the same as A1/A4.** The game reads this constant
at two sites next to each other (the compare and the limit). They must have
the same value for the effect to work. This code patches both, so it is a
2-byte code (below the 3-byte limit). No other code reads these bytes, only
`HandleLives`. The `BMI` check above the patched lines means the game-over
path (negative `PlayerLives`) does not change.

## Bonus stars required (bonus game triggers after 5 stars)

**Code:** `D961-AD67` + `D961-A7A7` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `008F62:05` + `008F6F:05` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:52:24

**Mechanism:** `HandleBonusStars` (`bank_00.asm`) runs on every frame. It
compares the current player's bonus star count with a limit. When the count
reaches the limit, it turns on the bonus game for the end of the level and
subtracts the same constant from the counter:

```
HandleBonusStars:                             ; Handle the current player's bonus stars.
    LDX.W PlayerTurnLvl                       ;\ 
    LDA.W PlayerBonusStars,X                  ;|
    CMP.B #!MaximumBonusStars                 ;| Number of bonus stars required to enter the bonus game (100).
    BCC DrawCoinCount                         ;|
    LDA.B #-1                                 ;|\ Set the flag to activate the bonus game after the level is beaten.
    STA.W BonusGameActivate                   ;|/
    LDA.W PlayerBonusStars,X                  ;|\ 
    SEC                                       ;||
    SBC.B #!MaximumBonusStars                 ;|| Number of bonus stars to subtract from the counter after getting a bonus game (100).
    STA.W PlayerBonusStars,X                  ;//
```

`!MaximumBonusStars` is `$64` (100). The game uses it in the same way at the
`CMP` (the limit) and at the `SBC` (the amount to subtract). This is the
same compare/subtract pair as `!CoinsPer1up` in `HandleCoins`. The code sets
both operands to `$05`, so the two values stay the same. The bonus game now
turns on (`BonusGameActivate = -1`) when `PlayerBonusStars` reaches 5, and
exactly 5 is subtracted. The counter works the same as before, but with a
much lower limit. Nothing is left over and the value does not go below zero.

**Evidence:** Patches `$008F62` (the `CMP.B #!MaximumBonusStars` operand,
opcode `$C9` is at `$008F61`) and `$008F6F` (the `SBC.B
#!MaximumBonusStars` operand, opcode `$E9` is at `$008F6E`). Both are in
`HandleBonusStars` (`bank_00.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source
and the built ROM. In the ROM, both addresses hold `$64` (100), as the
source predicts. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested
in play.

**Caveats:** **Two sites, the same as A1/A2.** The compare site and the
subtract site use the same named constant. This code patches both (2-byte
code) so the values stay the same. If you patch only one site, either the
bonus game never starts, or a large star count (or a value below zero) is
left after it starts. No other code reads these bytes, only
`HandleBonusStars`.

## Death launch velocity (much higher death hop)

**Code:** `6DED-6FAF`
**Raw form:** `00F607:80` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:52:44

**Mechanism:** The first step of `KillMario` (`bank_00.asm`) sets Mario's
vertical speed. The source comment says what the byte does:

```
KillMario:
    LDA.B #$90                                ; \ Mario Y speed = #$90
    STA.B PlayerYSpeed+1                      ; /
CODE_00F60A:
    LDA.B #!BGM_DEATH                         ; \
    STA.W SPCIO2                              ; / Change music
```

`PlayerYSpeed+1` is the signed whole-pixel byte of Mario's Y speed.
**Negative values move Mario up.** Other code confirms this. For example, in `bank_00.asm` a `BMI` branch after a load of this byte has the comment "Branch if Mario has upward speed". `$90` is
`-112` in 8-bit two's complement. This is already a large upward speed. It
makes Mario jump up in the normal death animation.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00F607` in `KillMario` (`bank_00.asm`). This is the
immediate operand of `LDA.B
#$90` (opcode `$A9` is at `$00F606`). Checked against the disassembly source
and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$00F607` holds `$90`, as the source
predicts. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in
play.

**Correction to the byte in the backlog:** the candidate list suggested
`$C0`. With the sign rule above, `$C0` is `-64`. This is a *smaller*
negative number than `-112` (`$90`). So `$C0` would make the death hop
**lower**, which is the opposite of the goal ("much higher"). To make the
hop higher, this code uses `$80` (`-128`) instead. This is the most
negative value an 8-bit signed byte can hold, so it is always a larger
upward speed than the original `-112`.

**Caveats:** Visual only. This changes only the launch speed of the death
animation. It does not change if or when Mario dies. No other code reads
this write. `PlayerYSpeed` is a common RAM variable, but this instruction
is the only one that writes it at this point in the program.

**`$80` is the maximum for this byte.** `PlayerYSpeed+1` is a signed 8-bit
value, so `-128` is the largest upward speed this immediate can hold. This
code cannot go higher. The hop *height* is `v²/(2·gravity)`. So to get a
much higher hop, you must lower the gravity. See "Death fall gravity"
below. That code does this, and you can use it together with this one.

## Fireball throwing pose duration (held three times as long)

CORRECTION (2026-08-09): the first version of this entry had the title
"Fireball cooldown (near-continuous fire)". It assumed that `ShootFireTimer`
controls how soon Mario can throw the next fireball. That was wrong. Every
reader of the variable uses it only to select Mario's *animation frame*.
The code and the address are the same. The mechanism and the effect below
are now correct.

**Code:** `F3E8-64A7`
**Raw form:** `00FEBB:1E` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:53:03 (mechanism corrected 2026-08-09)

**Mechanism:** `ShootFireball` (`bank_00.asm`) first looks for a free
extended-sprite slot. When it finds one, it sets `ShootFireTimer`, plays the
sound effect and creates the fireball:

```
ShootFireball:
    LDX.B #$09                                ; \ Find a free fireball slot (08-09)
CODE_00FEAA:
    LDA.W ExtSpriteNumber,X                   ; |
    BEQ CODE_00FEB5                           ; |
    DEX                                       ; |
    CPX.B #$07                                ; |
    BNE CODE_00FEAA                           ; |
    RTS                                       ; / Return if no free slots

CODE_00FEB5:
    LDA.B #!SFX_FIREBALL
    STA.W SPCIO3                              ; / Play sound effect
    LDA.B #$0A
    STA.W ShootFireTimer
    LDA.B #$05                                ; \ Extended sprite = Mario fireball
    STA.W ExtSpriteNumber,X                   ; /
```

`ShootFireTimer` (`$149C`) has exactly two readers in the disassembly.
**Both of them only select which pose to draw.** Neither one controls
firing:

- `bank_00.asm:9207` (`CODE_00CF62`, the pose selector on foot): while the
  timer is not zero, it uses pose `$3F` on the ground or `$16` in the air.
  These are the fire-throwing frames. Otherwise it uses the walk or stand
  pose from `PlayerAniTimer`.
- `bank_00.asm:10781` (`CODE_00DA7C`, the swimming pose selector): while
  the timer is not zero, it uses pose `$18`. Otherwise it uses the swim
  animation from `DATA_00D980`.

Both paths end in `STA.W PlayerPose`. The shared timer loop for
`$1496`-`$14A8` at `bank_00.asm:7907` decrements the timer once per frame
(`LDA ColorFadeTimer,X / BEQ + / DEC ColorFadeTimer,X`, with `X` going from
`$13` down to `$01`). The loop stops the timer at zero. It does not run at
all while `SpriteLock` is set.

So `$0A` is only **the number of frames that the throwing pose stays on
screen**. The code changes it to `$1E` (30, exactly 3x the normal 10). This
makes the hold 3 times longer. After each fireball, Mario keeps the
throwing pose (arm out) three times as long before he goes back to the
walk, stand or swim animation. Fireballs still come out at the normal rate.
Only the pose duration changes.

**Variant:** `EEE8-64A7` (`00FEBB:FF`) sets the same byte to a larger
value: 255 frames, about four seconds. After each fireball, Mario stays in
the throwing pose. Each new fireball starts the timer again. So if you keep
throwing fireballs, he stays in the pose all the time.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00FEBB` in `CODE_00FEB5` (`bank_00.asm`, part of the
`ShootFireball` routine). This is the immediate operand of `LDA.B #$0A`,
which goes to `STA.W ShootFireTimer` (opcode `$A9` is at `$00FEBA`. The ROM
bytes at `$00FEBA`-`$00FEBE` are `a9 0a 8d 9c 14`). Checked against the
disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$00FEBB` holds `$0A`, as
the source predicts. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** **This code is visual only. It does not change gameplay
timing.** Two other things control the fire rate. This byte is not one of
them. First, the slot search at the start of `ShootFireball` (`LDX.B #$09`
down to `CPX.B #$07`) checks only slots `$08`-`$09`. If both are in use, it
does `RTS` at once. So there are never more than 2 fireballs. Second, the
caller (`CODE_00D081`, `bank_00.asm`) goes to `ShootFireball` only when Y
is pressed on this frame (`BIT.B byetudlrFrame / BVS`, the byte for buttons
pressed on this frame), or once every 16 frames during a spin jump (auto
fire). Holding the button does not fire.

## Fireball launch Y speed (launches about 3x as high as normal) REDISCOVERY

NOTE: The libretro database already has a code for this address ("Shoot
Fireballs Straight", which sets it to `$00`). This entry uses a different
value (`$B0`) for a different, new effect.

**Code:** `8DEA-6F07`
**Raw form:** `00FEC5:B0` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:53:23

**Mechanism:** `ShootFireball` (`bank_00.asm`) sets the start vertical
speed of a new fireball. It does this just after it sets the
extended-sprite type:

```
CODE_00FEB5:
    LDA.B #!SFX_FIREBALL
    STA.W SPCIO3                              ; / Play sound effect
    LDA.B #$0A
    STA.W ShootFireTimer
    LDA.B #$05                                ; \ Extended sprite = Mario fireball
    STA.W ExtSpriteNumber,X                   ; /
    LDA.B #$30
    STA.W ExtSpriteYSpeed,X
```

`ExtSpriteYSpeed` is a signed fixed-point speed. The high nibble is the
whole part and the low nibble is the fraction. Its reader, `CODE_02B560`
(`bank_02.asm`), confirms this. It adds the speed to the sprite position on
every frame:

```
CODE_02B560:
    LDA.W ExtSpriteYSpeed,X
    ASL A
    ASL A
    ASL A
    ASL A
    CLC
    ADC.W ExtSpriteYPosSpx,X          ; low nibble -> subpixel position
    STA.W ExtSpriteYPosSpx,X
    PHP
    LDY.B #$00
    LDA.W ExtSpriteYSpeed,X
    LSR A
    LSR A
    LSR A
    LSR A
    CMP.B #$08                        ; high nibble >= 8 -> negative (upward)
    BCC +
    ORA.B #$F0                        ; sign-extend
    DEY                                ; Y = $FF, sign-extends into the high byte add
  + PLP
    ADC.W ExtSpriteYPosLow,X
    STA.W ExtSpriteYPosLow,X
    TYA
    ADC.W ExtSpriteYPosHigh,X
    STA.W ExtSpriteYPosHigh,X
```

The high nibble of `ExtSpriteYSpeed` is the signed number of whole pixels
per frame. It is sign-extended when it is `>= 8`. The low nibble is a
subpixel fraction. The high nibble of `$30` is `3`. It is positive and not
sign-extended, so it is a small downward speed. This matches the normal
fireball, which moves down in a small arc as it bounces. The high nibble of
`$B0` is `$B` (11). This value *is* sign-extended (`CMP.B
#$08` / `BCC` is not taken), so the speed is `-5`, a medium upward speed.
The peak height depends on the square of this speed. So `-5` compared with
the normal `3` gives `(5/3)² ≈ 2.8`. The fireball goes up to about three
times its normal peak height, and does not arc down.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00FEC5` in `CODE_00FEB5` (`bank_00.asm`, part of
`ShootFireball`). This is the immediate operand of `LDA.B #$30`, which goes
to `STA.W
ExtSpriteYSpeed,X` (opcode `$A9` is at `$00FEC4`). Checked against the
disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$00FEC5` holds `$30`, as
the source predicts. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Another published code uses the same address.** The
"Shoot Fireballs Straight" cheat in the libretro-style DB sets this byte to
`$00`. That removes all vertical speed, so the shot goes straight across.
This entry sets the same byte to a different value (`$B0`) for a different
effect (a medium upward launch, not a flat shot). This code changes only
the *start* speed written here. Other extended-sprite update code changes
`ExtSpriteYSpeed` on each frame for gravity and bounces. We did not trace
that code, and this code does not change it. So this entry makes no claim
about how the fireball moves after the launch.

## Score-sprite float speed (no more slowdown before vanishing)

**Code:** `DDCB-0468`
**Raw form:** `02AD9A:00` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:53:59

**Mechanism:** `PointSpeedY` (`bank_02.asm`) is a table with 4 entries. The
game uses each entry as a bitmask. The mask decides if a floating score or
1-up popup moves up on a frame:

```
PointSpeedY:
    db $03,$01,$00,$00
```

The popup has a life timer (`ScoreSpriteTimer`). It is set to `$30` = 48
when the popup appears and decrements once per frame. The timer is shifted
right by 4 bits to get the table index. The table value is then used as an
`AND` mask on the global frame counter:

```
CODE_02AE38:
    LDA.W ScoreSpriteTimer,X
    LSR A
    LSR A
    LSR A
    LSR A
    TAY
    LDA.B TrueFrame
    AND.W PointSpeedY,Y
    BNE CODE_02AE5B                           ; nonzero -> skip the rise this frame
    LDA.W ScoreSpriteYPosLow,X
    TAY
    SEC
    SBC.B Layer1YPos
    CMP.B #$04
    BCC CODE_02AE5B
    DEC.W ScoreSpriteYPosLow,X                ; rise by 1 pixel
    ...
```

The popup moves up only on frames where `TrueFrame AND PointSpeedY,Y == 0`.
So a *larger* mask gives *fewer* frames that match. This is a **slower**
rise, not a faster one. `$00` always matches (it moves up on every frame,
the fastest). `$01` matches on every second frame. `$03` matches on one
frame in four. `ScoreSpriteTimer` counts *down* from 48, so index `Y`
(`timer >> 4`) also counts down. `Y=3`/`Y=2` (both `$00`, fastest) are used
at the start of the popup's life. `Y=1` (`$01`, medium) is used in the
middle. `Y=0` (`$03`, slowest) is used at the end, just before the popup
disappears. So popups already slow down as they get older. Entry `+0` is
the *last and slowest* phase, not the first.

The code changes `PointSpeedY+0` from `$03` to `$00`. This removes the
slowdown at the end. The popup now moves up at full speed (on every frame)
for all of the time it is visible. It does not slow down just before it
disappears.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02AD9A`, the first byte of `PointSpeedY` (offset
`+0`), in `bank_02.asm`. Checked against the disassembly source and the
built ROM. In the ROM, `$02AD9A` holds `$03`, as the source predicts. This
effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Correction to the byte in the backlog:** the candidate list suggested
`$0F`. It assumed that this table holds a simple speed value. The real
reader (`CODE_02AE38` above) uses it as a frame-skip **mask** with `AND` and
`BNE`. So a *larger* value gives a *slower* rise. `$0F` would skip 15 of
every 16 frames, so popups would be much slower, not faster. This entry
uses `$00`. The table already uses this value in its `+2`/`+3` entries for
the fast phase. This makes the popups faster, which is what the candidate
wanted.

**Caveats:** **Shared reader.** `CODE_02AE38` handles the vertical movement
of every score and 1-up popup. So this changes all of them in the same way.
You cannot make one popup type faster without the others. Only the last
(slowest) phase of the animation changes. The early and middle phases
(`PointSpeedY+1`/`+2`/`+3`) do not change. They already use the fast value
that this patch now also uses for the last phase.

## Walking-enemy base speed (basic enemies walk 4x faster)

**Codes:** `3D63-D701` + `4D63-D7D1` (apply both)
**Raw form:** `0188ED:E0` (original `$F8`) and `0188EC:20` (original `$08`)
(address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 18:57:46, second code added 2026-08-08 19:56:04,
green Koopa Paratroopa coverage confirmed 2026-08-11 01:24:00

Tags: `basic-enemies` `enemy-movement-collection` `play-start` `challenge`

**Mechanism:** `Spr0to13SpeedX` (`bank_01.asm`) is a table of 4 signed
speeds. The index is the sprite direction (`SpriteMisc157C`, 0 or 1). If
the sprite's "fast" property bit is set, the index is 2 higher:

```
Spr0to13SpeedX:
    db $08,$F8,$0C,$F4
```

`Spr0to13Main` calculates the index and sets the speed:

```
Spr0to13Main:
    JSR IsOnGround                            ; \ If sprite on ground...
    BEQ CODE_018B2E                           ; |
    LDY.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; |
    LDA.W Spr0to13Prop,Y                      ; | Set sprite X speed
    LSR A                                     ; |
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; |
    BCC +                                     ; |
    INY                                       ; | Increase index if sprite set to go fast
    INY                                       ; |
  + LDA.W Spr0to13SpeedX,Y                    ; |
    EOR.W SpriteSlope,X                       ; | what does $15B8,x do?
    ASL A                                     ; |
    LDA.W Spr0to13SpeedX,Y                    ; |
    BCC +                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |
    ADC.W SpriteSlope,X                       ; |
  + STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
```

Other code in the same file confirms that `SpriteMisc157C` is the direction
the sprite faces (`; \ Store sprite direction`, `bank_01.asm`,
`Spr0to13Gfx`). Entry `+0` (`$08` = +8, direction 0) and entry `+1` (`$F8`
= -8, direction 1) are the walking speeds on the ground. `SpriteXSpeed` is
signed, and positive means right. So direction 1 (`$F8`, negative) is the
entry for facing left. The two codes make both entries of the pair 4 times
larger:

| Byte | Entry | Original | Patched | Code |
|------|-------|----------|---------|------|
| `$0188EC` | `+0`, rightward | `$08` = +8 | `$20` = +32 | `4D63-D7D1` |
| `$0188ED` | `+1`, leftward | `$F8` = -8 | `$E0` = -32 | `3D63-D701` |

`$20` and `$E0` are exact two's-complement opposites (+32 / -32). So the
walk speed is the same in both directions: these sprites move 4x faster to
the left and to the right. The EOR/ASL/ADC code after the table read only
adds a correction on slopes. It does not change the sign or the relation
between the two values.

If you use only `3D63-D701` (the first, single-code version), the right
entry stays at `$08`. Then these enemies walk 4x faster to the left and at
normal speed to the right. You can see this in play: enemies move quickly
one way and slowly the other way. Use both codes for the same speed-up in
both directions.

`Spr0to13Start` (which continues into `Spr0to13Main`) is the shared
handler. The `CallSpriteMain` dispatch table (`bank_01.asm`) uses it for
sprite numbers `$04`-`$07`, `$0C`, `$0F`, `$11`, `$13`:

```
    dw Spr0to13Start                          ; 04 - Green Koopa
    dw Spr0to13Start                          ; 05 - Red Koopa
    dw Spr0to13Start                          ; 06 - Blue Koopa
    dw Spr0to13Start                          ; 07 - Yellow Koopa
    dw Spr0to13Start                          ; 0C - Yellow Koopa with wings
    dw Spr0to13Start                          ; 0F - Goomba
    dw Spr0to13Start                          ; 11 - Buzzy Beetle
    dw Spr0to13Start                          ; 13 - Spiny
```

So this one byte changes the walking speed of Green, Red, Blue and Yellow
Koopas, Yellow Koopas with wings, Goombas, Buzzy Beetles and Spinies, all
at the same time.

A second, different reader also uses this same pair. `GreenParaKoopa`
(`bank_01.asm`) is the routine for sprites `$08` (flying green Koopa) and
`$09` (bouncing green Koopa). It gets `SpriteXSpeed` directly from the
`SpriteMisc157C,X` index, with no check of the fast bit:

```
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X
    LDA.W Spr0to13SpeedX,Y
    EOR.W SpriteSlope,X
    ASL A
    LDA.W Spr0to13SpeedX,Y
    BCC +
    CLC
    ADC.W SpriteSlope,X
  + STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
```

For these two sprites, `SpriteMisc157C` is always `0` (right) or `1`
(left). `InitStandardSprite` (the init for sprite `$08`) and
`InitGrnBounceKoopa` (the init for sprite `$09`) both continue into
`FaceMario`, which sets this value. No code adds 2 for these sprites, so
they never use the "fast" entries. So `GreenParaKoopa` always reads offsets
`+0`/`+1`, the same two bytes that this code patches. This means that **the
flying and bouncing green Koopa Paratroopas are also 4x faster with this
code**. They do not need a separate patch.

**Evidence:** Patches `$0188EC`/`$0188ED`, the first two bytes of
`Spr0to13SpeedX` (offsets `+0`/`+1`), in `bank_01.asm`. Checked against the
disassembly source and the reference ROM. In the ROM, `$0188EC..EF` holds
`08 F8 0C F4`, as the source predicts. Both codes were encoded and then
decoded again, and they give the correct address and byte. This effect
comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Shared table used by many sprites.** Every sprite type listed
above uses this table and reader. The flying (`$08`) and bouncing (`$09`)
green Koopa Paratroopas also use it through `GreenParaKoopa`. So you cannot
limit the effect to one enemy type. This effect needs **2 codes**. Real
Game Genie hardware accepts 5 codes at the same time, so three code slots
are still free. The two "fast" entries (`+2`/`+3`) stay at their original
+12/-12. They are already the same in both directions. So sprites with the
fast bit set in `Spr0to13Prop` are now *slower* than the patched base
speed. The slope correction that is added after the table read also does
not change. This code does not change the bounce *height* of `$09` (that is
a different, vertical-only mechanism). For that, see "Bouncing green Koopa
Paratroopas bounce twice as high" below.

## Kicked-shell speed (shells kicked either way rocket off)

**Code:** `5EB1-A7D5` + `6FB1-A4A5` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `019F6C:7F` + `019F6B:81` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie
codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:00:20

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** `ShellSpeedX` (`bank_01.asm`) is a table of 4 signed 8-bit
speeds. It is inside a block that depends on the game version:

```
if ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)                         ;\================== J, U, & SS =================
ShellSpeedX:                                  ;!
    db $D2,$2E,$CC,$34                        ;!
else                                          ;<==================== E0 & E1 ==================
ShellSpeedX:                                  ;!
    db $C9,$37,$C2,$3E                        ;!
endif                                         ;/===============================================
```

Entry `+0` (`$D2` = -46) and entry `+1` (`$2E` = +46) are selected by
direction. The game uses them when Mario kicks a shell that he holds with
the run button. `+2`/`+3` are the pair for Mario on Yoshi. `SpriteXSpeed`
is signed. A positive value moves a sprite right on the screen, and a
negative value moves it left. `SubUpdateSprPos` (`bank_01.asm`) confirms
this: it adds this byte to the sprite X position with `ADC`. So `+1`
(positive `$2E`) is the entry for a kick to the right.

There are three readers. The first two are in the same routine
(`CODE_01A079`, the handler for a run-button kick):

```
CODE_01A079:
    ...
    LDY.B PlayerDirection
    LDA.W PlayerRidingYoshi                   ; \ Y += 2 if riding Yoshi
    BEQ +                                     ; |
    INY                                       ; |
    INY                                       ; /
  + LDA.W ShellSpeedX,Y                       ; reader 1: base kick speed
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    EOR.B PlayerXSpeed+1                      ; \ if Mario's own X-speed sign
    BMI CODE_01A0A6                           ; / differs, skip the boost below
    LDA.B PlayerXSpeed+1
    STA.B _0
    ASL.B _0
    ROR A                                     ; A = PlayerXSpeed+1 / 2 (sign-preserving)
    CLC
    ADC.W ShellSpeedX,Y                       ; reader 2: half Mario's speed + table entry
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
CODE_01A0A6:
```

Reader 1 sets the shell speed directly from the table. The `EOR`/`BMI` code
checks the signs. If Mario moves in the *same* direction as the kick,
reader 2 replaces that speed with half of Mario's X speed plus the same
table entry. This is a bonus for a kick while running. In both cases,
`ShellSpeedX,Y` is the final speed, or is part of it.

The third reader is in a different routine. It runs when a shell or enemy
is defeated by contact (stomp, touch, and others). The dispatch code above
it has special cases for Key, P-switch, Bob-omb, Baby Yoshi, MechaKoopa and
Goomba. All other sprites continue to this code:

```
CODE_01AA97:
    JSR PlayKickSfx
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1540,X
    STA.B SpriteTableC2,X
    LDA.B #$0A                                ; \ Sprite status = Kicked
    STA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; /
    LDA.B #$10
    STA.W SpriteMisc154C,X
    JSR SubHorizPos                           ; Y = 0 or 1, Mario's side of the sprite
    LDA.W ShellSpeedX,Y                       ; reader 3
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    RTS
```

`SubHorizPos` sets `Y=0` if Mario is at or to the right of the sprite, and
`Y=1` if Mario is to its left. So this reader always sends the shell away
from Mario. It does not add the Yoshi offset (it uses only `+0`/`+1`).

The code changes `ShellSpeedX+1` from `$2E` (+46) to `$7F` (+127, the
largest positive signed value). This makes every speed to the right that
uses this byte larger, in all three readers: a direct run-kick to the right
(reader 1, when there is no running bonus), the running bonus (reader 2,
because it adds this same byte), and a stomp or touch kick to the right,
away from Mario (reader 3). `ShellSpeedX+0` is the matching entry for a
kick to the left in the same three readers. The code changes it from `$D2`
(-46) to `$81` (-127, the same size as `$7F` but negative). This gives the
same large speed in the other direction. So a shell moves away very fast in
both directions.

**Evidence:** Patches `$019F6C` and `$019F6B`, the second and first bytes
(offsets `+1` and `+0`) of `ShellSpeedX` in the `ver_is_ntsc` block, in
`bank_01.asm`. Checked against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In
the ROM, `$019F6B`-`$019F6C` holds `$D2,$2E`, as the source predicts. This
effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **U-only address.** This table is inside an `if
ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)` block (present in J/U/SS). The E0/E1 (PAL) builds have
different bytes (`$C9,$37,$C2,$3E`) at a different address, so this code
does not work on those versions. **Three shared readers** (see above) use
these bytes. Reader 2 (the running bonus) runs only when Mario moves in the
same direction as the kick. Reader 3 (the touch or stomp kick) is a
different code path with no Yoshi handling. The pair for Mario on Yoshi
(`+2`/`+3`) does not change.

## Block-bounce sprite speed (hit blocks launch much further)

**Code:** `6D67-A46B`
**Raw form:** `02873A:80` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:02:30

**Mechanism:** `BlockBounceSpeedY` (`bank_02.asm`) is a table with 4
entries. Each entry is a signed fixed-point speed (nibble format) for one
hit direction:

```
BlockBounceSpeedY:
    db $C0,$00,$00,$40
```

The game reads it with a macro instruction. This sets the start vertical
speed of a new block-bounce sprite:

```
    LDX.B _6
    %LorW_X(LDA,BlockBounceSpeedY)            ; \ Set bounce y speed
    STA.W BounceSpriteYSpeed,Y                ; /
    %LorW_X(LDA,BlockBounceSpeedX)            ; \ Set bounce x speed
    STA.W BounceSpriteXSpeed,Y                ; /
```

`%LorW_X` (`macros.asm`) makes `LDA` into `.L` (long, 4 bytes) **only for
the Japanese version**. For all other regions, including U, it makes `.W`
(absolute, 3 bytes). This is the opposite of what the backlog entry
assumed. The instruction length is different in each region, so counting
bytes in the macro source line to find the table address is not reliable.
So this patch takes the address of `BlockBounceSpeedY` directly from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` (the line of the label). The built ROM confirms it:
the instruction bytes are `BD 3A 87`, which is `LDA
$873A,X`. This is an absolute (3-byte) instruction, as `%LorW_X` predicts for
a non-Japanese build.

`CODE_02B526` (`bank_02.asm`) adds `BounceSpriteYSpeed` to the sprite
position. It uses the same signed fixed-point format as `ExtSpriteYSpeed`
in the fireball speed code above (`CODE_02B560` is the matching routine for
extended sprites). The high nibble is a signed 4-bit number of whole pixels
per frame. When it is `>= 8`, it is sign-extended with `LSR A`x4 /
`CMP #$08` / `ORA #$F0`. The low nibble is a subpixel fraction that is
added directly to the position:

```
CODE_02B526:
    LDA.W BounceSpriteYSpeed,X
    ASL A
    ASL A
    ASL A
    ASL A
    CLC
    ADC.W BounceSpriteXPosSpx,X                ; (subpixel accumulator; likely a
    STA.W BounceSpriteXPosSpx,X                ;  mislabeled Y-subpixel address —
    PHP                                        ;  see caveats)
    LDA.W BounceSpriteYSpeed,X
    LSR A
    LSR A
    LSR A
    LSR A
    CMP.B #$08
    LDY.B #$00
    BCC +
    ORA.B #$F0                                 ; sign-extend
    DEY                                        ; Y = $FF, sign-extends into the high byte add
  + PLP
    ADC.W BounceSpriteYPosLow,X
    STA.W BounceSpriteYPosLow,X
    TYA
    ADC.W BounceSpriteYPosHigh,X
    STA.W BounceSpriteYPosHigh,X
```

The high nibble of `$C0` (`$C` = 12) sign-extends to -4. The high nibble of
`$80` (`$8`) sign-extends to -8. This is two times the upward speed. So the
direction of the change also matches the goal ("launch much further"), not
only the byte value.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02873A`, the first byte of `BlockBounceSpeedY`
(offset `+0`, the direction for a block hit from below), in `bank_02.asm`.
Checked against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM,
`$02873A` holds `$C0,$00,$00,$40`, as the source predicts. The next 4 bytes
(`$02873E`) also match `$00,$40,$C0,$00` of `BlockBounceSpeedX`. This
effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Correction to the mechanism in the backlog:** the backlog said that
`%LorW_X` "picks `LDA.L` for U." `macros.asm` shows the opposite: `LDA.L`
is only for the Japanese version. U (and SS/E0/E1) get `LDA.W`. The opcode
in the built ROM at the macro site confirms this (`$BD` = absolute `,X`, 3
bytes). This did not change the byte to patch, because the linemap gives
the table address directly, whatever the addressing mode of the reader.
But the reason that the backlog gave for using the linemap was wrong.

**Caveats:** **Shared reader.** `CODE_02B526` is the only routine that
updates the position of every block-bounce sprite on each frame. So this
changes the upward launch speed for every hit block, not only one type.
Only the `+0` (up) entry changes. `+1`-`+3` (the other three hit
directions) and the matching `BlockBounceSpeedX` table do not change. In
the RAM map, the subpixel value that this routine writes is named
`BounceSpriteXPosSpx`, but it holds the fraction of the Y speed. (The
matching `ExtSpriteYSpeed` routine writes to `ExtSpriteYPosSpx`, which has
the correct name.) This is almost certainly a naming error in the RAM map,
not a different mechanism. It does not change this patch. The "how far up"
effect depends only on the sign-extended whole-pixel value, which is added
to the `Y` position.

## Invert the cape check (Caped Mario loses the mid-flight hit exemption)

**Code:** `DFE2-046F`
**Raw form:** `00F5DA:01` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:04:32

**Mechanism:** `HurtMario` (`bank_00.asm`) compares `Powerup` with the
constant for Caped Mario (`rammap.asm`: `!Powerup_Small = 0`,
`!Powerup_Big = 1`, `!Powerup_Cape = 2`, `!Powerup_Flower = 3`). This
decides if a hit causes the normal power-down, or if Mario is protected
because he is flying:

```
  + LDA.B Powerup                             ; \ If Mario is small, kill him
    BEQ KillMario                             ; /
    CMP.B #$02                                ; \ Branch if not Caped Mario
    BNE PowerDown                             ; /
    LDA.W FlightPhase                         ; \ Branch if not soaring
    BEQ PowerDown                             ; /
    LDY.B #!SFX_FLYHIT                        ; \ Break Mario out of soaring
    STY.W SPCIO0                              ; | (Play sound effect)
    LDA.B #$01                                ; | (Set spin jump flag)
    STA.W SpinJumpFlag                        ; |
    LDA.B #$30                                ; | (Set flashing timer)
    STA.W IFrameTimer                         ; /
    BRA CODE_00F622
```

In the retail game, only `Powerup == 2` (Caped) gets to the `FlightPhase`
check. For all other values of `Powerup` that are not zero, the `BNE` goes
to `PowerDown`. If Caped Mario is hit while he flies (`FlightPhase != 0`),
he does not go to `PowerDown`. He flashes for a short time (i-frames), the
spin-jump flag is set, and a "stop flying" sound plays. He does not lose
his power-up. If Caped Mario is hit while he does *not* fly
(`FlightPhase == 0`), he goes to `PowerDown`, the same as Big or Fire Mario.

The code changes the `CMP.B #$02` operand to `$01`. Now the compare tests
for `Powerup == 1` (Big), not `2` (Caped). This is what changes for each
value of `Powerup`:

- **Caped Mario (`Powerup == 2`)**: `CMP #$01` now fails (`2 != 1`), so the
  `BNE` is always taken. Mario always goes to `PowerDown`, whatever the
  value of `FlightPhase`. The protection while flying is gone. If Mario is
  hit while flying, he loses the cape at once, the same as when he does not
  fly.
- **Big Mario (`Powerup == 1`)**: `CMP #$01` now matches, so the code
  continues to the `FlightPhase` check. But `FlightPhase` can be non-zero
  only while `Powerup == 2`. The only code that sets it, `CODE_00D7E4`
  (`bank_00.asm`), starts flight only after `LDX.B Powerup / CPX.B #$02 / BNE
  CODE_00D811` (branch away if not Caped). Also, every path that sets
  `Powerup` back to `0` (`PowerDown` itself, and the shared end of
  `KillMario`) also clears `FlightPhase` in the same instructions
  (`CODE_00F622: STZ.W
  FlightPhase`). So `FlightPhase` is always `0` when `Powerup
  == 1`. This means the `BEQ PowerDown` branch is taken every time. **When
  Big Mario is hit, nothing changes.**

**Evidence:** Patches `$00F5DA` in `HurtMario` (`bank_00.asm`). This is the
immediate operand of `CMP.B
#$02` (opcode `$C9` is at `$00F5D9`). Checked against the disassembly source
and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$00F5DA` holds `$02`, as the source
predicts. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in
play.

**Correction to the effect in the backlog:** the backlog said that with
this patch "Big Mario gets the cape's soaring-knockback treatment...
instead of powering down." The only code that writes `FlightPhase`
(`CODE_00D7E4`, shown above) shows that this cannot happen. `FlightPhase`
can be non-zero only while `Powerup == 2`. So when Big Mario is hit,
`FlightPhase` is always zero, and he always goes to `PowerDown`, the same
as without the patch. The real effect of this byte is the opposite: *Caped*
Mario loses his protection while flying. Big Mario does not get it.

**Caveats:** This changes only hits while Mario flies with the cape
(`FlightPhase != 0`). A hit on Caped Mario on the ground or not flying
already went to `PowerDown` before this patch, and it still does.
`HurtMario` handles all damage (see the "Always die on contact" code
above), so this applies to every source of damage in the same way. Hits on
Small, Big or Fire Mario do not change, as shown above.

## Which button triggers the level-gameplay Select action (moved to Y)

**Code:** `0DA1-07AF`
**Raw form:** `00C56F:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:09:10

**Mechanism:** During normal play in a level, `CODE_00C569` (`bank_00.asm`)
runs a Select action only if a button-mask test passes:

```
CODE_00C569:
    JSR ProcessPlayerAnimation
    LDA.B byetudlrFrame
    AND.B #$20
    BEQ CODE_00C58F
if ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)                         ;\================== J, U, & SS =================
    LDA.B byetudlrHold                        ;!
    AND.B #$08                                ;!
    BRA CODE_00C585                           ;! Change to BEQ to reach debug routine below
    ...
endif
CODE_00C585:
    PHB
    LDA.B #$02
    PHA
    PLB
    JSL CODE_028008
    PLB
CODE_00C58F:
    STZ.W NoteBlockActive
    RTS
```

`$20` is the Select bit in the `byetudlr` layout. `ControllerUpdate`
(`bank_00.asm`) calculates `byetudlrHold` and `byetudlrFrame` from the
controller data. `byetudlrHold` holds the button state on the current frame
("held"). `byetudlrFrame` is `(current XOR previous-frame)
AND current`. So its bits are set only on the frame when a button goes from
up to down. So `AND.B #$20` on `byetudlrFrame` tests if **Select was
pressed on this frame**. This matches the bit layout in the `!Valid
values` block of `rammap.asm`: `!ButB=$80 !ButY=$40 !ButSelect=$20 !ButStart=$10
!DpadUp=$08 !DpadDown=$04 !DpadLeft=$02 !DpadRight=$01`.

In the retail game, a Select press here calls `CODE_00C585`. That code
changes the data bank and does `JSL CODE_028008` (a bank 2 routine with no
name), then sets `NoteBlockActive` to zero. This action really runs on every
Select press during play in a level. It is separate from the NTSC debug
code for changing the power-up below it (which normally cannot run).

The code changes the mask operand from `$20` (Select) to `$40` (Y). This
moves the whole check to the Y button. Now a press of **Y** runs the
`CODE_00C585` call. On NTSC versions, Y also controls entry to the debug
code, which is still unreachable, in the same way that Select did. Select
alone no longer does anything here.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00C56F` in `CODE_00C569` (`bank_00.asm`). This is
the immediate operand of `AND.B #$20` (opcode `$29` is at `$00C56E`).
Checked against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM,
`$00C56F` holds `$20`, as the source predicts. This effect comes from the
disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Select loses its original action here.** The
`JSL CODE_028008` call (and, on NTSC builds, the check for the debug
power-up code) no longer runs on Select, only on Y. The same Select-press
test (`byetudlrFrame`/`byetudlrP1Frame AND #$20`) is also at a different
address in `bank_04.asm`. The "Change Yoshi colour" code above uses that
one. It is a different instruction at a different address, and this patch
does **not** change it. Select still works there as normal.

## Bob-omb redirected to the generic walking-enemy handler (dispatch swap)

**Code:** `EA63-0F69`
**Raw form:** `0185E6:FC` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:13:42

**Mechanism:** `CallSpriteMain` (`bank_01.asm`) runs the sprite code on
each frame. It reads the sprite number of the current slot and jumps
through a `dw` table with one entry for each sprite number. X is the
sprite slot (the caller sets it):

```
CallSpriteMain:
    STZ.W SpriteXMovement                     ; CallSpriteMain
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X
    JSL ExecutePtr

    dw ShellessKoopas                         ; 00 - Green Koopa, no shell
    ...
    dw Bobomb                                 ; 0D - Bob-omb
    ...
```

Entry `$0D` (Bob-omb) points to `Bobomb` (`bank_01.asm`). This code checks
the explosion values that `InitBomb` set when the sprite appeared
(`SpriteMisc1534`/`SpriteMisc1540`). Only when the sprite is not exploding
does it continue to the shared walking code `Spr0to13Start`:

```
Bobomb:
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1534,X                    ; \ Branch if exploding
    BNE -                                     ; /
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1540,X                    ; \ Branch if not set to explode
    BNE Spr0to13Start                         ; /
    LDA.B #$09                                ; \ Sprite status = Stunned
    STA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; /
    LDA.B #$40                                ; \ Time until explosion = #$40
    STA.W SpriteMisc1540,X                    ; /
    JMP SubSprGfx2Entry1                      ; Draw sprite
```

`Bobomb` (`$018AE5`) and `Spr0to13Start` (`$018AFC`) are both in bank `$01`
and have the same high byte in the pointer (`$8A`). Only the low byte is
different (`$E5` and `$FC`). The code changes the low byte of the table
entry. This sends Bob-omb's *main* handler directly to `Spr0to13Start`
(`bank_01.asm`). This is the shared walking-enemy handler that entries
`$04`-`$07`, `$0C`, `$0F`, `$11`, `$13` already use (Koopas, Goomba, Buzzy
Beetle, Spiny; see the "Walking-enemy base speed" code above). This is a
table-base redirect (pattern 7): the original target and the new target
are both named handlers with comments in the same dispatch table.

`Spr0to13Start` uses `SpriteNumber,X` directly as the index into its
property and speed tables (not the dispatch-table slot). One of these
tables is `Spr0to13Prop` (`bank_01.asm`), with 20 entries for sprite
numbers `$00`-`$13`. It already has a valid entry at index `$0D` (the
Bob-omb sprite number): `$05` (binary `00000101`). This is true even though
no dispatch-table entry normally goes there. Bit 0 (read with `LSR A` at
`bank_01.asm:1664`) selects the "fast" pair of `Spr0to13SpeedX` (`$0C`/`$F4`,
±12). Bit 2 (`AND.B #$04` at `:1699`) is the "follow Mario" flag. Bits 1, 3
and 6 (stay on ledges, jump over shells, 2 tiles high) are clear. So the
read is inside the table, and every property byte it uses is valid for this
sprite number. There is no undefined or out-of-bounds behavior.

**Evidence:** Patches `$0185E6`, the low byte of the `$0D` entry in the
`CallSpriteMain` table (`dw Bobomb`). Checked against the disassembly
source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$0185E6`/`$0185E7` hold `$E5`/`$8A`
(pointer `$8AE5` = `Bobomb`), as the source predicts. The label address of
`Spr0to13Start` (`$018AFC`) confirms that the new pointer `$8AFC` is
different only in the low byte. This effect comes from the disassembly. It
was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This changes only the *main* handler (`CallSpriteMain`). The
*init* handler (the `CallSpriteInit` table, which this code does not
change) still runs `InitBomb` when the sprite appears. So `SpriteMisc1540`
is still set to `$FF` and `FaceMario` still runs once. But nothing reads
those values again, because the new main handler (`Spr0to13Start`) never
uses `SpriteMisc1534`/`SpriteMisc1540`. Expected effect in the game:
Bob-ombs no longer start a timer or explode. They walk back and forth like
a Koopa and turn to face Mario from time to time. Mario can jump on them
and defeat them with the normal `MarioSprInteractRt` walking-enemy contact
code, not their usual contact behavior. `Spr0to13Start` is a shared reader
(several other sprite numbers use it; see the writeup for `G2` above). But
this patch changes only the *dispatch table entry* for Bob-omb, so no other
sprite number changes.

## Red Super Koopa loses its spawn hop (init-handler dispatch swap)

**Code:** `5969-67A0`
**Raw form:** `01825F:75` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:16:01

**Mechanism:** `CallSpriteInit` (`bank_01.asm`) runs the start code for
each sprite. It runs once, when a sprite slot becomes active. It jumps
through a `dw` table with the sprite number as the index (X already holds
the slot):

```
CallSpriteInit:
    LDA.B #$08                                ; \ Sprite status = Normal
    STA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; /
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X
    JSL ExecutePtr

    dw InitStandardSprite                     ; 00 - Green Koopa, no shell
    ...
    dw InitSuperKoopa                         ; 71 - Super Koopa, red cape
    ...
```

Entry `$71` (Super Koopa, red cape) points to `InitSuperKoopa`
(`bank_01.asm`). This gives the sprite a small upward hop at the start,
then continues into the shared `FaceMario` code:

```
InitSuperKoopa:
    LDA.B #$28
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    BRA FaceMario
```

`InitStandardSprite` (`bank_01.asm`) is the default init for most entries
in this table. It sets a random value for a turn timer, then continues into
the same `FaceMario` code:

```
InitStandardSprite:
    JSL GetRand
    STA.W SpriteMisc1570,X
FaceMario:
    JSR SubHorizPos
    TYA
    STA.W SpriteMisc157C,X
Return018583:
    RTS
```

`InitSuperKoopa` (`$018528`) and `InitStandardSprite` (`$018575`) are both
in bank `$01` and have the same high byte in the pointer (`$85`). Only the
