low byte is different (`$28` and `$75`). The code changes the low byte of
the table entry. This sends the Super Koopa *init* handler to
`InitStandardSprite`. Its *main* handler (`RedSuperKoopa` ->
`SuperKoopaMain`, `bank_02.asm`) does not change. This is a table-base
redirect (pattern 7) between two named handlers with comments in the same
dispatch table.

The code of `SuperKoopaMain` (`bank_02.asm:14216`+) has few comments. Most
labels are automatic (`CODE_02xxxx`). The rule is to explain only code with
comments, so this writeup does not try to explain all of it. But a text
search confirms the one fact that this redirect needs. Inside
`SuperKoopaMain`, nothing reads `SpriteMisc1570,X` (the value that
`InitStandardSprite` writes and `InitSuperKoopa` does not). The code uses
only `SpriteMisc157C,X` (direction, which both inits set the same way in the
shared `FaceMario` code) and `SpriteYSpeed,X`. So the extra write from the
new init has no effect for this sprite. The only real change is that the
`SpriteYSpeed = $28` value from `InitSuperKoopa` is *lost*.

**Evidence:** Patches `$01825F`, the low byte of the `$71` entry in the
`CallSpriteInit` table (`dw InitSuperKoopa`). Checked against the
disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$01825F`/`$018260` hold
`$28`/`$85` (pointer `$8528` = `InitSuperKoopa`), as the source predicts.
The label address of `InitStandardSprite` (`$018575`) confirms that the new
pointer `$8575` is different only in the low byte. This effect comes from
the disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** Only the red-cape Super Koopa (index `$71`) changes. The
Yellow Koopa (`$72`) also uses `InitSuperKoopa`, but its table entry is a
different byte, and this patch does not change it. The Feather Koopa
(`$73`) already uses a different init routine (`InitSuperKoopaFthr`), so it
does not change either. Expected effect in the game: when a Red Super Koopa
appears (usually from a generator, or when a Koopa loses its shell and
starts to fly), it no longer makes the small upward hop at the start.
`SpriteYSpeed` starts with the value left by the general sprite-slot reset
code, not the `$28` value. So its first frame of movement looks a little
different. It probably glides flat or falls at once, depending on the
gravity code later in `SuperKoopaMain`, which has no comments. No other
value changes. The direction code (`FaceMario`) still runs the same way.
The text search above confirms that the extra random write of
`InitStandardSprite` to `SpriteMisc1570,X` has no effect for this sprite.
This is a smaller, single-sprite example of the backlog pattern for
`InitStandardSprite` redirects, which removes a special start setup.

## Invert the L+R Destroyed-Castle overworld secret

**Code:** `DDB0-0FBD`
**Raw form:** `049146:00` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:17:47

**Mechanism:** `CODE_049120` (`bank_04.asm`) is one of the overworld
process states. It runs on every frame while `OverworldProcess` is in state
3, the state where the player is idle and can move on the map (the `dl`
jump table of `CODE_048576`, `bank_04.asm:588-596`). On the English builds
(U/SS/E0/E1), a hidden button-combination check runs before the normal
button code:

```
if ver_is_english(!_VER)                      ;\=============== U, SS, E0, & E1 ===============
  + LDA.B axlr0000Hold                        ;! \
    AND.B #$30                                ;! |If L and R aren't pressed,
    CMP.B #$30                                ;! |branch to OWPU_NoLR
    BNE +                                     ;! /
    LDA.W OverworldLayer1Tile                 ;! \
    CMP.B #$81                                ;! |If Mario is standing on Destroyed Castle,
    BEQ OWPU_EnterLevel                       ;! / branch to OWPU_EnterLevel
endif                                         ;/===============================================
```

`!ButL = %00100000` and `!ButR = %00010000` (`rammap.asm`). So
`AND.B #$30` keeps only the L and R held bits, and `CMP.B #$30` tests if
**both** are held. Only if L and R are both held **and** Mario stands on
overworld tile `$81` does the code go to `OWPU_EnterLevel` and enter the
level again. (Tile `$81` is "Destroyed Castle", as the comment two lines
below says.) This is the known Nintendo L+R secret for entering this tile
again.

The code changes the `CMP.B #$30` operand to `$00`. This inverts the
condition. Now `BNE +` skips when the masked L/R bits are **not zero**
(L or R held). It continues to the `OverworldLayer1Tile` / `$81` check only
when **neither** L nor R is held. This is the opposite of the original
check. The trigger changes from "hold L+R on the tile" to "stand on the
tile with neither shoulder button held". So normal movement onto Destroyed
Castle now enters the level again, and holding L or R on the tile stops
this.

**Evidence:** Patches `$049146`, the immediate operand of `CMP.B #$30`
in `CODE_049120` (`bank_04.asm`). The opcode `$C9` is at `$049145`. Checked
against the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$049146`
holds `$30`, as the source predicts. This effect comes from the
disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** `CODE_049120` runs on every frame while the overworld is in
the idle state (not only once when Mario arrives on a tile). And the
`OverworldLayer1Tile == $81` check now needs *no* shoulder button, not a
button combination. So if Mario stops on the Destroyed Castle tile, with no
input, the code goes to `OWPU_EnterLevel` on the next check. In practice,
Mario can no longer stand on the tile without entering the level. To walk
over it or stop on it without entering, you must hold L or R. This is the
`ver_is_english` block of the U build (present in U/SS/E0/E1, not present
in J). The address and the effect are only for the English builds. The
backlog's expected effect ("simply walking onto the tile re-enters it") has
the correct direction, so no correction is needed. This writeup only adds
that the check runs again on every idle frame, not only when Mario arrives.

## Level header table-base redirection (subscreen mirrors main screen)

**Code:** `756D-0799`
**Raw form:** `05850D:37` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:20:01

**Mechanism:** `CODE_0584E3` (`bank_05.asm`) decodes the level header. For
the level mode (`LevelModeSetting`, 0-31, `X` below), it reads one byte
from each of six parallel tables. Each table has 32 entries and its own
header comment:

```
VerticalTable:
    db $00,$00,$80,$01,$81,$02,$82,$03        ; Vertical level settings for each level mode
    ...
LevMainScrnTbl:
    db $15,$15,$17,$15,$15,$15,$17,$15        ; Main screen settings for each level mode
    ...
LevSubScrnTbl:
    db $02,$02,$00,$02,$02,$02,$00,$02        ; Subscreen settings for each level mode
    ...
LevCGADSUBtable:
    ...
SpecialLevTable:
    ...
LevXYPPCCCTtbl:
    ...
```

This is the code that reads them:

```
    LDA.L LevMainScrnTbl,X                    ; \Get main screen setting from table
    STA.W ThroughMain                         ; /
    LDA.L LevSubScrnTbl,X                     ; \Get subscreen setting from table
    STA.W ThroughSub                          ; /
```

All six tables are next to each other in bank `$05`, from
`LevMainScrnTbl` (`$058437`) to `LevXYPPCCCTtbl` (`$0584B7`). Each table
is exactly 32 bytes, which matches the index range 0-31 of
`LevelModeSetting`. So any table in the group can safely replace any other,
with no out-of-bounds risk. The tables have the same bank (`$05`) and the
same high byte (`$84`) in their long address. So the six `LDA.L <table>,X`
instructions that read them are different **only in the low byte of the
operand**. This means that a table-base redirect (pattern 7) needs only a
1-byte change here.

The code changes the low byte of the `LDA.L LevSubScrnTbl,X` operand from
`$57` (`LevSubScrnTbl`) to `$37` (`LevMainScrnTbl`). Now the *subscreen*
read uses the *main-screen* table. The main-screen read two instructions
before it does not change. When a level loads, the game copies
`ThroughMain`/`ThroughSub` once, directly into the PPU screen hardware
registers (`bank_05.asm:144-149`):

```
    LDA.W ThroughMain
    STA.W HW_TM
    STA.W HW_TMW
    LDA.W ThroughSub
    STA.W HW_TS
    STA.W HW_TSW
```

So the effect is clear and you can follow it from start to end. For every
level mode, the subscreen layer-enable register (`HW_TS`/`HW_TSW`) now gets
the same byte as the main-screen register (`HW_TM`/`HW_TMW`). Normally it
gets the value from `LevSubScrnTbl`, which usually enables far fewer
layers. For example, mode 0 changes from subscreen `$02` to `$15`, the same
as the main screen value `$15`.

**Evidence:** Patches `$05850D`, the low byte of the 3-byte long operand of
`LDA.L LevSubScrnTbl,X` (opcode `$BF` is at `$05850C`). Checked against the
disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM,
`$05850D`/`$05850E`/`$05850F` hold `$57`/`$84`/`$05` (long address
`$058457` = `LevSubScrnTbl`), as the source predicts. The label address of
`LevMainScrnTbl` (`$058437`) confirms that the new operand `$37` is
different only in the low byte. This effect comes from the disassembly. It
was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This changes the subscreen layers for **every** level mode at
the same time. All 32 entries of the table are affected, because the
redirect changes the table-base operand, not one table entry. The PPU uses
the subscreen layers for color math (`CGADSUB`, `LevCGADSUBtable` /
`ColorSettings`). So some BG/OBJ layers can now show on the subscreen when
they did not before. Also, transparency effects that depend on the
subscreen layers (water, lava, sunsets) can look different in some levels.
`HW_TM`/`HW_TS`/`HW_TMW`/`HW_TSW` are written once when the level loads
(`LevelLoadObject == $20`). This routine does not write them again on each
frame. So the effect stays the same for the whole level. It is not a glitch
that changes on each frame. `LevMainScrnTbl` does not change, and it still
sets `ThroughMain`/`HW_TM` as normal. Only the subscreen side changes.

## Overworld->level handoff: lives loaded from the saved coin count

**Code:** `81B8-072D`
**Raw form:** `0491BF:B6` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:21:22

**Mechanism:** `OWPU_EnterLevel` (`bank_04.asm`) moves data from the
overworld to the level. It runs once each time Mario enters a level. It
copies several saved values for the current character from the two-player
save slots into the variables used in the level. The index is the
character whose turn it is:

```
    LDX.W PlayerTurnLvl                       ; Get current character
    LDA.W SavedPlayerCoins,X                  ; \ Get character's coins
    STA.W PlayerCoins                         ; /
    LDA.W SavedPlayerLives,X                  ; \ Get character's lives
    STA.W PlayerLives                         ; /
    LDA.W SavedPlayerPowerup,X                ; \ Get character's powerup
    STA.B Powerup                             ; /
```

`rammap.asm` declares the three saved values next to each other. Each one
is `skip 2` (one byte for each player):

```
SavedPlayerLives: skip 2
SavedPlayerCoins: skip 2
SavedPlayerPowerup: skip 2
```

This confirms `SavedPlayerLives = $0DB4`, `SavedPlayerCoins = $0DB6` and
`SavedPlayerPowerup = $0DB8`. All three have the same high byte (`$0D`) in
their absolute address. Only the low byte is different. This is an operand
redirect (pattern 8). The code changes only the low byte of the
`LDA.W SavedPlayerLives,X` operand, from `$B4` to `$B6`. The read now uses
`SavedPlayerCoins`, the next variable, not `SavedPlayerLives`. The
`STA.W PlayerLives` after it (the write) does not change.

The result: when Mario enters a level, `PlayerLives` (the lives counter
used in the level) is now loaded from the same saved slot as `PlayerCoins`.
This is the saved coin count of the current character, not the saved life
count. The `LDA.W SavedPlayerCoins,X` / `STA.W PlayerCoins` pair two lines
above does not change. So after each level entry, `PlayerLives` and
`PlayerCoins` hold the *same* value.

**Evidence:** Patches `$0491BF`, the low byte of the `LDA.W
SavedPlayerLives,X` operand (opcode `$BD` is at `$0491BE`). Checked against
the disassembly source and the built ROM. In the ROM, `$0491BE`/`$0491BF`
hold `$BD`/`$B4` (absolute address `$0DB4` = `SavedPlayerLives`), as the
source predicts. The `rammap.asm` address of `SavedPlayerCoins` (`$0DB6`)
confirms that the new operand `$B6` is different only in the low byte. This
effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested in play.

**Caveats:** `X` (`PlayerTurnLvl`, loaded just above this code) is the same
index for both reads. So the redirect still uses the character who enters
the level, and the player slots do not get mixed up. The effect depends on
the saved player state. A character who saved with 0 coins enters the level
with 0 lives (so any hit gives a game over at once, because this patch does
not change the zero-lives path in `HurtMario`). A character who saved with
99 coins enters with the maximum life count. When Mario collects or loses
coins in the level, `PlayerCoins` still changes as normal through the
status-bar code (`HandleCoins`, see the "Coins per 1-up" note above). Only
the single copy into `PlayerLives` at level entry changes. The counters
during play do not. `SavedPlayerPowerup` and the Yoshi-colour copy on the
nearby lines do not change.

## Low gravity while the jump button is released (and a huge death hop)

**Code:** `DF2C-AF0F`
**Raw form:** `00D7A5:01` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 19:34:16
**Corrected:** 2026-08-08 19:45:12. See "Correction" below. An earlier version
of this entry said that this code changes *only* the death animation. That
was wrong. This is a general low-gravity code. The address, the byte and the
code string did not change.

Tags: `demo-ready`

Use this with "Death launch velocity" above. That code sets the launch
speed of Mario (and it is already at the largest signed-byte value). This
code sets how strongly gravity pulls him back down. Height is
`v²/(2·gravity)`, so gravity is the value that can still change.

**Mechanism:** `PlayerGravity` (`bank_00.asm`) is a table with one gravity
value for each air state. The shared player physics routine adds it to
Mario's vertical speed once per frame:

```
CODE_00D928:
    LDY.B #$01
    LDA.B byetudlrHold
    BMI +
CODE_00D92E:
    LDY.B #$00
  + LDA.B PlayerYSpeed+1                      ; \ If Mario's Y speed is negative (up),
    BMI CODE_00D948                           ; / branch to $D948
    CMP.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y                ;   (falling only: clamp to terminal velocity)
    ...
CODE_00D948:
    CLC
    ADC.W PlayerGravity,Y                     ;   gravity: speed += table[Y]
```

The code patches entry 0 of `PlayerGravity`
(`db $06,$03,$04,$10,$F4,$01,$03,$04,$05,$06`). Entry 0 is the gravity
**while the jump button is not held**. Entry 1 (`$03`) is the gravity while
it is held. These two values give SMW its variable jump height. The code
lowers entry 0 from `$06` to `$01`. So as soon as Mario releases jump, he
falls six times more slowly. Every normal jump floats, and the upward
launch of the death animation goes far above the top of the screen.

It also **inverts how jumps feel**. Normally, when you release jump, you
fall *faster* (`$06` against `$03`). With this code, when you release jump,
you fall *slower* (`$01` against `$03`). So a short press of jump floats,
and holding jump makes you fall faster. The fall speed limit in
`PlayerMaxFallSpeed` is skipped while Mario moves up (the `BMI` above it),
so nothing limits the rise.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00D7A5`, the first byte of `PlayerGravity` in
`bank_00.asm`. Checked against the built ROM. It holds
`06 03 04 10 F4 01 03 04 05 06` at `$00D7A5`, exactly the bytes that the
source declares. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not tested
in play.

**Correction (2026-08-08):** the first version of this entry said that only
the death animation used entry 0. The reason was that `CODE_00D92E` has
exactly one `JSR` in the disassembly (the one in `MarioDeathAni`). It is
true that there is only one caller, but the conclusion was wrong. Execution
also **falls through** into `CODE_00D92E` from the end of `CODE_00D928`,
when the `BMI` on `byetudlrHold` (bit 7, `!ButB`, "A or B") is not taken. If
you count only the references to a label, you miss code that falls through
into it. That is what happened here. So entry 0 controls normal jumps and
falls, and also the death arc, and this code affects the whole game. The
tables now have names and comments in the disassembly (`PlayerGravity` /
`PlayerMaxFallSpeed`), and the meaning of each index is documented where
the tables are defined.

**Caveats:**

- **This is a physics code for the whole game, not a death-animation
  code.** It changes every jump and every fall. It will probably break
  jumps that need the normal fall speed, and it can change anything that
  depends on exact timing.
- **NTSC-only data.** `PlayerGravity` is inside an `if ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)`
  block. It is a byte table in J/U/SS, but a **word** table with a
  different layout in E0/E1. This code is only for U. Do not use it on a
  PAL ROM.
- Entries 1 (jump held), 2 (winged Yoshi) and 4-7 (cape flight) do not
  change, so those states keep their normal gravity.
- The death sequence still ends when `PlayerAniTimer` ends, not when Mario
  lands. So it lasts the same time. Mario only moves much further in that
  time.
- You can use it together with "Death launch velocity" (`6DED-6FAF`). That
  is two codes, which is inside the hardware limit of five codes.

## Winged-Yoshi fall cap (even slower glide-fall)

**Code:** `FD28-AD0F`
**Raw form:** `00D7B1:10` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 20:36:35

`PlayerMaxFallSpeed` is `db $40,$40,$20,$40,$40,$40,$40,$40,$40,$40`. Every
entry is `$40` (64), except entry 2 for winged Yoshi, which is already half
of that (`$20`, 32). This code does not remove that special case (by
setting it back to `$40`). It does the opposite: it makes the value half
again, `$10` (16). This is a quarter of the normal maximum fall speed. So
Mario glides down very slowly on a winged Yoshi. This is different from
only removing the special case.

**Mechanism:** the same shared physics routine that adds gravity (above)
also applies the limit. A check makes sure the limit applies only while
Mario does not move up:

```
  + LDA.B PlayerYSpeed+1                        ; \ If Mario's Y speed is negative (up),
    BMI CODE_00D948                             ; / branch to $D948 (skip the cap)
    CMP.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y                  ;   compare current fall speed to the cap
    BCC +                                       ;   below the cap: leave it alone
    LDA.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y                  ;   at/above the cap: clamp down to it
  + LDX.B PlayerInAir
    ...
CODE_00D948:
    CLC
    ADC.W PlayerGravity,Y                       ; then gravity is added on top
```

The header comment and the code that sets `Y` both confirm that `Y` is `2`
(winged Yoshi) here. `CODE_00D8CD` does `LDY.B #$02` on a branch that runs
only when `PlayerRidingYoshi` is set and `YoshiHasWingsEvt` is set. (Both
are tested for non-zero with `BEQ` exits just above it.) That path then
continues into shared code used near cape flight (`CODE_00D8FF`). It joins
the gravity and limit routine again at `CODE_00D924: CPY.B
#$02 / BEQ +`, and arrives at the same `LDA PlayerYSpeed+1` limit code with
`Y` still `2`. So entry 2 of both tables (gravity and fall limit) is used
only by winged-Yoshi flight.

> **Correction (2026-08-08):** an earlier version of this paragraph said
> that entry 2 was used by "the winged-Yoshi-**with-Caped-Mario** state",
> and it treated `Powerup == 2` as part of the condition. That was wrong. In
> `CODE_00D8CD`, `LDY.B #$02` runs *before* the `CPY.B Powerup` compare
> after it, and *does not depend on* it. The power-up test only decides if
> the code does `INX`. That selects which byte `LDA.B byetudlrHold,X` reads
> at `CODE_00D8FF`. `Y` is `2` in both cases. So entry 2 applies to
> winged-Yoshi flight with **any** power-up, not only Caped Mario. The code,
> the address and the byte do not change. Only this explanation changed.

The code changes `PlayerMaxFallSpeed+2` from `$20` to `$10`. This lowers the
limit that this `CMP` and limit code applies. When the fall speed reaches
`$10`, it stays there on every frame after that (the
`LDA PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y` line sets it back to the limit). It does not
keep increasing to the old `$20` limit. The entry 2 gravity value
(`PlayerGravity+2` = `$04`, which this code does not change) is still added
on each frame. So Mario still reaches a maximum fall speed, but a lower one.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00D7B1`, the third byte of `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` in
`bank_00.asm`. Checked against the disassembly source (`db
$40,$40,$20,$40,...`, entry 2 = `$20`) and the reference ROM
(`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header). The ROM holds
`$20` at `$00D7B1`. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not
tested in play.

**Caveats:**

- **Shared reader** with every other `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` entry. The limit
  code is one `CMP.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y` / `LDA.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y`
  pair with `Y` as the index. This patch changes only entry 2 because of
  its address. Entries 0, 1 and 3-9 do not change.
- **Used only in one state**, as the disassembly note says: `Y=2` is used
  only while Caped Mario rides a winged Yoshi (`PlayerRidingYoshi` and
  `YoshiHasWingsEvt` both set, `Powerup == 2`). So this code cannot change
  normal jumps, normal falls, or cape flight without a winged Yoshi.
- **NTSC-only data.** `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` is inside the same `if
  ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)` block as `PlayerGravity`. It is a byte table in
  J/U/SS, but a **word** table (`dw $2000` for this entry) with a different
  layout in E0/E1. This code is only for U. Do not use it on a PAL ROM.
- The limit is skipped while Mario's Y speed is negative (moving up). This
  is the same `BMI` check as for the other `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` entries. So
  an upward cape flap on a winged Yoshi does not change. Only the downward
  glide is slower.

## General terminal velocity (gentle long falls)

**Code:** `FD2C-A7AF`
**Raw form:** `00D7AF:10` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 20:36:35

Tags: `demo-ready`

`PlayerMaxFallSpeed` entry 0 (`$40`) is the fall speed limit for the common
state where jump is released. The game uses it when the jump button is not
held. This is the same `Y` selection as in the "Low gravity while the jump
button is released" code above. This code lowers it to `$10` (16, a quarter
of the original 64). So normal falls have a much lower maximum speed. This
does not depend on gravity. Mario speeds up at the start of a fall in the
same way, but when he reaches the limit, the fall speed stops there. It
does not continue up to `$40`.

**Mechanism:** the same jump-button test sets `Y=0`. It is documented at
the `PlayerGravity` definition, and the code is in `CODE_00D928`:

```
CODE_00D928:
    LDY.B #$01                                  ; tentatively Y = 1 (jump held)
    LDA.B byetudlrHold
    BMI +                                       ; branch (keep Y=1) if jump (bit 7) held
CODE_00D92E:
    LDY.B #$00                                  ; else Y = 0 (jump released) -- this entry
  + LDA.B PlayerYSpeed+1                        ; \ If Mario's Y speed is negative (up),
    BMI CODE_00D948                             ; / branch to $D948 (skip the cap entirely)
    CMP.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y                  ;   compare current speed to the cap
    BCC +                                       ;   below cap: leave alone
    LDA.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y                  ;   at/above cap: clamp down to it
  + LDX.B PlayerInAir
    ...
CODE_00D948:
    CLC
    ADC.W PlayerGravity,Y                       ; gravity added after the clamp check
```

The header comment at the table definition says that entry 0 controls
*both* normal falls with jump released and the death fall of
`MarioDeathAni` (`JSR
CODE_00D92E` also sets `Y=0` there). So this code also limits the fall in
the death animation, not only in normal play. The `BMI CODE_00D948` two
lines above the `CMP` is the check that the backlog note described. When
`PlayerYSpeed+1` is negative (moving up), it goes directly to the gravity
add and skips the `CMP` and limit pair. The source code confirms this. So
this limit can only slow a fall, never a rise.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00D7AF`, the first byte of `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` in
`bank_00.asm`. Checked against the disassembly source (`db
$40,$40,$20,...`, entry 0 = `$40`) and the reference ROM
(`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header). The ROM holds
`$40` at `$00D7AF`. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was not
tested in play.

**Caveats:**

- **Uses the same table system as the index-0 gravity code** ("Low gravity
  while the jump button is released," `DF2C-AF0F`) and the jump-held
  gravity code above (`DF2C-AF6F`). All three use the same `Y` selection
  code. But this one patches `PlayerMaxFallSpeed`, not `PlayerGravity`. So
  it changes the maximum fall speed, not the acceleration. You can use it
  with either of them. Gravity codes change how fast the speed increases
  toward the limit. This code changes the limit.
- **Also changes the death fall animation.** As the Correction in the "Low
  gravity" entry explains, `Y=0` is also used there. `MarioDeathAni` uses
  index 0 for its fall. So the fall after the death hop is limited to `$10`,
  the same as normal falls with jump released.
- **Never changes a rise.** The `BMI CODE_00D948` check skips the
  `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` check while `PlayerYSpeed+1` is negative (moving
  up). The source quoted above confirms this, as the backlog note said.
- **NTSC-only data.** `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` is inside the same `if
  ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)` block as `PlayerGravity`. It is a byte table in
  J/U/SS, but a **word** table (`dw $4000` for this entry) with a different
  layout in E0/E1. This code is only for U. Do not use it on a PAL ROM.
- Entries 1-9 (jump held, winged Yoshi, cape flight, and others) do not
  change.

## Mario exhales bubbles on dry land (out-of-water bubble breathing)

**Codes:** `F930-67D4` `6DBF-AF08`
**Raw form:** `00EA4C:15` (original `$56`); `029F15:80` (original `$D0`)
(address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 20:42:17

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** When Mario swims, he breathes out bubbles. `CODE_00FD08`
(`bank_00.asm`) creates them. It finds a free extended-sprite slot and puts
extended sprite `$12` ("Water bubble") in it:

```
CODE_00FD08:
    LDY.B #$3F
    LDA.B byetudlrHold
    AND.B #$83                                ; B/A, left, or right held?
    BNE +
    LDY.B #$7F
  + TYA
    AND.B EffFrame                            ; \ only on frames where
    ORA.B SpriteLock                          ; | (EffFrame & mask) == 0
    BNE Return00FD23                          ; /
    LDX.B #$07                                ; \ Find a free extended sprite slot
CODE_00FD1B:
    LDA.W ExtSpriteNumber,X                   ; |
    BEQ CODE_00FD26                           ; |
    DEX                                       ; |
    BPL CODE_00FD1B                           ; |
Return00FD23:
    RTS                                       ; / Return if no free slots

CODE_00FD26:
    LDA.B #$12                                ; \ Extended sprite = Water buble
    STA.W ExtSpriteNumber,X                   ; /
```

No code in `CODE_00FD08` tests a water flag. The rate check is only a
frame-counter mask. The bubble position comes from `PlayerDirection`,
`PlayerXPosNext`/`PlayerYPosNext`, `Powerup` and `PlayerIsDucking`. The
routine works only underwater **because of the place that calls it**. It
has exactly one caller, at the end of the water-state code in
`bank_00.asm`:

```
  + STZ.W PlayerCanJumpWater
    LDA.B LevelIsWater
    BNE CODE_00EA5E                           ; water level -> always "in water"
    LSR.B InteractionPtsInWater               ; \ touching water this frame?
    BCC CODE_00EAA3                           ; / no -> clear the flag and leave
    ...
CODE_00EA5E:
    LDA.B #$01
    STA.B PlayerInWater
CODE_00EA62:
    JMP CODE_00FD08                           ; <- the only call to the emitter
    ...
CODE_00EAA3:
    STZ.B PlayerInWater
Return00EAA5:
    RTS
```

The first code patches the **operand of the `BCC`**. This is the exit for
"Mario does not touch water, so stop here". In the original ROM it is `$56`.
This is a relative branch from the next instruction at `$00EA4D` to
`$00EA4D + $56 = $00EAA3` (`CODE_00EAA3`). The code changes it to `$15`.
Now the same branch goes to `$00EA4D + $15 = $00EA62`, which is
`CODE_00EA62`, the `JMP CODE_00FD08`. So on a frame when Mario is *not* in
water, the game now goes to the bubble code and does not return.

This is important: the new target is **below** `STA.B PlayerInWater` at
`CODE_00EA5E`, not above it. So the dry-land path reaches the bubble code
*without* setting the in-water flag. Mario keeps the normal walk and jump
physics, and only breathes out bubbles. The stack does not change. The old
path ended in `RTS`, and both exits of `CODE_00FD08` end in `RTS`, so this
is still a tail call.

The second code keeps the bubbles alive out of water. Without it, a bubble
made on land would pop at once. `WaterBubble` (`bank_02.asm`) runs the
bubble. Every other frame, it checks the block that it is in and decides if
it stays:

```
    JSR CODE_02A56E                           ; block interaction; C = solid tile
    BCS CODE_029F27                           ; hit something solid -> erase
    LDA.B LevelIsWater                        ; \ water level: skip the test
    BNE CODE_029F2A                           ; / entirely, bubble always lives
    LDA.B _C                                  ; \ layer 1 Map16 tile number
    CMP.B #$06                                ; | < $06 = a liquid tile
    BCC CODE_029F2A                           ; / still in water -> live
    LDA.B _F                                  ; \ layer 2 interaction active?
    BEQ CODE_029F27                           ; / no -> erase
    LDA.B _D                                  ; \ layer 2 Map16 tile number
    CMP.B #$06                                ; |
    BCC CODE_029F2A                           ; / still in water -> live
CODE_029F27:
    JMP CODE_02A211                           ; STZ ExtSpriteNumber,X - pop
```

The second code patches the **opcode of the `BNE`** on `LevelIsWater`. `$D0`
(BNE) becomes `$80` (BRA). So the branch is always taken, and this test
treats every level as a water level. The "am I still inside water?" check
below it is skipped. A bubble keeps going up through the air, and the game
does not erase it.

Map16 tile numbers `$00-$05` are the liquid tiles. This does not come only
from this routine. The sprite buoyancy handler `CODE_019211` (`bank_01.asm`)
runs the same `LDA Map16TileNumber / CMP #$06` test. When the test passes,
it sets `SpriteInLiquid` (and tile `$04` gets extra handling in
`CODE_019330`). So the constant has the same meaning in both places.

Nothing else about the bubble changes. It still goes up one pixel on each
frame where `ExtSpriteMisc1765 & $30` is not zero. It is still erased when
it touches a **solid** tile. (That is the `BCS` above the patched branch,
and the code does not change it.) It is also still erased when it goes past
the top of the screen. The code at `CODE_029F2A` subtracts `Layer1YPos` from
the bubble's Y position, and it erases the sprite as soon as the 16-bit
result is outside the current screen. So the eight extended sprite slots
are still reused normally.

**Evidence:** Checked against the reference ROM. `$00EA45` holds
`A5 85 D0 15 46 8A 90 56`. This decodes exactly as the source predicts:
`LDA $85` (`LevelIsWater`), `BNE +$15` → `$00EA5E`, `LSR $8A`
(`InteractionPtsInWater`), `BCC +$56` → `$00EAA3`. `$029F0E` holds
`20 6E A5 B0 14 A5 85 D0 13 A5 0C C9 06 90 0D A5 0F F0 06 A5 0D C9 06 90 03
4C`. This decodes as the source listing says: `JSR $A56E`, `BCS +$14` →
`$029F27`, `LDA $85` (`LevelIsWater`), **`BNE +$13` → `$029F2A` at
`$029F15`**, `LDA $0C`, `CMP #$06`, `BCC +$0D` → `$029F2A`, `LDA $0F`,
`BEQ +$06` → `$029F27`, `LDA $0D`, `CMP #$06`, `BCC +$03`, `JMP`.
Both codes were encoded and then decoded again, and they give the correct address and byte. This effect comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**

- **The dry-land path no longer clears the in-water flag.** Only two places
  in the ROM write `PlayerInWater` (`$75`). `CODE_00EA5E` sets it, and
  `CODE_00EAA3` clears it. `ClearMemory` (`bank_00.asm`) sets it to zero
  only on **reset**, not at the start of each level. This code sends the
  land path away from the clear. Execution still reaches the clear at
  `CODE_00EAA3` when Mario jumps out of water (`LDA #$AA / STA
  PlayerYSpeed+1` continues directly into it). So jumping out of water
  still works normally. But if Mario finishes a **water level**, or leaves
  water in any other way, the flag stays set. Nothing clears it when a
  level loads. So Mario keeps **swimming physics on dry land** until the
  next time he jumps out of water. Before Mario touches any water (for
  example, after a reset and in the first levels without water), the code
  only makes bubbles and does not change physics. This swim-on-land state
  is a known side effect that stays active. It is not a separate code.
- **Water levels do not change.** On a level with `LevelIsWater` set, the
  `BNE` above the first patched branch is taken on every frame, and the
  patched `BCC` never runs. The `BNE` that the second code patches was
  already taken on every frame too. So swimming and bubbles are the same as
  in the original game.
- **Bubbles from swimming also leave the water.** In levels with a water
  *line*, Mario's swimming bubbles now go through the surface and keep
  rising.
- **Bubbles use extended-sprite slots.** The bubble code checks slots `$07`
  down to `$00` and stops if no slot is free. So in a room with many
  sprites, a land bubble can be skipped with no sign. Also, a continuous
  bubble stream (with the steady stream codes) uses slots that fireballs, sparkles
  and other extended sprites also need.
- **`BRA` is a 65816 opcode.** It has two bytes, like `BNE`, and the same
  relative operand. So the instruction length and everything after it do
  not change.
- **The tile test routine has automatic labels.** `CODE_02A56E` /
  `CODE_02A611` and the temporary variables `_C`/`_D`/`_F` have no header
  comments in the disassembly. Their jobs here come from the code that reads
  them, and from the matching `CODE_019211` test above. The patched byte
  itself is in a named routine and branches on a named variable, so the
  code's own mechanism does not depend on those names.
- **Only one path.** `$029F15` is only inside `WaterBubble`. Only extended
  sprite `$12` gets to it, so the block interaction of other sprites does
  not change.

## Winged-Yoshi flight gravity (near-weightless glide)

**Code:** `DD2C-AFAF`
**Raw form:** `00D7A7:00` (original `$04`)
(address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 20:47:05

**Mechanism:** `PlayerGravity` (`bank_00.asm`) is a table with one gravity
value for each air state. Entry 2 is the value added to `PlayerYSpeed` once
per frame while Mario flies on a winged Yoshi. On that path, `CODE_00D8CD`
always selects `Y=2`. The selection does **not** depend on Mario's
`Powerup`:

```
CODE_00D8CD:
    LDA.B PlayerInAir                         ; \ Branch if not flying
    BEQ CODE_00D928                           ; /
    LDX.B #$00                                ; X = #$00
    LDA.W PlayerRidingYoshi                   ; \ Branch if not on Yoshi
    BEQ CODE_00D8E7                           ; /
    LDA.W YoshiHasWingsEvt                    ; \ Branch if not winged Yoshi
    LSR A                                     ; |
    BEQ CODE_00D8E7                           ; /
    LDY.B #$02                                ; \ Branch if not Caped Mario
    CPY.B Powerup                             ; |
    BEQ +                                     ; /
    INX                                       ; X= #$01
  + BRA CODE_00D8FF
```

`LDY.B #$02` runs as soon as `PlayerRidingYoshi` and `YoshiHasWingsEvt` are
both set. It runs *before* the `CPY.B Powerup` after it. That compare only
decides if the code does `INX` (which selects the byte of `byetudlrHold`
that is read later, at `CODE_00D8FF`). It never changes `Y`. So `Y` is `2`
for *any* `Powerup` value during winged-Yoshi flight, not only for Caped
Mario. The comment on that line ("Branch if not Caped Mario") describes the
`INX` selection, not the gravity index. `Y=2` stays the same until the
shared limit and add routine. There, `CODE_00D924: CPY.B #$02 / BEQ +`
checks it again, then continues into the shared gravity add:

```
CODE_00D924:
    CPY.B #$02
    BEQ +
CODE_00D928:
    LDY.B #$01
    ...
  + LDA.B PlayerYSpeed+1                      ; \ If Mario's Y speed is negative (up),
    BMI CODE_00D948                           ; / branch to $D948 (skip the fall cap)
    CMP.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y
    BCC +
    LDA.W PlayerMaxFallSpeed,Y
  + LDX.B PlayerInAir
    ...
CODE_00D948:
    CLC
    ADC.W PlayerGravity,Y                     ; speed += PlayerGravity[2]
```

`PlayerGravity+2` is `$04`. This is a small downward pull, weaker than the
`$06` for a normal fall with jump released. The code changes it to `$00`,
which removes the pull. When this index is selected, gravity no longer
changes Mario's vertical speed toward the ground on each frame. So during a
winged-Yoshi glide, Mario keeps his height much more easily and does not
slowly go down. It is closer to a real hover than the original "float and
slowly go down" feel. The byte sets only the *acceleration* to zero. The
vertical speed that Mario already has (from a flap, or from the start of
flight) does not change. It stays the same from frame to frame until other
code changes it (the `byetudlrHold` adjustments in
`CODE_00D8FF`/`CODE_00D90D`, or the end of flight).

**Evidence:** Patches `$00D7A7`, the third byte of `PlayerGravity` in
`bank_00.asm`. Checked against the disassembly source (`db
$06,$03,$04,...`, entry 2 = `$04`) and the reference ROM
(`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header). The ROM holds
`$04` at `$00D7A7`. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not**
tested in play.

**Caveats:**

- **Shared reader** with every other `PlayerGravity` entry. The add is one
  `ADC.W PlayerGravity,Y` at `CODE_00D948`. This patch changes only entry
  2 because of its address. Entries 0, 1 and 3-9 (jump released or held,
  cape flight) do not change.
- **Correction to the earlier "Winged-Yoshi fall cap" entry above**
  (`FD28-AD0F`, which patches `PlayerMaxFallSpeed+2`). The caveats of that
  entry say that entry 2 is used "while riding a winged Yoshi as Caped
  Mario", and they give `Powerup == 2` as a condition. The code in
  `CODE_00D8CD` shows that this is not correct. `LDY.B #$02` runs whenever
  `PlayerRidingYoshi` and `YoshiHasWingsEvt` are set, with no other
  condition. The `CPY.B Powerup` compare just after it only controls the
  `INX` and the input-byte selection, not `Y`. Index 2 applies to
  winged-Yoshi flight with **any** `Powerup` value, not only Caped Mario. The
  mechanism section of this entry uses the correct explanation. The earlier
  entry was not changed.
- **NTSC-only data.** `PlayerGravity` is inside an `if ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)`
  block. It is a byte table in J/U/SS, but a **word** table with a
  different layout in E0/E1. This code is only for U. Do not use it on a
  PAL ROM.
- When Mario's Y speed is negative (moving up), the `BMI CODE_00D948` check
  skips the `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` limit. But the gravity add at `CODE_00D948`
  runs in both cases. So the effect of this code (no pull) applies in both
  cases.

## Cape-flight pull-up gravity (snappier climb after a flap)

**Code:** `3D2C-A40F`
**Raw form:** `00D7A9:E0` (original `$F4`)
(address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 20:47:05

**Mechanism:** `PlayerGravity` entry 4 is one of the four gravity entries
for cape flight (indices 4-7, selected as `FlightPhase+3`). `CODE_00D87E`
prepares the index, and the NTSC block calculates it:

```
CODE_00D87E:
    STX.W NextFlightPhase
    LDY.W FlightPhase
    BEQ CODE_00D8CD                           ; not flying: use the ordinary jump/fall table
    LDA.B PlayerYSpeed+1                      ; \ clamp: rise speed can't exceed -56 ($C8)
    BPL CODE_00D892                           ; |
    CMP.B #$C8                                ; |
    BCS +                                     ; |
    LDA.B #$C8                                ; |
    BRA +                                     ; /
CODE_00D892:
    CMP.W DATA_00D7C8,Y
    BCC +
    LDA.W DATA_00D7C8,Y
  + PHA
    CPY.B #$01                                ; FlightPhase == 1?
    BNE CODE_00D8C6
    LDX.W MaxStageOfFlight
    BEQ CODE_00D8C4                           ; MaxStageOfFlight == 0 -> diverts to LDY #$02
    LDA.B PlayerYSpeed+1
    BMI CODE_00D8AF
    LDA.B #!SFX_CAPE
    STA.W SPCIO0
    BRA +
CODE_00D8AF:
    CMP.W MaxStageOfFlight
    BCS +
    STX.B PlayerYSpeed+1
    STZ.W MaxStageOfFlight
  + LDX.B PlayerDirection
    LDA.B PlayerXSpeed+1
    BEQ CODE_00D8C4                           ; PlayerXSpeed+1 == 0 -> diverts to LDY #$02
    EOR.W DATA_00D535,X
    BPL CODE_00D8C6                           ; direction test negative -> diverts to LDY #$02
CODE_00D8C4:
    LDY.B #$02                                ; forced index 5 (fallback)
CODE_00D8C6:
    PLA
    INY
    INY
    INY                                       ; Y = FlightPhase+3 (or 2+3=5 on the fallback)
```

`LDY.W FlightPhase` (which is not zero here) and then three `INY`s give
gravity index `FlightPhase+3`. So index 4 is normally the
`FlightPhase == 1` case. **But** the `CPY.B #$01` / `BNE CODE_00D8C6` check
does not always decide. When `FlightPhase == 1` but `MaxStageOfFlight == 0`,
or `PlayerXSpeed+1 == 0`, or the `EOR.W DATA_00D535,X` direction test gives
a negative result, execution goes to `CODE_00D8C4: LDY.B #$02` instead.
After the same three `INY`s, this gives index **5**, not 4. So index 4 is
only the *pull-up* (climb) case: just after a flap, while Mario moves and
faces in the same direction. It is not used on every `FlightPhase == 1`
frame.

The code just above the index calculation limits the rise speed. `LDA
PlayerYSpeed+1` / `BPL CODE_00D892` / `CMP #$C8` / `BCS +` / `LDA #$C8`
means that the vertical speed on this frame, after the gravity add, can
never be more than `-56` ($C8) upward. This is a fixed maximum that does not
depend on the gravity table. The code changes entry 4 from `$F4` (-12) to
`$E0` (-32). This makes the upward acceleration during a cape pull-up more
than 2.5x stronger. So `PlayerYSpeed` reaches the `-56` maximum in fewer
frames, and the pull-up is faster and stronger. It does **not** raise the
maximum. Mario still cannot climb faster than `-56` per frame, however
negative this byte is.

**Evidence:** Patches `$00D7A9`, the fifth byte of `PlayerGravity` in
`bank_00.asm`. Checked against the disassembly source (`db
$06,$03,$04,$10,$F4,...`, entry 4 = `$F4`) and the reference ROM
(`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header). The ROM holds
`$F4` at `$00D7A9`. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not**
tested in play.

**Caveats:**

- **Shared reader** with every other `PlayerGravity` entry. The add is one
  `ADC.W PlayerGravity,Y` at `CODE_00D948`. This patch changes only entry
  4 because of its address. Entries 0-3 and 5-9 (jump, winged Yoshi, and
  the other three cape-flight phases) do not change.
- **Index 5 is used in some cases.** As shown above, `FlightPhase == 1` does
  not always give index 4. If `MaxStageOfFlight == 0`, `PlayerXSpeed+1 == 0`,
  or the `EOR.W DATA_00D535,X` direction result is negative, the
  `LDY.B #$02` at `CODE_00D8C4` gives index 5 instead (gravity `$01`, which
  this code does not change). This patch changes only frames where none of
  these conditions is true.
- **The -56 climb-speed maximum is a separate limit, and it does not
  change.** The `CMP.B
  #$C8` / `BCS` / `LDA.B #$C8` code just above the index calculation limits
  `PlayerYSpeed+1` to `-56`, whatever this byte is. A more negative entry 4
  reduces the number of frames needed to reach that limit. It cannot make
  the climb faster than the limit.
- **NTSC-only data.** `PlayerGravity` is inside an `if ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)`
  block. It is a byte table in J/U/SS, but a **word** table with a
  different layout in E0/E1. The E0/E1 code also calculates the index with
  different instructions (`INY` x3 comes *before* the `ASL`/`REP #$20`
  widening; the index is the same, but the bytes are different) at a
  different address. This code is only for U. Do not use it on a PAL ROM.

## Mega Mole charge speed (rightward charge 4x faster)

**Code:** `0D61-A762`
**Raw form:** `03876E:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `MegaMoleSpeed` (`bank_03.asm`) is a table with two signed X
speeds, `db $10,$F0` (+16 / -16). The index is the direction that the
sprite faces. The `MegaMole` main handler sets `SpriteXSpeed` from this
table on every frame:

```
MegaMoleSpeed:
    db $10,$F0

MegaMole:
    JSR MegaMoleGfxRt                         ; Graphics routine
    LDA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; \
    CMP.B #$08                                ; | If status != 8, return
    BNE Return038733                          ; /
    JSR SubOffscreen3Bnk3                     ; Handle off screen situation
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; \ Set x speed based on direction
    LDA.W MegaMoleSpeed,Y                     ; |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
```

The comment in the reader says what the table does ("Set x speed based on
direction"). `Y` is `SpriteMisc157C`, the temporary direction value of the
Mega Mole. The routine inverts it with `EOR.B #$01` each time
`SpriteBlockedDirs & $03` reports that the mole hit a wall:

```
MegaMoleOnGround:
    LDY.W SpriteMisc15AC,X                    ; \
    LDA.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X                 ; | If Mega Mole is in contact with an object...
    AND.B #$03                                ; |
    BEQ CODE_0387CD                           ; |
    ...
  + LDA.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; \ Flip the temp direction status
    EOR.B #$01                                ; |
    STA.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; /
```

So entry `+0` (`$10`) is the walk to the right, and `+1` (`$F0`) is the
walk to the left. The code changes `+0` from `$10` (+16) to `$40` (+64).
This makes a Mega Mole that moves right 4 times faster. Its speed to the
left stays at the normal -16. The write always runs, and it runs before
`UpdateSpritePos`. So the new speed starts on the next frame after the mole
turns. This applies to the mole as an obstacle, and also to Mario when he
rides on top of one.

**Evidence:** Patches `$03876E`, the first byte of `MegaMoleSpeed`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $10,$F0`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$10` at `$03876E`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$038780` holds `B9 6E 87` (`LDA.W $876E,Y`), which matches the source. This
effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W MegaMoleSpeed,Y` at `$038780` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. So the code changes only
Mega Moles. **The two directions are different on purpose.** Only the entry
for the right is patched. So a mole changes from +64 to -16 and back, and
you can see the difference. To make a mole that is fast in both directions,
add a second code that sets `$03876F` to `$C0`. The routine does not set
Mario's ride speed separately. He gets the speed of the platform. So a fast
mole also carries him fast, and it can move faster than the screen scrolls.

## Blurp swim speed (Blurps swim right 4x faster)

**Code:** `4D6A-DF62`
**Raw form:** `0384C6:20` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `BlurpSpeedX` (`bank_03.asm`) is a table with two signed X
speeds, `db $08,$F8` (+8 / -8). It holds the horizontal swim speed of the
Blurp fish. The `Blurp` handler writes it to `SpriteXSpeed` on every frame.
The index is the direction that the sprite faces:

```
BlurpMaxSpeedY:
    db $04,$FC

BlurpSpeedX:
    db $08,$F8

BlurpAccelY:
    db $01,$FF

Blurp:
    ...
    LDA.B SpriteTableC2,X
    AND.B #$01
    TAY
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CLC
    ADC.W BlurpAccelY,Y                       ; vertical weave: accelerate...
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CMP.W BlurpMaxSpeedY,Y                    ; ...until the turnaround speed is hit
    BNE +
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X
  + LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X
    LDA.W BlurpSpeedX,Y                       ; horizontal: constant, by facing
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    JSL UpdateXPosNoGvtyW
    JSL UpdateYPosNoGvtyW
```

The two axes work in different ways. The *vertical* movement is an up and
down wave that builds up over time (`BlurpAccelY` is added every 4th
frame, and it changes direction when it reaches `BlurpMaxSpeedY`). The
*horizontal* speed is loaded again from `BlurpSpeedX` on each frame as a
constant. So `BlurpSpeedX` is a direct speed byte. It does not build up,
and no state machine uses it. A patch to it cannot put anything out of
sync.

Entry `+0` (`$08`) is the swim to the right. The code changes it to `$20`
(+32). Blurps that face right now swim four times as fast. The speed to the
left stays at the normal -8.

**Evidence:** Patches `$0384C6`, the first byte of `BlurpSpeedX`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $08,$F8`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$08` at `$0384C6`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$038519` holds `B9 C6 84` (`LDA.W $84C6,Y`), which matches the source.
This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W BlurpSpeedX,Y` at `$038519` is the
only read of this table in the disassembly. So the effect changes only
Blurps. The two tables next to it in the same block, `BlurpMaxSpeedY`
(`$0384C4`) and `BlurpAccelY` (`$0384C8`), are **not** changed by this code.
Each of them has *two* readers (`Blurp` and `CODE_038936`). The second
reader of `BlurpMaxSpeedY` is a `CMP`/`BNE` test for an exact value, which
decides when to turn around. So it is not safe to change those two tables
without care, and this code does not change them. **The two directions are
different on purpose.** Only the entry for the right is patched. For a
Blurp that is fast in both directions, add a second code that sets
`$0384C7` to `$E0`.

## Flying turn-block drift speed (blocks sweep 4x faster on one half-cycle)

**Code:** `4D6E-0FD2`
**Raw form:** `0385F4:20` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `FlyingBlockSpeedY` (`bank_03.asm`) is a table with two
signed Y speeds, `db $08,$F8` (+8 / -8). It controls the vertical movement
of the flying turn-blocks that move past during the forced fast-scroll
sections. The `FlyingTurnBlocks` handler reads the table only while
`BGFastScrollActive` is set:

```
FlyingBlockSpeedY:
    db $08,$F8

FlyingTurnBlocks:
    JSR CODE_0386A8
    LDA.B SpriteLock
    BNE Return038675
    LDA.W BGFastScrollActive
    BEQ CODE_038629                  ; <- not scrolling: table never read
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1534,X
    INC.W SpriteMisc1534,X
    AND.B #$01
    BNE +
    DEC.W SpriteMisc1602,X           ; \ every other frame, tick a countdown;
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1602,X           ; | when it wraps past 0 it is reloaded
    CMP.B #$FF                       ; | and the direction index advances
    BNE +                            ; |
    LDA.B #$FF                       ; |
    STA.W SpriteMisc1602,X           ; |
    INC.W SpriteMisc157C,X           ; /
  + LDA.W SpriteMisc157C,X           ; \ index = direction counter & 1
    AND.B #$01                       ; |
    TAY                              ; |
    LDA.W FlyingBlockSpeedY,Y        ; |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X             ; /
```

So the blocks move down and up in turn. `SpriteMisc157C` increments each
time the `SpriteMisc1602` countdown ends. Its low bit selects `+0` (`$08`,
down) or `+1` (`$F8`, -8, up). The code changes `+0` from `$08` to `$20`
(+32). This makes the downward half of the cycle four times faster. The
upward half stays at the normal -8. So the blocks move down quickly and
then move back up slowly.

Two details of the routine change what you see. Know both before you use
this code:

```
CODE_038629:
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    PHA
    LDY.W SpriteMisc151C,X           ; \ half the blocks mirror the motion
    BNE +                            ; |
    EOR.B #$FF                       ; |  (two's-complement negate)
    INC A                            ; |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X             ; /
  + JSL UpdateYPosNoGvtyW
    PLA
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X             ; restore the un-negated value
    LDA.W BGFastScrollActive
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X             ; X speed comes from the scroll rate
    JSL UpdateXPosNoGvtyW
```

First, `SpriteMisc151C` puts the blocks into two mirrored groups. Blocks
with this value clear move by the *negative* of the table value. So one
byte still controls both directions of the group, but with opposite signs.
Second, the negative value is used only for the position update. The
original value is put back just after it. So nothing builds up, and each
frame loads the value from the table again.

**Evidence:** Patches `$0385F4`, the first byte of `FlyingBlockSpeedY`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $08,$F8`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$08` at `$0385F4`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$038624` holds `B9 F4 85` (`LDA.W $85F4,Y`), which matches the source.
This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Works only during a forced fast scroll.** The `LDA.W
BGFastScrollActive / BEQ CODE_038629` check above the table read means that
the speed is never loaded while the scroll is off. Outside those sections,
the blocks keep their last `SpriteYSpeed`, and this code does nothing.
**One byte, two directions on screen.** Because of the `SpriteMisc151C`
mirror above, the patched value controls the blocks that move down and the
blocks that move up (as its negative). So the whole wall speeds up on the
same half of the cycle, not only one column. **The two directions are
different on purpose.** Only the `+0` entry is patched, so the cycle is
uneven (fast one way, normal the other way). For a sweep that is fast in
both directions, add a second code that sets `$0385F5` to `$E0`. Horizontal
movement does not change. It comes directly from `BGFastScrollActive`, not
from this table.

## Porcu-Puffer pursuit speed cap (rightward chase 4x faster)

**Code:** `0D64-0702`
**Raw form:** `03852D:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** The Porcu-Puffer follows Mario horizontally. It does not
jump to a speed at once. It speeds up by ±1 every fourth frame until it
reaches a maximum speed for that direction:

```
PorcuPuffAccel:
    db $01,$FF

PorcuPuffMaxSpeed:
    db $10,$F0

PorcuPuffer:
    ...
    JSR SubHorzPosBnk3                        ; Y = which side Mario is on
    TYA
    STA.W SpriteMisc157C,X
    LDA.B EffFrame                            ; \ only act every 4th frame
    AND.B #$03                                ; |
    BNE +                                     ; /
    LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; \ Branch if at max speed
    CMP.W PorcuPuffMaxSpeed,Y                 ; |
    BEQ +                                     ; /
    CLC                                       ; \ Otherwise, accelerate
    ADC.W PorcuPuffAccel,Y                    ; |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
```

The comments in the disassembly on both readers say what they do ("Branch
if at max speed" / "Otherwise, accelerate"). `Y` comes from
`SubHorzPosBnk3`. It calculates `PlayerXPosNext - SpriteXPos`. It returns
**`Y = 0` when Mario is to the right** of the sprite (the result stays
positive), and **`Y = 1` when he is to the left** (the `BPL` is not taken
and `INY` runs):

```
SubHorzPosBnk3:
    LDY.B #$00
    LDA.B PlayerXPosNext
    SEC
    SBC.B SpriteXPosLow,X
    STA.B _F
    LDA.B PlayerXPosNext+1
    SBC.W SpriteXPosHigh,X
    BPL +
    INY
  + RTS
```

So entry `+0` (`$10` = +16, right) is the maximum speed when the fish
follows Mario to the right. Entry `+1` (`$F0` = -16) is the maximum to the
left. The matching accelerations are `+1` and `-1`. The code changes `+0`
from `$10` to `$40` (+64). The fish can now move to the right 4 times
faster. Its speed to the left stays at the normal -16.

**The value `$40` was selected so that the fish can reach it exactly. This
is important.** The test is `CMP` + `BEQ`. It checks for an **exact
value**, and it is not a `BCS` limit. So the maximum stops the acceleration
only if the ±1 steps land exactly on it. The speed changes in steps of
exactly +1 (or -1) from its current whole-number value. So it passes every
whole number in the range, and it reaches `$40` exactly. If a step went
*past* the value, the fish would speed up with no limit. This cannot happen
with a ±1 step and an 8-bit speed. But it can happen if the acceleration
byte is also changed to a step larger than 1. **Do not use this code with a
patch to `PorcuPuffAccel` (`$03852B`/`$03852C`), unless the distance to the
maximum is a multiple of the new step size.**

**Evidence:** Patches `$03852D`, the first byte of `PorcuPuffMaxSpeed`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $10,$F0`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$10` at `$03852D`. Both readers were also checked in the
ROM: `$038553` holds `D9 2D 85` (`CMP.W $852D,Y`) and `$038559` holds
`79 2B 85` (`ADC.W $852B,Y`), which match the source. This effect comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `CMP.W PorcuPuffMaxSpeed,Y` at `$038553` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. So the effect changes only
Porcu-Puffers. **The two directions are different on purpose.** Only the
maximum for the right is patched. So the fish follows to the right at up to
+64, but to the left at only -16. For a chase that is fast in both
directions, add a second code that sets `$03852E` to `$C0`. For the
position update, the sprite also adds the layer 1 scroll change
(`Layer1DXPos * 8`) to this speed, and then puts back the value without
scroll. So on screen, the speed at which it comes closer to Mario is the
patched speed plus the camera movement. The code changes the sprite's own
chase speed, not the scroll value.

## Blurp / Swooper dive amplitude (4x deeper downward swing)

**Code:** `FD6A-DFD2`
**Raw form:** `0384C4:10` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `BlurpMaxSpeedY` (`bank_03.asm`, `db $04,$FC` = +4 / -4) is
the speed where an up and down wave changes direction. The wave is made by
adding ±1 many times. With `BlurpAccelY` (`db $01,$FF`), it makes the
normal up and down movement. The sprite's `SpriteYSpeed` changes by ±1 at a
fixed frame rate. When it is exactly equal to the maximum, the phase index
changes and the change goes the other way.

```
BlurpMaxSpeedY:
    db $04,$FC

BlurpSpeedX:
    db $08,$F8

BlurpAccelY:
    db $01,$FF
```

**Two sprites use this wave**, and you must understand both before you use
this code. The first is the Blurp fish. It does a step every fourth frame,
with `SpriteTableC2` as the phase:

```
Blurp:
    ...
    LDA.B EffFrame
    AND.B #$03                                ; every 4th frame
    BNE +
    LDA.B SpriteTableC2,X
    AND.B #$01
    TAY
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CLC
    ADC.W BlurpAccelY,Y
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CMP.W BlurpMaxSpeedY,Y
    BNE +
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; reverse the weave
```

The second is the **Swooper** (the cave bat). It uses state 2 of its
three-state handler. The game gets there through the `JSL ExecutePtr` /
`dw CODE_0388E4 / dw CODE_038905
/ dw CODE_038936` dispatch below `BatTiles`. This state runs after the bat
drops from the ceiling and plays `!SFX_SWOOPER`. It uses the same two
tables, but it does a step every **second** frame and keeps its phase in
`SpriteMisc151C`:

```
CODE_038936:                                  ; Swooper, state 2
    LDA.B TrueFrame
    AND.B #$01                                ; every 2nd frame
    BNE +
    LDA.W SpriteMisc151C,X
    AND.B #$01
    TAY
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CLC
    ADC.W BlurpAccelY,Y
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CMP.W BlurpMaxSpeedY,Y
    BNE +
    INC.W SpriteMisc151C,X
  + BRA CODE_038915
```

The code changes `BlurpMaxSpeedY+0` from `$04` to `$10` (+16). The downward
half of the wave can now get 4 times faster before it changes direction. So
both sprites dive much deeper, and they take longer to come back. The
upward maximum (`+1`, `$FC` = -4) does not change, so the wave is uneven: a
long, fast dive, then the normal slow rise. The Swooper does steps twice as
often as the Blurp. So the bat reaches the new maximum in half the frames,
and its dive is larger.

**The value `$10` was selected so that the sprites can reach it exactly.**
Both readers test with `CMP` + `BNE`. This checks for an **exact value**,
and it is not a `BCS` limit. So the wave changes direction only if the
speed lands exactly on the maximum. `BlurpAccelY` is ±1, so the speed
passes every whole number, and it reaches `$10` exactly. **Do not also
change `BlurpAccelY` (`$0384C8`/`$0384C9`) to a step larger than 1.** A
step that goes past the maximum without being equal to it makes
`SpriteYSpeed` increase with no limit, and the sprite does not turn around.

**Evidence:** Patches `$0384C4`, the first byte of `BlurpMaxSpeedY`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $04,$FC`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$04` at `$0384C4`. **Both** readers were checked in the ROM:
`$03850F` (Blurp) and `$03894A` (Swooper state 2) both hold `D9 C4 84`
(`CMP.W $84C4,Y`), which matches the source. This effect comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Shared reader, two different sprites.** The other `bank_03`
speed codes here have one reader, but this table has two. So the code
changes Blurps *and* Swoopers together. With this byte, you cannot change
one without the other. The two sprites use different step rates (every 4th
frame and every 2nd frame) and keep the phase in different RAM slots
(`SpriteTableC2` and `SpriteMisc151C`). So the same maximum gives a
different dive for each one. `BlurpSpeedX` (`$0384C6`) is between the two
tables. It is only horizontal, and this code does not change it. See the
separate Blurp swim speed entry. **The two directions are different on
purpose.** Only the downward maximum is patched. For a deep wave in both
directions, add a second code that sets `$0384C5` to `$F0`.

## Bowser statue lunge speed (rightward lunge 4x faster)

**Code:** `0D68-67A3`
**Raw form:** `038ABF:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `BwsrStatueSpeed` (`bank_03.asm`) is a table with two signed X
speeds, `db $10,$F0` (+16 / -16). The Bowser statue handler reads it once
for each jump. The statue stays still on the ground until an internal timer
ends. Then it jumps up and selects a horizontal speed toward Mario:

```
    AND.B #$04                                ; \ (on-ground check)
    BEQ Return038AC6                          ; /
    LDA.B #$10
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    STZ.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; Sprite X Speed = 0
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1540,X                    ; \ tick the between-lunges timer
    BEQ CODE_038AC1                           ; |
    DEC A                                     ; |
    BNE Return038AC6                          ; / not expired yet: stay put
    LDA.B #$C0                                ; \ launch: Y speed = -64 (upward)
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; /
    JSR SubHorzPosBnk3                        ; \ Y = which side Mario is on
    TYA                                       ; |
    STA.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; /
    LDA.W BwsrStatueSpeed,Y                   ; \ horizontal lunge speed
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
    RTS

BwsrStatueSpeed:
    db $10,$F0
```

`Y` comes from `SubHorzPosBnk3`. It returns **`Y = 0` when Mario is to the
right** of the sprite, and **`Y = 1` when he is to the left** (the
Porcu-Puffer entry above shows the code of that routine). So entry `+0`
(`$10` = +16) is the jump toward Mario when he is to the right, and `+1`
(`$F0` = -16) is the jump to the left. The code changes `+0` to `$40`
(+64). A jump to the right now goes 4 times further horizontally. Jumps to
the left stay at the normal -16.

The vertical part of the jump (`LDA.B #$C0` → `SpriteYSpeed`, which is -64,
up) is a separate immediate value. This code does **not** change it. So
the statue jumps to the same height as before, but it moves much further
horizontally in that jump. It goes past Mario and does not land on him.

**Evidence:** Patches `$038ABF`, the first byte of `BwsrStatueSpeed`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $10,$F0`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$10` at `$038ABF`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$038AB9` holds `B9 BF 8A` (`LDA.W $8ABF,Y`), which matches the source.
This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W BwsrStatueSpeed,Y` at `$038AB9` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. So the effect changes only
Bowser statues. **Read once for each jump, not on each frame.** The speed
is set when the statue jumps, and it stays the same for the whole jump. So
Mario's position at the start of the jump decides the direction, and the
statue cannot change direction in the air. **The two directions are
different on purpose.** Only the entry for the right is patched. For a long
jump in both directions, add a second code that sets `$038AC0` to `$C0`.

## Grey castle blocks drift instead of oscillating

**Code:** `FD65-6D0E`
**Raw form:** `038E71:10` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** The grey blocks that slide in castle levels use a cycle with
four phases. Two parallel tables control it: a speed for each phase, and a
wait time for each phase:

```
GreyMoveBlkSpeed:
    db $00,$F0,$00,$10

GreyMoveBlkTiming:
    db $40,$50,$40,$50

GreyCastleBlock:
    JSR CODE_038EB4
    LDA.B SpriteLock
    BNE Return038EA7
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1540,X                    ; \ when the phase timer hits 0...
    BNE +                                     ; |
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; |  ...advance to the next phase
    LDA.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; |
    AND.B #$03                                ; |
    TAY                                       ; |
    LDA.W GreyMoveBlkTiming,Y                 ; |  ...and reload its dwell time
    STA.W SpriteMisc1540,X                    ; /
  + LDA.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; \ every frame: speed for this phase
    AND.B #$03                                ; |
    TAY                                       ; |
    LDA.W GreyMoveBlkSpeed,Y                  ; |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
    JSL UpdateXPosNoGvtyW
```

From the two tables, the normal cycle is: phase 0, **stopped** for `$40`
(64) frames. Phase 1, left at -16 for `$50` (80) frames. Phase 2, stopped
for 64 frames. Phase 3, right at +16 for 80 frames. The two moving phases
have opposite speeds and the same duration. So after each cycle, the block
is back at exactly its start position, and it moves back and forth in the
same place all the time.

The code changes `GreyMoveBlkSpeed+0` from `$00` to `$10` (+16). The *first
stop* becomes a third movement to the right. The cycle is now: right for
64 frames, left for 80, stopped for 64, right for 80. The movement to the
left and to the right no longer cancel. After each full cycle, the block is
`+16 x 64` further to the right. So the blocks do not move back and forth in
place. They move steadily across the room in steps. Their position resets
only when the sprite despawns.

**Evidence:** Patches `$038E71`, the first byte of `GreyMoveBlkSpeed`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $00,$F0,$00,$10`)
and the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier
header). The ROM holds `$00 F0 00 10` at `$038E71`, and the matching
`GreyMoveBlkTiming` (`$40 50 40 50`) at `$038E75`. The reader was also
checked in the ROM: `$038E97` holds `B9 71 8E` (`LDA.W $8E71,Y`), which
matches the source. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not**
tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W GreyMoveBlkSpeed,Y` at `$038E97` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. **The timing table does not
change**, so the phase durations are normal. The drift comes only from the
speed table, whose values no longer add up to zero. The block still calls
`InvisBlkMainRt` on each frame. So it is still solid, and Mario can still
ride it while it drifts. But when a block has moved away from its planned
position, it may no longer be the platform or wall that the room needs. This
can make some castle rooms impossible to pass. Only the `+0` phase is
patched. `+1` (left), `+2` (the second stop) and `+3` (right) keep their
normal values.

## Statue fireball speed (rightward fireballs 4x faster)

**Code:** `0D63-646E`
**Raw form:** `038EEA:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `StatueFireSpeed` (`bank_03.asm`) is a table with two signed
X speeds, `db $10,$F0` (+16 / -16). It holds the speed of the fireballs that
castle statues shoot. The handler sets `SpriteXSpeed` from it on every
frame. The index is the direction that the fireball faces:

```
StatueFireSpeed:
    db $10,$F0

StatueFireball:
    JSR StatueFireballGfx
    LDA.B SpriteLock
    BNE +
    JSR SubOffscreen0Bnk3
    JSL MarioSprInteract
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X
    LDA.W StatueFireSpeed,Y
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    JSL UpdateXPosNoGvtyW
  + RTS
```

`SpriteMisc157C` is the same direction value that the graphics routine
reads (`StatueFireballGfx` loads it at the start, to select the flipped
tiles). So entry `+0` (`$10` = +16) is a fireball that moves right, and
`+1` (`$F0` = -16) is a fireball that moves left. The code changes `+0` to
`$40` (+64). Fireballs that move right now cross the screen four times
faster. Fireballs that move left do not change.

The handler does very little else. It has no gravity, no acceleration and
no state machine. It only loads a constant again on each frame. So this
byte controls all of the fireball's horizontal movement.

**Evidence:** Patches `$038EEA`, the first byte of `StatueFireSpeed`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $10,$F0`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$10` at `$038EEA`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$038EFD` holds `B9 EA 8E` (`LDA.W $8EEA,Y`), which matches the source.
This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W StatueFireSpeed,Y` at `$038EFD` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. **Faster fireballs are
harder to avoid, but they also leave the screen sooner.** The handler calls
`SubOffscreen0Bnk3` on each frame. So a fireball that crosses the screen in
a quarter of the time also despawns in a quarter of the time. This means
fewer fireballs are on screen at the same time. **The two directions are
different on purpose.** Only the entry for the right is patched. For fast
fireballs in both directions, add a second code that sets `$038EEB` to
`$C0`.

## Block snake travel speed (rightward legs 4x faster)

**Code:** `0DB1-67AA`
**Raw form:** `03926F:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `CrtEatBlkSpeedX` / `CrtEatBlkSpeedY` (`bank_03.asm`) are two
tables of signed speeds with five entries each. The game reads them
together. One direction index selects one entry from each table:

```
CrtEatBlkSpeedX:
    db $10,$F0,$00,$00,$00
CrtEatBlkSpeedY:
    db $00,$00,$10,$F0,$00
```

If you read them as X/Y pairs, the five indices are clear: `0` = right
(+16, 0), `1` = left (-16, 0), `2` = down (0, +16), `3` = up (0, -16),
`4` = **stopped** (0, 0). The block snake handler selects the index and
sets the speed on both axes on each frame:

```
    LDY.B #$04                                ; default: index 4 (stopped)
    LDA.W BlockSnakeActive
    CMP.B #$FF
    BEQ CODE_0392C0                           ; inactive: keep index 4
    ...
  + LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; active: index = stored direction
CODE_0392C0:
    LDA.B SpriteLock
    BNE Return03932B
    LDA.W CrtEatBlkSpeedX,Y
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    LDA.W CrtEatBlkSpeedY,Y
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    JSL UpdateYPosNoGvtyW
    JSL UpdateXPosNoGvtyW
```

The default `LDY.B #$04` and the `BlockSnakeActive == $FF` check make index
4 the stopped entry. When the snake does not move, both tables are read at
`+4`, and both speeds are zero. The code changes `CrtEatBlkSpeedX+0` from
`$10` to `$40` (+64). The parts of the snake's path that go right are now 4
times faster. The part to the left, both vertical parts and the stopped
entry do not change.

**Evidence:** Patches `$03926F`, the first byte of `CrtEatBlkSpeedX`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source
(`db $10,$F0,$00,$00,$00`) and the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc`
without its 512-byte copier header). The ROM holds `$10 F0 00 00 00` at
`$03926F`, and the matching `CrtEatBlkSpeedY` (`$00 00 10 F0 00`) at
`$039274`. Both readers were also checked in the ROM: `$0392C4` holds
`B9 6F 92` (`LDA.W $926F,Y`) and `$0392C9` holds `B9 74 92`
(`LDA.W $9274,Y`), which match the source. This effect comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader for each table.** `LDA.W CrtEatBlkSpeedX,Y` at
`$0392C4` is the only read of the X table. So the effect changes only the
block snake. **The `+0` entry is only the direction to the right.** So on
a path that turns, the snake moves at normal speed on the left, up and down
parts, and very fast on the right parts. The path does not change. Only the
speed on each part changes. **Do not patch the `+4` entries**
(`$039273` / `$039278`). That is the stopped state that the default
`LDY.B #$04` selects while `BlockSnakeActive` is `$FF`. A speed that is not
zero there would make the snake move when it must stay still.

## Fishin' Boo horizontal chase cap (rightward pursuit 2.5x faster)

**Code:** `9DB9-D7AA`
**Raw form:** `03905F:50` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** The Fishin' Boo follows Mario on both axes. It uses the
same "speed up to a maximum" method as the Porcu-Puffer. Each axis has its
own pair of acceleration and maximum tables:

```
FishinBooAccelX:
    db $01,$FF
FishinBooMaxSpeedX:
    db $20,$E0
FishinBooAccelY:
    db $01,$FF
FishinBooMaxSpeedY:
    db $10,$F0
```

The horizontal part runs on every frame:

```
FishinBoo:
    ...
    JSR SubHorzPosBnk3                        ; Y = 0 if Mario is to the right
    ...
  + LDA.W SpriteWillAppear                    ; \ if set, invert the direction index
    BEQ +                                     ; |
    TYA                                       ; |
    EOR.B #$01                                ; |
    TAY                                       ; /
  + LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; \ If not at max X speed, accelerate
    CMP.W FishinBooMaxSpeedX,Y                ; |
    BEQ +                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |
    ADC.W FishinBooAccelX,Y                   ; |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
```

The acceleration and the maximum use the **same** `Y` index. So index `+0`
pairs the `+1` acceleration with the `$20` (+32) maximum, and index `+1`
pairs `-1` with `$E0` (-32). Each index always moves the speed toward its
own maximum. **So entry `+0` is always the maximum speed to the right.**
The index only decides if "right" is toward Mario or away from him at that
moment. The code changes it from `$20` (+32) to `$50` (+80). This makes that
maximum two and a half times larger. The maximum to the left stays at the
normal -32.

**The `SpriteWillAppear` inversion decides if the Boo chases or runs
away.** When the flag is clear (normal play), `Y` is the result of
`SubHorzPosBnk3`: 0 when Mario is to the right. So the Boo moves toward the
`+32` maximum while it follows him to the right. When the flag is set, the
index is inverted. The Boo moves toward the same `+32` maximum while Mario
is to its *left*, so it speeds up away from him. `TurnOffGen2`
(`bank_02.asm`) does `INC` on this flag when a generator is turned off.
Other code in `bank_01.asm` uses it to clear `SpriteStatus` and despawn the
sprite. It means "these sprites are leaving". The same flag also skips the
layer 1 scroll correction later in this routine:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    PHA
    LDY.W SpriteWillAppear
    BNE +
    LDA.W Layer1DXPos                         ; \ normal play: add the camera delta
    ASL A                                     ; |  to the speed for the position update...
    ASL A                                     ; |
    ASL A                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |
    ADC.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
  + JSL UpdateXPosNoGvtyW
    PLA
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; ...then restore the un-scrolled value
```

So in normal play, this code makes the Boo chase much harder. In the
leaving state, it makes the Boo leave the screen faster.

**The value `$50` was selected so that the Boo can reach it exactly. This
is important.** The test is `CMP` + `BEQ`. It checks for an **exact
value**, and it is not a `BCS` limit. So the maximum stops the acceleration
only if the speed lands exactly on it. `FishinBooAccelX` is ±1 and the code
runs on every frame. So the speed passes every whole number, and it reaches
