`$50` exactly (about 80 frames from a stop). **Do not use this with a patch
to `FishinBooAccelX` (`$03905D`/`$03905E`) that makes the step larger than
1.** A step that goes past the maximum without being equal to it would let
`SpriteXSpeed` increase with no limit.

**Evidence:** Patches `$03905F`, the first byte of `FishinBooMaxSpeedX`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $20,$E0`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$20 E0` at `$03905F`, and the matching `FishinBooAccelX`
(`$01 FF`) at `$03905D`. The reader was also checked in the ROM: `$0390A4`
holds `D9 5F 90` (`CMP.W $905F,Y`), which matches the source. This effect
comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `CMP.W FishinBooMaxSpeedX,Y` at `$0390A4`
is the only read of this table in the disassembly. So the effect changes
only Fishin' Boos. **Horizontal only.** The vertical wave has its own
maximum table (`FishinBooMaxSpeedY`, see the next entry), and this code
does not change it. **The two directions are different on purpose.** Only
the maximum to the right is patched. For a chase that is fast in both
directions, add a second code that sets `$039060` to `$B0`.

## Fishin' Boo vertical weave (2.5x deeper dive)

**Code:** `0DB1-DDAA`
**Raw form:** `039063:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `FishinBooMaxSpeedY` (`bank_03.asm`, `db $10,$F0` = +16 /
-16) is the speed where the Fishin' Boo's up and down movement changes
direction. It uses the same ±1 method as the Blurp/Swooper wave, but with
its own tables:

```
FishinBooAccelY:
    db $01,$FF
FishinBooMaxSpeedY:
    db $10,$F0
```

```
  + LDA.B TrueFrame
    AND.B #$01                                ; every other frame
    BNE +
    LDA.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; phase index, its own slot
    AND.B #$01
    TAY
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CLC
    ADC.W FishinBooAccelY,Y
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CMP.W FishinBooMaxSpeedY,Y
    BNE +
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; reverse the weave
```

The code changes `+0` from `$10` (+16) to `$40` (+64). The downward half of
the movement can now get 4 times faster before it changes direction. So the
Boo goes down much further, and it takes longer to come back up. The upward
maximum (`+1`, `$F0` = -16) does not change, so the wave is uneven: a long,
fast dive, then the normal slow rise.

**The `SpriteWillAppear` direction inversion does *not* apply to this
code.** That inversion controls the horizontal maximum (see the previous
entry). It changes `Y`, which comes from `SubHorzPosBnk3` (the side where
Mario is). But this code sets `Y` again from `SpriteTableC2 & 1` (its own
phase counter) before it reads either table. So any change that the flag
made to `Y` is lost here. The vertical wave runs on its own. It does not
depend on where Mario is, or on whether the Boo chases or runs away.

**The value `$40` was selected so that the Boo can reach it exactly.** As
with the horizontal maximum, the test is `CMP` + `BNE`. It checks for an
**exact value** and is not a limit. `FishinBooAccelY` is ±1, so the speed
passes every whole number, and it reaches `$40` exactly. **Do not also
change `FishinBooAccelY` (`$039061`/`$039062`) to a step larger than 1.** A
step that goes past the maximum without being equal to it would make
`SpriteYSpeed` increase with no limit, and the Boo would not turn around.

**Evidence:** Patches `$039063`, the first byte of `FishinBooMaxSpeedY`
(`bank_03.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $10,$F0`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$10 F0` at `$039063`, and the matching `FishinBooAccelY`
(`$01 FF`) at `$039061`. The reader was also checked in the ROM: `$0390C2`
holds `D9 63 90` (`CMP.W $9063,Y`), which matches the source. This effect
comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `CMP.W FishinBooMaxSpeedY,Y` at `$0390C2`
is the only read of this table in the disassembly. **You can use it with
the horizontal code above with no problems.** The two axes use completely
separate acceleration and maximum pairs, and separate phase values. So with
both codes, you get a fast Boo that dives deep, and the two codes do not
affect each other. **The two directions are different on purpose.** Only
the downward maximum is patched. For a deep wave in both directions, add a
second code that sets `$039064` to `$C0`.

## Pokey shuffle speed (Pokeys move 8x faster)

**Code:** `FD81-6DAB`
**Raw form:** `02B663:10` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `PokeySpeed` (`bank_02.asm`) is a table with two signed X
speeds, `db $02,$FE` (+2 / -2). This is the slowest walk speed of all the
enemies in this list. That is why Pokeys move so slowly that you can almost
not see it. The main handler sets `SpriteXSpeed` from it on every frame:

```
PokeySpeed:
    db $02,$FE
```

```
    INC.W SpriteMisc1570,X                    ; \ every 128 frames, re-aim
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1570,X                    ; |
    AND.B #$7F                                ; |
    BNE +                                     ; |
    JSR CODE_02D4FA                           ; |
    TYA                                       ; |
    STA.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; /
  + LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; \ speed for the stored direction
    LDA.W PokeySpeed,Y                        ; |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
    JSR UpdateXPosNoGrvty
    JSR UpdateYPosNoGrvty
```

The direction value `SpriteMisc157C` is updated only once every 128 frames
(`AND.B #$7F`). So a Pokey keeps one direction for more than two seconds at
a time, and the speed table decides how far it moves in that time. Entry
`+0` (`$02` = +2) is movement to the right. The code changes it to `$10`
(+16). A Pokey that moves right now goes eight times as far between
direction changes, so its slow movement becomes a fast walk. Movement to the
left stays at the normal -2. So when a Pokey turns around, you can see it
slow down again.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02B663`, the first byte of `PokeySpeed`
(`bank_02.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $02,$FE`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$02 FE` at `$02B663`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$02B6D2` holds `B9 63 B6` (`LDA.W $B663,Y`), which matches the source.
This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W PokeySpeed,Y` at `$02B6D2` is the
only read of this table in the disassembly. **Horizontal only.** The Pokey's
vertical movement is a separate `INC SpriteYSpeed` / `CMP #$40` gravity
block later in the same routine, and this code does not change it. **The
two directions are different on purpose.** Only the entry for the right is
patched. For a Pokey that is fast in both directions, add a second code that
sets `$02B664` to `$F0`.

## Angry Wiggler charge speed (stomped Wigglers charge 4x faster)

**Code:** `0DE7-DDA6`
**Raw form:** `02F033:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `WigglerSpeed` (`bank_02.asm`) is a table with **four**
signed X speeds, `db $08,$F8,$10,$F0`. The index calculation is the
interesting part. The low bit is the direction, and the game selects the
*upper* pair only after the Wiggler was stomped and became angry.

```
WigglerSpeed:
    db $08,$F8,$10,$F0
```

```
    LDA.W SpriteMisc151C,X                    ; \ (angry flag) every 64 frames...
    BEQ +                                     ; |
    INC.W SpriteMisc1570,X                    ; |
    INC.W SpriteMisc1534,X                    ; |
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1534,X                    ; |
    AND.B #$3F                                ; |
    BNE +                                     ; |
    JSR CODE_02D4FA                           ; |  ...re-aim at Mario
    TYA                                       ; |
    STA.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; /
  + LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; \ Y = direction (0 = right)
    LDA.W SpriteMisc151C,X                    ; | if angry, add 2 to the index
    BEQ +                                     ; |
    INY                                       ; |
    INY                                       ; |
  + LDA.W WigglerSpeed,Y                      ; |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
```

So the four entries are a 2x2 table. `+0`/`+1` are the slow walk of a
**calm** Wiggler, right and left (±8). `+2`/`+3` are the fast run of an
**angry** Wiggler, right and left (±16). The game gets to them with
`INY INY` when `SpriteMisc151C` is set. The same flag also controls the
direction update above. So only an angry Wiggler turns to follow Mario. A
calm Wiggler keeps the direction that it had.

The code changes `+2` from `$10` (+16) to `$40` (+64). This makes an angry
Wiggler run to the right four times faster. The calm walk and the angry run
to the left do not change. Only the angry state updates its direction, so
the result is an enemy that really hunts Mario: it turns toward him every 64
frames, and it now gets closer four times faster when it moves right.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02F033`, the **third** byte of `WigglerSpeed`
(`bank_02.asm`, offset `+2`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db
$08,$F8,$10,$F0`) and the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its
512-byte copier header). The ROM holds `$08 F8 10 F0` at `$02F031`. The
reader was also checked in the ROM: `$02F090` holds `B9 31 F0`
(`LDA.W $F031,Y`), which matches the source. This effect comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W WigglerSpeed,Y` at `$02F090` is the
only read of this table in the disassembly. **Angry state only.** A Wiggler
that was not stomped never uses index `+2`. So this code does nothing until
you make one angry. **The two directions are different on purpose.** Only
the angry entry for the right is patched. For a fast run in both directions,
add a code that sets `$02F034` to `$C0`. The calm entries at
`$02F031`/`$02F032` do not change.

## Torpedo Ted acceleration cap (rightward torpedoes 2.5x faster)

**Code:** `9D88-D4DC`
**Raw form:** `02B8B8:50` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** The Torpedo Ted does not move at a fixed speed. It speeds up
until it reaches a maximum for its direction. It uses the pair of
acceleration and maximum tables:

```
TorpedoMaxSpeed:
    db $20,$F0

TorpedoAccel:
    db $01,$FF
```

```
  + LDA.B TrueFrame                           ; \ Only increase X speed every 4 frames
    AND.B #$03                                ; |
    BNE +                                     ; /
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; \ If not at maximum, increase X speed
    LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; |
    CMP.W TorpedoMaxSpeed,Y                   ; |
    BEQ +                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |
    ADC.W TorpedoAccel,Y                      ; |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
```

The comments in the reader code give both jobs. The acceleration and the
maximum use the same index `Y`. So `+0` pairs the `+1` acceleration with the
`$20` (+32) maximum, and `+1` pairs `-1` with `$F0` (-16). Note that the
normal table is **already different for each direction**. A torpedo that
moves right gets to +32, but a torpedo that moves left gets only to -16. So
this code does not patch one half of a matching pair.

The code changes `+0` from `$20` to `$50` (+80). This makes the maximum to
the right two and a half times larger. The acceleration happens only every
fourth frame, so the torpedo also needs more time to get to the new top
speed: about 320 frames from a stop, not 128. So what you see is a torpedo
that keeps getting faster long after the point where it used to stop
speeding up.

**The value `$50` was selected so that the torpedo can reach it exactly.**
The test is `CMP` + `BEQ`. It checks for an **exact value**, and it is not a
`BCS` limit. So the maximum stops the acceleration only if the speed lands
exactly on it. `TorpedoAccel` is ±1, so the speed passes every whole number,
and it reaches `$50` exactly. **Do not use this with a patch to
`TorpedoAccel` (`$02B8BA`/`$02B8BB`) that makes the step larger than 1.** A
step that goes past the maximum without being equal to it would let
`SpriteXSpeed` increase with no limit.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02B8B8`, the first byte of `TorpedoMaxSpeed`
(`bank_02.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $20,$F0`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$20 F0` at `$02B8B8`, and the matching `TorpedoAccel`
(`$01 FF`) at `$02B8BA`. The reader was also checked in the ROM: `$02B8C7`
holds `D9 B8 B8` (`CMP.W $B8B8,Y`), which matches the source. This effect
comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `CMP.W TorpedoMaxSpeed,Y` at `$02B8C7` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. **Horizontal only.** The
torpedo's vertical movement is a separate `DEC SpriteYSpeed` block that runs
every other frame, and this code does not change it. **The two directions
are different on purpose, and the normal values were already different.**
Only the maximum to the right is patched. The maximum to the left stays at
its normal -16.

## Baseball throw speed (rightward baseballs 3x faster)

**Code:** `9DA1-DFDB`
**Raw form:** `02C464:50` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `BaseballSpeed` (`bank_02.asm`) is a table with two signed X
speeds, `db $18,$E8` (+24 / -24). The game uses it one time for each
baseball, when the pitching Chuck creates the ball as an extended sprite:

```
BaseballSpeed:
    db $18,$E8
```

```
CODE_02C479:
    LDA.B #$0D                                ; \ Extended sprite = Baseball
    STA.W ExtSpriteNumber,Y                   ; /
    ...
    PHX
    LDA.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; X = the Chuck's facing
    TAX
    LDA.B _0
    CLC
    ADC.W BaseballTileDispX,X                 ; spawn offset, by facing
    STA.W ExtSpriteXPosLow,Y
    LDA.B _1
    ADC.W DATA_02C462,X
    STA.W ExtSpriteXPosHigh,Y
    LDA.W BaseballSpeed,X                     ; \ launch speed, by facing
    STA.W ExtSpriteXSpeed,Y                   ; /
    PLX
    RTS
```

Note that this table uses the index **`X`, not `Y`**. The routine keeps the
free extended sprite slot in `Y`. Between `PHX` and `PLX`, it loads the
Chuck's direction (`SpriteMisc157C`) into `X`. So the same index also
selects the start offset from `BaseballTileDispX`. Entry `+0` (`$18` = +24)
is a baseball thrown to the right. The code changes it to `$50` (+80). Those
throws now move about three times faster. Throws to the left stay at the
normal -24.

The speed is written **only one time, when the ball is created**, into
`ExtSpriteXSpeed`. The extended sprite keeps that speed until it is gone. So
this code changes the throw. It does not add acceleration while the ball
flies.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02C464`, the first byte of `BaseballSpeed`
(`bank_02.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $18,$E8`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$18 E8` at `$02C464`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$02C4AD` holds `BD 64 C4`. This is `LDA.W $C464,X`, the opcode with the
`,X` index (`$BD`), not the `,Y` form (`$B9`) that most other tables in this
list use. It matches the source's `LDA.W BaseballSpeed,X` exactly. This
effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W BaseballSpeed,X` at `$02C4AD` is the
only read of this table in the disassembly. **Only when the ball is
created.** The value is stored in the extended sprite's speed when the ball
appears. So balls that are already in the air when you turn on the code keep
their old speed. **The limit of two balls does not change.** The slot search
above (`LDY.B #$07` down through `BPL`) still limits how many extended
sprites can exist, and this code does not change how often the Chuck
throws. **The two directions are different on purpose.** Only the entry for
the right is patched. For fast throws in both directions, add a code that
sets `$02C465` to `$B0`.

## Fireball-killed Chuck knockback (4x further death launch)

**Code:** `ADC9-0D06`
**Raw form:** `02A151:C0` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `FireKillSpeedX` (`bank_02.asm`) is a table with two signed X
speeds, `db $F0,$10` (-16 / +16). The game uses it for a sprite that dies
from many fireball hits. The fireball collision routine counts the hits. On
the fifth hit, it changes the sprite into a dead body and throws it:

```
    INC.W SpriteMisc1528,X                    ; Increase times Chuck hit by fireball
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1528,X                    ; \ If fire count >= 5, kill Chuck:
    CMP.B #$05                                ; |
    BCC FireRtNextSprite                      ; |
    LDA.B #!SFX_SPLAT                         ; | Play sound effect
    STA.W SPCIO0                              ; |
    LDA.B #$02                                ; | Sprite status = Killed
    STA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; |
    LDA.B #$D0                                ; | Set death Y speed
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; |
    JSR SubHorzPosBnk2
    LDA.W FireKillSpeedX,Y                    ; | Set death X speed
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; |
    LDA.B #$04                                ; | Increase points
    JSL GivePoints                            ; |
    BRA FireRtNextSprite                      ; /

FireKillSpeedX:
    db $F0,$10
```

`Y` comes from `SubHorzPosBnk2`. It is the same as the `SubHorzPosBnk3` in
the Porcu-Puffer entry: `Y = 0` when Mario is to the **right** of the
sprite. Note that the signs here are the **opposite** of the chase tables in
other entries of this list. Entry `+0` is `$F0` (-16, to the left) when
Mario is on the right, because a dying sprite is thrown *away* from the
player, not toward the player.

The code changes `+0` from `$F0` (-16) to `$C0` (-64). This makes the throw
four times stronger. So when you kill a Chuck with fireballs while you stand
to its right, it flies four times further off the screen. The death Y speed
(`LDA.B #$D0` = -48, up, two instructions above) is a separate immediate
value, and this code does **not** change it. So the body goes up to the same
height, but it moves much further to the side.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02A151`, the first byte of `FireKillSpeedX`
(`bank_02.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $F0,$10`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$F0 10` at `$02A151`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$02A117` holds `B9 51 A1` (`LDA.W $A151,Y`), which matches the source.
This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W FireKillSpeedX,Y` at `$02A117` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. But that reader is in the
shared **fireball collision** routine. So it applies to all sprites that die
on this path (the comments in the disassembly name Chuck, which is the case
with five hits). It does not apply to stomps, shell hits or star kills,
because they use different death paths. **Visual only.** The sprite already
has `SpriteStatus = 2` (killed) and already gave its points before the game
reads this byte. So the kill itself does not change. **The two directions
are different on purpose.** Only the "Mario on the right" entry is patched.
For the same throw in both directions, add a code that sets `$02A152` to
`$40`.

## One Wave Eerie in five dives faster

**Code:** `0DCB-AD08`
**Raw form:** `02AF91:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `Load5Eeries` (`bank_02.asm`) creates Wave Eeries in groups
of five. It counts from 4 down to 0 and reads **five parallel tables, with
one row for each member**. Each row is one eerie in the group:

```
EerieGroupDispXLo:
    db $E0,$F0,$00,$10,$20
EerieGroupDispXHi:
    db $FF,$FF,$00,$00,$00
EerieGroupSpeedY:
    db $17,$E9,$17,$E9,$17
EerieGroupState:
    db $00,$01,$00,$01,$00
EerieGroupSpeedX:
    db $10,$F0
```

```
CODE_02AFAF:
    JSL FindFreeSprSlot                       ; \ Return if no free slots
    BMI Return02AFFD                          ; /
    TYX
    LDA.B #$08                                ; \ Sprite status = Normal
    STA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; /
    LDA.B #$39                                ; \ Sprite = Wave Eerie
    STA.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; /
    JSL InitSpriteTables
    LDY.B _4                                  ; Y = member index, 4 down to 0
    LDA.B _0
    CLC
    ADC.W EerieGroupDispXLo,Y                 ; \ spread the five out horizontally
    STA.B SpriteXPosLow,X                     ; /
    ...
    LDA.W EerieGroupSpeedY,Y                  ; \ per-member vertical speed
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; /
    LDA.W EerieGroupState,Y                   ; \ per-member wave phase
    STA.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; /
    ...
    DEC.B _4
    BPL CODE_02AFAF
```

If you read the columns, the five rows describe the group. The members are
placed at `-$20, -$10, 0, +$10, +$20` horizontally. Their vertical speeds
change between `+$17 / -$E9 / +$17 / -$E9 / +$17` (+23 / -23), with
matching `EerieGroupState` phases that also change between two values. This
is why the group flies as a mixed wave and not as one solid block.

The code changes `EerieGroupSpeedY+0` from `$17` (+23) to `$40` (+64). This
changes the start speed of **one member of each group**. That is index 0:
the last one that the countdown creates, and the one furthest right of the
five (`EerieGroupDispXLo+0` = `$20`, because `_4` counts down). So each
wave now has one eerie that dives much faster than the other four and leaves
the group. The table has one entry for each member. That is why this
changes one eerie of five, and not the speed of the whole group.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02AF91`, the first byte of `EerieGroupSpeedY`
(`bank_02.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source
(`db $17,$E9,$17,$E9,$17`) and the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc`
without its 512-byte copier header). The ROM holds `$17 E9 17 E9 17` at
`$02AF91`, and the matching `EerieGroupState` (`$00 01 00 01 00`) at
`$02AF96`. The reader was also checked in the ROM: `$02AFDE` holds
`B9 91 AF` (`LDA.W $AF91,Y`), which matches the source. This effect comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W EerieGroupSpeedY,Y` at `$02AFDE` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. **Only when the eerie is
created.** The value is written into `SpriteYSpeed` one time, when the eerie
appears. So it sets the first dive. It does not change what the eerie's own
main handler does to its speed after that. **The wave phase is not
patched.** `EerieGroupState+0` still gives this member the same
`SpriteTableC2` phase as before. So the faster dive is added on top of the
normal wave pattern. It does not replace the pattern. `EerieGroupSpeedX`
(`$02AF9B`, `db $10,$F0`) is a separate table with two entries, and its
index comes from `SubHorzPosBnk2`. It is horizontal, it applies to the whole
group, and this code does not change it.

## Wave Eerie group horizontal speed (whole group flies right 4x faster)

**Code:** `0DCB-A4A8`
**Raw form:** `02AF9B:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** `EerieGroupSpeedX` (`bank_02.asm`) is a table with two signed
X speeds, `db $10,$F0` (+16 / -16). `Load5Eeries` uses it for each member of
a Wave Eerie group when it creates that member. It goes with
`EerieGroupSpeedY` (see the "One Wave Eerie in five dives faster" entry
above). But that table has **one entry for each member** (five rows, one for
each eerie). This table has **one pair for the whole group**: a single
direction pair that the same creation loop reads once for each of the five:

```
EerieGroupSpeedY:
    db $17,$E9,$17,$E9,$17                    ; five rows: one per member
EerieGroupState:
    db $00,$01,$00,$01,$00                    ; five rows: one per member
EerieGroupSpeedX:
    db $10,$F0                                ; two rows: direction pair
```

```
    LDA.W EerieGroupSpeedY,Y                  ; Y = member index (4 down to 0)
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    LDA.W EerieGroupState,Y
    STA.B SpriteTableC2,X
    CPY.B #$04
    BNE +
    LDA.B _2
    STA.W SpriteLoadIndex,X
  + JSR SubHorzPosBnk2                        ; <- Y is REPLACED here
    LDA.W EerieGroupSpeedX,Y
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    DEC.B _4
    BPL CODE_02AFAF
```

The `JSR SubHorzPosBnk2` is the important point. Before it, `Y` held the
member index 4..0. The call replaces it with the side where Mario is
(`Y = 0` when Mario is to the **right**). So the same `Y` register is the
index into a table with five entries before the call, and into a table with
two entries after it. `EerieGroupSpeedX+0` is the speed to the right that
*every* member of the group gets.

The code changes `+0` from `$10` (+16) to `$40` (+64). When a group of five
eeries appears with Mario on their right, the whole group now flies right
four times faster. The `EerieGroupSpeedY` code changes one member. This code
changes the whole group at the same time.

**Evidence:** Patches `$02AF9B`, the first byte of `EerieGroupSpeedX`
(`bank_02.asm`). Checked against the disassembly source (`db $10,$F0`) and
the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header).
The ROM holds `$10 F0` at `$02AF9B`. The reader was also checked in the ROM:
`$02AFF4` holds `B9 9B AF` (`LDA.W $AF9B,Y`), which matches the source.
This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** `LDA.W EerieGroupSpeedX,Y` at `$02AFF4` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. **Only when the eerie is
created.** It is written into `SpriteXSpeed` one time for each eerie when it
appears. So it sets the start speed, and it does not change what the
eerie's own handler does after that. **The direction is decided for each
group when it appears**, from where Mario was at that moment. A group that
appears with Mario to its left uses the `+1` entry, which does not change.
**You can use it with the code for one member.** Also patch `$02AF91` (see
the previous Wave Eerie entry) to get a fast group with one eerie that is
even faster.

## Iggy's ball rolls 4x faster

**Code:** `0DE9-6F61`
**Raw form:** `01FA56:40` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08

**Mechanism:** Sprite `$A7` is the rolling ball in the Iggy/Larry boss room.
The sprite main handler dispatch table (`bank_01.asm:1065`) names it
`; A7 - Iggy's ball`. Its handler sets `SpriteXSpeed` on every frame from a
table with two signed entries. The index is the ball's stored direction:

```
    db $10,$F0                                ; (the table, at $01FA56)

IggysBall:
    ...
    LDA.B SpriteLock                          ; \ Branch if sprites locked
    BNE Return01FAB3                          ; /
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X
    LDA.W DATA_01FA56,Y
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    JSR SubSprXPosNoGrvty
    JSR SubSprYPosNoGrvty
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; \ gravity: accumulate +4 per frame
    CMP.B #$40                                ; |  up to a terminal +$40
    BPL +                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |
    ADC.B #$04                                ; |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; /
  + JSR CODE_01FF98                           ; \ on a floor hit, bounce:
    BCC +                                     ; |
    LDA.B #$F0                                ; |  Y speed = -16
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; /
```

Entry `+0` (`$10` = +16) is the roll to the right, and `+1` (`$F0` = -16) is
the roll to the left. The code changes `+0` to `$40` (+64). The ball now
crosses the room to the right four times faster. Rolls to the left stay at
the normal -16.

The vertical part of the ball's movement is completely separate, and this
code does not change it. It adds `+4` gravity on each frame, up to a limit
of `+$40`. (Note that this is a real `CMP`/`BPL` **limit**, not the exact
value test that several other tables in this list use.) There is also a
fixed `-16` bounce each time `CODE_01FF98` reports that the ball hit the
floor. So the ball bounces at its normal rate, but it moves much further
between bounces.

**Evidence:** Patches `$01FA56`, the first byte of the speed table with two
entries at that address (`bank_01.asm`). Checked against the disassembly
source (`db
$10,$F0`) and the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header). The ROM holds `$10 F0` at `$01FA56`. The reader was also
checked in the ROM: `$01FA84` holds `B9 56 FA` (`LDA.W $FA56,Y`), which
matches the source. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not**
tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Only one reader.** The `LDA.W DATA_01FA56,Y` at `$01FA84` is
the only read of this table in the disassembly. **The table has no name in
the disassembly** (automatic label `DATA_01FA56`, no comment). So, not like
most codes in this list, its job comes from the *reader* and not from the
table's own name. The routine around it is named `IggysBall`, its dispatch
entry names the sprite, and the read of three instructions stores the value
directly into `SpriteXSpeed`, with the direction value as the index. This is
clear, but the table still needs a name in the disassembly. **The two
directions are different on purpose.** Only the entry for the right is
patched. For a ball that is fast in both directions, add a code that sets
`$01FA57` to `$C0`.

## Star power lasts about 16 times longer

**Code:** `7E32-670D`
**Raw form:** `00E2DD:3F:03` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; the SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 22:14:41

**Mechanism:** When Mario gets a star, the game sets `InvinsibilityTimer` to
`$FF` (`LDA.B #$FF ; \ Set star timer` / `STA.W InvinsibilityTimer`, called
from the named `GiveMarioStar` handler). Only one place in the whole game
decreases that counter. It is inside `DrawMarioAndYoshi`, on the branch that
runs while the star is active. The code is `LDA.B EffFrame` / `AND.B #$03` /
`BNE` / `DEC.W InvinsibilityTimer`, and the last line has the comment
`; Decrease star timer`. The `AND` mask divides the frame rate. The `BNE`
skips the decrease unless the low bits of the frame counter are zero. With
`#$03`, the timer goes down once every 4 frames, so the star lasts
255 × 4 ≈ 1020 frames. When the mask is `$3F`, the timer goes down once
every 64 frames. So the same 255 steps now take 255 × 64 ≈ 16320 frames,
about sixteen times as long. The mask must stay one less than a power of
two, so that the `BNE` runs the decrease on one frame in *n*.

**Evidence:** The byte is the operand of the `AND.B #$03` at `$00E2DD`,
inside `DrawMarioAndYoshi` (`bank_00.asm`, symbol `$0000E2BD` in
`SMW_U.sym`). The address came from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (its fingerprint
was checked, and it is current for this source tree). In the reference ROM
(`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header), `$00E2DA` holds
`A5 14 29 03 D0 03 CE 90 14`. This decodes exactly as the source listing
says: `LDA $14` (`EffFrame`), **`AND #$03` with the operand at `$00E2DD`**,
`BNE +$03`, `DEC $1490` (`InvinsibilityTimer`). The code was encoded and
then decoded again, and it gives `$00E2DD <- $3F`. This effect comes from
the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **The music and the flashing use the timer. They do not have a separate
  clock.** The same block controls the star palette colours. A few lines
  below it, the `CPY.B #con($1E,$1E,$1E,$18,$18)` limit is what restores
  `MusicBackup` when the star is almost over. Both become longer by the same
  amount. So the rainbow flashing and the star music continue for the full
  longer time.
- **`con(...)` on that nearby line means that it is different in each
  version.** The patched `AND` operand is not. But do not think that the
  nearby addresses are the same in the J/E releases.
- **This does not change how Mario *gets* a star.** `$01C581` (the `$FF`
  operand of the star timer store) does not change. `$FF` is already the
  largest byte value, so that byte could only make the star shorter.
- **It uses no bytes that other codes here use**, so you can use it with any
  of them.

## Every powerup you already have gives you a star instead

**Code:** `B4A9-0F69`
**Raw form:** `01C556:92:6F` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 22:14:41

**Mechanism:** All powerup pickups go through `TouchedPowerUp`. It makes one
index from the item and Mario's current state. The source shows this:
`SEC` / `SBC.B #$74` / `ASL A` / `ASL A` / `ORA.B Powerup` / `TAY`, with the
comments `; \ Index created from...` / `; | ... powerup touched (upper 2
bits)` / `; | ... Mario's status (lower 3 bits)`. That `Y` selects a
handler number from `GivePowerPtrIndex` (`; \ Call routine to change Mario's
status`). `ExecutePtr` then jumps through a `dw` table with six entries, and
the source names each row: `0 - Big`, `1 - No change`, `2 - Star`,
`3 - Cape`, `4 - Fire`, `5 - 1Up`. This code changes entry **1**, the
handler that does nothing, to point at `GiveMarioStar`. Five index rows use
entry 1: a mushroom taken as Big, Caped or Fire Mario, a fire flower taken
as Fire Mario, and a feather taken as Caped Mario. These are exactly the
cases where the game now only plays the sound and gives points. All five now
give a star.

**Evidence:** Patches the low byte of the second `dw` in the dispatch table
at `$01C554` (`bank_01.asm`, directly below `TouchedPowerUp`, symbol
`$0001C538`). The reference ROM holds `61 C5 6F C5 92 C5 98 C5 EC C5 FE C5`
at `$01C554`. This matches the six source labels exactly:
`GiveMarioMushroom` = `$01C561`, `CODE_01C56F` = `$01C56F`,
`GiveMarioStar` = `$01C592`, `GiveMarioCape` = `$01C598`,
`GiveMarioFire` = `$01C5EC`, `GiveMario1Up` = `$01C5FE`. All six were
checked against `SMW_U.sym`. **All six have the same high byte `$C5`**. So
you can point any entry at any other one by changing one byte, and there is
no page condition. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$01C556 <- $92`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- **The new handler does exactly what the caller expects.**
  `GiveMarioStar` is only `JSL CODE_01C580` / `BRA CODE_01C56F`. It sets the
  star timer and music, and then goes into the same handler that it
  replaces. So it only *adds* to entry 1, and it does nothing different from
  it: the points and the mushroom sound effect still happen. `ExecutePtr`
  jumps with `JML [_0]` while `X` still holds the sprite slot, and both
  handlers return with `RTS`. So the return path does not change.
- **The reserve item box does not change.** `TouchedPowerUp` reads
  `ItemBoxSprite` earlier, and that is not patched. So the box fills exactly
  as before.
- **A star taken while you have a star is not one of the five rows.** The
  star group in `GivePowerPtrIndex` is all `$02` (`GiveMarioStar`) already.
- It changes nothing for *small* Mario, because all of those rows point at
  real handlers.

## A mushroom turns small Mario straight into Fire Mario

**Code:** `D0A4-0FD9`
**Raw form:** `01C524:04:00` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 22:14:41

**Mechanism:** This is the same path as the code above, one step earlier.
`Y = (sprite − $74) × 4 + Powerup` selects a row of `GivePowerPtrIndex`.
Its 20 bytes are five groups of four: one group for each powerup sprite, and
one entry for each value of `Powerup` (0 small, 1 big, 2 cape, 3 fire). The
dispatch comments in `CallSpriteMain` name the sprite numbers
(`; 74 - Mushroom`, `; 75 - Flower`, `; 76 - Star`, `; 77 - Feather`,
`; 78 - 1-Up`), so the groups are certain. So offset `+0` is "mushroom,
taken by small Mario". Its normal value `$00` selects `GiveMarioMushroom`
(`; 0 - Big`). The code changes it to `$04`, which selects `GiveMarioFire`
(`; 4 - Fire`). So the weakest pickup in the game skips Big completely and
gives you the fire flower's powerup.

**Evidence:** Patches `GivePowerPtrIndex+0` at `$01C524` (`bank_01.asm`,
symbol `$0001C524`). The reference ROM holds
`00 01 01 01 04 04 04 01 02 02 02 02 03 03 01 03 05 05 05 05` there, which
is the same as the source listing byte for byte. The reader's operand at
`$01C54D` is `B9 24 C5` (`LDA $C524,Y`), so the instruction itself confirms
the table address. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$01C524 <- $04`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- **The reserve box still acts as if you took a mushroom.**
  The game reads `ItemBoxSprite+0` first, and it is not patched (its value
  there is `$00`, which means "do not change the box"). So when small Mario
  takes a mushroom, the box still gets nothing.
- **`GiveMarioFire` does not run the grow animation.** It sets
  `CyclePaletteTimer`, `SpriteLock`, `PlayerAnimation = $04` and
  `Powerup = $03` directly. So small Mario becomes Fire Mario with the fire
  flower palette animation, not with the mushroom's grow animation.
- **Only the small Mario row changes.** A mushroom taken as Big, Caped or
  Fire Mario still goes to the "no change" handler at rows `+1`/`+2`/`+3`.
  So this code and the star code above change different rows, and you can
  use them together.
- The same table has two other one-byte options if you want to change this:
  `$01C530` (feather as small Mario, `$03`) and `$01C534` (1-Up as small
  Mario, `$05`).

## The reserve item box can hold a star

**Code:** `D7AF-04D9`
**Raw form:** `01C518:03:00` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 22:14:41

**Mechanism:** Before it calls the powerup handler, `TouchedPowerUp` reads
the parallel table `ItemBoxSprite` with the same index. If the result is not
zero, it stores it in `PlayerItembox`: `LDA.W ItemBoxSprite,Y ; \ Put
appropriate item in item box` / `BEQ +` / `STA.W PlayerItembox`, and then
it plays the item-reserved sound effect. `$00` means "do not change the
box". All of the star group in the table (offsets `+8`..`+$0B`) is `$00`.
That is why the normal game never puts a star in the reserve box. This code
sets offset `+8` (star, taken by small Mario) to `$03`. The item numbers
come from a separate place: `DrawReserveItem` in `bank_00.asm`. It uses
`ItemBoxOBJNos-1` and `ItemBoxOBJProps-1` (`; item box item OBJ numbers`,
`; item box item palettes`), and it has a special case `CPY.B #3` that uses
`ItemBoxStarProps` (`; star item box palettes`) to animate the item. So item
3 is the star, and its own palette animation branch confirms this.

**Evidence:** Patches `ItemBoxSprite+8` at `$01C518` (`bank_01.asm`, symbol
`$0001C510`). The reference ROM holds
`00 01 01 01 00 01 04 02 00 00 00 00 00 01 04 02 00 00 00 00` at `$01C510`,
which matches the source. The reader's operand at `$01C540` is `B9 10 C5`
(`LDA $C510,Y`), so the instruction confirms the table address. The index
calculation (`SBC #$74` / `ASL` / `ASL` / `ORA Powerup`) was checked in the
ROM at `$01C538` as `38 E9 74 0A 0A 05 19 A8`. The code was encoded and then
decoded again, and it gives `$01C518 <- $03`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **Only the small Mario row.** When Mario takes a star as Big, Caped or
  Fire Mario, the box still gets nothing. Offsets `+9`/`+$0A`/`+$0B` do not
  change.
- **The evidence does not show what the box *drops*.** The reserve drop
  routine (`CODE_028008` in `bank_02.asm`) has an automatic label, and its
  `ADC.B #$73` conversion has no comment. So this entry does not say which
  sprite number appears when you press Select. What is certain: the box is
  filled from this table, item 3 is the star for the HUD, and the item is
  drawn with the flashing star palette. That routine still needs a name in
  the disassembly.
- **The item-reserved sound effect plays**, because the `BEQ` that skipped
  the store is no longer taken.

## Any Yoshi gets wings and the ground pound from any shell

**Code:** `D7E7-0FA0`
**Raw form:** `01F137:03:00` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 22:14:41

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** When Yoshi swallows a shell, the game finds his new ability in
`YoshiShellAbility`. The index is made from *both* palettes. The block has
the comment `; \ Set yoshi stomp/wing ability, based on palette of sprite
and Yoshi`. It sends `SpriteOBJAttribute` for Yoshi and for the shell through
`YoshiAbilityIndex` (`LSR A` / `AND.B #$07` / `TAY` / `LDA
YoshiAbilityIndex,Y`). It shifts the first result left two times and ORs in
the second. The two lines that use the result decide its meaning:
`PHA` / `AND.B #$02` / `STA.W YoshiHasWingsEvt` (`; \ Set yoshi wing ability
($141E = #$02)`) and `PLA` / `AND.B #$01` / `STA.W YoshiCanStomp` (`; | If
Yoshi gets stomp ability, $18E7 = #$01`). So **bit 0 is the ground pound,
bit 1 is the wings**, and `$03` is both. Entry `+0` is the combination that
now gives neither. It becomes `$03`, so that combination gives a Yoshi that
flies and stomps.

**Evidence:** Patches `YoshiShellAbility+0` at `$01F137` (`bank_01.asm`,
symbol `$0001F137`). The reference ROM holds `00 00 01 02 00 00 01 02 01 01
01 03 02 02` there, which matches the fourteen bytes of the source listing
exactly. The reader's operand at `$01F192` is `B9 37 F1` (`LDA $F137,Y`), so
the instruction itself confirms the table address. The code that uses the
value, at `$01F195`, reads `48 29 02 8D 1E 14 68 29 01 8D E7 18`: `PHA` /
`AND #$02` / `STA $141E` / `PLA` / `AND #$01` / `STA $18E7`. This proves the
bit meanings. They are not a guess. The code was encoded and then decoded
again, and it gives `$01F137 <- $03`. This comes from the disassembly. It
was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **The game calculates the abilities again for each swallow. It does not
  keep them.** `Yoshi` clears `YoshiHasWingsEvt` and `YoshiCanStomp` at the
  start of every frame (`; Clear real winged Yoshi flag` /
  `; Clear stomp Yoshi flag`), and the ability block runs again on each
  swallow. So when Yoshi eats a different shell, the ability still changes
  normally.
- **Only one combination.** The index is
  `(Yoshi's colour class × 4) | shell's colour class`, so `+0` is one pair,
  not all shells. This entry does
  not say which *visible* colours that pair is, on purpose.
  `YoshiAbilityIndex` has no header comment, and the disassembly does not
  document which palette is which colour. That still needs to be found.
- **Not the fire ability.** The disassembly clearly marks the
  `YoshiHasWingsGfx == $01` case as `; This never happens (fireball on Yoshi
  ability)`. This table cannot get to it, and no value here gives fire
  breath.
- **`YoshiHeavenFlag` overrides it separately.** A different path a few
  lines above sets `YoshiHasWingsEvt = $02` when that flag is set, whatever
  the table holds.

## The overworld runs the in-level main loop

**Code:** `2CB0-AF0D`
**Raw form:** `009345:DA:BE` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 22:14:41

**Mechanism:** `RunGameMode` controls the whole game: `LDA.W GameMode
; Load game mode` / `JSL ExecutePtr`, with a `dw` table of 41 entries. Each
row has a comment with its mode number and name (`dw GM0EOverworld
; 0E - overworld`, `dw GM14Level ; 14 - level`, and so on). Mode `$0E` is
the handler that runs the overworld on each frame. Its table entry is at
`$009345` and holds `$A1BE`. `GM14Level`, the level handler, is at `$A1DA`.
The two have the same high byte `$A1`. So if you replace one low byte, the
overworld mode runs the level main loop: while the overworld map is on the
screen, the game runs level physics, level sprites and level collision.

**Evidence:** Patches the low byte of dispatch entry `$0E` at `$009345`
(`bank_00.asm`, `RunGameMode` = symbol `$00009322`). The reference ROM holds
`AD 00 01 22 DF 86 00` at `$009322`: `LDA $0100` (`GameMode`) then
`JSL ExecutePtr`. The table starts at `$009329`. `BE A1` is at `$009345` and
`DA A1` is at `$009351`. These match `SMW_U.sym`'s `0000A1BE
GM0EOverworld` and `0000A1DA GM14Level`. The code was encoded and then
decoded again, and it gives `$009345 <- $DA`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **This code will probably be unstable, and that is the result.** The
  register requirements are easy to meet. `ExecutePtr` is documented as
  `; Basically JSR (addr,a)`, it jumps with `JML [_0]`, and neither handler
  reads anything from the caller. But the *state* requirements are not met:
  `GM14Level` reads level RAM that the overworld mode never set up. Broken
  graphics, a Mario that is frozen or jumps to other places, and hangs are
  all possible. None of them was seen, because nothing in this process plays
  the game.
- **It starts when you enter the overworld.** The game enters mode `$0E`
  after the fade-in (`$0D`). So this code has its effect as soon as the map
  appears, also the first time, directly after file select.
- **The code path to leave a level still works**, because only entry `$0E`
  is patched. No other mode changes, including `$0F`–`$14` (fade out, load,
  prepare, fade in, level).
- **The same table has gentler one-byte swaps**, if this code breaks too
  much. `$009337` `$64` → `$D1` makes the title screen run file select
  (`GM07TitleScreen`/`GM08FileSelect` both use `$9C`). The eleven
  `GMTransitionFade` entries (`$9F6F`) and the four `GMTransitionMosaic`
  entries (`$9F37`) all have the high byte `$9F`, so you can change any fade
  into any other.


## Ordinary levels draw sprites (and Mario) behind the scenery

**Code:** `DD68-DF29`
**Raw form:** `0584B7:00:20` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 23:50:27

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** `LevXYPPCCCTtbl` is the default OBJ priority table. It has
one entry for each level mode. The header decode routine `CODE_0584E3` reads
it one time for each level: `LDA.L LevXYPPCCCTtbl,X` (X = level mode) /
`STA.B SpriteProperties`. After that, `SpriteProperties` (`$64`) is ORed
into the OAM attribute byte of every sprite, at 71 `ORA $64` places in banks
01/02/03. It is also ORed into Mario's own attribute byte in `CODE_00E33E`.
So this one table entry sets the OBJ priority bits for the whole level, for
sprites and for Mario. The normal table has only two values: `$20`
(`!OBJ_Priority2`) for modes `$00`, `$01`, `$02`, `$0E`, `$0F`, and `$30`
(`!OBJ_Priority3`) for all other modes. Levels run in Mode 1 with the BG3
priority bit set (`RegularLevelNMI` writes `!HW_BG_BG3Pri|!HW_BG_Mode1`).
This gives the draw order from front to back:
`BG3hi, OBJ3, BG1hi, BG2hi, OBJ2, BG1lo, BG2lo, OBJ1, OBJ0, BG3lo`. So
priority 3 draws sprites in front of all Layer 1/2 tiles. Priority 2 puts
them only behind the high priority tiles (tiles with the Map16 priority
bit). Priority 0 (the new value from this code) puts them behind everything,
also behind normal low priority tiles. This code patches entry `$00` of the
table from `$20` to `$00` (`!OBJ_Priority0`). That is level mode `$00`, the
normal mode with a Layer 2 background, which most levels of the game use.

**Evidence:** Patches `LevXYPPCCCTtbl+0` at `$0584B7` (`bank_05.asm`, `ORG
$058000`). The reference ROM at file offset `0x284B7` holds `20 20 20 30 30 30
30 30 30 30 30 30 30 30 20 20`, then sixteen `$30` bytes. This matches the
source's four `db` rows exactly. The reader's instruction at `$0584FF` (ROM
`0x284FF`) reads `BF B7 84 05`, which is `LDA.L $0584B7,X`. So the opcode
bytes confirm the table address. The next instruction is `STA.B
SpriteProperties`. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$0584B7 <- $00`. It was also checked separately with romdev's
`cheats({op:'make', platform:'snes',
device:'game-genie'})` for this address and value, which made the same code
`DD68-DF29`. (That tool says that it encoded it for the SNES **Game Genie**
device: an address+value patch with no compare byte, which matches the
encoder in this process.) This comes from the disassembly. It was **not**
tested in play.

*Addressing note:* `bank_05.asm` has `ORG` `$058000`. That is the low bank
range (`$00`-`$7D`), where the CPU really runs this code, and where the
`LDA.L` operand points. `$85xxxx` is a LoROM mirror of the same physical ROM
bank with the same content. Nothing in this routine uses it. So there is no
separate mirror address that this code must also patch.

**Caveats:**
- **It applies to the whole level.** The byte also moves Mario and Yoshi,
  not only enemies. It is the default for the whole level, not a setting for
  one sprite.
- **Drawing only.** Collision does not change. A sprite that is hidden
  behind scenery can still hurt you, and a platform that Mario can no longer
  see still holds him up.
- **Temporary overrides ignore it.** `ClassicPiranhas` and `CODE_019546`
  push `SpriteProperties`, set it to `!OBJ_Priority1` for one sprite, and
  then restore it. Those sprites draw at their own priority, whatever this
  code does.
- **The Bowser fight replaces it completely.** `CODE_03A279` and
  `CODE_03A5D8` write `$64` directly during that fight. So Bowser's sprites
  ignore this code, whatever the table holds.
- **The status bar (BG3) does not change.** It is a separate layer, and this
  table does not apply to it.
- **Only level mode `$00` is patched.** The entries of all other modes
  (indices `$01`-`$1F`) do not change.
- **Same as backlog item F4.** F4 was the same finding. It was filed then
  under an old "sprite palette XOR" idea, before `LevXYPPCCCTtbl` had the
  correct annotation. This entry closes both W1 and F4.

## Level mode $00 draws sprites over everything

**Code:** `7D68-DF29`
**Raw form:** `0584B7:30:20` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 23:50:27

**Mechanism:** This uses the same table and reader as the code above:
`LevXYPPCCCTtbl+0`, read by `CODE_0584E3`'s
`LDA.L LevXYPPCCCTtbl,X / STA.B SpriteProperties`. But this time entry `$00`
(level mode `$00`) is set to `$30` (`!OBJ_Priority3`), not `$00`. So the
most common level mode of the game gets the same OBJ priority as the boss
modes and vertical modes. The level draw order is
`BG3hi, OBJ3, BG1hi, BG2hi, OBJ2, BG1lo, BG2lo, OBJ1, OBJ0, BG3lo`
(Mode 1 + BG3 priority, from `RegularLevelNMI`). Priority 3 is in front of
*every* Layer 1/2 tile. This includes the high priority tiles (tiles with
the Map16 priority bit), which sprites and Mario could go behind with the
normal priority 2 value. Result: in mode `$00` levels, bushes, pipe tops,
cave entrance tiles and other scenery marked as foreground, which Mario or a
sprite could walk behind, are now drawn under him.

**Evidence:** Same read address and table as above. The reference ROM
confirms `LevXYPPCCCTtbl+0` = `$20` at `$0584B7` (ROM `0x284B7`), and the
reader is confirmed at `$0584FF` (`BF B7 84 05`). The code was encoded and
then decoded again, and it gives `$0584B7 <- $30`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play. (It was not checked separately
with `cheats({op:'make'})`. See the code above for that check. The encode
and decode check is done for every code in all cases.)

**Caveats:**
- **You cannot use it with the code above.** Both patch `$0584B7`, so only
  one value can be active in one game session.
- **It applies to the whole level**, also to Mario and Yoshi, the same as W1.
- **Drawing only.** Collision does not change.
- **The `ClassicPiranhas`/`CODE_019546` temporary overrides** and the
  **Bowser fight writes** (`CODE_03A279`, `CODE_03A5D8`) still have priority
  over this table, exactly as above.
- **Only level mode `$00` is patched.** All other `$30` mode entries already
  have this value and do not change. So this code only changes behavior in
  the five modes that had `$20` (`$00`,`$01`,`$02`,`$0E`,`$0F`), and in
  practice it changes only the mode `$00` entry.

## A priority-3 level mode draws behind both background layers

**Code:** `FD6A-DD99`
**Raw form:** `0584C1:10:30` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 23:50:27

**Mechanism:** This uses the same `LevXYPPCCCTtbl` / `CODE_0584E3` mechanism
as the two codes above. This time it patches entry `$0A` (level mode `$0A`)
at `$0584C1` from `$30` (`!OBJ_Priority3`) to `$10` (`!OBJ_Priority1`). The
level draw order is
`BG3hi, OBJ3, BG1hi, BG2hi, OBJ2, BG1lo, BG2lo, OBJ1, OBJ0, BG3lo`. Priority
1 is completely behind BG1 and BG2 (it is only above `OBJ0`/`BG3lo`). So
levels in mode `$0A` draw sprites and Mario behind the whole background. The
other `$30` mode levels draw them on top of the high priority tiles. Mode
`$0A` was selected, and not one of the other 26 `$30` entries, because it is
confirmed to have one layer, and it is not one of the three modes that
`SpecialLevTable` marks as a boss fight. `LoadAgain` (`bank_05.asm`) compares
`LevelModeSetting` with `$0A` in its "is this a Layer 2 level?" test chain.
The branch has the comment `; If the current level isn't a Layer 2 level,
branch to LoadLevelDone`. This confirms that mode `$0A` has no Layer 2 for
the sprites to be drawn against. So the demo is simpler, because it does not
involve the modes with an interactive Layer 2 that use priority 2.

**Evidence:** In the reference ROM, `LevXYPPCCCTtbl+$0A` (`$0584C1`, ROM
`0x284C1`) is `$30`, which matches the source's "Modes `$08`-`$0F`" `db`
row. The same `CODE_0584E3` reader that was confirmed above is used for all
indices in this table, with X = `LevelModeSetting`. `SpecialLevTable`
(`$058497`) was read directly from the ROM during this check. It holds `$00`
at index `$0A`, which makes it different from the boss modes in the same
table: `$C0` at `$09` (Morton/Ludwig/Roy), `$80` at `$0B` (Iggy/Larry) and
`$C1` at `$10` (Bowser). So mode `$0A` has none of the boss data that would
make it harder to see this code's effect on the screen. The code was encoded
and then decoded again, and it gives `$0584C1 <- $10`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **It applies to the whole level**, it changes only drawing, and the same
  `ClassicPiranhas`/`CODE_019546` temporary overrides and Bowser fight
  writes apply as for the two codes above. (Mode `$0A` is not the Bowser
  mode, so those writes do not apply to it. But the general caveat is here
  because the mechanism is the same.)
- **Only the mode `$0A` entry is patched.** The other 26 `$30` mode entries
  (including the real boss modes) do not change.
- **All levels that use mode `$0A`** change in the same way. It is not
  limited to one stage.

## Repoint the sprite-priority read at the boss/special-level flags

**Code:** `B56D-0DF9`
**Raw form:** `058500:97:B7` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 23:50:27

**Mechanism:** `CODE_0584E3`'s `LDA.L LevXYPPCCCTtbl,X` at `$0584FF`
assembles to `BF B7 84 05`: opcode `BF` (`LDA.L abs,X`), then the 24-bit
little-endian operand `B7 84 05` = `$0584B7`. This code patches only the
low byte of the operand, at `$058500`, from `$B7` to `$97`. The instruction
now reads `$058497` = `SpecialLevTable`, the special level flag table for
each level mode (header comment: `00: Normal level`, `80: Iggy/Larry level`,
`C0: Morton/Ludwig/Roy level`, `C1: Bowser level`). Both tables are 32 bytes
(one entry for each level mode `$00`-`$1F`) and are on the same page. So the
index range of `LevelModeSetting` is safe with either table, and no read goes
outside it. After the patch, `SpriteProperties` (`$64`) is loaded from
`SpecialLevTable` and not from the priority table. It is still ORed into the
OAM attribute byte of every sprite and of Mario, in the same way as for the
three codes above. `SpecialLevTable` is `$00` at all indices except `$09`,
`$0B` and `$10`. So every normal level now gets `$00` ORed in. This is the
same as `!OBJ_Priority0`, with the same visual effect as the first code
above, but for *all* level modes at once and not only mode `$00`. The three
boss mode entries give `SpriteProperties` OAM **flip** bits, not priority
bits: `$C0` = `!OBJ_XFlip|!OBJ_YFlip` (mode `$09`, mirrored and upside
down), `$80` = `!OBJ_YFlip` (mode `$0B`, only upside down), and `$C1` (mode
`$10`, Bowser) adds bit 0 to the Y flip. Bit 0 is the 9th tile number bit.
It also changes which graphics page the game uses for a sprite's tile
number. So in Bowser mode, sprites are also drawn from the wrong graphics
page.

**Evidence:** Before patching, the low byte of the operand at `$058500` (ROM
`0x28500`) was checked as `B7`, and the full instruction at `$0584FF` (ROM
`0x284FF`) as `BF B7 84 05`, both in the reference ROM. All 32 bytes of
`SpecialLevTable` at `$058497` (ROM `0x28497`) were also checked against the
source's `db` rows: `00` ×8, then `00 C0 00 80 00 00 00 00`, then `C1 00 00
00 00 00 00 00`, then `00` ×8. They match exactly. So the `$00`/`$C0`/
`$80`/`$C1` values above are facts, not guesses. The code was encoded and
then decoded again, and it gives `$058500 <- $97`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **It changes a pointer, not data.** The content of neither table changes.
  This code only changes which table `CODE_0584E3` reads when it loads the
  priority bits.
- **It applies to all level modes at the same time.** The first code above
  changes only mode `$00`. This code changes all 32 entries with one patch,
  because it changes the read itself and not one table byte.
- **The Bowser fight still writes `$64` directly later**
  (`CODE_03A279`, `CODE_03A5D8`). So the value that `SpecialLevTable[$10]`
  gives the sprites when the level loads is replaced during the real fight.
  But the OAM flip effect from the level load is still real on the decor in
  Bowser's own room, and on any sprites that are active before the fight's
  own override runs.
- **The `ClassicPiranhas`/`CODE_019546` temporary overrides** still apply on
  top of the value that this code sets, the same as for the other three codes
  in this section.
- **Drawing only.** The OAM flip and page change bits only change how a
  sprite is drawn (mirrored, upside down, wrong tile page). They never change
  its collision box or position.
- **Other tables you can reach**, if you want a different redirect later:
  the same page also holds `LevMainScrnTbl` (`$37`), `LevSubScrnTbl` (`$57`)
  and `LevCGADSUBtable` (`$77`). You can reach any of them by changing only
  this same low byte.

## Carried items float 64 pixels ahead of Mario

**Code:** `0DB9-A4A5`
**Raw form:** `019F5B:40:0B` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 23:58:12

**Mechanism:** `CarrySprXDispLo` / `CarrySprXDispHi` are parallel tables of
low and high bytes. Together they hold the signed 16-bit X offset for a
sprite that Mario carries, so that the sprite is drawn in his hands and not
at his own X. `CODE_01A0B1` reads them. It runs on every frame while a
carried sprite is active (the `; B - Carried` entry of the
`HandleSprCarried` dispatch). It makes an index from 0 to 5 from
`PlayerDirection`, `FaceScreenTimer`, and the cases for turning, climbing
and entering a pipe. Index 0 is the normal "facing right" case, `$000B` =
**+11 pixels**. When the low byte is `$40`, the pair is `$0040` = **+64
pixels**. So anything that Mario picks up while he faces right (shells,
Yoshi eggs, springboards, P-switches, the blue POW) stays 64 pixels in front
of him, and it follows his movement on every frame like a tractor beam. The
high byte does not change and stays `$00`. So the offset stays positive and
small: the sign does not change, and the item does not despawn off the
screen. Index 1 (facing left) is a separate byte and does not change. So
when Mario turns around, the item goes back into his hands at once.

**Evidence:** `CarrySprXDispLo` at `$019F5B` (ROM `0x9F5B`) was read from
the reference ROM as `0B F5 04 FC 04 00`. This matches the source's
`db $0B,$F5,$04,$FC,$04,$00` exactly. `CarrySprXDispHi` at `$019F61` was
read as `00 FF 00 FF 00 00`. The address was also confirmed separately with
the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv`. The encoding was checked with romdev's
`cheats({op:'make'})`, which returned the same code and reported it as
`game-genie`, `verified`. This effect comes from the disassembly. It was
**not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- It changes only the *drawing and placement* position of the held sprite.
  The sprite's own collision box moves with it. So a carried shell now hurts
  enemies 64 pixels in front of Mario. Mario's own hitbox does not change.
- The item is placed relative to Mario on every frame, so it goes through
  walls and ceilings. If you carry something toward a wall, it goes into the
  tilemap, and there is no collision check.
- Only index 0 is patched. The swing toward the camera (indices 2–4) and the
  centred cases (index 5: turning, climbing, riding Yoshi into a pipe) still
  use their normal values. So you can see the item jump between +64 and its
  normal offsets when Mario changes pose.
- `CarrySprXDispLo[0]` `$0B` → `$00` is a smaller change (the item stays at
  Mario's centre). Do not use both, because they patch the same byte.
- Bank `$01` has a mirror at `$81`. This code matches `$019F5B`, the address
  that the CPU really reads. It would not patch a read that goes through the
  mirror.

## Facing left flings the carried item across the screen

**Code:** `DDB1-AD65`
**Raw form:** `019F62:00:FF` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 23:58:12

**Mechanism:** This uses the same two tables and the same reader
`CODE_01A0B1`, which runs on each frame, as the code above. But this code
patches the **high** byte of index 1, the normal "facing left" carry offset.
`CarrySprXDispHi[1]` = `$FF` with `CarrySprXDispLo[1]` = `$F5` gives
`$FFF5` = **−11 pixels**, the normal hold position when Mario faces left.
When the high byte is `$00`, the pair is `$00F5` = **+245**. A small
negative offset becomes a large positive one. When Mario faces left while
he carries something, the item goes 245 pixels to Mario's *right*, almost
the width of the screen. It goes back to his hands as soon as he faces right
again. `CarrySprXDispLo` and `CarrySprXDispHi` are separate byte arrays, not
mixed 16-bit words. So this is a simple change of the high byte only, with
no page alignment condition.

**Evidence:** `CarrySprXDispHi` at `$019F61` (ROM `0x9F61`) was read from
the reference ROM as `00 FF 00 FF 00 00`, which matches the source's
`db $00,$FF,$00,$FF,$00,$00`. The patched byte is index 1 at `$019F62`, read
as `FF`. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$019F62 <- $00`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- At +245 pixels, the sprite is at or past the right edge of the screen when
  the camera does not move. So it can be off the camera, and SMW's normal
  off-screen sprite handling applies (this includes despawn for sprite types
  that do not stay when they leave the screen). You may not always see it.
- Only the resting index for facing left is patched. Indices 2–4 (the swing
  toward the camera) and 5 (turning/climbing/pipe) do not change. So the
  item jumps back and forth when Mario's pose changes.
- The same drawing and collision note as above applies: the sprite's hitbox
  moves with it.

## Setting an item down places it 112 pixels away

**Code:** `5DB1-A4D5`
**Raw form:** `019F68:70:0D` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 23:58:12

**Mechanism:** `DropSprXDispLo` / `DropSprXDispHi` are a second pair of
separate low and high byte tables, with two entries each. They hold the
signed 16-bit X offset that the game adds **one time** when Mario lets go of
a carried sprite *gently*: when Down is held, or when no direction is held
for sprite numbers `>= $15`. The reader is `CODE_01A047`. Its index is
`PlayerDirection` (`0` = left, `$F3`/`$FF` = −13; `1` = right, `$0D`/`$00`
= +13), so the sprite is put down just in front of Mario. The code changes
the low byte of index 1 from `$0D` to `$70`, so the pair is `$0070` =
**+112 pixels**. When Mario gently puts down a sprite while he faces right,
the sprite moves almost a screen ahead with no warning. It does not go to
Mario's feet. The entry for facing left is a different byte and does not
change, so the effect is in one direction only. The kick path
(`CODE_01A079`, which uses `ShellSpeedX`) and the upward throw path
(`CODE_01A068`) do not read these tables and do not change.

**Evidence:** `DropSprXDispLo`/`DropSprXDispHi` at `$019F67` (ROM `0x9F67`)
were read from the reference ROM as `F3 0D FF 00`. This matches the source's
`db $F3,$0D` / `db $FF,$00` exactly. The patched byte is
`DropSprXDispLo[1]` at `$019F68`, read as `0D`. The address was confirmed
with the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_01.asm` `DropSprXDispLo` row →
`$019F67`). This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- The item is placed one time. It does not follow Mario on each frame. The
  sprite moves one time when Mario lets go, and then it acts normally.
- The game does not check collision at the new position. So an item that is
  put down next to a wall can go inside solid tiles. What happens next
  depends on the sprite's own interaction code.
- 112 pixels is far enough that the new position may be off the visible
  screen when Mario is near the right edge of the camera.
- It changes only the gentle put-down. Kicking (run button) and throwing up
  still use their own routines and speeds.

## Setting an item down throws it harder than kicking

**Code:** `0DBB-A465`
**Raw form:** `019F9A:40:04` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-08 23:58:12

**Mechanism:** `DropSprXSpeed` (`db $FC,$04` at `$019F99`) is the small X
*speed* (not an offset) that `CODE_01A047` gives to a sprite that Mario puts
down gently. It is added to Mario's own X speed. Its index is `SubHorizPos`'s
`Y`, so the push always points away from Mario: index 0 = `$FC` (−4, Mario
is to its right), index 1 = `$04` (+4, Mario is to its left). The code
changes index 1 to `$40`, so the +4 push becomes **+64**. A sprite that is
put down while Mario is to its left flies away to the right faster than a
kicked shell. The NTSC `ShellSpeedX` table is `db $D2,$2E,$CC,$34`, and its
largest value is `$34` (+52). So the gentle put-down input, which should put
the item down carefully, becomes a stronger ranged attack than the kick
button. A put-down to the left still moves at −4.

**Evidence:** `DropSprXSpeed` at `$019F99` (ROM `0x9F99`) was read from the
reference ROM as `FC 04`, which matches the source's `db $FC,$04`. The
patched byte is index 1 at `$019F9A`, read as `04`. The NTSC values of
`ShellSpeedX` were read from the `if ver_is_ntsc(!_VER)` branch that the U
build uses. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$019F9A <- $40`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- This is a speed, not a position. It is a different setting from the +112
  put-down offset code above. The two are separate and you can use them
  together, but you should understand each one alone.
- Mario's own X speed is still added. So if Mario lets go while he runs
  right, the sprite is even faster.
- `$40` is a signed byte in the upper part of the positive range. It stays
  positive, so the direction does not change.
- Only the "Mario is to the left" index is patched. A put-down on the other
  side still gives the normal −4 push.
- It applies only to the gentle put-down path, not to kicks or upward throws.

## Two point values at once render each other's digits

**Code:** `20CC-0DA8`
**Raw form:** `02ADA3:D4:D8` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:02:07

**Mechanism:** `ScoreSprOAMIndex` (`db $B0,$B8,$C0,$C8,$D0,$D8`) gives each
of the six score sprite slots (the floating point values and the 1-UP/item
text) the OAM byte offset that it draws into. It has only one reader, at
`$02AE9B`, in the draw code for each slot in `ScoreSprGfx`. That code loads
the byte into `Y`. Then it writes `OAMTileYPos,Y` / `OAMTileXPos,Y` /
`OAMTileNo,Y` / `OAMTileAttr,Y` for the first 8x8 tile, and the `,Y+4` forms
for the second. So each slot has 8 bytes = two OAM objects (`$B0` = object
44 through `$D8` = object 54, with no gaps). The code changes the entry of
slot 5 from `$D8` to `$D4`. This moves it by one object and not by a full
slot. So the *first* tile of slot 5 now goes on object 53, which is the
*second* tile of slot 4. When two point values are on the screen at the same
time, each one shows half of the other's digits, so the two-digit numbers
look broken. Slot 5 is the best byte to patch, because `CODE_02AD34` selects
slots: it checks `ScoreSpriteNumber` from 5 down to 0 and takes the first
empty one. So a single point value almost always uses slot 5.

**Evidence:** `ScoreSprOAMIndex` at `$02AD9E` (ROM `0x12D9E`) was read from
the reference ROM as `B0 B8 C0 C8 D0 D8`. This matches the source's
`db $B0,$B8,$C0,$C8,$D0,$D8` exactly. The patched byte is index 5 at
`$02ADA3`, read as `D8`. The reader's address was confirmed with the
regenerated `linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_02.asm` `LDY.W ScoreSprOAMIndex,X` →
`$02AE9B`). The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$02ADA3 <- $D4`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- **This is a display code, not a score code.** The same routine still adds
  the points to `PlayerScore`, wherever the sprite is drawn.
- With only one point value on the screen, nothing looks wrong. You need two
  score sprites at the same time (a shell that clears a row, a chain of
  stomps) to see the effect.
- **It does nothing in the Bowser fight**, and **the Reznor/Morton/Roy fights
  override it**. `ScoreSprGfx` returns without drawing anything under
  `!IRQNMI_Bowser` (`$C1`). Under `!IRQNMI_ReznorMortonRoy` (`$C0`), it sets
  `Y = $04` for every slot and does not use this table at all.
- The half-overlap variant `$D8` → `$D0` (a full slot collision, where you can
  see only one number at a time) patches the same byte. Use one or the other.

## Point values are drawn at the front of OAM

**Code:** `D0CC-0DA8`
**Raw form:** `02ADA3:04:D8` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:02:07

**Mechanism:** This uses the same table and the same single reader as the
code above. The OAM offset of slot 5 changes from `$D8` (objects 54/55, at
the end of the score sprites' range 44–55) to `$04` (objects 1 and 2, at the
start of OAM). So the score sprite slot that the game uses most writes its
two tiles on top of anything else that is drawn there on that frame. `$04`
was not selected at random. It is exactly the value that `ScoreSprGfx` itself
sets for every slot under the `!IRQNMI_ReznorMortonRoy` layout. Also, the
start of the same routine moves `OAMTileYPos+4` / `+8` (the same object pair)
off the screen to `$F0`. So the ROM already uses objects 1–2 as the backup
place for the score sprites when the boss IRQ layouts use the rest of OAM.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read as above: `ScoreSprOAMIndex` at
`$02AD9E` (ROM `0x12D9E`) reads `B0 B8 C0 C8 D0 D8`, with `D8` at the patched
index 5 byte `$02ADA3`. The `$04` value and the `$F0` move were read from
the boss IRQ branch of `ScoreSprGfx` in the annotated source. The code was
encoded and then decoded again, and it gives `$02ADA3 <- $04`. This comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **Display only.** Points are still added normally.
- In normal levels, what exactly overlaps depends on which sprite uses OAM
  objects 1–2 on a given frame. This was **not** found. The mechanism is that
  the slot moves to the start of OAM. The overlap that results depends on
  the game state, and this entry does not name a specific sprite.
- The same boss fight exceptions as above apply: it does nothing under
  `!IRQNMI_Bowser`, and `!IRQNMI_ReznorMortonRoy` overrides it (that layout
  sets this same value anyway).
- It patches the same byte as the mixed digits code above. Use only one at a
  time.

## Let go of the run button and the cape climbs instead of landing

**Code:** `DF22-A4DF`
**Raw form:** `00D7D8:01:00` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:06:33

**Mechanism:** `FlightPhase` is the angle of the cape during flight. It
selects the gravity for that frame through `PlayerGravity[FlightPhase+3]`.
Phase 1 gets `PlayerGravity` index 4, `$F4`, which is *upward*
acceleration. Phase 4 gets index 7, `$04`, the dive. On each frame, the
flight code selects a mode index `X`, and it moves `FlightPhase` by
`CapeSpeed[X]` toward `FlightPhaseLimit[X]`. Mode 4 is the "Y released"
case. When bit 6 of `byetudlrHold` is clear at `CODE_00D85B`, mode 4
replaces the mode that the direction logic selected. Its limit of `$00` is
what brings the flight back down to phase 0 and ends it. The code changes
`FlightPhaseLimit[4]` from `$00` to `$01`. So when you release Y, the phase
stops at 1, the lift phase. If you let go of the run button during flight,
Mario speeds up *upward* on every frame and does not come down. With one
byte, this reverses the input that cape flight uses most.

**Evidence:** `FlightPhaseLimit` at `$00D7D4` (ROM `0x57D4`) was read from
the reference ROM as `01 06 03 01 00`. This matches the source's
`db $01,$06,$03,$01,$00` exactly. The patched byte is index 4 at `$00D7D8`,
read as `00`. `PlayerGravity` was read as `06 03 04 10 F4 01 03 04`
(+ `05 06`), which confirms index 4 = `$F4`. The address was confirmed with
the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_00.asm` `FlightPhaseLimit` row →
`$00D7D4`). The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$00D7D8 <- $01`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- **The flight is not really permanent.** `FlightPhase` is set to zero when
  Mario lands (`CODE_00EF99`), when he takes damage, and by `CODE_00D988`.
  So the climb ends as soon as one of those happens.
- **The address is for U only, even more than usual.** These tables come
  directly after a large `if ver_is_ntsc` block, and its two branches have
  different lengths (the PAL `PlayerGravity` has 16-bit `dw` rows, and NTSC
  has `db`). So the labels are almost certainly at other addresses in the
  E0/E1 ROMs. Do not expect this code to work there.
- Only the Y-released mode changes. The direction modes (0–3) still work
  normally, so normal left/right pumping does not change.

## Hands-off cape flight gains altitude

**Code:** `DF22-AF6F`
**Raw form:** `00D7D6:01:03` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:06:33

**Mechanism:** This uses the same table and the same step logic as the code
above, but for mode 2: takeoff, or in the air with no direction held and a
phase below 4. Its limit of `$03` is what makes a cape with no input go down
slowly. The code changes `FlightPhaseLimit[2]` to `$01`. So the same
hands-off state stops at phase 1, the lift phase (`PlayerGravity` index 4 =
`$F4`, upward acceleration). If you hold Y and press no direction, Mario
climbs and does not drift down. This is the gentler and more playable
version of the Y-released code above. Releasing Y is mode 4, and it does not
change, so the cape still lands normally.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read: `FlightPhaseLimit` at `$00D7D4`
(ROM `0x57D4`) reads `01 06 03 01 00`, with `03` at the patched index 2 byte
`$00D7D6`. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$00D7D6 <- $01`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- The same U-only address warning as above: because of the `if ver_is_ntsc`
  block before it, the E0/E1 labels are at other addresses.
- Mode 2 is also the **takeoff** mode. So the change applies from the start
  of the flight, not only while Mario glides.
- `FlightPhase` is still set to zero when Mario lands, when he takes damage,
  and by `CODE_00D988`.

## Any dive banks the maximum cape swoop

**Code:** `A622-A7DF`
**Raw form:** `00D7DC:C8:F8` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:06:33

**Mechanism:** `CapeDiveLift` is the upward speed that the cape saves from a
dive. At `CODE_00D94F`, its index is the fall speed `>> 3`. The entries are
signed lift values: `$F8` = −8, `$F4` = −12, `$F0` = −16, `$C8` = −56.
`CODE_00D94F` keeps the more negative value. So `MaxStageOfFlight` holds the
strongest lift from the dive, and `CODE_00D8AF` uses it on `PlayerYSpeed`
when the player pulls up at phase 1. Index 3 is for fall speeds
`$18`–`$1F`, the slowest dive that saves any lift. The code changes it from
`$F8` (−8) to `$C8` (−56). So the smallest downward movement saves the same
lift as a full speed dive, and any dive gives the largest pull-up swoop. The
same byte has a second effect, which is documented: `CODE_00D874` compares
`MaxStageOfFlight` with `#$C8`, and when they are equal, it sets
`CapePumpTimer` to 2 and not 8. So after a gentle dive, the flight phase
can also change four times as fast on the way out.

**Evidence:** `CapeDiveLift` at `$00D7D9` (ROM `0x57D9`) was read from the
reference ROM as `00 00 00 F8 F8 F8 F4 F0 C8 02 01`. This matches the
source's two `db` rows exactly. The patched byte is index 3 at `$00D7DC`,
read as `F8`. The `CapePumpTimer` behaviour was read directly from the
`LDA #$08 / LDY MaxStageOfFlight / CPY #$C8 / BNE + / LDA #$02` code in
`CODE_00D874`. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$00D7DC <- $C8`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- The same U-only address warning as the two codes above.
- Indices 4 and 5 (fall speeds `$20`–`$2F`) are still `$F8`. So this does not
  change all dive speeds. Only the `$18`–`$1F` range now gives the maximum.
- `CapeDiveLift` entries 9 and 10 (`$02,$01`) need a fall speed of `$48` or
  more. That is above the `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` limit of `$40`, and the source
  marks them as unverified because the game cannot reach them. This code
  does not change them.
