## The full-speed cape dive stops paying off

**Code:** `DD23-AD0F`
**Raw form:** `00D7E1:00:C8` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:06:33

**Mechanism:** This uses the same table and the same reader as the code
above, but index 8. That is the entry for fall speed `$40`, which is
`PlayerMaxFallSpeed`: a dive at full speed. Its value `$C8` (−56) is the
largest lift in the table, and it is the purpose of the mechanic: dive
fast, then pull up into a big swoop. Setting it to zero reverses this. A
full speed dive now saves **no** lift. A medium dive (indices 3–7, still
`$F8`/`$F4`/`$F0`) saves a lot. So to get a swoop, you must now dive
*slowly*, and the game's famous power dive gives nothing. `CODE_00D874` uses
`MaxStageOfFlight == $C8` for its fast pump shortcut. So a full speed dive
also no longer starts the 2-frame `CapePumpTimer`.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read: `CapeDiveLift` at `$00D7D9` (ROM
`0x57D9`) reads `00 00 00 F8 F8 F8 F4 F0 C8 02 01`, with `C8` at the patched
index 8 byte `$00D7E1`. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it
gives `$00D7E1 <- $00`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not**
tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- The same U-only address warning as the rest of section T.
- Indices 0–2 are already `$00` (fall speeds below `$18` save nothing). So
  after this patch, both ends of the speed range save nothing, and only the
  middle range gives lift. That reversal is the effect. It is not a bug in
  the code.
- It patches a different byte from the "any dive banks the maximum" code
  above, so you can use the two together. Together, gentle dives give the
  maximum and fast dives give nothing. This is the most complete form of the
  reversal.

## Come out of a horizontal pipe or door invisible

**Code:** `5E2B-0F6D`
**Raw form:** `00D196:7F:00` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:09:30

**Mechanism:** `DoorPipeHideTiles` (`db $00,$63,$1C,$00`) gives the
`PlayerHiddenTiles` masks for the horizontal pipe / door transition
(`DoorPipeAni`, `PlayerAnimation` = 5). The routine calculates
`Y = (PlayerPipeAction >> 1) + 1` and reads the table two times. It uses
entry `Y-1` as the mask for the first half while `PipeTimer >= $1D`, and
entry `Y` as the mask for the second half after the timer goes below that.
Only `PlayerPipeAction` 0/1 (entering) and 4/5 (exiting) get to this
routine. So the pairs that the game really uses are `(0,1)` for entering and
`(2,3)` for exiting. Entry 3, the second half mask for exiting, is normally
`$00`, which means nothing is hidden. This code sets it to `$7F`
(`!PlayerHide_All`: both body halves, the extra tiles, the cape tile and the
other cape tiles). This hides every tile that Mario is drawn with. When
Mario exits on foot, `PipeTimer` starts at `$1C`, which is already below the
`$1D` limit. So this one entry covers the *whole* exit animation. Mario
walks out of the pipe or door completely invisible, and he appears only
when the animation ends and the player has control again.

**Evidence:** `DoorPipeHideTiles` at `$00D193` (ROM `0x5193`) was read from
the reference ROM as `00 63 1C 00`. This matches the source's
`db $00,$63,$1C,$00` exactly. The patched byte is entry 3 at `$00D196`, read
as `00`. The address was confirmed with the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv`.
`rammap.asm` documents what each bit of `PlayerHiddenTiles` means
(`sabcxylu`: `$03` body, `$0C` extra tiles, `$10` cape, `$60` other cape
tiles, bit 7 = do not decrease the star timer). The code was encoded and
then decoded again, and it gives `$00D196 <- $7F`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **It ends by itself, by design.** `CODE_00C47E` sets `PlayerHiddenTiles`
  to zero at the start of every level frame. So the effect lasts only as
  long as the pipe/door animation. The player cannot stay invisible.
- **`$7F`, not `$FF`, on purpose.** `DrawMarioAndYoshi` has a special case
  for `PlayerHiddenTiles == $FF`: it skips both `CODE_01EA70` and the star
  timer decrease. So `$FF` would be a different (and less clean) change.
  `$7F` keeps bit 7 clear, so the star timing does not change.
- It applies only to horizontal pipes and doors. Vertical pipes select
  `PlayerAnimation` = 6 (`VertPipeAni`) and never use this table.
- When Mario rides Yoshi, `PipeTimer` starts at `$36`. So entry 2 covers the
  first 26 frames, and this code's entry is used only after that.

## Walk into the pipe fully drawn

**Code:** `DD2B-0FDD`
**Raw form:** `00D194:00:63` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:09:30

**Mechanism:** This uses the same table and the same reader, but entry 1:
the second half mask for **entering** a horizontal pipe or door. When Mario
enters, `PipeTimer` starts at `$20` (`$30` when he rides Yoshi). So entry 0
(`$00`, nothing hidden) covers the first four frames, and entry 1 covers
the other ~28. Its normal value `$63` hides both body halves (`$03`) and the
outer cape tiles (`$60`). That is what makes Mario disappear into the pipe
opening. When it is zero, Mario is fully drawn for the whole transition. So
you can see him walk *across* the pipe opening (through the tiles, not into
them) until the sublevel has loaded. This is the exact opposite of the
invisible exit code above.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read: `DoorPipeHideTiles` at `$00D193`
(ROM `0x5193`) reads `00 63 1C 00`, with `63` at the patched entry 1 byte
`$00D194`. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$00D194 <- $00`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- It also ends by itself: `CODE_00C47E` clears `PlayerHiddenTiles` on every
  level frame, so nothing continues after the animation.
- `IsCarryingItem` applies an `EOR #$1C` only to the *first* half mask. So
  carrying an item does not affect this byte.
- Only horizontal pipes and doors. Vertical pipes use `VertPipeAni`.

## Vanish while riding Yoshi out of a pipe

**Code:** `5E2B-0F0D`
**Raw form:** `00D195:7F:1C` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:09:30

**Mechanism:** The same table again, entry 2: the *first* half mask for
exiting. This is the only entry in the table that is used only when Mario
rides Yoshi. When Mario exits on foot, `PipeTimer` starts at `$1C`, which is
already below the `$1D` limit. So the game never reads the first half mask,
and entry 2 is never used. When Mario rides Yoshi, `DATA_00A61D[4/5] = $1A`
is added, so the timer starts at `$36`. Then entry 2 gives the mask for the
first 26 frames. Its normal value `$1C` hides the extra tiles and the cape
tile (`!PlayerHide_Extra | !PlayerHide_Cape`). The code changes it to `$7F`
(`!PlayerHide_All`). This hides Mario and Yoshi completely for those 26
frames. After that, entry 3's `$00` shows them again, and the two suddenly
appear while they walk.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read: `DoorPipeHideTiles` at `$00D193`
reads `00 63 1C 00`, with `1C` at the patched entry 2 byte `$00D195`. The
table's header comment in the source says as fact that only the Yoshi case
reaches entry 2, and that the start value is `$36`. The code was encoded and
then decoded again, and it gives `$00D195 <- $7F`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **You need Yoshi.** On foot, the game never reads this byte, so the code
  seems to do nothing. You must test it while you ride Yoshi.
- `IsCarryingItem` changes the first half mask with `EOR #$1C`. So if Mario
  carries an item while he rides Yoshi, the patched `$7F` becomes `$63`: a
  partial hide and not a full one.
- The same `$7F`-not-`$FF` reason, and the same clear on each frame, as for
  the codes above.

## Hidden the instant you touch the pipe

**Code:** `EE22-076D`
**Raw form:** `00D1DE:FF:1D` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:09:30

**Mechanism:** This is not a table byte. It is the immediate limit value that
decides *which* of the two `DoorPipeHideTiles` entries the game reads.
`DoorPipeAni` does `LDX PipeTimer / CPX #$1D / BCS CODE_00D1F0`. It uses the
first half mask while the timer is at or above `$1D`, and otherwise it
continues to the second half mask. When Mario enters, `PipeTimer` counts
down from `$20` (`$30` on Yoshi). So the limit is what gives Mario his four
visible steps into the pipe before he is hidden. The code changes the
immediate value to `$FF`. The compare can then never pass, because
`PipeTimer` never gets to that value. So the game uses the second half mask
from the first frame. When Mario enters, that is entry 1's `$63`: Mario's
body and outer cape tiles are hidden as soon as he touches the pipe, and you
do not see him walk in at all.

**Evidence:** Before encoding, the instruction at `$00D1DD` (ROM `0x51DD`)
was checked as `E0 1D` (`CPX #$1D`), followed by `B0` (`BCS`). So the
patched byte at `$00D1DE` is clearly the immediate operand and not an
opcode. The reference ROM had `e0 1d b0` at that offset, and the address was
confirmed with the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_00.asm` `CPX.B #$1D`
line → `$00D1DD`). The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$00D1DE <- $FF`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- **It changes both entering and exiting**, because the same compare
  controls both pairs. On foot, the exit already starts below the limit, so
  that case does not change. On Yoshi, the exit loses its 26 frames of the
  first half mask.
- The opposite value also works and patches the same byte: `$1D` → `$01`
  keeps the *first* half mask for almost the whole animation. Use one or the
  other, not both.
- This changes an operand inside a routine. So it is the only item in this
  group that is not only a data table change. But the opcode itself does not
  change.
- The same clear on each frame by `CODE_00C47E` applies. Nothing continues
  after the animation.

## One shard of a broken block falls instead of flying

**Code:** `D960-A46B`
**Raw form:** `02874A:05:FB` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:11:11

**Mechanism:** `ShatterBlock` breaks a 16×16 block into four pieces. It
creates minor extended sprite `#$01` four times, with `Y` counting 3→0. Four
parallel tables (`ShatterPieceYDisp`, `ShatterPieceXDisp`,
`ShatterPieceYSpeed`, `ShatterPieceXSpeed`) make one set of records with the
same `Y` as the index. So each index is one quarter of the block: offset
`(+0,+0)` `(+8,+0)` `(+0,+8)` `(+8,+8)` and start speed `(-1,-5)` `(+1,-5)`
`(-1,-3)` `(+1,-3)`. The sign of the X speed always matches the column that
the piece came from, and the top row moves away faster than the bottom row.
The handler `CODE_028F8B` uses the X speed on 3 frames of 4
(`TrueFrame AND #$03`) and the Y speed on every frame. It adds gravity with
one `INC MinExtSpriteYSpeed` every 4th frame, and that is what makes the
start speeds into the normal arc. `ShatterPieceYSpeed[0]` is the top left
piece's `$FB` (−5, fast up). The code changes it to `$05` (+5). That one
piece now flies *down* out of the block, and the other three go up in the
normal arc.

**Evidence:** All four tables were read from the reference ROM at `$028742`
(ROM `0x10742`) as `00 00 08 08 / 00 08 00 08 / FB FB FD FD / FF 01 FF 01`.
This matches the four source `db` rows exactly. The patched byte is
`ShatterPieceYSpeed[0]` at `$02874A`, read as `FB`. The addresses were
confirmed with the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv`. The code was encoded and then
decoded again, and it gives `$02874A <- $05`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **Visual only.** The pieces are debris. They have no collision, and no
  game state depends on them.
- **All block breaks use these tables.** Six places in `bank_01`, `bank_02`
  and `bank_03` call `ShatterBlock`: Mario breaking a turn block, sprites
  breaking one, and the case of a block two tiles high, which calls it two
  times. There is no separate version for each source, so this changes every
  broken block in the game.
- Only the top left piece changes. You can see the effect clearly because it
  is different from the other three pieces, which do not change.

## One shard rockets off the top of the screen

**Code:** `2D60-A7DB`
**Raw form:** `02874C:D0:FD` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:11:11

**Mechanism:** This uses the same set of records and the same handler.
`ShatterPieceYSpeed[2]` is the bottom left piece, normally `$FD` (−3). It is
one of the two *weaker* starts, because the design makes the top row move
away faster. The code changes it to `$D0` (−48). The piece that should only
jump a little now leaves the top of the screen almost at once. This reverses
the plan where the top row is faster. Gravity is still added at one unit
every four frames by `CODE_028F8B`'s `INC MinExtSpriteYSpeed`. But at −48,
the piece is gone long before that has an effect.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read of all four rows at `$028742`. The
patched byte is `ShatterPieceYSpeed[2]` at `$02874C`, read as `FD`. The code
was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives `$02874C <- $D0`. This comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- Visual only, and all block breaks use it, the same as above.
- `$D0` is a large negative value in a signed byte. The piece leaves the
  visible area in a few frames. So the player sees a piece that disappears,
  not a piece that makes an arc.
- It patches a different byte from the falling piece code above, so you can
  use them together.

## One shard shoots sideways across the screen

**Code:** `0D60-A7AB`
**Raw form:** `02874F:40:01` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:11:11

**Mechanism:** `ShatterPieceXSpeed[1]` is the horizontal start speed of the
top right piece. It is normally `$01`: one pixel per frame to the right,
which matches the column that the piece came from. The code changes it to
`$40` (+64), so that piece crosses the screen in about four frames. To be
exact: `CODE_028F8B` uses the X speed on only 3 frames of 4
(`TrueFrame AND #$03`). So the real movement rate is three quarters of the
byte, not the full value. The Y speed does not change, so the piece still
goes up in its normal arc while it flies to the side.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read of all four rows at `$028742`. The
patched byte is `ShatterPieceXSpeed[1]` at `$02874F`, read as `01`. The
source header comment of the tables, which describes `CODE_028F8B`, gives the
¾ rate as fact. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$02874F <- $40`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- Visual only, and all block breaks use it.
- `$40` stays in the positive signed range, so the piece still moves right.
  The direction still matches its original column. Only the size of the
  speed changes.
- Only the top right piece changes.

## Debris appears half a screen away from the block

**Code:** `6D60-AFAB`
**Raw form:** `028747:80:08` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:11:11

**Mechanism:** This one is different from the others in this group. It is a
start *offset*, not a speed. `ShatterPieceXDisp[1]` is added to
`TouchBlockXPos`. It puts the top right piece 8 pixels to the right of the
block's origin, which is the offset that puts it in its own quarter. The
code changes it to `$80` (+128). So that one piece appears half a screen to
the right of the block that the player really broke. From there it moves in
its normal arc, because its start speeds do not change. The other three
pieces still appear correctly on the block. So the extra piece looks like
debris from a completely different place.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read of all four rows at `$028742`. The
patched byte is `ShatterPieceXDisp[1]` at `$028747`, read as `08`. The code
was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives `$028747 <- $80`. This comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- Visual only, and all block breaks in the game use it.
- The offset is added to the block's X position, and the game does not check
  the screen edges. So when the block is near the right edge of the level,
  the piece may appear outside the camera, and you will not see it.
- This byte and the sideways speed code above both change the top right
  piece. But they are different bytes, so if you use both, you get one piece
  that is very far away and very fast.

## Rubble and pipes become enterable levels

**Code:** `65BB-04BD`
**Raw form:** `04919A:87:81` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:16:24

**Mechanism:** `OverworldLayer1Tile` holds the number of the Map16 tile that
the player stands on. `rammap.asm` documents the numbers: blank `$00`, paths
`$01-$55`, level tiles `$56-$80` (the range that `CODE_04D832` gives
translevel numbers to), rubble and pipes after events `$81-$86`, and
`$87-$FF` cannot be passed. `OWPU_NotOnPipe` sets the upper end of the range
that can be entered with `CMP #$81 / BEQ / BCS`. It refuses everything at or
above the Destroyed Castle, so pressing A/B/X/Y on rubble does nothing. The
code changes the immediate value to `$87`. This moves the limit past the
whole rubble range. So you can enter tiles `$81-$86` with a normal button
press: the Destroyed Castle's back door without L+R, and also destroyed
fortresses, switch palaces, and the `$81`/`$82` pipes, which the game now
treats as levels.

**Evidence:** The instruction at `$049199` (ROM `0x21199`) was read from the
reference ROM as `C9 81 F0`: `CMP #$81`, then `BEQ`. So the patched byte at
`$04919A` is clearly the immediate operand. It was also confirmed that this
is the correct one of the two: there is a second `C9 81 F0` at `$04914C`. It
is part of a different check, and this code does **not** change it. The
address was confirmed with the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv`. The code was
encoded and then decoded again, and it gives `$04919A <- $87`. This comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **The correct level loads.** `CODE_04D832` gives translevel numbers only
  to tiles `$56-$80`. But it does this on the *original* map:
  `CODE_04DC09` copies `OWL1TileData` with MVN from bank `$0C` into
  `Map16TilesLow`, and then at once calls `CODE_04D7F2`, before any events
  run again. Nothing else in the ROM writes `OWLayer1Translevel`. So the tile
  position of a structure keeps the level number that it had before the
  event changed it into rubble. This is also why the normal L+R back door of
  the Destroyed Castle enters the correct castle. (An earlier version of this
  entry said the opposite.)
- Only the entry check moves. The walk check is a separate compare. So this
  code alone does not let the player get to tiles that they could not
  already stand on.
- The second `C9 81` at `$04914C` still refuses its own case.

## Walk anywhere on the overworld map

**Code:** `EEBE-64FD`
**Raw form:** `0492F8:FF:87` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:16:24

**Mechanism:** The walk check at `CODE_0492BC` reads the target tile and
allows `$01-$86`: `AND #$00FF / BEQ block / CMP #$0056 / BCC ok /
CMP #$0087 / BCC ok / BRA block`. The upper limit is the 16-bit
`CMP.W #$0087`, which assembles to `C9 87 00`. This code patches the low
byte of its operand. The code changes it to `$FF`. The allowed range then
includes everything except blank (`$00`) and `$FF`. So the player can step
off the paths and walk on the decorative parts of the map. The direction
and step animation still come from `OWSpecialStepTiles`. None of these tiles
are in it, so every tile off the path uses the default 8-pixel step.

**Evidence:** The instruction at `$0492F7` (ROM `0x212F7`) was read from the
reference ROM as `C9 87 00`, then `90` (`BCC`). This confirms both the
position of the operand and the 16-bit form. The address was confirmed with
the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv`. The code was encoded and then decoded again,
and it gives `$0492F8 <- $FF`. This comes from the disassembly. It was
**not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- The `CMP #$0056` part of the pair is **not needed**. Both of its branches
  go to the same "walkable" target. So it is not changed, and a patch there
  would do nothing.
- Only the low byte of the 16-bit operand changes. The high byte stays
  `$00`, so the compare is still a simple 0–255 range test.
- There is a **second `CMP.W #$0087` that is the same** in another place in
  `bank_04` (at `$0495E3`). It controls a different path. This code does not
  change it, so anything that it controls does not change.
- Walking off the paths does not make level entrances. To enter, you still
  need a tile that the entry check accepts.

## Clearing a castle leaves a Star Road warp behind

**Code:** `9E38-0D2F`
**Raw form:** `04E5B3:5F:81` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:16:24

**Mechanism:** When a level-clear event destroys a structure, `CODE_04E68A`
finds the tile in `OWCrushTiles` (`db $77,$79,$58,$4C,$A6`) and writes the
matching entry of `OWCrushRubbleTile` (`db $85,$86,$81,$81,$81`) back to the
map. Index 2 is the Castle case: `$58` becomes `$81`, the Destroyed Castle.
The code changes that entry to `$5F`. So when you clear a castle, it leaves
a **Star Road warp** tile and not rubble. `$5F` is inside the `$56-$80`
level range, so you can still enter it. `CODE_04D832` gives translevel
numbers one time when the map loads and does not calculate them again. So
the tile keeps the castle's own level number. The castle can still be
played again, but it has a different graphic.

**Evidence:** `OWCrushTiles` / `OWCrushUpperTile` / `OWCrushRubbleTile` were
read from the reference ROM at `$04E5A7`, `$04E5AC`, `$04E5B1` (ROM
`0x265A7` onward) as `77 79 58 4C A6` / `85 86 00 10 00` /
`85 86 81 81 81`. These match the source `db` rows exactly. The patched byte
is `OWCrushRubbleTile[2]` at `$04E5B3`, read as `81`. `rammap.asm`'s
`OverworldLayer1Tile` numbers document that `$5F` = Star Road warp. The code
was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives `$04E5B3 <- $5F`. This
comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- There is one writer, `CODE_04E68A`, and it runs one time for each
  level-clear event. So you see the change only on castles that you clear
  *after* you turn on the code.
- For indices below 3, the game writes only `OWCrushRubbleTile`. The Castle
  is one of those, so no upper tile is used.
- `$56` (Yoshi's House) also works as a replacement at the same byte. Use
  one value or the other.
- The other entries 0/1 (`$85`/`$86`, the results for fortress and switch
  palace) and 3/4 (the structures with two tiles) do not change, and they
  are still destroyed normally.

## The clear event crushes pipes instead of castles

**Code:** `983C-049F`
**Raw form:** `04E5A9:5B:58` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:16:24

**Mechanism:** This is the other half of the same mechanism. This code
patches the *search key* and not the result. `OWCrushTiles`
(`db $77,$79,$58,$4C,$A6`) is the list that `CODE_04E68A` compares with the
tile at the event position, with X counting from 4 down to 0. Index 2 is
`$58`, the Castle. The code changes it to `$5B` (Pipe). So when you clear a
level whose event is on a pipe tile, that pipe becomes a Destroyed Castle.
The search no longer finds real castles, so they stay as they are after the
clear.

**Evidence:** The same reference ROM read as above: `OWCrushTiles` at
`$04E5A7` reads `77 79 58 4C A6`, with `58` at the patched index 2 byte
`$04E5A9`. `rammap.asm`'s `OverworldLayer1Tile` numbers document that
`$5B` = Pipe, and `$5B` is not already in `OWCrushTiles`. The code was
encoded and then decoded again, and it gives `$04E5A9 <- $5B`. This comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **The search starts at the highest index.** So indices 3 and 4
  (`$4C`/`$A6`, the structures with two tiles) are tested before index 2.
  `$5B` was selected because it is not already at a higher index. If the
  value were there twice, the search would never get to the patched entry.
- Castles stay after the clear, so the map keeps the castle graphic. Nothing
  else about level completion changes.
- It goes well with the rubble tile code above (they are different bytes of
  the same set of records), but each one is useful alone.

## A stretch of path offers to save instead of the castle

**Code:** `DF65-A727`
**Raw form:** `048F7F:01:58` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:16:24

**Mechanism:** `OWSavePromptTiles` (`db $58,$59,$5D,$63,$77,$79,$7E,$80`) is
the list of eight overworld tiles that offer to save. `CODE_048F87` compares
each one with `OverworldLayer1Tile`. When one matches, it writes the current
progress to the save buffer (events, the positions of both players,
animations and submaps) and sets `ShowSavePrompt`. Index 0 is `$58`, the
Castle. The code changes it to `$01`, a normal path tile. This moves the
save offer to that part of the path. If you stop there, the game offers to
save. When you clear a castle, it no longer offers to save.

**Evidence:** `OWSavePromptTiles` at `$048F7F` (ROM `0x20F7F`) was read from
the reference ROM as `58 59 5D 63 77 79 7E 80`. This matches the source `db`
row exactly. The patched byte is index 0, read as `58`. `OWSaveArmTiles` at
`$04E5E6` (ROM `0x265E6`) was read as the same eight bytes, which confirms
that the two lists start the same. The address was confirmed with the
regenerated `linemap_U.tsv`. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and
it gives `$048F7F <- $01`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not**
tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **This makes the two lists different on purpose.** `OWSaveArmTiles` has
  the same eight tiles again, and the level-clear handler checks it. If the
  player stands on one of them, `CODE_04E61C` sets `OWLevelExitMode = $E0`
  and `KeepModeActive = $0F`. `CODE_048F87` uses these later to show the
  prompt. If you patch only `OWSavePromptTiles`, the castle still *prepares*
  the prompt but no longer matches it. And the path tile matches, but a level
  clear never prepares it. To keep them the same, you must also patch
  `$04E5E6`, with a second code.
- `$01` is a very common path tile. So the save offer may start on a large
  part of the map, not at one place.
- The other seven prompt tiles do not change.

## The L+R overworld back door moves to Yoshi's House

**Code:** `91B0-079D`
**Raw form:** `04914D:56:81` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte
is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:29:23

**Mechanism:** `OWPlayerUpdate` runs one time on each frame while the
player stands still on the overworld. Inside an `if ver_is_english` block, it
checks if L+R is held (`LDA axlr0000Hold / AND #$30 / CMP #$30`). If it is,
it does `LDA OverworldLayer1Tile / CMP #$81 / BEQ OWPU_EnterLevel`. `$81` is
the Destroyed Castle. It is above the `$56-$80` range that you can enter, so
the normal A/B/X/Y path refuses it. L+R is the only way back into a castle
that you already beat. It is the game's "back door". The code changes the
compare operand to `$56`, which moves that back door to Yoshi's House. If
you hold L+R while you stand on it, the game jumps directly to
`OWPU_EnterLevel`, and the Destroyed Castle loses its secret. This branch
jumps directly into the entry path, so it skips the `>= $81` check that the
normal button path does. So any tile value works here, also values that the
normal path would refuse.

**Evidence:** The instruction at `$04914C` (ROM `0x2114C`) was read from the
reference ROM as `C9 81 F0`: `CMP #$81`, then `BEQ`. So the patched byte at
`$04914D` is clearly the immediate operand. This is the *second* of the two
`C9 81 F0` sequences in `bank_04`. The other, at `$049199`, is the
`OWPU_NotOnPipe` range check, which a different code in this file patches.
The two were told apart by their addresses before encoding. `rammap.asm`'s
`OverworldLayer1Tile` numbers document that `$56` = Yoshi's House. The
address was confirmed with the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv`. The code was
encoded and then decoded again, and it gives `$04914D <- $56`. This comes
from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **The Destroyed Castle's back door is gone.** This moves the secret. It
  does not add one. So you cannot enter a castle that you beat again in any
  way.
- You can already enter Yoshi's House with the normal A/B/X/Y path, so the
  L+R way is not needed there. The part of this code that you notice is
  mostly what it *removes*. `$5F` (Star Road warp) also works as a
  replacement at the same byte, if you prefer a different tile. Use one
  value or the other.
- The whole check is inside an `if ver_is_english` block. So it exists in U,
  SS, E0 and E1, but not in the Japanese release. This address is for the U
  build.
- When you enter this way, the game uses the translevel number that the tile
  has, the same as for any other entry.

## Reserve item drops as a P-Balloon / flying red coin / key instead of a powerup

**Code:** `5A60-D466`
**Raw form:** `02804A:7C:73` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:12:41

**Mechanism:** `DropReserveItem` (`$028008`) is the routine that empties the
item box. Two places in bank_00 call it: `CODE_00C585`, when the player
presses Select during normal level play, and `PowerDown`, when damage drops
the item automatically. `PlayerItembox` holds a small *item* number
(1 Mushroom, 2 Flower, 3 Star, 4 Feather), not a sprite number. So after the
routine gets a sprite slot, it changes one into the other with one addition
at `$028049`:

```
    PLA
    CLC
    ADC.B #$73        ; <- $02804A is the byte this code patches
    STA.B SpriteNumber,X
```

`1 + $73 = $74` Mushroom, `2 + $73 = $75` Flower, `3 + $73 = $76` Star,
`4 + $73 = $77` Feather. These are exactly the sprite numbers that the
dispatch table of `CallSpriteMain` gives those four. The code changes the
added value to `$7C`. This moves the whole mapping up eight numbers, into the
group of flying objects:

| Box contents | Normal sprite | With this code |
|---|---|---|
| 1 Mushroom | `$74` Mushroom | `$7D` P-Balloon |
| 2 Flower | `$75` Flower | `$7E` Flying red coin |
| 3 Star | `$76` Star | `$7F` Flying yellow 1-Up |
| 4 Feather | `$77` Feather | `$80` Key |

One routine, `BalloonKeyFlyObjs`, handles all four replacements. That is
why the change works cleanly. The caller only needs "a sprite number that
the dispatch table can reach", and the routine's own `JSL InitSpriteTables`
sets up the slot in both cases.

**Evidence:** `DropReserveItem` in `bank_02.asm` was read from the reference
ROM at `$028049` (`0x10049`) as `69 73 95`: `ADC #$73`, then `STA dp,X`. So
the patched byte at `$02804A` is clearly the immediate operand and nothing
else. The sprite numbers come from the annotated dispatch table of
`CallSpriteMain` in `bank_01.asm` (`74 - Mushroom`, `75 - Flower`,
`76 - Star`, `77 - Feather`, `7D - Balloon`, `7E - Flying Red coin`,
`7F - Flying yellow 1-Up`, `80 - Key`). The status bar reads
`ItemBoxOBJNos-1,X` with the same values. This confirms separately that the
box's numbers 1-4 are item numbers and not sprite numbers. The address was
confirmed with the regenerated `linemap_U.tsv`. The code was encoded and then
decoded again, and it gives `$02804A <- $7C`. It was also checked with a
separate encoder, which returned the same code. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **You can no longer use a stored powerup.** Both the Select press path and
  the damage path go through this one instruction. So this replaces the
  reserve item completely. It does not add an option. The drop on damage
  that normally gives you a second chance now gives you a balloon or a key.
- In normal play, the game never gets to the Star row. `TouchedPowerUp`
  stores only 1, 2 or 4 in `PlayerItembox` (its `ItemBoxSprite` table has no
  3s). So nothing normally puts a Star in the box, and the `$7F` flying 1-Up
  does not appear without a second code.
- The replacements appear at the fixed screen position of the item box:
  `$78` to the right of and `$20` below the layer 1 origin. That is where
  these sprites are drawn, but it is not where they normally come from. A key
  or flying coin that appears in the air at the top of the screen is
  expected. It is not a fault.
- `$7D` P-Balloon is the same sprite number that the routine already handles
  in a special way when it must replace a used slot. So a balloon from this
  code can go through that path. The routine clears `PBalloonInflating`
  there, which is the planned handling.

## Iggy's and Larry's ball floats instead of dropping

**Code:** `DFEB-6FA1`
**Raw form:** `01FA97:01:04` (address:new-byte:original-byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 00:41:07

**Mechanism:** `IggysBall` (`$01FA58`) is the main routine for sprite `$A7`,
the ball that Iggy and Larry shoot at Mario. The ball has almost no AI. Its X
speed is set again from `IggyBallXSpeed` on every frame, so it can never
speed up, slow down or turn. Only its vertical movement changes, and that
comes from these four instructions at `$01FA8F`:

```
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CMP.B #$40                                ; terminal fall speed
    BPL +
    CLC
    ADC.B #$04                                ; <- $01FA97 is the byte this code patches
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
```

`$04` is the ball's gravity: 4/16 of a pixel per frame, added on each frame,
until the fall speed gets to the `$40` limit (4 px/frame). The code changes
it to `$01`, which makes that acceleration four times smaller. So the ball
needs four times as long to get any downward speed. When the ball touches
the tilting platform, the bounce is a fixed `LDA #$F0` (one pixel per frame
up, at `$01FA9F`), and gravity does *not* change it. So the balance between
the two changes completely. A bounce that normally ends in four frames now
carries the ball for sixteen. Between bounces, the ball drifts across the
room and does not fall onto it.

**Evidence:** `IggysBall` in `bank_01.asm` was read from the reference ROM at
`$01FA96` (`0xFA96`) as `69 04`, which is `ADC #$04`. So the patched byte at
`$01FA97` is the immediate operand. The constants around it were checked in
the same way: `C9 40` at `$01FA91` (the terminal speed compare) and `A9 F0`
at `$01FA9F` (the bounce). The disassembly shows in three ways that the index
into `IggyBallXSpeed` is a direction, `0` right and `1` left:
`Spr0to13SpeedX`'s `db $08,$F8`, `SubHorizPos` returning `Y=0` when Mario is
to the right, and `GenerateBall`'s `BallPositionDispX: db $08,$F8`.
`GenerateBall` copies it from Iggy one time when the ball appears, so nothing
else in the routine changes. The address was confirmed with the regenerated
`linemap_U.tsv`. The code was encoded and then decoded again, and it gives
`$01FA97 <- $01`. It was also checked with a separate encoder, which returned
the same code. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- **One reader, one sprite.** Only `IggysBall` uses `$01FA97`. So this
  changes nothing outside the Iggy and Larry fights. It is a fun change for a
  boss room, not a physics change for the whole game.
- The ball destroys itself in a puff of smoke (`CODE_019ACB`, status `$04`)
  while the *low byte* of its Y position is in `$44`-`$4F`. If the ball falls
  at a different speed, it needs a different time to cross that
  twelve-pixel range. So the code also changes when balls disappear, and
  probably makes them last longer. The disassembly gives the exact range, but
  not what place on the screen it is.
- Larry's fight uses the same sprite and the same routine, so it changes in
  the same way.
- `$01FA97` is not inside a version-conditional block, but this is the
  address for the U build. The other releases were not checked.

## Mario throws hammers instead of fireballs (D0EA-6DD7)

**Code:** `D0EA-6DD7`
**Raw form:** `00FEC0:04` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Original byte:** `$05`
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09

**Effect:** Fire Mario still throws, with the same button, the same sound and
the same launch arc. But what comes out is a Hammer Bro's hammer. It kills
nothing, and it hurts *Mario* when it touches him.

**Mechanism:** SMW has ten "extended sprite" slots. This is a simple group
of slots, separate from the twelve real sprite slots, for projectiles and
effects. A slot's `ExtSpriteNumber` ($170B..$1714) has three jobs at the
same time. It shows if the slot is used (`$00` = free), it is the dispatch
index, and it selects the appearance. `RunOneExtendedSprite`
(`bank_02.asm`) runs one slot per frame. It jumps through a table with 19
entries:

```
    dw Return029B15   ; 00 - Empty slot        dw LauncherArm       ; 08 - Torpedo Ted shooter's arm
    dw SmokePuff      ; 01 - Puff of smoke     dw UnusedExtendedSpr ; 09 - Unused
    dw ReznorFireball ; 02 - Reznor fireball   dw CloudCoin         ; 0A - Coin from cloud game
    dw FlameRemnant   ; 03 - Tiny flame        dw Hammer            ; 0B - Piranha fireball
    dw Hammer         ; 04 - Hammer            dw VolcanoLotusFire  ; 0C - Volcano lotus fire
    dw MarioFireball  ; 05 - Mario fireball    dw Baseball          ; 0D - Baseball
    dw Baseball       ; 06 - Bone              dw CloudCoin         ; 0E - Flower of Wiggler
    dw LavaSplash     ; 07 - Lava splash       dw SmokeTrail        ; 0F - Trail of smoke
                                               dw SpinJumpStars     ; 10 - Spin Jump stars
                                               dw YoshiFireball     ; 11 - Yoshi fireballs
                                               dw WaterBubble       ; 12 - Water bubble
```

`ShootFireball` (`bank_00.asm`) is the code that writes `$05` into that
byte:

```
ShootFireball:
    LDX.B #$09                                ; \ Find a free fireball slot (08-09)
CODE_00FEAA:
    LDA.W ExtSpriteNumber,X                   ; |
    BEQ CODE_00FEB5                           ; |
    DEX                                       ; |
    CPX.B #$07                                ; |
    BNE CODE_00FEAA                           ; |
    RTS                                       ; / Return if no free slots

CODE_00FEB5:
    LDA.B #!SFX_FIREBALL
    STA.W SPCIO3                              ; / Play sound effect
    LDA.B #$0A
    STA.W ShootFireTimer
    LDA.B #$05                                ; \ Extended sprite = Mario fireball
    STA.W ExtSpriteNumber,X                   ; /
    LDA.B #$30
    STA.W ExtSpriteYSpeed,X
    LDY.B PlayerDirection
    LDA.W DATA_00FE94,Y                       ; db $FD,$03
    STA.W ExtSpriteXSpeed,X
```

The code changes the `$05` to `$04`. This sends the same slot to `Hammer` and
not to `MarioFireball`. Nothing else that `ShootFireball` sets up changes.
So the hammer gets the fireball's start state: `ExtSpriteYSpeed = $30`
(down) and `ExtSpriteXSpeed` from `DATA_00FE94` (`db $FD,$03`: three pixels
per frame in the direction that Mario faces). The different handler causes
three clear differences:

- **It makes an arc and does not bounce.** `MarioFireball` bounces off the
  floor. `Hammer` has no ground interaction at all. It only adds gravity
  (`CMP #$40 / BPL / INC / INC`, +2 per frame up to a limit of `$40`). So the
  hammer flies out with the fireball's start speed and falls in a smooth
  parabola. It disappears as soon as it leaves the screen (`CODE_02A1A4`
  continues to `CODE_02A211`, which sets `ExtSpriteNumber` to zero).
- **It kills nothing.** `ProcessFireball` is the routine that checks the
  sprite slots and destroys what a fireball touches. It has exactly two
  callers in the disassembly: `MarioFireball` (`bank_02.asm:4245`) and
  `YoshiFireball` (`4194`). `Hammer` is not one of them. So a hammer goes
  through every enemy in the level.
- **It hurts you.** `Hammer` calls `CODE_02A3F6`. That routine checks if the
  projectile touches Mario. For any extended sprite number except `$0A` (the
  coin of the cloud game), it continues to `CODE_02A469` → `JSL HurtMario`.
  If you ride Yoshi, it goes to the routine that knocks you off him. The
  hammer handler never checks who threw it, so your own hammer hurts you
  when it touches you. Because of the launch arc, the most likely ways to get
  hit are to throw one while you run and catch up with it, or to throw one
  down a slope and follow it.

It still *looks* like a hammer. The draw path of `Hammer` checks
`CMP.B #$0B` to select between the Piranha fireball graphics and the hammer
graphics, and `$04` takes the hammer branch (`HammerTiles` /
`HammerGfxProp`, a spin of four frames with `ExtSpriteMisc1765` as the
index).

**Evidence:** Patches `$00FEC0`, the immediate operand of the `LDA.B #$05` at
`$00FEBF` in `CODE_00FEB5` (`bank_00.asm`). The reference ROM reads
`a9 05 9d 0b 17` across `$00FEBF`-`$00FEC3`. Opcode `$A9` at `$00FEBF`
confirms that the operand is the next byte, and `STA.W $170B,X` follows. The
address was found with `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, which was regenerated for this
check and verified as byte for byte the same as `comparison_U.smc`. The code
was encoded, decoded again to `($00FEC0, $04)`, and checked with romdev's
separate encoder, which returned the same string. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **Only Mario's own fireballs change.** Yoshi's fire breath is extended
  sprite `$11`, created in another place, and it does not change. Hammer
  Bros still throw their own hammers as before. `Hammer` is a shared handler,
  and this code adds a caller. It does not change the existing callers.
- **The automatic fire during a spin jump also changes.** `CODE_00D081`
  calls `ShootFireball` on a new Y press, and also once every 16 frames while
  Fire Mario spin jumps. So a spin jump throws many hammers that hurt you.
- **This makes the fire flower worse. It is not a different weapon.** You
  keep the powerup's extra hit point and its behaviour without Yoshi, but the
  attack is gone, and you get a way to hurt yourself. Use it as a hard mode or
  fun code, not as a power boost.
- The two fireball slots (`$08`-`$09`) are still reserved in the same way, so
  at most two hammers can exist at the same time.
- `$00FEC0` is not inside a version-conditional block, but this is the
  address for the U build. The other releases were not checked.

## Yoshi ground pound on every landing (DD36-AD67 + DD36-A4A7)

**Codes:** `DD36-AD67` **and** `DD36-A4A7`. You need both.
**Raw form:** `00EF82:00` and `00EF8B:00` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie
codes carry no compare byte)
**Original bytes:** `$12` at `$00EF82`, `$09` at `$00EF8B`
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Effect:** Each time Mario lands from a jump or a fall, he does the Yoshi
ground pound. The screen shakes, the KAPOW sound plays, two puffs of smoke
go out to the sides from his feet, and every enemy that stands on the ground
is knocked over. You do not need Yoshi or a shell. It works as Small Mario,
in any level, on any landing.

**Mechanism:** The landing handler at `CODE_00EF60` (`bank_00.asm`) runs on
the frame when the ground stops Mario's fall. After it clears the in-air
flags, it checks if this landing should start Yoshi's stomp. There are three
checks:

```
CODE_00EF60:
    STA.B PlayerYSpeed+1
    ...
    STZ.B PlayerInAir
    ...
    LDY.W FlightPhase
    BNE CODE_00EF99                           ; cape dive-bomb path, not this one
    LDA.W PlayerRidingYoshi                   ; gate 1: must be on Yoshi
    BEQ +
    LDA.B TempPlayerAir                       ; gate 2: must have been airborne
    BEQ +
    LDA.W YoshiCanStomp                       ; \ gate 3: Yoshi has stomp ability,
    BEQ +                                     ; |
    JSL YoshiStompRoutine                     ; | Run routine
    LDA.B #!SFX_YOSHISTOMP                    ; | Play sound effect
    STA.W SPCIO3                              ; /
  + STZ.W SpriteStompCounter
    RTS
```

The two codes set the **branch offsets** of checks 1 and 3 to zero. Each
`BEQ +$nn` becomes `BEQ +$00`. A branch to the next instruction does the
same thing as no branch. So both tests still run and still set the Z flag,
but they no longer skip anything. Check 2 is not changed, on purpose.
`TempPlayerAir` is the copy of `PlayerInAir` from the previous frame, so it
is not zero only on the one frame when Mario lands. That is what makes this
happen "once for each landing" and not "all the time while standing".

This works without Yoshi because `YoshiStompRoutine` (`bank_02.asm`) reads
**no Yoshi state at all**. All of its inputs come from the player or from
blocks:

```
YoshiStompRoutine:
    LDA.W SpriteStompCounter
    BNE +
    PHB / PHK / PLB
    JSR SprBlkInteract                        ; claim a free quake-sprite slot
    LDA.B #$02
    STA.W QuakeSpriteNumber,Y                 ; the shockwave
    LDA.B PlayerXPosNext ...                  ; positioned at Mario, +$20 in Y
    JSR CODE_029BE4
    PLB
  + RTL
```

`CODE_029BE4` is the sound and graphics part: `ScreenShakeTimer` = `$05`,
`!SFX_KAPOW`, and two `$0F` "Yoshi stomp smoke" extended sprites thrown to
the left and right of Mario's feet from `DATA_029BDE`/`DATA_029BE2`. The
quake sprite itself is the part that does damage. Its handler (`CODE_029398`)
runs on each frame and counts down a timer. In its last three frames, it
checks all twelve sprite slots (`LDX #$0B`). It skips sprites that are
already being eaten, that the cape cannot hurt, or that have interaction
turned off. It applies the stomp result to the others: `SpriteMisc154C` =
`$08`, `SpriteMisc1540` = `$FF`, then `JSL CODE_01AB6F`. **These codes
change none of that.** They change only *when* the game calls the routine,
never what it does. So the effect is exactly the normal Yoshi stomp that the
game already has.

**Evidence:** Both patched bytes are branch operands, and each was checked
against the reference ROM. `$00EF7B`-`$00EF98` reads:

```
14 d0 1b ad 7a 18 f0 12 a5 8f f0 0e ad e7 18 f0 09 22 bf 86 02 a9 25 8d fc 1d 9c 97 16 60
```

This decodes as `BNE $EF99` at `$00EF7C`; `LDA $187A` at `$00EF7E`; **`BEQ`
opcode `$F0` at `$00EF81` with operand `$12` at `$00EF82`**; `LDA $8F` at
`$00EF83`; `BEQ +$0E` at `$00EF85`; `LDA $18E7` at `$00EF87`; **`BEQ` opcode
`$F0` at `$00EF8A` with operand `$09` at `$00EF8B`**; `JSL $0286BF` at
`$00EF8C`. Both `$12` and `$09` go to `$00EF95`, the shared `+` target. This
confirms that the two checks are the skips that the codes remove. `$187A` =
`PlayerRidingYoshi`, `$18E7` = `YoshiCanStomp` and `$0286BF` =
`YoshiStompRoutine`, from `SMW_U.sym`. The addresses were found with
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`, which was regenerated for this check and verified as
byte for byte the same as `comparison_U.smc`. Both codes were decoded again
to their `(address, $00)` pairs and checked with romdev's separate encoder,
which returned the same strings. This comes from the disassembly. It was
**not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **You need both codes.** `00EF8B:00` alone is still a useful code: "any
  Yoshi does a ground pound on every landing, no shell needed". But
  `00EF82:00` alone is almost useless. The `Yoshi` sprite routine clears
  `YoshiCanStomp` again at its start on every frame. So it reads `$00` when a
  Yoshi is on the screen without the correct shell.
- **One pound for each landing, and only if the stomp chain is clear.**
  `YoshiStompRoutine` returns at once when `SpriteStompCounter` is not zero,
  and that counter is set to zero at `$00EF95`, directly after this block. So
  a landing that ends a series of enemy stomps is skipped, and the pound
  happens on the *next* landing. The normal game does this too. The codes do
  not add it.
- **The cape dive-bomb is a separate path, and it does not change.**
  `LDY.W FlightPhase / BNE CODE_00EF99` sends caped landings to
  `CallGroundPound` before the game gets to these checks. So with a cape and
  a `FlightPhase` that is not zero, you get the old cape slam and not the
  Yoshi stomp.
- **Only four shockwaves can exist at the same time.** `SprBlkInteract`
  checks the four `QuakeSpriteNumber` slots. If none is free, it uses slot 0
  again with no warning. In practice, one landing makes one shockwave, so
  normal play does not get to this case.
- **It keeps a quirk of the normal game in the shockwave's X high byte.**
  `YoshiStompRoutine` writes `PlayerXPosNext+1` into
  `QuakeSpriteYPosHigh,Y`, not into `QuakeSpriteXPosHigh,Y`. The real Y high
  byte then replaces that value. So the shockwave's X page keeps the value
  that `SprBlkInteract` copied from `TouchBlockXPos+1`. This landing handler
  is the block interaction path, so that value is the block that Mario just
  landed on, and the shockwave is in the correct place. This is the same as
  in the normal game.
- `$00EF82` and `$00EF8B` are not inside a version-conditional block, but
  this is the address for the U build. The other releases were not checked.

## Fireballs drop straight down (BAEA-67D7)

`BAEA-67D7` — `00FECC:9C` (original `$94`)

Mario's fireballs come out with no horizontal speed at all. If you fire
while you stand still, the ball drops out of Mario's mouth and bounces up
and down in one place. It never moves left or right. Every fireball becomes
a vertical pogo that stays in place, and it only moves relative to Mario
when Mario moves or the level scrolls. If you fire while you run, you leave
it behind at once, because it no longer gets its own start speed.

**Mechanism.** `ShootFireball` (`$00FEA8`) sets the start X speed of a
fireball from a table with two entries. The index is the direction that
Mario faces:

```
FireballXSpeed:
    db $FD,$03                                ; -3 left, +3 right
...
    LDY.B PlayerDirection                     ; $00FEC9
    LDA.W FireballXSpeed,Y                    ; $00FECB  b9 94 fe
    STA.W ExtSpriteXSpeed,X                   ; $00FECE
```

This **moves the table base**. It does not change a value. The code changes
the low byte of that `LDA`'s operand from `$94` to `$9C`. So the instruction
reads `FireballSpawnXOffHigh`, and that table starts with `db $00,$00`. So
both directions load `$00`, and one byte sets the start speed to zero for a
fireball thrown in either direction. The two useful entries are at exactly
the correct offsets for this reason: the fireball's start position offset is
stored as a signed 16-bit value, split into low and high halves, and the
high half is only the sign extension. It is `$00` for the two entries on
foot, and `$FF` under each negative low byte later in the row.

Nothing else reads `FireballXSpeed`. This is its only reader. The redirect
does not change the normal use of `FireballSpawnXOffHigh`, which is a
separate instruction at `$00FEEA` that reads the same table at the same
index as before. The rest of the launch does not change. The ball still
appears in the correct place, still gets `ExtSpriteYSpeed` = `$30` down,
still plays `!SFX_FIREBALL`, and still acts as extended sprite `$05` after
that. Only the horizontal part of its start speed is gone.

It is useful to explain why the index has only two entries, because that is
what makes the one-byte version possible. The three *position* tables after
it have six entries each: direction, plus two more rows for riding Yoshi and
for ducking on Yoshi. But `ShootFireball` does the `INY` pairs that select
those rows *after* it loads the speed. So the speed table uses only
`PlayerDirection` as the index, and it is exactly two bytes long.
`PlayerDirection` is 0 = left, 1 = right (`CODE_00D6B1` makes it as
`byetudlrHold AND #$01`, and `!DpadRight` is bit 0). This agrees with entry
0 being `$FD` = -3.

**Evidence:** the patched byte is the operand of `LDA.W FireballXSpeed,Y`.
Its address `$00FECB` came from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (regenerated for this
check; the instrumented build was byte for byte the same as
`comparison_U.smc`). The reference ROM at `$00FEC9` reads:

```
a4 76 b9 94 fe 9d 47 17
```

This is `LDY $76` (`PlayerDirection`), then `B9 94 FE` = `LDA $FE94,Y` with
the low operand byte `$94` at `$00FECC`, then `9D 47 17` = `STA $1747,X`
(`ExtSpriteXSpeed`). The table bytes were also confirmed at `$00FE94`
(`fd 03`) and `$00FE9C` (`00 00 ff 00 ff 00`). The code was decoded again to
`($00FECC, $9C)` and checked with romdev's separate encoder, which returned
the same string. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Variants**, all at the same byte, each one code:

| Code | Byte | Reads | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `BAEA-67D7` | `$9C` | `$00,$00` | no horizontal speed in either direction |
| `B1EA-67D7` | `$96` | `$00,$08` | throws to the left stay in place, throws to the right fly at +8, almost three times normal |
| `C4EA-67D7` | `$A2` | `$08,$08` | every fireball flies right at +8, whatever direction Mario faces |

If you do not want to move the pointer, you can get the same fireball that
does not move by setting the table entries to zero directly. This needs a
second code: `DDEB-6FD7` (`00FE94:00`) and `DDEB-6F07` (`00FE95:00`).

**Caveats:**
- **The ball still moves vertically.** `ExtSpriteYSpeed` = `$30` and gravity
  do not change. So it bounces off the floor exactly as before, but in one
  column. On a slope it drifts, because the bounce reflects off the surface
  and does not use the start speed again.
- **This does not make fireballs useless.** A fireball that stays in front
  of Mario still kills anything that walks into it. On flat ground, it
  becomes a short-range trap and not a projectile.
- **Fireballs thrown from Yoshi also change.** The posture rows change only
  the start *position*, never the speed. So a fireball thrown while riding or
  ducking on Yoshi comes out further from Mario, but it also does not move.
- `$00FECC` is not inside a version-conditional block, but this is the
  address for the U build. The other releases were not checked.

## Holding the cape climbs forever instead of gliding down

**Code:** `ED28-A40F`
**Raw form:** `00D7B9:F0` (address:new-byte; the original byte is `$10` — SNES
Game Genie codes carry no compare byte, so it is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:30:00

**Mechanism:** `CapeTargetYSpeed` (`bank_00.asm`) is the table of vertical
speeds for continuous flight. It is read at
`CODE_00D8FF`/`CODE_00D90D`/`CODE_00D91B`. The index is the flight *mode*
that the three paths from `CODE_00D8CD` select: entry 0 = caped Mario
floating, entry 1 = the caped takeoff climb, entry 2 = flying on a winged
Yoshi. Entry 0 is `$10` (+16), the slow float down of the cape. The game
*sets the speed to* the table value. It does not add the value.
`CODE_00D91B` loads the entry and compares it with `PlayerYSpeed+1`. On
`BEQ`/`BMI` it jumps to `CODE_00D94C`, which stores that value directly into
`PlayerYSpeed+1` and returns. This skips the `ADC PlayerGravity,Y` step
completely. The code changes entry 0 to `$F0` (-16). So the float mode keeps
a steady *rise* of the same size. If you hold A or B with a cape in the air,
Mario now goes up with no end and does not glide down.

Two details make this clean and not glitchy. First, the check in
`CODE_00D90D`, `LDX CapeTargetYSpeed,Y / BPL CODE_00D924`, exists so that a
*downward* target is not used on a Mario who already goes up. With a
negative entry, that check no longer runs, and the negative target applies
in both directions. Second, `CapeFloatTimer` is set to `$10` again each time
the button check passes. So the climb continues for 16 frames after you
release the button, exactly like the normal float.

**Evidence:** the byte is entry 0 of `CapeTargetYSpeed`. Its header comment
in `bank_00.asm` names the three modes (`0=cape float 1=cape takeoff
2=winged Yoshi`) and marks entries 3-14 as never used. The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` (checked as current in this session). The reference
ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header) reads `10 c8 e0
02 03 03 04 03 02` at `$00D7B9`. This matches the source row
`db $10,$C8,$E0,$02,$03,$03,$04,
$03`. It was encoded by `tools/gg_encode.py`, which decodes every code again
with its own decoder and tests itself against 11 known good vectors from
romdev's cheat DB. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in
play.

**Caveats:**
- **The `$C8` flight speed limit at `CODE_00D87E` does not limit this.** The
  game gets to that limit only when `FlightPhase` is not zero. Every
  `CapeTargetYSpeed` path comes through `CODE_00D8CD`, which is the
  `FlightPhase == 0` branch. The rise is a direct store, with no limit.
- It interacts with any code that changes cape flight gravity. The gravity
  step is the step that is skipped, so the two codes affect each other, and
  their effects do not simply add.
- No other reader uses entry 0 of this table. Entries 1 and 2 (the takeoff
  climb and winged Yoshi) do not change with this code.
- PAL (E0/E1) has its own `CapeTargetYSpeed` at a different address. This is
  the byte for the U build.

## A phase-1 cape cannot descend at all

**Code:** `DD2A-A40F`
**Raw form:** `00D7C9:00` (address:new-byte; original byte `$10`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:30:00

**Mechanism:** `CapeMaxFallSpeed` (`bank_00.asm`) is the limit on downward
speed for each `FlightPhase`. It is applied at `CODE_00D892`:
`CMP CapeMaxFallSpeed,Y / BCC + /
LDA CapeMaxFallSpeed,Y`. The row is `db $01,$10,$30,$30,$38,$38,$40`:
phase 1 = `$10`, phases 2-3 = `$30`, phases 4-5 = `$38`, phase 6 = `$40`.
This row is the whole reason why a cape goes down more slowly than a normal
fall. Phase 6 is the same as `PlayerMaxFallSpeed`, and every less steep
angle is slowed. The game never uses entry 0 (`CODE_00D87E` branches to
`CODE_00D8CD` when `FlightPhase` is 0, before the limit runs). The code sets
entry 1 to `$00`. Then the `BCC` can never be taken for any speed that is not
negative. So a phase 1 cape has its fall speed set to zero on every frame,
and the gentlest glide becomes a hover.

**Evidence:** entry 1 of `CapeMaxFallSpeed`, source row
`db $01,$10,$30,$30,$38,
$38,$40`. The reference ROM reads `01 10 30 30 38 38 40` at `$00D7C8`, so the
phase 1 byte is `$10` at `$00D7C9`, as the source says. The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Caveats:**
- **Not a perfect hover.** The limit runs *before* the
  `ADC PlayerGravity,Y` step at `CODE_00D948`. So the speed is set to zero,
  and then it gets one frame of gravity again. The result is a very slow
  sink, not a stop.
- Only phase 1 changes. If you angle the cape down into phases 2-6, the
  normal descent comes back. So this changes the shallow glide and nothing
  else.
- `$00` is a correct value for this table. The `CMP`/`BCC` pair reads it as
  "never go above zero", not as a special marker. So nothing else goes wrong.

## The full-speed dive stops building speed

**Code:** `DD2A-A76F`
**Raw form:** `00D7CE:00` (address:new-byte; original byte `$40`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:30:00

**Mechanism:** The same `CapeMaxFallSpeed` limit at `CODE_00D892`, but entry
6. That is the steepest dive, and the only phase whose limit (`$40`) is the
same as `PlayerMaxFallSpeed`. So it is the one angle where the cape does not
slow Mario down at all. The code sets it to `$00`, which reverses that. The
fastest dive becomes the *slowest* descent in the game. It stops and does
not speed up. Every less steep phase keeps its normal limit.

**Evidence:** entry 6 of `CapeMaxFallSpeed`. The reference ROM reads
`01 10 30 30 38 38 40` at `$00D7C8`, so `$40` is at `$00D7CE`. The address is
from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Caveats:**
- The *other* effects of the dive stay. `CODE_00D94F` saves lift into
  `MaxStageOfFlight` from `CapeDiveLift`, with fall speed / 8 as the index.
  So a dive that can no longer get speed also saves no lift. The pull-up that
  `CODE_00D8AF` uses is also lost with the dive.
- The cape ground pound needs `FlightPhase >= 5`, and the game can still get
  to it. So a code that depends on phase 6 still works.
- If you use it with the phase 1 code above, the cape loses both ends of its
  speed range. That uses two of the five codes that a real Game Genie can
  hold.

## The cape's climb ceiling doubles

**Codes:** `6D26-D4A4` **and** `6D26-D7A4` (both needed)
**Raw form:** `00D88B:80` and `00D88F:80` (address:new-byte; both original bytes
are `$C8`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:30:00

**Mechanism:** The upward half of the flight limit at `CODE_00D87E` is one
constant and not a table: `LDA PlayerYSpeed+1 / BPL CODE_00D892 / CMP #$C8 /
BCS + / LDA #$C8 / BRA +`. `$C8` is -56. It is the fastest speed at which
the cape can ever raise Mario, at *any* `FlightPhase`. It is also what
limits the pull-up lift that `CapeDiveLift` saves during a dive.
`CapeDiveLift`'s own largest entry is also `$C8`. So with the normal values,
a full speed dive becomes exactly this rise and no more. The constant is
there two times: once as the `CMP` operand (the test) and once as the `LDA`
operand (the value that replaces the speed). So to raise the limit cleanly
to `$80` (-128), you need both codes.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM at `$00D886` reads
`a5 7d 10 08 c9 c8 b0 0c a9 c8 80 08 d9 c8 d7 90 03 b9 c8 d7`, which is
`LDA $7D / BPL +8 / CMP #$C8 / BCS +$0C / LDA #$C8 / BRA +8 /
CMP $D7C8,Y / BCC +3 / LDA $D7C8,Y`. So the `CMP` operand is at `$00D88B`
and the `LDA` operand is at `$00D88F`, exactly as the source shows. The
addresses are from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`. Both were encoded and verified with
a decode by `tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was
**not** tested in play.

**Variants.** Each code alone has its own effect. It is not a broken half:

| Code | Byte | What it changes | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `6D26-D4A4` + `6D26-D7A4` | both `$80` | test and value | clean climb limit of -128 |
| `6D26-D7A4` alone | `LDA` only | the value that replaces the speed | any climb faster than -56 is *set to -128*, not cut to -56. This is a boost, and maybe the more interesting single code |
| `6D26-D4A4` alone | `CMP` only | the test | climbs between -56 and -128 are not limited, but anything past -128 is still set back to -56 |

**Caveats:**
- This limit is only on the `FlightPhase != 0` path. So it controls cape
  *flight*, not the float/takeoff/winged Yoshi modes that `CapeTargetYSpeed`
  controls.
- If the limit is above `CapeDiveLift`'s largest entry, the two values are no
  longer the same as in the normal game. So a maximum dive no longer becomes
  exactly the limit rise.
- Two codes for one effect leave three Game Genie slots free.

## The cape takeoff climb doubles

**Code:** `6D28-A46F`
**Raw form:** `00D7BA:80` (address:new-byte; original byte `$C8`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:30:00

**Mechanism:** `CapeTargetYSpeed` entry 1 is the takeoff climb. `CODE_00D8E7`
selects this mode when Mario has a cape, `PlayerInAir` is `$0C`, and
`TakeoffTimer` is still below 2. Its normal value `$C8` (-56) has the same
size as the flight speed limit at `CODE_00D87E`, on purpose. The code
changes it to `$80` (-128). So the launch after a running start throws
Mario twice as high per frame. Like all `CapeTargetYSpeed` entries, it is
stored directly into `PlayerYSpeed+1` at `CODE_00D94C`, and the gravity step
is skipped. So Mario gets the value at once. He does not speed up to it.

**Evidence:** entry 1 of `CapeTargetYSpeed`. The reference ROM reads
`10 c8 e0 02 ...` at `$00D7B9`, so `$C8` is at `$00D7BA`. The address is
from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Caveats:**
- Takeoff is short by design (`TakeoffTimer` ends it at 2). So this is a
  single boost at the start of a flight, not a change that lasts.
- Not like the flight limit, nothing limits this value. It is a direct store
  on the `FlightPhase == 0` path.

## Winged Yoshi climbs twice as fast

**Code:** `AD28-A4AF`
**Raw form:** `00D7BB:C0` (address:new-byte; original byte `$E0`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:30:00

**Mechanism:** `CapeTargetYSpeed` entry 2 is the winged Yoshi flight mode.
`CODE_00D8CD` selects it when `PlayerRidingYoshi` and `YoshiHasWingsEvt` are
both set. Its normal value `$E0` (-32) is the gentlest of the three climbs.
`$C0` (-64) makes it twice as fast. Note that this mode handles input
differently from the others. `CODE_00D8CD` sets X = 1 for a winged Yoshi
that carries a Mario *without* a cape. So that combination reads
`byetudlrFrame` (pressed on this frame) and not `byetudlrHold`, and you must
tap the button to stay in the air. This code changes how much each tap
lifts, not how often you must tap.

**Evidence:** entry 2 of `CapeTargetYSpeed`. The reference ROM reads
`10 c8 e0 02 ...` at `$00D7B9`, so `$E0` is at `$00D7BB`. The address is
from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Caveats:**
- A Mario *with a cape* on a winged Yoshi gets X = 0 and holds the button.
  He also uses this same entry. So the code changes both types of winged
  flight, and the tap or hold difference does not change.
- Winged Yoshi comes from an event, so this code does nothing during most of
  a normal game.

## Iggy's and Larry's ball bounces three times as hard

**Code:** `2DEC-6DD1`
**Raw form:** `01FAA0:D0` (address:new-byte; original byte `$F0` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:29:30

**Mechanism:** `IggysBall` (`bank_01.asm`, sprite `$A7`) checks the tilting
Mode 7 platform on every frame with `JSR CODE_01FF98`. If carry is set, the
ball is on solid ground, and the routine responds with a fixed
`LDA.B #$F0 / STA SpriteYSpeed,X`. That is the whole bounce: a fixed upward
speed that never gets smaller and does not depend on how fast the ball hit.
That is why the normal ball jumps in the same arcs for its whole life. `$F0`
is -16, and `SubSprYPosNoGrvty` shifts the sprite speed right by 4 to get
whole pixels. So the normal bounce is 1 px/frame up. `$D0` (-48) makes it
3 px/frame. The ball jumps about three times as high off the platform before
the `ADC.B #$04` gravity below it pulls it back.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `20 98 ff 90 04 a9 f0 95 aa` at `$01FA99`, which is
`JSR $FF98 / BCC +4 /
LDA #$F0 / STA $AA,X`. So the `LDA` operand is at `$01FAA0`, which matches
the source. The address is from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (checked as current in
this session). It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Caveats:**
- **The despawn range still catches it.** `IggysBall` destroys the ball with
  `JSR CODE_019ACB` while `SpriteYPosLow` is in `$44`-`$4F`, a range of 12
  pixels. A rise of 3 px/frame cannot jump over a 12-pixel range. So a harder
  bounce does not make balls last forever. It only changes how soon they get
  to the range.
- Iggy and Larry both use sprite `$A7`, so both fights change.
- The game loads the ball's X speed again from `IggyBallXSpeed` on every
  frame, and this code does not change it. Only the vertical arc changes.

## Iggy's and Larry's ball creeps downward

**Code:** `FDEB-6D61`
**Raw form:** `01FA92:10` (address:new-byte; original byte `$40`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:29:30

**Mechanism:** The ball's gravity in `IggysBall` is
`LDA SpriteYSpeed,X / CMP.B #$40 / BPL + / CLC / ADC.B #$04 / STA SpriteYSpeed,X`.
It adds +4 on each frame until the fall speed gets to `$40`, the ball's
terminal velocity. `$40` is 4 px/frame after `SubSprYPosNoGrvty` divides by
16. The code lowers the limit to `$10`, which is 1 px/frame. The ball still
speeds up at the normal rate, but it stops speeding up four times sooner. So
it drifts across the room and does not drop. The `CMP` is a signed `BPL`
test, so negative (rising) speeds are still below the limit, and gravity
still applies normally. The bounce gets smaller at its normal rate, and only
the descent is slower.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM reads `b5 aa c9 40 10 05 18 69 04 95 aa` at
`$01FA90`, which is `LDA $AA,X / CMP #$40 / BPL +5 / CLC / ADC #$04 / STA $AA,X`.
So the limit operand is `$40` at `$01FA92`. The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Caveats:**
- **Do not use this with the published `DFEB-6FA1`** (`01FA97:01`, which
  makes the `ADC.B #$04` acceleration four times smaller). Both change the
  same descent in two different ways, and the disassembly cannot clearly
  predict what they do together.
- A slower descent means the ball spends more time between bounces. So it
  also spends more time crossing the `$44`-`$4F` despawn range, and balls
  last longer in general.
- Iggy and Larry both use sprite `$A7`.

## Iggy's and Larry's balls never disappear

**Code:** `DDEC-6701`
**Raw form:** `01FAAD:00` (address:new-byte; original byte `$50`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:29:30

**Mechanism:** The last thing that `IggysBall` does on each frame is a range
test with two sides on the low byte of the ball's Y position:
`LDA SpriteYPosLow,X / CMP.B #$44 / BCC ret / CMP.B #$50 / BCS ret /
JSR CODE_019ACB`. `CODE_019ACB` is what really removes the ball. It sets the
sprite's status to `$04` and leaves a puff of smoke for `$1F` frames. The
range `$44 <= Y < $50` is the strip that the ball goes through when it
leaves the platform area. So the despawn depends on position, not on a
timer. The code sets the upper limit to `$00`. The range is then empty
(`$44 <= Y < $00` is never true), so the `JSR` never runs, and **the balls
keep bouncing for the whole fight** and fill the room.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM reads `b5 d8 c9 44 90 07 c9 50` at `$01FAA6`,
which is `LDA $D8,X / CMP #$44 / BCC +7 / CMP #$50`. So the lower limit is at
`$01FAA9` and the upper limit is at `$01FAAD`. The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Variants:**

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `DDEC-6701` | `01FAAD:00` | range is empty, balls never destroy themselves |
| `DDEC-6401` | `01FAA9:00` | range goes down to zero, balls die much sooner, so the boss can almost never hit you |

**Caveats:**
- **This cannot fill the sprite table.** `ThrowBall` uses slots from
  `Y = $05` down, so at most six balls can exist at the same time. The code
  makes each of those six stay. It does not make an unlimited number.
- The puff of smoke from `CODE_019ACB` never plays, because that is the call
  that is skipped.
- Balls that would have been removed now stay on the screen as dangers. So
  both fights become harder, not easier.

## Mario gets four fireballs at once

**Code:** `D9E8-6D07`
**Raw form:** `00FEB1:05` (address:new-byte; original byte `$07`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:29:30

**Mechanism:** The extended sprite pool has ten slots. A slot is free exactly
when `ExtSpriteNumber` is `$00`. There is no separate status byte. Every
place in the game that creates one looks for a slot with `LDY #$07` and
counts down. That is why slots `$08` and `$09` are reserved in practice.
`ShootFireball` (`bank_00.asm`) starts with `LDX.B #$09` and counts down with
`DEX / CPX.B #$07 / BNE`. It stops as soon as X gets to 7. Because of that
window of two slots, Mario can have exactly two fireballs on the screen. The
code lowers the bottom value to `$05`. So the search runs from `$09` down
to `$06`, and **four** fireballs can be active at the same time.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM reads `a2 09 bd 17 17 f0 06 ca e0 07 d0 f6 60`
at `$00FEA8`, which is
`LDX #$09 / LDA $1717,X / BEQ +6 / DEX / CPX #$07 / BNE -10 / RTS`. So the
bottom value operand is `$07` at `$00FEB1`. The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Variants:** `D1E8-6D07` (`00FEB1:06`) is the gentler version with three
fireballs. It competes for only one slot, not two.

**Caveats:**
- **Slots `$06`-`$07` are not free extras.** They are the top of the general
  extended sprite pool, and every other creator takes slots from it with
  `LDY #$07`. Mario's fireballs now compete for them. So a fireball can
  replace, or be replaced by, a Piranha Plant fireball, a lava splash, a spin
  jump star or a cloud game coin. On a busy screen, expect that projectiles
  sometimes do not appear.
- Nothing else changes. `ShootFireball`'s cooldown, the start offsets and the
  launch speeds do not change. So the extra fireballs exist only if you can
  press the button fast enough to fill the slots.

## Fireballs spawn but never move (extended-sprite slot leak)

**Code:** `D5BD-A4AC`
**Raw form:** `029B0B:07` (address:new-byte; original byte `$09`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:29:30

**Mechanism:** `RunExtendedSprites` (`bank_02.asm`) is the only code that runs
the ten-slot extended sprite pool on each frame:
`LDX.B #$09 / - STX CurSpriteProcess /
JSR RunOneExtendedSprite / DEX / BPL -`. The start index is both the highest
slot that runs and the full size of the loop. If you lower it to `$07`, the
top two slots never run. These are exactly the two slots that
`ShootFireball` reserves for Mario. The slots are still *allocated* (the
spawn writes `ExtSpriteNumber`), but they never *run*. So the fireball does
not move, is not drawn, and never clears its own slot. After two shots, the
fireball slots stay full, and Mario cannot shoot again for the rest of the
level.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM reads `a2 09 8e e9 15 20` at `$029B0A`, which
is `LDX #$09 / STX $15E9 / JSR …`. So the loop start value is `$09` at
`$029B0B`, which matches the first line of `RunExtendedSprites`. The address
is from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Caveats:**
- **This code shows how the pool works. It is not a fun code.** The slots
  stay full until the level loads again. Losing fire flower attacks for a
  whole level is more of a handicap than a cheat.
- Lower values stop more of the pool. At `$05`, two more general slots stop
  running, so the same problem also affects Piranha Plant fireballs and puffs
  of smoke.
- This loop writes `CurSpriteProcess` for the handlers to read. Slots that
  never run also never write their index. Nothing else reads it for the
  skipped slots, but keep this in mind if you use this code with other pool
  codes.

## Pitching the cape into a dive makes Mario rocket upward

**Code:** `ED2C-A76F`
**Raw form:** `00D7AE:F0` (address:new-byte; original byte `$06` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:34:40

**Mechanism:** `PlayerGravity` (`bank_00.asm`) is a table with 10 entries.
`CODE_00D948` adds an entry to `PlayerYSpeed` on each frame
(`CLC / ADC PlayerGravity,Y`). During cape flight, `CODE_00D8C6` sets the
index to `FlightPhase + 3`. The NTSC path is only `PLA / INY / INY / INY`,
and it does not double the value. (The `ASL` in the block next to it is part
of the PAL branch, which uses a 16-bit table.) So entries 4 to 9 are the cape
gravity for each flight angle. Entry 9 is `$06`, the strongest downward pull
in the table, and it is used for `FlightPhase` 6, the steepest forward dive.
The code changes it to `$F0` (-16). The strongest downward acceleration
becomes the strongest *upward* one. So when you hold the direction Mario
faces to go into a dive, he shoots up into the sky.

Phase 6 is part of normal flight, not a rare case. In mode 1 you hold the
direction you face (`FlightPhaseLimit[1] = 6`), and `FlightPhase` goes up one
step each time `CapePumpTimer` runs out. Also, `CODE_00EF99` separately tests
`FlightPhase >= 5` to start the cape's landing slam, and players do that move
all the time.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `10 f4 01 03 04 05 06 40 40 20` at `$00D7A8`. So the
base of `PlayerGravity` is at `$00D7A5`, its entry 9 (`$06`) is at `$00D7AE`,
and `PlayerMaxFallSpeed`'s `db $40,$40,$20,…` starts directly after it at
`$00D7AF`. This is the same layout that the source shows
(`db $06,$03,$04,$10,$F4,$01,$03,$04` / `db $05,$06`). The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` (checked as current in this session). It was encoded
and verified with a decode by `tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- **The `$C8` climb ceiling at `CODE_00D87E` still applies** to this code.
  This is different from the `CapeTargetYSpeed` codes. This code is on the
  `FlightPhase != 0` path, so the climb is limited to -56 per frame, however
  large the negative gravity is. Use it with `6D26-D4A4` + `6D26-D7A4` to
  remove that ceiling, but that uses all three Game Genie slots.
- Only phase 6 uses entry 9. All less steep angles keep the normal gravity,
  so the cape still acts normally until you go fully into the dive.
- `CODE_00D8C4` (`LDY #$02` then `+3`) also reads entry 5 (`$01`), for the
  case with no X speed. Entry 9 has no second reader like this.
- Entry `+3` of the same table (`$00D7A8`) is still not checked in the
  disassembly. No traced path reads it. Do not change it.

## Cape slam on every caped landing

**Code:** `DD3C-ADD7`
**Raw form:** `00EFA0:00` (address:new-byte; original byte `$05`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:34:40

**Mechanism:** `CODE_00EF99` is the landing handler's path for when Mario is
not on Yoshi. It clears `SpriteStompCounter` and `FlightPhase`. Then it
starts the cape's ground slam only if the flight was steep enough:
`CPY.B #$05 / BCS CallGroundPound`. `CallGroundPound` checks `TempPlayerAir`
and calls `GroundPound` (`bank_02.asm`). That routine sets `ScreenShakeTimer`
to `$30` and goes through the sprite table, and it kills everything on the
