ground. The code sets the compare value to `$00`. Every unsigned value is
`>= 0`, so the `BCS` is always taken, and **every** landing does the slam.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM reads `9c 97 16 9c 07 14 c0 05 b0 0b a5 19 c9 02`
at `$00EF99`, which is
`STZ $1697 / STZ $1407 / CPY #$05 / BCS +$0B / LDA $19 / CMP #$02`. So the
`CPY` operand is `$05` at `$00EFA0`. The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

> **Backlog correction:** during the sweep, this byte was recorded as
> `$00EFA2`. But `$00EFA2` is the *offset* of the `BCS` (`$0B`), not the
> `CPY` operand. The `C0 05` pair is two bytes earlier, at `$00EF9F`/`$00EFA0`.
> The ROM read above found this error.

**Caveats:**
- **`TempPlayerAir` still controls it.** So the slam happens once per
  landing, not on every frame while Mario stands.
- **`GroundPound` kills enemies on the ground.** The Yoshi stomp
  (`YoshiStompRoutine`) only flips them. So this is the stronger of the two,
  and it really changes combat. It is not only a visual change.
- This path is the landing handler for when Mario is **not** on Yoshi. So it
  adds to the published Yoshi ground pound codes (`DD36-AD67` + `DD36-A4A7`)
  and does not repeat them.
- At this point, `Y` is the flight phase that was saved before
  `STZ FlightPhase`. So the code does not need Mario to still have the cape
  at the moment he lands. It only uses the value that the landing handler
  started with.

## The reserve item drops at the edge of the screen

**Code:** `D669-DD66`
**Raw form:** `028052:08` (address:new-byte; original byte `$78`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:34:40

**Mechanism:** `DropReserveItem` (`bank_02.asm`) creates the item box's
contents at a fixed *screen* position, not near Mario:
`LDA.B #$78 / CLC / ADC.B Layer1XPos / STA SpriteXPosLow,X`. The
`LDA Layer1XPos+1 / ADC #$00` pair below it adds the carry into
`SpriteXPosHigh`. A matching `LDA.B #$20 / ADC Layer1YPos` sets the vertical
offset. `$78` is 120, the middle of the 256-pixel screen, directly below the
item box on the screen. The code changes it to `$08`, so the item appears at
the left edge of the screen.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM reads `a9 78 18 65 1a 95 e4 a5 1b 69 00 9d e0 14
a9 20 18 65 1c` at `$028051`, which is `LDA #$78 / CLC / ADC $1A / STA $E4,X /
LDA $1B / ADC #$00 / STA $14E0,X / LDA #$20 / CLC / ADC $1C`. So the X offset
is at `$028052` and the Y offset is at `$028060`. The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

**Variants**, each one is a single code:

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `D669-DD66` | `028052:08` | item drops at the far left of the screen |
| `3669-DD66` | `028052:E8` | item drops at the far right of the screen |
| `CD61-DDD6` | `028060:A0` | item drops near the *bottom* of the screen, not the top (`$20` → `$A0`) |

**Caveats:**
- The drop position is relative to `Layer1XPos`, the camera position, not to
  Mario. So the item appears at a fixed place on the screen, wherever Mario
  is. At an edge, it can appear inside a wall or above a pit.
- `DropReserveItem` has two callers: pressing Select, and `PowerDown` when
  Mario takes damage. Both use this position. So a mushroom that drops
  because of damage also appears at the edge, and that is when you least want
  to chase it.
- The vertical variant also depends on the sprite's own gravity. A mushroom
  that appears low has less distance to fall before it gets to the floor. This
  changes how far it walks before you can catch it.

## The reserve item flies up out of the item box

**Code:** `DA60-DDA6`
**Raw form:** `028043:0C` (address:new-byte; original byte `$08` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:40:01

**Mechanism:** `DropReserveItem` (`bank_02.asm`) starts its spawn block with
`LDA.B #$08 / STA SpriteStatus,X`. Status `$08` means "Normal". `HandleSprite`
(`bank_01.asm`) uses that byte to send every sprite through a documented
table with 13 entries. Status `$0C` is `HandleGoalPowerup`. This is the
routine that runs the powerup you get when you carry a sprite past the goal
tape:

```
HandleGoalPowerup:
    JSR CallSpriteMain
    JSR SubOffscreen0Bnk1
    JSR SubUpdateSprPos
    DEC.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    DEC.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    JSR IsOnGround
    BEQ +
    JSR SetSomeYSpeed__
  + RTS
```

The first line is the same `CallSpriteMain` that status `$08` uses.
(`HandleSprite` has status 8 hardcoded as `JMP CallSpriteMain`, only to make
it faster.) So the item keeps all of its normal behavior, including the
Mario contact check in `CODE_01C4AC` and the `TouchedPowerUp` collection
path. What `$0C` *adds* is the two `DEC.B SpriteYSpeed,X` instructions. They
give a constant upward acceleration of -2 on each frame. So when the reserve
item comes out, it now rises slowly up out of the box like the goal tape
powerup, and it does not drop.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `a9 08 9d c8` at `$028042`, which is
`LDA #$08 / STA $14C8,X`. So the status immediate is `$08` at `$028043`. This
matches the source line `LDA.B #$08 ;
Sprite status = Normal`. Each entry of the `HandleSprite` dispatch table has
a comment in `bank_01.asm`. This is what shows that `$0C` is a real status
that the game can use, not a guess. The address is from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` (checked as current in this session). It was encoded
and verified with a decode by `tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

> **Backlog gate resolved.** The sweep suggested status `$09` ("Carryable"),
> so that the powerups would already be held when they come out. It also
> noted that the status table must be read again first, because this could
> soft-lock the game. Reading it again shows that `$09` does not work. Status
> `$09` goes to `HandleSprStunned`, which never calls `CallSpriteMain`. Only
> the powerup's own main routine can get to `TouchedPowerUp`. So you could
> never collect a `$09` mushroom. `$0C` is the status that keeps the item
> working, and that is why it was published.

**Caveats:**
- Both callers of `DropReserveItem` are affected: pressing Select, and
  `PowerDown` when Mario takes damage. A mushroom that comes out because of
  damage also flies upward, so it is easier to lose.
- The rise works against the item's own gravity, which `CallSpriteMain`
  applies. The total movement is upward, but the disassembly does not give
  the exact rate, because it depends on which powerup was in the box.
- `SetSomeYSpeed__` runs only when `IsOnGround` finds contact. A sprite that
  appears in the air near the top of the screen usually does not touch the
  ground.

## A 1-up on every coin (REDISCOVERY)

NOTE: The libretro cheat database already has "extra life at N coins" codes
that change these same two bytes. This code was found again separately, from
the disassembly.

**Codes:** `DF64-A7D7` **and** `DF67-AFA7` (both needed)
**Raw form:** `008F2C:01` and `008F37:01` (address:new-byte; both original bytes
are `$64`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:40:01

**Mechanism:** `HandleCoins` (`bank_00.asm`) runs once per frame as part of
the status bar update. But the whole block is behind
`LDA CoinAdder / BEQ
HandleLives`, so it only does something on a frame when a coin is added.
When that happens, it increments `PlayerCoins`. Then it uses the same
constant `!CoinsPer1up` (`$64`, 100, from `constants.asm`) two times:
`CMP.B #!CoinsPer1up / BCC HandleLives / INC GivePlayerLives`, and then
`LDA PlayerCoins / SEC / SBC.B #!CoinsPer1up / STA PlayerCoins`. The constant
is assembled into two separate instruction operands. So you can change the
limit and the amount that is subtracted separately. If you set **both** to
`$01`, you get a life for every coin, *and* the counter stays correct
(1 − 1 = 0).

**Evidence:** the reference ROM has `$64` at both `$008F2C` (the `CMP`
operand) and `$008F37` (the `SBC` operand). These match the two
`#!CoinsPer1up` places in `HandleCoins`. The addresses are from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`. Both were encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. These two bytes are also among the 11 known-good test
vectors that the encoder checks itself against. They come from romdev's
bundled cheat DB, which is a separate implementation, and it agrees. This
comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Variants:** `DC64-A7D7` + `DC67-AFA7` sets both to `$0A`. This gives a 1-up
every ten coins. It is a gentler version, and the coin counter still means
something.

> **Backlog correction:** the sweep said to change only the `CMP`. It said
> "the counter still resets correctly as long as the new value ≤ the
> subtract value". That is wrong. If the compare is `$01` and the subtract
> value is still `$64`, the first coin calculates `1 − 100`, and
> `PlayerCoins` wraps to `$9D`. After that, the coin count on the screen has
> no meaning and changes on every pickup. The code with one byte still gives
> a life for each coin, but it is not the clean version. Use the pair.

**Caveats:**
- **This uses two codes for one effect**, so only one Game Genie slot is left.
- `GivePlayerLives` is a queue that other code empties. So the lives come
  with the normal sound and animation, not all at once.
- Nothing else reads `!CoinsPer1up`. The bonus star limit is a different
  constant, and it has its own pair of places.

## Start with 99 lives (REDISCOVERY)

NOTE: The libretro cheat database already has a "start with N lives" code that
changes this byte. This code was found again separately, from the
disassembly.

**Code:** `17B4-6F07`
**Raw form:** `009E25:63` (address:new-byte; original byte `$04`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:40:01

**Mechanism:** `LoadSaveAndFadeToOW` (`bank_00.asm`) runs when you choose a
save file on the title screen. It fades out the music and sets player 2's
life count to `-1`. Then it loops to write the start life value into
`SavedPlayerLives` for each player in the game (`LDX IsTwoPlayerGame`). It
also writes the same value into the current `PlayerLives`:

```
    LDA.B #4                                  ; Set initial lives to 4
  - STA.W SavedPlayerLives,X
    DEX
    BPL -
    STA.W PlayerLives                         ; Current lives is also 4
```

The `#4` is one immediate value that all of those writes use. If you change
it to `$63` (99), the file starts with 99 lives, and so do both saved slots.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM has `$04` at `$009E25`. This is the operand
of the `LDA.B #4` shown above. The address is from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It
was encoded and verified with a decode by `tools/gg_encode.py`. This byte is
also one of the encoder's 11 known-good self-test vectors from romdev's
bundled cheat DB, and it agrees. This comes from the disassembly. It was
**not** tested in play.

**Variants:** `DFB4-6F07` (`009E25:01`) does the opposite. Every file starts
with only one life.

**Caveats:**
- **The code must be on before file select**, not after. This value is used
  only one time, when the save loads. If you turn it on during a level,
  nothing happens.
- On every frame, `HandleLives` limits the count on the screen to
  `!MaximumLives-1` (`$62`, 98). So when the status bar updates, a value of
  99 from this code is reduced to 98. Use `$62` if you want the value to
  stay without a visible correction.
- The `LDA.B #-1 / STA SavedPlayerLives+1` above the loop sets player 2 to
  "no game". In a two-player game, the loop writes this value over it, so
  both players get the new count.

## Green Yoshi gets the ground pound from any shell

**Code:** `D4E0-0460`
**Raw form:** `01F14A:02` (address:new-byte; original byte `$00` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:46:17

**Mechanism:** `CODE_01F14B` (`bank_01.asm`) decides what a Yoshi gets for
holding a shell. It uses the *palettes* of the two sprites, not their sprite
numbers. That is why one small pair of tables covers all Koopa types at the
same time. It gets CCC (bits 3-1 of `SpriteOBJAttribute`) with
`LSR / AND #$07` **two times**: once for the Yoshi and once for the shell in
its mouth. It converts each one with `YoshiAbilityIndex` into a color class
from 0 to 3. Then it combines them as `(YoshiClass * 4) | ShellClass`, and
uses that as the index into `YoshiShellAbility`. That table's value is a pair
of bits: bit 0 = ground pound (`YoshiCanStomp`), bit 1 = wings
(`YoshiHasWingsEvt`).

`YoshiAbilityIndex` is `db $03,$02,$02,$03,$01,$00`, and CCC is its index.
Entry 5 is green. The code changes it from `$00` (class 0, green) to `$02`
(class 2, yellow). Then **everything green counts as yellow**. The table is
read two times, so this also includes the normal green Yoshi that you ride.
So a green Yoshi uses the yellow row of `YoshiShellAbility`
(`db $01,$01,$01,$03`). That row gives the ground pound for *every* shell
color, and stomp plus wings for a blue shell. The first Yoshi acts like a
yellow Yoshi for the whole game.

**Evidence:** the color mapping was worked out from the ROM data. It was not
assumed. `LoadSpriteTables` (`bank_07.asm`) sets `SpriteOBJAttribute` to
`Sprite166EVals[SpriteNumber] AND #$0F`. For the sprites that give abilities
(sprite numbers `< $0D`, the limit that `CODE_01F14B`'s `CMP.B #$0D` checks),
those values are `$0A $08 $06 $04`, repeated. That gives CCC 5 = green,
4 = red, 3 = blue, 2 = yellow for all 13 entries. This agrees with the color
names in the dispatch comments of `CallSpriteInit`. `YoshiPal`
(`db $09,$07,$05,$07`, used by `InitYoshiEgg`) separately gives CCC 4/3/2/3 =
red/blue/yellow/blue by the same rule. The reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc`
without its 512-byte copier header) reads `03 02 02 03 01 00` at `$01F145` and
`00 00 01 02 00 00 01 02 01 01
01 03 02 02` at `$01F137`, which matches both source rows. It was encoded and
verified with a decode by `tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the
disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

> This code was blocked during the sweep. The tables had names, but nothing
> recorded which palette is which color, so no entry could be described by
> color. It was unblocked when the mapping was worked out from
> `Sprite166EVals` and comments were added to both tables in `bank_01.asm`.
> That build was checked to be byte-identical to `comparison_U.smc`, so the
> comments changed nothing else.

**Variants:**

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `D4E0-0460` | `01F14A:02` | green counts as yellow: ground pound from any shell |
| `D7E0-0460` | `01F14A:03` | green counts as blue: **wings from any shell**, so a green Yoshi flies with anything in its mouth |
| `DDE0-0400` | `01F149:00` | red counts as green, not class 1, so red shells are no longer special |

**Caveats:**
- **The table is read two times, so a changed entry changes both the Yoshi
  and the shell.** That is how the code works, not a side effect. But it
  means that you cannot change a shell color without also changing a Yoshi of
  that color.
- **Fire breathing is not in these tables.** `YoshiShellAbility` has only the
  stomp and wings bits. The fire ability is handled in a different place.
  That is why a red shell gives `$00` for a green Yoshi in the normal table.
  This code cannot give or remove fire.
- The `$03` (blue) variant depends on a real read past the end of the table.
  The blue Yoshi row of `YoshiShellAbility` has only two of its four bytes. So
  indices `$0E`/`$0F` read the first two bytes of `YoshiAbilityIndex` (`$03`,
  `$02`). Those give stomp plus wings, and wings. That is exactly the "blue
  Yoshi always flies" behavior that the rest of the row has. So the result is
  well-defined, but you cannot move one of the two tables without the other.
- `YoshiHasWingsEvt` is cleared on each frame at the start of `Yoshi`, and it
  is calculated again for each shell. So the ability does not stay. It lasts
  only while the shell is in Yoshi's mouth.

## Stomping a Para-Koopa's wings off leaves a live Bob-omb

**Code:** `D2C2-AD09`
**Raw form:** `01A7D1:0D` (address:new-byte; original byte `$04` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 02:54:33

**Mechanism:** in SMW, winged enemies do not die when Mario stomps them.
Instead they *change into a simpler enemy*. `CODE_01A95D` (`bank_01.asm`)
handles the stomp. If a sprite has bit `$40` set in `SpriteTweakerE`, the
routine looks up the new sprite in `SpriteToSpawn` (`$01A7C9`), with the
sprite number as the index. It writes the result directly back into
`SpriteNumber,X`:

```
CODE_01A998:
    LDA.W SpriteToSpawn,Y
CODE_01A99B:
    STA.B SpriteNumber,X
    ...
    JSL LoadSpriteTables
```

Index `$08` is "Green Koopa, flying left", and its normal entry is `$04`, a
normal green Koopa. That is why a stomped Para-Koopa leaves a normal Koopa
shell. The code changes that entry to `$0D`. Then the same stomp makes a
**Bob-omb**: the walking bomb that explodes a few seconds after *it* is
stomped. The change works cleanly, because `CODE_01A99B` calls
`LoadSpriteTables` with the new sprite number. So the new sprite gets the
Bob-omb's own tweaker bytes, palette and clipping, not the Koopa's.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `00 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 04 04 05 05 07 00 00 0f 0f 0f 0d`
at `$01A7C9`. So index `$08` is the ninth byte, `$04`, at `$01A7D1`. The read
at `$01A998` is `b9 c9 a7` = `LDA $A7C9,Y`, which checks the table base.
`$01A95D` reads `20 46 ab b4 9e bd 86 16 29 40 f0 55` = `JSR CODE_01AB46 /
LDY SpriteNumber,X / LDA SpriteTweakerE,X / AND #$40 / BEQ …`. This checks the
`$40` test and that `Y` is the sprite number. The addresses are from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`. It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

> This code was blocked during the sweep. `SpriteToSpawn`/`SpriteToSpawn2`
> had names but no documentation. Nothing recorded which indices the game can
> use, and the read at `SpriteToSpawn2-$40,Y` looked like an off-by-one error.
> It was unblocked in three steps: the `$40` tweaker test was worked out from
> `Sprite1686Vals` (`$0007F590`), the indices that the game uses were listed,
> and comments were added to both tables in `bank_01.asm`. That build was
> checked to be byte-identical to `comparison_U.smc`, so the comments changed
> nothing else.

**Variants:**

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `D2C2-AD09` | `01A7D1:0D` | green Para-Koopa changes into a **Bob-omb** |
| `FDC2-A409` | `01A7D9:10` | winged Goomba changes into a **winged Goomba**. The wings come back when you stomp them off, so it can never lose them |
| `D0C2-A4A9` | `01A7DB:04` | Para-Bomb (the Bob-omb with a parachute) changes into a green Koopa, not a Bob-omb. The bomb is never live when it lands |

**Caveats:**
- **Four readers use the table, with two different tests, and the game uses
  only ten of its eighteen entries.** *(Corrected 2026-08-09: this entry
  first named only the stomp reader and said that indices `$00`–`$07` were
  never used. That was wrong. See below.)* Three readers test
  `SpriteTweakerE` bit `$40` ("has wings"): `CODE_01A95D` (this stomp path),
  `CODE_01F2DF` (Yoshi spits out what is in its mouth) and `CODE_029448` in
  `bank_02` (a killed sprite that you can jump on, but that does not die when
  you jump on it, becomes carryable). `Sprite1686Vals` sets bit `$40` for
  `$08 $09 $0A $0B $0C $10 $3F $40 $6D $6E
  $73 $C6 $D7 $E7 $F2 $F5 $F6 $F8 $FE`. Of those, only `$08`–`$0C` and `$10`
  are inside the table's range and below the `CPY #$3F` / `CPY #$72` limits.
  The fourth reader is `CODE_01F344` (Yoshi's mouth handles a sprite it has
  chewed). It tests bit **`$02`** ("has a shell") and a sprite number
  `< $0D`. `Sprite1686Vals` gives bit `$02` to `$04`–`$07`, and `$42`/`$52`
  to `$08`–`$0C`. So **indices `$04` to `$0C` are all used**, through the
  mouth. Only `$00`–`$03`, `$0D`, `$0E`, `$0F` and `$11`
  (`$01A7C9`–`$01A7CC`, `$01A7D6`–`$01A7D8`, `$01A7DA`) are really never
  used. If you change `$04`–`$07`, it changes what a Koopa that Yoshi has
  chewed turns into, and nothing else.
- Index `$08` is only "flying left". The other Para-Koopa types have their own
  entries: `$09` bouncing, `$0A` red vertical, `$0B` red horizontal, `$0C`
  yellow. So this one code changes only the green one that flies left. Also
  change `$09` (`$01A7D2`) if you want both green types.
- The normal Para-Bomb path at `CODE_01A98A` sets `SpriteMisc1540` to `$80`
  before it creates its `$0D`. The `SpriteToSpawn` path at `CODE_01A998` does
  not. So a Bob-omb made this way starts with the `$1540` value that the Koopa
  had, not a new value. Its fuse behavior in the first frames may not match a
  Bob-omb that was created normally.
- The winged Goomba variant means you cannot really kill that enemy by
  stomping it. Shells, fireballs, capes and spin jumps still hurt it (the
  spin jump path branches at `CODE_01A91C`, before the code gets to this
  table). So it is an annoyance, not a soft-lock. But a level that needs you
  to defeat one to continue will get stuck.

## Yoshi never swallows the shell in its mouth

**Code:** `EEEC-0F00`
**Raw form:** `01F1A5:FF` (address:new-byte; original byte `$03` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 03:37:04

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** when Yoshi chews something that has a shell, the shell is not
destroyed. It stays in Yoshi's mouth with a countdown, and Mario can spit it
out again until the countdown ends. `CODE_01F344` (`bank_01.asm`) is the step
that handles the chew. It checks `SpriteTweakerE` bit `$02` ("has a shell").
If the bit is set, it keeps the sprite alive with status `$07` ("in Yoshi's
mouth"), and it sets `YoshiSwallowTimer` to `$FF`:

```
CODE_01F344:
    LDA.W SpriteTweakerE,Y
    AND.B #$02          ; no shell -> just kill it
    BEQ CODE_01F373
    LDA.B #$07          ; status = in Yoshi's mouth
    STA.W SpriteStatus,Y
    LDA.B #$FF          ; the hold timer
    STA.W YoshiSwallowTimer
```

That timer does **not** count down on every frame. `CODE_01F1A2` puts it
behind a frame counter mask, so it decrements on only one frame out of four:

```
CODE_01F1A2:
    LDA.B EffFrame
    AND.B #$03          ; <- the patched byte, at $01F1A5
    BNE +               ; 3 frames out of 4: skip the swallow timer entirely
    LDA.W YoshiSwallowTimer
    BEQ +
    DEC.W YoshiSwallowTimer
    BNE +
    ...                 ; expired: destroy the sprite, empty the mouth, gulp
```

`$FF` steps at one step per four frames is 1020 frames, about
**17 seconds** of holding a shell. This is the normal time in which you can
carry a Koopa in Yoshi's mouth and spit it at something. If the mask is
`$FF`, the branch is taken on every frame *except* the frame when `EffFrame`
wraps to `$00`. So the timer steps once per 256 frames: 65280 frames, about
**18 minutes**. In practice, Yoshi never swallows a shell. It stays in the
mouth for the rest of the level, and you can always spit it out.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `a5 14 29 03 d0 1e ad ac 18 f0 19 ce` at `$01F1A2` =
`LDA $14 / AND #$03 / BNE + / LDA $18AC / BEQ + / DEC $18AC`. So the mask byte
is at `$01F1A5`. `$01F35B` reads `a9 ff 8d ac 18 b9 9e 00 c9 0d b0 09` =
`LDA #$FF / STA $18AC / LDA $009E,Y / CMP #$0D / BCS …`. This checks both the
`$FF` reload and the `< $0D` Koopa test. The addresses are from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` (made again, and `--check` passes against the current
sources). It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

> This code was blocked during the sweep. The Yoshi eat and swallow timers
> had names, but nothing documented how fast they count. So nothing recorded
> that the two timers in `CODE_01F1A2` run at different speeds. It was
> unblocked when comments were added to `CODE_01F0A2`, `CODE_01F1A2` and
> `CODE_01F344` in `bank_01.asm`. That build was checked to be byte-identical
> to `comparison_U.smc`, so the comments changed nothing else.

**Variants:**

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `EEEC-0F00` | `01F1A5:FF` | swallow timer steps once per 256 frames, so in practice a shell is **never** swallowed |
| `DDEC-0F00` | `01F1A5:00` | timer steps on every frame, so the shell is gone in about 4.25 s, four times faster than normal |
| `D6E9-A7D0` | `01F35C:08` | set the hold timer to `$08`, not `$FF`, so Yoshi swallows a shell after about **half a second** |
| `DFE9-A7D0` | `01F35C:01` | set it to `$01`, so the shell is swallowed almost as soon as it is chewed |
| `0DEA-DDD0` | `01F0C0:40` | the *other* timer: `$40`, not `$06`, for the delay between the tongue catching an enemy and the mouth taking it. Caught enemies hang on the tongue for about a second |
| `D2CA-A709` | `01A7CD:0D` | Yoshi chews a **green Koopa**, and what stays in its mouth becomes a **Bob-omb**. You spit out a live walking bomb |

**Caveats:**
- **The mask changes only the swallow timer.** The eat timer
  (`YoshiStartEatTimer`) is decremented *after* the `BNE +`, on the side that
  always runs. So it still steps once per frame, whatever `$01F1A5` contains.
  So both `$01F1A5` variants change only how long a shell stays in the mouth,
  and nothing else about eating.
- **`EffFrame` (`$14`) is the global frame counter, not a Yoshi variable.**
  But `$01F1A5` is the operand of *this* `AND` only, and no other routine
  reads that byte. Nothing other than the mouth timer changes.
- The `$01F0C0` variant delays when the mouth takes the enemy, so it also
  delays when `CODE_01F344` runs. It does not make the tongue itself stay out
  longer (`YoshiTongueTimer` is a different timer). So an enemy hangs at the
  end of the tongue. With a large enough value, you can spit it out before it
  is ever chewed.
- The `$01A7CD` redirect goes through the mouth's `SpriteToSpawn` lookup, and
  that path **does not run `LoadSpriteTables` again**. A Bob-omb made this
  way keeps the green Koopa's tweaker bytes, clipping and palette. Only its
  sprite number changes. So its graphics and hitbox will not match a normal
  Bob-omb, and its fuse starts from the value that the Koopa had.
- Only Koopas can get to the `$01A7CD` path. `CODE_01F344` needs a sprite
  number `< $0D` *and* `SpriteTweakerE` bit `$02`, and `Sprite1686Vals` gives
  that bit to `$04`–`$0C`. A chewed Goomba, Rex or Chuck has no shell. It is
  destroyed at once at `CODE_01F373` and never gets to either timer.

## Morton, Roy and Ludwig die in one stomp

**Code:** `DFAA-A705`
**Raw form:** `01CFCD:01` (address:new-byte; original byte `$03` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 03:52:11

**Mechanism:** all seven Koopa Kids are one sprite (`$29`). The only thing
that decides which one you fight is the Y position where the level designer
put the sprite. `InitKoopaKid` shifts that position right four times and
stores the 4-bit value as `SpriteTableC2`. The three Mode 7 bosses (`$00`
Morton, `$01` Roy, `$02` Ludwig) run `WallKoopaKids` in `bank_01.asm`. This is
a state machine with six phases in `SpriteMisc151C`: wait, fall in, fight,
get stomped, die, clear the level.

Phase 3 (stomped) counts a timer down through three parts. On the one frame
when that timer equals `$40`, it counts the hit at `CODE_01CFC6`:

```
CODE_01CFC6:
    INC.W SpriteMisc1626,X    ; one more stomp landed
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1626,X
    CMP.B #$03                ; <- the patched byte, at $01CFCD
    BCC +                     ; fewer than three: survive, go back to fighting
CODE_01CFD0:
    LDA.B #!SFX_BOSSDEAD
    STA.W SPCIO0
    LDA.B #$04                ; phase 4: the death animation
    STA.W SpriteMisc151C,X
    ...
```

`SpriteMisc1626` is the hit counter, and this `CMP` is the **only** place
that tests it. So the `$03` means exactly "how many stomps kill this boss".
If you set it to `$01`, the first stomp already passes the `BCS`, and the boss
goes directly into its death spin. The sound effect, the shrinking Mode 7
layer, the puff of smoke and the castle clear cutscene all happen on the
first hit.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `fe 26 16 bd 26 16 c9 03 90 0f a9 1f 8d f9 1d a9` at
`$01CFC6` =
`INC $1626,X / LDA $1626,X / CMP #$03 / BCC +$0F / LDA #$1F / STA $1DF9`. So
the compare operand is at `$01CFCD`, and the `BCC` skips exactly the
eight-byte death block. `$01CD92` reads `01 01 00 02 02 03 03`. These are the
seven arena types, one for each boss. This is what puts Morton with Roy and
Iggy with Larry, and it checks the `SpriteTableC2` order. The addresses are
from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (made again, and `--check` passes against the
current sources). It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

> This code was blocked during the sweep, and it was the largest blocked
> area left. `WallKoopaKids`, `PlatformKoopaKids` and `PipeKoopaKids` had
> names, but their state code was only bare `CODE_*` labels, with 8 comment
> lines in 242. So no byte in them could be explained. It was unblocked when
> comments were added in `bank_01.asm` to `InitKoopaKid`, the `KoopaKid`
> dispatch, all six `SpriteMisc151C` phases and Ludwig's three sub-states.
> That build was checked to be byte-identical to `comparison_U.smc`, so the
> comments changed nothing else.
>
> This work also **fixed the dispatch table's own comments**, which were
> wrong by two. The seven `dw` entries had the labels `02 - Ludwig` to
> `06 - Wendy` on entries 0–4. The seven arena types in `DATA_01CD92` and the
> `CMP #$05` / `CMP #$03` group tests in `InitKoopaKid` both show that the
> table starts at 0: Morton, Roy, Ludwig, Iggy, Larry, Lemmy, Wendy.

**Variants:**

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `DFAA-A705` | `01CFCD:01` | one stomp kills Morton, Roy or Ludwig |
| `D4AA-A705` | `01CFCD:02` | two stomps, not three |
| `D6AA-A705` | `01CFCD:08` | eight stomps, so the boss fight is much longer |
| `D9A8-A4D5` | `01CFB8:05` | skip the hit counter completely. The first stomp sends the boss to **phase 5**, so the boss clear music and castle cutscene start at once, and the boss only disappears, with no death animation |
| `0DAB-6405` | `01CE99:40` | Ludwig never spits fireballs (the trigger compares against a value that the masked counter can never have) |
| `7EAC-6405` | `01CEA9:3F` | Ludwig's standing phase is a quarter as long. So he charges much more often and spits one fireball per cycle, not four |
| `DDAB-0D65` | `01CD92:00` | Morton gets Ludwig's arena type: no falling ceiling pillar and no sprite lock when he enters, and he turns to face Mario as he moves |

**Caveats:**
- **This is three bosses, not all seven.** Iggy and Larry
  (`PlatformKoopaKids`) and Lemmy and Wendy (`PipeKoopaKids`, whose fight code
  is in bank 03) have their own ways to lose, and they never use `$01CFCD`.
  Reznor and Bowser are completely different sprites.
- The hit counter increments on the one frame when the stomp timer passes
  `$40`, not at contact. So with `$01`, the full squash and flash still plays
  before the death spin starts. The boss does not die on the same frame that
  you land on it.
- `$01CFB8:05` does not use `SpriteMisc1626` at all. So it also skips
  `!SFX_BOSSDEAD` and the shrink animation in phase 4. Phase 5 runs on its
  first frame, because the timer it checks is already zero at that time. The
  level does end correctly (`CutsceneID` is incremented and `EndLevelTimer`
  is decremented in the same way), but the boss disappears and does not die
  on the screen.
- `$01CD92:00` changes Morton's *arena*, not his moves. He still runs the wall
  climb routine at `CODE_01D116`. Without the entrance, `HorizLayer1Setting`
  is never set to zero and `SpriteLock` is never set, so the camera acts
  differently before the fight. Nobody has seen whether the room looks
  correct without the pillar.
- Ludwig's fireballs come from `CODE_01D059`. It checks sprite slots `$04`
  down to `$00`, and it stops with no error if all five are in use. So codes
  that make him shoot more often are limited by free slots, not only by
  timing.

## Mode 7 bosses take 255 stomps

**Code:** `EEAA-A705`
**Raw form:** `01CFCD:FF` (address:new-byte; original byte `$03` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 03:52:11

Tags: `challenge`

**Mechanism:** this is the same byte as "Morton, Roy and Ludwig die in one
stomp" above. The `CMP` at `$01CFCD` is the only test of the hit counter
`SpriteMisc1626`, and its operand is the number of stomps that kills Morton,
Roy or Ludwig. With `$FF`, the boss dies on the 255th stomp. Each stomp
plays the full squash and flash, so in practice the three Mode 7 bosses
cannot be killed.

**Evidence:** see the entry above. The ROM reads `c9 03` at `$01CFCC`, and the
code decodes to `$01CFCD <- $FF`. This comes from the disassembly. It was
**not** tested in play.

**Caveats:**
- Only Morton, Roy and Ludwig. Iggy, Larry, Lemmy and Wendy never use
  `$01CFCD`.
- `SpriteMisc1626` is one byte, and it is compared after the `INC`, so the
  255th stomp still ends the fight. It never wraps to 0 first.
- Do not use this with the other `$01CFCD` codes. They patch the same byte.

## Iggy and Larry fall off their platform the moment the fight starts

**Code:** `DDE5-DFD5`
**Raw form:** `01FC74:00` (address:new-byte; original byte `$D8` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 03:28:14

**Mechanism:** Iggy and Larry are the two Koopa Kids (`SpriteTableC2` `$03`
and `$04`) that `InitKoopaKid` sends to `PlatformKoopaKids` in `bank_01.asm`.
This is the fight on the tilting Mode 7 platform above lava. Morton, Roy and
Ludwig have a hit counter, but these two have **no hit counter at all**.
Nothing in `PlatformKoopaKids` uses `SpriteMisc1626`. You win the fight by
position. The boss walks and gets pushed around in screen X, and the only
thing that ends the fight is when that X leaves the area of the platform.
That test is four instructions long, and both of its numbers are immediates:

```
CODE_01FC62:
    ...
    LDA.B SpriteXPosLow,X
    CMP.B #$20                ; left edge  (operand at $01FC70)
    BCC CODE_01FC77
    CMP.B #$D8                ; right edge (operand at $01FC74)
    BCC +                     ; still on the platform
CODE_01FC77:
    LDA.W IggyLarryTempXPos   ; \ start falling from where it was drawn
    STA.B SpriteXPosLow,X     ; |
    LDA.W IggyLarryTempYPos   ; |
    STA.B SpriteYPosLow,X     ; |
    INC.W SpriteMisc160E,X    ; / from now on: gravity, not walking
```

`SpriteMisc160E` is the "off the edge" flag. When it is set, `CODE_01FB36`
stops running the walking code. It applies gravity instead (+2 per frame, up
to a terminal speed of `$40`) until the boss's Y gets into the lava range
`$58`–`$7F`. That plays `!SFX_BOSSINLAVA`, kills every sprite and prepares
the level clear.

The code changes the right edge to `$00`. Then `CMP #$00 / BCC +` is a branch
that can never be taken, because carry is always set after a compare with
zero. So on the first frame that the interaction routine runs, the game
decides that the boss is off the platform. It falls into the lava, and the
castle clear cutscene starts before Mario has done anything.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `c9 20 90 04 c9 d8 90 0d ad b8 14` at `$01FC6F` =
`CMP #$20 / BCC +$04 / CMP #$D8 / BCC +$0D / LDA $14B8`. So the left edge
operand is at `$01FC70`, and the right edge operand is at `$01FC74`. The
addresses are from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (made again, and `--check` passes
against the current sources). It was encoded and verified with a decode by
`tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested
in play.

> This code was blocked during the sweep. `PlatformKoopaKids` was a named
> label followed by about 380 lines of bare `CODE_*` code, so no byte in it
> could be explained. It was unblocked when comments were added in
> `bank_01.asm` to these parts: the state variables (`SpriteMisc1534`,
> `1564`, `154C`, `1558`, `160E`, `163E`), the falling and walking branches of
> `CODE_01FB36`, the shell sequence at `CODE_01FC2A`, the edge and contact
> test at `CODE_01FC62` and the fireball handler at `CODE_01FD0A`. That build
> was checked to be byte-identical to `comparison_U.smc`, so the comments
> changed nothing else.

**Variants:**

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `DDE5-DFD5` | `01FC74:00` | the boss is off the platform on the first frame |
| `6DE5-DFD5` | `01FC74:80` | the right half of the platform is gone, so one good push wins |
| `56E5-DDD5` | `01FC70:78` | the same on the left. With the code above, there is no area left to walk on |
| `DDE5-DDD5` | `01FC70:00` | the left edge test can never be true, so you can only push the boss off the right side |
| `0DED-0DD5` | `01FD00:40` | a stomp pushes the boss for `$40` frames, not `$18`, so each hit moves it about three times as far |
| `DFED-0DD5` | `01FD00:01` | stomps almost do not move it, so the fight becomes very long |
| `0DE0-0F65` | `01FD46:40` | fireballs push harder than a normal stomp, so Fire Mario can win from far away |
| `DDE7-D7D5` | `01FC3C:00` | the boss never throws its ball (the throw happens on the one step when the shell timer equals the changed value, and zero is skipped) |
| `DEEF-AD61` | `01FB12:0F` | goes into its shell every `$10` qualifying frames, not every `$80`, so eight times as often |
| `96E9-A701` | `01FB5D:58` | the lava is never found: the boss falls off and keeps falling forever, and the level never ends |
| `DFE1-AF61` | `01FB66:01` | the clear cutscene starts on the frame when the boss touches the lava, not `$50` frames later |

**Caveats:**
- **This is only Iggy and Larry.** Morton, Roy and Ludwig run
  `WallKoopaKids`, and the three-stomp counter at `$01CFCD` kills them (see
  the previous entry). Lemmy and Wendy run `PipeKoopaKids`, whose code is in
  bank 03. Nothing here changes Reznor or Bowser.
- The edge test reads `SpriteXPosLow,X`, the sprite's own screen X. But the
  boss is *drawn* at `IggyLarryTempXPos`/`YPos`. `CODE_01CC9D` calculates
  that by rotating the platform position around the Mode 7 center. The two
  values are close enough that this is how the fight is meant to be won. But a
  code that makes the walking area smaller does it in sprite space, not in
  what you see.
- `CODE_01FC62` runs only when `PlayerAnimation < $01` and `SpriteMisc160E`
  is clear. So none of these codes do anything during pipe, door or death
  animations, or after the boss already falls.
- `$01FB5D:58` leaves the boss falling with nothing to stop it. It cannot come
  back, because `SpriteMisc160E` is never cleared. So you must leave the room
  in some other way. It is only a curiosity, not a playable code.
- `$01FB12:0F` also changes *when* the ball is thrown, because the shell timer
  is reset to `$7F` on the same frame. If the timer is set again before the
  previous sequence counts down past `$28`, the throw can be skipped
  completely on some cycles.
- The knockback codes change `SpriteMisc154C`. This is the timer during which
  the boss slides and cannot act. With very large values, it slides for so
  long that it never goes into its shell, because `PlatformKoopaKids` steps
  the shell counter only while `SpriteMisc154C` is zero.

## Lemmy and Wendy can be beaten by walking into them

**Code:** `DDA8-6DDE`
**Raw form:** `03CEB0:00` (address:new-byte; original byte `$10` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 03:35:20

**Mechanism:** Lemmy (`SpriteTableC2` `$05`) and Wendy (`$06`) are the last
two Koopa Kids. Their whole fight is in `bank_03.asm`, and the
`PipeKoopaKids` trampoline in bank 01 jumps to it. Three copies of sprite
`$29` are on the screen: the real boss and two decoys that `CODE_03CCE2`
creates in sprite slots `$00` and `$01`. `SpriteMisc1570` tells them apart:
`$00` is the real one, and `$10` and `$20` are decoys. The same value is also
the offset for their read of `DATA_03CC5A`. So one random number sends all
three to different pipes.

Every contact, with the real boss or a decoy, goes through `CODE_03CEA7`:

```
CODE_03CEA7:
    JSL MarioSprInteract
    BCC Return03CEF1          ; no contact
    LDA.B PlayerYSpeed+1
    CMP.B #$10                ; <- the patched byte, at $03CEB0
    BMI CODE_03CEED           ; too slow: HurtMario instead
    JSL DisplayContactGfx
    ...
```

`PlayerYSpeed+1` is the integer half of Mario's 4.12 fixed-point vertical
speed. So the normal `$10` means "you must already fall at 16 or more". The
code changes it to `$00`. Then the test is `CMP #$00 / BMI`, which is taken
only when that byte is *negative*, so only when Mario moves **up**. Every
other contact now counts as a hit: walking into the boss, standing still
against it, or moving down at any speed. You can win the three-hit fight by
just walking into the pipes.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `c9 10 30` at `$03CEAF` = `CMP #$10 / BMI`, so the
operand is at `$03CEB0`. `$03CE19` reads `c9 03 d0` = `CMP #$03 / BNE`, the
three-hit counter. `$03CC38` reads `18 38 58 78 98 b8 d8 78`, the seven pipe X
positions. The addresses are from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (made again, and
`--check` passes against the current sources). It was encoded and verified
with a decode by `tools/gg_encode.py`. This comes from the disassembly. It
was **not** tested in play.

> This code was blocked during the sweep. `PipeKoopaKids` in bank 01 was a
> trampoline of two instructions into `CODE_03CC09`, and everything after it
> was bare `CODE_*`/`DATA_*` labels. It was unblocked when comments were
> added in `bank_03.asm` to the seven-phase `SpriteMisc151C` dispatch, all
> five parameter tables, the decoy creator `CODE_03CCE2`, and the contact
> handler `CODE_03CEA7`. That build was checked to be byte-identical to
> `comparison_U.smc`, so the comments changed nothing else. With this entry,
> all seven Koopa Kids have comments and have been searched for codes.

**Variants:**

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `DDA8-6DDE` | `03CEB0:00` | any contact that is not an upward jump counts as a hit |
| `5EA8-6DDE` | `03CEB0:7F` | the opposite: no fall is ever fast enough, so you cannot hit Lemmy and Wendy at all, and every touch hurts Mario |
| `DFAF-646E` | `03CE1A:01` | one hit, not three |
| `D6AF-646E` | `03CE1A:08` | eight hits, so the fight is much longer |
| `D5A2-6FDE` | `03CED4:07` | the decoys are not removed from the screen on the last hit, so they keep coming out of their pipes while the boss falls |
| `79A3-D76E` | `03CCEE:35` | the two decoys appear as **green Yoshis**, not copies of the boss |
| `DDAB-D40E` | `03CC99:00` | the random pipe choice is always zero, so all three use the same three pipes every time |
| `FDA4-0FAE` | `03CD27:10` | out of the pipe for `$10` frames, not `$40`, so there is almost no time to jump on one |
| `EEA4-0FAE` | `03CD27:FF` | stays out about four times as long |
| `EEA3-6D0E` | `03CEE1:FF` | a hit stuns the real boss for `$FF` steps, not `$50` |
| `D9A8-DDDE` | `03CCB0:05` | all of Lemmy's pipes are at Wendy's fixed height of `$50` |
| `D5A8-DDDE` | `03CCB0:07` | the opposite: Wendy's flat row of pipes gets Lemmy's different heights from `DATA_03CC40` |
| `EEA5-6D0E` | `03CE71:FF` | the game never finds that the beaten boss hit the lava, so it falls forever, and the level never ends |

**Caveats:**
- **This is only Lemmy and Wendy.** The counter at `$01CFCD` kills Morton,
  Roy and Ludwig. Iggy and Larry have no counter at all, and you push them
  off a platform. All three fights are separate code.
- `CODE_03CEA7` also runs for the decoys, and they use the same byte. So every
  one of these codes also applies to the two fakes. With `$03CEB0:00`, if you
  touch a decoy, it also "hits" it. You get the wrong-answer sound and the
  short `$1F` stun, but no progress.
- `$03CCEE:35` writes the sprite number **after** `SpriteStatus` is already
  set to `$08` (Normal). So the new sprite never runs its `$01` init phase,
  and `InitYoshi` is skipped. `InitSpriteTables` still runs, and then the
  boss's `SpriteMisc1570`, `SpriteTableC2` and position are copied on top.
  Expect a Yoshi whose state is not initialized. This is a curiosity code, and
  nobody has seen what it looks like.
- `$03CE71:FF` leaves the boss falling with nothing to stop it. It cannot come
  back, because the phase never moves on to the level clear. So you must leave
  the room in some other way.
- The `$03CD27` codes change how long the boss stays out **and** its
  animation. `CODE_03CDC7` chooses a frame with
  `(set << 4) | (timer >> 2)`. That is an `ORA`, not an `ADC`, so a timer
  above `$3F` makes the two fields overlap. So with `$FF`, the first part
  reads frames from the row where the overlap lands, not from the boss's own
  row.
- `$03CCB0` is compared with `SpriteTableC2`, which is the boss identity for
  *all seven* Koopa Kids. Only Lemmy and Wendy ever get to this instruction,
  so the other five do not change. But the value must stay in `$00`–`$07` to
  mean anything.

## The Big Boo goes down in one hit

**Code:** `DF6C-0D6A`
**Raw form:** `0381A2:01` (address:new-byte; original byte `$03` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 03:43:37

**Mechanism:** The Big Boo of Big Boo's Fort is sprite `$C5`. All the other
bosses in the game can be stomped, but he is **never stomped**. `BigBooBoss`
(`bank_03.asm`) runs a state machine with seven phases in `SpriteTableC2`:

```
    dw CODE_0380BE      ; 00 - away, counting down to return
    dw CODE_0380D5      ; 01 - fading in
    dw CODE_038119      ; 02 - drifting: can be hit
    dw CODE_03818B      ; 03 - hit: flash and score it
    dw CODE_0381BC      ; 04 - fading out
    dw CODE_038106      ; 05 - gone; wait, then start over
    dw CODE_0381D3      ; 06 - beaten: fall off the screen
```

Phase 2 is the only phase in which he can be hurt, and Mario is not what
hurts him. `CODE_0381E4` checks the sprite slots for one with status `$09`
(stunned, or waiting to be carried) or `$0A` (kicked), and tests it for
contact:

```
CODE_0381E4:
    LDY.B #$0B                ; highest sprite slot
CODE_0381E6:
    LDA.W SpriteStatus,Y
    CMP.B #$09                ; <- $0381EA
    BEQ CODE_0381F5
    CMP.B #$0A                ; <- $0381EE
    BEQ CODE_0381F5
```

That is why his room has grab blocks. A hit sets phase 3. That phase flashes
his palette for `$40` steps and then counts the hit:

```
CODE_03818B:
    ...
    INC.W SpriteMisc1534,X    ; one more hit landed
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1534,X
    CMP.B #$03                ; <- the patched byte, at $0381A2
    BNE +
    LDA.B #$06                ; straight to phase 6 instead
    STA.B SpriteTableC2,X
    JSL KillMostSprites
  + RTS
```

`SpriteMisc1534` starts at zero, and `INC` adds 1 to it before the compare. So the
normal `$03` means three thrown blocks. The code changes the operand to `$01`,
so the first block matches: the counter gets to 1, the phase jumps to 6,
`KillMostSprites` clears the room, and `CODE_0381D3` sends the Boo up at
`$D0` as a killed sprite. The start of `BigBooBoss` watches for his
`SpriteStatus` to become `$00`. As soon as he floats off the screen, it ends
the level.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `c9 03 d0` at `$0381A1` = `CMP #$03 / BNE`, so the operand
is at `$0381A2`. `$0381E9` reads `c9 09 f0` and `$0381ED` reads `c9 0a f0`,
the two status tests. `$0380B0` reads
`be 80 d5 80 19 81 8b 81 bc 81 06 81 d3 81`, the phase table with seven
entries. The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again after the
comments added in this pass. The build with comments is byte-identical to the
reference ROM.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `DB6C-0D6A` | `0381A2:09` | nine thrown blocks, not three |
| `D663-046A` | `0381EA:08` | the check matches status `$08` (a live, normal sprite). The Big Boo himself has that status while he drifts. So he finds his own slot, tests himself for contact with himself, and hits himself three times without the player doing anything |
| `D863-076A` | `0381EE:0B` | status `$0B` (carried), not `$0A` (kicked): you beat him by *walking into him while you hold* a grab block, not by throwing it |
| `D16D-6FAA` | `038207:06` | a hit sets phase 6 directly, not phase 3. One block ends the fight, with no flash and no `KillMostSprites` |
| `DD6D-6FAA` | `038207:00` | a hit sends him back to phase 0 instead: he disappears, comes back, and can never be beaten |
| `2768-DFDA` | `0380B4:D3` | the phase 2 table entry points to `CODE_0381D3`, not `CODE_038119`, so he gives up as soon as he finishes fading in |
| `2968-DDDA` | `0380B0:D5` | the phase 0 entry points to the fade-in handler: there is no wait at the start, and he is there at once |
| `D463-D7AA` | `0380EF:02` | `CODE_0380D5` ends the fade when `BooTransparency` is `$02`, not `$07`, so you fight him while he is still almost invisible |
| `DF6A-D46A` | `0380CA:01` | `SpriteMisc1570` only has to get to `$01`, not `$90`, before he first appears |
| `DF6A-076A` | `0381CE:01` | he stays away for `$01` frame after a hit, not `$C0`, so the fight almost never stops |
| `6D6E-D7DA` | `0380FC:80` | the left end of his X speed range changes from `$F0` (16 left) to `$80`. So he speeds up to full speed and flies across the room |
| `DD62-04AA` | `0381DB:00` | when he is beaten, his Y speed is `$00`, not `$D0`: he falls out of the bottom of the room and does not float up |

**Caveats:**
- All of these affect only Big Boo's Fort. The normal Boos (sprite `$37`) and
  the Boo ring and stream generators are different code, and they do not
  change.
- `0381EA:08` depends on the Boo's own status being `$08` while phase 2 runs.
  `BigBooBoss` only runs the phase machine after `CMP #$08`, so he always
  matches himself. It does not depend on the slot order. Between each hit on
  himself, he still does the full `$40` flash, the fade out and the `$C0` away
  timer. So the fight ends by itself over a few seconds, not at once. Nobody
  has seen it on the screen.
- `038207:06` skips `JSL KillMostSprites`. That call normally removes the grab
  blocks from the room before the level ends. Anything on the screen when the
  hit happens stays there during the fall.
- `038207:00` changes only the phase value. The
  `LDA #$40 / STA SpriteMisc1540` two instructions later still runs, so the
  phase 0 handler starts with its timer already loaded. But `CODE_0380BE`
  ignores `SpriteMisc1540` and counts `SpriteMisc1570` instead, so the wait
  time does not change. The only thing lost is that phase 3 can never happen.
- `0380B4:D3` and `0380B0:D5` change only the low byte of a pointer, so they
  need both handlers to be on the same page. `CODE_038119`/`CODE_0381D3` are
  both `$81xx`, and `CODE_0380BE`/`CODE_0380D5` are both `$80xx`. A handler
  from the other page would also need the high byte at `$0380B5`/`$0380B1`,
  so the effect would need more than one code.
- With `0380EF:02`, `CODE_0380D5`'s chime test (`CMP #$02` at `$0380E6`) also
  matches on the same frame. So the magic sound and the change to phase 2 now
  happen together.
- `0380FC` uses `SpriteMisc151C & 1` as its index, and `$0380FD` (`$10`) is
  the right limit of the same range. If you change only the one byte, his
  movement is not the same on both sides.

## Magikoopa's magic turns every block it hits into a 1-Up

**Code:** `5686-D7A5`
**Raw form:** `01BC8F:78` (address:new-byte; original byte `$07` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 07:30:56

**Mechanism:** Magikoopa is sprite `$1F`. The magic that he throws is a
different sprite, `$20`, and `MagikoopasMagic` in `bank_01.asm` handles it.
The magic flies in a straight line with no gravity. When it hits a block,
the *magic's own sprite slot is used again* for the sprite that the block
turns into. A chain of four choices decides which sprite that is:

```
    LDA.W SprMap16TouchVertLow
    SEC
    SBC.B #$11
    CMP.B #$1D                ; <- $01BC6E: only tiles $11-$2D are turnable
    BCS CODE_01BCB9
    JSL GetRand               ; \ four sources stirred together, so the
    ADC.W RandomNumber+1      ; | outcome cannot be read off the RNG alone
    ADC.B PlayerXSpeed+1      ; |
    ADC.B TrueFrame           ; /
    LDY.B #$78                ; \ exactly $35 -> 1-Up      (1 in 256)
    CMP.B #$35                ; |
    BEQ +                     ; /
    LDY.B #$21                ; \ below $08 -> moving coin (8 in 256)
    CMP.B #$08                ; |
    BCC +                     ; /
    LDY.B #$27                ; \ $F7 and up -> Thwimp     (9 in 256)
    CMP.B #$F7                ; |
    BCS +                     ; /
    LDY.B #$07                ; <- the patched byte, at $01BC8F
  + STY.B SpriteNumber,X      ; the magic's slot becomes that sprite
```

The last `LDY` is the default case, and it gets 238 of the 256 random values.
So a changed block almost always becomes a yellow Koopa (sprite `$07`). The
code changes that operand to `$78`, so the common case is a 1-Up mushroom
instead. All values except the eighteen special ones give you an extra life.
The block itself is used up in both cases: `Map16TileGenerate` is loaded with
`$02`, and `GenerateTile` clears the tile.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM (`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte
copier header) reads `a0 07 84` at `$01BC8E` = `LDY #$07 / STY dp`, so the
operand is at `$01BC8F`. The three tests above read `c9 35 f0`, `c9 08 90`
and `c9 f7 b0` at `$01BC7E`, `$01BC84` and `$01BC8A`. The range of tiles
that can change reads `c9 1d b0` at `$01BC6D`. The sprite numbers are from
the bank 01 dispatch table (`; 07 - Yellow Koopa`, `; 21 - Moving coin`,
`; 27 - Thwimp`, `; 78 - 1-Up`, `; 1F - Magikoopa`,
`; 20 - Magikoopa's magic`). The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`,
made again after the comments added in this pass. The build with comments is
byte-identical to the reference ROM.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `4586-D7A5` | `01BC8F:27` | the common case becomes a Thwimp, so every block he hits drops a crusher on you |
| `4F86-D7A5` | `01BC8F:21` | the common case becomes a moving coin |
| `EE81-D765` | `01BC6E:FF` | the range of tiles that can change grows from 29 tiles to 255: almost anything the magic touches becomes a sprite, not only the few block types that are normally allowed |
| `DF81-D765` | `01BC6E:01` | the opposite: only Map16 tile `$11` changes, so the magic almost always just disappears |
| `DD86-D4A5` | `01BC8B:00` | the Thwimp test `CMP #$F7 / BCS` is always taken, so every value above `$07` is a Thwimp |
| `EE86-DF05` | `01BC85:FF` | the same trick on the coin test: every value except `$35` and `$FF` is a moving coin |
| `FE87-ADA5` | `01BF33:1F` | he creates *another Magikoopa*, not magic. It is aimed at Mario, and it can start its own teleport cycle |
| `1D89-A4D5` | `01BF58:60` | the magic is aimed at Mario at speed `$60`, not `$20`, so it is three times as fast |
| `D689-A4D5` | `01BF58:08` | ...or at `$08`, so it moves across the room slowly enough that you can walk around it |
| `5F86-6FA5` | `01BE87:71` | he casts only when the phase 2 timer is exactly `$40`. The timer never has the value `$71`, so he appears, poses and disappears without casting |
| `DD86-6FA5` | `01BE87:00` | the opposite: `$00` matches both the last frame of his stay *and* the `JSR CODE_01BE82` that phase 0 makes as he enters, so he casts two times each time he appears |
| `DD87-6405` | `01BE39:00` | removes the rule that he must appear "at least `$20` away from Mario", so he can now appear directly on top of you |
| `FD8D-6705` | `01BE0D:10` | the random Y offset is rejected unless it is under `$10`. So he only appears again on the top row of the screen (and much less often, because most values are rejected) |
| `EEA4-DDA0` | `01C023:FF` | he stays visible for `$FF` frames, not `$70`. He still casts only once, at `$40`, so he stays a long time after that |
| `DD8E-A465` | `01BFFA:00` | no pause after he fades out, before he starts to look for the next place |

**Caveats:**
- All of these are about Magikoopa's magic: the blocks that he hits, not the
  blocks that Mario hits. Nothing else in the game reads
  `SprMap16TouchVertLow` through this path.
- The new sprite is written directly into the magic's slot, and its
  `SpriteStatus` is already `$08` (Normal). So the new sprite's `$01` init
  phase **never runs**. Only `InitSpriteTables` runs. This is also true in
  the normal game (a yellow Koopa works fine without it), but be careful
  about this when you use a sprite that needs real init work. `$78` (1-Up)
  and `$21` (moving coin) both use `PowerUpRt`, which has the same form as
  `Spr0to13Start`, so they are safe. `$27` (Thwimp) also has a simple
  handler.
- `01BF33:1F` skips `InitMagikoopa`. That is the routine that allows only one
  Magikoopa at a time. So the copies add up. Each one runs its own teleport
  cycle, and each one creates more copies. Expect the sprite table to fill
  quickly. When it is full, `CODE_01BF1D` finds no free slot, and the cast is
  lost with no error. That is what stops it from growing without end. Nobody
  has seen it on the screen.
- `01BC6E:FF` lets the magic change tiles that were never meant to become
  sprites, including tiles with their own block behavior. The tile is still
  replaced with `$02` after that, so the level shape changes wherever the
  magic hits.
- `01BE39:00` removes a safety check. It is not a difficulty setting. The
  place must still be solid ground away from walls, but nothing now stops him
  from appearing inside Mario's hitbox.
- `01BE87` is an exact-equality test against a timer that *counts down*. So it
  can never make him cast more than once each time the timer passes the value.
  To make him cast more often, you need a different byte.
- `01C023:FF` also makes the `$34` visible palette setting stay longer.
  `01BFFA:00` shortens only the time between disappearing and the next
  search. The fade steps themselves are `$04` frames in (`$01C00A`) and `$02`
  frames out (`$01BFE9`).

## The net Koopas never cross to the other side of the fence

**Code:** `DD8B-0F61`
**Raw form:** `01B996:00` (address:new-byte; original byte `$01` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 07:42:26

**Mechanism:** The four net Koopas (`$22`/`$23` climbing and `$24`/`$25`
walking) use one handler, `ClimbingKoopa` in `bank_01.asm`. They move along
the chain-link fence until they get to its edge. Then they swing around it
and go back the way they came, now on the *other* side of the fence. Only
the timer in `SpriteMisc1540` controls that swing. It is set to `$50` as soon
as the Koopa steps off the net. The side change happens on the one frame when
the timer is exactly `$40`. The special swing frames are drawn from `$3F`
down to `$30`. Below that, he walks normally again, and the timer only counts
down to zero.

```
ClimbingKoopa:
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1540,X
    BEQ CODE_01B9FB           ; not mid-swing: normal movement
    CMP.B #$30                ; <- $01B985: under $30, the swing is over
    BCC CODE_01B9A0
    CMP.B #$40                ; <- $01B989: $30-$3F, draw the swing frames
    BCC CODE_01B9A3
    BNE CODE_01B9A0           ; above $40: still winding up
    LDY.B SpriteLock          ; \ exactly $40: the flip itself
    BNE CODE_01B9A0           ; /
    LDA.W SpriteBehindScene,X ; \ change sides of the net
    EOR.B #$01                ; | <- the patched byte, at $01B996
    STA.W SpriteBehindScene,X ; /
    JSR FlipSpriteDir         ; turn around
    JSR CODE_01BA7F           ; ...and reverse the climb too
```

`SpriteBehindScene` is the only thing that decides "which side of the fence
am I on". It chooses the graphics (`STA SpriteMisc1602` at `CODE_01BA53`). It
decides if the Koopa is drawn behind the foreground layer
(`!OBJ_Priority1`). It is also why a Koopa on the far side cannot hurt you
until he comes back around. The code changes `EOR #$01` to `EOR #$00`, so the
value does not change. Everything else in the move still happens: he still
swings, still turns around, and still reverses his climb. But he ends on the
same side where he started. A Koopa that started in front of the net stays in
front of it forever, and you can jump on him at any point in the loop. A
Koopa that started behind it can never be reached.

The level designer does not choose the side where each Koopa *starts*.
`InitVertNetKoopa` takes it directly from bit `$10` of the sprite's X
position, so the columns of the fence change between front and back.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `EE8B-0F61` | `01B996:FF` | `EOR #$FF` instead: `$00` becomes `$FF` and `$01` becomes `$FE`. Both are non-zero, so after his first swing every net Koopa is *behind* the fence forever, and you cannot reach him |
| `DD87-6DA1` | `01BA33:00` | the swing timer is set to `$00`, so the move never starts: he walks directly off the end of the fence and keeps going through the air |
| `EE87-6DA1` | `01BA33:FF` | set to `$FF`, not `$50`. Everything above `$40` is wind-up, during which he still moves. So he goes about 190 frames past the fence before he swings back to it |
| `7E87-6DA1` | `01BA33:3F` | set to `$3F`, which is below the `$40` flip frame. He stops at the edge for the sixteen swing frames, never flips, and then continues off the net |
| `0D86-0F01` | `01B985:40` | the `< $30` test becomes `< $40`, so the swing frames never happen. The side change still happens at exactly `$40`, and he jumps to the other side with no animation |
| `DD86-0401` | `01B989:00` | the `< $40` test becomes `< $00`, so the `BNE` below it is taken for every timer value that is not zero: the flip never runs, and he walks off the fence |
| `5280-0D61` | `01B942:7D` | points `LDA HorzNetKoopaSpeed,Y` to `DATA_01B97D` (same page). So the walkers' start speed comes from the blocked-direction masks `$03`/`$0C`. Both are positive, so they always start to the right, fast or slow depending on where Mario is |
| `4D87-07D1` | `01B93C:20` | the walking speed for "Mario is to the right" goes from `$08` to `$20`, and it is doubled again to `$40` for the type with OBJ bit `$02` clear. They race along the fence |
| `D680-0701` | `01B94D:08` | the climbers' start Y speed changes from `$F8` (up) to `$08`, so they start to go *down* the fence |
| `3D80-0701` | `01B94D:E0` | the climbers start at `$E0`, not `$F8`: four times the climb speed, and eight times for the doubled type |
| `DD89-0F01` | `01B955:00` | `AND #$10` on the X position becomes `AND #$00`. The test always fails, so every net Koopa in the game starts behind the fence |
| `DD81-0D01` | `01B961:00` | `AND #$02` on the OBJ attribute becomes `AND #$00`. So *every* net Koopa, red and green, takes the double speed branch |
| `DD85-0701` | `01B97D:00` | the horizontal walkers' blocked-direction mask becomes `$00`: they never find that they hit a wall, and they stop turning around |
| `DD85-0761` | `01B97E:00` | the same for the climbers' up/down mask |
| `F284-6DD1` | `01BA20:1D` | a climber that goes down tests "still on the net?" with `< $1D`, which is true for every net tile. He turns around as soon as he starts to go down, so the climbers can only go up |
| `F284-64A1` | `01BA2B:1D` | the same trick on the other test: any net tile now counts as the *edge*. So they start a new swing each time one ends, and spend the level flipping back and forth in one place |
| `DD84-64A1` | `01BA2B:00` | the opposite: the `< $07` "off the net" test becomes `< $00`. So empty air (Map16 `$00`) counts as fence, and they walk off the end and keep going |
| `DD89-64A1` | `01BA5B:00` | `AND #$08` on the animation clock becomes `AND #$00`. The two-frame walk cycle stays on its first frame, so they slide along the fence without moving their legs |
| `6D88-04A1` | `01B9BB:80` | during the swing, the climbers are normally drawn `$0C` pixels above their real position. `$80` draws them 128 pixels up, so they jump most of a screen height during the swing and then jump back |

**Caveats:**
- Other sprites also use `SpriteBehindScene`, which is a field for each slot.
  But `$01B996` is inside `ClimbingKoopa`, and it runs only for sprites
  `$22`-`$25`. Nothing else in the game gets to this instruction.
- The main code does **not** stop the Koopa from turning around.
  `FlipSpriteDir` and the climb reversal at `CODE_01BA7F` are separate
  instructions after the changed one. He still turns around. He only does it
  without changing sides.
- `01BA33:00` and `01BA2B:00` both let net Koopas leave the fence. They keep
  their speed, and no gravity is applied (`SubSprXPosNoGrvty` /
  `SubSprYPosNoGrvty`). So they move in a straight line until
  `SubOffscreen0Bnk1` removes them. Nobody has seen it on the screen.
- `01B93C` is only the *start* speed. But `FlipSpriteDir` negates the speed
  and does not load it again, so the size of the speed set at init stays for
  the sprite's whole life. The second entry of that table (`$01B93D`, `$F8`)
  is the mirror case, and it is the code to use with it.
- `01B961:00` doubles the speed of both types. For the green ones, `$08`/`$F8`
  becomes `$10`/`$F0`, so there is no longer any speed difference between red
  and green.
- The horizontal walkers (through `CODE_01BA27`) and the climbers that move
  *up* (`BMI CODE_01BA2A`) both use `01BA2B`. Climbers that move down use
  `$01BA20` instead. Changing one does not change the other.
- One byte in this routine was **not** searched for codes on purpose.
  `CODE_01B9A3` reads `OWLevelTileSettings+$49` (`$7E1EEB`) to change to a
  different set of five frames. Nothing else in the disassembly writes that
  byte, so it is not known what sets it.

**Verification:** all twenty bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` (without
its 512-byte copier header), and they matched the disassembly exactly.
`$01B996` has `49 01` (`EOR #$01`). `$01B985`/`$01B989` have `c9 30`/`c9 40`.
`$01BA33` has `a9 50`. `HorzNetKoopaSpeed` at `$01B93C` has `08 f8`, and
`DATA_01B97D` has `03 0c`. `$01B94D` has `a9 f8`. `$01B955`/`$01B961` have
`29 10`/`29 02`. The net tile ranges read `c9 07`/`c9 1d` at `$01BA1F`,
`$01BA23`, `$01BA2A` and `$01BA2E`. The sprite numbers are from the bank 01
dispatch table (`; 22 - Green vertical net Koopa` … `; 25 - Red horizontal net
Koopa`). The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again after the
comments added in this pass. The build with comments is byte-identical to the
reference ROM.

## Piranha Plants come up even while you are standing on the pipe

**Code:** `DD62-6405`
**Raw form:** `018ED9:00` (address:new-byte; original byte `$37` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 07:49:27

**Mechanism:** Sprites `$1A` and `$2A` are the Piranha Plants that live in a
pipe, the normal one and the upside-down one. Both use `ClassicPiranhas` in
`bank_01.asm`. They run a cycle of four states. `SpriteTableC2` counts the
state, and `SpriteMisc1540` times it: hidden in the pipe, rising, fully out,
sinking back. `PiranhaSpeed` gives the Y speed of each state (`$00`, `$F0`,
`$00`, `$10`, which is one pixel per frame up or down). `PiranTimeInState`
gives the length of each state. So the rise of `$20` frames and the sink of
`$20` frames each move exactly the `$20` pixels of the pipe.

The well-known rule that a plant does not come out while Mario stands on its
pipe is one compare, in `ChangePiranhaState`:

```
    BNE CODE_018EE1           ; only state 0 (hidden) is refusable
    JSR SubHorizPos           ; _F = Mario X - sprite X, signed
    LDA.B _F
    CLC
    ADC.B #$1B                ; <- $018ED7: slide the window onto zero
    CMP.B #$37                ; <- the patched byte, at $018ED9
    LDA.B #$01                ; <- $018EDB: the "stay hidden" flag
    STA.W SpriteMisc1594,X
    BCC +                     ; carry clear = too close: stay down, RTS
CODE_018EE1:
    STZ.W SpriteMisc1594,X
    LDY.B _0                  ; \ arm the next state's timer
    LDA.W PiranTimeInState,Y  ; |
    STA.W SpriteMisc1540,X    ; /
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X
  + RTS
```

`+$1B` and then `< $37` make a range that goes `$1B` pixels to each side of
the plant. The code changes the width to `$00`. Then carry is always set, so
the branch is never taken, and the plant comes out of the pipe wherever Mario
is. This includes when he stands directly on top of it, which is exactly
where the level design expects him to be safe. The path without the branch
also clears `SpriteMisc1594`, so the plant is drawn and interacts normally the
whole time.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `EE62-6405` | `018ED9:FF` | the opposite: carry is set only when the shifted distance is exactly `$FF`. So almost every plant in the game does not come up, and the pipes stay empty |
| `DD62-6FA5` | `018ED7:00` | the range is no longer centered on the plant: the plant stays down only when Mario is up to `$36` pixels to its *right*, and coming from the left no longer works |
| `6D62-6FA5` | `018ED7:80` | the range moves 128 pixels left. So the plant hides when you are some distance to its left, and it comes up happily when you are on the pipe |
| `DD62-64A5` | `018EDB:00` | the "stay hidden" flag is stored as `$00`, not `$01`. So a plant that does not come up still runs its contact check, and a Piranha Plant that is down inside its pipe can hurt you |
| `FD61-67A5` | `018E6F:10` | the rising state's speed changes from `$F0` to `$10`. So both moving states go down, and the plants dig down out of the level and do not appear |
| `ED65-6D05` | `018E71:F0` | the mirror case: the sinking state also goes up. So the plants climb out of their pipes and keep going up the screen |
| `ED65-6DD5` | `018E70:F0` | the "fully out" state gets an upward speed. So the plant does not stay still at the top of its cycle. It keeps rising for another `$30` frames each cycle |
| `ED61-6765` | `018E6E:F0` | the *hidden* state gets an upward speed. So the plant rises out of the pipe during the time it should be in the pipe. It comes out early, and higher on every cycle |
| `D665-6DA5` | `018E73:08` | the time a plant stays fully out goes from `$30` frames to `$08`: it puts its head up and goes down again at once |
| `EE65-6DA5` | `018E73:FF` | ...or `$FF`, so when it is up, it stays up for four seconds each time |
| `EE65-6F05` | `018E75:FF` | the hidden state grows from `$30` frames to `$FF`, so the plants appear only about a quarter as often |
| `DF65-6F05` | `018E75:01` | ...or `$01`, so a plant starts to come up again on the frame after it finishes sinking |
| `FC68-67D5` | `018EBC:1A` | the speed inversion checks sprite `$1A`, not `$2A`. This swaps which plant is upside down: the normal ones go down into their pipes, and the ceiling ones drop out of theirs |
| `DD68-67D5` | `018EBC:00` | no sprite is `$00`, so the inversion never happens. The upside-down plants move the same way as normal ones: directly up into their own pipe, where you never see them |
| `DD6C-67A5` | `018EAF:00` | the state index in the main handler is always `0`, so the speed from the table is always `$00`. The plants never move at all, but the cycle keeps running, and they flash on and off at the top of the pipe |
| `DD6A-64A5` | `018ECB:00` | the same mask in `ChangePiranhaState`. It makes *every* state look like state 0. So every change of state now needs Mario to be far away, and a plant stops and disappears in the middle of its rise as soon as you get near it |
| `5468-6FA5` | `018EB7:72` | points `LDA PiranhaSpeed,Y` to `PiranTimeInState` on the same page. The speeds become `$20`/`$30`, all fast and down, and the plants dive directly out of the bottom of the level |
| `1363-6FA5` | `018EE7:6E` | the mirror redirect: `LDA PiranTimeInState,Y` now reads `PiranhaSpeed`. So the two moving states get a length of `$00` frames and are skipped completely. The plant jumps directly between hidden and fully out |
| `DF6B-6DA5` | `018E93:01` | the stem's OAM attribute changes from `$0B` to `$01`. This changes the palette of the plant's stem, but not the head |

**Caveats:**
- Every byte here is inside `ClassicPiranhas` / `ChangePiranhaState`, and
  only sprites `$1A` and `$2A` read it. The jumping Piranha Plants (`$4F`,
  `$50`) use a different handler, and they do not change.
- The rise and the sink are equal only because `$F0`×`$20` frames and
  `$10`×`$20` frames both move the same `$20` pixels. Any code that changes
  one speed or one length, but not its partner, leaves a net movement in each
  cycle. Then the plant moves a little further up or down the level each
  time. That is how most of the variants above work, and the effect adds up.
  Nobody has seen it on the screen.
- `018EDB:00` does not make the plant come out. It only stops the game from
  hiding it. The plant is drawn with `!OBJ_Priority1` (behind the
  foreground), so mostly you notice that something you cannot see hurts you.
- `PiranTimeInState` uses the state that is *ending* as its index, not the
  one that is starting. So `$018E72` sets the length of the rise, `$018E73`
  the time out, `$018E74` the sink and `$018E75` the time hidden.
- `018EAF:00` and `018ECB:00` change the same `AND #$03`, which is written
  two times: in the main handler and in the state change routine. They are
  separate bytes, and you can use them alone or together.

**Verification:** all twenty bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` (without
its 512-byte copier header), and they matched the disassembly exactly.
`PiranhaSpeed` at `$018E6E` has `00 f0 00 10`, and `PiranTimeInState` at
`$018E72` has `20 30 20 30`. The distance test reads `69 1b c9 37 a9 01` at
`$018ED6`. The upside-down check reads `c0 2a` at `$018EBB`. The two table
loads read `b9 6e 8e` at `$018EB6` and `b9 72 8e` at `$018EE6`. The stem
attribute reads `29 f1 09 0b` at `$018E90`. The sprite numbers are from the
bank 01 dispatch table (`; 1A - Classic Piranha Plant`,
`; 2A - Upside down Piranha Plant`). The addresses come from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again after the comments added in this pass. The
build with comments is byte-identical to the reference ROM.

## Bullet Bills hang motionless in the air

**Code:** `2E6E-A7A5`
**Raw form:** `018FFF:DF` (address:new-byte; original byte `$D7` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 07:57:43

**Mechanism:** Everything about a Bullet Bill (sprite `$1C`, `BulletBill` in
`bank_01.asm`) comes from one number: `SpriteTableC2`, the direction it was
shot in. This number is the index into four tables at the same time. The
eight entries are the eight compass directions, in this order: right, left,
up, down, up-right, down-right, down-left, up-left:

```
BulletGfxProp:  db $42,$02,$03,$83,$03,$43,$03,$43   ; $018FC7 - OAM attribute
DATA_018FCF:    db $00,$00,$01,$01,$02,$03,$03,$02   ; $018FCF - frame
BulletSpeedX:   db $20,$E0,$00,$00,$18,$18,$E8,$E8   ; $018FD7
BulletSpeedY:   db $00,$00,$E0,$20,$E8,$18,$18,$E8   ; $018FDF
```

A bullet placed in a level uses only directions `$00` and `$01`.
`InitBulletBill` calls `SubHorizPos`, which returns `$00` when Mario is to the
right and `$01` when he is to the left. So the shot is always aimed at him.
The vertical and diagonal entries are for the shooter clusters. Those choose
an index from `DATA_02B10C` in `bank_02.asm` and write it into
`SpriteTableC2` themselves.

The four tables are read again *on every frame*. That is why nothing can slow
down a Bullet Bill, turn it, or push it off its path. It just continues in
its direction. It also means that one operand byte can redirect everything a
bullet does, because all four tables are on the same page `$018F`:

```
    LDY.B SpriteTableC2,X     ; Y = direction, $00-$07
    LDA.W BulletGfxProp,Y     ; B9 C7 8F   <- table base low byte at $018FF3
    STA.W SpriteOBJAttribute,X
    LDA.W DATA_018FCF,Y       ; B9 CF 8F   <- $018FF9
    STA.W SpriteMisc1602,X
    LDA.W BulletSpeedX,Y      ; B9 D7 8F   <- the patched byte, at $018FFF
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
    LDA.W BulletSpeedY,Y      ; B9 DF 8F   <- $019004
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
```

The code changes `$018FFF` from `$D7` to `$DF`, so the X speed lookup reads
`BulletSpeedY`. Directions `$00` and `$01` are the only two that a bullet
placed in a level uses. They have `$00` in that column, and their own Y speed
is also `$00`. So the bullet leaves the shooter with no speed at all, and it
just stays in the air at the front of the shooter. It is still solid, it
still kills you when you touch it, and the shooter still fires without end.
So the screen slowly fills with bullets that do not move. Diagonal bullets
from shooters get `$E8`/`$18` from the Y column instead, and they fly at new
angles.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `AE6E-A7A5` | `018FFF:CF` | X speed is read from the *frame* table instead. The two horizontal directions are `$00` again, so bullets in a level still stay in the air, and bullets from shooters move very slowly, a subpixel or two per frame |
| `A56E-A7A5` | `018FFF:C7` | X speed is read from `BulletGfxProp`. A bullet shot to the right flies off fast at `$42` (four pixels per frame), and one shot to the left moves slowly *right* at `$02`. Nothing ever moves left again |
| `25BD-DFD0` | `019004:D7` | the mirror redirect: Y speed is read from `BulletSpeedX`. So a bullet to the right also goes down two pixels per frame, and a bullet to the left goes up. Every shot leaves the shooter at an angle |
| `A5BD-DFD0` | `019004:C7` | Y speed from `BulletGfxProp`: bullets to the right drop fast at `$42`, and bullets to the left go down slowly at `$02` |
| `256E-ADA5` | `018FF3:D7` | the OAM attribute table points to `BulletSpeedX`, so the palette, flip and priority bits come from the speed column. `$20` draws bullets to the right in the wrong palette and in front of the foreground. `$E0` also draws bullets to the left flipped both ways |
| `A56E-A405` | `018FF9:C7` | the frame table points to `BulletGfxProp`, so the frame index becomes `$42`/`$02`. That is far past the four frames the bullet really has, so it is drawn from the tile data that comes after them |
| `3D62-AFA5` | `018FD7:E0` | the X speed for "shot right" is negated. A bullet aimed at Mario on its right goes the other way, so every Bullet Bill in the game now moves left |
| `DD62-AFA5` | `018FD7:00` | ...or `$00`, so shots to the right stay at the shooter, and shots to the left still fly |
| `5E62-AFA5` | `018FD7:7F` | ...or `$7F`, almost eight pixels per frame, so a bullet to the right crosses the screen in about half a second |
| `4D62-A4D5` | `018FD8:20` | the "shot left" entry is made positive, so bullets move right on whichever side of the shooter you stand |
