| `6D62-A4D5` | `018FD8:80` | ...or `$80`, eight pixels per frame to the left, so you almost cannot see it before it hits you |
| `3D62-A7A5` | `018FDF:E0` | the Y speed for the right direction becomes `$E0`: those bullets go up as they fly and leave the top of the level |
| `4D63-ADD5` | `018FE0:20` | the same for the left direction, but down: they go down as they move and go into the floor |
| `4D63-AD05` | `018FE1:20` | the *up* direction, used only by the diagonal shooter clusters, is reversed to `$20`: shooters that shoot up now shoot down |
| `3D63-AD65` | `018FE2:E0` | ...and the down direction is reversed to `$E0`, so shooters that shoot down now shoot up |
| `D46A-AFA5` | `018FC7:02` | the OAM attribute for the right direction loses its X flip bit. So bullets shot to the right face backwards and fly tail first |
| `D46A-A7A5` | `018FCF:02` | the frame index for the right direction changes from `$00` to `$02`, so horizontal bullets use the diagonal graphics |
| `EE63-DFD9` | `0184E4:FF` | `InitBulletBill` sets `SpriteMisc1540` to `$10`. This is the number of frames that a new bullet is drawn *behind* the foreground while it leaves the shooter. `$FF` keeps it hidden behind the scenery for about four seconds, which is most of its flight |
| `DD63-DFD9` | `0184E4:00` | ...or `$00`, so the bullet is drawn in front from its first frame, and you can see it come out of the wall |
| `2DB4-DF60` | `019026:D0` | the `BEQ` that tests that timer becomes a `BNE`, which reverses it: bullets are in front for their first `$10` frames, and behind the foreground for the rest of their flight |
| `DDBF-D700` | `01901D:00` | the erase check `CMP #$F0` ("is this bullet more than `$F0` pixels below the top of the screen?") becomes `CMP #$00`, which is always true. So every Bullet Bill is erased on the frame it appears: the shooters fire, and nothing ever comes out |
| `FDBF-D700` | `01901D:10` | ...or `$10`, so a bullet lives only while it is within 16 pixels of the top of the screen, and it disappears as soon as it is anywhere else |

**Caveats:**
- Only sprite `$1C` reads these bytes (`dw BulletBill ; 1C - Bullet
  Bill` and `dw InitBulletBill ; 1C - Bullet Bill` in the bank 01 dispatch
  tables). Banzai Bill is sprite `$9F`, with its own handler, and it does not
  change.
- Bullets placed in a level and bullets from shooter clusters use the same
  four tables. So a code for directions `$00`/`$01` changes horizontal
  shooters everywhere and does not change the diagonal ones, and the other
  way around.
- The speeds are written again on every frame, so the effect of a speed code
  never goes away. But also, nothing else in the game can push a bullet. So a
  bullet that stays in the air stays exactly where it appeared, until the
  offscreen check removes it.
- `019026:D0` and the two `01901D` codes change how a bullet is drawn or when
  it is erased, not whether it hurts you. A bullet that `01901D:00` erases is
  gone before it can hurt you, but a bullet hidden behind the foreground is
  still there.
- Not tested in play. Every effect above comes from the disassembly, and the
  byte at each address was checked against the reference ROM.

**Provenance:** the bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` (the U release,
without its 512-byte copier header) and compared with the disassembly.
`$018FF2` and onward has `b9 c7 8f 9d f6 15 b9 cf 8f 9d 02 16 b9 d7 8f 95 b6 b9 df 8f`.
The four table base operands come from there. `$019017` has `b5 d8 38 e5 1c c9
f0 90 03 9e c8 14 bd 40 15 f0 03 4c 46 95` (the offscreen erase and the test
for behind the foreground). `InitBulletBill` at `$0184DE` has `30 ad 98 95 c2
a9 10 9d 40 15`. The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again
after the comments added in this pass. The build with comments is
byte-identical to the reference ROM.

## Lakitu's cloud never runs out

**Code:** `C238-A4A9`
**Raw form:** `01E7BB:AD` (address:new-byte; original byte `$CE` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 15:32:00

**Mechanism:** Lakitu has two parts. Sprite `$1E` is only the man, and sprite
`$87` (`LakituCloud` in `bank_01.asm`) is the cloud that carries him around.
`InitLakitu` creates the cloud together with him. It does not run at all if
either part is already active, so a level can never have two Lakitus, however
many are placed in it. All the flying, aiming and throwing is in the
*cloud's* routine, which finds the man by his slot. The man's own handler
only poses.

When you beat Lakitu, `HandleSprKilled` writes `$FF` to `LakituCloudTimer`,
and the cloud stays for Mario to ride. But it has a time limit:

```
  + LDY.W LakituCloudTimer    ; $01E7B6
    BEQ +
    LDA.B EffFrame
    AND.B #$03                ; $01E7B3 - tick once every four frames
    BNE +
    LDA.W LakituCloudTimer
    BEQ +
    DEC.W LakituCloudTimer    ; $01E7BB - the opcode this code replaces
    BNE +
    LDA.B #$1F                ; $01E7C1 - frames of flashing before it goes
    STA.W SpriteMisc1540,X
```

`$FF` counts down once every four frames, so the ride lasts about `$3FC`
frames, which is seventeen seconds. Then the cloud flashes for `$1F` frames,
and then it erases itself and starts the respawn timer for sprite `$1E`
again. So killing Lakitu only gives you a short break.

`$01E7BB` is the opcode of that `DEC.W`. The code changes `$CE` (`DEC abs`)
to `$AD` (`LDA abs`), which reads the timer and does not decrement it. So the
timer stays at `$FF` forever. The `BNE` on the next line now tests the value
that `LDA` just loaded, not the result of a decrement, so it is always taken.
So the flashing never starts. The changed accumulator does not matter: the
first instruction after the branch target loads `A` again from
`SpriteMisc1540`. The cloud that you take from Lakitu is yours for the rest of
the level.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `EE38-ADA9` | `01E7B3:FF` | do not change the `DEC`, but make the timer step less often: the timer goes down once every 256 frames, not every four. So the cloud lasts about eighteen minutes. That is long enough to feel permanent, but it still ends |
| `DD38-ADA9` | `01E7B3:00` | ...or `$00`, so the timer goes down on every frame: the cloud is gone about four seconds after you take it |
| `EE3A-AD09` | `01E7C1:FF` | the flashing time becomes `$FF` frames. So the cloud flashes for four seconds before it goes, not half a second, and you can still ride it the whole time |
| `FD32-AD09` | `01E7D1:10` | when the cloud finally goes, it sets `SpriteRespawnTimer` to `$FF`. `$10` brings Lakitu back almost as soon as his cloud goes away |
| `BE32-AF69` | `01E7D6:9F` | the matching `SpriteRespawnNumber` is `$1E`, Lakitu himself. `$9F` brings back a Banzai Bill in his place. Beat Lakitu, and something much larger comes where he was |
| `FD3F-DDD1` | `01E810:10` | to get on the cloud, `PlayerYSpeed` must not be negative: you must fall onto the cloud, not rise into it. The `BMI` becomes a `BPL`, which reverses the test. Now the only way to get on is to jump up into the cloud from below, and landing on it does nothing |
| `ED37-DDA1` | `01E833:F0` | when you get on, the cloud gets `$10` as its Y speed, and that speed becomes yours on every frame. `$F0` makes it rise one pixel per frame, not sink one, so the cloud carries you slowly up through the level |
| `6D39-DD01` | `01E851:80` | while you ride, `$03` is added to the cloud's speed before it is written over your fall speed. `$80` changes the slow sink into a fixed `$90`: a fast climb that you cannot stop or fall out of |
| `D636-D401` | `01E889:08` | B makes you step off the cloud (`AND #$80` against `byetudlrFrame`). `$08` moves that to Up, so B no longer makes you step off, and Up does |
| `0D36-D401` | `01E889:40` | ...or `$40`, which moves it to Y |
| `EE36-D401` | `01E889:FF` | ...or `$FF`, so any new button press throws you off. This includes the d-pad, so it is almost impossible to steer the cloud while you ride |
| `6D36-D701` | `01E88D:80` | stepping off gives a fixed `$C0` jump with no variable height. `$80` doubles it into a big launch |
| `DD3B-DD01` | `01E891:00` | stepping off also sets a cooldown of `$10` frames, so you cannot land on the cloud again at once. `$00` removes it: you get on again as soon as you start to fall, so if you tap B again and again, you bounce along on top of the cloud |
| `1D36-0401` | `01E989:60` | Lakitu never gets a speed directly. The cloud is pushed one unit every other frame toward a limit, `$20` when Mario is to the right. `$60` makes his chase speed to the right three times as fast |
| `CD36-0461` | `01E98A:A0` | the same for the limit to the left (`$E0` → `$A0`) |
| `0D36-04A1` | `01E98B:40` | the two ends of his idle up-and-down movement are `$10` down and `$F0` up. `$40` makes the down half four times as deep, so he dives and does not only bob |
| `AD36-07D1` | `01E98C:C0` | ...and the same for the up end, so he swings wildly through four times the vertical range |
| `DD3A-0DD1` | `01E9C0:00` | the whole acceleration step runs every other frame (`TrueFrame AND #$01`). `$00` runs it on every frame, so he turns toward you twice as sharply. He becomes jumpy and much harder to get away from |
| `DD32-0FD1` | `01E9D4:00` | bit 0 of `SpriteMisc1534` chooses the up or down half of the movement. A mask of `$00` keeps it on the down entry forever. So Lakitu stops bobbing and slowly sinks to the floor of the level, while he still chases you sideways |
| `DD3D-64D1` | `01EA08:00` | he throws when `TrueFrame AND #$7F` is zero, once every 128 frames. `$00` makes that test pass on every frame: Spinies come without stopping, limited only by how many sprite slots are free |
| `DE3D-64D1` | `01EA08:0F` | ...or `$0F`, one Spiny every sixteen frames. That is fast, but not a solid wall of them |
| `EE3D-67A1` | `01EA0F:FF` | each throw sets `SpriteMisc1558` to `$20`, the number of frames that Lakitu is drawn in his throw pose. `$FF` keeps him in the middle of a throw forever |
| `0D3F-6FA1` | `01EA17:40` | a thrown Spiny moves toward you at one pixel per frame. `$40` throws it four times as fast, so they fly far past you and do not drop in front of you |
| `DD37-6DD1` | `01EA30:00` | the throw normally checks `SilverPSwitchTimer` (`CMP #$01`), and while that timer runs, he throws a moving coin, not a Spiny. `CMP #$00` always sets carry, so the Spiny branch is never taken: Lakitu always throws coins at you |
| `4F37-6D61` | `01EA32:21` | the same effect from the other side: the sprite number `$14` (falling Spiny) changes directly to `$21` (moving coin), and the P-switch test does not change |
| `C639-6FA1` | `01EA57:A8` | Spinies are thrown up at `$D8`, and they fall back down past Lakitu. `$A8` throws them much higher, so they leave the top of the screen and come down several seconds later |
| `DD62-DD09` | `0184D1:00` | `InitMontyMole` is the shared end of the init code that Lakitu uses. It copies bit `$10` of the sprite's X position into `SpriteMisc151C`, and a Lakitu throws only when that byte is zero. A mask of `$00` makes it always zero, so *every* Lakitu throws, wherever he was placed |
| `EE62-DD09` | `0184D1:FF` | ...or `$FF`, which keeps the whole low byte of the X position. That is almost never zero, so almost no Lakitu ever throws anything |

**Caveats:**
- The main code and every `$01E7xx` variant change `LakituCloudTimer`, which
  is one global value, not a field for each sprite. That is safe here only
  because `InitLakitu` makes sure that at most one Lakitu and one cloud exist
  at the same time.
- `0184D1` is the only code here with a shared reader. `InitMontyMole` is also
  the whole init routine for the Monty Moles (`$4D`/`$4E`), the flying gray
  turn blocks (`$C1`) and `InitCreateEatBlk`. All of them set the same
  `SpriteMisc151C` from the same bit, and each one reads it in its own way.
  Expect those sprites to act differently too. Only the meaning of that bit
  for Lakitu is documented.
- `01E7D6:9F` brings back the sprite number you choose at `SpriteRespawnYPos`
  through the normal respawn path, so the new sprite gets its normal init.
  Sprites whose init needs some state that Lakitu's death does not leave may
  still act wrong.
- The ride codes (`01E833`, `01E851`) work by writing over `PlayerYSpeed` on
  every frame while you are on the cloud. You still have normal walking and
  jumping control the whole time. Riding the cloud really only replaces
  gravity. So you cannot fight an upward variant with the d-pad. You can only
  get away by stepping off.
- `01E889:FF` means that you cannot hold a direction while you ride, which is
  a real loss. The other two changes only move the step-off action to a button
  that you did not use in the air anyway.
- Not tested in play. Every effect above comes from the disassembly, and the
  byte at each address was checked against the reference ROM.

**Provenance:** the bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` (the U release,
without its 512-byte copier header) and compared with the disassembly.
`$01E7B0` has
`a5 14 29 03 d0 0f ad e0 18 f0 0a ce e0 18 d0 05 a9 1f 9d 40` (the timer
countdown, with the `ce` at `$01E7BB` that this code replaces). `$01E886` has

0b a9 c0 85 7d a9 10 9d 4c` (stepping off). `$01E989` has `20 e0 10 f0` (the

15` (the throw test). `$01EA2C` has `ad ae 14 c9 01 a9 14 90 02 a9` (the

## Chargin' Chuck splits when stomped

**Code:** `D9AE-A7DB`
**Raw form:** `02C7FC:05` (address:new-byte; original byte `$03` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 16:41:00

Tags: `video-ready` `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** There is no separate Chargin' Chuck routine. All eight Chuck
sprites (`$91` Chargin', `$92` Splittin', `$93` Bouncin', `$94`
Whistlin', `$95` Clapin', `$96` the unused copy, `$97` Puntin', `$98`
Pitchin') and also `$46`, the Diggin' Chuck, run the same routine,
`ChucksMain` in `bank_02.asm`. Which Chuck you see depends on one number:
`SpriteTableC2`, an index into a state dispatch table with thirteen entries.
The eight init routines in `bank_01.asm` do nothing else:

```
$00  Looking around      <- $91, which has no init and takes the $00
$01  Walking / charging      InitSpriteTables leaves behind
$02  Bracing before a charge
$03  Stomped, getting back up
$04  Diggin' Chuck       <- $46
$05  Splittin'/Bouncin'  <- $92, $93
$06  Bouncin', airborne
$07  Bouncin', landed
$08  Clapin' Chuck       <- $95
$09  Puntin' Chuck       <- $97
$0A  Pitchin' Chuck      <- $98
$0B  Whistlin', silent   <- $94
$0C  Whistlin', whistling
```

All nine sprites share everything outside that dispatch: gravity, the jump
over walls, breaking turn blocks, and death after three stomps.

A stomp that does not kill (`CODE_02C7F6`) puts the Chuck in state `$03` to
get up, with `$03` frames in `SpriteMisc1540`:

```
CODE_02C7F6:
    LDA.B #!SFX_ENEMYHURT
    STA.W SPCIO3
    LDA.B #$03                ; $02C7FC - the operand this code changes
    STA.B SpriteTableC2,X
    LDA.B #$03
    STA.W SpriteMisc1540,X
```

The code changes the state to `$05`, the Splittin'/Bouncin' state
(`CODE_02C582`). That state acts when `SpriteMisc1540` reaches `$01`, so two
frames after the stomp. It then checks the sprite number. Only `$93` (Bouncin')
bounces. Every other Chuck takes the split branch: he plays `!SFX_MAGIC`, goes
back to state `$00`, and creates two new Chargin' Chucks (`$91`) that are
thrown off to the left and right. Stomp any Chuck, and there are three
Chargin' Chucks.

The two new Chucks start with a stomp count of 0, so they split too when you
stomp them. The first Chuck keeps his count and still dies on his third stomp.

**Variant `BFA5-A46B`, Super Koopas:** the game checks the sprite *number* in
only three places. One of them is the end of the get-up sequence after a
stomp, at `CODE_02C777`:

```
CODE_02C777:
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X
    CMP.B #$94                ; $02C77A - the operand BFA5-A46B changes
    BEQ CODE_02C794           ; Whistlin' Chuck -> start whistling
    CMP.B #$46                ; $02C782
    BNE +                     ; Diggin' Chuck -> becomes a Chargin' Chuck
    LDA.B #$91
    STA.B SpriteNumber,X
  + ...brace, then charge, angry...
```

That `CMP #$94` is why a stomp on a Whistlin' Chuck calls the Super Koopas.
Nothing else in his state `$0B` works on dry land, so the stomp is the only
way into state `$0C`. `BFA5-A46B` changes the operand to `$91`, which moves that
way in to the normal Chargin' Chuck. Jump on any Chuck in the game, and he
does not get back up. He stands still, whistles, and sets
`ChuckIsWhistling`. If bit `$10` of his X position is set, he also starts
generator `$09`. He never leaves state `$0C`, so the whistling and the Super
Koopas continue for the rest of the level. The real Whistlin' Chuck loses the
change of state, and he only braces and charges at you like all the others.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `DFA3-A7AB` | `02C7EF:01` | the stomp counter in `SpriteMisc1528` is tested once, against `$03`. `$01` kills any Chuck with one stomp |
| `D6A3-A7AB` | `02C7EF:08` | ...or `$08`, so every Chuck needs eight |
| `EEA3-AF0B` | `02C7E5:FF` | stomps are not counted while the Chuck is already in state `$03` (`CMP #$03`). `$FF` never matches, so stomps add up while he is on the ground, and three fast jumps kill him |
| `EAAA-A46B` | `02C7CA:FC` | the stomp-or-hurt test compares Mario's vertical offset with `$EC`. `$FC` makes almost any contact from above count as a stomp |
| `ADAA-A46B` | `02C7CA:C0` | ...or `$C0`, so you must be more than `$40` pixels above him, and most jumps only hurt you |
| `EEAA-A76B` | `02C7CE:FF` | the contact cooldown of `$05` frames becomes `$FF`: after one touch, nothing can touch the Chuck for four seconds, and you can run directly through him |
| `BFA5-A46B` | `02C77A:91` | stomp a Chargin' Chuck and he whistles up a squadron of Super Koopas (see the mechanism above) |
| `EEAD-DDDC` | `02C800:FF` | the `$03` frames of stagger after a stomp become `$FF` |
| `D9AB-AF0B` | `02C795:05` | the other end of `BFA5-A46B`'s change: the state that a stomped *Whistlin'* Chuck goes to. `$05` makes him split, not whistle |
| `B0A6-AD6B` | `02C782:94` | when you stomp a Diggin' Chuck, his sprite number is normally changed to `$91`, and that makes him a normal charger for good. `$94` makes him a Whistlin' Chuck instead, so if you dig him out and stomp him two times, you get Super Koopas |
| `DA6D-0D09` | `018501:0C` | `InitWhistlinChuck` sets state `$0B`. `$0C` starts him in the whistling state, so he whistles as soon as he appears, and you never need to stomp him |
| `DC6D-0F09` | `018505:0A` | `InitChuck` sets `$05` for the Splittin' and Bouncin' Chucks. `$0A` makes them Pitchin' Chucks, with baseballs |

  the nine Chuck sprites changes. But for the same reason, a code for the

  `FindFreeSprSlot` fails and fewer Chucks appear.

  `$07`. So a Bouncin' Chuck still falls between bounces.

## Every Goomba, Koopa and Buzzy Beetle turns round and comes after you

**Code:** `EE69-A761`
**Raw form:** `018B5E:FF` (address:new-byte; original byte `$04` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 17:58:00

Tags: `basic-enemies` `play-start`

**Mechanism:** Sprite numbers `$00` to `$13` all run one handler,
`Spr0to13Main` in `bank_01.asm`. These are the four Koopas without shells,
the four with shells, the four para-Koopas, the Bob-omb, the keyhole, both
Goombas, the Buzzy Beetle and the Spiny. The only difference between a Goomba
and a red Koopa is one byte for each in `Spr0to13Prop`. This is a bit field
table with twenty entries, and the sprite number is its index:

```
$01  fast (use the second pair of Spr0to13SpeedX entries)
$02  turn round at a ledge
$04  face Mario
$08  jump over a kicked shell
$40  two tiles tall
$80  keep animating while airborne (the para-Koopas' flutter)
```

Only three sprites have bit `$04` set: the yellow Koopas `$03` and `$07`, and
the Bob-omb. Once per frame, while the sprite is on the ground, the handler
does this:

```
    LDA.W Spr0to13Prop,Y
    PHA
    AND.B #$04                ; $018B5E - the operand this code changes
    BEQ +                     ; not a chaser -> skip
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1570,X    ; \ ...and only every $80th animation frame
    AND.B #$7F                ; |
    BNE +                     ; /
    ...JSR FaceMario, and start the turning animation if he really turned...
```

`AND #$FF` can never give zero for a sprite whose property byte is not zero.
So the `BEQ` is no longer taken, and the chase code runs for every sprite in
the group whose property byte is not zero. Goombas and Koopas of every color
now turn toward Mario about once every two seconds. They also play the
eight-frame turn animation, which before only the yellow Koopa played. The
`AND` still reads the *table*, so the sprites whose property byte is `$00`
still do not chase: the green Koopa without a shell, the Buzzy Beetle and the
Spiny. (The keyhole and the unused `$12` also have `$00`, but they do not use
this handler.) Use this with `D96D-0D01` below for the Beetle, or `696D-0DA1`
for the Spiny.

## Swap the two green para-Koopas: the one that flies in bounces, and the bouncer takes to the air

**Code:** `DB65-DFD5`
**Raw form:** `018C74:09` (address:new-byte; original byte `$08` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 20:05:00

**Mechanism:** Sprites `$08` and `$09` are one routine, `GreenParaKoopa` in
`bank_01.asm`. One `CMP` is the only difference between them:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteNumber,X
    CMP.B #$08                ; $018C74 - the operand this code changes
    BNE CODE_018C8C
    JSR SubSprXPosNoGrvty     ; $08: no gravity at all...
    LDY.B #$FC                ; ...just a $FC/$04 bob driven by bit $20
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1570,X    ;    of the animation counter
    AND.B #$20
    BEQ +
    LDY.B #$04
  + STY.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    JSR SubSprYPosNoGrvty
    BRA +

CODE_018C8C:
    JSR SubUpdateSprPos       ; $09: ordinary gravity, and a bounce off
    DEC.B SpriteYSpeed,X      ;    the floor of $B0 or $D0
```

Sprite `$08` is the green Koopa that flies in from the right in a slow wave.
`$09` is the one that bounces along the ground. If you change the `$08` to
`$09`, the test matches the other sprite. `$09` now gets the up-and-down
movement with no gravity and floats across the screen. `$08` gets real
gravity and starts to bounce. `SpriteMisc160E` decides which of the two
bounce heights `$08` uses. `InitGrnBounceKoopa` sets it from bit `$10` of the
Y position where the level designer put him. Half a tile up or down chooses a
high or low bounce. The level designer never set that bit on purpose for a
flier, so his bounce height depends only on where he happened to be placed.

The red pair `$0A`/`$0B` work in the same way, and they share one oscillator
(`CODE_018CFD`). The trick there is that the oscillator writes its value to
*both* `SpriteXSpeed` and `SpriteYSpeed` every time. The axis along which the
Koopa really moves depends only on which of the two values is written over
after that. `$0A` skips `CODE_018CEA` and updates only its Y position, so it
moves vertically. `$0B` goes through `CODE_018CEA`, which writes over the Y
speed with the same `$FC`/`$04` up-and-down movement that the green flier
uses, and leaves the X speed to do the work. `EE63-DD65` changes that test in
the same way.

| `3D65-D4A5` | `018C7B:E0` | the flier's upward movement is eight times stronger |
| `D666-DDD5` | `018C80:08` | the flier's wave is four times faster, a tight zigzag |

**Caveats:** When the green flier `$08` gets real gravity, he bounces at the
height that `SpriteMisc160E` has. That value is set once, when he appears,
from bit `$10` of his placement Y. A flier placed anywhere in the top half of
his tile bounces high, and one placed anywhere in the bottom half bounces
low. Level designers never had to think about this difference. When the
bouncer `$09` gets the up-and-down movement with no gravity, he keeps his
floor collision code, but he never goes down far enough to use it. So he
flies directly through solid ground. The speed codes are two's-complement
byte speeds in units of 1/16 pixel: `$00`-`$7F` is right or down, and
`$80`-`$FF` is left or up. So the very fast values move the sprite off the
screen quickly, and `SpriteOffscreen` erases it. Sprite `$10` is only the
*jumping* form of the winged Goomba. The normal walking one uses the same walk
speed bytes at `018DBC`/`018DC3`, so you can see those two codes on both. Not
tested in play. Every effect above comes from the disassembly, and the byte at
each address was checked against the reference ROM.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again after
the comments added in this pass. The build with comments is byte-identical to
the reference ROM. All 29 different bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc`
(without its 512-byte copier header) at the LoROM offsets above, and they
matched the source operands exactly. Every code in the tables decodes back to
its own `address:byte` pair with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Lakitu's cloud: start levels with it

**Codes:** `D7C1-AFAB` + `65EB-D767` (both are needed)
**Raw form:** `02A767:03` (original byte `$09`) and `00FC9E:87` (original byte
`$35`) — address:new-byte; SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the
originals are recorded here instead
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 20:15:00

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** Nothing in the game can create a sprite at the start of any
level you choose. A level's sprites come from its own sprite data, which is
data and not code, and the cloud exists only where a Lakitu was placed. There
is only one exception: Yoshi coming back. If Mario goes into a pipe or door
while he rides Yoshi, `CarryYoshiThruLvls` is set. At the end of the sprite
part of level loading, the game puts Yoshi back under him. That is the only
sprite in Super Mario World that exists before the level's own sprite data is
read, and these two codes take control of it.

The first code opens the way. In `CODE_02A751` (`bank_02.asm`):

```
  + LDA.W CarryYoshiThruLvls     ; $02A763
    BEQ +                        ; $02A766, displacement at $02A767 = $09
    LDA.W RemoveYoshiFlag        ; $02A768
    BNE +                        ; $02A76B
    JSL CODE_00FC7A              ; $02A76D
  + PLB                          ; $02A771
```

`$09` sends the branch to the `PLB`: no Yoshi was carried, so Yoshi does not
come back. If you change the offset to `$03`, the branch goes to the `BNE`
instead. The accumulator is still zero from the load that set `Z`, so the
`BNE` is not taken, and the `JSL` runs. Now Yoshi comes back in **every**
level.

The second code decides which sprite comes back. `CODE_00FC7A`
(`bank_00.asm`) builds the sprite step by step:

```
  + LDA.B #$08                   ; Status = Normal, so the sprite's own
    STA.W SpriteStatus,X         ;   init routine is skipped entirely
    LDA.B #$35                   ; $00FC9D; operand at $00FC9E = Sprite $35, Yoshi
    STA.B SpriteNumber,X
    ...                          ; plant it at Mario's position, lift Mario $10 up
  + INC.W PlayerRidingYoshi
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X        ; <- this is the lever
```

Sprite `$87` is Lakitu's cloud. For `LakituCloud`, `SpriteTableC2` is exactly
the "Mario is on board" flag. The cloud sets the same byte for itself in
`CODE_01E7DB` when he lands on one. So the routine that should put Mario on
Yoshi puts him on a cloud instead, already riding it, on the first frame of
the level. The status is set directly to `$08`, so the cloud never runs its
own init, and no Lakitu needs to drop it.

After that, `CODE_01E840` works normally. On every frame it moves the cloud to
Mario's position, replaces his fall speed with a slow sink of `$13`, and marks
him as standing on something solid. B makes him step off with a fixed `$C0`
jump.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `65EB-D767` | `00FC9E:87` | used alone: you still get the cloud only where Yoshi would have come back, but if you go into a pipe on Yoshi, you now get a cloud instead |
| `D7C1-AFAB` | `02A767:03` | used alone: Yoshi is under you at the start of every level, whether you brought him or not |
| `DDC1-A7DB` | `02A76C:00` (orig `$04`) | a third way in: disables the `RemoveYoshiFlag` branch, so levels that should take Yoshi away can no longer do it |

**Caveats:** `PlayerRidingYoshi` is set together with the cloud flag, and
nothing clears it. So Mario is drawn in the riding pose the whole time. The
cloud stays at the Yoshi bob distance (the second half of `DATA_01E793`,
`$1A`-`$1E`) and not the normal `$0E`-`$12`. So he floats clearly higher
above it than on a cloud that he got on normally. `YoshiColor` is written into
the sprite's OAM attribute, so the cloud's palette is the color of the last
Yoshi you had. `CurrentYoshiSlot` and `YoshiIsLoose` both point to the cloud.
This means you cannot ride Yoshi at all for the rest of the game. The Yoshi
drum roll sound plays at the start of every level. In a level that already has
a live Lakitu, the check at `CODE_01E7DB` finds him and jumps to
`CODE_01E898`, so he takes your cloud from you and rides it himself. Also, with
the first code on, Yoshi comes back before the level's own sprites are read.
So this uses a sprite slot in every level: slot `$05` normally, or the slot
that `FindFreeSprSlot` returns, with slot `$03` if none is found. In crowded
rooms, this can cost you a sprite. Not tested in play. Every effect above
comes from the disassembly, and the byte at each address was checked against
the reference ROM.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again after
the comments added to `CODE_02A751` and `CODE_00FC7A` in this pass. The build
with comments is byte-identical to the reference ROM. The original bytes `$09`
at `02A767`, `$04` at `02A76C` and `$35` at `00FC9E` were read from
`comparison_U.smc` (without its 512-byte copier header) at LoROM offsets
`$012767`, `$01276C` and `$007C9E`, and they matched the source operands
exactly. Every code above decodes back to its own `address:byte` pair with
`tools/gg_encode.py
decode`.

## Bullet Time for Banzai Bill

**Code:** `EE2B-040B`
**Raw form:** `02D599:FF` (address:new-byte; original byte `$E8` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 20:30:00

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** Sprite `$9F` is the biggest enemy in the game, but it has the
smallest main routine of all the enemies. It has no state machine, no gravity
and no aiming. All of it is `CODE_02D587` in `bank_02.asm`:

```
CODE_02D587:
    JSR CODE_02D5E4              ; draw the 4x4 block of 16x16 tiles
    LDA.W SpriteStatus,X
    CMP.B #$02                   ; $02D58D; operand at $02D58E
    BEQ +                        ;   killed-and-falling: draw only
    LDA.B SpriteLock
    BNE +
    JSR SubOffscreen0Bnk2
    LDA.B #$E8                   ; $02D598; operand at $02D599
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X         ;   the only speed he ever has
    JSR UpdateXPosNoGrvty
    JSL MarioSprInteract
  + RTS
```

On every frame, he is drawn again, gets the same fixed X speed, moves by that
speed, and is checked for a collision with Mario. `$E8` is `-$18` in two's
complement, which is one and a half pixels left per frame. It is not a start
speed or a maximum. It is written again on every frame, so if you change this
one byte, his flight changes completely and for good. `$FF` is `-$01` in
two's complement: a sixteenth of a pixel per frame, the smallest leftward
speed that is not zero and fits in a signed byte. He still flies toward Mario
exactly as `InitBanzai` wants (he appears to Mario's right, by `SubHorizPos`,
and `OffScrEraseSprite` deletes any that would appear on the wrong side). But
he is so slow that crossing the screen takes minutes, not seconds. In
practice, he stays in the air and moves forward very slowly.

The status test is the other thing you can change. `$02` is the
killed-and-falling status. So the branch normally means "after he is beaten,
only keep drawing him". That is why a dying Banzai Bill stops in the air and
does not keep moving. If you change the operand to `$08`, the normal live
status, the test matches *live* Bills instead. They stop where they are. The
branch skips `MarioSprInteract` and also the movement, so they can no longer
hurt Mario at all. He can walk directly through a Bill that hangs still in the
sky.

**Variants:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `EE2B-040B` | `02D599:FF` (orig `$E8`) | he flies left again, but at the slowest possible speed that is not zero, a sixteenth of a pixel per frame |
| `F62B-040B` | `02D599:18` (orig `$E8`) | he flies right, away from Mario, and not left |
| `2D2B-040B` | `02D599:D0` | he flies left at twice the speed |
| `6D2B-040B` | `02D599:80` | he flies left eight times as fast, so he is only a quick flash across the screen |
| `E02B-040B` | `02D599:F4` | half speed, a slow and scary movement |
| `EA2B-040B` | `02D599:FC` | very slow, a quarter of a pixel per frame |
| `DD2B-040B` | `02D599:00` | he stays still in the air where he appeared |
| `D626-076B` | `02D58E:08` (orig `$02`) | live Bills match the killed test: they stop *and* skip the collision check completely, so they become harmless scenery |
| `DD26-076B` | `02D58E:00` | nothing ever matches, so a Bill that you already killed keeps flying and keeps hurting you as it falls |
| `B32F-670B` | `02D61D:9E` (orig `$9F`) | the ball-and-chain and the Banzai Bill swap routines |
| `C72F-670B` | `02D61D:A3` | the gray chain platform swaps routines with the Banzai Bill |
| `DD2F-670B` | `02D61D:00` | nothing matches, so the Banzai Bill runs the chain rotation code and does not fly |

The last three are in `Banzai_Rotating`. This is the shared entry point for the
three sprites that use it: `$9E` the ball and chain, `$9F` the Banzai Bill and
`$A3` the gray platform on a chain. One `CMP` separates them:

```
Banzai_Rotating:
    PHB : PHK : PLB
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X
    CMP.B #$9F                   ; $02D61C; operand at $02D61D
    BNE CODE_02D625
    JSR CODE_02D587              ; the flat leftward flight
    BRA +
CODE_02D625:
    JSR CODE_02D62A              ; the chain rotator
  + PLB
    RTL
```

`CODE_02D62A` swings a sprite around a center, at the radius that
`InitBallNChain` and `InitGreyChainPlat` put in `SpriteMisc187B`. If the test
checks `$9E`, the ball-and-chain flies in a straight line, and the Banzai Bill
swings on a chain. `$00` matches nothing, so only the Bill swings on the chain.

**Caveats:** Each sprite's *init* routine fills `SpriteMisc187B`, and
`InitBanzai` never fills it. It only does the horizontal position test and
plays the boom sound. So a Banzai Bill that runs the chain rotation code swings
at whatever radius the byte happened to have, which is not a designed value.
Expect an irregular path, not a clean circle, and expect it to be different
each time one appears. The same is true the other way for a ball-and-chain that
gets the flight routine. It keeps the chain state that its init gave it, and
this is harmless, because the flight path never reads it. The speed codes are
two's-complement byte speeds in units of 1/16 pixel. So `$00`-`$7F` is right,
and `$80`-`$FF` is left. The very fast values move the Bill off the screen
quickly enough that `SubOffscreen0Bnk2` erases him. `02D58E:00` leaves a dead
Bill flying *and* still colliding. This means the same Bill can kill you after
you already beat him. Sprite `$9F` is only the giant Banzai Bill. The normal
Bullet Bill is sprite `$2E`, which is a completely different routine, and none
of the above changes it. Not tested in play. Every effect above comes from the
disassembly, and the byte at each address was checked against the reference
ROM.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again after
the comments added to `CODE_02D587`, `InitBanzai` and `Banzai_Rotating` in this
pass. The build with comments is byte-identical to the reference ROM. The
original bytes `$E8` at `02D599`, `$02` at `02D58E` and `$9F` at `02D61D` were
read from `comparison_U.smc` (without its 512-byte copier header) at LoROM
offsets `$015599`, `$01558E` and `$01561D`, and they matched the source
operands exactly. All eleven codes decode back to their own `address:byte`
pair with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`. The sprite tweaker parameter tables in
`bank_07.asm` (`Sprite1656Vals` and after) also have behavior bits for each
sprite, including `$9F`. But they are bare `db` rows with no comments, so they
were **not** searched for codes on purpose. They are recorded as blocked until
they get comments.

## Shrink the Wiggler's body, or make him actually hunt you

**Code:** `D1ED-0FA6`
**Raw form:** `02F107:06` (address:new-byte; original byte `$7E` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 21:00:00

**Mechanism:** Sprite `$86`, the Wiggler, looks like a caterpillar with five
parts. But it is one sprite that remembers where it has been. `WigglerTable`
is 512 bytes of RAM, divided into four ring buffers of `$80` bytes, one for
each Wiggler. (The low two bits of the sprite slot choose the buffer. This is
the real reason why only four can be on the screen.) On every frame,
`WigglerPushTrail` moves the whole history two bytes along with one `MVP`,
and it writes the head's current position into the free space at offset
`$00`:

```
WigglerPushTrail:
    REP #$30
    LDA.B WigglerSegmentPtr : CLC : ADC.W #$007D : TAX
    LDA.B WigglerSegmentPtr : CLC : ADC.W #$007F : TAY
    LDA.W #$007D
    MVP WigglerTable>>16,WigglerTable>>16      ; the whole trail, moved back one slot
    SEP #$30
    ...                                        ; head position -> offset $00
```

So offset `$2n` has the position of the head *n* frames ago. The body parts
are never simulated at all. They are the head's own past positions, shown
again after a delay, and one table decides how long that delay is:

```
WigglerSegmentTrailOfs:
    db $00,$1E,$3E,$5E,$7E      ; $02F103..$02F107
```

The head is at "now", and the four parts are at 15, 31, 47 and 63 frames ago.
That table multiplied by his walking speed *is* his length. Nothing else in
the sprite knows how long he is. If you lower the tail's `$7E` to `$06`, it
uses three frames of history, not sixty-three. So the whole body collects in a
short lump directly behind the head.

The same table is why an angry Wiggler looks different. When
`SpriteMisc151C` is set, the draw routine halves every offset before it reads
it (`TYA : LSR A : AND
#$FE`), and the speed table moves on by two to the doubled charge speeds. He
moves twice as fast and uses half as much history, so on the screen he stays
about the same length, but you can see that he hurries.

The one thing a Wiggler does that is not on a fixed path is to turn toward
Mario. When he is angry, every `$40` frames he checks where Mario is and turns
to face him:

```
    INC.W SpriteMisc1534,X
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1534,X
    AND.B #$3F                  ; $02F07C
    BNE +
    JSR CODE_02D4FA             ; Y = 1 if Mario is to the left
    TYA
    STA.W SpriteMisc157C,X
```

`D7E5-D7D6` cuts that to `$03`, and the stomped Wiggler turns toward Mario
fifteen times a second. This changes the enemy that most blindly walks in a
straight line into something that follows you around the room. A calm Wiggler
never changes direction at all, except when he walks into a wall.

The stomp handler always bounces Mario. But everything after that (the
flower, the points, the stun flash) is skipped when `SpriteMisc151C` is
already set. That is the flag the first stomp sets. So you can never stomp an
angry Wiggler again, whatever these codes do to the numbers. Star power
(`ADDR_02F29D`) is the only path in the routine that sets a killed status. The
hitbox codes change five boxes that are read directly from the OAM entries
that were just written. So if you make the drawn body smaller with `02F107`,
the hitboxes also get smaller. `02F11B:00` goes further. Only the head can
touch Mario at all, and you can walk directly through the four body parts.
Segment count values above `$05` at `02F147` would make the draw loop go past
the end of `WigglerSegmentTrailOfs` into `WigglerSegmentYDisp`, so they are
not listed here. The `02F2E3` stomp reward codes change the extended sprite
that comes out of his head. Every replacement in the list is a real entry in
the extended sprite dispatch table. But all of them get
`ExtSpriteMisc1765 = $01` and the Wiggler's position. That is what the flower
expects, but maybe not what they expect. So expect a fireball with a strange
start state, not a clean shot. Only one is created, and only if a free
extended sprite slot exists, so in a busy room you get nothing. Speeds are
two's-complement bytes in units of 1/16 pixel (`$00`-`$7F` right, `$80`-`$FF`
left). Not tested in play. Every effect above comes from the disassembly, and
the byte at each address was checked against the reference ROM.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again after
the comments added in this pass to `WigglerInit`, `WigglerSetBufferPtr`,
`WigglerMainRt`, `WigglerPushTrail`, `WigglerSegmentTrailOfs`,
`WigglerSegmentYDisp`, `WigglerTiles`, `WigglerSpawnFlower` and
`WigglerGroundYSpeed`. The build with comments is byte-identical to the
reference ROM. All 30 different bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc`
(without its 512-byte copier header) at the LoROM offsets above, and they
matched the source operands exactly. All 54 codes decode back to their own
`address:byte` pair with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Give every Thwomp a hair trigger, or make him climb back so fast he never comes down again

**Code:** `EEC3-64A5`
**Raw form:** `01AEEB:FF` (address:new-byte; original byte `$50` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 21:35:00

**Mechanism:** Sprite `$26`, the Thwomp, is a state machine with three states.
`ExecutePtr` chooses the state from `SpriteTableC2`: 0 hanging, 1 falling,
2 sitting and then climbing back. Everything dangerous about him is in state
0. It is two ranges, one inside the other, measured on the low byte of Mario's
X minus his own X:

```
CODE_01AEC3:
    ...
    LDA.B _F
    CLC
    ADC.B #$40                  ; operand at $01AEDB
    CMP.B #$80                  ; operand at $01AEDD
    BCS +
    LDA.B #$01                  ; within $40 either side: turn the eyes only
    STA.W SpriteMisc1528,X
  + LDA.B _F
    CLC
    ADC.B #$24                  ; operand at $01AEE9
    CMP.B #$50                  ; operand at $01AEEB - the drop trigger
    BCS Return01AEF9
CODE_01AEEE:
    LDA.B #$02                  ; angry face
    STA.W SpriteMisc1528,X
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X       ; -> falling
```

The outer range only changes his face. The inner range (`$24` pixels to the
left, `$2C` to the right) is the whole area he can reach. If you walk one
pixel outside it, a Thwomp never moves. If you make the `CMP` operand `$FF`,
the compare always passes. So every Thwomp in the game drops as soon as he
comes onto the screen, wherever Mario is.

The climbing state has something more interesting. He goes back home by
comparing the low byte of his Y with the value that `InitThwomp` saved when
he appeared:

```
CODE_01AF24:
    LDA.B SpriteYPosLow,X
    CMP.W SpriteMisc151C,X      ; exact byte equality
    BNE +
    LDA.B #$00
    STA.B SpriteTableC2,X       ; home again - back to hanging
    RTS
  + LDA.B #$F0                  ; operand at $01AF39
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
```

That equality test is safe only because `$F0` is exactly *minus one pixel per
frame* (sprite speeds are in 1/16ths, and `-$10/16 = -1`). He rises one pixel
at a time, so he must land on the exact byte where he started. If you change
the rise to `$E0`, he moves two pixels per frame. Then whether he ever gets to
his home byte depends on whether the distance he fell is even or odd. Half the
time, he goes directly past it and keeps climbing, through the ceiling and off
the top of the level, forever.

Sprite `$27`, the Thwimp, is a completely different routine with no state
pointer at all, and nothing in it ever looks at Mario. He falls at `$08` per
frame, up to `$40`. He rises at only `$03`, and bounces off ceilings at `$10`.
When he lands, he sits for `$40` frames, then jumps up at `$A0` and one step
to the side. The low bit of his landing count decides left or right. That is
why he moves between two positions forever and does not chase anything.

**Caveats:** `01AF39:E0` and the other fast climb values are an interesting
glitch, not a clean effect. A Thwomp that misses his home byte keeps rising
forever and leaves the level. `01AF39:10` reverses the sign, so he goes down
instead and sinks through the floor, and does not return. `01AEE9:04` makes
the left half of the trigger range smaller and does not change the right
half. So he drops only after Mario walks past under him. The two halves are
also not equal in the original (`$24` left, `$2C` right), because one `ADC`
shifts the range. `01AEE7`/`01AEE9` are also used for the face choice, so if
you change the trigger, it also changes when he shows the angry face. The
placement change at `01AE9F` moves *every* Thwomp in the game from where the
level data puts him. In rooms that were built close around him, this can put
one inside a wall. The Thwimp's `01AFEA:40` jump goes down and not up, which
keeps him on the floor forever. It is boring to watch, and it is only listed
to be complete. All speeds are two's-complement bytes in units of 1/16 pixel
(`$00`-`$7F` down/right, `$80`-`$FF` up/left). Not tested in play. Every
effect above comes from the disassembly, and the byte at each address was
checked against the reference ROM.

## Monty Moles dig climbable vines out of the ledges instead of holes

**Code:** `D737-A7D0`
**Raw form:** `01E33C:03` (address:new-byte; original byte `$08` — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte, so the original is recorded here instead)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 14:05:00

**Mechanism:** Sprite `$4E` is the Monty Mole that jumps out of a ledge and
not out of the floor. It is the only sprite in the game that changes the level
as it moves. On the frame when it jumps out, it copies its own position into
the block creation variables and asks `GenerateTile` for Map16 tile `$08`:

```
    CMP.B #$4E                ; $01E326 - which sprite digs
    BNE MontyMoleDrawBuried
    LDA.B SpriteXPosLow,X     ; \ $9A = sprite X
    STA.B TouchBlockXPos      ; | for block creation
    ...
    LDA.B #$08                ; $01E33C - the operand this code changes
    STA.B Map16TileGenerate   ; Block to generate = Mole hole
    JSL GenerateTile
```

`Map16TileGenerate` is a small documented index, and other parts of the game
name its entries where they use them: `$02` is the blank tile that a used-up
block leaves, `$03` is the vine that a vine block grows, `$04` the tree behind
a berry, `$06` a coin, `$08` the mole hole, `$09` an invisible solid block,
`$0D` a used block. Any of those is a valid value here, so the hole that the
mole leaves can become any of them. `$03` is the most interesting one. Every
ledge mole in the level makes a climbable vine in the wall that he came out
of. Vines grow, so one mole can build a ladder up to the ceiling.

The rest of the routine depends on one bit. `InitMontyMole` copies bit `$10`
of the mole's placement X (half a tile of the level editor grid) into
`SpriteMisc151C`. The chase state reads exactly that byte to decide if he
walks or jumps. Nothing else makes them different:

```
MontyMoleChase:
    JSR MontyMoleMoveAndDraw
    LDA.W SpriteMisc151C,X    ; the placement bit, and nothing else
    BNE MontyMoleHop          ; $01E39A
```

The walker never turns around directly. On each frame, a random choice decides
if he turns toward Mario, and his X speed moves *one 1/16th of a pixel* toward
`$18`/`$E8`. So he slows down through zero and speeds up again in the other
direction. That is why a mole that you run past needs a visible moment before
he comes after you, and why he makes dust while his speed still has the wrong
sign. The jumper never reads Mario's position at all. On every landing, he
gets a fixed `$10`/`$F0` again, and he jumps again at `$D8` when a cooldown
of `$50` frames ends. So he only bounces along a line. He only seems to hunt
you because the shared movement code turns him around at walls.

The third finding is how the difficulty increases. When a mole wakes up, he
does not jump out at once. A timer starts in `SpriteMisc1540`, and the
overworld submap of the level chooses that timer's value:

```
    LDY.W PlayerTurnLvl
    LDA.W OWPlayerSubmap,Y
    TAY
    LDA.B #$68                ; $01E2FB - Yoshi's Island's fuse
    CPY.B #$01                ; $01E2FD - submap $01 is Yoshi's Island
    BEQ +
    LDA.B #$20                ; $01E301 - everywhere else
  + STA.W SpriteMisc1540,X
```

`$68` gives almost two seconds of warning. `$20` gives half a second. It is the
same sprite and the same level data, but a Monty Mole is three times slower to
jump out in world 1 than anywhere after it.

| | | **Burrow graphics** |

**Caveats:** The tile that the mole makes is written into the level's Map16
layer. So it stays after the mole dies, and leaving the screen does not undo
it. A room with several ledge moles collects whatever you told them to leave.
`$09` (invisible solid block) can block a path that the level expected you to
walk through. `$02` removes the visual sign that a mole came out of that
place. The placement bit codes at `0184D1` change `InitMontyMole`, which is a
*shared* init. Lakitu (`$1E`), the flying gray turn blocks (`$C1`), the wooden
spike (`$AD`) and the creating/eating block (`$B1`) all run the same two
instructions. For a Lakitu, the same bit decides if he ever throws a Spiny. So
those two codes change six sprites, not one. `DD3B-A460` is the version of the
same effect for moles only (it disables the branch that chooses the jumper),
and it is the safer choice. Speeds are two's-complement bytes in units of
1/16 pixel: `$00`-`$7F` is right/down, `$80`-`$FF` left/up, so `$F0` is
exactly one pixel per frame. `01E2F0` is a branch offset, not a value. If you
set it to zero, the branch goes to the next instruction, and that is what lets
a mole that is off the screen wake up. The only difference between the timer
codes at `01E2FB`/`01E301` is which submap you are on. On Yoshi's Island only
the first applies, and everywhere else only the second. Not tested in play.
Every effect above comes from the disassembly, and the byte at each address
was checked against the reference ROM.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`, made again after
the Monty Mole comments added in this pass. The build with comments is
byte-identical to the reference ROM. All 20 different bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` (without its 512-byte copier header) at the LoROM offsets
above, and they matched the source operands exactly. All 49 codes decode back
to their own `address:byte` pair with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`. The
`Map16TileGenerate` index values used above are each documented in the places
where other parts of the disassembly use them. They were not guessed from this
routine.

## The Volcano Lotus showers you with coins instead of fireballs

**Code:** `DC3B-DD06`

**Raw form:** `$02E091` ← `$0A` (originally `$0C`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09

**Mechanism:** The Volcano Lotus (sprite `$2A`, the plant in a pot on a
pedestal) does not own his fireballs. He creates them as *extended sprites*,
and the extended sprite number he asks for is one immediate byte in
`VolcanoLotusSpawnFire`:

```
VolcanoLotusSpawnFire:
    LDA.B #$0C                                ; \ Extended sprite = Volcano Lotus fire
    STA.W ExtSpriteNumber,Y                   ; /
```

`$0C` is his own fire. `$0A` is the coin that the cloud bonus game creates. It
is a real coin that you can collect. The spawner does not check which number it
gets. It writes the number into the free slot, copies his own position into it,
and then loads the slot's X and Y speeds from his two tables of four entries.
So whatever you put here is launched in the same fan of four directions, at the
same speeds, on the same schedule. He fires four at a time, and the whole cycle
of idle, warning and spit is `$100` frames, a little more than four seconds. So
one Lotus becomes a coin fountain that keeps paying for as long as he is on the
screen.

The rest of him is a loop of three states on one countdown, `SpriteMisc1540`.
`SpriteTableC2` tells what the count means: idle (`$80` frames), warning
(`$40`), mouth open (`$40`). The shots are not fired when the mouth opens. They
are fired on the one frame when the countdown is `$38`:

```
VolcanoLotusSpit:
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1540,X
    BNE +
    LDA.B #$80
    JSR VolcanoLotusNextState
    STZ.B SpriteTableC2,X
  + CMP.B #$38
    BNE +
    JSR VolcanoLotusSpitFire
```

That is an equality test, not a limit. So `$38` is a more sensitive byte than it
looks. If you set it above the state's own `$40`, the compare never matches.
Then he opens his mouth on schedule forever and never spits.

harmless decoration. All ten numbers used above are documented in the places

## The Torpedo Ted launcher fires a continuous stream

**Code:** `D688-A7D6`

**Raw form:** `$02B3BC` ← `$08` (originally `$50`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09

**Mechanism:** Torpedo Teds are not placed in a level. A *generator* makes
them. `LaunchTorpedo` is generator type `$01`, and the first thing it does is
reset a simple 80-frame timer:

```
LaunchTorpedo:
    LDA.W ShooterTimer,X
    BNE Return02B42C
    LDA.B #$50
    STA.W ShooterTimer,X
```

If you lower that `$50` to `$08`, the launcher fires every eight frames. The
interesting detail is what comes *after* the reset: three tests, and each one
can cancel the shot. The launcher must be on the camera's screen on both axes,
and it must be at least `$10` pixels in from the left edge of the screen. The
timer is already reset at that point, so a failed test does not delay the
shot. It *loses* it. That is why a launcher that scrolls in from the left seems
to wait, and it is also why the two dead zone bytes below change how often it
fires without changing the timer at all.

The Ted himself is an unusual sprite. He has no init routine, no gravity, and
one byte of state that means "still in the launcher". While `SpriteMisc1540`
counts down, he is drawn behind the level, sinks slowly, and does not move
sideways. The movement part of the routine is physically *after* his two speed
tables, and only the branch taken when the timer ends gets to it. Also, the two
directions are not the same:

```
TorpedoMaxSpeed:
    db $20,$F0

TorpedoAccel:
    db $01,$FF
```

`$20` is two pixels per frame, and `$F0` is one. The same sprite is twice as
fast when he comes at you from the left as when he comes from the right. There
is no comment about this difference in the original code and nothing in the
game shows it. `02B8B9:E0` below makes the two speeds equal.

table, with its own copy of this logic, so it does not change. A fast reload
cannot make sprites from nothing. The launcher still needs a free sprite slot,
so on a busy screen the extra shots are lost. The top speed test is
`CMP`/`BEQ`, an equality and not a limit. So any code that makes the
acceleration and the limit point in opposite directions (`02B8B8:F0`,
`02B8BA:FF`) means the speed byte never equals its limit. It keeps changing
until it wraps around through zero, and the Ted turns around and does not
stop. The sag codes affect the launch timer. `02B8B4` is written on every frame
*during* the launch and only starts to go away after the timer ends. So
`02B8B4:80` is a climb that moves away from zero, not toward it, and it never
becomes level. The exhaust puffs use a side table of four slots that every
other smoke effect on the screen also uses. A Ted takes a slot and does not
wait, so a long trail (`02B99F:40`) visibly pushes out other puffs. The two
graphics offset tables overlap on purpose. `02B8F1` is both the second entry of
the nose table and the first entry of the tail table, so that one byte moves
two different tiles. Not tested in play. Every effect above comes from the
disassembly, and the byte at each address was checked against the reference
ROM.
