## Getting hit powers you up instead of shrinking you

**Code:** `05AB-04AF`

**Raw form:** `$00C59B` ← `$47` (originally `$29`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

**Mechanism:** `ProcessPlayerAnimation` is a simple jump table: `LDA.B
PlayerAnimation / JSL ExecutePtr`, followed directly by fourteen `dw` entries.
The source gives each one a name and a comment:

```
ProcessPlayerAnimation:
    LDA.B PlayerAnimation
    JSL ExecutePtr

    dw ResetAni                               ; 0 - Reset
    dw PowerDownAni                           ; 1 - Power down
    dw MushroomAni                            ; 2 - Mushroom power up
    dw CapeAni                                ; 3 - Cape power up
    dw FlowerAni                              ; 4 - Flower power up
    ...
```

Entry 1 is the only thing that `HurtMario` starts when an enemy takes a powerup
away. The damage path itself does not animate anything. It drops the reserve
item, sets the animation number, clears the powerup and passes control on:

```
PowerDown:
    LDY.B #!SFX_PIPE
    STY.W SPCIO0
    JSL DropReserveItem
    LDA.B #$01                                ; \ Set power down animation
    STA.B PlayerAnimation                     ; /
    STZ.B Powerup                             ; Mario status = Small
    LDA.B #$2F
```

The interesting part is where the *growth* happens. `GiveMarioMushroom` also
does not make Mario big. It only sets animation 2 and the same `$2F` timer. The
real change to Big is one instruction at the end of the grow animation:

```
CODE_00D156:
    INC.B Powerup
CODE_00D158:
    LDA.B #$00
    STA.B PlayerAnimation
    STZ.B SpriteLock
```

`PowerDownAni` and `MushroomAni` are `$D129` and `$D147`, on the same page. So
one byte is enough to point entry 1 at `$47`. A hit then runs the *mushroom*
animation. `HurtMario` has already set `Powerup` to zero, the grow sequence
plays, and `INC.B Powerup` sets it back to 1. You cannot be made smaller than
Big. Both paths load the same `$2F` into `PlayerAniTimer`, and `MushroomAni`
reads `GrowingAniImgs` at index `$0B - (timer >> 2)`. So `$2F` gives exactly
the last entry of the table, and the animation fits the timer with nothing left
over.

**Variants:**

| Code | Address:Value | Effect |
|------|---------------|--------|
| `05AB-04AF` | `00C59B:47` | a hit makes you small and then at once grows you back to Big (orig `$29`) |
| `9EAB-04AF` | `00C59B:5F` | a hit makes Mario disappear for `$2F` frames, and then he appears again without his powerup (orig `$29`) |
| `4BAB-070F` | `00C59D:29` | mushrooms no longer make you big. You get the `$7F` invincibility frames of `PowerDownAni` instead (orig `$47`) |
| `9EAB-070F` | `00C59D:5F` | a mushroom makes Mario disappear for the length of the animation and does nothing else (orig `$47`) |
| `05AB-07AF` | `00C59F:47` | a feather gives you the cape, and then the `INC Powerup` of the grow animation takes you to Fire (orig `$5F`) |
| `4BAC-0D0F` | `00C5A1:29` | a fire flower also gives you `$7F` invincibility frames (orig `$6F`) |

**Evidence:** `ProcessPlayerAnimation` is at `$00C593` in `bank_00.asm`. So the
table starts at `$00C599`, and entry *n* is at `$00C599 + 2n`. `UnknownAniB` at
`$00C5B5` is exactly `$1C` bytes later, which is the fourteen entries. The
reference ROM at `$00C599` has `68 CC 29 D1 47 D1 5F D1 6F D1 97 D1`. This
matches `ResetAni $CC68`, `PowerDownAni $D129`, `MushroomAni $D147`,
`CapeAni $D15F`, `FlowerAni $D16F`, `DoorPipeAni $D197` from `SMW_U.sym`. The
`STA.B PlayerAnimation` / `STZ.B Powerup` of `HurtMario` were read at `$00F5FE`
(`85 71 64 19`), and the `INC.B Powerup` at the end of `MushroomAni` at
`$00D156`. Not tested in play. The effects come from the disassembly.

**Caveats:** `PowerDownAni` is the only handler that sets `IFrameTimer` (`$7F`,
at `CODE_00D140`). So with `00C59B:47` you lose the invincibility after a hit:
on the frame when the grow animation ends, you can be hit again. None of these
codes change Small Mario, because `HurtMario` branches to `KillMario` before it
gets to `PowerDown`. `00C59F:47` runs `MushroomAni` with the shorter `$18` timer
of the cape animation, and *without* the `PlayerHiddenTiles = $7F` of `CapeAni`.
So Mario is visible where the game normally hides him behind the smoke puff. It
only gets to Fire because `GiveMarioCape` has already written `Powerup = 2`
before the animation starts. If you get a feather as Fire Mario
(`GivePowerPtrIndex` row `$0F`), `Powerup` would go to `$04`, which is not a
defined status. `00C5A1:29` skips the part of `FlowerAni` that clears
`FlightPhase` and the cape pose. So if you get a flower while you fly, that
state stays. It also depends on `PlayerAniTimer` being 0 on that path
(`GiveMarioFire` sets `CyclePaletteTimer`, not the animation timer). With an
old timer value that is not zero, you would see the shrink poses first.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`8f74b96d62115a17`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offset
`0x04599`. The codes decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`, and
`00C59B:47` was also checked with romdev's own encoder
(`cheats({op:'make'})` → `05AB-04AF`, identical).

## Dying costs you the level but not a life

**Code:** `31AC-04AF`

**Raw form:** `$00C5AB` ← `$E6` (originally `$B6`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

**Mechanism:** Entry 9 of the same `ProcessPlayerAnimation` table is
`dw MarioDeathAni ; 9 - Mario Death`. `MarioDeathAni` is the whole death
sequence: the death pose, the four-frame countdown on `PlayerAniTimer`, the
bounce, and, when the timer ends, the updates to the game state:

```
    LDA.B #$80
    STA.W OWLevelExitMode
    LDA.W RemoveYoshiFlag
    BNE +
    STZ.W CarryYoshiThruLvls
  + DEC.W PlayerLives                         ; Decrease amount of lifes
    BPL DeathNotGameOver
```

`DeathNotGameOver` is the last part, which decides where you go next:

```
DeathNotGameOver:
    LDY.B #$0B                                ; Set Y (game mode) to x0B (Fade to overworld)
    LDA.W InGameTimerHundreds
    ORA.W InGameTimerTens
    ORA.W InGameTimerOnes
    BNE +
    LDX.B #$1D                                ; Set X (Death message) to x1D (Time Up)
...
  + STY.W GameMode
```

`MarioDeathAni` is at `$D0B6` and `DeathNotGameOver` at `$D0E6`, on the same
page. So one byte points entry 9 at the last part and not the start. The death
animation never runs. On the first frame, `PlayerAnimation` becomes 9, the
handler writes game mode `$0B`, and the game fades back to the overworld. The
`DEC.W PlayerLives` comes before the new entry point, so it never runs.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM at `$00C5AB` has `B6 D0`, which matches
`MarioDeathAni` `$00D0B6` in `SMW_U.sym`. `$00D0E6` has `A0 0B AD 31 0F` = `LDY #$0B / LDA.W
InGameTimerHundreds`, the first two instructions of `DeathNotGameOver`. The
level init path clears `PlayerAnimation` when a level starts:
`LDX.B #$23 / - STZ.B Map16HighPtr+2,X / DEX / BNE -` at `CODE_00A660` sets
`$71`-`$93` to zero, and `$71` is `PlayerAnimation`. So the animation number
that is left does not follow you into the next level. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** Every death goes through this entry, including a fall off the
bottom of the level (`CODE_00F595` calls `KillMario`) and running out of time.
So all of them become instant, free returns to the map. Two writes that
normally happen on death are skipped with the rest of `MarioDeathAni`. One is
`OWLevelExitMode = $80`. It is not documented in this disassembly's RAM map,
so all we can say is that it keeps its last value. The other is the
`STZ.W CarryYoshiThruLvls` that would take your Yoshi away. If you die with the
timer at zero, you still go to `DeathShowMessage` and get the Time Up screen
and game mode `$15`, exactly as before. This code stops the cost of dying, not
of running out of time. The handler writes `GameMode` on the same frame that
the death starts, so the fade cuts off the death music that `KillMario` starts.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`8f74b96d62115a17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x045AB`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Enemies can no longer take your powerup

**Code:** `65ED-6D0F`

**Raw form:** `$00F601` ← `$87` (originally `$19`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** The `PowerDown` branch of `HurtMario` is six instructions, and
only one of them really takes something from you:

```
PowerDown:
    LDY.B #!SFX_PIPE                          ; \ Play sound effect
    STY.W SPCIO0                              ; /
    JSL DropReserveItem
    LDA.B #$01                                ; \ Set power down animation
    STA.B PlayerAnimation                     ; /
    STZ.B Powerup                             ; Mario status = Small
    LDA.B #$2F
    BRA +
```

`STZ.B Powerup` assembles to `64 19`, a direct-page store. So its whole
destination is one byte, and it can point at any of the 256 direct-page
variables that `rammap.asm` documents. `$7E0087` is documented there as
unused:

```
; === $7E0087 ===
; 1 byte
; unused
WRAM_0087: skip 1
```

If you point the store at `$87`, the "you are small now" write goes to a byte
that nothing reads. Nothing else on the damage path changes. The pipe sound
plays, `DropReserveItem` still throws your reserve item out of the box, and
`PlayerAnimation = 1` still runs the shrink animation. The animation still ends
in the `LDA.B #$7F / STA.W IFrameTimer` of `CODE_00D140`, so you still get the
normal ~2 seconds of flashing invincibility after the hit. You just stay Fire,
Caped or Big.

**Variants:**

| Code | Address:Value | Effect |
|------|---------------|--------|
| `65ED-6D0F` | `00F601:87` | a hit takes your reserve item and nothing else (orig `$19`) |
| `5FED-6D0F` | `00F601:71` | the store writes to `PlayerAnimation` instead, and cancels the animation that the line above it just started. You keep the powerup, but get no shrink animation and no invincibility frames, and sprites still freeze for `$2F` frames (orig `$19`) |

**Evidence:** `HurtMario` has comments from start to end in `bank_00.asm`. The
reference ROM at `$00F5FE` has `85 71 64 19 A9 2F 80 17`, which is exactly
`STA.B PlayerAnimation / STZ.B Powerup / LDA.B #$2F / BRA`. `Powerup` is `$19`
and `WRAM_0087` is `$87` in `SMW_U.sym`, and the `$7E0087` block above is
copied exactly from `rammap.asm`. The `IFrameTimer = $7F` of `PowerDownAni` was
read at `CODE_00D140`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** Small Mario is not protected. `HurtMario` tests `LDA.B Powerup /
BEQ KillMario` *before* it gets to `PowerDown`, so when you have nothing to
lose, you still die. The reserve item still drops on every hit. With this code,
this means that repeated contact can empty your item box. When Caped Mario is
hit while he flies, he takes the earlier `FlightPhase` branch (the one that
plays `!SFX_FLYHIT` and sets the spin jump flag) and never gets to `PowerDown`.
So that knock-down does not change. `00F601:71` leaves `SpriteLock` and
`PlayerAniTimer` set to `$2F`, and no animation runs to clear them. So sprites
freeze for those frames each time you are hit.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`8f74b96d62115a17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
512-byte copier header at LoROM offset `0x07600`. The codes decode back
correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Mario has no gravity

**Code:** `6520-0704`

**Raw form:** `$00D94D` ← `$87` (originally `$7D`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

**Mechanism:** All of Mario's vertical movement goes through three
instructions. This includes normal falling, the weaker gravity while the jump
button is held, winged Yoshi, and every phase of cape flight. The
disassembly's own header for the parameter tables says it directly:
*"PlayerGravity is added to PlayerYSpeed+1 once per frame at CODE_00D948"*.

```
CODE_00D948:
    CLC
    ADC.W PlayerGravity,Y
...
CODE_00D94C:
    STA.B PlayerYSpeed+1
    RTS
```

`STA.B PlayerYSpeed+1` is `85 7D`. If you point it at `$87`, the byte that
`rammap.asm` documents as unused, the result is lost. Then gravity never
changes Mario's fall speed at all. The cape also uses this store. The two
branches above it (`BEQ CODE_00D94C` / `BMI CODE_00D94C` at `CODE_00D91B`) jump
directly here to write `CapeTargetYSpeed`, so the cape logic that keeps a
speed also stops writing.

Every *other* write to the fall speed still works: the jump impulse, a bounce
off an enemy, water, and the `STZ.B PlayerYSpeed+1` that lands Mario. That is
why the result is interesting and not just frozen. If you walk off a ledge with
zero vertical speed, you keep walking on air. If you jump, the impulse that
starts the jump never gets smaller, so Mario keeps rising at the same speed
until something else writes the byte.

**Variants:**

| Code | Address:Value | Effect |
|------|---------------|--------|
| `6520-0704` | `00D94D:87` | gravity is written to an unused RAM byte, so Mario never falls (orig `$7D`) |
| `5820-0704` | `00D94D:7B` | gravity is written to Mario's *horizontal* speed instead. He never falls, and on every frame the collected fall value replaces his running speed (orig `$7D`) |

**Evidence:** The reference ROM at `$00D94C` has `85 7D 60`, the store and its
`RTS`. `PlayerYSpeed` is `$7C` (so `+1` is `$7D`), `PlayerXSpeed` is `$7A` (so
`+1` is `$7B`) and `WRAM_0087` is `$87`, all from `SMW_U.sym`. The `$7E0087`
"unused" comment is from `rammap.asm`. The gravity and limit block above it was
read at `$00D948` in the `if ver_is_ntsc` part. So this address is only for the
U (and J/SS) build. The PAL builds run a 16-bit version of the same routine at
a different address. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This is a physics code, and physics codes break level design. Any
jump that you cannot stop takes Mario off the top of the screen. Only the other
writes to `PlayerYSpeed+1` (landing, a ceiling, water, a bounce) bring him
down. The `$00D948` block also applies `PlayerMaxFallSpeed`, so nothing limits
any speed now. The death fall uses the same routine (`MarioDeathAni` does
`JSR CODE_00D92E` to force gravity index 0). So the death jump also changes, and
Mario does not fall off the bottom of the screen after he dies. The address is
only for the U build, because of the `ver_is_ntsc` block noted above.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`8f74b96d62115a17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x0594C`. The codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every level is built from the next level's Layer 1 data

**Codes:** `D72A-DD21` + `D02A-D4F1` + `D92A-D791` (all three needed)

**Raw form:** `$05D8C3` ← `$03` (originally `$00`), `$05D8C8` ← `$04`
(originally `$01`), `$05D8CD` ← `$05` (originally `$02`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

**Mechanism:** When a level loads, the game changes the level number into an
index. It uses that index to read the level's Layer 1 (foreground) pointer from
a table of three-byte entries that starts on a page boundary:

```
CODE_05D8B7:
    REP #$30                                  ; AXY->16
    LDA.B _E                                  ; \
    ASL A                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |Multiply level number by 3 and store in Y
    ADC.B _E                                  ; |(Each L1/2 pointer table entry is 3 bytes long)
    TAY                                       ; /
    SEP #$20                                  ; A->8
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs,Y                        ; \
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr                       ; |
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs+1,Y                      ; |Load Layer 1 pointer into $65-$67
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr+1                     ; |
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs+2,Y                      ; |
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr+2                     ; /
```

`Layer1Ptrs` is `$05E000`, a page boundary. So the low bytes of those three
absolute operands are `$00`, `$01`, `$02`, and adding to them can never carry
into the high byte. Each table entry is three bytes. So if you add `3` to all
three operands (`$00`→`$03`, `$01`→`$04`, `$02`→`$05`), the read moves one whole
entry further along the table: level *n* is built from the Layer 1 data of
level *n+1*.

That means the foreground: the ground, the platforms, the pipes, the blocks,
the whole shape of the level. It also means more than the shape, because the
level's **5-byte header is at the start of the Layer 1 data** and is read
through this same pointer (`CODE_0584E3` does `LDA.B [Layer1DataPtr],Y` five
times, then adds 5 to the pointer to get to the object list). So the
replacement level brings its music, time limit, level mode, screen length,
foreground/background/sprite palettes, tileset and scroll settings together
with its terrain. What stays is this level's own sprite list, its background,
its exits, and Mario's start position. Three codes are needed because the
24-bit pointer is read one byte at a time, and each read is a separate
instruction. The "level number" used as the index is the internal one that the
game builds just above this code (the translevel number, `+$100` when you are
on a submap). It is not the number shown on the overworld map.

**Evidence:** `Layer1Ptrs $05E000` is from `SMW_U.sym`, and the label is
defined at `bank_05.asm:7769`. The reference ROM confirms all three operands:
`$05D8C2` = `B9 00 E0`, `$05D8C7` = `B9 01 E0`, `$05D8CC` = `B9 02 E0`, which
is `LDA.W Layer1Ptrs+k,Y` for k = 0, 1, 2. These three reads are the only
references to `Layer1Ptrs` in the whole disassembly, so nothing else in the ROM
changes. The statement that the header is read through the same pointer comes
from `CODE_0584E3` (`bank_05.asm:547`). It reads bytes 0-4 with
`[Layer1DataPtr],Y` and ends with `LDA.B Layer1DataPtr : CLC : ADC.B #$05`
("Level data comes right after the header"). Mario's start position is *not*
in that header. It comes from `DATA_05F200`/`DATA_05FE00`, with the original
level number as the index, so it does not follow the change. A dump of the
table from the reference ROM shows that its 512 entries use 194 different
pointers, all in banks `$06` (446 entries) and `$07` (66). So almost every level
gets really different terrain. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** The index is a full 16-bit level number (the `REP #$30` above
makes `LDA.B _E` read `_E`/`_F` as a word), so the table has 512 entries.
512 × 3 bytes puts its end at `$05E600`, which is exactly where the *Layer 2*
pointer table starts. So the highest level, moved by one entry, reads the first
entry of that next table and not a level, and it loads garbage terrain. Only
the foreground moves, so the level's own sprite list stays where it is. This
will often leave enemies inside walls or in the air above holes. Mario's start
position also does not follow, so expect to start some levels inside solid
ground, and some levels cannot be finished. The header that comes with the new
data also changes the time limit and the level mode. This can put a horizontal
level into a vertical mode, or the other way around.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0x2D8C2`-`0x2D8CE`. All three codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every level is populated with the next level's enemies

**Codes:** `D423-D7F1` + `D72E-DD91` (both needed)

**Raw form:** `$05D8EC` ← `$02` (originally `$00`), `$05D8F1` ← `$03`
(originally `$01`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** After the level loader finds the level's graphics pointers, it
uses the level number as an index into a separate table of two-byte sprite data
pointers, which also starts on a page boundary. Then it reads the sprite header
through the pointer that it just built:

```
    REP #$20                                  ; A->16
    LDA.B _E                                  ; \
    ASL A                                     ; |Multiply level number by 2 and store in Y
    TAY                                       ; / (Each sprite pointer table entry is 2 bytes long)
    LDA.W #$0000
    SEP #$20                                  ; A->8
    LDA.W Ptrs05EC00,Y                        ; \
    STA.B SpriteDataPtr                       ; |Store location of sprite level Y in $CE-$CF
    LDA.W Ptrs05EC00+1,Y                      ; |
    STA.B SpriteDataPtr+1                     ; /
    LDA.B #$07                                ; \ Set highest byte to x07
    STA.B SpriteDataPtr+2                     ; / (All sprite data is stored in bank 07)
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr]                     ; \ Get first byte of sprite data (header)
    AND.B #$3F                                ; |Get level's sprite memory
    STA.W SpriteMemorySetting                 ; / Store in $1692
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr]                     ; \ Get first byte of sprite data (header) again
    AND.B #$C0                                ; |Get level's sprite buoyancy settings
    STA.W SpriteBuoyancy                      ; / Store in $190E
```

`Ptrs05EC00` is `$05EC00`, a page boundary. So the low bytes of the two
absolute operands are `$00` and `$01`, and adding to them cannot carry into the
high byte. Entries are two bytes. So if you add `2` to both operands
(`$00`→`$02`, `$01`→`$03`), the read moves one whole entry along: level *n*
gets the enemy list of level *n+1*.

Two codes are enough, not three, because the sprite pointer is only 16 bits.
The bank byte is the constant `$07` loaded just below, because all sprite data
is in bank `$07`. Nothing else about the level changes. The terrain, the
background, the level header (and so the music, timer and palettes), the exits
and Mario's start position all stay this level's own. The "level number" used
as the index is the internal one that the game builds just above this code
(the translevel number, `+$100` when you are on a submap). It is not the number
shown on the overworld map.

**Evidence:** `Ptrs05EC00 $05EC00` is from `SMW_U.sym`, and the label is
defined at `bank_05.asm:8797`. The reference ROM confirms both operands:
`$05D8EB` = `B9 00 EC` and `$05D8F0` = `B9 01 EC`, which is
`LDA.W Ptrs05EC00+k,Y` for k = 0, 1. These two reads are the only references to
`Ptrs05EC00` in the whole disassembly, so nothing else in the ROM changes. Not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** The index is a full 16-bit level number (the `REP #$20` above
makes `LDA.B _E` read `_E`/`_F` as a word), so the table has 512 entries.
512 × 2 bytes puts its end at `$05F000`, where a different table
(`DATA_05F000`) starts. So the highest level, moved by one entry, reads two
bytes of that table as a pointer and creates garbage. The change also moves the
*header* byte that the loader reads through the same pointer. That is the
`LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr]` pair above, which gives `SpriteMemorySetting` and
`SpriteBuoyancy`. So the level also gets the sprite memory and buoyancy
settings of the replacement level. This is consistent and not a glitch: the
enemy list and the settings it needs move together. The terrain does not
change, so expect enemies inside walls or in the air above holes. Also expect
swimming enemies to flop around in a dry level wherever the new buoyancy
setting says there is water. Boss rooms and other levels with short or empty
sprite lists exist, so a level that gets its list from one of those will be
almost empty.

The enemies are drawn with this level's sprite graphics files, not the next
level's, so they often show the wrong tiles. "Every level is populated with
the next level's enemies, with their graphics" in
`smw_game_genie_big_codes.md` fixes that, with 32 codes.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0x2D8EC` and `0x2D8F1`. Both codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every level gets the next level's background

**Codes:** `D722-DDB1` + `D022-DF21` + `D922-D7F1` (all three needed)

**Raw form:** `$05D8D2` ← `$03` (originally `$00`), `$05D8D7` ← `$04`
(originally `$01`), `$05D8DC` ← `$05` (originally `$02`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

**Mechanism:** The level loader changes the level number into an index. It uses
that index to read the level's Layer 2 (background) pointer from a table of
three-byte entries that starts on a page boundary:

```
CODE_05D8B7:
    REP #$30                                  ; AXY->16
    LDA.B _E                                  ; \
    ASL A                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |Multiply level number by 3 and store in Y
    ADC.B _E                                  ; |(Each L1/2 pointer table entry is 3 bytes long)
    TAY                                       ; /
    SEP #$20                                  ; A->8
    ...
    LDA.W Layer2Ptrs,Y                        ; \
    STA.B Layer2DataPtr                       ; |
    LDA.W Layer2Ptrs+1,Y                      ; |Load Layer 2 pointer into $68-$6A
    STA.B Layer2DataPtr+1                     ; |
    LDA.W Layer2Ptrs+2,Y                      ; |
    STA.B Layer2DataPtr+2                     ; /
```

`Layer2Ptrs` is `$05E600`, a page boundary. So the low bytes of those three
absolute operands are `$00`, `$01`, `$02`, and adding to them can never carry
into the high byte. Each table entry is three bytes. So if you add `3` to all
three operands (`$00`→`$03`, `$01`→`$04`, `$02`→`$05`), the read moves one whole
entry further along the table: level *n* gets the background of level *n+1*.

Layer 2 has two types, and the loader uses the bank byte of the pointer to tell
them apart. `CMP.B #$FF` means "this entry is one of the drawn background
images in bank `$0C`". Any other value means "this is a second object list,
read like terrain". The change moves the whole three-byte entry, so a level can
get either type from the next level. It can get a new sky, or a whole second
layer of objects where it had a flat background before. Nothing else about the
level changes. The terrain, the sprite list, the level header (and so the
music, timer and palettes), the exits and Mario's start position all stay this
level's own. Three codes are needed because the 24-bit pointer is read one byte
at a time, and each read is a separate instruction. The "level number" used as
the index is the internal one that the game builds just above this code (the
translevel number, `+$100` when you are on a submap). It is not the number
shown on the overworld map.

**Evidence:** `Layer2Ptrs $05E600` is from `SMW_U.sym`, and the label is
defined at `bank_05.asm:8283`. The reference ROM confirms all three operands:
`$05D8D1` = `B9 00 E6`, `$05D8D6` = `B9 01 E6`, `$05D8DB` = `B9 02 E6`, which
is `LDA.W Layer2Ptrs+k,Y` for k = 0, 1, 2. These three reads are the only
references to `Layer2Ptrs` in the whole disassembly, so nothing else in the ROM
changes. The bank byte rule comes from `CODE_05801E` (`bank_05.asm:32`):
`LDA.B Layer2DataPtr+2 : CMP.B #$FF`, with the comment "If the layer 2 data is
a background". Further down comes `LDA.B #$0C : STA.B Layer2DataPtr+2` ("All
backgrounds are stored in bank 0C"). A dump of the table from the reference ROM
shows 486 of the 512 entries with bank `$FF` (background images) and 26 with
banks `$06`/`$07` (object lists). Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** The index is a full 16-bit level number (the `REP #$30` above
makes `LDA.B _E` read `_E`/`_F` as a word), so the table has 512 entries.
512 × 3 bytes puts its end at `$05EC00`, which is exactly where the sprite
pointer table starts. So the highest level, moved by one entry, reads the first
entry of that next table and not a level, and it loads a garbage background.
**In most levels you cannot see the effect.** The same ROM dump shows that the
512 entries use only 34 different pointers, and one of them is used 283 times.
So most levels have the same background as the next level, and they get exactly
what they already had. Where it does change something, the change is not always
only visual. In levels that use Layer 2 as solid, scrolling or crushing
terrain, that terrain is replaced, and this changes what Mario can stand on. The
Layer 2 *scroll and interaction settings* are read further down from
`DATA_05F000` → `DATA_05D710`/`DATA_05D720`, with this level's own number as the
index, so they do not change. This means a new background can scroll in a way
it was never drawn for.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0x2D8D2`-`0x2D8DC`. All three codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every level's foreground is read from the background pointer table

**Codes:** `312A-DFF1` + `312A-D491` + `312A-D7B1` (all three needed)

**Raw form:** `$05D8C4` ← `$E6` (originally `$E0`), `$05D8C9` ← `$E6`
(originally `$E0`), `$05D8CE` ← `$E6` (originally `$E0`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

**Mechanism:** The level loader reads a level's Layer 1 (foreground) pointer
from one table and its Layer 2 (background) pointer from another. Both tables
start on a page boundary, and the loader uses the same index for both:

```
CODE_05D8B7:
    REP #$30                                  ; AXY->16
    LDA.B _E                                  ; \
    ASL A                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |Multiply level number by 3 and store in Y
    ADC.B _E                                  ; |(Each L1/2 pointer table entry is 3 bytes long)
    TAY                                       ; /
    SEP #$20                                  ; A->8
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs,Y                        ; \
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr                       ; |
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs+1,Y                      ; |Load Layer 1 pointer into $65-$67
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr+1                     ; |
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs+2,Y                      ; |
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr+2                     ; /
```

`Layer1Ptrs` is `$05E000` and `Layer2Ptrs` is `$05E600`. Both start on a page
boundary, so the only difference between the two tables is the **high** byte
of the absolute operand, `$E0` or `$E6`. There is no low byte or carry problem
at all. If you change the high byte of all three Layer 1 reads from `$E0` to
`$E6`, the foreground pointer comes from the *background* table, and the index
does not change. Every level then tries to build its terrain from its own
Layer 2 entry.

The problem is what a Layer 2 entry really contains. Most of them are not
pointers to object data at all. The loader recognizes a background *image* by
the bank byte `$FF` (`CMP.B #$FF`, "If the layer 2 data is a background") and
uses bank `$0C` in its place. That check is only on the Layer 2 path. The
Layer 1 path has nothing like it. So for the 486 levels whose Layer 2 entry is
an image, `Layer1DataPtr` stays pointing at `$FF????`. That address has no
cartridge ROM, and both the level header and the object list are read from
whatever the console returns there. The 26 levels whose Layer 2 really is an
object list (banks `$06`/`$07`) are the ones that do what the name says: their
background objects are built as solid foreground. Three codes are needed
because the 24-bit pointer is read one byte at a time, and each read is a
separate instruction.

**Evidence:** `Layer1Ptrs $05E000` and `Layer2Ptrs $05E600` are from
`SMW_U.sym`, with the labels defined at `bank_05.asm:7769` and
`bank_05.asm:8283`. The reference ROM confirms all three Layer 1 operands:
`$05D8C2` = `B9 00 E0`, `$05D8C7` = `B9 01 E0`, `$05D8CC` = `B9 02 E0`. The
Layer 2 reads a few instructions later confirm the target high byte:
`$05D8D1` = `B9 00 E6`. These are the only references to either table in the
whole disassembly, so nothing else in the ROM changes. The `$FF` rule comes
from `CODE_05801E` (`bank_05.asm:32`): `LDA.B Layer2DataPtr+2 : CMP.B #$FF`
followed by `LDA.B #$0C : STA.B
Layer2DataPtr+2`. The code that uses Layer 1 data never tests the bank byte.
This is the header reads in `CODE_0584E3` (`bank_05.asm:547`) and the object
loop in `LoadLevelData` (`bank_05.asm:701`), all `LDA.B [Layer1DataPtr],Y`. A
dump of `Layer2Ptrs` from the reference ROM gives the split: 486 of 512 entries
have bank `$FF`, 18 have `$06` and 8 have `$07`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This is the most destructive of the level pointer changes, and the
one least likely to give a level that you can play. For the 486 levels with
images, the foreground pointer goes to bank `$FF`, outside the 512 KB
cartridge. What is read there depends on mirror/open-bus behavior. So the
result is not well-defined, and it can be different on emulators and on real
hardware. The level **header** is read through the same pointer (`CODE_0584E3`
reads five bytes with `[Layer1DataPtr],Y` before it moves past them). So that
garbage also sets the level mode, screen length, music, time limit, palettes
and tileset. A level can become vertical, black, silent, or have no timer. A
first byte of `$FF` is the "level is empty" marker tested in `LoadAgain`
(`bank_05.asm:430`). So some levels load no terrain at all, and Mario falls
through empty space. The 26 levels with a real object list in Layer 2 are the
interesting ones, and even those get a header that was meant for background
data. The sprite list, the real background, the exits and Mario's start
position do not change. So enemies still appear where the original level put
them, whether or not there is now a floor under them.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0x2D8C4`-`0x2D8CE`. All three codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Stars and 1-Ups promote you up the powerup ladder instead

**Code:** `FDA0-0769`

**Raw form:** `$01C54E` ← `$10` (originally `$24`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

**Mechanism:** Every powerup that you pick up in the game goes through
`TouchedPowerUp`. It builds one index from *what you touched* and *what you
already are*, `Y = (sprite - $74) * 4 + Powerup`, and then reads two 20-byte
tables with it. One table decides what goes into the reserve box. The other
decides which of six named handlers runs:

```
    LDA.W ItemBoxSprite,Y                     ; \ Put appropriate item in item box
    BEQ +
    STA.W PlayerItembox
  + LDA.W GivePowerPtrIndex,Y                 ; \ Call routine to change Mario's status
    JSL ExecutePtr

    dw GiveMarioMushroom                      ; 0 - Big
    dw CODE_01C56F                            ; 1 - No change
    dw GiveMarioStar                          ; 2 - Star
    dw GiveMarioCape                          ; 3 - Cape
    dw GiveMarioFire                          ; 4 - Fire
    dw GiveMario1Up                           ; 5 - 1Up
```

Both tables are in page `$01C5`: `ItemBoxSprite` at `$01C510` and
`GivePowerPtrIndex` at `$01C524`. So one byte can point the *base* of the
second read at the first table. If you change `$24` to `$10`, the handler index
comes from the item box table:

```
ItemBoxSprite:      00 01 01 01 | 00 01 04 02 | 00 00 00 00 | 00 01 04 02 | 00 00 00 00
GivePowerPtrIndex:  00 01 01 01 | 04 04 04 01 | 02 02 02 02 | 03 03 01 03 | 05 05 05 05
                    mushroom    | flower      | star        | feather     | 1-Up
```

The mushroom row is the same in both tables, so mushrooms work exactly as
before. The Star and 1-Up rows are all `$00` in the item box table, so they go
to handler 0. Handler 0 is not "become Big". It is `GiveMarioMushroom`, which
starts animation 2 and lets the `INC.B Powerup` of `MushroomAni` do the work.
So a Star or a 1-Up moves you *up one step*: Small becomes Big, Big becomes
Caped, Caped becomes Fire. A flower or feather that you get as Fire Mario reads
`$02` and gives you a Star instead.

**Evidence:** Both tables were read from the reference ROM. `$01C510` has
`00 01 01 01 00 01 04 02 00 00 00 00 00 01 04 02 00 00 00 00` and `$01C524` has
`00 01 01 01 04 04 04 01 02 02 02 02 03 03 01 03 05 05 05 05`, which matches the
source. The changed instruction at `$01C54D` has `B9 24 C5` =
`LDA.W GivePowerPtrIndex,Y`, and the read above it at `$01C540` has
`B9 10 C5` = `LDA.W ItemBoxSprite,Y`. The index calculation and the group
layout (`$74` Mushroom, `$75` Flower, `$76` Star, `$77` Feather, `$78` 1-Up)
come from the comments in `TouchedPowerUp` and the dispatch table comments in
`CallSpriteMain`. The fact that `GiveMarioMushroom` leaves the growth to
`MushroomAni` was read at `$01C561` and `$00D156`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** Handler 0 adds 1 to `Powerup` without any check. So if you get a
Star or a 1-Up as **Fire Mario**, it goes from `$03` to `$04`. The game never
makes that status in any other way, and it has no graphics or logic for it.
This is the known failure of this code, not a surprise. 1-Ups no longer give
lives at all (handler 5, `GiveMario1Up`, is no longer used by any row), and
Stars no longer give invincibility. So this code takes away two of the game's
mechanics to add one. The reserve box read comes *before* the changed
instruction and does not change, so the item box still fills exactly as
before. The `$04` entries of `ItemBoxSprite` (a flower or feather that you get
as Caped Mario) go to handler 4 = Fire. For the flower, that is what the game
already did.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`8f74b96d62115a17`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets `0x0C510`, `0x0C524` and `0x0C54D`. The
code decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Goombas, Koopas and Buzzy Beetles walk up and down instead of sideways

**Code:** `CC64-A701`

**Raw form:** `$018B2D` ← `$AA` (originally `$B6`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 18:44:01

**Mechanism:** Sprite numbers `$00`-`$13` all use one handler: the four Koopas
without shells, the four with shells, the four para-Koopas, the Bob-omb, the
keyhole, both Goombas, the Buzzy Beetle and the Spiny. Its walking code is six
lines long:

```
Spr0to13Main:
    JSR IsOnGround                            ; \ If sprite on ground...
    BEQ CODE_018B2E                           ; |
    LDY.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; |
    LDA.W Spr0to13Prop,Y                      ; | Set sprite X speed
    LSR A                                     ; |
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; |
    BCC +                                     ; |
    INY                                       ; | Increase index if sprite set to go fast
    INY                                       ; |
  + LDA.W Spr0to13SpeedX,Y                    ; |
    EOR.W SpriteSlope,X                       ; |
    ASL A                                     ; |
    LDA.W Spr0to13SpeedX,Y                    ; |
    BCC +                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |
    ADC.W SpriteSlope,X                       ; |
  + STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /
```

`STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X` is `95 B6`, a direct-page indexed store. The sprite speed
tables are next to each other in the direct page: `SpriteXSpeed` is `$B6`, and
`SpriteYSpeed` is `$AA`. If you change that one byte, the walk speed goes to the
vertical table instead. This store is the *only* thing that sets a basic
enemy's horizontal speed while it is on the ground. (The source notes that the
speed is read again on every frame, and that is why nothing can push a walking
enemy along.) So the whole group stops walking. Instead, they get the value of
`Spr0to13SpeedX` on the wrong axis: `$08` (half a pixel per frame, down) for
one direction and `$F8` (half a pixel per frame, up) for the other. It is only
applied on the frames when they stand on something.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM at `$018B2C` has `95 B6`, and the instruction
above it at `$018B29` has `7D B8 15` = `ADC.W SpriteSlope,X`. This matches the
source exactly. `SpriteXSpeed $B6` and `SpriteYSpeed $AA` are from `SMW_U.sym`.
The sprite number range and the statement that they share one handler come from
the header comment of `Spr0to13Start` and the comments on each entry in
`CallSpriteMain`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This describes the *store*, not the movement that you see. An
enemy pushed up leaves the ground. Then `IsOnGround` fails and the store no
longer happens, so gravity brings it back down and the cycle repeats. So you
see enemies that hover, jerk and do not move forward, not enemies that fly
cleanly. Enemies that face the other way are pushed down into the floor that
they already stand on, and they just stay there. Nothing else about them
changes. They still turn around at walls (`IsTouchingObjSide` /
`FlipSpriteDir`), still hurt you, and can still be stomped. The
`STZ.B SpriteXSpeed,X` in the blocked direction check a few lines below still
runs. So their horizontal speed is whatever was left when they appeared,
usually zero. Sprites outside `$00`-`$13` have their own handlers and do not
change. The Bob-omb and keyhole are inside the range, although neither is a
normal walker.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`8f74b96d62115a17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x08B2C`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Falling into a pit launches Mario back up instead of killing him

**Code:** `6DEF-6F0F` + `52EF-6FAF` (add `DDED-64AF` to keep the level music)

**Raw form:** `$00F615 ← $80 (originally $09)` and `$00F617 ← $7D (originally
$71)`; optional third code `$00F60B ← $00 (originally $09)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 19:12:40

**Mechanism:** `CODE_00F595` handles a fall off the bottom of the screen. It
runs on every frame and ends with a `JSL` into the last part of `KillMario`:

```
    LDA.B PlayerYPosScrRel+1
    DEC A
    BMI Return00F5B6
    LDA.W YoshiHeavenFlag
    BEQ +
    JMP CODE_00C95B
  + JSL CODE_00F60A
```

`PlayerYPosScrRel+1` is the high byte of Mario's position relative to the top
of the screen. So the `DEC A / BMI` only continues when he is more than 255
pixels below the camera, about 32 pixels below the visible bottom. What it then
calls is the death routine without its first two instructions:

```
KillMario:
    LDA.B #$90                                ; \ Mario Y speed = #$90
    STA.B PlayerYSpeed+1                      ; /   (skipped by the pit path)
CODE_00F60A:
    LDA.B #!BGM_DEATH                         ; \
    STA.W SPCIO2                              ; / Change music        <- $00F60B
    LDA.B #$FF
    STA.W MusicBackup
    LDA.B #$09                                ; \ Animation sequence = Kill Mario
    STA.B PlayerAnimation                     ; /   <- $00F615 / $00F617
```

The two changed bytes are the immediate value and the destination of that last
store. `STA.B PlayerAnimation` is `85 71`. `PlayerYSpeed+1` is `$7D`, so
`85 7D` points the store there, and `#$80` replaces the animation number with a
signed speed of -128. Both halves are needed, and each does a different job.
The death is cancelled because `PlayerAnimation` is never set to `$09`.
Animation `$09` is `MarioDeathAni`, the routine that really plays the death
jump, subtracts 1 from `PlayerLives` and sets `GameMode` to the value that
fades to the overworld. The launch happens because the value goes into the Y
speed instead. `KillMario` itself uses the same method one instruction earlier
for the death hop (`#$90`). This is just stronger, and it is on the pit path,
which normally skips it.

The rise has no limit. `LDA.B PlayerYSpeed+1 / BMI CODE_00D948` in
`CODE_00D928` skips the `PlayerMaxFallSpeed` limit when the signed speed is
negative. So only gravity slows Mario down: `$06` per frame when the jump
button is not held, and `$03` when it is held (`PlayerGravity` index 0 and 1).
For comparison, a normal jump starts at `DATA_00D2BD` = `$B0`…`$9F`, so `$80` is
about 40% stronger than the strongest jump in the game. It is also applied
again on *every frame* that Mario is below the screen. So he is pushed up at a
constant speed until he comes back into view, and then he moves another 80-170
pixels up with the speed that is left. The player can steer during that jump
with normal air control.

The optional third code is for the sound. `$00F60B` is the `#!BGM_DEATH`
immediate value. `$00` is the idle value that the NMI music handler checks for
(`LDA.W SPCIO2 / BNE +` at `$008179`). So if you store zero, the level music
keeps playing, and the death music does not start again on every frame of the
fall.

**Variants:** the launch strength is the `$00F615` byte. It is signed, and a
negative value is up.

| Code | Value | Effect |
|------|-------|--------|
| `6DEF-6F0F` | `$80` | -128, the strongest value a byte can hold; a very high launch |
| `BDEF-6F0F` | `$90` | -112, exactly the death hop that `KillMario` uses |
| `CDEF-6F0F` | `$A0` | -96, about one full jump |
| `ADEF-6F0F` | `$C0` | -64, a small bounce, often not enough to get out of the pit |

**Evidence:** The reference ROM at `$00F60A` has
`A9 09 8D FB 1D A9 FF 8D DA 0D A9 09 85 71 9C 0D 14 A9 30`. This is the source
byte for byte, and it puts the music immediate at `$00F60B`, the animation
immediate at `$00F615` and the store destination at `$00F617`. `PlayerYSpeed+1
$7D`, `PlayerAnimation $71` and `SPCIO2 $1DFB` are from `SMW_U.sym` and
`rammap.asm`. The statement that the rise has no limit comes from the commented
`BMI CODE_00D948` in `CODE_00D928`. The gravity and jump numbers are from
`PlayerGravity` and `DATA_00D2BD`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** `CODE_00F60A` is shared, so *every* death that goes through it
becomes a launch. This includes a hit by an enemy as Small Mario (the
`BEQ KillMario` in `HurtMario`), the timer getting to zero (`JSL KillMario` in
the status bar timer code), and `CODE_00F629`. Enemy deaths get the launch
*plus* the `#$90` death hop that `KillMario` applies first. The timer case runs
again while the timer is zero, so Mario keeps being pushed up and the level can
no longer be finished. Drowning and the Yoshi wings bonus exit use other paths
and do not change. If the pit has no ground that Mario can get to, he falls out
again and is launched again. It is an endless trampoline, not a death. The rest
of `CODE_00F60A` still runs on every launch. `SpriteLock` is set to `$30` again,
so enemies freeze for about a second after it. `FlightPhase` is set to zero,
which cancels cape flight. `MusicBackup` is set to `$FF`, the "nothing to
restore" marker. So if a P-switch or star was running when Mario fell, the
level music does not come back when it ends. Without the third code, the death
music starts again on every frame that Mario is below the bottom, and it sounds
like a stutter. Mario cannot fly up into nothing. The ceiling limit in the same
routine, `LDA.W #$FF80 / ADC.B Layer1YPos / CMP.B
PlayerYPosNext / BMI + / STA.B PlayerYPosNext`, holds him 128 pixels above the
top of the camera.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`8f74b96d62115a17`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offsets `0x0760B`, `0x07615`, `0x07617`. The codes decode
back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Falling into a pit drops Mario back in from the top of the level

**Code:** `DDEF-6F0F` + `B5EF-6FAF` (add `DDED-64AF` to keep the level music)

**Raw form:** `$00F615 ← $00 (originally $09)` and `$00F617 ← $97 (originally
$71)`; optional third code `$00F60B ← $00 (originally $09)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 19:12:40

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** This uses the same place as the launch code above: the
`LDA.B #$09 /
STA.B PlayerAnimation` pair at the start of the death routine `CODE_00F60A`.
`CODE_00F595` calls it when Mario is more than 255 pixels below the camera.
Here the store points at `PlayerYPosNext+1` (`$97`, `85 97`) and the value is
zero. So the pit does not start the death animation. It *teleports* Mario:

```
PlayerYPosNext: skip 2   ; vertical position of the player within the level,
                         ; forward calculation for the next frame
```

If the high byte of that 16-bit position is zero, Mario is in the top 256
pixels of the level. His horizontal position and his downward speed do not
change at all. So he appears again at the top of the level at the same X, and
he is already falling. `AdvancePlayerPosition` copies `PlayerYPosNext` into
`PlayerYPosNow` on every frame, so the write has an effect at once. The death
never happens, for the same reason as above: `PlayerAnimation` is never set to
`$09`, so `MarioDeathAni` never runs and you lose no life. The move to the top
also does not happen again. When Mario is at the top of the level, he is above
the camera, not 255 pixels below it, so the `DEC A / BMI Return00F5B6` in
`CODE_00F595` exits early.

**Evidence:** This is the same ROM read as the entry above (`$00F60A` =
`A9 09 8D FB 1D A9 FF 8D DA 0D A9 09 85 71 …`). `PlayerYPosNext $96` and its
description are from `rammap.asm`. The copy on each frame is
`AdvancePlayerPosition` in `bank_00.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** All the caveats of the launch entry also apply here.
`CODE_00F60A` is the shared last part for enemy deaths and for the timer
running out, so those also move Mario to the top of the level.
`SpriteLock`/`FlightPhase`/`MusicBackup` are still written, and the death music
still plays unless you use the third code. Mario moves to the top of the
*level*, not the top of the screen. In a tall vertical level, he appears far
above the camera and must fall back into view. In a level with no vertical
scrolling, this means he drops in from off the screen. He lands wherever his X
was, directly above the pit. So if there is a ceiling above the pit, he can
drop straight back into it.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`8f74b96d62115a17`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offsets `0x0760B`, `0x07615`, `0x07617`. The codes decode
back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## The screen never scrolls

**Code:** `46CB-646D`

**Raw form:** `$00A29A ← $28 (originally $DB)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 20:24:00

**Mechanism:** This code changes where a call goes. The last part of
`GM14Level`, the work that a normal level does on each frame, runs a fixed list
of calls at `$00A28A`:

```
CODE_00A28A:
    LDA.W IRQNMICommand
    BPL +
    JSR ProcessMode7Room                      ; Mode 7 rooms take their own path
    JMP CODE_00A2A9

  + JSL OAMResetRoutine
    JSL UpdateScreenPosition                  ; <- $00A299, operand $DB F6 00
    JSL ProcScreenScrollCmds
    JSL UploadScrolledTiles
    JSL QueueAnimatedTiles
```

`UpdateScreenPosition` (`$00F6DB`) is the camera. It copies `NextLayer1XPos` /
`NextLayer1YPos` / `NextLayer2XPos` / `NextLayer2YPos` into the live
`Layer1XPos` / `Layer1YPos` / `Layer2XPos` / `Layer2YPos`. It sets
`CameraLeftBuffer` / `CameraRightBuffer` from `CameraMoveTrigger`. Then it
calculates where the camera must be next, from Mario's position and the level's
horizontal and vertical scroll settings.

The code changes the low byte of that `JSL`'s operand from `$DB` to `$28`. The
call then goes to `$00F628`, which is `Return00F628`: a single `RTL` at the end
of a nearby routine in the same 256-byte page:

```
CODE_00F622:
    STZ.W FlightPhase
    STZ.W Empty188A
Return00F628:
    RTL
```

The call still returns correctly, because a `JSL` needs an `RTL`, and that is
exactly what it now gets to. But no camera work happens, so the layer
positions keep the values that `GM11LoadLevel` gave them when the level
started. If you walk right, Mario just leaves the screen. The view stays on the
first frame of the level for as long as you are in it.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$00A299` has `22 DB F6 00` (`JSL $00F6DB`), and at
`$00F628` it has `6B` (`RTL`). `UpdateScreenPosition` and `Return00F628` are
both in `bank_00.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** Only the level path changes. `GM11LoadLevel` calls
`UpdateScreenPosition` once when the level loads, and that is why the camera
starts in the right place. `ProcM7BossRoom` also calls it, so the Mode 7 boss
rooms still scroll normally. `Layer1YPos` does not change, so the pit death
check in `CODE_00F595`, which kills Mario 255 pixels below the top of the
camera, now measures from the *start* position of the camera. So if you go down
far enough in a tall level, he dies even on solid ground. `UploadScrolledTiles`
sees no scrolling, so it uploads nothing. That is why the frozen view stays
clean and does not fill with garbage tiles.
