## The clock stops, and so does the whole status bar

**Code:** `B0C2-6FAD`

**Raw form:** `$00A2D7 ← $94 (originally $8E)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 20:32:00

**Mechanism:** This code also changes where a call goes in the same `GM14Level`
list, but this one changes the *high* byte. At `$00A2D5`, the level frame does
`JSR UpdateStatusBar` (`20 1A 8E` → `$008E1A`). If you change the high byte from
`$8E` to `$94`, the call goes to `$00941A` instead. That is `FinishGameMode`, the
shared `RTS` that the game mode handlers branch to when they have nothing to do:

```
GM01Presents:
    DEC.W VariousPromptTimer
    BNE FinishGameMode
    JSR CODE_00B888
NextGameMode:
    INC.W GameMode
FinishGameMode:
    RTS
```

A `JSR` needs an `RTS`, and `FinishGameMode` is one. So the call returns
correctly, and `UpdateStatusBar` never runs during play. That routine does much
more than drawing, and that is why one byte stops so many things at once:

- It controls the countdown. `DEC.W InGameTimerFrames` and the three-digit
  borrow chain over `InGameTimerHundreds`/`Tens`/`Ones` are here, together with
  the `JSL KillMario` that runs when they all get to zero. If it is skipped, the
  timer never moves: unlimited time, no hurry-up music, no time-up death.
- It adds up your coins. `HandleCoins` moves `CoinAdder` (the queue that a
  collected coin adds to) into `PlayerCoins`, and it is the only place that
  increases `GivePlayerLives` at 100 coins. Coins still disappear when you touch
  them, but the counter never moves, and you never get a 1-up for 100 coins.
- It starts the bonus game. `HandleBonusStars` is the only code that writes
  `BonusGameActivate`, so 100 bonus stars no longer open the bonus room.
- It draws. Score, lives, coins and both bonus star counters are written into
  the `StatusBar` tilemap here. So the HUD stays at the values it got when the
  level started.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$00A2D5` has `20 1A 8E` (`JSR $008E1A`), and at
`$00941A` it has `60` (`RTS`). `UpdateStatusBar` and `FinishGameMode` are both
in `bank_00.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** Only the call in `GM14Level` changes. `UpdateStatusBar` is also
called once from the level start path in `CODE_00A5B9`, and that is why the HUD
shows correct values before it freezes. Your score still goes up in
`PlayerScore`. Only the drawing and the 999999 limit stop. So the display is
old, not wrong forever, and it is correct again as soon as you leave the level.
The timer freeze applies to every level, including boss rooms. So you can no
longer fail any level by running out of time.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x022D7`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Enemies aim at the spot where you started the level

**Code:** `6BC2-670D`

**Raw form:** `$00A2DD ← $89 (originally $F3)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 20:41:00

**Mechanism:** SMW keeps two copies of Mario's position. `PlayerXPosNext` /
`PlayerYPosNext` (`$D1`/`$D3`) are the working pair that the physics code moves
on each frame. `PlayerXPosNow` / `PlayerYPosNow` (`$94`/`$96`) are the final
pair that the rest of the game reads. One routine in the level frame copies one
pair into the other:

```
AdvancePlayerPosition:
    REP #$20
    LDA.B PlayerXPosNext
    STA.B PlayerXPosNow
    LDA.B PlayerYPosNext
    STA.B PlayerYPosNow
    SEP #$20
    RTS
```

The code changes the `JSR AdvancePlayerPosition` at `$00A2DC` (`20 F3 A2`) so
that it goes to `$00A289` and not `$00A2F3`. `$00A289` is `Return00A289`, a
single `RTS` a few bytes earlier in the same page. The call still works (a
`JSR` gets its `RTS`), but the copy never happens. So `PlayerXPosNow` /
`PlayerYPosNow` stay at the value that the level start code put there: Mario's
start point.

Mario himself does not change. He runs, jumps and collides using the `Next`
pair. But the *sprites* read the `Now` pair. `SubHorizPos` is the helper that
39 different sprite routines call to find which side Mario is on. It subtracts
the sprite's position from `PlayerXPosNow` and returns the sign.
`CODE_01AD42` does the same thing vertically. So every enemy that turns toward
you, walks toward you, aims at you or checks if you are above it now gets an
answer about the door you came in through. Koopas face the wrong way, Chucks
charge at nothing, and Lakitu stays above the start of the level and throws
Spinies there.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$00A2DC` has `20 F3 A2` (`JSR $00A2F3`), and at
`$00A289` it has `60` (`RTS`). `AdvancePlayerPosition`, `Return00A289` and the
call are all in `bank_00.asm`. `SubHorizPos` and `CODE_01AD42` are in
`bank_01.asm`. `PlayerXPosNow`/`PlayerYPosNow` are documented in `rammap.asm` as
"horizontal/vertical position of the player within the level". Not tested in
play.

**Caveats:** Contact does *not* change. `GetMarioClipping` in `bank_03.asm`
builds Mario's hitbox from `PlayerXPosNext`/`PlayerYPosNext`. So enemies still
hurt you where you really are, even though they cannot find you. A few sprite
routines write `PlayerXPosNow`/`PlayerYPosNow` themselves, and this makes the
pair correct again. `CODE_01EDCE` moves Mario onto a sprite that he stands on
or that carries him, and `CODE_01F989` moves it and puts it back. If you ride
those, the "ghost" position jumps forward. Mode 7 rooms do not change, because
`ProcessMode7Room` calls `AdvancePlayerPosition` from its own place.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x022DD`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Levels run with no enemies, items or Yoshi at all

**Code:** `FCC3-6DAD`

**Raw form:** `$00A2E3 ← $1A (originally $8C)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 20:52:00

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** `JSL ProcessAllSprites` at `$00A2E2` (`22 8C 80 01`) is the
whole sprite frame. It is the loop that runs all twelve sprite slots, highest
first, and gives each one its OAM share, its timers and its state machine. It
also runs the cluster sprites after that. The code changes the low byte of the
operand from `$8C` to `$1A`. The call then goes to `$01801A`, which is
`UpdateYPosNoGvtyW`. This is one of the small wrappers at the start of bank 01
that let other banks `JSL` into its sprite helpers:

```
UpdateYPosNoGvtyW:
    PHB
    PHK
    PLB
    JSR SubSprYPosNoGrvty
    PLB
    RTL
```

This is more important than it looks. A `JSL` must go to something that ends in
`RTL`, and that something must be *balanced*. Most of the interesting routines
in bank 01 push the data bank when they start. If you jump into the middle of
one, the `PLB` takes the bank byte that the `JSL` pushed, and the `RTL` returns
to a wrong address. These wrappers are whole routines with their own
`PHB`…`PLB` pair, so they are the only group of safe replacements in the page.

The result is that the sprite engine never runs. Enemies, shells, coins that
are sprites, springboards, platforms, Yoshi and cluster sprites all stay in
their slots, and nothing updates or draws them. Mario, the level, the blocks
and the scenery work exactly as normal, so you walk through an empty level. The
replacement adds the Y speed of one sprite slot to its Y position on each
frame. That has no effect, because nothing reads those slots again.

**Variants** — each of these is a different wrapper in the same page. All of
them have the same "no sprites" effect, with a different harmless side effect:

| Code | Byte | Substitute |
|---|---|---|
| `FCC3-6DAD` | `$1A` | `UpdateYPosNoGvtyW` |
| `44C3-6DAD` | `$22` | `UpdateXPosNoGvtyW` |
| `4CC3-6DAD` | `$2A` | `UpdateSpritePos` |
| `74C3-6DAD` | `$32` | `SprSprInteract` |
| `7CC3-6DAD` | `$3A` | `SprSpr_MarioSprRts` |
| `04C3-6DAD` | `$42` | `GenericSprGfxRt0` |

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$00A2E2` has `22 8C 80 01` (`JSL $01808C`), and at
`$01801A` it has `8B 4B AB` (`PHB / PHK / PLB`). The wrapper block and
`SubSprYPosNoGrvty` are in `bank_01.asm`. Every address it uses is either
direct-page indexed or `abs,X` with the bank 01 data bank below `$2000`. So it
stays inside the WRAM mirror, whatever index the calling code leaves in X. Not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** You cannot finish any level whose exit is a sprite. The goal tape
and every boss are sprites. So use this on levels that you leave by a pipe or
door, or together with an exit code. `ProcessAllSprites` is also the routine
that clears the flags that tell, on each frame, how Mario and the sprites
touch. It also copies `IsCarryingItem` into `CarryingFlag` and
`CurrentYoshiSlot` into `YoshiIsLoose`. So if you turn the code on in the middle
of a level while Mario carries something or rides Yoshi, that state stays. The
Mode 7 boss rooms and the level load path call `ProcessAllSprites` from their
own places, so they do not change. `RunSpriteSubsystems` still runs, so 1-ups in
the queue are still given, and star invincibility still cycles the palette.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x022E3`. The codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Message boxes never appear

**Code:** `6DC2-070D`

**Raw form:** `$00A1DD ← $80 (originally $F0)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 21:08:00

**Mechanism:** A message box does not draw itself from the place that started
it. It takes control of the whole frame. `GM14Level` checks for one before it
does anything else. If it finds one, it gives the whole level frame to
`ProcessMessageBox`:

```
GM14Level:
    LDA.W MessageBoxTrigger                   ; AD 26 14
    BEQ +                                     ; F0 05   <- $00A1DD
    JSL ProcessMessageBox                     ; 22 0C B1 05
    RTS

  + LDA.W BonusGameActivate
    ...
```

The code changes that `BEQ` (`$F0`) into a `BRA` (`$80`). The branch keeps its
`$05` displacement and the same target. So the level frame always runs, and
the `JSL` below it is never reached. Nothing else in the game reads
`MessageBoxTrigger`. `bank_00`, `bank_01` and `bank_03` only write it, and the
only other reads are inside `ProcessMessageBox` itself. So it is harmless if it
stays set forever.

If you touch a message box block, it still plays the message sound and still
stops the block's bounce. But no window opens, no text is built into
`DynamicStripeImage`, and the level never freezes to wait for a button. This
covers all three sources at once: the two `InfoBox` message blocks that a level
can have, the "you rescued a Yoshi" message, and the switch palace message.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$00A1DA` has `AD 26 14 F0 05 22 0C B1`, which is
`LDA.W $1426 /
BEQ +5 / JSL $05B10C`. `$F0` is `BEQ` and `$80` is `BRA`. Both are two-byte
relative branches, so the displacement byte does not change.
`MessageBoxTrigger` is documented in `rammap.asm`, and `ProcessMessageBox` has
comments in `bank_05.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** There is one real trap. When you finish a **Switch Palace**, the
game goes through `CODE_00C948`. At the end of the level, it checks
`SwitchPalaceColor`. If that is set, it starts the message box and does an
`RTS`. The message *is* the exit sequence. When the message is blocked, that
path never moves the game mode on, so after you hit the switch you are stuck in
the palace. The switch itself is still saved (the switch block writes
`SwitchPalacePressed`, not the message). So the colored blocks do appear when
you get back to the overworld in some other way. If you want to remove the
message blocks without that risk, use `4A6B-0DDE` instead (`$038D90 ← $2C`,
originally `$8D`). It changes the `STA.W MessageBoxTrigger` at the end of
`InfoBox` into a `BIT.W $1426`. So the message *blocks* start nothing, and the
Yoshi and switch palace messages still work. `BIT` only reads, and the next
instruction loads A again, so there it really does nothing.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offsets `0x021DD` and `0x18D90`. The codes decode back
correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Message boxes close the moment you let go of the buttons

**Code:** `2D85-0DB0` (add `ED8D-0420` to make the closing animation 4x faster)

**Raw form:** `$05B172 ← $D0 (originally $F0)`; optional second code
`$05B10B ← $F0 (originally $FC)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 21:31:00

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** `ProcessMessageBox` runs in two phases, and `MessageBoxExpand`
stores which one: phase 0 opens the window, and phase 1 closes it. Between them
is a wait for input with no time limit, at `CODE_05B16E`. It is strict: it
wants a button that is *newly* pressed. It tests this with an EOR of the hold
mask and this frame's press mask:

```
CODE_05B16E:
    LDA.B byetudlrHold                        ; A5 15
    AND.B #$F0                                ; 29 F0   B / Y / Select / Start
    BEQ CODE_05B18E                           ; F0 1A   <- $05B172, nothing held: keep waiting
    EOR.B byetudlrFrame                       ; 45 16
    AND.B #$F0
    BEQ +                                     ; a fresh press: close the box
    ...
  + INC.W MessageBoxExpand                    ; -> phase 1, closing
```

The first code changes that `BEQ` (`$F0`) into a `BNE` (`$D0`), and this
reverses the whole test. When no buttons are held, `AND #$F0` gives zero, and
the `BNE` is not taken. The `EOR` with `byetudlrFrame` is also zero, because
nothing was pressed either. So the code goes directly through the `BEQ +` into
`INC.W MessageBoxExpand`. The box starts to close on the first frame when it is
fully open. If you hold B, Y, Select or Start, the `BNE` *is* taken, so the box
stays open for as long as you hold the button.

That reversal works well in practice, because you usually still hold the run
button when you hit the block. The message opens, waits while you hold, and
closes as soon as you let go.

The optional second code makes the closing animation itself faster.
`DATA_05B10A,X` is added to `MessageBoxTimer` on every frame, and the phase ends
on an exact `CMP` against `DATA_05B108,X` (`$50` open, `$00` closed). So the
closing step `$FC` (-4) needs 20 frames. `$F0` (-16) does it in 5.

**Variants** — closing step, second code only. **The value must divide `$50`
exactly.** If not, the timer steps past `$00`, the phase never ends, and the box
stays open forever:

| Code | Byte | Closing animation |
|---|---|---|
| `E68D-0420` | `$F8` | 10 frames |
| `ED8D-0420` | `$F0` | 5 frames |
| `3A8D-0420` | `$EC` | 4 frames |
| `268D-0420` | `$D8` | 2 frames |
| `8D8D-0420` | `$B0` | 1 frame, so the box disappears at once |

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$05B16E` has `A5 15 29 F0 F0 1A 45 16 29 F0 F0 0C A5 17
29 C0 F0 0E`. So the branch opcode is at `$05B172`, with displacement `$1A`
(target `$05B18E` = `CODE_05B18E`). The swap does not change the target, because
`$F0` and `$D0` are both two-byte relative branches. The ROM at `$05B106` has
`4C 50 50 00 04 FC`, which covers all three of `DATA_05B106` / `DATA_05B108` /
`DATA_05B10A`. The code that adds the step is `CODE_05B250` (`LDA MessageBoxTimer / CLC / ADC DATA_05B10A,X / STA
MessageBoxTimer`). It is a simple 8-bit add, and that is why the value must
divide `$50`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **Switch palaces are safe.** The palace message and the
`OverworldOverride` side exit prompt never get to `CODE_05B16E` at all. They
close with `VariousPromptTimer`, and at `CODE_05B14F` they set `GameMode` to
`$0B` and leave the level directly from phase 0. They never go into phase 1
either, so neither code changes the palace exit. This is the difference between
this entry and the code above that *blocks* message boxes, which does leave you
stuck there.

**Do not make the opening step faster** (`$05B10A`, the `$04`). The message
text is built into `DynamicStripeImage` on the one frame when `MessageBoxTimer`
equals `DATA_05B106` = `$4C`, one step before fully open. Any larger opening
step jumps over `$4C`, and the box opens empty.

You can still read a message if you hold a button. But the box no longer waits
for you, so a message that you did not expect goes past quickly. Nothing is
lost. `MessageBoxTrigger` is cleared normally, and if you touch the block again,
it shows the message again.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offsets `0x2B172` and `0x2B10B`. The codes decode back
correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Running out of time no longer kills Mario

**Code:** `4661-67D7`

**Raw form:** `$008E6C ← $28 (originally $06)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 22:41:10

**Mechanism:** This code changes where a call goes. `UpdateStatusBar` (with the
header "Routine to update the status bar.") controls the in-game clock. Once
per second, it subtracts 1 from the three timer digits, and then:

```
  + LDA.W InGameTimerHundreds                 ;\
    ORA.W InGameTimerTens                     ;|
    ORA.W InGameTimerOnes                     ;| If time is 0, kill Mario.
    BNE UpdateTime                            ;|
    JSL KillMario                             ;/   <- $008E6B, operand $06 F6 00
```

The code changes the low byte of that `JSL`'s operand from `$06` to `$28`. So
the call does not go to `KillMario` (`$00F606`). It goes to `Return00F628`, a
single `RTL` at the end of a nearby routine in the same 256-byte page:

```
CODE_00F622:
    STZ.W FlightPhase
    STZ.W Empty188A
Return00F628:
    RTL
```

A `JSL` needs an `RTL`, and that is exactly what it now gets to. So the call
returns correctly, and `UpdateStatusBar` continues to draw the timer. The clock
still counts down normally and still starts the hurry-up music at 100. But when
it gets to 000, nothing happens at all. Then it stays at 000. The routine's own
"If timer is already zero, skip time up" check (`LDA InGameTimerHundreds / ORA
Tens / ORA Ones / BEQ UpdateTime`) is *above* the subtraction. So the digits
never go below zero to 999, and the death call only runs on the one frame when
the timer becomes zero. This code removes that call.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$008E6B` has `22 06 F6 00` (`JSL $00F606`), and at
`$00F628` it has `6B` (`RTL`). `UpdateStatusBar`, `KillMario` and
`Return00F628` are all in `bank_00.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This one byte controls the time-out death alone. `KillMario` has
only two `JSL` calls in the whole ROM: this one and the one at the start of
`CODE_00F629`. But it is *only* the time-out death. No other way of dying
changes. When small Mario is hit, the code gets to `KillMario` by falling
through a branch, not by a call. The pit fall comes in lower down at
`CODE_00F60A`, after the `LDA #$90 / STA PlayerYSpeed+1` that this code skips.
The Bowser fight does not change either way, because `UpdateStatusBar` stops
counting down the clock while `IRQNMICommand` is `!IRQNMI_Bowser`.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x00E6C`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## The camera is never placed on Mario, in any room

**Code:** `46BF-ADAF` + `46B9-6404` + `46CB-646D` (three codes)

**Raw form:** `$009713 ← $28 (originally $DB)`, `$009A59 ← $28 (originally
$DB)`, `$00A29A ← $28 (originally $DB)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 22:41:10

**Mechanism:** This is the version of "The screen never scrolls" above that
changes every call to the routine. `UpdateScreenPosition` (`$00F6DB`) is the
camera. It copies the `Next*` layer positions into the live `Layer1XPos` /
`Layer1YPos` / `Layer2XPos` / `Layer2YPos`. Then it calculates where the view
must be next, from Mario's position and the level's scroll settings. It has
exactly **three** `JSL` calls in the ROM, and for all three, one low byte change
sends them to the same single `RTL`, `Return00F628`:

```
JSL $009712   [GM11LoadLevel]   "Reset layer positions."   <- $009713
JSL $009A58   [ProcM7BossRoom]  "Morton, Ludwig, Roy, Reznor"  <- $009A59
JSL $00A299   [the GM14Level frame]                        <- $00A29A
```

`$DB` → `$28` at all three sends every one of them to `Return00F628` instead.
The version with one code only changes the call on each frame. So
`GM11LoadLevel` still *places* the camera correctly when the level loads, and
then the camera stays there. If you change all three, the camera is never
placed at all. When the level loads, it keeps whatever `Layer1XPos` /
`Layer1YPos` the previous screen left. So a level starts with the view at a
random place, and Mario is usually completely off the screen. The third code
covers the Mode 7 boss rooms. The header of `ProcM7BossRoom` says that they get
"the ordinary camera work (`UpdateScreenPosition` and `ProcScreenScrollCmds`,
the same two `GM14Level` would have called)".

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$009712`, `$009A58` and `$00A299` has `22 DB F6
00` (`JSL $00F6DB`) at each, and `$00F628` = `6B` (`RTL`). This list of calls is
complete: `tools/callsites.py --callers UpdateScreenPosition` reports exactly
these three. All four labels are in `bank_00.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This includes all of `46CB-646D` ("The screen never scrolls"), so
do not count that as a separate slot. Real Game Genie hardware takes five
codes, and this effect uses three of them. `ProcScreenScrollCmds`,
`UploadScrolledTiles` and `QueueAnimatedTiles` still run, and they see no
scrolling, so the frozen view stays clean and does not fill with garbage.
`Layer1YPos` never moves, so the pit death check in `CODE_00F595`, which kills
Mario 255 pixels below the top of the camera, measures from wherever the camera
was left. So in a tall level he can die on solid ground. Expect that you cannot
see the player in most levels. This code shows what the engine does without its
camera. It is not a code for playing.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offsets `0x01713`, `0x01A59` and `0x0229A`. The codes
decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every sprite is treated as an end-of-level goal-tape sprite

**Code:** `1268-DDD0`

**Raw form:** `$0180B0 ← $6D (originally $27)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 22:52:30

**Mechanism:** This code changes where a call goes, at the most used call in
the ROM. `ProcessAllSprites`, with the header "The sprite frame: run all 12
sprite slots, highest slot first", is the whole sprite loop for each frame:

```
    LDX.B #$0B
  - STX.W CurSpriteProcess
    JSR CODE_0180D2                           ; OAM allotment + timer ageing
    JSR HandleSprite                          ; <- $0180AF, operand $27 $81
    DEX
    BPL -
```

`HandleSprite` (`$018127`) is the dispatcher for sprite *status*. It reads
`SpriteStatus,X` and jumps to the handler for that status. All of those
handlers are in page `$0181` and end in `RTS`, so one low byte change can send
the call to any of them. Because the code changes the call and not the
dispatch, the status check never happens. So the replacement runs for **every
slot, whatever its status**, twelve times per frame, with X already holding the
slot index.

`$27` → `$6D` sends the call to `HandleSprLvlEnd` (`$01816D`), the handler for
status `$06`, which is `JSL LvlEndSprCoins / RTS`. `LvlEndSprCoins` is the code
that changes enemies into coins when you cross the goal tape. It does not use
the sprite's AI at all. It moves the sprite with `Layer1DXPos` so that it
follows the scroll. When `SpriteMisc1540` is zero, it goes on into
`CODE_00FBF0`. That code adds 2 per frame to `SpriteYSpeed,X`. When that gets to
`$20`, it calls `GivePoints` with `SilverCoinsCollected` (limited to `$0D`) as
the award index, adds 2 to `SilverCoinsCollected`, and sets `SpriteStatus,X` to
zero.

So from the first frame of a level, no sprite acts like a sprite. Each one
sinks away and starts to make score sprites. The status check is skipped, so
setting `SpriteStatus,X` to zero does not stop the slot. It keeps running the
same handler, so the payment repeats for as long as `SpriteYSpeed,X` stays in
the range that pays. `SilverCoinsCollected` gets to its limit after a few
payments and stays there.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$0180AF` has `20 27 81` (`JSR $018127`).
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` gives `$01816D` for `HandleSprLvlEnd` and `$018127` for
`HandleSprite`, the same page, so the one-byte change is valid. The loop, the
dispatcher and the handlers are all in `bank_01.asm`. `LvlEndSprCoins` and
`CODE_00FBF0` are in `bank_00.asm`, and `GivePoints` is in `bank_02.asm`. Not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** The twelve slots include *empty* ones. Status `$00` normally exits
at once through `EraseSprite`, and this code skips exactly that check. So
unused slots also run the goal tape change and also pay out. Expect the score
to go up all the time, even in an empty room. The graphics are whatever the
change draws. While `SpriteMisc1540` is not zero, `GenericSprGfxRt2` draws the
sprite with palette A and a tile from `LvlEndSmokeTiles` (the goal tape puff).
After that, `CoinSprGfx` draws it. So nothing on the screen looks like the enemy
that it replaced. Nothing here calls the off-screen handling, so slots are only
used again when the level's spawner uses them.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x080B0`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Everything that leaves the ground keeps rising

**Code:** `9568-DDD0`

**Raw form:** `$0180B0 ← $57 (originally $27)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 22:52:30

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** This is the same changed call as above, the `JSR HandleSprite`
inside the twelve-slot loop of `ProcessAllSprites`, but it points at a
different handler in the same page. `$27` → `$57` sends it to
`HandleGoalPowerup` (`$018157`), the handler for status `$0C`. The dispatch
table comment calls it "Power up from carrying a sprite past the goal tape":

```
HandleGoalPowerup:
    JSR CallSpriteMain
    JSR SubOffscreen0Bnk1
    JSR SubUpdateSprPos
    DEC.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    DEC.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    JSR IsOnGround
    BEQ +
    JSR SetSomeYSpeed__
  + RTS
```

This handler is different from the others, because it calls `CallSpriteMain`
*first*. So every sprite still runs its normal AI. What it adds is a second
position update and a fixed −2 per frame on `SpriteYSpeed,X`. That is a
constant upward acceleration on all twelve slots. Only the last part stops it.
`IsOnGround` returns `SpriteBlockedDirs,X & $04`. When the sprite *is* standing
on something, `SetSomeYSpeed__` replaces `SpriteYSpeed,X` with `$00` or `$18`
and removes the upward speed that was collected. So enemies that walk on flat
ground mostly stay where they are. Anything in the air, like a flying Koopa, a
jumping enemy, an enemy that walks off a ledge or a thrown shell, rises away
and never comes back down.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$0180AF` has `20 27 81` (`JSR $018127`).
`HandleGoalPowerup` is at `$018157`, in the same `$0181` page as the
dispatcher, so the low byte change can get to it. `HandleGoalPowerup`,
`IsOnGround` and `SetSomeYSpeed__` are all in `bank_01.asm`. Not tested in
play.

**Caveats:** Because the status check is skipped, slots with status `$00`
(empty) also get to `CallSpriteMain`. That dispatches on whatever old
`SpriteNumber,X` the slot still has. A slot that was not used since
`ClearMemory` has `$00`, which is a green Koopa without a shell. So the result
is limited and not a wild jump, but expect ghost sprites to appear in unused
slots. The killed, stunned and kicked states are also skipped. So a stomped
enemy runs its normal main routine and not its death animation.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x080B0`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## No sprite ever runs, and none is ever marked for reloading

**Code:** `9F68-DDD0`

**Raw form:** `$0180B0 ← $51 (originally $27)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 22:52:30

**Mechanism:** This is the same `JSR HandleSprite` operand inside
`ProcessAllSprites`, and this time it points at `EraseSprite` (`$018151`).
`HandleSprite` normally uses that handler only for status `$00`. The
disassembly's comment on it is "Permanently erase sprite … the actual sprite
won't get marked for reloading":

```
EraseSprite:
    LDA.B #$FF                                ; \ Permanently erase sprite:
    STA.W SpriteLoadIndex,X                   ; | By changing the sprite's index
Return018156:                                 ; | into the level tables
    RTS                                       ; / the actual sprite won't get
                                              ;   marked for reloading
```

The replacement takes the place of the dispatcher itself, so every slot runs it
on every frame, whatever its status. No sprite ever runs its init or its main.
The main routines are what draw sprite graphics, so nothing moves and nothing
is drawn. Also, `SpriteLoadIndex,X` is set to `$FF` twelve times per frame. So
a sprite that scrolls away is also never marked to appear again.

Two simpler variants go to a single `RTS` instead and skip the
`SpriteLoadIndex` write. They do not change the records that the spawner keeps:

| Code | Byte | Lands on |
|---|---|---|
| `4168-DDD0` | `$26` | `Return018126` — bare `RTS` |
| `9168-DDD0` | `$56` | `Return018156` — bare `RTS`, the tail of `EraseSprite` |

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$0180AF` has `20 27 81` (`JSR $018127`).
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` puts `EraseSprite` (`$018151`), `Return018126`
(`$018126`) and `Return018156` (`$018156`) all in page `$0181`. So one low byte
change can send the call to each of them. All are in `bank_01.asm`. Not tested
in play.

**Caveats:** This is a *different* method from "Levels run with no enemies,
items or Yoshi at all" (`FCC3-6DAD`), which disables the whole
`JSL ProcessAllSprites` from the calling side. Here the loop still runs. So
`CODE_0180D2` still gives out OAM and counts down the timers of each slot on
every frame, and the cluster sprites and the `CurrentYoshiSlot` check after the
loop still happen. `CurrentYoshiSlot` is cleared at the top of
`ProcessAllSprites`, and only Yoshi's own main sets it again, which now never
runs. So `PlayerRidingYoshi` is cleared on every frame, and you cannot ride
Yoshi. Anything that a level needs a sprite for (a moving platform, a P-switch,
a goal tape sprite, Bowser) also disappears, so most levels cannot be finished.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x080B0`. The codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every sprite re-runs its spawn setup every frame and never acts

**Code:** `5468-DDD0`

**Raw form:** `$0180B0 ← $72 (originally $27)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 22:52:30

**Mechanism:** This is the same `JSR HandleSprite` operand, pointed at
`CallSpriteInit` (`$018172`). That is the handler for status `$01`, the
*initialization* dispatch for each sprite:

```
CallSpriteInit:
    LDA.B #$08                                ; \ Sprite status = Normal
    STA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; /
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X
    JSL ExecutePtr
    dw InitStandardSprite                     ; 00 - Green Koopa, no shell
    …
```

So every slot is forced to status `$08` (Normal) and initialized again on every
frame. This has two results. First, killed, stunned, kicked and smushed sprites
are set back to Normal before their state handler can run. The dispatcher would
have chosen those handlers, and this code skips exactly them. So a sprite can
never stay in a death state. Second, `CallSpriteMain` is never reached, so no
sprite runs its behavior or draws itself. The whole frame is used to fill the
sprite tables again from the `Init*` routines.

What you see is a level with no visible enemies. But their slots are still
alive and are set up again all the time. Any side effects of the separate
`Init*` routines (sounds, helper sprites that they create, table resets) repeat
sixty times per second for each slot that is in use.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$0180AF` has `20 27 81` (`JSR $018127`).
`CallSpriteInit` is at `$018172`, in the same page as the dispatcher.
`ProcessAllSprites`, `HandleSprite` and `CallSpriteInit` are all in
`bank_01.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This code is chaotic by design, and it is the least predictable in
this group. The `Init*` table has about 200 entries, and their side effects are
different. So what a room does depends on which sprites it has. Empty slots
become live sprites of whatever `SpriteNumber,X` they had last, forced to status
`$08`. `SpriteStatus,X` is `$08` for every slot, so any other part of the engine
that looks for a Normal sprite (interaction checks, Yoshi's tongue) finds twelve
of them.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x080B0`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Sprite timers never tick down and sprite tiles pile up

**Code:** `546C-D700`

**Raw form:** `$0180AD ← $72 (originally $D2)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 22:52:30

**Mechanism:** This is the *other* call for each slot in the loop of
`ProcessAllSprites`. Its header states the job of this routine: before the
state machine itself, each slot goes through a routine "which allots it OAM
from the level's `SpriteMemorySetting` and ages its timers":

```
  - STX.W CurSpriteProcess
    JSR CODE_0180D2                           ; <- $0180AC, operand $D2 $80
    JSR HandleSprite
```

`$D2` → `$72` at `$0180AD` sends the call to `Return018072`, a single `RTS` in
the same `$0180` page. So the call returns at once, and that work never
happens. This has two results. First, `SpriteOAMIndex,X` is never set, so every
slot keeps the index from the last frame, and sprite tiles are written on top of
each other. Second, the seven `SpriteMisc*` countdowns never go down. So any
sprite timer that is running when you turn the code on stays where it is. A
stunned sprite or a sprite in its shell never wakes up, an invulnerability time
never ends, and a sprite that waits for a phase timer waits forever.

Another code with the same effect is `A46C-D760` (`$0180AE ← $C2`, originally
`$80`). It changes the high byte of the operand instead, and the call goes to
`Return01C2D2`, another single `RTS`.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$0180AC` has `20 D2 80` (`JSR $0180D2`).
`Return018072` is at `$018072` (in the same page as `$0180D2`, so the low byte
change can get to it). `Return01C2D2` is at `$01C2D2` (with the same low byte
`$D2`, so the high byte change can get to it). Both are in `bank_01.asm`. Not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** The OAM part of this gives visual noise, not a clean effect.
Expect sprite tiles that overlap and flicker, not a neat freeze. The sprites
themselves still run their AI normally, because `HandleSprite` does not change.
Only their timers and their tile allocation stop. Sprites whose main routine
sets a timer and then waits for it stay in that phase forever.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offsets `0x080AD` and `0x080AE`. The codes decode back
correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every Chargin' Chuck stands there and does nothing

**Code:** `496D-DFA1` + `4961-D4A1` (two codes)

**Raw form:** `$018807 ← $25 (originally $F5)`, `$01886B ← $25 (originally $F5)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 23:04:20

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** These are two changed call operands with one target.
`ChucksMain` (`$02C1F5`) is documented as the one routine for the whole group:
"Every Chuck in the game runs this one routine: sprites `$91`-`$98` (Chargin',
Splittin', Bouncin', Whistlin', Clapin', the unused clone, Puntin' and Pitchin')
and `$46`, the Diggin' Chuck. Which one you are looking at is a single number —
`SpriteTableC2` … Everything below that dispatch, including the gravity, the
block smashing and the three-stomp death, is shared by all of them."

The game gets to it through exactly two of the one-line wrappers of
`CallSpriteMain` in `bank_01.asm` that call into another bank:

```
DigginChuck:
    JSL ChucksMain                            ; <- $018806, operand $F5 $C1 $02
    RTS

Chucks:
    JSL ChucksMain                            ; <- $01886A, operand $F5 $C1 $02
    RTS
```

Both codes change the low byte of that operand from `$F5` to `$25`. The call
then goes to `Return02C125`, a single `RTL` at the end of a nearby routine in
the same `$02C1` page. A `JSL` needs an `RTL`, so each call returns correctly
and does nothing. So every Chuck skips its state dispatch, its gravity, its
block smashing and its stomp handling. They stay still wherever they appear,
they are not drawn (the graphics come from inside `ChucksMain`), and they never
charge, jump, whistle, split or throw anything.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$018806` and at `$01886A` has `22 F5 C1` (`JSL
$02C1F5`), and `$02C125` = `6B` (`RTL`). `tools/callsites.py --callers
ChucksMain` reports exactly these two calls, so the pair covers all nine Chuck
sprites. The wrappers are in `bank_01.asm`, and `ChucksMain` and `Return02C125`
are in `bank_02.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** Two codes are needed for one effect, because `$46` and
`$91`-`$98` use separate wrappers. `496D-DFA1` alone stops only the Diggin'
Chuck, and `4961-D4A1` alone stops only the eight `$9x` Chucks. The sprites
still exist. They use their slots, their OAM share and their timers still run,
and their `Init*` routines still set `SpriteTableC2`. So in a room where a Chuck
must break a block or open a path, that never happens. Chucks are the planned
obstacle in several Vanilla Dome and Chocolate Island levels, so this makes
those rooms easier, not stranger.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offsets `0x08807` and `0x0886B`. The codes decode back
correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Bouncing footballs fight you like the Big Boo boss

**Code:** `65C7-070A`

**Raw form:** `$03A13D ← $87 (originally $12)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 23:04:20

**Mechanism:** This code changes a call operand inside a dispatch on the sprite
number. `Bnk3CallSprMain` (`$03A118`) is a chain of `CMP #num / BNE / JSR <Main>`
that sends seventeen sprite numbers to their main routines. So each `JSR`
operand *is* the byte that says "which AI does this sprite run", and the other
main routines in the chain are the choices:

```
  + CMP.B #$1B
    BNE +
    JSR Football                              ; <- $03A13C, operand $12 $80
    PLB
    RTL
```

Sprite `$1B` is "Bouncing football in place" (that is its label in the table of
`CallSpriteMain`). `$12` → `$87` changes the operand from `Football`
(`$038012`) to `BigBooBoss` (`$038087`). The two are in the same `$0380` page,
so one byte is enough. `BigBooBoss` is fully documented in `bank_03.asm`: it is
"The Big Boo of Big Boo's Fort — sprite `$C5` … He is never stomped: the only
thing that hurts him is a sprite in status `$09` (stunned/carryable) or `$0A`
(kicked) touching him … Three of those beat him". It runs a state machine of
seven phases from `SpriteTableC2`: away, fading in, drifting (can be hit), hit,
fading out, gone, beaten.

So every bouncing football becomes a Big Boo. It starts in phase 0, invisible,
and counts `SpriteMisc1570` up to `$90`. Then it fades in one step every eight
frames, drifts around the room, and can only be hurt if you throw a stunned or
kicked sprite into it.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$03A13C` has `20 12 80` (`JSR $038012`).
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` gives `$038012` for `Football` and `$038087` for
`BigBooBoss`. They are in the same page, so the low byte change can get to it.
`tools/callsites.py --in Bnk3CallSprMain` confirms that both are targets of the
same chain of seventeen. So the calling rules are the same for both: the
chain's `PHB / PHK / PLB` has already set the bank, X holds the slot index, and
the routine returns with `RTS`. Both routines are in `bank_03.asm`. Not tested
in play.

**Caveats:** Only the *main* routine is swapped. The tweaker table bits of
sprite `$1B` and its `Init*` entry do not change. (That entry is
`Return0185C2`, a single `RTS`. The football has no initialization at all.) So
the Big Boo logic runs with the football's clipping and interaction flags, not
the boss's. It also does not get the `FaceMario` init that sprite `$C5` normally
runs. That difference is the interesting part of this code. But it means the
result is a Big Boo *with the interaction rules of a football*, not an exact
second boss. `BooTransparency`, the fade level that the phase machine controls,
is one global byte, not one per slot. So two footballs on the screen both change
it, and the fade will not work correctly. Big Boo's Fort itself does not
change, because sprite `$C5` still points at `BigBooBoss`.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`281aef4b1edd8d17`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x1A13D`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## The Big Boo boss is replaced by a bouncing football

**Code:** `F4C1-0D0A`

**Raw form:** `$03A161 ← $12 (originally $87)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 23:58:10

**Mechanism:** This is the football/Big Boo swap above, in the other direction.
`Bnk3CallSprMain` (`$03A118`) sends seventeen sprite numbers to their main
routines with a chain of `CMP #num / BNE / JSR <Main>`. So each `JSR` operand is
the byte that says "which AI does this sprite run":

```
  + CMP.B #$C5
    BNE +
    JSR BigBooBoss                            ; <- $03A160, operand $87 $80
    PLB
    RTL
```

Sprite `$C5` is "Big Boo Boss" (that is its label in the table of
`CallSpriteMain`). `$87` → `$12` changes the operand from `BigBooBoss`
(`$038087`) to `Football` (`$038012`). Both are in the `$0380` page, so one byte
is enough.

`Football` is now documented in `bank_03.asm` as the bouncing football, sprite
`$1B`: "a purely ballistic hazard that bounces off whatever it hits". Bits 0/1
of `SpriteBlockedDirs` negate `SpriteXSpeed`, bit 3 sets `SpriteYSpeed` to zero,
and bit 2 starts a bounce. On each bounce on the ground, it flips bit `$40` of
`SpriteOBJAttribute`, chooses a new random upward speed from `DATA_03800E`, and
adds `DATA_038007[SpriteSlope+3]` to the horizontal speed before it limits it to
`$E0`-`$20`. So the boss of Big Boo's Fort is no longer a boss, and he bounces
around his room like a football.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$03A160` has `20 87 80` (`JSR $038087`).
`tools/callsites.py --in Bnk3CallSprMain` gives `$038087` for `BigBooBoss` and
`$038012` for `Football`. They are in the same page, so the low byte can get to
it. It lists both as targets of the same chain of seventeen, so the calling
rules are the same for both: the chain's `PHB / PHK / PLB` has already set the
bank, X holds the slot index, and both routines end in `RTS`. Both are in
`bank_03.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **This makes Big Boo's Fort impossible to finish.** `BigBooBoss`
itself ends the level. The first thing it does on each frame is to check
`SpriteStatus`. When the boss is gone, it does `INC CutsceneID` /
`STA EndLevelTimer` and plays `!BGM_BOSSCLEAR`. With the main routine changed,
that code never runs, so no number of thrown grab blocks can finish the room.
Only the *main* routine is swapped. Sprite `$C5` keeps its own tweaker bits and
its `FaceMario` init, so the football logic runs with the boss's clipping and
interaction flags. The graphics will also be wrong. `Football` draws through
`GenericSprGfxRt2`, which finds the sprite's tile as
`SprTilemap[SpriteMisc1602 + SprTilemapOffset[number]]`. `SprTilemapOffset` has
only 84 entries, so sprite number `$C5` reads past its end into the data after
it. That is also why the disassembly's comment calls the routine "the routine
for sprites <= 53". Sprite `$1B` itself does not change and still runs
`Football`.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x1A161`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`, and it matches `cheats({op:'make'})` for the same
address/byte pair.

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 23:59:05

the same chain:


constant horizontal speed of `$08`/`$F8` from `BlurpSpeedX[SpriteMisc157C]`. Every

`BlurpAccelY` / `BlurpMaxSpeedY`, and `SpriteTableC2` flips at each limit.

shallow zigzag. `Blurp` never calls `InvisBlkMainRt`, so **they are no longer
solid**, and Mario falls directly through the place where a platform was.

same. Both are in `bank_03.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** This makes any level whose path goes over gray falling platforms
impossible to cross. That is the point, but it is good to know before you start
one. The init of sprite `$C4` is `Return0185C2`, so it has none.
`InitSpriteTables` leaves `SpriteMisc157C` at 0, and every platform swims in the
same direction (`BlurpSpeedX[0]` = `$08`). The drawing uses `Blurp`'s own code.
It calls `GenericSprGfxRt2` and then *replaces* the tile number with `$A2` or
`$EC`. So the tile itself is a real Blurp tile, even though `SprTilemapOffset`

`Blurp` unless you also use `90C5-0DAA`.

**Recorded:** 2026-08-09 23:59:30

```

    PLB
    RTL
```

`PorcuPuffer` (`$03852F`) to `FlyingTurnBlocks` (`$0385F6`). Both are in `$0385`.

`FlyingTurnBlocks` is now documented in `bank_03.asm` as sprite `$C1`. It "is
solid (`InvisBlkMainRt`) and sits still until Mario stands on it; landing on one
starts the level's auto-scroll and sets the whole formation moving". Landing on
it writes `$08` into `BGFastScrollActive`. That is the trigger that the layer 2
scroller in `bank_05` reads, and the routine then copies the same byte into
`SpriteXSpeed`. Landing also sets `SpriteMisc1602` to `$7F` as the countdown to
turn around, and it searches the slots for one *other* sprite `$C1` to set up so
that it moves in step.

stand on one, the level's fast background scroll starts. Then they move up and
down (`FlyingBlockSpeedY`, `$08`/`$F8`, chosen by `SpriteMisc157C`) and move
sideways with the scroll.

`$0385F6` for `FlyingTurnBlocks`. They are in the same page and the same chain,
with the same calling rules. Both are in `bank_03.asm`. Not tested in play.

to start `BGFastScrollActive` in any level that has a Porcu-Puffer. A level
whose layer 2 was never designed to scroll will do whatever the `bank_05`
scroller makes it do. The loop at the end that sets up one other sprite `$C1`
looks for sprite number `$C1` only, and these sprites do not have that number.
So the loop ends with Y = 0 and writes `SpriteMisc1602` of slot 0 anyway. This

Only the main routine is swapped: sprite `$C3` keeps its `FaceMario` init and
its own tweaker bits. The drawing is `CODE_0386A8` of `FlyingTurnBlocks` itself,
so there is no tile lookup outside the table. Sprite `$C1` does not change
unless you also use `4EC6-0F0A`.

behaviour of its own: it waits, unseen, until Mario walks into it and then turns
itself into a real mushroom on the spot. `GetDrawInfoBnk3` is called only to set

sprite up `$0F` pixels, and runs `PopupMushroom`. That gives it Mario's facing
direction, an upward speed of `$C0` and the item block sound.

get to it. Both are targets of the same chain, so the calling rules are the
same. Both are in `bank_03.asm`. Not tested in play.

`FaceMario` init and its own tweaker and clipping bits. The contact test is the

mushroom's. The change goes one way only and stays for that slot. The sprite

this chain. Sprite `$C7` still runs `InvisMushroom` unless you also use
`0AC4-04AA`. A Ninji that you never touch is just gone from the level, so the
levels that use them are clearly emptier.

always turned toward Mario, and does nothing else: this routine never touches
`SpriteXSpeed`". `SubHorzPosBnk3` writes `SpriteMisc157C` again on every frame,
so it faces Mario even in the air. When it lands, it loads `SpriteMisc1540`
with `$60` again and takes the height of the next hop from
`NinjiSpeedY[SpriteTableC2 AND $03]`. That cycles through `$D0`, `$C0`, `$B0`,

hopping Ninji that faces Mario and hurts him through `SprSpr_MarioSprRts`. The

reward becomes a trap.

`tools/callsites.py --in Bnk3CallSprMain` puts both routines in the `$03C3`
page as targets of the same chain, with the same calling rules. Both are in
`bank_03.asm`. Not tested in play.

sprites <= 53". The sprite also still has the tweaker and clipping bits of the
invisible mushroom. So it hurts Mario with the mushroom's interaction shape, not
a Ninji's. Sprite `$51` still runs `Ninji` unless you also use `DEC7-0FDA`.

**Mechanism:** `GM00LoadPresents` (game mode `$00`) builds the "Nintendo
Presents" logo from four sprites in OAM, plays the "bing" with `!SFX_COIN`, and
then starts the hold timer:

```

    STA.W VariousPromptTimer
```

`!NintendoPresentsTimer` is `64` in `constants.asm`. The next mode only counts
that timer down:

```
GM01Presents:

    BNE FinishGameMode
    JSR CODE_00B888                           ; Decompress GFX32/GFX33.
    INC.W GameMode
```

of mode `$02` starts. If you store `$01` instead, the first `GM01Presents` frame
counts down to zero, continues, and moves on at once. The logo is drawn for one
frame and then it is gone.

`STA VariousPromptTimer`), which matches the source line exactly.
`GM00LoadPresents`, `GM01Presents` and `!NintendoPresentsTimer` all have names
and comments in `bank_00.asm` / `constants.asm`. Not tested in play. The effect
comes from the disassembly.

`$FF`, and the logo would stay for 255 frames, four times *longer* than normal.
The "bing" sound is started in `GM00LoadPresents` and does not depend on the
timer. So it still plays, and now it plays after the logo is already gone. This
store is the only write to `VariousPromptTimer` in the boot path. The title
screen sets it again from `TitleScreenInputSeq` in `GM07TitleScreen`, so nothing
later changes.

## The title screen's opening circle is skipped — boot goes straight to file select

**Code:** `2DB4-DD0F`

**Raw form:** `$009421 ← $D0 (originally $F0)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-10 00:32:10

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** `GM06TitleSpotlight` (game mode `$06`) is the circle that opens
on the title screen. The first thing it does is to let the player skip it:

```
GM06TitleSpotlight:
    JSR DetermineJoypadInput
    JSR IsFaceButtonPressed                   ;\ Branch if A/B/X/Y is not pressed.
    BEQ +                                     ;/ <- $009421, opcode $F0
    LDA.B #4*!MaxTitleSpotlightSize           ; Size to make the window if the opening animation is skipped
    JSR CODE_009440
    INC.W GameMode                            ;\ Prepare the file select menu.
    JMP PrepareFileSelect                     ;/
```

`IsFaceButtonPressed` returns with Z set when no button is held. So the normal
`BEQ` takes the *slow* path, and the window grows four units per frame. If you
change the opcode to `BNE` (`$D0`), the test is reversed. When no button is
held, the skip path runs on the first frame of mode `$06`. The window jumps to
its full size of `4*59 = 236`, `GameMode` is increased past `$07`, and
`PrepareFileSelect` runs (it ends in `JMP NextGameMode`, which goes to
`GM08FileSelect`). The boot goes logo → fades → file select, with no circle
animation and no title screen demo.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$009421` has `F0 0B A9 EC`: `BEQ +$0B` followed by the
`LDA #$EC` of the skip path (`= 4*!MaxTitleSpotlightSize`, `$EC` = 236). This
matches the source. `GM06TitleSpotlight`, `IsFaceButtonPressed` and
`PrepareFileSelect` all have names and header comments in `bank_00.asm`. Not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** The branch is reversed, not removed. So if you *hold* A, B, X, Y,
Select or Start during mode `$06`, the normal behavior comes back and the
animation plays. Skipping and watching have just changed places.
`IsFaceButtonPressed` reads the *hold* variables (`axlr0000Hold` /
`byetudlrHold`), not new presses, so a button that is still held from a reset
counts. The window is set to the same full size that the normal skip uses, so
no dark ring stays on the screen.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x1421`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## The title screen's circle irises open in 3 frames instead of 59

**Code:** `7AB7-D4AF`

**Raw form:** `$00943B ← $3C (originally $04)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-10 00:32:10

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** When the player does *not* skip it, `GM06TitleSpotlight` makes
the window wider by a fixed step on each frame. When the next step would go too
far, it moves on to the next game mode:

```
  + DEC.W VariousPromptTimer                  ; A/B/X/Y is not pressed, handle the window.
    BNE FinishGameMode
    INC.W VariousPromptTimer
    LDA.W SpotlightSize
    CLC
    ADC.B #4                                  ; <- $00943A, operand $04
    CMP.B #4*(!MaxTitleSpotlightSize+1)       ; = $F0
    BCS NextGameMode
CODE_009440:
    STA.W SpotlightSize
```

`!MaxTitleSpotlightSize` is 59. So normally `SpotlightSize` goes
`0, 4, 8, … 236`, which is 59 drawn frames, and it stops when the sum gets to
`$F0`. If you change the step to `$3C` (60), it goes `0, 60, 120, 180`, and then
`180 + 60 = 240 = $F0` ends it: three drawn frames.

You cannot see that the final size is smaller. `CODE_00CA88` builds the window
table for each scanline around a center of (128, 112), with `SpotlightSize` as
a radius in scanlines. The farthest corner of the screen is ~170 scanlines away.
So any final size above that already covers the whole 256×224 frame. 180 does,
and so does the normal 236.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$00943A` has `69 04 C9 F0 B0 D7`: `ADC #$04` /
`CMP #$F0` / `BCS`. This matches the source and confirms the `$F0` end value.
`GM06TitleSpotlight`, `SpotlightSize`, `!MaxTitleSpotlightSize` and the window
builder `CODE_00CA88` are documented in `bank_00.asm` / `constants.asm`. Not
tested in play.

**Caveats:** You must choose the step so that the sum that *ends* the growth is
not more than 255. The `ADC` is 8-bit, and the code only checks `BCS` against
`$F0`, never the carry. A step of `$3B` (59) would get to exactly 236 and then
wrap around to `$27` on the next add. `$27 < $F0`, so `BCS` would not be taken,
and the circle would shrink to a very small point and not move on. `$3C`, `$14`
and `$04` all get exactly to 240. A softer variant is below. This code is not
needed if `2DB4-DD0F` is also on, because that code never goes into the growth
path.

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `7AB7-D4AF` | `$3C` | 3 frames (`0→60→120→180`), final size 180 |
| `F0B7-D4AF` | `$14` | 12 frames (`0→20→…→220`), final size 220 |

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x143A`. Both codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every fade and mosaic transition in the game runs twice as fast

**Code:** `DDB4-A467`

**Raw form:** `$009F2A ← $00 (originally $01)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-10 00:32:10

**Mechanism:** All of SMW's transition modes slow themselves down with one
shared helper. These are the eleven `GMTransitionFade` entries and the four
`GMTransitionMosaic` entries in the dispatch table of `RunGameMode`:

```
KeepGameModeActive:                           ; This game mode will last 1 more frame
    LDA.B #1                                  ; <- $009F29, operand $01
CODE_009F2B:
    STA.W KeepModeActive
    RTS
```

and each transition frame starts with

```
GMTransitionFade:
    DEC.W KeepModeActive
    BPL Return009F6E
    JSR KeepGameModeActive
```

When `$01` is stored, the `DEC` gives 0, `BPL` is taken, and the mode does
nothing. Only every *second* frame gets past it to change the brightness. If you
store `$00` instead, the `DEC` gives `$FF`. That is negative, so `BPL` is never
taken, and every frame does work. Both parts of the mosaic transitions get
faster together (brightness and `MosaicSize` change in the same block), so
nothing gets out of step. The fade-out to the title, the fade-in to the title,
the fade to the overworld, the mosaic into and out of every level, and the
credits fades all take half as many frames.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$009F29` has `A9 01 8D B1 0D 60` (`LDA #$01` /
`STA $0DB1` / `RTS`), which matches the source. `KeepGameModeActive`,
`KeepModeActive`, `GMTransitionFade` and `GMTransitionMosaic` all have names and
comments in `bank_00.asm`. The dispatch table in `RunGameMode` labels every
transition mode by number. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** Four other routines call `KeepGameModeActive` to stay for one more
frame: `CODE_009622` (enemy credits preparation), `FadeToOverworld`,
`CODE_00A11B` (overworld load) and `CODE_00A5B9` (in `GM12PrepLevel`). Each of
those loading modes now ends one frame sooner. You cannot see this, but it is a
real change in behavior. `bank_04.asm` writes `KeepModeActive` directly in
several overworld places, and those do not change. This is the *safe* way to
make the fades faster. See the two codes below for the stronger version, and for
why they do not work well with the mosaic.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x1F2A`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every fade-in is instant

**Code:** `DEB4-A7A7`

**Raw form:** `$009F2F ← $0F (originally $01)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-10 00:32:10

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** Every fade in the game uses one two-byte rate table and one
two-byte limit table. Both are indexed by `MosaicDirection`:

```
BrightnessRate:
    db 1,-1                                   ; <- $009F2F / $009F30
MosaicRate:
    db -1<<4,1<<4
BrightnessLimits:
    db 15,0
```

They are read by the shared body of both transition handlers:

```
CODE_009F4C:
    LDA.W Brightness                          ;\
    CLC                                       ;| Adjust brightness
    ADC.W BrightnessRate,Y                    ;|
    STA.W Brightness                          ;/
    CMP.W BrightnessLimits,Y
    BNE +
NextGameModeMosaic:
    INC.W GameMode                            ; Go to next game mode
```

Index 0 is the fade *in* direction: `+1` per step, with a limit of `15`. So a
fade-in is 15 brightness steps (30 frames, because `KeepGameModeActive` only
lets every second frame through). If you replace the `+1` with `$0F`, the one
step goes `0 → 15`. That is equal to `BrightnessLimits[0]` at once, so the mode
moves on in its first working frame. The title screen, and every other screen,
goes to full brightness at once instead of fading up.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$009F2F` has `01 FF F0 10 0F 00`: `BrightnessRate`
(`01`, `FF`), `MosaicRate` (`F0`, `10`) and `BrightnessLimits` (`0F`, `00`), in
exactly the order the source declares them. All three tables and both handlers
that read them (`GMTransitionFade`, `GMTransitionMosaic`) have names and comments
in `bank_00.asm`. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** The end test is an exact `CMP`, so the new rate must divide 15.
`$01`, `$03`, `$05` and `$0F` are the only clean choices. The game does not lock
up if a fade starts from a brightness that is not on the step grid (15 and 256
have no common factor, so the steps still get to `$0F` in the end). But the
values in between go to `HW_INIDISP` in the NMI with no mask, so bit 7 would
blank the screen for part of those steps. In practice, every fade-in starts from
exactly 0, because the fade-out before it ends there.

The real cost is the **mosaic**. `GMTransitionMosaic` (the level fades, modes
`$0F` and `$13`) ends on *brightness* only. So a brightness change of one step
ends the mode after `MosaicSize` has moved only one `$10` step, and levels can
start with some blockiness left on BG1/BG2. Adding `FDB7-AD07` (`$009F31 ← $10`)
and `EDB7-AD67` (`$009F32 ← $F0`) makes the mosaic finish in one step too.
That is four codes, which still fits on real Game Genie hardware (it takes
five). `DDB4-A467` above does not have this problem, because it makes both parts
faster by the same amount.

| Code | Byte | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `DEB4-A7A7` | `$0F` | 1 step — instant |
| `D9B4-A7A7` | `$05` | 3 steps instead of 15 |

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x1F2F`. Both codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

**Code:** `EFB7-ADD7`

**Raw form:** `$009F30 ← $F1 (originally $FF)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-10 00:32:10

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** The second byte of `BrightnessRate` is the fade-*out* direction:
`-1` per step, with a limit of `BrightnessLimits[1]` = `0`. That is 15 steps
down from full brightness. `$F1` is `-15`, so `15 - 15 = 0` matches the limit in
the first working frame, and the transition mode moves on at once. When the game
boots, this is game mode `$02`, the fade-out from "Nintendo Presents" to the
title screen. The same table is used for the fade to the overworld, to game
over, and to every credits scene.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$009F2F` has `01 FF F0 10 0F 00`. The `FF` at
`$009F30` is the second entry of `BrightnessRate`, and the `00` at `$009F34` is
the `BrightnessLimits` entry that it is compared with. `BrightnessRate`,
`BrightnessLimits`, `GMTransitionFade` and `GMTransitionMosaic` all have names
and comments in `bank_00.asm`. Not tested in play.

must divide 15 (`$FF`, `$FD`, `$FB`, `$F1`). The same mosaic problem also
applies to the level transitions, and you can fix it only with two more codes.
Use it with `DEB4-A7A7` to make both directions instant. That uses two of your

|---|---|---|
| `EFB7-ADD7` | `$F1` (-15) | 1 step — instant |
| `E8B7-ADD7` | `$FB` (-5) | 3 steps instead of 15 |

## Level transitions are instant — entering a level costs 98 frames instead of 154

**Codes (all four):** `DEB4-A7A7` + `FDB7-AD07` + `EFB7-ADD7` + `EDB7-AD67`

**Raw form:** `$009F2F ← $0F (originally $01)`, `$009F31 ← $10 (originally $F0)`,
`$009F30 ← $F1 (originally $FF)`, `$009F32 ← $F0 (originally $10)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-10 01:00:30

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** The two fade-rate entries above mention the mosaic pair only in
their caveats. This entry gives it its own section, because this pair is what
really makes the "MARIO START!" screen shorter. `GMTransitionMosaic` (game modes
`$0F` and `$13`, the fades out of and into every level) changes two values on
each working frame and ends on brightness only:

```
GMTransitionMosaic:
    DEC.W KeepModeActive
    BPL Return009F6E
    JSR KeepGameModeActive
    LDY.W MosaicDirection                     ;\
    LDA.W MosaicSize                          ;| Adjust mosaic size
    CLC                                       ;|
    ADC.W MosaicRate,Y                        ;|
    STA.W MosaicSize                          ;/
CODE_009F4C:
    LDA.W Brightness / CLC / ADC.W BrightnessRate,Y / STA.W Brightness
    CMP.W BrightnessLimits,Y
    BNE +
```

If you make only `BrightnessRate` faster, the mode ends while `MosaicSize` is
still only part of the way there, and some blockiness stays on BG1/BG2. The two
tables are next to each other, so if you patch both, they stay in step:

| Direction | Y | Brightness | `BrightnessRate` | `MosaicSize` | `MosaicRate` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fade **in** (mode `$13`) | 0 | `$00 → $0F` | `$01` → `$0F` | `$F0 → $00` | `$F0` → `$10` |
| fade **out** (mode `$0F`) | 1 | `$0F → $00` | `$FF` → `$F1` | `$00 → $F0` | `$10` → `$F0` |

Each direction now finishes in one step. `$F0 + $10` wraps around to exactly
`$00`, and `$00 + $F0` gets to exactly `$F0`. This matches the one brightness
step to its `BrightnessLimits` entry.

**Evidence — this one was measured, not only derived.** The U ROM was run in
snes9x, and `GameMode` (`$7E0100`) was logged on every frame. A level entry from
the overworld, without patches:

| Mode | Stock | With these four codes |
|---|---|---|
| `$0F` fade out to level | 31 frames | **3** |
| `$10` `GM10FadeToLevel` | 1 frame | 1 |
| `$11` `GM11LoadLevel` | 37 frames | 37 |
| `$12` `GM12PrepLevel` | 55 frames | 55 |
| `$13` fade in to level | 30 frames | **2** |
| **total** | **154 frames (~2.6 s)** | **98 frames (~1.6 s)** |

A screenshot 120 frames into the level shows full brightness, correct palettes
and **no mosaic left over**. That is the failure that the mosaic pair is there
to prevent. The ROM at `$009F2F` has `01 FF F0 10 0F 00`. This covers all four
patched bytes and the `BrightnessLimits` values that end the fades.
`GMTransitionMosaic`, `BrightnessRate`, `MosaicRate` and `BrightnessLimits` all
have names and comments in `bank_00.asm`.

**Caveats:** **Four codes.** Real Game Genie hardware takes five, so this fits,
with one slot free. For a shorter set, use `DDB4-A467` instead. It makes both
parts twice as fast with one code, and they cannot get out of step. If you want
a subset of two codes, take the fade-*in* pair (`DEB4-A7A7` + `FDB7-AD07`).
That is the part you wait through *after* the level has loaded, and it leaves
three slots free. The codes change every fade in the game, not only
level entry. This includes the overworld and the credits. Each rate must divide
15 exactly, because the end test is a `CMP`. See the two fade-rate entries above
for the full list of safe values.

**The remaining 93 frames are not patchable.** Modes `$11` and `$12` have no
timer at all. They are `GM11LoadLevel` and `GM12PrepLevel` doing real work
(level data, GFX decompression, palette upload) with NMI off. So the PPU keeps
showing the black "MARIO START!" screen while the CPU loads. There is no byte to
make shorter. Only the 61 frames of fading around it can be changed.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`). The bytes were read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offsets `0x1F2F`-`0x1F32`. All four codes decode back to
their own `address:byte` pair with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`. The frame counts
were measured in snes9x through the romdev MCP, with the codes applied at load.
