## "MARIO START!" never appears

**Code:** `6DBB-67AF`

**Raw form:** `$00969F ← $80 (originally $D0)`

**Recorded:** 2026-08-10 01:00:30

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** `GM10FadeToLevel` uses a short series of tests to decide if it
draws the message on the loading screen:

```
GM10FadeToLevel:
    JSR ClearOutLayer3
    LDA.W BonusGameActivate                   ;\ Branch if bonus game should be loaded.
    BNE .ShowText                             ;/
    LDA.W SublevelCount                       ;\ Don't show "MARIO START!" if:
    ORA.W ShowMarioStart                      ;|  - entering sublevel
    ORA.W OverworldOverride                   ;|  - no yoshi intro
    BNE .DontShowText                         ;| <- $00969F, opcode $D0
    LDA.W OverworldLayer1Tile                 ;|  - entering yoshi's house
    CMP.B #!LevelTileNoStart                  ;||
    BEQ .DontShowText                         ;/
.ShowText:
    JSR ShowLevelLoadingText                  ; Show MARIO START!
.DontShowText:
    JMP CODE_0093CA
```

If you change that `BNE` to `BRA` (`$80`, same operand, same target), the skip
always happens for every level that is not a bonus game. `ShowLevelLoadingText`
never runs. So `CODE_00A82D` never builds the message tiles, `UploadMarioStart`
is never set, and the twenty OAM letters are never placed. The loading screen is
all black.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$00968E` has `20 FA 85 AD 25 14 D0 12 AD 1A 14 0D 1D 14
0D 09 01 D0 0A AD C1 13 C9 56 F0 03 20 B1 91`. This decodes to exactly the
listing above. `D0 0A` at `$00969F` branches to `.DontShowText` at `$0096AB`,
and `C9 56` confirms that `!LevelTileNoStart` = `$56`. `GM10FadeToLevel`,
`ShowLevelLoadingText`, `CODE_00A82D` and all four test variables have names and
comments in `bank_00.asm` / `constants.asm`. Nobody saw on screen that the
message is gone. See the caveats.

**Caveats:** **This removes the message, it does not shorten the wait.** The
black screen that you wait through is `GM11LoadLevel` + `GM12PrepLevel` loading
the level with NMI off, which was measured at 92 frames. `ShowLevelLoadingText`
runs inside `GM10FadeToLevel`, which was measured at one frame. So expect the
same pause, with nothing written on the screen. The `BRA` comes *after* the
`BonusGameActivate` test, so bonus games still show "BONUS GAME". That branch is
taken earlier and goes directly to `.ShowText`. The message is never built, so
the `UploadMarioStart` path in the NMI and the `CODE_00A436` tile restore that
goes with it also never run. Both already test the flag, so this is the same
path that a sublevel transition takes every time.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`). The byte was read from `comparison_U.smc` without its
copier header at LoROM offset `0x169F`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Rex walks at 4x speed, both directions

**Code:** `4DBF-0DA2` + `3DBF-0FD2` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `039513:20` + `039514:E0` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie
codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 00:46:16

Tags: `demo-ready` `basic-enemies` `enemy-movement-collection` `play-start` `curated` `challenge`

**Mechanism:** `RexMainRt` (`bank_03.asm`) loads Rex's horizontal speed again
from a table with 4 entries on every frame that he is on the ground. The index
is his facing direction (`SpriteMisc157C`), plus 2 after he has been hit once
(`SpriteTableC2 != 0`, "smushed"):

```
RexSpeed:
    db $08,$F8,$10,$F0

    ...
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; Load, y = Rex direction, as index for speed
    LDA.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; \ If hits on Rex == 0...
    BEQ +                                     ; /    ...goto DONT_ADJUST_SPEED
    INY                                       ; \ Increment y twice...
    INY                                       ; /    ...in order to get speed for smushed Rex
  + LDA.W RexSpeed,Y                          ; \ Load x speed from ROM...
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; /    ...and store it
```

Index `0` (`$08`, half a pixel per frame to the right) and index `1` (`$F8` =
`-8`, half a pixel to the left) are the speeds used for all the time that Rex
walks normally. The smushed pair at indices `2`/`3` is only used for the short
time after his first hit. If you make the two normal bytes four times larger,
`$20` (32, two pixels to the right) and `$E0` (`-32`, two pixels to the left),
Rex runs back and forth four times as fast in both directions. The smushed speed
after a hit does not change.

**Evidence:** This patches `$039513`/`$039514` in `RexSpeed` (`bank_03.asm`).
These are the first two bytes of the table, read by `LDA.W RexSpeed,Y` with `Y`
= 0 or 1 for a Rex that is not smushed. This was checked against the disassembly
source and against the built ROM, where `$039513`-`$039516` has `08 f8 10 f0`,
as the source says.

**Caveats:** Only the two normal entries are patched. A Rex that has already
been hit once (and is in the smushed pose for a short time before the second
hit defeats him) still moves at the original `$10`/`$F0` speed for that short
time. Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## Jumping Piranha Plant moves very slowly

**Code:** `DF31-0DA6`
**Raw form:** `02E163:01` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no
compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 00:53:11

**Mechanism:** Sprites `$4F`/`$50` (the normal Jumping Piranha Plant and the one
that spits fire) both run `JumpingPiranhaMain` -> `CODE_02E0CD` in
`bank_02.asm`. Its state machine runs every frame, and `SpriteTableC2` selects
the state:

```
    dw CODE_02E13C                            ; 0 - waiting in the pipe
    dw CODE_02E159                            ; 1 - rising out of the pipe
    dw CODE_02E177                            ; 2 - falling back in
```

State `0` picks a random time to jump. It sets a fixed start speed upward and
moves on to state `1`:

```
CODE_02E13C:
    ...
    LDA.B #$C0                                ; upward launch speed (-64)
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X
```

State `1` is gravity, applied on every frame while the plant rises:

```
CODE_02E159:
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    BMI CODE_02E161                           ; still rising: always accelerate
    CMP.B #$40                                ; already falling: cap at terminal speed $40
    BCS +
CODE_02E161:
    CLC
    ADC.B #$02                                ; <- patched byte, at $02E163
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
  + INC.W SpriteMisc1570,X
    LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    CMP.B #$F0                                ; once speed climbs to -16 or better...
    BMI Return02E176
    LDA.B #$50
    STA.W SpriteMisc1540,X
    INC.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; ...move to state 2 (falling/spitting)
Return02E176:
    RTS
```

`$02` is added to `SpriteYSpeed` on every frame, if the plant is still rising or
already falling. It is the one acceleration value that controls the whole jump.
If you lower it to `$01`, its speed changes half as fast on each frame. So the
whole jump takes twice as long to get to the `$F0` (-16) limit that ends state
`1`. The fall in state `2` also becomes longer to match. (State `2` has its own
separate, softer +1 every 4 frames, and that does not change.) The plant rises
and falls in slow motion that you can see, instead of doing the jump quickly.
`$01` is the smallest value this byte can have without breaking the sprite.
`$00` would mean no acceleration at all. A plant that jumps at the fixed `-64`
speed of state `0` would then fly up forever and never come back down.

**Evidence:** This patches `$02E163` in `CODE_02E159` (`bank_02.asm`). It is the
immediate operand of `ADC.B #$02`, which goes into `STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X`. The
opcode `$69` is at `$02E162`, and the ROM has `18 69 02 95 aa fe` at
`$02E161`-`$02E166`, which is `CLC / ADC #$02 / STA SpriteYSpeed,X / INC
SpriteMisc1570,X`. This was checked against the disassembly source and against
the built ROM, where `$02E163` has `$02`, as the source says. The effect comes
from the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** Both sprite numbers (`$4F` and `$50`) are changed, because they run
the same main code. The fire-spitting plant shoots its fireball from state `2`
on a separate timer (`SpriteMisc1540`), and this byte does not change that
timer. So it still spits at the normal rate, even though the jump that carries
it up and down is now much slower. This code does not change the fixed jump
speed of state `0` (`$C0`) or the softer acceleration of state `2`.

## Mario can't voluntarily jump off Yoshi's back

**Code:** `6D3B-07D5`
**Raw form:** `01ED9C:80` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no
compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 01:04:02

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** While Mario rides Yoshi (`SpriteTableC2` state `$01`), Yoshi's
sprite routine (`bank_01.asm`) runs a block on every frame that lets Mario get
off when the player chooses. Holding a direction sets a turn timer. Then, if the
P-balloon is not inflating (that always forces Mario off), the routine checks
if a button in the A/X/L/R group was pressed on this frame. If so, it continues
into the dismount code at `CODE_01ED9E`:

```
  + LDA.W PBalloonInflating
    BNE CODE_01ED9E
    BIT.B axlr0000Frame                       ; <- patched instruction, at $01ED9C
    BPL Return01EDCB                          ; no A/X/L/R press this frame: stay mounted
CODE_01ED9E:
    LDA.B #$02
    STA.W SpriteMisc1FE2,X
    STZ.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; unmount
    ...
    STZ.W PlayerRidingYoshi
```

`BIT axlr0000Frame` sets the negative flag from the top bit of that byte (the
`A` in the name `axlr0000Frame`). So `BPL` skips the dismount unless a button in
the A/X/L/R group was pressed. If you change the `BPL` opcode (`$10`) to `BRA`
(`$80`), the branch is always taken. The routine always goes to `Return01EDCB`
instead of `CODE_01ED9E`. The player can no longer choose to get off, whatever
they press, on the ground or in the air. The forced dismount when the P-balloon
inflates, a few lines earlier, does not change. It branches directly to
`CODE_01ED9E` and never gets to the patched instruction.

**Evidence:** This patches `$01ED9C` in the handler for riding Yoshi
(`bank_01.asm`). It is the opcode byte of `BPL Return01EDCB`. This was checked
against the disassembly source and against the built ROM, where
`$01ED9A`-`$01ED9D` has `24 18 10 2D` (`BIT $18` / `BPL +$2D`, which goes to
exactly `Return01EDCB` at `$01EDCB`), as the source says. The effect comes from
the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** This fully turns off the A/X/L/R dismount, on the ground and in the
air. The game does not check `PlayerInAir` for this input, so you cannot patch
only the case in the air. Mario can still be knocked off Yoshi in other ways
(touching an enemy, the forced P-balloon dismount, taking damage). Yoshi can
still be lost in the normal way at the end of a level or when going back to the
overworld.

## Enemies can't knock Mario off Yoshi (and Yoshi never runs off scared)

**Code:** `6DEF-AD09` + `1DC5-DDAB` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `01F711:80` + `02A473:60` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie
codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 01:07:28

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** When something touches Mario while he rides Yoshi, one of two
separate routines runs, depending on what touched him. Both end the same way:
Yoshi gets scared and goes into `SpriteTableC2` state `$02` (run away), and
`PlayerRidingYoshi` is cleared.

Normal sprites go through Yoshi's own collision check in `bank_01.asm`
(`CODE_01F668`). First it filters out a few special sprite numbers. Then it
checks for a star before it knocks Mario off:

```
CODE_01F70E:
    LDA.W InvinsibilityTimer                  ; \ Branch if Mario has star
    BNE Return01F74B                          ; /  <- patched instruction, at $01F711
    LDA.B #$10
    STA.W SpriteMisc163E,X
    ...
    LDA.B #$02
    STA.B SpriteTableC2,X                     ; Yoshi -> scared/run-away state
    STZ.W PlayerRidingYoshi                   ; Mario dismounted
    ...
```

Extended sprites (fireballs, Bullet Bills, and similar) go through a separate
check in `bank_02.asm` (`CODE_02A469`). It is called from the player's own
damage collision code. It does the same job, knocking Mario off with no damage,
instead of continuing to `HurtMario`:

```
    LDA.W InvinsibilityTimer                  ; \ Branch if Mario has star
    BNE CODE_02A4B5                           ; /
    LDA.W PlayerRidingYoshi
    BEQ +                                     ; not riding Yoshi -> HurtMario normally
CODE_02A473:
    PHX                                       ; <- patched instruction, at $02A473
    LDX.W CurrentYoshiSlot
    ...
    LDA.B #$02
    STA.B SpriteTableC2-1,X                   ; Yoshi -> scared/run-away state
    STZ.W PlayerRidingYoshi                   ; Mario dismounted
    ...
  + JSL HurtMario
```

Both routines already handle the star case as a simple early return (`BNE`, or
a skip past the whole knock-off sequence). The patches only make that same
early return happen in every case. The `BNE` at `$01F711` becomes a `BRA` that
is always taken, so Yoshi's own collision check always returns before the
knock-off code. The first instruction at `$02A473` (`PHX`) becomes an `RTS`, so
the extended sprite path returns at once instead of running the knock-off
sequence. That path's only other exit (`JSL HurtMario`) is behind the earlier
`BEQ`, which already excludes riding Yoshi. So Mario also takes no damage from
these sprites while he rides Yoshi. This matches the protection that normal
sprites already give to a Yoshi rider. State `$02` (run away) is only written to
`SpriteTableC2` inside these two blocks, which can no longer run. So no contact
with an enemy can scare Yoshi into running away either. The two effects have
one cause and one pair of patches.

**Evidence:** This patches `$01F711` in `CODE_01F70E` (`bank_01.asm`), the
`BNE` opcode byte. This was checked against the built ROM, where
`$01F70E`-`$01F711` has `AD 90 14 D0` (`LDA InvinsibilityTimer` / `BNE +$38`,
which goes to `Return01F74B` at `$01F74B`), as the source says. It also patches
`$02A473` in `CODE_02A473` (`bank_02.asm`), the `PHX` opcode byte. This was
checked against the built ROM, where `$02A469`-`$02A473` has
`AD 90 14 D0 47 AD 7A 18 F0 3B DA` (`LDA InvinsibilityTimer` / `BNE +$47` to
`CODE_02A4B5` / `LDA
PlayerRidingYoshi` / `BEQ +$3B` to the `JSL HurtMario` fallback / `PHX`), as the
source says. The effect comes from the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** You need both codes for full protection. With only `01F711:80`, the
extended sprite path (Bullet Bills, etc.) can still knock Mario off, and the
other way around. This only covers damage from contact. Other ways to lose Yoshi
do not change: the A/X/L/R dismount, the forced P-balloon dismount, falling in a
pit, and finishing or leaving a level. Not tested in play. The effect comes from
the disassembly.

## Mario (and Yoshi, since he shares the same speed) walks and runs much faster, both directions

**Code:** `6627-0F0F` + `5627-0F6F` + `6627-0FAF` + `5627-04DF` + `6627-040F`
+ `5627-046F` + `6627-04AF` + `5627-07DF` (apply all eight together)
**Raw form:** `00D535:88` + `00D536:78` + `00D537:88` + `00D538:78` +
`00D539:88` + `00D53A:78` + `00D53B:88` + `00D53C:78` (address:new-byte —
SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte; the original bytes are
`EC 14 DC 24 DC 24 D0 30`)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 01:12:10

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** Mario's horizontal top speed (`bank_00.asm`, the physics routine
that starts near `CODE_00D6B1`) is a simple system: speed up toward a limit,
then stop speeding up. On every frame that a direction is held, the code picks
a byte in `DATA_00D535`. This is a table of signed-byte speed limits, with one
8-byte row for each `SlopeType` (flat ground is `SlopeType` `$00`, so row 0,
`$00D535`-`$00D53C`). The code stops adding acceleration when the high byte of
`PlayerXSpeed` gets to that limit:

```
DATA_00D535:
    db $EC,$14,$DC,$24,$DC,$24,$D0,$30        ; flat ground (SlopeType 0)
CODE_00D742:
    LDA.B PlayerXSpeed+1
    SEC
    SBC.W DATA_00D535,Y                       ; already at (or past) the limit?
    BEQ CODE_00D76B
    EOR.W DATA_00D535,Y
    BPL CODE_00D76B                           ; yes -> stop speeding up
    ...
    LDA.W MarioAccel_,X                       ; otherwise add this frame's acceleration
    ...
    ADC.B PlayerXSpeed
```

`Y` is made as `SlopeType | (tier * 2) | direction`, and there are four tiers:

| Tier | When | Offsets | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | walking | 0/1 | `$EC`/`$14` = -20/+20 |
| 1 | run button (`Y`/`X`) held | 2/3 | `$DC`/`$24` = -36/+36 |
| 2 | run button held, speed at least `$23` | 4/5 | `$DC`/`$24` = -36/+36 |
| 3 | tier 2 and `PlayerPMeter` full (`$70`) | 6/7 | `$D0`/`$30` = -48/+48 |

Tier 3 comes from `CODE_00D96A`. It fills `PlayerPMeter` while in tier 2,
and when the meter reaches `$70` it does one more `INY`. That is how Mario
gets to his full running speed.

The code sets all eight bytes to `$88`/`$78` (-120/+120). Now every tier has
the same, much higher limit in both directions. So Mario always speeds up
toward 120, whether he walks or runs.

Nothing here checks `PlayerRidingYoshi`. The only use of it in this whole
routine is an unrelated branch for the spin jump sound effect. So Yoshi does not
have his own top speed. When Mario rides Yoshi, Mario's own `PlayerXSpeed` moves
Yoshi on each frame (see the note about `CODE_02A751` and the Yoshi hand-off in
the "ghost house" code elsewhere in this doc for how the two are linked). So the
same table change makes Yoshi with a rider run exactly as much faster as Mario
on foot.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$00D535`-`$00D53C` has `EC 14 DC 24 DC 24 D0 30`,
as the source says. All eight codes decode back to their addresses and bytes.
A headless Mesen run on flat ground in Yoshi's Island 2 logged the high byte of
`PlayerXSpeed`:

| Codes | Walk right | Run right | Run left |
|---|---|---|---|
| None | 21 | 48 | -48 |
| First six only (the old version of this entry) | 121 | 118, then back to 48 | — |
| All eight | 121 | 121 | -96 and still speeding up when Mario hit the left edge of the level |

**Revised 2026-10-01.** This entry used to have only the first six codes. It
said tier 2 was the top tier and that offsets 6/7 were never used. That was
wrong: when the P-meter filled, the limit went back to `$30` and Mario slowed
down to his normal running speed. Walking was fast, but running was not.

**Caveats:** You need all eight codes together. If you leave the pair for one
tier unpatched, Mario slows back down to the old limit as soon as he gets to
that tier. Eight codes is more than a real Game Genie holds, so use an
emulator's cheat list. Only the flat ground row (`SlopeType` `$00`) is patched.
The seven other rows, for slopes of different angles, do not change, so speed
on slopes is normal. This does not change `MarioAccel_`, the table of
acceleration per frame. So it still takes the same time to speed up as before.
Mario just keeps getting faster past the old limit, and reaches 120 in about
80 frames. Not played by hand.

## Yoshi's tongue stays out three times as long

**Code:** `1DEF-A700` + `F6E4-A400` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `01F31D:60` + `01F329:18` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie
codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 01:16:57

**Mechanism:** The state machine for Yoshi's mouth (`bank_01.asm`) controls the
length you see of the tongue with `SpriteMisc151C`, not with
`YoshiTongueTimer`. (That separate counter only starts the catch delay and picks
Mario's riding pose. It is not what keeps the tongue out.) State `1` makes the
tongue 3 longer on each frame until it goes past a limit. Then it waits for a
short time, and state `2` makes it 4 shorter on each frame:

```
CODE_01F314:                                  ; state 1: extending
    LDA.W SpriteMisc151C,X
    CLC
    ADC.B #$03
    STA.W SpriteMisc151C,X
    CMP.B #$20                                ; <- patched immediate, at $01F31D
    BCS +
CODE_01F321:
    ...
    RTS

  + LDA.B #$08                                ; <- patched immediate, at $01F329
    STA.W SpriteMisc1558,X                    ; brief hold at full extension
    INC.W SpriteMisc1594,X                    ; advance to state 2
    BRA CODE_01F321

CODE_01F332:                                  ; state 2: retracting
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1558,X
    BNE CODE_01F321                           ; still holding
    LDA.W SpriteMisc151C,X
    SEC
    SBC.B #$04
    BMI CODE_01F344                           ; fully retracted -> back to idle
    STA.W SpriteMisc151C,X
    BRA CODE_01F321
```

`SpriteMisc1558` (the wait counter) counts down by itself on every frame, in
the shared per-sprite counter block in `CODE_0180D2`. So it is enough to set it
once. If you make the extend limit three times larger (`$20` -> `$60`), state 1
takes three times as many `+3` steps to get past it. State 2 always counts down
from where state 1 stopped, so pulling the tongue back also takes three times as
long. One value controls both halves. If you also make the wait at full length
three times longer (`$08` -> `$18`), that pause in the middle keeps the same 3x
ratio as the rest.

**Evidence:** This patches `$01F31D` in `CODE_01F314` (`bank_01.asm`), the
immediate of `CMP.B #$20`. It also patches `$01F329` in the same routine, the
immediate of `LDA.B #$08` that sets `SpriteMisc1558`. This was checked against
the disassembly source and against the built ROM, where `$01F31D`-`$01F31E` has
`C9 20` and `$01F328`-`$01F329` has `A9 08`, as the source says. The effect
comes from the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** You need both codes together to get 3x for every part. If you
patch only the limit, extending and pulling back take three times as long, but
the wait in the middle stays at its original 8 frames, which is now short in
comparison. This does not change how long Yoshi *holds* what the tongue caught
(that is `YoshiSwallowTimer`, an unrelated timer). It only changes how long the
tongue animation takes to shoot out and pull back. Not tested in play. The
effect comes from the disassembly.

## Bouncing green Koopa Paratroopas bounce twice as high

**Code:** `6E6C-DDA5` + `8A6C-D465` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `018CA3:8F` + `018CAA:BC` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie
codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 01:20:26

**Mechanism:** Sprites `$08` (flying) and `$09` (bouncing) both run
`GreenParaKoopa` (`bank_01.asm`). The source describes this routine as "the two
green para-Koopas, sharing one routine and told apart by a single CMP." The
floor bounce of sprite `$09` is picked at random when the sprite is placed: `high`
(`$B0`, -80) or `low` (`$D0`, -48). This depends on a bit that
`InitGrnBounceKoopa` stores in `SpriteMisc160E`:

```
    JSR SetSomeYSpeed__
    LDA.B #$D0                                ; <- patched immediate, at $018CA3
    LDY.W SpriteMisc160E,X
    BNE +
    LDA.B #$B0                                ; <- patched immediate, at $018CAA
  + STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
```

Bounce height is `v²/(2·gravity)`. So to make the *height* twice as large, you
multiply the start speed by `√2` (≈1.414), not the byte value by 2.
`-80 * √2 ≈ -113.1` rounds to `-113` (`$8F`), and `-48 * √2 ≈ -67.9` rounds to
`-68` (`$BC`). Both bounce types are patched together, so the effect works for
every Koopa, whatever placement bit it started with.

**Evidence:** This patches `$018CA3` and `$018CAA` in `GreenParaKoopa`
(`bank_01.asm`), the immediates of `LDA.B #$D0` and `LDA.B #$B0`. This was
checked against the disassembly source and against the built ROM, where
`$018CA3`-`$018CA4` has `A9 D0` and `$018CAA`-`$018CAB` has `A9 B0`, as the
source says. The effect comes from the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** You need both codes together. Sprite `$09` (the bouncing type) can
start with the high or the low placement bit, depending on the level data. If
you patch only one immediate, the bounce for the other placement does not
change. Sprite `$08` (the flying type) never runs this bounce branch, so it does
not change. The `√2` factor is exact for the physics model (constant gravity,
one push). Nobody has checked that it looks like a clean "twice as high" in real
play. Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## Monty Mole moves much faster, both left and right

**Code:** `1D36-A7A0` + `CD3B-ADD0` + `1D3B-AD00` + `CD3B-AD60` (apply all
four together)
**Raw form:** `01E38F:60` + `01E390:A0` + `01E391:60` + `01E392:A0`
(address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 01:21:40

Tags: `demo-ready` `basic-enemies` `enemy-movement-collection` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** `MontyMole` (`bank_01.asm`) has two different ways to move:
walking on the ground, or hopping along a fixed line. The choice is made when
the sprite is placed, from a bit that `InitMontyMole` stores in
`SpriteMisc151C`. Each way reads its own two-byte speed table (right, left):

```
MontyMoleHopXSpeed:                           ; <- patched, at $01E38F/$01E390
    db $10,$F0                                ; hopper: fixed launch speed

MontyMoleWalkTopSpeed:                        ; <- patched, at $01E391/$01E392
    db $18,$E8                                ; walker: speed eased toward
```

The hopper (`MontyMoleHop`) writes `MontyMoleHopXSpeed` directly to
`SpriteXSpeed` every time it lands. The walker (`MontyMoleChase`) instead moves
`SpriteXSpeed` one `DATA_01EBB4` step per frame toward `MontyMoleWalkTopSpeed`,
and stops speeding up when it matches. So this table sets a top speed, not the
speed itself. Both tables are patched to the same faster right/left pair
(`$18`/`-24` and `$10`/`-16` both become `$60`/`-96`, and `$E8`/`$F0` both
become `$A0`). So the mole moves much faster, whichever of the two behaviors it
was placed with.

**Evidence:** This patches `$01E38F`-`$01E392`, which is `MontyMoleHopXSpeed`
followed directly by `MontyMoleWalkTopSpeed` in `bank_01.asm`. This was checked
against the disassembly source and against the built ROM, where
`$01E38F`-`$01E390` has `10 F0` and `$01E391`-`$01E392` has `18 E8`, as the
source says. The effect comes from the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** You need all four codes together. Which pair is used depends on the
mole's placement bit. If you patch only one table, the other type of movement
does not change. The walker still speeds up *slowly* to this new top speed with
the unchanged `DATA_01EBB4` acceleration table. So it gets up to speed faster in
absolute terms, but not at once. Not tested in play. The effect comes from the
disassembly.

## Shell-less Koopas never retreat into their shells

**Code:** `6D6C-6DD1`
**Raw form:** `018AA0:80` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no
compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 01:22:51

**Mechanism:** Sprites `$00`-`$03` are Koopa Troopas that already had their
shell stomped off. They run a small state machine in `bank_01.asm`. When the
Koopa has hopped over to its dropped shell, `SpriteMisc1558` counts down.
`CODE_018A9B` is the check that runs on the one frame when it gets to `$01`:

```
CODE_018A9B:
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1558,X
    CMP.B #$01
    BNE Spr0to13Main                          ; <- patched, at $018AA0
    LDY.W SpriteMisc1594,X                    ; shell to interact with
    ...
    JSL CheckForContact
    BCC +
    JSR OffScrEraseSprite                     ; erase the walking Koopa
    LDY.W SpriteMisc1594,X
    LDA.B #$10
    STA.W SpriteMisc1558,Y                    ; \ hatch a fresh Koopa back
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; | out of the shell later
    STA.W SpriteMisc160E,Y                    ; /
  + RTS
```

On that one frame, the routine continues on to check for contact with the
shell. If they touch, it erases the Koopa with no shell, and sets the shell to
let the Koopa come back out later. If you change the opcode of the `BNE`
(`$D0`) to `BRA` (`$80`), it always branches to `Spr0to13Main`. So the check for
climbing back in, and everything after it, never runs, whatever value
`SpriteMisc1558` counts down to. The Koopa just keeps walking.

**Evidence:** This patches `$018AA0` in `CODE_018A9B` (`bank_01.asm`), the
opcode of `BNE Spr0to13Main`. This was checked against the disassembly source
and against the built ROM, where `$018AA0`-`$018AA1` has `D0 68`, as the source
says. The effect comes from the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** This only stops the Koopa with no shell from climbing back *into* a
shell that it finds on the ground. It does not change how it pushes or kicks a
stunned or kicked shell (`SpriteMisc1528`/
`SpriteMisc1534`). That code runs earlier in the same state machine and does not
change. Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## Red (walking) Koopas behave like Yellow Winged Koopas

**Code:** `226E-DF01`
**Raw form:** `0188F5:DD` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie codes carry no
compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 18:59:48

**Mechanism:** Sprite `$05` (walking Red Koopa) and sprite `$0C` (Yellow Koopa
with wings) already use exactly the same init routine (`InitStandardSprite`) and
main loop routines (`Spr0to13Start`/`Spr0to13Main`). The only thing that makes
them different at run time is one byte of behavior flags in `Spr0to13Prop`
(`bank_01.asm`), indexed by `SpriteNumber`:

```
Spr0to13Prop:
    db $00,$02,$03,$0D,$40,$42,$43,$45        ; 00-07 shell-less then shelled Koopas: green, red, blue, yellow
                                               ; <- $05 (Red) patched at $0188F5, $42 -> $DD
    db $50,$50,$50,$5C,$DD,$05,$00,$20        ; 08-0F para-Koopas, yellow winged Koopa, Bob-omb, keyhole, Goomba
```

`$42` (Red Koopa's original byte) has bits `$40` (two tiles tall, which every
Koopa with a shell already has because of the shell) and `$02` (turn around at a
ledge). The byte for `$0C`, `$DD`, adds these bits:

- `$01` (fast walk: uses the second, faster pair of `Spr0to13SpeedX` entries).
- `$04` (face Mario: turns toward Mario from time to time, instead of only
  walking back and forth).
- `$08` (jump over a kicked shell instead of walking into it).
- `$80` (flutter: keep animating in the air instead of stopping).

If you write Yellow Winged Koopa's byte over Red Koopa's byte, Red Koopa gets
all of those behaviors at once.

**Evidence:** This patches `$0188F5` in `bank_01.asm`, which is offset `+5` of
`Spr0to13Prop` (sprite `$05`). This was checked against the disassembly source
and against the reference ROM, where `$0188F5` has `42`, as the source says. The
effect comes from the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** **Behavior only, not graphics.** Red Koopas keep their normal red
sprite with no wings, and their normal shell. This code does not make them look
like Yellow Winged Koopas. A separate check in `Spr0to13Gfx` controls the wing
*graphic* (`LDA SpriteNumber,X` / `CMP.B #$08` / `BCC`: no wings if the sprite
number is below `$08`). That check is one shared limit that every sprite with
wings uses (`$08`, `$09`, `$0C`, and others). You cannot add sprite `$05` to
that check with one byte without also breaking it for the sprites that already
pass it. That would remove the wings from the flying and bouncing green Koopa
Paratroopas and from Yellow Winged Koopa itself, so it was left alone on
purpose. If you stomp a patched Red Koopa, you still get a normal red shell (the
shell color code is not related to this byte). Jumping over a kicked shell now
uses the same code path that yellow Koopas use (logic near `CODE_018526`, which
checks bit `$08` of `Spr0to13Prop`). Not tested in play. The effect comes from
the disassembly.

## Every landing shakes the ground like a cape dive-bomb

**Code:** `6D35-A7D7` + `6D3C-AD07` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `00EF7C:80` + `00EFA1:80` (address:new-byte — SNES Game Genie
codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 19:12:17

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** The shockwave of the cape dive-bomb (the screen shakes, and any
nearby enemy on the ground that the cape can kill is killed) is its own
subroutine, `GroundPound` (`bank_02.asm`):

```
GroundPound:
    LDA.B #$30                                ; \ Set ground shake timer
    STA.W ScreenShakeTimer                    ; /
    STZ.W GroundPoundTimer
    ...                                       ; loop over sprite slots $00-$09,
                                               ; kill any grounded, cape-killable
                                               ; sprite via CODE_029404
    RTL
```

Mario's landing handler runs every frame (`bank_00.asm`, right after
`PlayerInAir` is cleared for the frame). It only calls `GroundPound` from deep
inside the cape flight branch:

```
    LDY.W FlightPhase
    BNE CODE_00EF99                           ; <- patched, at $00EF7C
    LDA.W PlayerRidingYoshi                   ; (normal-landing path: Yoshi-
    ...                                       ;  stomp handling, skipped once
    RTS                                       ;  patched)

CODE_00EF99:
    STZ.W SpriteStompCounter
    STZ.W FlightPhase
    CPY.B #$05                                ; FlightPhase >= 5? (deep dive)
    BCS CallGroundPound                       ; <- patched, at $00EFA1
    ...
    RTS

CallGroundPound:
    LDA.B TempPlayerAir                       ; was Mario airborne this frame?
    BEQ +
    JSL GroundPound
    LDA.B #!SFX_KAPOW
    STA.W SPCIO3
  + RTS
```

`FlightPhase` is Mario's cape flight state, and `CPY.B #$05` is the test for "was
this dive fast enough". Normally both must be true (Mario is flying with the
cape, and he is deep into a dive) before `GroundPound` runs. If you change both
branch opcodes (`BNE`→`BRA` at `$00EF7C`, `BCS`→`BRA` at `$00EFA1`, that is
`$D0`→`$80` and `$B0`→`$80`), both are always taken. So every landing gets to
`CallGroundPound`, whatever Mario's powerup or flight state is. `TempPlayerAir`
(a copy of `PlayerInAir` taken each frame before this frame's ground collision
is done) does not change. So the shake still happens only once, on the real
landing frame, not on every frame that Mario stands still.

**Evidence:** This patches `$00EF7C` (the opcode of `BNE CODE_00EF99`) and
`$00EFA1` (the opcode of `BCS CallGroundPound`) in `bank_00.asm`. This was
checked against the disassembly source and against the built ROM, where
`$00EF7C`-`$00EF7D` has `D0 1B` (branches to `$00EF99`, the address of
`CODE_00EF99`) and `$00EFA1`-`$00EFA2` has `B0 0B` (branches to `$00EFAE`, the
address of `CallGroundPound`), as the source says. Both codes keep the original
relative branch distance byte and change only the opcode, so the branch targets
do not change. The effect comes from the disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** You need both codes together. The first (`$00EF7C`) is what lets a
*normal* landing, without flying, get to the dive-bomb logic at all. The second
(`$00EFA1`) then removes the fall speed test ("was this deep into a dive").
Forcing the first branch also always skips the other code path that it
controlled. Yoshi's ability to stomp through blocks (`YoshiStompRoutine`, which
`YoshiCanStomp` turns on after Yoshi eats some shells) no longer happens by
itself on landing, because that logic was on the side of the branch that this
code makes unreachable. The shake radius is what the sprite kill loop in
`GroundPound` already checks (on the ground, can be killed by the cape, sprite
slots `$00`-`$09` only). This code does not change who or what the shockwave
hits, only how often it happens. Not tested in play. The effect comes from the
disassembly.

## Yoshi always spits triple fireballs, no matter what's in his mouth

**Code:** `F5E1-6FD0` + `DDE5-64A0` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `01F264:17` + `01F27B:00` (address:new-byte — SNES Game
Genie codes carry no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-11 19:47:20

**Mechanism:** When you press B while Yoshi has something in his mouth
(`SpriteTableC2==$01`), the spit dispatcher at `CODE_01F1DF` (`bank_01.asm`)
runs. Normally it only shoots the three "Yoshi fireballs" (`CODE_01F27C`, which
creates three `$11` extended sprites with three calls to `CODE_01F295`) when the
item in his mouth is a Koopa with a red shell, or when Yoshi himself is red. For
anything else, it continues to `CODE_01F2DF`, which only spits the item out
again with no change:

```
    LDA.W SpriteNumber,Y
    CMP.B #$0D
    BCS CODE_01F2DF                           ; <- patched, at $01F264
    LDA.W SpriteMisc187B,Y
    BNE CODE_01F27C
    LDA.W SpriteOBJAttribute,Y                ; held item's palette
    AND.B #$0E
    CMP.B #$08                                ; CCC==red?
    BEQ CODE_01F27C
    LDA.W SpriteOBJAttribute,X                ; Yoshi's own palette
    AND.B #$0E
    CMP.B #$08                                ; CCC==red?
    BNE CODE_01F2DF                           ; <- patched, at $01F27B
CODE_01F27C:
    PHX
    TYX
    STZ.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; the held item is destroyed
    ...                                        ;  (not respawned as itself)
    JSR CODE_01F295                           ; x3: spawn the fireball trio
    ...
```

The usual method in this file is to change a branch opcode so that it is always
taken. Here, both branches stay conditional. Instead, their **displacement
byte** is changed so that *every* result goes to `CODE_01F27C`.

- The first test (`BCS CODE_01F2DF` at `$01F263`) skips the fire for anything
  that is not a Koopa: Bob-omb, Goomba, Buzzy Beetle, Spiny, keyhole. Its
  displacement changes from `$7A` to `$17`, so when the branch is taken, it now
  goes to `CODE_01F27C` instead of `CODE_01F2DF`.
- The last test (`BNE CODE_01F2DF` at `$01F27A`) skips the fire when neither the
  item nor Yoshi is red. Its displacement changes from `$63` to `$00`.
  `CODE_01F27C` is the next instruction after this branch, so a branch with zero
  displacement does nothing in practice. Taken or not, the code continues at
  `$01F27C`.

With both targets changed, every path through the dispatcher gets to the fire
branch, whatever Yoshi has in his mouth, whatever color it is, and whatever
color Yoshi is.

**Evidence:** This patches `$01F264` (the displacement byte of `BCS
CODE_01F2DF`) and `$01F27B` (the displacement byte of `BNE CODE_01F2DF`) in
`bank_01.asm`. This was checked against the disassembly source and against the
built ROM, where `$01F263`-`$01F264` has `B0 7A` and `$01F27A`-`$01F27B` has
`D0 63`. Both branches decode to a target of `$01F2DF` (`CODE_01F2DF`: the PC
after the instruction, `$01F265` + `$7A` and `$01F27C` + `$63`), which matches
the source. The new displacements (`$17` and `$00`) were calculated the same
way, and checked again to go to `$01F27C` (`CODE_01F27C`): `$01F265` +
`$17 = $01F27C`, and `$01F27C` + `$00 = $01F27C`. The effect comes from the
disassembly and was not seen in play.

**Caveats:** You need both codes together. With only one, one path (items that
are not Koopas, or items that are not red caught by a Yoshi that is not red) can
still get to the unchanged spit in `CODE_01F2DF`. The item in Yoshi's mouth when
he spits is always destroyed (`STZ.W SpriteStatus,X` inside `CODE_01F27C`), not
shot out as itself. This is now also true for shells and enemies that he used to
spit out normally, so Yoshi can spit only fireballs. The special cases in
`CODE_01F2DF` (changing some sprites to a different thrown form through
`SpriteToSpawn` when bit 6 of `SpriteTweakerE` is set) also can no longer run,
together with the rest of the normal spit path in that routine. This only
changes the dispatcher for spitting from the mouth. Yoshi's fire *breath* when
he stands still with an empty mouth, and the swallow path
(`YoshiSwallowTimer`/`CODE_01F309`), do not change. Not tested in play. The
effect comes from the disassembly.

## Cleared Switch Palaces stay on the map and can be re-entered

**Code:** `5538-0D9F` and `5B38-0DBF` (two codes, both needed)
**Raw form:** `04E5B1:77:85` and `04E5B2:79:86` (address:new-byte:original-byte
— the original byte is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has
no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 16:52:10

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** A Switch Palace uses one Map16 tile on the overworld. The tile is
`$76` or `$78` before the palace is beaten. After it is beaten, it becomes `$77` /
`$79`, through the beaten tile change `DATA_04DA1D` -> `DATA_04DA33` that
`CODE_04ED83` applies.

Then the level clear event destroys the building. `CODE_04E68A` reads the Map16
tile at the event's position and looks for it in `OWCrushTiles`
(`$77,$79,$58,$4C,$A6`). It then writes the matching `OWCrushRubbleTile` byte
over it: `$85` for `$77`, `$86` for `$79`, and `$81` for the three castle and
fortress tiles. `$81`-`$86` are above the range `$56`-`$80` that can be entered,
which `OWPU_NotOnPipe` checks with `CMP #$81 / BEQ / BCS`. That is exactly why
you cannot enter a cleared Switch Palace.

These two codes change the first two `OWCrushRubbleTile` entries, which are the
two for the Switch Palace tiles. So the destroy step writes back `$77` / `$79`,
the *beaten Switch Palace* tile, instead of rubble. The tile that stays is still
a level tile in the range that can be entered, so if you press A/B/X/Y on a
cleared palace, you enter it again. Castles and fortresses do not change. They
are the other three bytes of the same table.

**Evidence:** `OWCrushTiles` and `OWCrushRubbleTile` were read from the
reference ROM at `$04E5A7` and `$04E5B1` as `77 79 58 4C A6` and
`85 86 81 81 81`, which matches the tables with comments in `bank_04.asm`.

Two separate checks show that `$77` / `$79` are the Switch Palace tiles and not
fortresses:

1. `ProcessMessageBox` picks the switch palace message and sets
   `SwitchPalaceColor` for the first four entries of `DATA_05A590`. Their
   translevel numbers are `$14, $45, $3F, $08`. Number the unchanged overworld
   tilemap `OWL1TileData` the way `CODE_04D832` does: go through all `$800`
   Map16 entries and number every tile in `$56`-`$80` in order. This puts those
   four translevels at map positions `$0212`, `$06AC`, `$062A`, `$00D1`, and their
   tiles are `$76`, `$78`, `$78`, `$76`. So all four Switch Palaces are on the two
   tiles that entries 0 and 1 of `OWCrushTiles` cover, and the eleven castles and
   fortresses are the `$58` / `$4C` / `$A6` entries.
2. All four of those map positions are in `DATA_04E5B6`, the destroy routine's
   own list of event positions. So this routine is what removes them.

The level number is kept after the destroy step. `OWLayer1Translevel` is written
in only one place in the whole ROM, `CODE_04D7F2`. `CODE_04DC09` calls it right
after it uses MVN to copy the unchanged `OWL1TileData` from bank `$0C` into
`Map16TilesLow`, and before any event is played again. So the position keeps the
palace's level number, whatever its tile becomes.

Decoded back: `5538-0D9F` decodes to `$04E5B1 <- $77` and `5B38-0DBF` to
`$04E5B2 <- $79`. The effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** seen in
play.

**Caveats:**
- You need both codes for all four palaces. Two are on the `$76`/`$77` tile and
  two are on `$78`/`$79`. Each code alone opens only its own pair again.
- A fifth building uses the `$78`/`$79` tile: the destroy event at map position
  `$0572`, translevel `$36`. `5B38-0DBF` also keeps that one on the map and lets
  you enter it. Which level it is is not known yet.
- The crumble animation and sound still play. Only the tile that stays changes.
  The rubble graphics come from a separate stripe image (`CODE_04EEAA` /
  `DATA_04EE7A`). So the palace looks destroyed for the rest of that visit to the
  map, and is drawn as a palace again when the map is built again.
- If you enter a palace again, you can press the switch again. It is not known
  if the game runs the palace's overworld event again on a second clear, or what
  that would do to `ExitsCompleted`.
- Castles and fortresses still crumble to `$81` and stay locked. The wider
  option is the one code `65BB-04BD` above. It moves the limit in
  `OWPU_NotOnPipe` instead, and opens rubble of every kind again.

## Every sprite counts as already killed, so nothing ever spawns

**Code:** `6DC9-D40C`

**Raw form:** `$02A859` ← `$80` (originally `$D0`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 17:31:00

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** SMW remembers which enemies you have already dealt with in
`SpriteLoadStatus`, a table of 128 bytes at `$7E1938`. It has one flag for each
entry in the level's sprite list, "not just those onscreen". `LoadSprFromLevel`
goes through that list every second frame as the screen edge moves forward, and
it checks the flag just before it creates anything:

```
    LDA.W SpriteLoadStatus,X                  ; \ This table has a flag for every sprite in the level (not just those onscreen)
    BNE LoadNextSprite                        ; / Skip sprite if it's already been loaded/permanently killed
    STX.B _2                                  ; $02 = Number of sprite in level
    INC.W SpriteLoadStatus,X                  ; Mark sprite as loaded
    INY                                       ; Next byte
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr],Y                   ; Byte format: Sprite number
```

The patched byte is the opcode of that `BNE`. `$D0` → `$80` makes it `BRA`, so
the "already been loaded/permanently killed" branch is always taken. Every entry
in the list is handled as a sprite that you have already killed, and the loader
goes on to the next one without ever creating it. The flag itself is not used.
The `LDA` above still runs, but its result no longer decides anything.

Two facts make this a clean change of one byte. First, `LoadSpriteLoopStrt` is
the **only** place in the ROM that reads `SpriteLoadStatus`. All eleven other
references write it. So this one branch makes the whole "has this sprite been
used up?" decision. Second, `LoadNextSprite` is the loop's own step forward
(`INY : INY : INX : BRA LoadSpriteLoopStrt`). It moves forward by exactly one
sprite entry of three bytes. So forcing the branch keeps the scan in step, and
it still stops normally at the `$FF` at the end of the list.

Note where the test is: it runs **before** the sprite number is read. That
`LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr],Y ; Byte format: Sprite number` is three instructions
later. So the test cannot tell an enemy from a platform, and no change of one
byte here can affect only enemies.

**Evidence:** `SpriteLoadStatus $7E1938` comes from `SMW_U.sym` and
`rammap.asm` (`SpriteLoadStatus: skip 128`). `LoadNextSprite $02A846` and
`LoadSprFromLevel $02A7FC` come from `SMW_U.sym`. The reference ROM confirms the
sequence: `$02A856` = `BD 38 19` (`LDA.W SpriteLoadStatus,X`), `$02A859` =
`D0 EB` (`BNE`, and `$02A85B` − `$15` = `$02A846` = `LoadNextSprite`), `$02A85D`
= `FE 38 19` (`INC.W SpriteLoadStatus,X`). `$02A846` = `C8 C8 E8 80`, the
`INY : INY : INX : BRA` step. `grep SpriteLoadStatus` over the disassembly finds
exactly one read (`bank_02.asm:5380`) and eleven writes. The routine runs once
per frame from the chain of sprite routines. It has one caller,
`JSR LoadSprFromLevel` at `$028B1D` (`bank_02.asm:1479`), so it applies in every
level, horizontal and vertical. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** The effect is much wider than enemies. SMW's sprite list has
everything the level places that is not a Map16 block, and the test runs before
the type is known. Things that are lost include:

- the **Goal Point tape** (`$7B`) and the **Goal Point Question Sphere** (`$4A`)
- the **key** (`$80`) and the P-switch (`$3E`)
- both springboards (`$6B`/`$6C`)
- every platform sprite (`$55`–`$68`: checkerboard, flying rock, line-guided,
  turn-block bridges, floating platforms)
- the switch palace switch (`$60`), the growing vine (`$79`), the climbing net
  door (`$54`) and Princess Peach (`$7C`)

**No level can be completed with this code
on**, because every level clear trigger in the game is a sprite. Levels that are
built on line-guided or floating platforms cannot be passed.

The dispatch for the high sprite numbers is also after the test. So shooters
(`$C9`–`$CA`) and generators (`$CB`–`$D9`) never start. The entries `$E7` and up
are not objects at all. They are **Layer 1/2 scroll commands** that feed
`Layer1ScrollCmd`/`Layer1ScrollBits`, and they never run either. Levels that
need a layer scroll trigger will not move.

Only the level's own sprite list is affected. Anything that is created in
another way still appears: powerups and items that come out of blocks, sprites
created by other sprites, extended sprites (fireballs, and so on), and the Yoshi
that the remount routine creates. Map16 blocks, pipes and doors do not change,
so you can still move around a level and between its sublevels. There is just
nothing in it. The address was checked for the U release. The code around it
has no `ver_is_ntsc`-style check, but the other four releases have not been
checked.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The byte was read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offset
`0x12859`. `6DC9-D40C` decodes back to `$02A859 <- $80` with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every level loads the next level's terrain, enemies and enemy graphics together

**Codes:** `D72A-DD21` + `D02A-D4F1` + `D92A-D791` + `D423-D7F1` + `D72E-DD91`
(all five needed)

**Raw form:** `$05D8C3` ← `$03` (originally `$00`), `$05D8C8` ← `$04`
(originally `$01`), `$05D8CD` ← `$05` (originally `$02`), `$05D8EC` ← `$02`
(originally `$00`), `$05D8F1` ← `$03` (originally `$01`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 17:46:22

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** One RAM byte, `SpriteTileset` (`$7E192B`), decides which enemy
graphics a level uploads to VRAM. `UploadSpriteGFX` multiplies it by four and
reads four GFX file numbers from `SPRITEGFXLIST`:

```
UploadSpriteGFX:
    ...
    LDA.W SpriteTileset                       ; $192B = current sprite GFX list index
    ASL A                                     ; \
    ASL A                                     ;  }4A -> Y
    TAY                                       ; /
  - LDA.W SPRITEGFXLIST,Y                     ; |
    STA.B _4,X                                ; |
```

The problem is where `SpriteTileset` comes from, and this is why you cannot
simply make the enemy graphics follow the enemy list. For a normal level, only
one place writes it, and that is the **level header**:

```
    INY                                       ; \Get third byte
    LDA.B [Layer1DataPtr],Y                   ; /
    STA.B _0                                  ; "Push" third byte
    TAX                                       ; "Push" third byte
    AND.B #$0F                                ; \Load sprite set
    STA.W SpriteTileset                       ; /
```

That header is not stored with the sprite data. It is at the **front of the
Layer 1 data**, and it is read through `Layer1DataPtr`, the foreground pointer.
So the sprite tileset goes with Layer 1, not with the sprite list. The only
pointer in the ROM that can be changed to get to the next level's header is the
Layer 1 pointer.

That is what this set does. Three pointer tables, each starting on a page
boundary, control level loading. Each is read one byte at a time through
absolute operands whose low bytes are `$00`/`$01`/`$02`:

```
CODE_05D8B7:
    REP #$30                                  ; AXY->16
    LDA.B _E                                  ; \
    ASL A                                     ; |
    CLC                                       ; |Multiply level number by 3 and store in Y
    ADC.B _E                                  ; |(Each L1/2 pointer table entry is 3 bytes long)
    TAY                                       ; /
    SEP #$20                                  ; A->8
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs,Y                        ; \
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr                       ; |
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs+1,Y                      ; |Load Layer 1 pointer into $65-$67
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr+1                     ; |
    LDA.W Layer1Ptrs+2,Y                      ; |
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr+2                     ; /
```

`Layer1Ptrs` is at `$05E000` and has three-byte entries, so `+3` on all three
operands moves it forward one whole entry. `Ptrs05EC00` is at `$05EC00` and has
two-byte entries, so `+2` on both of its operands does the same. So level *n*
gets these from level *n+1*:

- the Layer 1 data
- the header, and with it the `SpriteTileset`, so `UploadSpriteGFX` uploads
  exactly the enemy graphics that those enemies were drawn for
- the sprite list

Terrain, enemies and enemy graphics all match.

The header carries the foreground/background tileset in the same way (byte 5,
`AND.B #$0F : STA.W ObjectTileset`). So the terrain graphics also match the
terrain, and so do the music, time limit, level mode, screen length and palettes.

**Evidence:** `SpriteTileset $7E192B`, `SPRITEGFXLIST $00A8C3`,
`Layer1Ptrs $05E000` and `Ptrs05EC00 $05EC00` come from `SMW_U.sym`.
`UploadSpriteGFX` is at `bank_00.asm:5343`, and the header parser `CODE_0584E3`
is at `bank_05.asm:547`. `grep SpriteTileset` over the disassembly finds one
writer for normal levels (`bank_05.asm:598`, the header). Every other writer is
a special mode that writes a fixed value: the castle and credits cutscenes
(`GM19LoadCutscene`, `GM1DLoadThankYou`, `GM23PrepEnemyList` in `bank_00.asm`),
the Reznor room (`bank_00.asm:2807`) and the vertical bonus mode
(`bank_04.asm:5664`). The reference ROM confirms every patched operand:
`$05D8C2` = `B9 00 E0`, `$05D8C7` = `B9 01 E0`, `$05D8CC` = `B9 02 E0`,
`$05D8EB` = `B9 00 EC`, `$05D8F0` = `B9 01 EC`.

Going through `Layer1Ptrs` in the reference ROM and reading byte 3 of each
level's header shows how large the problem is that this fixes. Of the 511 pairs
of levels next to each other, 340 (67%) already use the same sprite tileset.
Those are the levels where the enemy change looks right by itself. The other 171
are the ones with broken graphics without these three extra codes. Not tested in
play.

**Caveats:** **Five codes is the most a real Game Genie holds.** With
`DDB8-DD07` (see below) it is six, so on a new save file this set needs an
emulator's cheat list.

- **On a new save file, also turn on `DDB8-DD07`** ("A new game skips the
  intro message and starts on the map"). A new file first loads the intro
  level (`$C5`, the "Welcome! This is Dinosaur Land" message). With this
  set on, that level loads level `$C6`'s data instead, and the game gets
  stuck there, so it never reaches the map. `DDB8-DD07` skips the intro
  level, so the game goes straight to the map. A file that already has a
  save does not need it. Turn `DDB8-DD07` on before file select opens
  (see its own entry).
- Both tables have 512 entries, indexed by a full 16-bit level number. Each
  table ends exactly where the next table starts (the 512 × 3 bytes of
  `Layer1Ptrs` end at `$05E600` = `Layer2Ptrs`, and the 512 × 2 bytes of the
  sprite table end at `$05F000` = `DATA_05F000`). So the level with the highest
  number reads the wrong table for both and loads garbage.
- The **background does not move**. Layer 2 comes from its own pointer table,
  which is still indexed by this level's number. So a level keeps its old sky
  behind the new terrain. In levels that use Layer 2 as solid terrain, that Layer
  2 will conflict with the new foreground.
- Exits do not move either. A level's pipes and doors still go where they always
  did, whatever the new layout is.
- Mario's start position comes from `DATA_05F200`/`DATA_05FE00`, indexed by the
  original level number. So expect to enter some levels inside solid ground, and
  some levels cannot be finished.
- The new level mode can put a horizontal level into a vertical one.
- The sprite list also brings its own `SpriteMemorySetting` and `SpriteBuoyancy`
  (read through `SpriteDataPtr`). This is consistent, because those settings
  belong to the enemies that came with them.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0x2D8C2`-`0x2D8F1`. All five codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Yoshi's House is replaced by the unused "No Yoshi" sign level

**Code:** `033D-A7F0`

**Raw form:** `$05E30C` ← `$4E` (originally `$2D`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 18:24:40

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** SMW keeps six small entrance scenes in bank `$07`. These are the
rooms that play when Mario walks into a castle or ghost house and Yoshi is sent
away. `CODE_05DA38` picks one with an index `X` and reads its Layer 1 pointer
from `PtrsLong05D766`:

```
    LDA.W PtrsLong05D766,Y                    ; Y = X * 3
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr
    LDA.W PtrsLong05D766+1,Y
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr+1
    LDA.W PtrsLong05D766+2,Y
    STA.B Layer1DataPtr+2
```

`X` is picked by comparing the **object tileset** of the level being entered
(header byte 5, low nibble) with a table of six bytes:

```
CODE_05DA24:
    LDX.B #$04
    LDY.B #$04
    LDA.B [Layer1DataPtr],Y                   ; header byte 5
    AND.B #$0F
CODE_05DA2C:
    CMP.L DATA_05D760,X
    BEQ CODE_05DA38
    DEX
    BPL CODE_05DA2C
```

`DATA_05D760` is `05 01 02 06 08 01`. So `X` = 2, the scene named
`NoYoshiEntrance1`, is picked only by a level whose object tileset is `$02`.
**Only one level in the ROM has tileset `$02`: level `$12C`, "Way Cool". And
that level sets the flag that turns the scene off completely.** `CODE_05DA38`
starts with three early exits, and one of them is `DisableNoYoshiIntro`:

```
CODE_05DA38:
    LDA.W SublevelCount
    BNE -
    LDA.W ShowMarioStart
    BNE -
    LDA.W DisableNoYoshiIntro
    BNE -
```

`DisableNoYoshiIntro` comes from `DATA_05F600,Y AND #$80`, indexed by level
number, and `DATA_05F600[$12C]` is `$80`. So the only level that could ever get
to `NoYoshiEntrance1` refuses the scene before it is built. Nothing in the
released game shows it.

The patch makes Yoshi's House load it instead. Level data is found through
`Layer1Ptrs`. Its entry for level `$104` (Yoshi's House) is the
`dl YHLevel104` at `bank_05.asm:8030`, assembled to `$05E30C`. `YHLevel104` is
`$07802D` and `NoYoshiEntrance1` is `$07804E`. They are in the same bank with
the same high byte, so **only the low byte is different**, and one code moves
the pointer: `$2D` → `$4E`.

The 5-byte level header is at the front of the Layer 1 data and is read through
the same pointer. So the scene also brings its own header: its music, object
tileset (`$02`), level mode, palettes and back area color all come with it. This
is what makes the room look like the scene, and not like Yoshi's House with the
scene's tiles.

**Evidence:** `Layer1Ptrs $05E000`, `YHLevel104 $07802D` and
`NoYoshiEntrance1 $07804E` come from `SMW_U.sym`. `bank_05.asm:8030` is
`dl YHLevel104`, and `tools/linemap_U.tsv` puts that line at `$05E30C`. The
reference ROM has `2D 80 07` there (`$05E000 + $104 × 3 = $05E30C`), and
`DATA_05D760` has `05 01 02 06 08 01`. Going through `Layer1Ptrs` for all 512
levels and taking the low nibble of header byte 5 gives a count of the
tilesets: tileset `$02` is used once, at level `$12C`, and
`DATA_05F600[$12C]` = `$80` sets `DisableNoYoshiIntro`. The six scene headers
are `GhostHouseEntrance $078000`, `CastleEntrance1 $07801E`,
`NoYoshiEntrance1 $07804E`, `NoYoshiEntrance2
$07809F`, `NoYoshiEntrance3 $0780B1`, `CastleEntrance2 $078090`. The header of
`NoYoshiEntrance1`, `20 4E 29 11 02`, confirms that its object tileset is `$02`,
the value that only `X` = 2 matches. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **The ending uses this level too.** `GM1DLoadThankYou` loads
`!YoshisHouse` (`$28`, which the loader changes to level `$104`) for the "Thank
You" scene at the end of the game. So that scene also gets the sign room.

The swap is correct but not complete, because only the Layer 1 pointer moves.

- The **background needs no code at all**. `Layer2Ptrs[$104]` is already
  `00 D9 FF`, the same bytes as the entry that the scene itself would use
  (`PtrsLong05D778[2]`). So Yoshi's House and the sign scene use the same
  background.
- The sprites stay the ones from Yoshi's House. `Ptrs05EC00[$104]` does not
  change, so the message boxes, the birds and Yoshi still appear inside the
  scene. In the original game, the scene forces `SpriteDataPtr` to `$07C3EE`.
  Their graphics at least stay correct, because both headers use sprite tileset
  `$09`.
- Mario's start position also stays the one from Yoshi's House, because it comes
  from `DATA_05F200`/`DATA_05FE00` indexed by level number. Both rooms are one
  screen wide (header byte 1 `$20`), so he should land inside the room.
- When the game builds this scene in the normal way, `CODE_05DA38` also forces
  `ScreenMode`, the Layer 1/2 scroll settings and `Layer3Setting`. When it is
  entered as a normal level, none of that happens. So the room may scroll or use
  layers differently than the unused scene would have.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offset
`0x2E30C`. `033D-A7F0` decodes back to `$05E30C <- $4E` with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Yoshi's House is replaced by the orphaned "unused ghost house exit" level

**Code:** `1D3D-A7F0`

**Raw form:** `$05E30C` ← `$60` (originally `$2D`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 19:13:24

**Mechanism:** The foreground data of every level is found through
`Layer1Ptrs`, a table of 512 three-byte pointers at `$05E000`. The entry for
level `$104`, Yoshi's House, is the `dl YHLevel104` at `bank_05.asm:8030`. It is
assembled to `$05E30C` and has `2D 80 07`, the address `$07802D`.

The disassembly puts the game's special level data in bank `$07` page `$80`. So
each of those rooms is at a `$0780xx` address, which is different from Yoshi's
House only in the **low** byte. `UnusedGHExit2Level` is at `$078060`. So if you
write `$60` over that low byte, Yoshi's House points to it. It is one code, with
no carry into the high byte, and nothing else in the table changes.

## Yoshi's House is replaced by the game's blank placeholder level

**Code:** `F63D-A7F0`

**Raw form:** `$05E30C` ← `$18` (originally `$2D`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 19:15:40

**Mechanism:** The foreground data of every level is found through
`Layer1Ptrs`, a table of 512 three-byte pointers at `$05E000`. The entry for
level `$104`, Yoshi's House, is the `dl YHLevel104` at `bank_05.asm:8030`. It is
assembled to `$05E30C` and has `2D 80 07`, the address `$07802D`.

The disassembly puts the game's special level data in bank `$07` page `$80`. So
each of those rooms is at a `$0780xx` address, which is different from Yoshi's
House only in the **low** byte. `EmptyLevel` is at `$078018`. So if you write
`$18` over that low byte, Yoshi's House points to it. It is one code, with no
carry into the high byte, and nothing else in the table changes.

`EmptyLevel` is six bytes long: a five-byte header and then one `$FF`. That
`$FF` is the loader's end-of-data marker. It is tested as soon as the header has
been read:

```
    LDY.B #$00                                ; \
    LDA.B [Layer1DataPtr],Y                   ; |
    CMP.B #$FF                                ; |If level isn't empty, load the level.
    BEQ +                                     ; |
    JSR LoadLevelData                         ; /
```

`CODE_0584E3` reads the five header bytes and then moves `Layer1DataPtr` past
them ("Level data comes right after the header"). So byte 0 of the object data
is that `$FF`, and `LoadLevelData` is skipped completely. The result is a level
that loads its settings and then has nothing in it at all. It is the game's own
blank placeholder, and the simplest way to see what Yoshi's House looks like
with every object removed.

The header still loads, so the room brings its own: one screen wide, level mode
`$0F`, object tileset `$05`, music track index 4, foreground palette 4,
background palette 6, back area color 3, and no time limit.

**Evidence:** `Layer1Ptrs $05E000`, `YHLevel104 $07802D` and `EmptyLevel $078018`
come from `SMW_U.sym`. `bank_05.asm:8030` is `dl YHLevel104`, and
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` puts that line at `$05E30C` (`$05E000 + $104 × 3`). The
reference ROM has `2D 80 07` there, and `$078018` has `C0 6F 49 04 05 FF`: the
five header bytes and the end marker, with `CastleEntrance1` starting right
after at `$07801E`. Decoded: screens `($C0 & $1F) + 1 = 1`, mode
`$6F & $1F = $0F`, object tileset `$05 & $0F = $05`, sprite tileset `$49 & $0F =
$09`, music `($49 >> 4) & $07 = 4`, time index `$04 >> 6 = 0` → `TimerTable[0]` =
`$00`. The empty level test is in `LoadAgain` (`bank_05.asm:430`). A check
against the reference ROM shows that the only pointer in the game to `$078018`
is `PtrsLong05D778[0]`. There it is used as a *Layer 2* pointer for one of the
entrance scenes. No level's Layer 1 pointer uses it. Not tested in play.

**Caveats:** **The ending uses this level slot too.** `GM1DLoadThankYou` loads
`!YoshisHouse` (`$28`, which the loader changes to level `$104`) for the "Thank
You" scene at the end of the game. So that scene also gets this room.

Only the Layer 1 pointer moves, so the room is not as empty as its name says.
`Layer2Ptrs[$104]` does not change, so the background image of Yoshi's House
(`00 D9 FF`, the bank-`$FF` background flag that points into bank `$0C`) is
still drawn behind the empty room. `Ptrs05EC00[$104]` does not change either, so
the sprites of Yoshi's House (the message boxes, the birds, Yoshi) still appear,
floating in an empty room. Their graphics at least stay correct, because this
header uses sprite tileset `$09`, the same value as Yoshi's House. **There is no
floor.** With no object data, nothing is solid anywhere. So Mario starts at the
entry position of Yoshi's House (from `DATA_05F200`/`DATA_05FE00`, indexed by
level number, so it does not change) and falls straight out of the level.
Expect to lose a life every time you enter, with no way to look around.

`0x2E30C`. `F63D-A7F0` decodes back to `$05E30C <- $18` with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

entered as a normal level, none of that happens. `Layer2Ptrs[$104]` does not
change, so the background image of Yoshi's House (`00 D9 FF`) is drawn instead
of the scene's background. `Ptrs05EC00[$104]` does not change, so the sprites of
Yoshi's House (the message boxes, the birds, Yoshi) appear inside the scene.
Their graphics do stay correct, because this header uses sprite tileset `$09`,
the same value as Yoshi's House. Mario's start position also stays the one from
Yoshi's House, from `DATA_05F200`/`DATA_05FE00`. Both rooms are one screen wide,
so he should land inside the room. The room is a background for a cutscene, so
it has no exit. Expect to need a reset or a death to leave, and there is no
timer to run out.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offset
`0x2E30C`. `8F3D-A7F0` decodes back to `$05E30C <- $B1` with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

## Every level is populated with the previous level's enemies

**Codes:** `E323-D7F1` + `EE2E-DD91` (both needed)

**Raw form:** `$05D8EC` ← `$FE` (originally `$00`), `$05D8F1` ← `$FF`
(originally `$01`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 22:44:01

**Mechanism:** After the level loader has found the level's graphics pointers,
it indexes a separate table of two-byte sprite data pointers that starts on a
page boundary. Then it reads the sprite header through the pointer it just
built:

```
    REP #$20                                  ; A->16
    LDA.B _E                                  ; \
    ASL A                                     ; |Multiply level number by 2 and store in Y
    TAY                                       ; / (Each sprite pointer table entry is 2 bytes long)
    LDA.W #$0000
    SEP #$20                                  ; A->8
    LDA.W Ptrs05EC00,Y                        ; \
    STA.B SpriteDataPtr                       ; |Store location of sprite level Y in $CE-$CF
    LDA.W Ptrs05EC00+1,Y                      ; |
    STA.B SpriteDataPtr+1                     ; /
    LDA.B #$07                                ; \ Set highest byte to x07
    STA.B SpriteDataPtr+2                     ; / (All sprite data is stored in bank 07)
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr]                     ; \ Get first byte of sprite data (header)
    AND.B #$3F                                ; |Get level's sprite memory
    STA.W SpriteMemorySetting                 ; / Store in $1692
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr]                     ; \ Get first byte of sprite data (header) again
    AND.B #$C0                                ; |Get level's sprite buoyancy settings
    STA.W SpriteBuoyancy                      ; / Store in $190E
```

`Ptrs05EC00` is `$05EC00`, a page boundary, so the low bytes of the two
absolute operands are `$00` and `$01`. Entries are two bytes, so if you subtract
`2` from both operands, the read moves one whole entry *back*. Level *n* gets the
enemy list of level *n-1*. `$00 - 2` and `$01 - 2` are `$FE` and `$FF`, so the
subtraction borrows from the byte that the codes write. That is exactly why this
works with two codes: the operands become `$ECFE` and `$ECFF`, and the high byte
`$EC` stays the same in both. The loader now indexes from the base address
`$05EBFE`, two bytes below the table.

It needs two codes, not three, because the sprite pointer is only 16 bits wide.
The bank byte is the constant `$07` loaded just below, because all sprite data is
in bank `$07`. Nothing else about the level changes: the terrain, the
background, the level header (and with it the music, timer and palettes), the
exits and Mario's start position all stay this level's own. The "level number"
that is indexed is the internal one that the game builds just above this code
(the translevel number, `+$100` when you are on a submap). It is not the number
shown on the overworld map.

**Evidence:** `Ptrs05EC00 $05EC00` comes from `SMW_U.sym`, and the label is
defined at `bank_05.asm:8797`. The reference ROM confirms both operands:
`$05D8EB` = `B9 00 EC` and `$05D8F0` = `B9 01 EC`, which is
`LDA.W Ptrs05EC00+k,Y` for k = 0, 1. These two reads (`bank_05.asm:7342` and
`:7344`) are the only references to `Ptrs05EC00` in the whole disassembly, so
nothing else in the ROM is affected. Not tested in play.

The two bytes that the moved base now reads for the level with the lowest number
were also read from the reference ROM. `$05EBFE`/`$05EBFF` = `DF FF`. This is
the end of the last entry of the Layer 2 pointer table (`Layer2Ptrs` is
`$05E600`, 512 three-byte entries, so entry `$1FF` is at `$05EBFD`–`$05EBFF` and
has `59 DF FF`). So level `$000` builds `SpriteDataPtr` = `$07FFDF`. That
address is in the padding at the end of bank `$07`. The last byte of real data
in the bank is at `$07FC8F`, and `$07FC90`–`$07FFFF` is 880 bytes of `$FF`
(`%insert_empty($370, …)` at the end of `bank_07.asm`, `$370` = 880 for the U
release). `$FF` is the sprite list's own end marker, so the list ends before it
starts.

**Caveats:** **Level `$000` gets no enemies at all.** As shown above, its moved
pointer goes into the `$FF` padding of bank `$07`. So the loader reads a header
byte of `$FF` and then finds the end marker at once. `SpriteMemorySetting`
becomes `$3F` (`$FF AND #$3F`), `SpriteBuoyancy` becomes `$C0` (`$FF AND #$C0`),
and the level creates nothing. This is a read out of range by design, but it
gives an empty list and not garbage: no crash, and no random sprites.

The change also moves the *header* byte that the loader reads through the same
pointer. That is the `LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr]` pair above, which gives
`SpriteMemorySetting` and `SpriteBuoyancy`. So the level also gets the sprite
memory and buoyancy settings of the other level. This is consistent and not a
glitch: the enemy list and the settings it needs go together. The terrain does
not change, so expect enemies inside walls or floating over holes. Also expect
swimming enemies flopping around a dry level wherever the new buoyancy setting
says water. Boss rooms and other levels with short or empty sprite lists exist,
so the level after one of those will be almost empty. Enemy *graphics* are not
changed either. The sprite tileset comes from the level's own 5-byte header, so
borrowed enemies whose tileset does not match the level will be drawn as broken
tiles.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0x2D8EC` and `0x2D8F1`. Both codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`: `E323-D7F1` → `$05D8EC <- $FE`, `EE2E-DD91` →
`$05D8F1 <- $FF`.

## Each enemy spawns several copies, and comes back after you kill it

**Code:** `B3C9-D70C`

**Raw form:** `$02A85D` ← `$9E` (originally `$FE`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 232301

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated` `challenge`

**Mechanism:** This is the opposite of "Every sprite counts as already killed,
so nothing ever spawns" above. It uses the same three lines of
`LoadSprFromLevel`, forced the other way. SMW keeps one flag for each entry in
the level's sprite list in `SpriteLoadStatus` (`$7E1938`, 128 bytes). That one
bit has two meanings: *"this entry is already on screen"* and *"this entry has
been used up and must not come back"*. The loader sets it as soon as it decides
to create something:

```
    LDA.W SpriteLoadStatus,X                  ; \ This table has a flag for every sprite in the level (not just those onscreen)
    BNE LoadNextSprite                        ; / Skip sprite if it's already been loaded/permanently killed
    STX.B _2                                  ; $02 = Number of sprite in level
    INC.W SpriteLoadStatus,X                  ; Mark sprite as loaded
    INY                                       ; Next byte
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr],Y                   ; Byte format: Sprite number
```

The patched byte is the opcode of that `INC`. `$FE` is `INC abs,X`, and `$9E` is
`STZ abs,X`. Both are three bytes long, and both take the same `$1938` operand.
So the instruction still uses exactly `SpriteLoadStatus,X`. It just writes zero
instead of adding one. The line becomes `STZ.W SpriteLoadStatus,X`, which is
the disassembly's own way to write "Allow sprite to be reloaded by level loading
routine" (that exact comment is at four other places in the ROM).

The write does not change the value that is already there. The code only gets
to this line when the `BNE` above was not taken, which means the flag was
`$00`. So the patch does not clear anything that was set. It stops the flag from
*ever* being set. Then the "already been loaded/permanently killed" test in
`LoadSpriteLoopStrt` is never true for any entry. Every sprite that the level
places can always be loaded, however many times it has already been loaded or
killed.

Two things happen because of this, and both are the purpose of the code.

First, **death stops being permanent.** Nothing in the ROM writes a "killed"
mark anywhere else. An enemy stays dead only because its loaded flag was not
cleared when it went away. (`OffScrEraseSprite` clears it only for sprites whose
status is still `>= $08`, that is, sprites that left the screen alive.) If the
flag is never set at all, that difference is gone. A stomped Goomba, a Koopa
killed by a shell, an enemy that was spin-jumped into smoke, and a dead enemy
that fell off the bottom of the screen are all loaded again the next time the
loader's scan gets to their column, the same as an enemy you never touched.

Second, **the same entry can load several times at once.** `LoadSprFromLevel`
runs every second frame. It creates any list entry whose 16-pixel column matches
the scroll edge `$00`/`$01` that it just calculated from `Layer1XPos`. That edge
only moves when the camera crosses a 16-pixel line. So one column stays selected
for several loader passes in a row: about three at a full run, more when you
move slower, and *forever* if the camera stops while a sprite's column is
selected. Normally the loaded flag turns all of those passes into one spawn.
Without it, each pass creates another copy. So enemies come in groups, and a
camera that does not move turns one list entry into a fountain.

It limits itself and does not crash. The slot search at `CODE_02A918` goes
through the range for the level's sprite memory setting. When it finds no free
slot, it goes to `CODE_02A936`, which does `STZ.W SpriteLoadStatus,X` and
returns. The patch does not change that path. The loader just stops making
copies when the sprite table is full, and starts again when slots become free.

**Evidence:** `SpriteLoadStatus $7E1938` comes from `SMW_U.sym` and
`rammap.asm` (`SpriteLoadStatus: skip 128`). `LoadSprFromLevel $02A7FC` and
`LoadNextSprite $02A846` come from `SMW_U.sym`. The reference ROM confirms the
instruction and the ones around it: `$02A856` = `BD 38 19` (`LDA.W
SpriteLoadStatus,X`), `$02A859` = `D0 EB` (`BNE`, which goes to `$02A846` =
`LoadNextSprite`), `$02A85B` = `86 02` (`STX.B _2`), `$02A85D` = `FE 38 19`
(`INC.W SpriteLoadStatus,X`), `$02A860` = `C8` (`INY`), `$02A861` = `B7`
(`LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr],Y`). So `$FE` → `$9E` replaces a three-byte instruction
with a three-byte instruction, and the two bytes after the opcode keep their
meaning. Nothing after it moves.

The change is also safe for the flags. `INC` sets N and Z from the result, and
`STZ` changes no flags at all. In both cases, the next instruction is the `INY`
at `$02A860`, which sets N and Z itself. The first branch after that
(`BCC CODE_02A88C`) reads carry from the `CMP.B #$E7` two lines later. No branch
in between depends on what the `INC` left.

`grep SpriteLoadStatus` over the disassembly finds exactly one read
(`bank_02.asm:5380`, the `BNE` test) and eleven writes. So nothing else uses
this flag, and turning off the one write that sets it cannot confuse anything
else. The effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Alternative bytes**, all the same effect:

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `B3C9-D70C` | `02A85D:9E` (orig `$FE`) | `INC` becomes `STZ`: the flag is cleared instead of set |
| `82C9-D70C` | `02A85D:BD` | `INC` becomes `LDA.W SpriteLoadStatus,X`: the flag is read and not used, instead of written. A is loaded again three instructions later, so the read does no harm |
| `DDC9-D46C` | `02A85A:00` | does not change the `INC`, and turns off the test instead: the displacement of the `BNE` becomes `$00`, so the branch goes to the next instruction, and nothing uses the flag, even though it is still set |

The third one is the exact opposite of the code in the other entry. `6DC9-D40C`
changes that same `BNE` into `BRA` so it is always taken. `DDC9-D46C` changes its
displacement so that taking it changes nothing.

**Caveats:** Expect **several copies of the same enemy**, not a clean
one-for-one respawn. The worst case is standing still where the scroll edge is
on a column with sprites. Copies keep coming every second frame until the sprite
