table is full. The table then has no room, so other sprites nearby will not load
while the pile-up lasts. Using many slots also causes the usual SNES sprite
flicker and slowdown.

The test that this code defeats runs **before** the sprite number is read. So,
like the other entry, it cannot tell an enemy from anything else the level
places. Everything in the sprite list loads again: platforms (`$55`–`$68`),
springboards, the P-switch, the key, the goal tape and the Goal Point Question
Sphere, the growing vine, the climbing net door. Copies of moving platforms
cause the most problems, because two copies of a line-guided or floating
platform can be on the same guide. Items that are placed as sprites (dragon
coins, 1-up mushrooms, powerups) also load again. So you can collect them again
after you scroll away and come back. Nobody has checked if a dragon coin that is
collected again counts a second time toward the 1-up for five coins.

Sprite numbers `$E7` and up are not objects. They are Layer 1/2 scroll commands,
and they load again too. The scroll handler has a guard: it only runs when
`Layer1ScrollCmd` and `Layer2ScrollCmd` are both zero, so it cannot stack. But
it can be set again and run again as soon as the previous scroll ends. So a
level built on a triggered layer scroll may repeat that scroll while the camera
stays on the trigger column.

Shooters (`$C9`–`$CA`) and generators (`$CB`–`$D9`) do not change in kind. Their
own handlers already clear this flag on purpose (`STZ.W SpriteLoadStatus,X` at
`$02A8BB`, `STA.W SpriteLoadStatus,Y` at `$02AB9B`), so they could always load
again. Respawning applies only to the level's own sprite list. Sprites that come
from somewhere else (items from blocks, sprites created by other sprites,
extended sprites, the Yoshi that the remount routine creates) never had a list
entry, and they do not change.

A killed enemy comes back when the loader's edge gets to its column again. In
practice, this means you scroll far enough away and come back. In a level where
the camera never takes you back through, nothing seems to respawn. The address
was checked for the U release. The code around it has no `ver_is_ntsc`-style
check, but the other four releases have not been checked.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The byte was read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offset
`0x1285D`. All three codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`: `B3C9-D70C` → `$02A85D <- $9E`, `82C9-D70C` →
`$02A85D <- $BD`, `DDC9-D46C` → `$02A85A <- $00`.

## Killing an enemy no longer keeps it away — it reloads like one you never touched

**Code:** `DDCB-DD65`

**Raw form:** `$01AC92` ← `$00` (originally `$08`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 232750

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** Nothing in SMW writes a "this enemy is dead for good" mark
anywhere. An enemy stays gone because something is *not* done. The routine that
erases a sprite when it leaves the screen clears that sprite's
`SpriteLoadStatus` entry. That is the level list flag that `LoadSprFromLevel`
checks before it creates anything. But it only clears it if the sprite was still
alive when it left. If you kill it first, the clear is skipped, the flag stays
set, and the loader never uses that list entry again. All of "death is
permanent" is one compare:

```
OffScrEraseSprite:
    ...
  + LDA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; \ If sprite status < 8, permanently erase sprite
    CMP.B #$08                                ; |
    BCC +                                     ; /
    LDY.W SpriteLoadIndex,X                   ; \ Branch if should permanently erase sprite
    CPY.B #$FF                                ; |
    BEQ +                                     ; /
    LDA.B #$00                                ; \ Allow sprite to be reloaded by level loading routine
    STA.W SpriteLoadStatus,Y                  ; /
  + STZ.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; Erase sprite
```

Sprite statuses `$08` and up are the living ones (`$08` normal, `$09` stunned,
`$0A` kicked, `$0B` carried). Everything below is a dead sprite at some stage of
being removed. The patched byte is the operand of the `CMP`. `$08` → `$00` makes
it `CMP #$00`, which sets carry for every possible value. So the `BCC` is never
taken, and the clear runs for *every* sprite that this routine erases, dead or
alive. A killed enemy is now marked as able to load again, the same as one that
only scrolled away, and the loader creates it again the next time you come back
through.

This is the gentle version of "Each enemy spawns several copies, and comes back
after you kill it" above. That code stops the flag from ever being set. This
brings enemies back, but it also lets the loader create the same list entry
several times. This code keeps the flag's other job ("this entry is already on
screen, don't spawn it twice") completely, and removes only the special case
for dead sprites. The result is a simple one-for-one respawn with no copies. A
level that you go back through gets its enemies back the way it had them the
first time.

One code covers every kill in the game, even though there are three identical
copies of this routine (`OffScrEraseSprite` in bank `$01`, `OffScrEraseSprBnk2`
at `$02D07A`, `OffScrEraseSprBnk3` at `$03B8AC`, one for each bank of sprite
code). The reason is that the sprite's own main routine does not handle death at
all. The status dispatch table of `HandleSprite` is in bank `$01` and runs for
every sprite, whatever bank its main routine is in. The handlers for dead states
that it picks use the bank `$01` copy:

- status `$02` (killed by a shell, a fireball, a star, a thrown block) is
  `HandleSprKilled`. It calls `SubOffscreen0Bnk1` on every frame while the dead
  sprite falls, and gets to `OffScrEraseSprite` when it falls off the bottom;
- status `$04` (spin-jumped, or any sprite whose "disappears in puff of smoke"
  tweaker is set) is `HandleSprSpinJump`. When its timer ends, it does
  `JSR OffScrEraseSprite` directly. The disassembly's own comment there is
  "Permanently kill the sprite";
- status `$05` gets to the same `SpinJumpEraseSpr` in the same way.

The copies in bank `$02` and bank `$03` only ever get living sprites, which
already take the clear path now. So patching them would change nothing.

**Evidence:** `OffScrEraseSprite $01AC80` comes from `SMW_U.sym`. The routine
is at `bank_01.asm:6329`. The reference ROM confirms the sequence byte for byte:
`$01AC8E` = `BD C8 14 C9 08 90 0C BC 1A 16 C0 FF F0 05 A9 00 99 38 19 9E C8 14`,
which is `LDA.W SpriteStatus,X` / `CMP.B #$08` / `BCC +$0C` (which goes to
`$01ACA1`, the `STZ.W SpriteStatus,X`) / `LDY.W SpriteLoadIndex,X` /
`CPY.B #$FF` / `BEQ` / `LDA.B #$00` / `STA.W SpriteLoadStatus,Y`. The patched
byte is the `$08` at `$01AC92`.

The `CPY.B #$FF` guard two instructions later does not change and still does its
job. `EraseSprite` sets `SpriteLoadIndex` to `$FF` for anything that has no
level list entry. Those sprites still skip the write, so the patch cannot write
outside the table.

`tools/callsites.py --callers OffScrEraseSprite` lists six direct call sites in
addition to the offscreen path: `InitBanzai` (`$01838D`), `ADDR_018468`
(`$018468`), `CODE_018A9B` (`$018AC9`), `SpinJumpEraseSpr` (`$019A77`),
`CODE_019FC4` (`$019FC7`) and `CODE_01C1C8` (`$01C1C8`). Every one of them
except `SpinJumpEraseSpr` is a living sprite that erases itself (a Banzai Bill
that appeared on the wrong side of Mario, a second Lakitu that removes itself, a
P-Balloon whose time ran out). So its status is `$08`, and it already took the
clear path before this patch. The code only changes behavior for statuses below
`$08`. The effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `DDCB-DD65` | `01AC92:00` (orig `$08`) | the compare can never fail, so every erased sprite is marked as able to load again |
| `DDCB-DFD5` | `01AC94:00` (orig `$0C`) | same effect in a different way: the displacement of the `BCC` becomes `$00`, so taking the branch goes to the next instruction and skips nothing |
| `EECB-DD65` | `01AC92:FF` | **the opposite**: `CMP #$FF` fails for every real status, so the clear *never* runs, and even enemies that you walked past without hurting are gone for good when they scroll off |
| `EE25-D766` | `02D07E:FF` | the same reversal in `OffScrEraseSprBnk2`, for sprites whose code is in bank `$02` |
| `EE88-DDD3` | `03B8B0:FF` | the same reversal in `OffScrEraseSprBnk3`, for sprites whose code is in bank `$03` |

The last three go together. Living sprites are erased by the copy that their own
bank uses, so "every sprite you have seen is gone forever" needs all three. The
respawn code needs only the bank `$01` one.

**Caveats:** One kind of death is **not** covered. Enemies with tweaker bit
`$20` set in `SpriteTweakerA` ("dies when jumped on") are flattened into status
`$03` instead. `HandleSprSmushed` frees their slot with only
`STZ.W SpriteStatus,X` when the squash timer ends. It never uses
`OffScrEraseSprite`, so their flag is never cleared, and they stay dead. Reading
`Sprite1656Vals` (`bank_07.asm:736`) for that bit gives the full list: the four
Koopas with no shell (`$00`–`$03`), the Sliding Koopa without a shell (`$BD`),
the Para-Goomba (`$3F`), the Para-Bomb (`$40`), the Dino Torch (`$6F`) and the
feather Super Koopa (`$73`). Sprites `$04`–`$10` (the Koopas with shells and
wings) are also flattened and not killed, but only when they are stomped while
`FlightPhase` is not zero, that is, during cape flight. Everything else in the
game dies through a status that is covered.

Respawning does not happen at once. It happens when the scan edge of
`LoadSprFromLevel` gets to the entry's 16-pixel column again. In practice, this
means you scroll far enough away and come back. A level where the camera never
comes back will not look any different.

Items do not change, which is probably what you want. A powerup that Mario takes
is freed by `STZ.W SpriteStatus,X` in the collision handler itself
(`bank_01.asm:9775`), not by the offscreen erase. So eaten mushrooms and
collected coins do not come back. What does come back, in addition to enemies,
is anything in the level's sprite list that you can *destroy*: a throw block
that was thrown and broken, a Bob-omb that exploded, a shell kicked off the
screen.

Sprite slots are freed normally, and no entry is ever created twice at the same
time. So this code does not itself fill the sprite table or cause flicker or
slowdown. A screen that gets its enemies back is exactly as busy as it was the
first time. The address was checked for the U release. The code around it has
no `ver_is_ntsc`-style check, but the other four releases have not been checked.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0xAC92`, `0xAC94`, `0x1507E` and `0x1B8B0` (all four have `$08`, `$0C`, `$08`,
`$08`, as stated). All five codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`: `DDCB-DD65` → `$01AC92 <- $00`, `DDCB-DFD5` →
`$01AC94 <- $00`, `EECB-DD65` → `$01AC92 <- $FF`, `EE25-D766` →
`$02D07E <- $FF`, `EE88-DDD3` → `$03B8B0 <- $FF`.

## No enemy can be stomped — every sprite in the game behaves like a Spiny

**Code:** `DDCA-D701`

**Raw form:** `$01A8CD` ← `$00` (originally `$10`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 233421

Tags: `challenge`

**Mechanism:** One bit for each sprite decides if Mario can stand on its head:
`SpriteTweakerA` bit `$10`, "can be jumped on". The routine for contact between
the player and a sprite reads it when Mario comes down on something:

```
CODE_01A8C9:
    LDA.W SpriteTweakerA,X                    ; \ Branch if can be jumped on
    AND.B #$10                                ; |
    BNE CODE_01A91C                           ; /
    LDA.W SpinJumpFlag
    ORA.W PlayerRidingYoshi
    BEQ CODE_01A8E6
CODE_01A8D8:
    LDA.B #!SFX_SPLAT
    STA.W SPCIO0                              ; / Play sound effect
    JSL BoostMarioSpeed
    JSL DisplayContactGfx
    RTS
```

The patched byte is the mask of the `AND`. `$10` → `$00` leaves A at zero,
whatever the sprite's tweaker says. So the `BNE` is never taken, and nothing
ever gets to `CODE_01A91C`. That is the whole stomp result, where an enemy is
flattened, killed, turned onto its back or changed into a shell. Every sprite in
the game now says "cannot be jumped on".

This is not a new state that the game must handle. It is the state that Spinies
are already in. Reading `Sprite1656Vals` (`bank_07.asm:736`) for bit `$10` shows
that only **48 of the 201 sprites** can be stomped at all. The Spiny (`$13`), the
Chargin' Chuck family (`$91`–`$98`, `$46`), Rex (`$AB`), every Piranha Plant
(`$1A`, `$2A`, `$4F`, `$50`) and the Koopa Kids (`$29`) already have the bit
clear. What happens when you land on one of those is exactly what will now
happen on every enemy: the path above when the branch is not taken. So the code
does not make new behavior. It uses a behavior that already exists for all
sprites.

Note what that path does, because it is not just "nothing". If Mario is
spin-jumping or riding Yoshi, the code gets to `CODE_01A8D8`. The splat sound
plays, `BoostMarioSpeed` bounces him back up, and `DisplayContactGfx` draws the
contact puff. This is a harmless bounce off an enemy that takes no damage. If
not, it goes to `CODE_01A8E6`, the damage path, and **the enemy hurts Mario
instead**. Landing on a Goomba now costs a powerup, the same as walking into it.

**Evidence:** `SpriteTweakerA $7E1656` comes from `rammap.asm`
(`SpriteTweakerA: skip 12`). `LoadSpriteTables` (`bank_07.asm:990`) loads it for
each sprite from `Sprite1656Vals`. The reference ROM confirms the instruction:
`$01A8C9` = `BD 56 16 29 10 D0 4C`, which is `LDA.W SpriteTweakerA,X` /
`AND.B #$10` / `BNE` with displacement `$4C`, and `$01A8D0 + $4C = $01A91C =
CODE_01A91C`, the stomp handler. The patched byte is the `$10` at `$01A8CD`.

Bit `$10` is read in exactly two places, and the code can only get to one of
them at a time. `CODE_01A87E` (`bank_01.asm:5766`) tests the sprite's status
first. `$09`, stunned, goes to `CODE_01AA42` and returns, and everything else
continues to the stomp test patched here. The read of the bit in `CODE_01AA42`
(`bank_01.asm:6011`) only decides if spin-jumping onto an *already stunned*
sprite kills it, and this code does not change that read. The effect comes from
the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `DDCA-D701` | `01A8CD:00` (orig `$10`) | the mask is empty, so no sprite can be jumped on |
| `DDCA-D7A1` | `01A8CF:00` (orig `$4C`) | same effect in a different way: the displacement of the `BNE` becomes `$00`, so even when the bit is set, the branch goes to the next instruction and the stomp handler is skipped |
| `DDC2-0DD1` + `DDC3-0F61` | `01A9D0:00` (orig `$20`) + `01A9E6:00` (orig `$80`) | **the gentle version**: stomping still works and still bounces Mario safely, but it cannot kill. The "dies when jumped on" test and the "falls off the screen when killed" test both fail, so every stomped enemy is only stunned on its back, ready to be picked up or kicked |

The gentle pair matches "immune to *death* by stomping" more closely, and it
needs both codes. `$01A9D0` blocks the death where the enemy is flattened
(status `$03`), and `$01A9E6` blocks the death where it is knocked off the
screen (status `$02`). This leaves `CODE_01AA01`, which sets status `$09`,
stunned. Sprites whose tweaker says they change when stomped (Koopas that turn
into shells) take that branch earlier, and neither code affects them.

**Caveats:** With the main code, **jumping on an enemy hurts you**. So this
makes the game harder. It is not a way to keep enemies around. Small Mario dies.
Levels where you must kill a specific enemy from above, or use an enemy's head
as a platform, cannot be passed. Note that Yoshi still attacks normally. He eats
enemies with his tongue, which is a completely separate interaction, and riding
him turns the landing into the harmless bounce above.

Carrying still works. A stunned sprite (status `$09`, which is the status of a
loose shell, a throw block, a P-switch and the key) goes to `CODE_01AA42` one
branch before this test and never gets to it. So picking those up, kicking them
and spin-jumping on them do not change. Springboards and note blocks are Map16
blocks or have their own contact code. Mario rides line-guided and floating
platforms through the clipping code for sprites and Mario, not through this
branch. None of those are affected.

Sprites that already cannot be stomped do not change. Nothing that kills enemies
in another way changes either: fireballs, cape spins, thrown shells, star power,
Yoshi and falling off the screen all still work. The address was checked for
the U release. The code around it has no `ver_is_ntsc`-style check, but the
other four releases have not been checked.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0xA8CD`, `0xA8CF`, `0xA9D0` and `0xA9E6` (they have `$10`, `$4C`, `$20`,
`$80`). All four codes decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`:
`DDCA-D701` → `$01A8CD <- $00`, `DDCA-D7A1` → `$01A8CF <- $00`, `DDC2-0DD1` →
`$01A9D0 <- $00`, `DDC3-0F61` → `$01A9E6 <- $00`.

## Fireballs bounce off every enemy — nothing can be killed with fire

**Code:** `CBCE-DD06`

**Raw form:** `$02A0F1` ← `$A9` (originally `$29`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 233639

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** Fire immunity is one bit for each sprite, `SpriteTweakerC` bit
`$10`. For each active fireball, `ProcessFireball` goes through sprite slots
`$09` down to `$00`. When it has confirmed that a fireball touches a sprite, it
checks if fire works on that sprite:

```
  + LDA.W SpriteTweakerC,X                    ; \ Skip sprite if fire killing is disabled
    AND.B #$10                                ; |
    BNE FireRtNextSprite                      ; /
    LDA.W SpriteTweakerF,X                    ; \ Branch if takes 1 fireball to kill
    AND.B #$08                                ; |
    BEQ TurnSpriteToCoin                      ; /
```

The patched byte is the **opcode** of the `AND`, not its operand. `$29` is
`AND #const` and `$A9` is `LDA #const`. Both have the same two-byte immediate
form, with the same `$10` byte after it. So nothing moves, and the instruction
becomes `LDA #$10`. A is now loaded with `$10` directly, instead of being masked
from the sprite's real tweaker. So it is never zero, the `BNE` is always taken,
and every sprite in the game says "fire killing is disabled". The two results
below the branch can no longer run: `TurnSpriteToCoin`, the normal fireball kill
that changes an enemy into a moving coin (sprite `$21`), and the Chargin' Chuck
path that counts hits in `SpriteMisc1528` and kills him on the fifth.

The check comes *after* the collision test, and after the call to
`CODE_02A045`, which plays the bonk sound and removes the fireball. So the
fireball still acts normally on contact: it makes its sound and disappears. It
just does nothing to what it hit.

**Evidence:** `SpriteTweakerC $7E166E` comes from `rammap.asm`
(`SpriteTweakerC: skip 12`). `bank_01.asm:3331` shows that bit `$10` is the fire
flag and bit `$20` is the cape flag. There, a sprite that is kicked turns *both*
off at once with one `ORA.B #$30`, under the comment "Disable fireball/cape
killing". The fire check here reads `$10`, and the two cape checks
(`GroundPound` at `bank_02.asm:2761` and `CODE_0293AE` at `:2621`) read `$20`.

The reference ROM confirms the instruction and the ones around it: `$02A0EE` =
`BD 6E 16 29 10 D0 4E`, which is `LDA.W SpriteTweakerC,X` / `AND.B #$10` / `BNE`
with displacement `$4E`, which goes to `FireRtNextSprite`. The patched byte is
the `$29` at `$02A0F1`. `$29` and `$A9` are both two-byte immediate opcodes. So
the `$10` after it stays an operand and does not become an instruction, and the
`BNE` after it keeps its address. Neither instruction changes memory, X or Y.
The only flags that either sets are N and Z, which are exactly what the `BNE`
uses. The effect comes from the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `CBCE-DD06` | `02A0F1:A9` (orig `$29`) | `AND #$10` becomes `LDA #$10`: every sprite says it is immune to fire |
| `6DCE-DDA6` | `02A0F3:80` (orig `$D0`) | same effect one instruction later: the `BNE` becomes `BRA`, so the fireball always skips to the next sprite, whatever the flag says |

**Caveats:** Fire is only one of Mario's weapons, and only this one path is
closed. Stomping, cape spins, thrown shells, star power, Yoshi and being knocked
off the screen all still kill normally. Enemies that were already immune to fire
do not change. **Bosses and set pieces that must be beaten with fireballs cannot
be beaten at all.** Check before you use it in a castle.

This covers Mario's fireball *and* Yoshi's. `ProcessFireball` handles extended
sprite `$05` (Mario's) and `$11` (the fireball that Yoshi spits after he eats a
red shell). The routine tells them apart a few lines above, only to decide if it
runs `CODE_02A045`. Both then continue to the patched check, so a Yoshi that
breathes fire also loses his attack. Enemy fireballs do not change. They hurt
Mario through a completely different routine and never check this bit.

The loop covers sprite slots `$09` down to `$00`, so fire could never kill
sprites in slots `$0A` and `$0B`. That is the original behavior, and this code
does not change it. The opposite code, which lets fire kill more enemies, is
the next entry. The address was checked for the U release. The
code around it has no `ver_is_ntsc`-style check, but the other four releases
have not been checked.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0x120F1`, `0x120F2` and `0x120F3` (they have `$29`, `$10`, `$D0`). All three
codes decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`: `CBCE-DD06` →
`$02A0F1 <- $A9`, `6DCE-DDA6` → `$02A0F3 <- $80`, `DDCE-DD66` →
`$02A0F2 <- $00`.

## Fireballs kill more enemy types

**Code:** `DDCE-DD66`

**Raw form:** `$02A0F2` ← `$00` (originally `$10`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 233639

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** This is the opposite of the previous entry, and it patches the
same check in `ProcessFireball`. The byte is the operand of `AND.B #$10`, the
mask for the fire flag in `SpriteTweakerC`. With `$00`, the result is always
zero, so the `BNE FireRtNextSprite` is never taken. Every sprite that a fireball
touches then goes on to the kill code, even when its `SpriteTweakerC` bit `$10`
says fire does not work on it. Most of them become a moving coin through
`TurnSpriteToCoin`.

Chargin' Chucks still take five fireballs. The next test, `SpriteTweakerF` bit
`$08`, comes after the patched one and is not changed. It sends Chucks to the
hit counter in `SpriteMisc1528`, which kills them on the fifth hit.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `$02A0EE` = `BD 6E 16 29 10 D0 4E`, which is
`LDA.W SpriteTweakerC,X` / `AND.B #$10` / `BNE`. The patched byte is the `$10`
at `$02A0F2`. It is an operand, so no instruction moves. The effect comes from
the disassembly. It was **not** tested in play.

**Caveats:** The guard on `SpriteTweakerD` bit `$02` ("invincible to
fire/cape/etc") at the top of the loop still works. So scenery and platforms do
not turn into coins. But the code does apply to sprites that the designers made
immune for a reason, so expect odd results.

Like the previous entry, this covers Mario's fireballs and the ones that Yoshi
spits after he eats a red shell. Sprites in slots `$0A` and `$0B` still cannot
be killed by fire, because the loop never reaches them.

## The cape spin passes through every enemy without hurting it

**Code:** `CBBA-AD06`

**Raw form:** `$0293C1` ← `$A9` (originally `$29`)

**Recorded:** 2026-08-21 233745

**Mechanism:** Cape immunity is next to fire immunity in the same tweaker byte:
`SpriteTweakerC` bit `$20`, "can't be killed by cape". When Mario swings the
cape, `CODE_00D044` sets `CapeInteracts` and fills in
`CapeInteractionXPos`/`CapeInteractionYPos` with the collision box of the swing.
`CODE_0294F5` is called once per frame from the chain of sprite routines
(`bank_02.asm:1478`). It sees that flag and runs the sprite loop at
`CODE_0293AE` every second frame. That loop checks if the cape works on each
sprite before it tests the boxes at all:

```
    LDA.W SpriteTweakerC,X
    AND.B #$20
    ORA.W SpriteOnYoshiTongue,X
    ORA.W SpriteMisc154C,X
    ORA.W SpriteMisc1FE2,X
    BNE CODE_0293F7
```

The patched byte is the **opcode** of the `AND`. `$29` is `AND #const`, and
`$A9` is `LDA #const`. Both have the same two-byte immediate form, and the `$20`
after it stays an operand, so the line becomes `LDA #$20`. A is loaded with `$20`
directly, instead of being masked from the sprite's real tweaker. The three
`ORA`s can only keep it non-zero, so the `BNE` always takes the skip. Every
sprite in the game says "can't be killed by cape". The clipping test below never
runs, and this path never calls `CODE_029404`, the routine that knocks a sprite
over and sets its status to `$02`, killed.

Nothing about swinging the cape changes. The animation, the timing and the
`CapeInteracts` flag all come before this test and do not change. The swing just
passes through enemies now.

**Evidence:** `SpriteTweakerC $7E166E` comes from `rammap.asm`
(`SpriteTweakerC: skip 12`). `CapeInteracts $7E13E8` comes from `rammap.asm`.
`CODE_00D044` (`bank_00.asm:9372`) writes it together with the cape's collision
coordinates, and this is what connects this loop to the cape. `bank_01.asm:3331`
shows that bit `$20` is the cape flag and bit `$10` is the fire flag. There, a
kicked sprite turns both off at once with `ORA.B #$30`, under the comment
"Disable fireball/cape killing". The two cape checks (here and `GroundPound` at
`bank_02.asm:2761`) use `$20`, and the fire check (`bank_02.asm:4417`) uses
`$10`.

The reference ROM confirms the instruction and everything that the patch must
not change: `$0293BE` = `BD 6E 16 29 20 1D D0 15 1D 4C 15 1D E2 1F D0 29`, which
is `LDA.W SpriteTweakerC,X` / `AND.B #$20` / `ORA.W SpriteOnYoshiTongue,X` /
`ORA.W SpriteMisc154C,X` / `ORA.W SpriteMisc1FE2,X` / `BNE` with displacement
`$29`. The patched byte is the `$29` opcode at `$0293C1`. `$A9` is also a
two-byte immediate opcode, so the `$20` stays an operand, and the three `ORA`s
and the `BNE` keep their addresses. `LDA` changes no memory and no index
register, and only N and Z, which is what the `BNE` five instructions later uses.
The `ORA`s set those flags again anyway. The effect comes from the disassembly.
It was **not** tested in play.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `CBBA-AD06` | `0293C1:A9` (orig `$29`) | `AND #$20` becomes `LDA #$20`: every sprite says it is immune to the cape |
| `6DBA-A7D6` | `0293CC:80` (orig `$D0`) | same effect at the branch: the `BNE` becomes `BRA`, so the loop always skips to the next sprite |
| `CBB2-D7AB` | `0294DF:A9` (orig `$29`) | the partner code for the **dive-bomb**: `GroundPound` has its own copy of this test, so add this code to make the cape harmless in the air *and* on landing |
| `DDBA-AD66` | `0293C2:00` (orig `$20`) | **the opposite**: the mask is empty, so the test always fails, and the cape spin kills sprites that are normally immune to it |

**Caveats:** The dive-bomb is a separate move with a separate copy of the check,
and the main code does **not** cover it. When Mario lands from a cape dive,
`GroundPound` (`bank_02.asm:2746`) runs its own loop over sprite slots
`$09`–`$00`, reads the same bit at `$0294DF`, and calls the same `CODE_029404`
to kill what it finds. Use `CBB2-D7AB` as well if you want the cape to be fully
harmless.

One other routine also uses the loop that this code patches. `CODE_029398` runs
the **quake sprite**. That is the short shock that a bumped block leaves behind.
It is kept in the four bounce sprite slots as `QuakeSpriteNumber`, and
`BounceSpriteIntTimer` counts down the time it can interact. It enters the same
`CODE_0293AE` with `$0E` cleared, instead of set to `CapeInteracts`. The two
paths only become different *after* the patched test (`LDA.B _E : BEQ
CODE_0293EB`, which picks a different clipping routine). So this code also stops
a quake from flipping enemies: hitting a block under a Koopa will no longer knock
it over. It is the same bit doing the same job in both cases, not a side effect.
But it affects more than just the cape.

Everything else still kills: stomps, fireballs, thrown shells, star power, Yoshi
and falling off the screen. Sprites that are already immune to the cape do not
change. A sprite that has been kicked is immune to the cape anyway.
`bank_01.asm:3331` sets both immunity bits on a kicked sprite. That is the
original behavior, and this code does not change it. The cape's other uses
(flying, the slow fall, blocking projectiles) do not go through this loop and
still work. The address was checked for the U release. The code around it has
no `ver_is_ntsc`-style check, but the other four releases have not been checked.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets
`0x113C1`, `0x113C2`, `0x113CC` and `0x114DF` (they have `$29`, `$20`, `$D0`,
`$29`). All four codes decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`:
`CBBA-AD06` → `$0293C1 <- $A9`, `6DBA-A7D6` → `$0293CC <- $80`, `CBB2-D7AB` →
`$0294DF <- $A9`, `DDBA-AD66` → `$0293C2 <- $00`.

## Enemies face away from Mario instead of toward him

**Code:** `7DC7-0765`

**Raw form:** `$01AD3E` ← `$30` (originally `$10`)

**Recorded:** 2026-09-11 230425

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** This code patches `SubHorizPos`. Not one byte of `FaceMario`
changes. `FaceMario` is only the caller that the effect was aimed at, and it is
one of 37 routines that use the result.

`SubHorizPos` is the game's basic "which side of me is Mario on" routine, and
it returns the answer in `Y`:

```
SubHorizPos:
    LDY.B #$00
    LDA.B PlayerXPosNow
    SEC
    SBC.B SpriteXPosLow,X
    STA.B _F
    LDA.B PlayerXPosNow+1
    SBC.W SpriteXPosHigh,X
    BPL +                 ; $01AD3E: 10 01
    INY
  + RTS
```

The 16-bit subtraction is *Mario minus sprite*. So a positive result means Mario
is to the **right**, and `Y` stays 0. A negative result takes the `INY`, and `Y`
becomes 1. If you change the `BPL` (`$10`) to `BMI` (`$30`), this is reversed:
Mario on the right now gives `Y` = 1, and Mario on the left gives 0.

`FaceMario`, the shared "turn toward the player" helper, uses that result to set
the facing when a sprite appears. It is four instructions. It only copies the
answer into `SpriteMisc157C`, the sprite's facing byte, which is also the index
that every walk speed table in the game reads:

```
FaceMario:
    JSR SubHorizPos
    TYA
    STA.W SpriteMisc157C,X
Return018583:
    RTS
```

So with the test reversed, every sprite that is initialized through `FaceMario`
appears facing **away** from Mario and walks off in that direction.

You cannot make the patch in `FaceMario` itself, with this code or with any
number of codes. To reverse it there, you must insert `EOR #$01` between the
`TYA` and the `STA`. The game uses that longer form in other places, for example
`JSR SubHorizPos : TYA : EOR #$01 : STA SpriteMisc157C,Y` in `GeneralResetSpr`,
under the comment "Make Shelless Koopa face away from Mario". That makes the
routine 10 bytes. `FaceMario` uses 8, `$01857C`–`$018583`, and `InitBowsersFire`
starts right after it at `$018584`. Game Genie codes replace bytes and cannot
insert them. No change of one byte helps either. The `TYA` (`$98`) would have to
become an opcode that puts `Y EOR 1` into `A`, and the 65816 has no implied
instruction for that. Changing the `JSR` operand or the `STA` changes where the
value comes from or where it goes, not what it is.

**Evidence:** `$01AD3E` was found with `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_01.asm`
line 6432, the `BPL +` in `SubHorizPos`). It was read back from the ROM with
`memory({op:'readCart', romPath:'comparison_U.smc', platform:'snes',
cpuAddress:0x01AD30})`: `A0 00 A5 D1 38 F5 E4 85 0F A5 D2 FD E0 14 10 01 C8 60`,
that is `LDY #$00` / `LDA $D1` / `SEC` / `SBC $E4,X` / `STA $0F` / `LDA $D2` /
`SBC $14E0,X` / `BPL +1` / `INY` / `RTS`. This matches the source instruction by
instruction, and puts the `$10` at `$01AD3E`. The bytes of `FaceMario` at
`$01857C` are `20 30 AD 98 9D 7C 15 60`. This confirms the `JSR` target, and that
the routine is the eight bytes shown above. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `DDC7-07A5` | `01AD3F:00` (orig `$01`) | the branch displacement becomes zero, so `BPL` always continues into the `INY`: `Y` is always 1, and every sprite always faces **left**, wherever Mario is |
| `3CC0-0DD5` | `01AD40:EA` (orig `$C8`) | the `INY` becomes `NOP`, so `Y` is always 0: the opposite of the code above, every sprite always faces **right** |

**Caveats:** The patch is in `SubHorizPos`, so what it affects depends on the
**37 call sites** of that routine in bank 01. `FaceMario` is only one of them.
There is no way to limit it to only the sprites of `FaceMario`. The other 36 ask
the same question for their own reasons, so the change goes far beyond the
facing when sprites appear. `InitBanzai`, `InitSpikeTop`, `InitBulletBill`,
`InitFish`, `InitHorzNetKoopa`, `InitEerie`, `ChangePiranhaState`,
`MontyMoleWait`, `PlatformKoopaKids`, `YoshiEgg`, `ProcessInteract`,
`GeneralResetSpr` (twice) and two dozen sprite routines with no names all call
it.

If a caller is affected depends on **which of the two outputs it reads**.
`SubHorizPos` returns the side in `Y` *and* the low byte of the distance in
`$0F`, and this code only changes `Y`. Callers that use `$0F` do not change.
`ProcessInteract` does `JSR SubHorizPos : LDA $0F : CLC : ADC #$50 : CMP #$A0 :
BCS` as a distance test, and `MontyMoleWait` does the same with `#$60`/`#$C0`.
So contact detection and the Monty Mole's jump range still work normally.
Callers that index a table with `Y` do change. `CODE_01A847` reads
`DATA_01A839,Y` for the X speed of a sprite that was just killed. So enemies
killed by a star or a shell will now fly off the other way.

Three call sites reverse the result **back**, because they already apply
`EOR #$01` to it themselves.

- Two are the `GeneralResetSpr` paths. One is the Koopa with no shell that runs
  away from Mario on purpose after its shell is knocked off. The other sets a
  Koopa's speed from `DATA_0197AD,Y` and then stores the reversed facing.
- The third is `InitSpikeTop`. It does `TYA : EOR #$01 : ASL A` four times and
  gives the result, `$00`/`$10`, to `CODE_01841D`. There it becomes
  `SpriteMisc151C` and picks the Spike Top's starting crawl direction from
  `DATA_0183EF`/`DATA_0183F0`.

With this code, all three become "face toward Mario", the exact opposite of
everything else. A Koopa knocked out of its shell will now run *at* you, and
Spike Tops start crawling toward you.

Note also that `FaceMario` runs more often than its direct calls show.
`InitStandardSprite` is right above it and **continues** into it. So all 18
sprites whose init dispatch entry is `InitStandardSprite` also run it. This is in
addition to the 12 sprites that are dispatched to `FaceMario` directly (`21`
moving coin, `30`/`32` Dry Bones, `31` Bony Beetle, `51` Ninji, `90` large green
gas bubble, `AB` Rex, `B4` grinder, `BF` Mega Mole, `C2` Blurp, `C3`
Porcu-Puffer, `C5` Big Boo Boss), the 15 routines that `JSR`/`JMP` to it, and
five that get to it with `BRA` (`InitSuperKoopa`, `InitPokey`, `InitBomb`,
`InitBubbleSpr`, `InitBowsersFire`).

It works with the Super Koopa code `1D64-07D9` in the way you would expect. That
code removes the call to `FaceMario` from `InitSuperKoopa` completely. So the
Super Koopas with capes are not affected by this code, while everything else is
reversed.

The address was checked for the U release. The code around it has no
`ver_is_ntsc`-style check, but the other four releases have not been checked.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The byte was read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offset `0xAD3E`
(it has `$10`). The call site counts come from `tools/callsites.py --callers
SubHorizPos` (37 sites) and `--callers FaceMario` (20 sites), plus the five
`BRA FaceMario` sites that the tool does not index, and the `dw` rows in the
dispatch table of `CallSpriteInit`. All three codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`: `7DC7-0765` → `$01AD3E <- $30`, `DDC7-07A5` →
`$01AD3F <- $00`, `3CC0-0DD5` → `$01AD40 <- $EA`.

## Sprites behave like a Chargin' Chuck (or another enemy)

**Codes:** `CB6A-0F69` + `BF6A-0FA9`

**Raw form:** `$0185C6` ← `$A9` (originally `$B5`), `$0185C7` ← `$91`
(originally `$9E`)

**Recorded:** 2026-09-11 235825

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start`

**Mechanism:** `CallSpriteMain` is the start code of three instructions that
every sprite in the game runs once per frame. The second instruction is what
decides what each sprite is:

```
CallSpriteMain:
    STZ.W SpriteXMovement                     ; $0185C3: 9C 91 14
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; $0185C6: B5 9E
    JSL ExecutePtr                            ; $0185C8: 22 DF 86 00

    dw ShellessKoopas                         ; 00 - Green Koopa, no shell
    dw ShellessKoopas                         ; 01 - Red Koopa, no shell
    ...                                       ; 201 rows, $00-$C8
```

`ExecutePtr` (`bank_00.asm:847`) pulls the caller's return address from the
stack, and uses the `dw` rows after the `JSL` as its jump table. It indexes that
table with the value in `A`. So `LDA.B SpriteNumber,X` ("load the sprite number
of slot X") is the one place where a sprite becomes itself.

The first code replaces that load with a constant. `B5 9E` is `LDA $9E,X` and
`A9 9E` is `LDA #$9E`. Sprite code runs with the accumulator in 8-bit mode, so
both are exactly two bytes. The change fits exactly, and no second code is needed
to handle a change in length. Every sprite now gives `ExecutePtr` the same index,
and every sprite runs the same main routine.

The second code is the operand, which picks *which* routine. `$91` is a
Chargin' Chuck. So with the pair above, every Rex, Banzai Bill, Koopa, coin
block and platform in the level runs `Chucks`. See the caveats for how each
sprite enters the Chuck's state machine. Any value `$00`–`$C8` works. See the
table below. For example, `$35` (`796A-0FA9`) is Green Yoshi, and the whole
level fills with dinosaurs you can ride.

There is one limit to state. The code cannot break it, but a value that you
change by hand could. The dispatch table has 201 rows, and `ExecutePtr` masks
its index with `#$00FF` with no range check. So `$C9`–`$FF` would read a pointer
from the opcodes of `InvisSolid_Dinos`, which is assembled right after the last
row at `$01871D`. Keep the value of the second code at `$C8` or below.

**Selector codes.** These are sprites picked from the ones that the Yoshi's
Island levels really contain:

| Second code | Value | Every sprite becomes | Handler |
|------|-------|----------------------|---------|
| `DF6A-0FA9` | `$01` | a Koopa whose shell has been stomped off | `ShellessKoopas` |
| `D96A-0FA9` | `$05` | a Red Koopa Troopa | `Spr0to13Start` |
| `4A6A-0FA9` | `$2C` | a Yoshi egg | `YoshiEgg` |
| `796A-0FA9` | `$35` | a Green Yoshi | `Yoshi` |
| `026A-0FA9` | `$4D` | a ground-dwelling Monty Mole | `MontyMole` |
| `0E6A-0FA9` | `$4F` | a Jumping Piranha Plant | `JumpingPiranha` |
| `596A-0FA9` | `$75` | a Fire Flower | `FireFlower` |
| `556A-0FA9` | `$77` | a Feather | `Feather` |
| `586A-0FA9` | `$7B` | a Goal Point tape | `GoalTape` |
| `6C6A-0FA9` | `$8A` | a bird from Yoshi's house | `YoshisHouseBirds` |
| `686A-0FA9` | `$8B` | a puff of smoke from Yoshi's house | `YoshisHouseSmoke` |
| `BF6A-0FA9` | `$91` | a Chargin' Chuck — *see caveats* | `Chucks` |
| `BE6A-0FA9` | `$9F` | **not** a Banzai Bill — *see caveats* | `BanzaiBnCGrayPlat` |
| `C86A-0FA9` | `$AB` | **not** a Rex — *see caveats* | `Bank3SprHandler` |
| `8B6A-0FA9` | `$B9` | **not** an Info Box — *see caveats* | `Bank3SprHandler` |

Use `$7B` if you want something other than chaos. Every sprite becomes goal
tape, so touching anything at all ends the level.

**Evidence:** `$0185C3` was found with `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_01.asm` line
936). It was read back from the ROM with `memory({op:'readCart',
romPath:'comparison_U.smc', platform:'snes', cpuAddress:0x0185C3})`:
`9C 91 14 B5 9E 22 DF 86 00 04 89 04 89 04 89 04 89 FC 8A ...`, that is
`STZ $1491` / `LDA $9E,X` / `JSL $0086DF` / `dw $8904` ×4 / `dw $8AFC`. This
matches the source instruction by instruction. It puts the `$B5` at `$0185C6`
and the `$9E` at `$0185C7`, and confirms that the table starts at `$0185CC`, with
`ShellessKoopas` = `$018904` in rows `$00`–`$03`. The 402-byte table read from
`$0185CC` ends at `$01871C` and has 104 different handlers. Both codes decode
back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`: `CB6A-0F69` → `$0185C6 <- $A9`,
`BF6A-0FA9` → `$0185C7 <- $91`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was
not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** Three of the fifteen selectors above do not do what their name
says. The reason is the same for each: **the code changes what the dispatch
reads, not what is in RAM.** `SpriteNumber` does not change. So any handler that
reads the sprite number a second time still sees the real one.

- `$9F` **Banzai Bill** does not work. Its row points to `BanzaiBnCGrayPlat`.
  The Ball and Chain (`$9E`) and the gray platform on a chain (`$A3`) also use
  that routine. It starts with `PHB : PHK : PLB : LDA SpriteNumber,X : CMP #$9F`
  (`bank_02.asm:11756`). The compare is against the sprite's own number, which
  will not be `$9F`. So everything goes to `CODE_02D62A`, the ball and chain
  path. You get a level full of balls and chains, which is also what `$9E` and
  `$A3` give you.
- `$AB` **Rex** and `$B9` **Info Box** do not work, for a bigger version of the
  same reason. Both rows point to `Bank3SprHandler`, a jump of two instructions
  into `Bnk3CallSprMain` (`bank_03.asm:4427`). That is a chain of 36 `CMP`s
  against `SpriteNumber,X` that picks out `RexMainRt`, `InfoBox`, `MegaMole`,
  `Swooper` and the rest. Every one of those compares uses the real number. So a
  sprite only gets Rex's behavior if it was already a Rex. Anything that matches
  nothing in the chain goes past the end into
  `JSL CODE_03DFCC : JSR CODE_03A279 : JSR CODE_03B43C`. That is the handler of
  sprite `$A0`, the Bowser scene activator, the only `Bank3SprHandler` sprite
  that the chain does not name. That routine writes `BowserPalette` from
  `Mode7XScale`, and the game cannot survive it as the main routine for each
  sprite. Expect the level to fall apart.
- `$91` **Chargin' Chuck** works, but not in a predictable way. `ChucksMain`
  does not read the sprite number. The eight types of Chuck are told apart by
  `SpriteTableC2`, which is both the state and the type. It is dispatched
  through a second `ExecutePtr` over 13 rows (`$00` looking around … `$0C`
  Whistlin' Chuck, whistling). For a real Chuck, its init set that byte. For
  anything else, it has whatever that sprite uses `SpriteTableC2` for. So each
  sprite enters the Chuck state machine in a random state. A sprite with `$0D` or
  more there goes past the end of that 13-row table. This is the one selector in
  the list that can crash by itself.

Remember the general form of that rule for any value you pick. About a dozen
main routines in the game are **shared** by several sprite numbers, and read
`SpriteNumber,X` again to tell them apart. The selectors in the table that do
this show it in their results, and do not fail completely:

- `$4D`/`$4E` **Monty Mole** share `MontyMole`. It does `CMP #$4E` to choose the
  ledge behavior, and `CMP #$4D` in `MontyMoleDrawBuried` to choose the dirt
  puff animation. So both selector values give the same results for every sprite
  that is not itself a mole.
- `$4F`/`$50` **Jumping Piranha Plant** share `JumpingPiranha`. It does
  `LDY SpriteNumber,X : CPY #$50` to decide if it spits fire. It is the same
  here: the fire depends on the real number, so neither selector value gives it.
- `$00`–`$03` **shell-less Koopas** share `ShellessKoopas`. It reads the number
  again two times: once for `CMP #$02`, to give the blue one a different jump
  speed, and once to record which color of shell to climb back into.

Two results apply to every selector value, including the ones that work well:

**Sprites keep their own appearance.** The shared graphics helpers
`SubSprGfx0Entry1`, `SubSprGfx1`, `SubSprGfx1Hlpr1` and `SubSprGfx2Entry1` all
do `LDY SpriteNumber,X`, and index `SprTilemapOffset,Y` and the palette tables
with it. So a Rex that runs Yoshi's main routine is still drawn from Rex's
tilemap with Rex's palette. The level behaves the same everywhere, but looks as
varied as it always did. That is most of the fun.

**Nothing is re-initialised.** `CallSpriteInit` is a *separate* dispatch table
at `$018179`, and this code does not change it. Every sprite is still set up as
its original type. So the new main routine reads misc bytes that were filled in
for something else. `Spr0to13Start` (`$05`, Red Koopa) shows this most clearly.
It does `LDY SpriteNumber,X : LDA Spr0to13Prop,Y` for the walk speed, and
`Spr0to13Prop` is twenty bytes that cover only `$00`–`$13`. If it gets a sprite
with a number of `$14` or more, it reads past the end of the table into the
opcode bytes of `ShellessKoopas`, and walks at whatever speed those bytes give.
Its graphics path does a limited version of the same thing on purpose.
`Spr0to13Gfx` does `LDA SpriteNumber,X : CMP #$08 : BCC + : JSR KoopaWingGfxRt`.
So with this selector, every sprite with a number of `$08` or more is drawn
**with Koopa wings attached**.

Like the sprite status codes, this is one of the codes in the list that makes
glitches on purpose. The interesting results are the ones where a sprite that is
only half set up does something the game never meant to happen. You cannot have
the swap without them.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets `0x85C6`
(it has `$B5`) and `0x85C7` (it has `$9E`). The places that dispatch again were
found by searching the whole cart for `B5 9E` (`LDA $9E,X`, 121 matches) and
`B4 9E` (`LDY $9E,X`, 21 matches) with `memory({op:'readCart', findHex:...})`,
and mapping every match back through the line map to the routine that contains
it. All sixteen codes decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every enemy in the level flies, and the only things left wingless are the Koopas

**Codes:** `CB6A-0F69` + `D96A-0FA9` + `6D63-AF01`

**Raw form:** `$0185C6` ← `$A9` (originally `$B5`), `$0185C7` ← `$05`
(originally `$9E`), `$018BE5` ← `$80` (originally `$D0`)

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 001757

**Mechanism:** The wings of a para-Koopa are not part of its tilemap. They are an
overlay of four tiles that `KoopaWingGfxRt` (`$019E28`) draws on top of the
sprite that was just drawn. `tools/callsites.py --callers KoopaWingGfxRt` finds
**exactly one call site** in the whole ROM. It is at the end of `Spr0to13Gfx`,
the draw routine that the twenty basic sprites share:

```
    JSR SubSprGfx1                            ; Draw sprite
    ...
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; \ Add wings if sprite number > #$08
    CMP.B #$08                                ; | $018C0C: C9 08
    BCC +                                     ; | $018C0E: 90 03
    JSR KoopaWingGfxRt                        ; / $018C10: 20 28 9E
```

No code runs into `KoopaWingGfxRt` from above either. The bytes above it are its
own data tables. So **no enemy outside the Koopa family can be given wings while
being left otherwise alone.** The only way to send another sprite past that
`JSR` is the `CallSpriteMain` override. That changes what the sprite *is*, as
well as how it looks. These three codes accept that cost.

The first two codes are the override. `CB6A-0F69` changes the
`LDA SpriteNumber,X` at `$0185C6` in `CallSpriteMain` to `LDA #imm`, and
`D96A-0FA9` sets that immediate to `$05`. So sprites run
`Spr0to13Start`, the main routine of the Red Koopa Troopa, and so they draw
through `Spr0to13Gfx`.

Getting there is not enough by itself, because the routine splits on height
before it gets to the wing test:

```
CODE_018BDE:
    LDY.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; \ Branch if sprite is 2 tiles high
    LDA.W Spr0to13Prop,Y                      ; |
    AND.B #$40                                ; |
    BNE CODE_018BEC                           ; / $018BE5: D0 05
    JSR SubSprGfx2Entry1                      ; \ Draw 1 tile high sprite and return
    BRA +                                     ; /
```

The branch for one tile returns before the wing test. `6D63-AF01` changes that
`BNE` into a `BRA` (`$D0` → `$80`, same displacement, same target). So the
height test is skipped completely, and **every** sprite takes the path for two
tiles high and gets to the wing test.

That test still reads the **real** sprite number, which none of these codes
change. So it uses its original rule: `$08` or more gets wings. Almost every
enemy in the game has a number of `$08` or more, so almost every enemy flies.
The exception is the good part. The sprites that come out without wings are
`$00`–`$07`: **the Koopas**, the one family that the wings were made for.

To close that gap you need a fourth code, `DD6D-D705` (`018C0D:00`). It removes
the `CMP #$08` test, so every sprite passes. That code is already in this file as
a variant of "Every Goomba, Koopa and Buzzy Beetle turns round and comes after
you". There it is the way to give the four Koopa Troopas with shells wings with
one code, in a game with no other changes. Four codes fit on real Game
Genie hardware, which takes five.

**Evidence:** `$018BE5` was found with `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_01.asm`
line 1886). It was read back from the ROM with `memory({op:'readCart',
romPath:'comparison_U.smc', platform:'snes', cpuAddress:0x018BDB})`:
`9D 7C 15 B4 9E B9 F0 88 29 40 D0 05 20 0D 9F 80 27 BD 02 16 ...`, that is
`STA $157C,X` / `LDY $9E,X` / `LDA $88F0,Y` / `AND #$40` / `BNE +5` /
`JSR $9F0D` / `BRA +$27`. This matches the source instruction by instruction,
and puts the `$D0` at `$018BE5`, with displacement `$05` going to `$018BEC`. The
wing test was read separately at `$018C08`: `95 D8 B5 9E C9 08 90 03 20 28 9E 68
9D 7C 15 60`. `$0185C6`/`$0185C7` were checked for the `CallSpriteMain` entry in
this file, and read again the same way. All codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`: `CB6A-0F69` → `$0185C6 <- $A9`, `D96A-0FA9` →
`$0185C7 <- $05`, `6D63-AF01` → `$018BE5 <- $80`, `DD6D-D7A5` →
`$018C0F <- $00`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in
play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `DD6D-D7A5` | `018C0F:00` (orig `$03`) | in a game with no other changes, the four Koopa Troopas with shells get the para-Koopa's wings. The displacement of the wing test's `BCC` becomes zero, so taking the branch goes to the next instruction and runs the `JSR` anyway. Same result as `DD6D-D705`, from the branch instead of the comparison |

**Caveats:** Two other things change in addition to the wings, and both come
from forcing the taller draw path.

Sprites that are normally one tile high are now drawn by `SubSprGfx1` from the
rows of the two-tile tilemap, at a position `$0F` pixels higher. Most of them
have no second tile, so the game uses whatever is above them in the sprite
graphics page. Expect garbage above each enemy's head, not a taller enemy.

Also, `Spr0to13Start` reads its walk speed from `Spr0to13Prop`, indexed by the
real sprite number. So any sprite with a number of `$14` or more reads past the
end of that twenty-byte table. The table is at `$0188F0`, so `$0188F0 + $14` is
`$018904`. That is the first opcode of `ShellessKoopas`, which is also the
handler address that the dispatch table of `CallSpriteMain` gives for sprites
`$00`–`$03`. Those enemies walk at whatever speed the opcode bytes give.

The note under "Every Goomba, Koopa and Buzzy Beetle turns round and comes after
you" uses `018C0D:00` together with `018BE4:FF` to get to the same place. That
works on the `AND #$40` operand instead, and it depends on the sprite.
`AND #$FF` is only non-zero if the sprite's property byte is non-zero. So the
four sprites whose entry is `$00` (green Koopa with no shell, keyhole, Buzzy
Beetle and the unused `$12`) still take the path for one tile. `018BE5:80` does
not have that gap, because it removes the test instead of making it wider.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session). The bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header at LoROM offsets `0x8BE5`
(it has `$D0`), `0x8C0F` (it has `$03`), `0x85C6` (it has `$B5`) and `0x85C7`
(it has `$9E`). The `Spr0to13Prop` base `$0188F0` is the operand of the
`LDA $88F0,Y` read back at `$018BE0`. The call site count comes from
`tools/callsites.py --callers KoopaWingGfxRt`.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## The turn-block bridges drag you sideways

**Codes:** `C66A-0FD9`

**Raw form:** `$0185C4` ← `$A8` (originally `$91`)

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 010149

**Mechanism:** `CallSpriteMain` (`$0185C3`) starts by clearing one byte. It does
this before it has found out which sprite it will run:

```
CallSpriteMain:
    STZ.W SpriteXMovement                     ; $0185C3: 9C 91 14
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; $0185C6: B5 9E
    JSL ExecutePtr                            ; $0185C8: 22 DF 86 00
```

`SpriteXMovement` (`$7E1491`) is **one global byte, not a table of twelve
entries**. It holds "how far the sprite that is being processed now moved
horizontally in this frame". Exactly three places write it. The important one is
`CODE_01AC09` (`$01AC09`), the shared end of `SubSprXPosNoGrvty` and
`SubSprYPosNoGrvty`. Almost every sprite that moves uses these helpers:

```
    ADC.B #$00
CODE_01AC09:
    STA.W SpriteXMovement                     ; $01AC09: 8D 91 14
    RTS
```

Both paths get to that end, including the early exit at the top of
`SubSprYPosNoGrvty` (`$01ABD8: B5 AA F0 2D`, `LDA SpriteYSpeed,X / BEQ
CODE_01AC09`). So a sprite with a speed of zero stores `$00`, and does not leave
the byte alone. This means that any sprite that calls a movement helper writes
its own movement into `$1491`.

Ten routines read the byte. **Nine of them call a movement helper just before
they read it**, so they read the movement of their own sprite. They are the
orange platform, the skull raft, the Carrot Top lift, the Mega Mole, the timed
lift, the brown swinging platform (which calculates and stores `$1491` itself at
`$01C795`), and three places in sprite bookkeeping that copy it into
`SpriteMisc1528`.

The tenth does not. `CODE_01B852` (`$01B852`) is the "Mario is standing on me"
code. Exactly two sprites share it: `TurnBlockBridge` (sprite `$59`, the
turn-block bridge that turns in both directions) and `HorzTurnBlkBridge` (sprite
`$5A`, the one that is only horizontal). At its end, it moves Mario by the value
in `$1491`, with the sign extended:

```
    LDY.B #$00                                ; $01B89F: A0 00
    LDA.W SpriteXMovement                     ; $01B8A1: AD 91 14
    BPL +                                     ; $01B8A4: 10 01
    DEY                                       ; $01B8A6: 88
  + CLC                                       ; $01B8A7: 18
    ADC.B PlayerXPosNext                      ; $01B8A8: 65 94
    STA.B PlayerXPosNext                      ; $01B8AA: 85 94
```

A turn-block bridge never moves by sprite speed. It turns by moving
`SpriteMisc151C` forward against a table of lengths, so **nothing writes `$1491`
for it**. Its whole main routine is `JSR SubOffscreen0Bnk1 / JSR CODE_01B710 /
JSR CODE_01B852 / JSR CODE_01B6B2` (`$01B6A5: 20 31 AC 20 10 B7 20 52 B8 20 B2
B6`), and none of those four uses the byte. The bridge needs the `STZ` in
`CallSpriteMain` to make `$1491` zero when it reads it.

This code removes that clear. `STZ.W SpriteXMovement` becomes
`STZ.W EmptyTimer14A8`. The low byte of the operand changes from `$91` to `$A8`.
So the instruction still runs and still writes a zero, but it writes it to a
place where it does no harm. `$7E14A8` is really unused RAM. The only code that
names it is the timer loop in `ProcessLevelEffects`:

```
    LDX.B #$06                                ; $00C55C: A2 06
CODE_00C55E:
    LDA.W EmptyTimer14A8,X                    ; $00C55E: BD A8 14
    BEQ +
    DEC.W EmptyTimer14A8,X
  + DEX
    BNE CODE_00C55E
```

This loop runs indices `6` down to `1`, and stops before index `0`. So the game
never reads or writes `$14A8` itself.

When `$1491` is not cleared, it keeps the last value written to it.
`ProcessAllSprites` goes through the sprite slots from `11` down to `0`. So a
bridge in slot *N* reads the movement of the higher slot that last called a
movement helper. If nothing in the level did, the value stays from an earlier
frame, because nothing else ever resets it. Stand on a turn-block bridge, and it
moves you sideways.

**Evidence:** `$0185C4` was found with `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_01.asm`
line 937). It was read back from `comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier
header at LoROM offset `0x85C3`: `9C 91 14 B5 9E 22 DF 86`, that is
`STZ $1491` / `LDA $9E,X` / `JSL $0086DF`. This puts `$91` at `$0185C4`. The
reader at `$01B89A` has `14 E9 00 85 97 A0 00 AD 91 14 10 01 88 18 65 94 85 94`.
This matches the source instruction by instruction and puts `LDA $1491` at
`$01B8A1`. The writer at `$01AC06` has `28 69 00 8D 91 14` (`PLP` /
`ADC #$00` / `STA $1491`). The claim that the RAM is unused was checked at
`$00C55C`: `A2 06 BD A8 14 F0 03 DE A8 14 CA D0 F5`. `C66A-0FD9` decodes back to
`$0185C4 <- $A8` with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `3C6A-0DA9` + `3C6A-0FD9` + `3C6A-0F09` | `0185C3:EA` + `0185C4:EA` + `0185C5:EA` (orig `$9C $91 $14`) | the same thing with more codes: three `NOP`s replace the whole `STZ`. The behavior is the same, with three times the codes. The form with one code only works because `$14A8` is not used |

**Caveats:** **Narrow by design.** Nine of the ten readers write `$1491` before
they read it. So this code changes nothing for any other platform, lift, raft or
Mega Mole. The two turn-block bridges are the only sprites in the game that read
the byte without writing it first. That is the only reason the clear exists.

**Unpredictable magnitude.** How far you move depends on what else is loaded in
the level and which slot it is in, not on the bridge. A sprite in a higher slot
that moves one or two pixels a frame gives a steady sideways pull. In a level
where nothing else moves horizontally, an old value stays, which may or may not
be zero.

**Stale across frames.** Without the clear, nothing resets `$1491`. So a value
written by a sprite that has since been removed is still applied, until another
sprite writes over it.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`a1e74db189ce8ab8`, `--check` clean this session) and `SMW_U.sym`
(`CallSpriteMain` `$0185C3`, `CODE_01AC09` `$01AC09`, `CODE_01B852` `$01B852`,
`TurnBlockBridge` `$01B6A5`, `HorzTurnBlkBridge` `$01B6DA`, `CODE_00C55E`
`$00C55E`, `SpriteXMovement` `$1491`, `EmptyTimer14A8` `$14A8`). Every reader
and writer of `SpriteXMovement` in the disassembly was listed with grep over all
sixteen bank files: three writers (`$0185C3` the clear, `$01AC09`, and the store
at `$01C795` for the swinging platform, plus the `UpdateYPosNoGrvty` end in
bank 2 at `$02D2C3` and the second clear in bank 1 at `$01B2B0`) and ten readers.
The sprite numbers `$59`/`$5A` come from the dispatch table of `CallSpriteMain`.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Nothing in the game is random any more

**Code:** `65C4-0705`
**Raw form:** `01AD2D:87` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 02:05:59

**Mechanism:** `GetRandStep` ends with `STA RandomNumber,Y` (`99 8D 14`). That
one store is the only write to `RandomNumber` anywhere in the ROM. This code
changes the low byte of the operand from `$8D` to `$87`, so the instruction
becomes `STA $1487,Y`. That writes to the four bytes `$7E1487`-`$7E148A`, which
`rammap.asm` marks as unused. The generator still runs. `RNGCalc` still gets its
`*5 + 1` step and its shift-register step two times per call. But the result is
not kept. So both bytes of `RandomNumber` keep the value that the RAM clear at
power-on gave them, for the rest of the session.

About fifty call sites in banks 01, 02 and 03 read that pair: the sprite
generators (fire, Bullet Bills, fish, Super Koopas, bubbles, Eeries, winged
enemies), Magikoopa's magic, Big Boo, the Fishbone, Reznor, Peach, the winged
Goomba, and some smoke and spark effects. All of them still ask for a random
number, and all of them always get the same one. So every choice that the game
makes by chance becomes a fixed choice.

**Evidence:** `GetRand` at `$01ACF9` and `GetRandStep` at `$01AD07` in
`bank_01.asm`. They were annotated in this session, and a rebuild that is
identical byte for byte to the reference ROM confirmed them. The three bytes of
the store were read from `comparison_U.smc` (without its 512-byte copier header)
at `$01AD2C`: `99 8D 14`. That `$1487` is unused RAM comes from the comment
`; 7E1487 - 7E148A unused` in `rammap.asm`, above the `skip 4` that comes before
`RNGCalc`. `65C4-0705` decodes back to `$01AD2D <- $87` with
`tools/gg_encode.py decode`, and matches `cheats({op:'make'})` for the same
address and byte. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in
play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `3CCD-0DD5` | `01AD00:EA` (orig `$88`) | half of the randomness stops. The `DEY` between `GetRand`'s two `JSL`s becomes a `NOP`, so both steps store into `RandomNumber+1`, and `RandomNumber` is never written. Code that reads the high byte still gets random values. Code that reads the low byte gets a constant |
| `F6CD-07D5` | `01AD0C:18` (orig `$38`) | the low half of the seed stops working. `SEC` becomes `CLC`, so the step of the low byte changes from `RNGCalc * 5 + 1` to `RNGCalc * 5`. That is a multiply whose only fixed point is zero, and a seed of `$00` from cleared RAM never leaves it. Every random byte then comes only from the shift-register half, and the sequence repeats every 255 numbers instead of every 65280 |

**Caveats:** **The frozen value is whatever the RAM clear left.** The code only
stops new values from being written. It does not choose a value. In practice
that value is `$00` for both bytes. So every masked read (`AND #$01` for a
direction, `AND #$03` for a variant) always picks option zero. But if a boot
leaves those bytes non-zero, they stay at that value instead.

**Some sprites will look broken rather than fixed.** Some routines use the
random byte to spread out the members of a group: the Eerie waves, the bubble
generator, the Super Koopa squadron. Every member now gets the same offset, so
they are drawn on top of each other and are not spread out.

**Not the same as "no enemies".** Generators still make sprites on their own
timers. Only their choices are frozen. Expect the same enemy, from the same
side, at the same height, again and again.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `SMW_U.sym` (`GetRand` `$01ACF9`,
`CODE_01AD07`/`GetRandStep` `$01AD07`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc`. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was out of date this session and was
not used. `RNGCalc` `$7E148B` and `RandomNumber` `$7E148D` were found by
following the `ORG`/`skip` chain in `rammap.asm`. The list of call sites is every
`JSL GetRand` in `bank_01.asm`, `bank_02.asm` and `bank_03.asm` (53 sites). The
label that contains each site was taken from the source.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Random numbers stop being evenly spread, so the game keeps making the same choice

**Code:** `42C4-0405`
**Raw form:** `01AD29:2D` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 02:06:00

**Mechanism:** `GetRandStep` makes each random byte by combining the two halves
of the seed with EOR: `LDA RNGCalc+1` / `EOR RNGCalc` / `STA RandomNumber,Y`. The
`EOR` is `4D 8B 14`. If the opcode changes to `2D`, it becomes `AND RNGCalc`.
Both halves of the seed are still evenly spread, and the generator keeps its full
period, so the sequence is as long as before. But each bit of the *output* is
now set only when both bits of the seed are set. That happens one time in four,
not one time in two. So the random byte is small much more often than not, and
is exactly `$00` about one time in ten.

Almost all code that uses the byte masks it down to a choice (`AND #$01` for a
left/right or up/down decision, `AND #$03` to pick one of four). With the bias,
those masks give zero three times out of four. Enemies pick the same direction,
generators pick the same spawn slot, and Magikoopa's magic and the smoke effects
pick the same variant. But the game never becomes fully predictable.

**Evidence:** `GetRandStep` at `$01AD07` in `bank_01.asm`. It was annotated in
this session, and a rebuild that is identical byte for byte to the reference ROM
confirmed it. The three bytes of the combine were read from `comparison_U.smc`
(without its 512-byte copier header) at `$01AD29`: `4D 8B 14`. `42C4-0405`
decodes back to `$01AD29 <- $2D` with `tools/gg_encode.py decode`, and matches
`cheats({op:'make'})` for the same address and byte. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `D2C4-0405` | `01AD29:0D` (orig `$4D`) | the bias goes the other way. `ORA` replaces `AND`, so each output bit is set three times in four, and the random byte is large much more often than not. Masked reads give every bit set most of the time, so the game keeps picking the *last* option, not the first |

**Caveats:** **This changes the output only, not the generator.** `RNGCalc`
still steps exactly as before. So the full 65280-step cycle of the seed does not
change, and you can use the codes here with no other changes. It also means that
the bias is statistical. A run that looks really evenly spread can still happen,
but it is rare.

**How visible it is depends on the mask.** A sprite that tests one bit shows the
bias clearly (three to one instead of even). A sprite that uses the whole byte as
a position or a timer only gets values that are more often short (`AND`) or long
(`ORA`). It does not settle on one behavior.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `SMW_U.sym` (`CODE_01AD07`/`GetRandStep`
`$01AD07`), and was checked against a direct read of `comparison_U.smc`.
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` was out of date this session and was not used. `RNGCalc`
`$7E148B` and `RandomNumber` `$7E148D` were found by following the
`ORG`/`skip` chain in `rammap.asm`.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Swim in the air

**Code:** `6D30-6FA4`
**Raw form:** `00EA47:80` (address:new-byte:original-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 02:19:00

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** At the end of the player update, one short block decides if
`PlayerInWater` (`$7E0075`) is set for the next frame. First it clears
`PlayerCanJumpWater`. Then it reads `LevelIsWater` (`$7E0085`) and branches. A
level that is all water is always wet, so the block skips the tile test and goes
directly to `LDA #$01 / STA PlayerInWater`. A normal level continues into the
tile test. That test shifts the two low bits of `InteractionPtsInWater`
(`$7E008A`) to find out if the player's upper and lower interaction points are on
water tiles. The branch is `D0 15` (`BNE`) at `$00EA47`. If the opcode changes to
`80`, it becomes `BRA`: the same displacement and the same target, but it is now
always taken. The tile test never runs, and `PlayerInWater` is set on every
frame, in every level.

So everything that reads `PlayerInWater` acts as if the player is always under
water:

- The player update runs the swim handler instead of the ground handler.
- The jump pose becomes the swim pose.
- The cape animation slows to its underwater speed.
- The X and Y speed tables are indexed at their water entries. So the player
  drifts instead of walking, and each press of the jump button is a swim stroke:
  one small push up, and then the player sinks again.
- The block also ends with a jump to the bubble spawner. So the player breathes
  out a steady stream of bubbles on dry land.

There is no way out. `PlayerCanJumpWater` is cleared at the top of the block on
every frame. Only the surface case in the tile test sets it, and that case can
no longer run. So the jump that sends the player up out of the water can never
happen. Swimming is the only movement left in the game.

**Evidence:** The block is just after `CODE_00EA32` in `bank_00.asm`, and was
annotated in this session. The rebuild after that was identical byte for byte to
the reference ROM, so the annotation moved nothing. The five bytes were read from
`comparison_U.smc` (without its 512-byte copier header) at `$00EA45`:
`A5 85 D0 15 46`, that is `LDA $85` / `BNE +$15` / `LSR $8A`. `6D30-6FA4`
decodes back to `$00EA47 <- $80` with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches
`cheats({op:'make'})` for the same address and byte. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Raw | Effect |
|------|-----|--------|
| `6530-6F64` | `00EA46:87` (orig `$85`) | the opposite. The `LDA $85` operand now points at `$7E0087`. The RAM map records that byte as unused, so it always reads zero, and the shortcut for levels that are all water never runs. The real underwater levels continue into the tile test and come out dry, so the player walks, runs and jumps on the bottom of the sea |

**Caveats:** **The camera reads the same flag.** The vertical scroll routine
checks `PlayerInWater` before it decides if the screen can follow the player up
and down. So in every level the camera acts as it does under water, not only the
movement.

**Levels built around walking still have to be swum.** There is no ground speed,
so long runs take much longer, and you cannot do a running jump across a gap.
Some levels become slow but still possible. A few gaps that need a jump at full
speed cannot be crossed at all.

**The mirror code is not a way to walk through water levels comfortably.** Water
levels are made for swimming. Without the water, the player falls down shafts
that were made to float up through.

**Provenance:** The address comes from the annotated water state block in
`bank_00.asm` (the block after `CODE_00EA32`, which ends at `CODE_00EAA3`), and
was checked against a direct read of `comparison_U.smc`. `PlayerInWater`
`$7E0075`, `LevelIsWater` `$7E0085`, `WRAM_0087` `$7E0087` (documented as unused,
and not used anywhere in the disassembly), `InteractionPtsInWater` `$7E008A` and
`PlayerCanJumpWater` `$7E13FA` were all found by following the `ORG`/`skip`
chain in `rammap.asm`.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Select inflates and deflates Mario like a P balloon, at any time

**Codes:** `4DCF-676D` **and** `E7C7-6FDD` **and** `E7C7-640D` (all three needed)
**Raw form:** `00A21E:20` (orig `$10`), `00A234:F3` (orig `$D4`) and
`00A239:F3` (orig `$D4`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation,
not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 02:30:00

**Mechanism:** In a level, the pause toggle is the only place where a button
press switches a flag between two values and debounces itself. So it is the
obvious place to give a button a new job. It reads a new press of Start, refuses
during the end of level sequence and the death animation, sets a lockout of 60
frames, and then does the toggle:

```
CODE_00A21B:
    LDA.B byetudlrFrame
    AND.B #$10                                ; <- $00A21E, bit 4 = Start
    BEQ CODE_00A242
    ...
    LDA.B #$3C
    STA.W PauseTimer                          ; 60-frame lockout
    LDY.B #!SFX_UNPAUSE
    LDA.W PauseFlag                           ; <- $00A234, operand $D4
    EOR.B #$01
    STA.W PauseFlag                           ; <- $00A239, operand $D4
    BEQ +
    LDY.B #!SFX_PAUSE
  + STY.W SPCIO0
```

Three bytes change. The mask becomes `$20`, bit 5, so **Select** runs the toggle
instead of Start. Then both operands of the toggle point somewhere else.
`PauseFlag` is `$13D4` and `PBalloonInflating` is `$13F3`. They are on the same
page, so only the low byte of each absolute operand has to change, from `$D4` to
`$F3`. The instructions become `LDA PBalloonInflating / EOR #$01 /
STA PBalloonInflating`. Now Select switches the P-balloon flag between 0 and 1,
at most once per second, and plays the pause sound.

The player update tests `PBalloonInflating` before it does any movement:

```
CODE_00CD39:
    STZ.W PlayerTurningPose
    LDY.W PBalloonInflating
    BNE CODE_00CD95                           ; inflated: nothing below runs
```

When the flag is set, climbing, the water and ground handlers, gravity, friction,
the input reads and Yoshi are all skipped. `CODE_00CD95` only picks a pose:
`$42` small, `$43` powered up, the balloon frames. The position update
`CODE_00DC2D` runs *before* this test. So Mario's position still changes by his
speed on every frame, but nothing is left to change that speed. He keeps exactly
the speed he had when you pressed the button, and moves in a straight line. If
you press Select while standing still, he stays still in the air. If you press it
in the middle of a jump, he moves away at a constant speed. Press it again, and
normal physics start again from where he is.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `A5 16 29 10 F0 21` at `$00A21B`, that is
`LDA $16` / `AND #$10` / `BEQ +$21`, and
`A9 3C 8D D3 13 A0 12 AD D4 13 49 01 8D D4 13 F0 02 A0 11` at `$00A22C`. This
is the listing above byte for byte. It puts the mask at `$00A21E`, and the low
bytes of the two `$13D4` operands at `$00A234` and `$00A239`. `PauseFlag`
`$7E13D4` and `PBalloonInflating` `$7E13F3` come from `SMW_U.sym`. The pause
block and the P-balloon test were both annotated in this session, and the rebuild
after that was identical byte for byte to the reference ROM. All three codes
decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and match `cheats({op:'make'})`
for the same addresses and bytes. The effect comes from the disassembly and
**was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **The game can no longer be paused.** After the patch, nothing
writes `PauseFlag`. So you cannot pause in a level, and you also lose the
Start+Select level skip, which needs the game to be paused. In a level, Start
now does nothing at all. The "look around" on the overworld has its own writes to
the same flag, and does not change.

**Inflating is not the same as having a balloon.** The real P-balloon keeps the
balloon sprite alive, and that sprite steers the player while the flag is set.
Here there is no sprite, so there is no steering. You cannot control the drift
until you press Select again.

**Only the ceiling still stops him.** Only one speed test still runs: the
`LDA PlayerYSpeed+1 / BMI / LDA PlayerBlockedDir / AND #$08 / STZ PlayerYSpeed+1`
above the flag test. It runs first, and stops upward speed at a ceiling. Nothing
stops horizontal or downward speed, so in every other direction Mario drifts into
and through terrain.

**Anything that clears the flag ends it early.** The goal tape clears
`PBalloonInflating`. Taking and then losing a real P-balloon also clears it. So
those deflate Mario without a button press.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`1fe094b881d08cd0`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header. `PauseFlag` `$7E13D4`,
`PauseTimer` `$7E13D3` and `PBalloonInflating` `$7E13F3` were found in
`SMW_U.sym` and `rammap.asm`.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Bullet Bills fire constantly

**Codes:** `DD85-D7A6` + `E18D-DDD6` (use both)
**Raw form:** `02B07F:00` (orig `$7F`) + `02B000:F6` (orig `$18`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 03:05:00

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `video-ready` `bullet-bill-generator-collection` `challenge`

**Mechanism:** Generator `$0B` (sprite `$D5`) is the plain Bullet Bill
generator. It runs `GenerateBullet`, which starts with a rate test:

```
GenerateBullet:
    LDA.B EffFrame
    AND.B #$7F                                ; <- $02B07F
    BNE +                                     ; return
    JSL FindFreeSlotLowPri
    ...
```

With the mask `$7F`, the test passes once every 128 frames. With `$00`, the
result is always zero, so the generator fires on every frame. Each shot is one
Bullet Bill just off the left or right edge of the screen, at a random height.
One random byte picks both the height and the edge, and the edge also picks the
direction, so a bullet from the left always flies right.

Sprite `$D5` is placed only once in the whole game, in Valley of Bowser 4. So
the second code, `E18D-DDD6`, turns the generator on in every level.
`CallGenerator` reads the generator type with `LDA.W CurrentGenerator` (`AD B9
18` at `$02AFFE`). The code changes the operand's high byte from `$18` to
`$F6`, so it reads the ROM byte at `$02F6B9` instead, which is `$0B`. Each
frame of every level, `CallGenerator` then runs the plain Bullet Bill
generator, whatever the level placed. The level's own generators and "turn off
