generators" sprites are ignored. `E18D-DDD6` also has its own entry: it is the
Bullet Bill row of "A chosen generator runs in every level from the start".

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `A5 14 29 7F D0 46` at `$02B07C`, which is
`LDA.B EffFrame` / `AND.B #$7F` / `BNE`, and puts the `$7F` at `$02B07F`. It
has `AD B9 18` at `$02AFFE`, which puts the `$18` at `$02B000`, and `$0B` at
`$02F6B9`. The codes decode back to `$02B07F <- $00` and `$02B000 <- $F6`.
The effect comes from the disassembly.

**Caveats:**

- Not tested.
- No level can use its own generator while this is on (no Super Koopas,
  dolphins, Eeries and so on).

- The sprite table fills up. `FindFreeSlotLowPri` refuses without an error
  when there is no free slot, so the real rate is whatever the slot table can
  hold.
- `GenerateBullet` calls `GetRand` for every shot, so `GetRand` now runs on
  every frame instead of every 128th frame. This changes the stream of random
  numbers that the rest of the game uses.
- The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have
  not been checked.

## Hold Select and every enemy in the level thinks it is standing on solid ground

**Codes:** `C26D-D760` + `F96D-D7A0` + `DD6F-DDD0` + `4D6F-DD60`
**Raw form:** `01800E:AD` (orig `$BD`), `01800F:15` (orig `$88`),
`018010:00` (orig `$15`) and `018012:20` (orig `$04`) (address:new-byte — the
original byte is documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no
compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 03:45:00

**Mechanism:** In Super Mario World, sprites do not test the ground themselves.
The collision code writes a contact byte for each sprite, `SpriteBlockedDirs`
at `$7E1588` plus the sprite index. Three very small helper routines at the start
of bank `$01` read it back. They are next to each other, and each is six bytes:

```
IsTouchingObjSide:                            ; $018008
    LDA.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X
    AND.B #$03                                ; the two walls
    RTS

IsOnGround:                                   ; $01800E
    LDA.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X                 ; BD 88 15
    AND.B #$04                                ; 29 04  <- the floor bit
    RTS                                       ; 60

IsTouchingCeiling:                            ; $018014
    LDA.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X
    AND.B #$08                                ; the ceiling
    RTS
```

`IsOnGround` is called from 38 places in bank `$01`, and from nowhere else. Every
one of those 38 calls is a `JSR IsOnGround` with a `BEQ` or `BNE` right after it.
No code looks at which bit came back. So the routine is only a yes/no answer. This
means it can be changed to answer a completely different question, as long as it
still returns zero for no and a non-zero value for yes.

The four codes change it to read the controller instead:

```
IsOnGround:                                   ; $01800E
    LDA.W $0015                               ; AD 15 00  buttons currently held
    AND.B #$20                                ; 29 20     the Select button
    RTS                                       ; 60
```

`$7E0015` is the byte of held buttons for the active player, and bit 5 is Select.
The new routine fits in the same space, so the original `RTS` at `$018013` still
ends it. Only four bytes change: the opcode `$BD` becomes `$AD` (absolute
instead of absolute indexed), the two operand bytes become `$0015`, and the mask
`$04` becomes `$20`. The `AND #` opcode and the `RTS` stay exactly as they were.

Hold Select, and all 38 questions get the answer yes at the same time. Every
sprite that asks "am I standing on something?" gets yes, wherever it really is.
Koopas and goombas walk in the air, shells keep sliding after they leave the
ledge, Chargin' Chucks charge across empty space, Wigglers keep crawling off the
end of their platform, and anything that is falling acts as if it has just
landed.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `80 40 20 10 08 04 02 01 BD 88 15 29 03
60 BD 88 15 29 04 60 BD 88 15 29 08 60` at `$018000`. That is the table of
eight bit masks and then the three routines, byte for byte. It puts
`IsOnGround` at `$01800E`, with its mask at `$018012`. The 38 call sites were
listed with grep, and the line after each one was checked: all 38 are `BEQ` or
`BNE`. `$7E0015` is `byetudlrHold` in `rammap.asm`. The pause code and Yoshi's
carry check read the same byte with the same `$20` bit. The routines were
annotated in this session, and the rebuild after that was identical byte for
byte to the reference ROM. Every code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from
the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Let go of Select and nothing is ever on the ground.** The routine
does not look at the contact byte at all now. So the answer is no for every
sprite until you press Select again. Enemies that need ground contact to turn
around at a ledge will not turn around. Shells that need it to bounce will not
bounce. Sprites that only act when they are on the ground will stand still. You
must hold the button for this cheat to work. It does not work in the background.

**It is sprites only.** Mario has his own separate ground flag,
`PlayerIsOnGround` `$7E13EF`. The player collision code in bank `$00` writes it.
Nothing here changes it, so Mario falls normally.

**Select loses nothing.** In the unmodified game, Select does nothing during a
level, so you lose no function. The overworld does not change. These are sprite
routines, and the overworld does not call them.

**Four codes fit on real hardware.** A SNES Game Genie holds five codes at
once, so this leaves one slot free.

**A one-code relative:** If you change `$018011` from `$29` to `$09`, the
`AND #$04` becomes `ORA #$04`. `IsOnGround` then returns `$04` or more for every
sprite all the time: always on the ground, with no button. That is a different
cheat, and is not part of this entry.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`b688b5478d5d3033`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header. `SpriteBlockedDirs`
`$7E1588` and `byetudlrHold` `$7E0015` were found in `rammap.asm`, and the ROM
bytes above confirm them.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Everything is permanently standing on solid ground, until you hold Select

**Codes:** `C96D-D760` + `F96D-D7A0` + `DB6F-DDD0` + `2E6F-DD00` + `FC6F-DD60`
**Raw form:** `01800E:A5` (orig `$BD`), `01800F:15` (orig `$88`),
`018010:09` (orig `$15`), `018011:DF` (orig `$29`) and `018012:1A`
(orig `$04`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of
the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 04:05:00

**Mechanism:** This is the opposite of the "hold Select and every enemy thinks
it is standing on solid ground" cheat above, and it changes the same six bytes.
`IsOnGround` at `$01800E` is the routine that 38 places in bank `$01` call to ask
if a sprite is touching the floor. All 38 of them only do `BEQ` or `BNE` on the
answer:

```
IsOnGround:                                   ; $01800E
    LDA.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X                 ; BD 88 15
    AND.B #$04                                ; 29 04
    RTS                                       ; 60
```

The five codes replace it with this:

```
IsOnGround:                                   ; $01800E
    LDA $15                                   ; A5 15  buttons currently held
    ORA #$DF                                  ; 09 DF  set every bit except Select
    INC A                                     ; 1A     $FF rolls over to $00
    RTS                                       ; 60     (unchanged)
```

`$DF` is `%11011111`: every bit is set except bit 5, which is Select. So after
the `ORA`, the accumulator is `$FF` when Select is held, and `$DF` when it is
not. `INC A` then changes `$FF` to `$00`, and `$DF` to `$E0`. Zero means no. So
if you hold Select, all 38 questions get the answer no at the same time. If you
let go, all of them get yes.

This form fits, and the obvious form `LDA $15 / AND #$20 / EOR #$20` does not.
The obvious form is seven bytes, and `IsOnGround` has only six before
`IsTouchingCeiling` starts at `$018014`. `ORA` plus `INC A` is six bytes. So the
original `RTS` still ends the routine, and the ceiling test next to it does not
change.

When Select is not held, sprites think they have just landed,
wherever they really are. Enemies that are falling run their landing behavior,
things that only act on the ground never stop acting, and nothing acts as if it
is in the air. Hold Select and this reverses: nothing in the level is on the
ground at all. Sprites that turn around at a ledge walk straight off it, shells
stop bouncing, and anything that waits for ground contact waits forever.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `BD 88 15 29 03 60 BD 88 15 29 04 60 BD
88 15 29 08 60` at `$018008`. That is `IsTouchingObjSide`, `IsOnGround` and
`IsTouchingCeiling` byte for byte, and it puts `IsOnGround` at `$01800E`. The 38
call sites were listed, and the line after each one was checked: all 38 are `BEQ`
or `BNE`, so no code depends on which bit comes back. `$7E0015` is
`byetudlrHold` in `rammap.asm`, and bit 5 is Select. Yoshi's carry check reads
the same byte with `BIT byetudlrHold / BVC`. Immediates like `ORA #$09` are one
byte here, because sprite code runs with an 8-bit accumulator. The original
`AND.B #$04` confirms this. Every code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from
the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Normal ground detection is gone in both directions.** The routine
does not read the sprite's contact byte at all now. Sprites are never told the
truth: the answer is yes for everything or no for everything, depending on the
button. Six bytes is not enough space to keep the real test and add the button
override. Every form of that needs seven or eight bytes, and the seventh byte is
the first instruction of `IsTouchingCeiling`.

**It is sprites only.** Mario has his own ground flag, `PlayerIsOnGround`
`$7E13EF`. The player collision code in bank `$00` writes it. Nothing here
changes it.

**Select loses nothing.** In the unmodified game, Select does nothing during a
level. The overworld does not change, because these are sprite routines and the
overworld does not call them.

**Five codes is the most real hardware takes.** A SNES Game Genie holds five
codes at once, so this set fills it.

**Do not combine it with the Select-makes-everything-grounded cheat.** Both
change the same six bytes, so the two sets of codes would conflict.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`77f1cef29d459d20`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header. `SpriteBlockedDirs`
`$7E1588` and `byetudlrHold` `$7E0015` were found in `rammap.asm`, and the ROM
bytes above confirm them.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## No sprite ever notices a ceiling

**Codes:** `DD6F-D4D0`
**Raw form:** `018018:00` (orig `$08`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 04:20:00

**Mechanism:** `IsTouchingCeiling` is at `$018014`. It is the third of the three
six-byte sprite contact tests at the start of bank `$01`. It reads the contact
byte of the current sprite and keeps one bit:

```
IsTouchingCeiling:                            ; $018014
    LDA.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X                 ; BD 88 15
    AND.B #$08                                ; 29 08   <- bit 3, the ceiling
    RTS                                       ; 60
```

If the mask changes from `$08` to `$00`, the `AND` gives zero whatever the
contact byte holds, so the answer is always no. One byte, one code.

Ten sprite handlers call it, and all ten test the answer with `BEQ`. Nine of
them use it for the same thing: to stop a sprite's upward speed when it hits a
ceiling. `CODE_018B2E`, `CODE_018C8C`, `WingedGoomba`, `CODE_0198D0`,
`CODE_01E4ED` and `SpringBoard` do `STZ SpriteYSpeed,X`. `CODE_019598` and
`CODE_01AFC8` set a downward speed of `$10` instead. `CODE_01C437` stores zero.
The tenth, `MagikoopasMagic`, plays the `BONK` sound effect when a magic blast
hits a ceiling on the screen.

With the mask at zero, none of that happens. A sprite that is going up keeps its
upward speed for as long as it goes up, and a Magikoopa's magic makes no sound.

The block collision code does not change, so sprites are still pushed out of the
ceiling they hit. `CODE_019414` moves the sprite's Y position to the edge of the
block, and *then* sets the contact bit. This code only hides the second part. So
what you see is a sprite held under the ceiling while it tries to go up: it is
pushed down on one frame and goes up again on the next, and it does not stop and
fall away.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `BD 88 15 29 08 60` at `$018014`. That is
`IsTouchingCeiling` byte for byte, and it puts the `$08` at `$018018`. The ten
call sites were listed, and the line after each one was checked: all ten are
`BEQ`, and the instructions on the taken path are as described above. The
contact bit itself comes from `DATA_019134: db $01,$02,$04,$08` (right, left,
floor, ceiling). `CODE_019435` ORs it in, and `CODE_019414` calls that right
after it moves the sprite's Y position. The routine was annotated in the earlier
pass over the three contact tests in this session. The code decodes back
correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches `cheats({op:'make'})`. The
effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Mario is not affected.** He has his own ceiling handling in bank
`$00`. This is only the test for sprites.

**It does not make sprites pass through ceilings.** The position correction is
separate from the flag and still runs. The code removes every reaction to the
contact, not the contact itself.

**Two of the ten are the same sprite twice.** `CODE_019598` and `CODE_01AFC8`
both set a downward speed, not zero. So those sprites now continue up, where
before they were knocked back down. That is the most visible part of the effect.

**Do not combine it with either `IsOnGround` cheat above.** Those change
`$01800E`-`$018013`, the routine just before this one. The byte counts do not
overlap, but with both effects together, very little of the sprite contact system
works normally.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`77f1cef29d459d20`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header. `SpriteBlockedDirs`
`$7E1588` was found in `rammap.asm`, and the ROM bytes above confirm it.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## All sprites use underwater physics

**Codes:** `6DBF-6FD0` + `40BF-6F00`
**Raw form:** `019214:80` (orig `$F0`), `019215:24` (orig `$45`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 04:45:00

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** `SpriteInLiquid` is `$7E164A`, one byte for each sprite slot. Bit
0 means "this sprite is in liquid". At the start of every frame, the sprite block
interaction clears the byte, keeps the old value in `SpriteInterIndex`, and then
calls the liquid test at `$019211` to set it again:

```
CODE_019211:                                  ; $019211
    LDA.W SpriteBuoyancy                      ; AD 0E 19
    BEQ CODE_01925B                           ; F0 45   <- both patched bytes
    LDA.B LevelIsWater                        ; A5 85
    BNE CODE_019258                           ; D0 3E
    LDY.B #$3C                                ; A0 3C
    JSR CODE_01944D                           ; 20 4D 94   read the Map16 tile
    ...
CODE_01923A:                                  ; $01923A
    TAY                                       ; A8
    LDA.W SpriteInLiquid,X                    ; BD 4A 16
    ORA.B #$01                                ; 09 01   <- bit 0, "in liquid"
    CPY.B #$04                                ; C0 04   acts-like $04 is lava
    BNE CODE_019258                           ; D0 14
    ...
CODE_019258:
    STA.W SpriteInLiquid,X                    ; 9D 4A 16
CODE_01925B:
    ...
```

The two codes change `BEQ CODE_01925B` (`F0 45`) to `BRA CODE_01923A`
(`80 24`). The branch is now always taken, and it goes to the path that sets the
bit, not the path that skips the whole test. So `SpriteInLiquid` is set to `$01`
for every sprite on every frame, in every level, whatever tile the sprite is on.

Three things must be true for this to work, and all three are.

1. At the branch, the accumulator holds `SpriteBuoyancy`, the sprite buoyancy
   setting from the level header. It is always `$00`, `$40`, `$80` or `$C0`.
   `CODE_01923A` does `TAY` and then `CPY #$04` to test for lava. None of the
   four possible values is `$04`. So the lava path is never taken, and the cheat
   kills no sprite.
2. `CODE_019258` continues directly into `CODE_01925B`, which is where the
   original branch went. So nothing after the liquid test is skipped. The rest of
   the block interaction runs exactly as before.
3. The tile read at `CODE_01944D` is skipped, but that already happens normally:
   in any level whose header has no buoyancy bits, the original `BEQ` skipped it
   too.

**What it does:** `SpriteInLiquid` is what selects water physics instead of air
physics. `SubUpdateSprPos` reads it and changes to the other gravity and
terminal speed tables: `DATA_019030: db $03,$01` for gravity and
`DATA_01902E: db $40,$10` for maximum fall speed, where the second entry of each
is the water value. It also halves the sprite's X speed, and limits upward speed
to `$E8`. So every enemy in the game falls slowly, moves at half speed and bobs,
as if the whole level were under water.

Some sprites also read the byte themselves, and take their path for water.
Jumping Fish act as if they were in their pond. Rip Van Fish, Blurps and
Porcu-Puffers swim on dry land.

The splash only happens once for each sprite. The change test at `$019248` is
`SpriteInLiquid EOR SpriteInterIndex`. After the first frame both are `$01`, so
no more splashes are made.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `AD 0E 19 F0 45 A5 85 D0 3E A0 3C 20 4D
94` at `$019211`, which puts the `F0 45` at `$019214`-`$019215`. `$01923A`
minus `$019216` is `$24`, the new branch offset. `SpriteInLiquid` `$7E164A` and
`SpriteBuoyancy` `$7E190E` come from `rammap.asm` and `SMW_U.sym`.
`SpriteBuoyancy` is written in three places in `bank_05.asm`, always as
`AND #$C0` (or `AND #$80`) of the level's sprite header byte. This is why it has
only four possible values. The codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`, and match `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Mario is not affected.** `PlayerInWater` is a separate byte with
its own test in bank `$00`. Mario still walks and jumps normally, among enemies
that all swim.

**Sprites that skip block interaction are not affected.** If a sprite's tweaker
bits turn off object interaction, it never gets to `$019211`, so its
`SpriteInLiquid` keeps its old value. Most enemies do interact, so most enemies
swim.

**In a real water level nothing changes.** The flag was already set there.

**It does not make anything float upward.** Water gravity still pulls down, only
more gently. So enemies sink slowly and do not go up.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Walking enemies never turn round at a wall

**Codes:** `1DB6-D400`
**Raw form:** `019089:60` (orig `$BD`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 05:05:00

**Mechanism:** `FlipIfTouchingObj` is the shared "you walked into a wall, turn
around" helper. It is at `$019089`:

```
FlipIfTouchingObj:                            ; $019089
    LDA.W SpriteMisc157C,X                    ; BD 7C 15   direction, 0 = right
    INC A                                     ; 1A         -> 1 = right, 2 = left
    AND.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X                 ; 3D 88 15   contact byte
    AND.B #$03                                ; 29 03      keep the two wall bits
    BEQ +                                     ; F0 03
    JSR FlipSpriteDir                         ; 20 98 90
  + RTS                                       ; 60
```

If the first byte changes from `$BD` to `$60`, the first instruction, `LDA`,
becomes an `RTS`. The routine now returns as soon as it starts, and never gets to
the test or the flip. One byte, one code.

All six callers do a plain `JSR`, and the next instruction is another `JSR` or
`JSL`. So none of them looks at the accumulator or the flags after the call.
That is why an `RTS` at the start is safe here: the caller can only see the
difference in how the sprite behaves.

**What it affects:** The six call sites cover most of the normal walking enemies
in the game.

| caller | sprites |
|---|---|
| `Spr0to13Start` | Koopas `$04`-`$07`, yellow winged Koopa `$0C`, Goomba `$0F`, Buzzy Beetle `$11`, Spiny `$13` |
| `SpinyEgg` | falling Spiny `$14` |
| `GreenParaKoopa` (via `CODE_018CAE`) | `$08`, `$09` |
| `WingedGoomba` (via `CODE_018DA5`) | `$10` |
| `HoppingFlame` (via `CODE_018F43`) | `$1D` |
| `DryBonesAndBeetle` (via `CODE_01E5B6`) | Dry Bones `$30`, Bony Beetle `$31`, Dry Bones on ledge `$32` |

A Koopa that walks into a wall now stays there. The game still detects the wall
contact: `Spr0to13Main` runs its own copy of the same test at `CODE_018B2E`, and
does `STZ SpriteXSpeed,X`. But at the start of the next frame, the walk speed is
loaded again from `Spr0to13SpeedX`. Nothing changes the direction, so the enemy
keeps pushing into the wall forever.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `BD 7C 15 1A 3D 88 15 29 03 F0 03 20 98
90 60` at `$019089`, which is `FlipIfTouchingObj` byte for byte. All seven
references to `FlipIfTouchingObj` in `bank_01.asm` were listed: one is the label
and six are `JSR`s. The instruction after each `JSR` was checked. The code
decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches
`cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen
in play**.

**Caveats:** **This is not every turn-around in the game.** `FlipSpriteDir` at
`$019098` does not change, and thirteen other places still call it directly.
Some sprites also run their own `IsTouchingObjSide` and `FlipSpriteDir` pair
instead of this helper. Rexes, Chargin' Chucks, Mega Moles and others still turn
normally.

**Ledge behaviour is unchanged.** The flip for "stay on ledges" is in
`CODE_018B90`, and it calls `FlipSpriteDir` directly. So enemies still turn at
the edge of a platform. Only the flip at walls is gone.

**Enemies can still be pushed.** The block interaction still keeps sprites out
of solid tiles, so nothing goes into a wall. The enemies stand against it.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every enemy falls in slow motion

**Codes:** `D0B4-D760`
**Raw form:** `01902E:04` (orig `$40`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 15:40:00

**Mechanism:** `SubUpdateSprPos` is the routine that adds a sprite's speed to its
position. It is called from 23 places in `bank_01.asm`, and together these cover
almost every sprite in the game that moves. Two tables of two bytes are directly
above it:

```
DATA_01902E:                                  ; $01902E
    db $40,$10                                ; terminal fall speed: air, liquid
DATA_019030:                                  ; $019030
    db $03,$01                                ; gravity per frame:   air, liquid
```

`Y` is 0 for a sprite in air and 1 for a sprite in liquid. So entry 0 of each
table is the one that is used almost all the time. This is the gravity step:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $019049
    CLC
    ADC.W DATA_019030,Y                       ; speed += gravity
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    BMI +                                     ; rising? no cap, leave it alone
    CMP.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; \ falling: clamp to the
    BCC +                                     ; | terminal speed
    LDA.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; /
  +
```

The patched byte is entry 0 of `DATA_01902E`, the terminal fall speed in air.
`$40` becomes `$04`, one sixteenth of the normal value. Gravity does not change,
so a falling sprite still speeds up by 3 per frame. But it gets to the new limit
after two frames and stays there. So everything in the game that falls, falls
slowly at a constant speed.

**What it affects:** Everything that uses `SubUpdateSprPos`. Enemies that walk
off a ledge float down. The shell of a stomped Koopa comes down gently. A thrown
shell or a kicked item goes much further before it lands. Falling platforms sink
slowly. Anything sent upward still goes up at full speed, because the limit is
skipped for negative speeds (`BMI +`). So the path is a fast rise and then a long,
slow fall.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `40 10 03 01` at `$01902E`, which is the two
tables byte for byte. `DATA_01902E` and `DATA_019030` are used in exactly three
places, all in `SubUpdateSprPos` (`bank_01.asm` lines 2346, 2349 and 2351). So
no other code reads the patched byte. The 23 `JSR
SubUpdateSprPos` call sites were counted in `bank_01.asm`. There are none in
`bank_02.asm` or `bank_03.asm`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from
the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Mario is not affected.** He has his own gravity and fall limit
tables (`PlayerGravity` and the table that goes with it) in bank `$00`. This
only changes sprites.

**A sprite standing on the ground is unaffected.** `SetSomeYSpeed__` writes `$00`
or `$18` to `SpriteYSpeed,X` whenever the sprite is on something. So walking
enemies look completely normal until they leave the ground.

**In water nothing changes.** Entry 1 of the table (`$10`) is the limit in liquid,
and it does not change.

**It is not zero gravity.** Sprites still fall, only slowly. Nothing floats or
stays in one place.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Hold Select and sprites stop dead

**Codes:** `EEB7-DFD0` + `C9E2-A4D5` + `F9E2-A405` + `4BE2-A465` + `4DE2-A4A5` +
`2DE2-A7D5` + `D7E2-A705` + `0AE2-A765` + `26E2-A7A5` + `C8E3-ADD5` +
`16E3-AD05` + `16E3-AD65` + `1DE3-ADA5`

**Raw form:** (address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part
of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `EEB7-DFD0` | `019034:FF` | `$AB` | `JSR $ABD8` becomes `JSR $FFD8` |
| `C9E2-A4D5` | `01FFD8:A5` | `$FF` | `LDA $15` |
| `F9E2-A405` | `01FFD9:15` | `$FF` | operand `$15`, `byetudlrHold` |
| `4BE2-A465` | `01FFDA:29` | `$FF` | `AND #` |
| `4DE2-A4A5` | `01FFDB:20` | `$FF` | mask `$20`, Select |
| `2DE2-A7D5` | `01FFDC:D0` | `$FF` | `BNE` |
| `D7E2-A705` | `01FFDD:03` | `$FF` | branch `+3` |
| `0AE2-A765` | `01FFDE:4C` | `$FF` | `JMP` |
| `26E2-A7A5` | `01FFDF:D8` | `$FF` | target low byte |
| `C8E3-ADD5` | `01FFE0:AB` | `$FF` | target high byte, `$01ABD8` |
| `16E3-AD05` | `01FFE1:68` | `$FF` | `PLA` |
| `16E3-AD65` | `01FFE2:68` | `$FF` | `PLA` |
| `1DE3-ADA5` | `01FFE3:60` | `$FF` | `RTS` |

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 15:45:00

**Mechanism:** `SubUpdateSprPos` at `$019032` is the routine that moves a
sprite. It adds gravity, limits the fall speed, moves the sprite by its X and Y
speeds, and then runs the block interaction. It is called from 23 places in
`bank_01.asm`, and together these cover almost every sprite in the game that
moves. Its first instruction is the Y position update:

```
SubUpdateSprPos:                              ; $019032
    JSR SubSprYPosNoGrvty                     ; 20 D8 AB
    LDY.B #$00                                ; $019035
    ...
    JSR SubSprXPosNoGrvty                     ; move by X speed
    ...
    JSR CODE_019140                           ; block interaction
    RTS
```

The cheat puts a short new routine in the unused space at the end of bank `$01`,
and sends that first call to it instead. Only one byte of the original routine
changes: the high byte of the call target, `$AB` to `$FF`. So `JSR $ABD8`
becomes `JSR $FFD8`. The low byte `$D8` is already correct. That is why the new
routine is at `$01FFD8` and not at another place in the free space.

The new routine is twelve bytes:

```
$01FFD8  A5 15      LDA $15                   ; buttons held this frame
$01FFDA  29 20      AND #$20                  ; Select
$01FFDC  D0 03      BNE +                     ; held -> take the exit below
$01FFDE  4C D8 AB   JMP SubSprYPosNoGrvty     ; not held -> the original call
$01FFE1  68         PLA                       ; + drop this routine's own
$01FFE2  68         PLA                       ;   return address
$01FFE3  60         RTS                       ; return to the sprite instead
```

When Select is not held, it jumps directly to `SubSprYPosNoGrvty`. That routine
ends with `RTS`, which returns to `$019035`, exactly where the original `JSR`
would have returned. So all of `SubUpdateSprPos` runs normally, and nothing is
slower or different.

When Select is held, the two `PLA`s remove the return address that `JSR $FFD8`
pushed. The `RTS` then pops the address that the *sprite* pushed when it called
`SubUpdateSprPos`. So the sprite's own code continues, and all of
`SubUpdateSprPos` is skipped: no Y position update, no gravity, no fall limit, no
X position update, and no block interaction.

**What it affects:** Hold Select, and every sprite that moves with
`SubUpdateSprPos` stops where it is. Walking enemies stop walking, thrown shells
stay in the air, falling platforms stop falling, and anything in the middle of a
jump stops there. Let go, and everything continues with exactly the speed it had.
Mario is not affected, because he has his own movement code in bank `$00`. So
this is a button that freezes the room.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `20 D8 AB` at `$019032`, so the high byte of
the call target is at `$019034`. `SubSprYPosNoGrvty` is at `$01ABD8`. This was
confirmed with `tools/linemap_U.tsv` and `SMW_U.sym`. The 23 callers were counted
in `bank_01.asm`. Every one of them is a `JSR`, never a `JSL`, and this is what
makes the stack trick safe. The routine ends with `RTS`, so no caller could use
`JSL` anyway. The 65 bytes from `$01FFBF` to `$01FFFF` are unused filler.
`bank_01.asm` ends with `%insert_empty($3E,$41,$41,$41,$41)`, which for the U
release writes `$41` = 65 bytes of `$FF`, and the reference ROM does have 65
`$FF` bytes there. Nothing in the ROM reads or calls that space. All thirteen
codes decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and match
`cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen
in play**.

**Caveats:** **Thirteen codes.** Real Game Genie hardware takes five, so this
one is only for emulators.

**Mario is not affected.** Nothing else that bank `$00` code controls is
affected either. The screen still scrolls, the timer still counts down, and the
music keeps playing.

**A few sprites will keep moving.** The 23 call sites cover most of the game. But
a sprite with its own movement code, one that calls `SubSprXPosNoGrvty` or
`SubSprYPosNoGrvty` directly and does not use `SubUpdateSprPos`, is not affected
by this cheat.

**Sprites stop interacting with blocks as well as moving.** At its end,
`SubUpdateSprPos` calls `CODE_019140`, the test for sprites against blocks. So
while Select is held, a frozen sprite does not test the ground under it either.
It does not fall through the floor, because it does not move at all. But a sprite
that is inside a block when you let go of Select may act strangely on the first
frame after.

**The early exit returns with `A` = `$20`.** The normal exit from
`SubUpdateSprPos` leaves whatever value the last instruction loaded. No caller
was found that tests it, but this is the one register that is different between
the two paths.

**Select does nothing in a level normally**, so you lose no control that exists.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked. The free space at the end of bank `$01` is `$41` bytes in J and U.
In the other three releases it is filled from a different file, so the new
routine would have to be placed again for those.

## Enemies that scroll off the sides of the screen never disappear

**Codes:** `826A-D760` + `822A-D7D6` + `828E-D763`
**Raw form:** `0180CE:BD` (orig `$1D`), `02D0CC:BD` (orig `$1D`),
`03B8FE:BD` (orig `$1D`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 15:47:00

**Mechanism:** There is one copy of the same routine of three instructions in
each sprite bank, so that each bank can call it with a `JSR`:

```
IsSprOffScreen:                               ; $0180CB, bank $01
    LDA.W SpriteOffscreenX,X                  ; BD A0 15
    ORA.W SpriteOffscreenVert,X               ; 1D 6C 18   <- the patched byte
    RTS                                       ; 60
IsSprOffScreenBnk2:                           ; $02D0C9, identical
IsSprOffScreenBnk3:                           ; $03B8FB, identical
```

`SpriteOffscreenX` (`$7E15A0`) is set for a sprite that is to the left of the
camera, or more than 255 pixels to the right of it. `SpriteOffscreenVert`
(`$7E186C`) is set for a sprite that is above or below the screen. The `ORA`
combines the two, so the routine answers "is this sprite off the screen in any
direction".

If the `ORA abs,X` opcode `$1D` changes to the `LDA abs,X` opcode `$BD`, the
second instruction replaces the first value instead of combining with it. The
horizontal flag is loaded and then lost, and the routine answers "is this sprite
off the top or the bottom".

The despawn test is the first thing that `SubOffscreen0Bnk1` does:

```
SubOffscreen0Bnk1:
  + JSR IsSprOffScreen                        ; \ if the sprite is not off
    BEQ Return01ACA4                          ; / screen, return
    ...                                       ; erase logic below
```

A sprite that has only scrolled off the side now gives zero. So the routine
returns before any of the erase logic: before the test for falling off the
bottom, before the `SpriteTweakerD & $04` "process offscreen" check, and before
`OffScrEraseSprite`.

**What it affects:** Every enemy that walks or scrolls out of view stays loaded
and keeps running. Walk right past a line of Koopas and walk back, and they are
all still there. They are where they walked to, not back where they started.
Level sprites stay behind you for the whole level.

The three codes cover the three banks that hold the main routines of sprites.

- Bank `$01` is Bullet Bill, Thwomp, Thwimp, Monty Mole, Yoshi, the Boos, the
  Grinder, the Springboard, the winged Goomba, both para-Koopas and the platform
  families.
- Bank `$02` is Torpedo Ted, Rip Van Fish, Pea Bouncer, Volcano Lotus and 17
  more.
- Bank `$03` is the Football, PorcuPuffer, Swooper, Bowser Statue, Rex,
  Fishbone, Rhino, Blargg, Mecha-Koopa, Ninji and the lift family.

Use only one code if you want only the sprites of one bank to stay.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `BD A0 15 1D 6C 18 60` at `$0180CB`,
`$02D0C9` and `$03B8FB`, the same seven bytes three times. So the `ORA` opcode is
at `$0180CE`, `$02D0CC` and `$03B8FE`. The despawn routines `SubOffscreen0Bnk1`
through `SubOffscreen3Bnk1` are called from 41 places in `bank_01.asm`. The
routines in bank `$02` are called from 27 places, and those in bank `$03` from
24. `IsSprOffScreen` itself has 12 more direct callers in bank `$01`, and 2 in
each of the other two banks. `SpriteOffscreenX` and `SpriteOffscreenVert` are
both written by `GetDrawInfo2` (`bank_02.asm`). The first gets an `INC` when the
16-bit `sprite X - camera X` has a non-zero high byte. The second is ORed with
`$01` or `$02` for the top and bottom edges of the sprite. The codes decode back
correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and match `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect
comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **The twelve sprite slots fill up.** Sprites that go off the side
never free a slot. So when twelve sprites are loaded, the game cannot make any
more. A long level will become empty: no new enemies appear in front of you,
because sprites behind you use every slot. This is the main effect you will see,
and it is not a crash.

**Dead sprites are still cleaned up.** A stomped enemy falls off the bottom of
the screen. That sets the vertical flag, which is the half that the patch keeps.
So kills still free their slots, and the game keeps working. This is the safe
half of the test to remove. If you remove the vertical half instead, slots are
lost much faster.

**Cosmetic effects now play off screen.** Twelve routines in bank `$01` use the
same test the other way (`BNE` → skip), to skip work for sprites that cannot be
seen: kick smoke, contact puffs, the throw-block shatter, the Yoshi egg,
`SmushedGfxRt` and three OAM helpers. Without the horizontal half, they no longer
skip a sprite that is only off to the side. So each frame does a little more work
than the game intends.

**Sprites still respawn as usual.** This only changes what happens to a sprite
that is already loaded. The level's own sprite loader does not change, so walking
back and forth over a spawn point works as it always did.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every enemy steals the horizontal speed of the sprite in the next slot

**Codes:** `85B9-D760`
**Raw form:** `01905E:B7` (orig `$B6`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 15:52:00

Tags: `interesting` `play-start` `challenge` `video-ready`

**Mechanism:** `SpriteXSpeed` is a RAM table of 12 bytes at `$7E00B6`, one byte
for each sprite slot. Sprite code reads it as direct page `$B6,X`, with `X` set
to the slot that is being processed. The X half of `SubUpdateSprPos` saves the
speed, moves the sprite, and then writes the speed back:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; $01905D  B5 B6  <- operand patched
    PHA                                       ; save it
    LDY.W SpriteInLiquid,X                    ; in water? halve the stored speed
    BEQ +
    ...
  + JSR SubSprXPosNoGrvty                     ; $019076  move by the table value
    PLA                                       ; $019079
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; $01907A  put the speed back
```

The patch changes the operand of that first load from `$B6` to `$B7`. So it reads
one byte further along the table: the X speed of the **next sprite slot up**. The
move itself does not change, because `SubSprXPosNoGrvty` reads the RAM table and
not the accumulator. What changes is the write at the end: the speed that is
written back to this sprite now comes from the sprite next to it.

The sprite loop counts **down**:

```
    LDX.B #$0B                                ; bank_01.asm:132
  - STX.W CurSpriteProcess
    JSR CODE_0180D2
    JSR HandleSprite
    DEX
    BPL -
```

So slot 11 is processed first and slot 0 last. When slot 5 runs, slot 6 has
already taken the speed of slot 7, which took the speed of slot 8, and so on. The
whole table moves down by one slot on every frame. A speed that enters at the top
gets to the bottom in the same frame, and does not need twelve frames to get
there. In practice, every sprite on the screen that uses `SubUpdateSprPos` soon
moves sideways at the same speed.

Slot 11 has no next slot. `$B7 + $0B` is `$C2`, the first byte of
`SpriteTableC2` ("various sprite properties"). So the speed that goes into the
whole chain is a state byte of sprite slot 0.

**What it affects:** Enemies slide along together. A Koopa next to a kicked shell
moves off at the speed of the shell. Put a sprite that is not moving in a high
slot, and everything on the screen stops. The source byte is a state value and
not a speed. So the value changes whenever sprite slot 0 changes state, and the
shared speed changes suddenly by itself.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `B5 B6 48` at `$01905D`, that is `LDA $B6,X /
PHA`. So the operand byte is at `$01905E`. `rammap.asm` gives `SpriteYSpeed` =
`$7E00AA`, `SpriteXSpeed` = `$7E00B6` and `SpriteTableC2` = `$7E00C2`. Each is
twelve bytes, and they are next to each other. This is why `$B7,X` reads the next
slot for slots 0-10, and `SpriteTableC2` for slot 11. The mapping from line to
address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_01.asm:2353` -> `$01905D`). The
code decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches
`cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen
in play**.

**Caveats:** **Sprites that set their speed every frame are unaffected.** If a
sprite's main routine writes `SpriteXSpeed,X` on each frame, for example one
that chases Mario or one that is being carried, it replaces the stolen value
before it is used. You see the cheat most on sprites that set a speed once and
then keep it. Most walking sprites do this.

**Mario is not affected.** His movement code is in bank `$00`, and has its own
speed variables.

**Sprites that never call `SubUpdateSprPos` keep their own speed.** The routine
has 23 callers. They cover most of the sprites in the game, but not all.

**In water nothing else changes.** The liquid branch that halves the speed still
reads and writes the sprite's own slot. Only the copy that is saved and written
back comes from the sprite next to it.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## How fast an enemy falls depends on which sprite slot it is in

**Codes:** `C8B0-D460`
**Raw form:** `01904A:AB` (orig `$AA`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 15:53:00

Tags: `interesting` `play-start` `challenge` `video-ready`

**Mechanism:** `SpriteYSpeed` is a RAM table of 12 bytes at `$7E00AA`, one byte
for each sprite slot, read as direct page `$AA,X`. The gravity step of
`SubUpdateSprPos` reads it, adds the gravity for this frame, writes it back, and
limits the result to the terminal fall speed:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $019049  B5 AA  <- operand patched
    CLC
    ADC.W DATA_019030,Y                       ; + gravity (3 in air, 1 in liquid)
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; back into THIS sprite's slot
    BMI +                                     ; rising? no cap
    CMP.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; \ falling: clamp to the
    BCC +                                     ; | terminal speed ($40 in air)
    LDA.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; /
```

The patch changes the operand of the load from `$AA` to `$AB`. So the speed that
gravity is added to is read from the **next sprite slot up**, but the result is
still written to the sprite that is being processed. The sprite no longer builds
up its own speed. On every frame, its fall speed is made again from the speed of
the sprite next to it.

The sprite loop counts down from slot 11 to slot 0 (`LDX #$0B ... DEX / BPL`,
`bank_01.asm:132`). So the next slot has usually already been updated in this
frame. This means each step down the slot list adds one more gravity step: the
sprite in slot 11 gets *(seed + 3)*, slot 10 gets *(seed + 6)*, and so on, all
limited to `$40`. The lower the slot number, the faster the sprite falls, and the
lowest few slots stay at the terminal speed.

The seed at the top of the chain is `$AB + $0B` = `$B6`, which is
`SpriteXSpeed` slot 0. So **the horizontal speed of sprite slot 0 is used as the
vertical speed of sprite slot 11**. When sprite 0 moves left, this is a negative
number, so the whole chain starts by going up.

**What it affects:** Everything that falls with `SubUpdateSprPos`. Two identical
enemies dropped next to each other fall at different speeds, because they are in
different slots. Falling platforms, thrown shells and stomped enemies all fall in
order of slot number. Nothing speeds up any more: each sprite falls at a constant
speed while the sprite in the next slot keeps the same speed.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `B5 AA 18 79` at `$019049`, that is
`LDA $AA,X /
CLC / ADC abs,Y`. So the operand byte is at `$01904A`. `rammap.asm` gives
`SpriteYSpeed` = `$7E00AA` and `SpriteXSpeed` = `$7E00B6`. Each is twelve bytes,
and they are next to each other. This is why `$AB,X` reads the next slot for
slots 0-10, and `SpriteXSpeed` for slot 11. The gravity and terminal speed tables
`DATA_019030` and `DATA_01902E` are read from exactly three places, all in
`SubUpdateSprPos`. The mapping from line to address comes from
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_01.asm:2344` -> `$019049`). The code decodes back
correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches `cheats({op:'make'})`. The
effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Enemies on the ground still look normal.** `SetSomeYSpeed__`
writes `$00` or `$18` into the sprite's own slot whenever it stands on something.
The block interaction at the end of the routine also stops a sprite that lands.
So walking sprites are not affected until they leave the ground.

**Mario is not affected.** He has his own gravity and fall limit in bank `$00`.

**The liquid rise clamp is untouched.** The other read of the table, which limits
how fast a sprite can go up in water (`$01903D`), still reads the sprite's own
slot.

**It can send sprites upward.** The chain starts from a horizontal speed. That
speed is negative whenever sprite slot 0 moves left, and a negative fall speed
means going up. The limit is skipped for negative values (`BMI +`), so sprites
can drift up off the top of the screen. When they do, they are erased normally.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every enemy is invisible and does nothing, but a kicked shell still works

**Codes:** `1D6A-04D9`
**Raw form:** `0185C8:60` (orig `$22`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 15:56:00

**Mechanism:** `CallSpriteMain` is the start code of three instructions that
runs a sprite's own behavior routine:

```
CallSpriteMain:                               ; $0185C3
    STZ.W SpriteXMovement                     ; 9C 91 14
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; B5 9E
    JSL ExecutePtr                            ; 22 DF 86 00   <- the patched byte
    dw ShellessKoopas                         ; 00 - the 104-entry handler table
    ...
```

`ExecutePtr` uses the accumulator as an index into the table of `dw` pointers
after the `JSL`. So this one instruction is what changes "sprite number `$0F`"
into "run the Goomba routine". If the `JSL` opcode `$22` changes to `$60`, the
start code ends with `RTS` instead. The sprite number is still loaded, and
`SpriteXMovement` is still cleared, but the game never gets to a behavior
routine. The three bytes `DF 86 00` become operand bytes that never run. The
stack stays balanced, because `CallSpriteMain` was called with a `JSR`.

In this game, a sprite's main routine does everything: it moves the sprite, tests
it against Mario, tests it against blocks, and writes its tiles to the OAM
buffer. Without the call, all four are gone at once. That is why the enemies
become invisible and do not only stand still.

**What it affects:** Everything in the normal sprite status. `HandleSprite`
dispatches on `SpriteStatus`, and status `$08` ("normal") has a fixed fast path
that jumps directly here:

```
HandleSprite:
    LDA.W SpriteStatus,X
    BEQ EraseSprite
    CMP.B #$08
    BNE +
    JMP CallSpriteMain                        ; status 8 goes here
```

Sprites still load and are still set up. `CallSpriteInit` (status `$01`) is a
different table with its own `JSL`, and it does not change. So each sprite is set
up and put into status `$08` as usual. It then stays in its slot and does nothing
for the rest of the level.

**The exceptions are the interesting part.** Four statuses do not use this start
code at all, so they still work:

- `$09` stunned, `$0A` kicked, `$0B` carried: `HandleSprStunned`,
  `HandleSprKicked` and `HandleSprCarried` have their own code. A shell that you
  have already kicked keeps sliding, spinning and killing.
- `$02` killed, `$03` smushed, `$04` spin-jumped and the rest also have their own
  handlers, so death animations still play.

Only three special cases come back here: `HandleGoalPowerup` (status `$0C`), the
Wiggler branch of `HandleSprKilled` (`CMP #$86`), and `HandleSpriteDeath` when
tweaker D bit 0 says that the main routine handles its own death. All three now
return at once.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `9C 91 14 B5 9E 22 DF 86 00` at `$0185C3`,
and the handler table starts at `$0185CC` with `04 89` (`dw ShellessKoopas` =
`$018904`). So the `JSL` opcode is at `$0185C8`. `CallSpriteMain` has exactly
four callers, all in `bank_01.asm`: the fast path for status 8,
`HandleGoalPowerup`, the Wiggler branch of `HandleSprKilled`, and
`HandleSpriteDeath`. Every one of them is reached from the main loop's
`JSR HandleSprite`, so an `RTS` here cannot unbalance the stack. The code decodes
back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and matches `cheats({op:'make'})`. The
effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Nothing despawns.** A sprite's main routine also calls the
offscreen check, so no sprite ever frees its slot. When twelve are loaded, the
game cannot make any more.

**The level can become impossible to finish.** The goal tape, the goal sphere and
every other object that ends a level are sprites, so they do nothing either. Keep
a way out that does not need one, or expect to leave with the pause menu.

**Yoshi, platforms and item boxes are sprites too.** This cheat does not only
affect enemies. Moving platforms stop moving and are no longer solid, and message
boxes say nothing.

**Mario is unaffected**, so he runs, jumps and dies when the time runs out, as
usual.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every sprite moves at one fixed speed, left or right

There are four versions of this cheat. For each frame, each version ignores the
sprite's real horizontal speed and moves the sprite at a fixed speed instead. The
sprite keeps the direction it was already moving in. Pick one. They patch the
same bytes, so you cannot combine them.

### Version 1 — everything moves at 4 pixels a frame (speed ±64)

**Codes:** `4BB1-DDD0` + `6DB1-DD00` + `DBB1-DD60` + `0DB1-DDA0` +
`B9B1-DFD0` + `81B1-DF00` + `6DB1-DF60` + `D3B1-DFA0`

**Raw form:** (address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part
of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `4BB1-DDD0` | `019060:29` | `$BC` | `AND #` |
| `6DB1-DD00` | `019061:80` | `$4A` | mask `$80`, keep only the sign bit |
| `DBB1-DD60` | `019062:09` | `$16` | `ORA #` |
| `0DB1-DDA0` | `019063:40` | `$F0` | value `$40`, so `$40` or `$C0` |
| `B9B1-DFD0` | `019064:95` | `$11` | `STA dp,X` |
| `81B1-DF00` | `019065:B6` | `$0A` | operand `$B6`, `SpriteXSpeed` |
| `6DB1-DF60` | `019066:80` | `$76` | `BRA` |
| `D3B1-DFA0` | `019067:0E` | `$B6` | branch `+14`, to `$019076` |

### Version 2 — everything moves at 2 pixels a frame (speed ±32)

**Codes:** `DCB1-DDD0` + `CBB1-DD00` + `4DB1-DD60` + `BDB1-DDA0` +
`D4B1-DFD0` + `0BB1-DF00` + `ADB1-DF60` + `B9B1-DFA0` + `81B1-D4D0` +
`6DB1-D400` + `D8B1-D460`

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DCB1-DDD0` | `019060:0A` | `$BC` | `ASL A`, sign bit into carry |
| `CBB1-DD00` | `019061:A9` | `$4A` | `LDA #` |
| `4DB1-DD60` | `019062:20` | `$16` | value `$20`, +32 |
| `BDB1-DDA0` | `019063:90` | `$F0` | `BCC` |
| `D4B1-DFD0` | `019064:02` | `$11` | branch `+2`, taken when positive |
| `0BB1-DF00` | `019065:49` | `$0A` | `EOR #` |
| `ADB1-DF60` | `019066:C0` | `$76` | value `$C0`, turns `$20` into `$E0` |
| `B9B1-DFA0` | `019067:95` | `$B6` | `STA dp,X` |
| `81B1-D4D0` | `019068:B6` | `$B5` | operand `$B6`, `SpriteXSpeed` |
| `6DB1-D400` | `019069:80` | `$B6` | `BRA` |
| `D8B1-D460` | `01906A:0B` | `$48` | branch `+11`, to `$019076` |

### Version 3 — everything crawls at 1/16 of a pixel a frame (speed ±1)

**Codes:** `DCB1-DDD0` + `CBB1-DD00` + `DFB1-DD60` + `BDB1-DDA0` +
`D4B1-DFD0` + `0BB1-DF00` + `E3B1-DF60` + `B9B1-DFA0` + `81B1-D4D0` +
`6DB1-D400` + `D8B1-D460`

These are the same eleven bytes as version 2, with two values changed:

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DFB1-DD60` | `019062:01` | `$16` | value `$01`, +1 |
| `E3B1-DF60` | `019066:FE` | `$76` | value `$FE`, turns `$01` into `$FF` |

### Version 4 — everything moves as fast as the game can count (speed +127 / -128)

**Codes:** `DCB1-DDD0` + `CBB1-DD00` + `5EB1-DD60` + `1BB1-DDA0` +
`DDB1-DFD0` + `B9B1-DF00` + `81B1-DF60` + `6DB1-DFA0` + `D2B1-D4D0`

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DCB1-DDD0` | `019060:0A` | `$BC` | `ASL A`, sign bit into carry |
| `CBB1-DD00` | `019061:A9` | `$4A` | `LDA #` |
| `5EB1-DD60` | `019062:7F` | `$16` | value `$7F`, the largest positive speed |
| `1BB1-DDA0` | `019063:69` | `$F0` | `ADC #` |
| `DDB1-DFD0` | `019064:00` | `$11` | value `$00`, so the carry adds 1 |
| `B9B1-DF00` | `019065:95` | `$0A` | `STA dp,X` |
| `81B1-DF60` | `019066:B6` | `$76` | operand `$B6`, `SpriteXSpeed` |
| `6DB1-DFA0` | `019067:80` | `$B6` | `BRA` |
| `D2B1-D4D0` | `019068:0D` | `$B5` | branch `+13`, to `$019076` |

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:07:28

**Mechanism:** `SubUpdateSprPos` at `$019032` moves a sprite by its speeds. It
is called from 23 places in `bank_01.asm`, and together these cover almost every
sprite in the game that moves. This is its horizontal half:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X        ; $01905D  the sprite's X speed
    PHA                         ; $01905F  keep the real value
    LDY.W SpriteInLiquid,X      ; $019060  \
    BEQ +                       ; $019063  |
    ASL A                       ; $019065  | in water: write 3/4 of the
    ROR.B SpriteXSpeed,X        ; $019066  | speed back into SpriteXSpeed
    LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X        ; $019068  |
    PHA / STA $00 / ASL A       ; $01906A  |
    ROR $00 / PLA / CLC         ; $01906E  |
    ADC $00                     ; $019072  |
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X        ; $019074  /
  + JSR SubSprXPosNoGrvty       ; $019076  move by SpriteXSpeed
    PLA                         ; $019079  \ put the real value back
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X        ; $01907A  /
```

Two things about this code make the cheat possible.

`SubSprXPosNoGrvty` does not get the speed in a register. It adds 12 to X and
then continues into `SubSprYPosNoGrvty`, which reads `SpriteYSpeed,X`. And
`SpriteYSpeed + 12` is `SpriteXSpeed`. So the value that really moves the sprite
is whatever value is in `SpriteXSpeed,X` at `$019076`.

The water block is 22 bytes long. All it does is write a different value into
that byte before the call. That is exactly what the cheat needs to do. So each
version writes its own few instructions over the start of the water block, and
branches to `$019076`.

At `$019060`, the accumulator still holds the sprite's X speed from the `LDA` at
`$01905D`, so the new code already has the value.

**Version 1** keeps only the sign bit, and sets bit 6:

```
$019060  29 80   AND #$80          ; $00 if moving right, $80 if moving left
$019062  09 40   ORA #$40          ; -> $40 (+64) or $C0 (-64)
$019064  95 B6   STA SpriteXSpeed,X
$019066  80 0E   BRA +             ; to $019076
```

`$40` and `$C0` are the same distance from zero. That is why 64 is the only speed
that fits in four bytes. The other versions must test the sign separately:

```
$019060  0A      ASL A             ; sign bit into the carry
$019061  A9 20   LDA #$20          ; assume moving right
$019063  90 02   BCC +             ; it was, so keep $20
$019065  49 C0   EOR #$C0          ; it was not: $20 -> $E0, which is -32
$019067  95 B6 + STA SpriteXSpeed,X
$019069  80 0B   BRA ++            ; to $019076
```

Version 3 is the same code with `$01` and `$FE` instead of `$20` and `$C0`. This
gives `$01` and `$FF`.

Version 4 uses the carry as a number, not as a branch:

```
$019060  0A      ASL A             ; sign bit into the carry
$019061  A9 7F   LDA #$7F          ; +127
$019063  69 00   ADC #$00          ; add the carry: $7F, or $80 when negative
$019065  95 B6   STA SpriteXSpeed,X
$019067  80 0D   BRA +             ; to $019076
```

`$80` is -128. So this is the fastest speed that the byte can hold in each
direction.

**What the speeds mean.** `SubSprYPosNoGrvty` multiplies the speed by 16 and
adds it to the sub-pixel position. So a speed of 16 is one pixel a frame. Version
1 is 4 pixels a frame, version 2 is 2, version 4 is a little less than 8, and
version 3 is 1/16 of a pixel. At that speed a sprite needs about four seconds to
move one pixel.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `BC 4A 16 F0 11 0A 76 B6 B5 B6 48` at
`$019060`, which is the water block above, and `20 CC AB` at `$019076`. The
`BEQ` at `$019063` is `F0 11`, so its target is `$019076`. It is the only branch
into the block, and every version writes over it, so no path can skip the new
code. All four versions decode back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`, and
match `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not
seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **The real speed is not changed.** The `PHA` at `$01905F` and the
`PLA` at `$019079` write the sprite's own X speed back after the move. So
everything that reads `SpriteXSpeed` later (turning at walls, being kicked,
bouncing off other sprites) still sees the normal value. Only the distance moved
on each frame is fixed.

**Sprites that were standing still start moving right.** A speed of `$00` has
its sign bit clear, so it counts as positive. Sprites that are not moving,
sprites at the top of a jump, and platforms that never move sideways all drift
to the right. In version 4 they go off the screen very fast.

**Sprites no longer slow down in water.** The block that the cheat writes over is
the one that reduces a sprite's speed to 3/4 while it is in liquid. So that no
longer happens.

**Not every sprite goes through this routine.** The 23 callers cover most walking
and flying enemies. But sprites that move themselves, such as Lakitu, the
rotating platforms and some bosses, set their positions directly and are not
affected.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Gravity barely pulls on enemies at all

There are two versions of this one-code cheat. They patch the same byte, so pick
one.

### Version 1 — a third of normal gravity

**Codes:** `DFB7-DDD0`
**Raw form:** `019030:01` (orig `$03`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)

### Version 2 — no gravity at all

**Codes:** `DDB7-DDD0`
**Raw form:** `019030:00` (orig `$03`)

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:07:28

**Mechanism:** `SubUpdateSprPos` is the routine that adds a sprite's speed to its
position. It is called from 23 places in `bank_01.asm`, and together these cover
almost every sprite in the game that moves. Two tables of two bytes are directly
above it:

```
DATA_01902E:                                  ; $01902E
    db $40,$10                                ; terminal fall speed: air, liquid
DATA_019030:                                  ; $019030
    db $03,$01                                ; gravity per frame:   air, liquid
```

`Y` is 0 for a sprite in air and 1 for a sprite in liquid. So entry 0 of each
table is the one that is used almost all the time. This is the gravity step:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $019049
    CLC
    ADC.W DATA_019030,Y                       ; speed += gravity
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    BMI +                                     ; rising? no cap, leave it alone
    CMP.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; \ falling: clamp to the
    BCC +                                     ; | terminal speed
    LDA.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; /
  +
```

The patched byte is entry 0 of `DATA_019030`, the amount added to a sprite's Y
speed on every frame while it is in the air. This works the opposite way from the
"Every enemy falls in slow motion" code above. That code lowers the speed limit
and does not change the acceleration. This code lowers the acceleration and does
not change the limit.

**Version 1** sets it to `$01`, the same value that the game already uses under
water. Sprites still speed up, and still get to the normal terminal speed of
`$40`, but this takes 64 frames instead of 21. So everything falls in a long,
gentle curve, and a thrown shell or an enemy sent into the air goes about three
times as far before it comes down.

**Version 2** sets it to `$00`. Nothing is ever added, so a sprite's Y speed only
changes when another routine sets it. A sprite keeps its vertical speed forever,
whatever that speed is.

**What version 2 actually looks like.** Not everything floats. `SetSomeYSpeed__`
writes `$00` or `$18` into `SpriteYSpeed,X` for any sprite that stands on
something. So walking enemies stay on the ground as usual. When one walks off a
ledge, it keeps the `$18` it was given, and sinks at a steady 1.5 pixels a frame
forever, without speeding up. A sprite that is thrown or knocked upward never
slows down. It goes up at a constant speed until it leaves the level.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `40 10 03 01` at `$01902E`, which is the two
tables byte for byte. `DATA_019030` and `DATA_01902E` are used in exactly three
places, all in `SubUpdateSprPos` (`bank_01.asm` lines 2346, 2349 and 2351). So
no other code reads the patched byte. Both codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`, and match `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Mario is not affected.** He has his own gravity table in bank
`$00`. This only changes sprites.

**In water nothing changes.** Entry 1 of the table (`$01`) is the gravity in
liquid, and it does not change. This also means that with version 1, air and
water work in the same way.

**Sprites that set their own speed are unaffected.** Anything that writes
`SpriteYSpeed,X` directly on each frame (thwomps, some bosses, sprites on a fixed
path) keeps doing exactly what it did.

**Version 2 can strand things.** A sprite that drifts up at a constant speed never
comes back. A sprite whose speed is `$00` in the air stays there until something
hits it.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Enemies are slammed to the ground by huge gravity

There are two versions of this one-code cheat. They patch the same byte, so pick
one.

### Version 1 — about ten times normal gravity

**Codes:** `4DB7-DDD0`
**Raw form:** `019030:20` (orig `$03`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)

### Version 2 — the hardest pull the routine can take

**Codes:** `7EB7-DDD0`
**Raw form:** `019030:3F` (orig `$03`)

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:07:28

**Mechanism:** The patched byte is entry 0 of `DATA_019030`, the amount added to
a sprite's Y speed on every frame while it is in the air. The tables and the
gravity step are described in full under "Gravity barely pulls on enemies at
all" above. This is the short form:

```
DATA_01902E:  db $40,$10                      ; $01902E terminal fall speed
DATA_019030:  db $03,$01                      ; $019030 gravity per frame
...
  + LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $019049
    CLC
    ADC.W DATA_019030,Y                       ; speed += gravity
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
    BMI +                                     ; rising? no cap
    CMP.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; falling: clamp to $40
    BCC +
    LDA.W DATA_01902E,Y
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X
  +
```

Normally a sprite that starts from rest needs 21 frames to get to the terminal
speed of `$40`. **Version 1** gets there in two frames, and **version 2** in one.
Upward movement also stops just as fast. An enemy knocked into the air goes up for
a frame or two, and is then pulled straight back down. Jumping enemies no longer
get over anything, thrown shells fall almost straight down, and anything that
leaves a ledge is on the floor again at once.

**Why `$3F` is the limit.** The limit on speed only runs when the new speed is
positive (`BMI +` skips it). A sprite that is at the limited speed `$40` gets the
gravity added again on the next frame. So the sum must stay below `$80`, or it
becomes negative and the limit is skipped. `$40 + $3F = $7F`, which is still
limited. At `$40` and above, the sum wraps to a negative speed, and the sprite
goes up very fast instead. Then it wraps again. So everything in the level would
bounce up and down every few frames and would not fall. That is a different
cheat, not this one.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `40 10 03 01` at `$01902E`, which is the two
tables byte for byte. `DATA_019030` and `DATA_01902E` are used in exactly three
places, all in `SubUpdateSprPos` (`bank_01.asm` lines 2346, 2349 and 2351). So
no other code reads the patched byte. Both codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`, and match `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Mario is not affected.** He has his own gravity table in bank
`$00`. This only changes sprites.

**In water nothing changes.** Entry 1 of the table (`$01`) is the gravity in
liquid, and it does not change. So sprites in water fall normally.

**Walking enemies look the same on flat ground.** `SetSomeYSpeed__` writes `$00`
or `$18` to `SpriteYSpeed,X` for any sprite that stands on something. So you only
see the change when a sprite is in the air.

**Sprites that set their own speed are unaffected**, so thwomps, sprites on a
fixed path and some bosses act normally.

**Some levels may become unwinnable.** Jumping and flying enemies that are part of
a route, and any platform that uses this routine, no longer get to where they did
before.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every sprite rises or falls at one fixed speed

There are four versions of this cheat. Each one replaces the gravity step with
a fixed vertical speed. The sprite keeps the direction it was already moving in.
Pick one. They patch the same bytes, so you cannot combine them.

### Version 1 — 4 pixels a frame (Y speed ±64), four codes

**Codes:** `4BB0-D4A0` + `6DB0-D7D0` + `DBB0-D700` + `0DB0-D760`

of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `4BB0-D4A0` | `01904B:29` | `$18` | `AND #` |
| `6DB0-D7D0` | `01904C:80` | `$79` | mask `$80`, keep only the sign bit |
| `DBB0-D700` | `01904D:09` | `$30` | `ORA #` |
| `0DB0-D760` | `01904E:40` | `$90` | value `$40`, so `$40` or `$C0` |

| `0BB9-DDD0` | `019050:49` | `$AA` | `EOR #` |
| `ADB9-DD00` | `019051:C0` | `$30` | value `$C0`, turns `$20` into `$E0` |

`0BB9-DDD0` + `E3B9-DD00` + `B9B9-DD60` + `CCB9-DDA0` + `6DB9-DFD0` +
`D5B9-DF00`

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |

**Codes:** `DCB0-D4A0` + `CBB0-D7D0` + `5EB0-D700` + `1BB0-D760` +
`DDB0-D7A0` + `B9B9-DDD0` + `CCB9-DD00` + `6DB9-DD60` + `DBB9-DDA0`

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `DCB0-D4A0` | `01904B:0A` | `$18` | `ASL A`, sign bit into carry |
| `CBB0-D7D0` | `01904C:A9` | `$79` | `LDA #` |
| `5EB0-D700` | `01904D:7F` | `$30` | value `$7F`, the largest positive speed |
| `1BB0-D760` | `01904E:69` | `$90` | `ADC #` |

| `6DB9-DD60` | `019052:80` | `$0A` | `BRA` |
| `DBB9-DDA0` | `019053:09` | `$D9` | branch `+9`, to `$01905D` |

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:13:22

**Mechanism:** This is the vertical version of "Every sprite moves at one fixed
speed, left or right". It works in a different way, because the vertical part of
`SubUpdateSprPos` has a different layout. The routine moves the sprite by its Y
speed *first*, and then updates that speed for the next frame:

```
SubUpdateSprPos:                              ; $019032
    JSR SubSprYPosNoGrvty                     ; move by the current Y speed
    ...                                       ; liquid rise cap
  + LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $019049
    CLC                                       ; $01904B \
    ADC.W DATA_019030,Y                       ; $01904C | speed += gravity
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $01904F /
    BMI +                                     ; $019051 rising? leave it alone
    CMP.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; $019053 \ falling: clamp to
    BCC +                                     ; $019056 | the terminal speed
    LDA.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; $019058 |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $01905B /
  + LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; $01905D
```

So the cheat does not need to get to the movement routine at all. The value
written into `SpriteYSpeed,X` here is what moves the sprite on the next frame.
The cheat writes over the gravity step, starting at the `CLC` at `$01904B`. The
new code changes the speed that is already in the accumulator into a fixed value
with the same sign.

**Version 1 is only four codes**, because the four bytes after it are already
what it needs:

```
$01904B  29 80   AND #$80          ; $00 if falling, $80 if rising
$01904D  09 40   ORA #$40          ; -> $40 (+64) or $C0 (-64)
$01904F  95 AA   STA SpriteYSpeed,X   <- original bytes, unchanged
$019051  30 0A   BMI +                <- original bytes, unchanged
```

The original `BMI` and the terminal speed limit below it stay in place, and by
chance they do the right thing. A sprite going up has speed `$C0`, so the `BMI`
is taken and the limit is skipped. A falling sprite has speed `$40`, which is
exactly the terminal speed in the table. So the limit runs, compares equal, and
writes `$40` back. `$40` and `$C0` are the same distance from zero, and that is
why 64 is the cheap case.

The other three versions must jump over that last part, because it would change
`$20`, `$01` and `$7F`:

```
$01904B  0A      ASL A             ; sign bit into the carry
$01904C  A9 20   LDA #$20          ; assume falling
$01904E  90 02   BCC +             ; it was, so keep $20
$019050  49 C0   EOR #$C0          ; it was not: $20 -> $E0, which is -32
$019052  95 AA + STA SpriteYSpeed,X
$019054  80 07   BRA ++            ; to $01905D, past gravity and the clamp
```

The `BCC` opcode `$90` goes on a byte that is already `$90` in the ROM, so that
byte needs no code. Version 3 is the same, with `$01` and `$FE` instead of `$20`
and `$C0`. Version 4 uses the carry as a number, not as a branch:

```
$01904B  0A      ASL A             ; sign bit into the carry
$01904C  A9 7F   LDA #$7F          ; +127
$01904E  69 00   ADC #$00          ; add the carry: $7F, or $80 when rising
$019050  95 AA   STA SpriteYSpeed,X
$019052  80 09   BRA +             ; to $01905D
```

**What the speeds mean.** `SubSprYPosNoGrvty` multiplies the speed by 16 and
adds it to the sub-pixel position. So a speed of 16 is one pixel a frame. Version
1 is 4 pixels a frame, version 2 is 2, version 4 is a little less than 8, and
version 3 is 1/16 of a pixel, about four seconds for each pixel.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `B5 AA 18 79 30 90 95 AA 30 0A D9 2E 90
90 05 B9 2E 90 95 AA` at `$019049`. This is the load, the gravity step and the
limit, byte for byte. `$019049` is the target of all three branches above it
(`F0 0D` at `$01903A`, `10 08` at `$01903F`, `B0 04` at `$019043`). So every path
gets there with the Y speed in the accumulator, and nothing branches into the
middle of the replaced bytes. All four versions decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`, and match `cheats({op:'make'})`. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **There is no gravity left.** The cheat replaces the instruction
that adds gravity, so sprites do not speed up at all. Every curved path in the
game becomes a straight line.

**Sprites that were not moving vertically start falling.** A speed of `$00` has
its sign bit clear, so it counts as falling.

**Walking enemies still walk.** `SetSomeYSpeed__` writes `$00` or `$18` into
`SpriteYSpeed,X` for any sprite that stands on something. The block interaction
at the end of `SubUpdateSprPos` also still pushes a sprite out of the floor. So
enemies on the ground stay on the ground.

**Version 4 may push sprites through thin floors.** A little less than 8 pixels a
frame is fast enough for a sprite to go through a platform one tile thick between
two collision checks.

**Mario is not affected.** He has his own gravity and his own movement code in
bank `$00`.

**Sprites that set their own Y speed are unaffected**: thwomps, sprites on a
fixed path and some bosses write `SpriteYSpeed,X` themselves on every frame.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Star power is cancelled the moment any enemy is loaded

**Codes:** `BD6A-0FD9`
**Raw form:** `0185C4:90` (orig `$91`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:25:32

**Mechanism:** `CallSpriteMain` starts with an `STZ` that clears one global byte
before it runs a sprite's own behavior routine:

```
CallSpriteMain:                               ; $0185C3
    STZ.W SpriteXMovement                     ; 9C 91 14   <- $91 is the patched byte
    LDA.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; B5 9E
    JSL ExecutePtr                            ; 22 DF 86 00
```

`SpriteXMovement` is `$7E1491`. The byte just below it, `$7E1490`, is
`InvinsibilityTimer`, the star timer. If the low byte of the operand changes from
`$91` to `$90`, the start code writes its zero into the star timer instead. It
runs once per frame for every sprite in the normal status (`$08`), before that
sprite's own routine. So the star timer is zero before any enemy can check it.

**What the player sees:** Mario touches a star. `CODE_01C580` sets
`InvinsibilityTimer` to `$FF` and starts the star music. The next sprite in the
loop clears the timer again. Every sprite checks `InvinsibilityTimer` before it
hurts Mario or is killed by him (`LDA.W InvinsibilityTimer` / `BEQ`, in all three
sprite banks). So Mario gets no protection and kills nothing with the star.

**The star music never stops.** The normal music comes back in only one place:
in `DrawMarioAndYoshi`, while the timer counts down, at the moment the timer is
`$1E`. That code only runs while the timer is non-zero (`LDY.W InvinsibilityTimer`
/ `BEQ`). The timer never counts down through `$1E`, so the star music plays
until Mario dies or leaves the level.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `9C 91 14 B5 9E 22 DF 86 00` at `$0185C3`,
so the low byte of the `STZ` operand is at `$0185C4`. `rammap.asm` puts
`InvinsibilityTimer: skip 1` directly before `SpriteXMovement: skip 1`. The
order in each frame comes from `GM14Level`: `DrawMarioAndYoshi`, then the player
update, then `CODE_01808C` (the sprite loop). The sprite loop counts down from
slot 11, and `CallSpriteMain` is the fast path of `HandleSprite` for status 8.
The code decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from
the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **"Any enemy" means any sprite in status `$08`**, in any of the 12
slots, on the screen or not. That includes platforms, Yoshi, the goal tape and
many level objects. So in most places the star stops working at once. In a room
with no sprites loaded, the star works normally until the first sprite loads, and
then it stops.

**One frame may survive.** If the star is in a low slot, and no other normal
sprite runs after it in that frame, the timer is still `$FF` on the next frame
when `DrawMarioAndYoshi` runs. Mario can flash for that frame. Then the first
sprite of that frame clears it.

**`SpriteXMovement` is no longer cleared.** This is the same side effect as "The
turn-block bridges drag you sideways" (`C66A-0FD9`), which patches the same byte.
Nine of the ten readers of `SpriteXMovement` call a movement routine just before
