they read it, so they are not affected. The turn-block bridges
(`TurnBlockBridge`, `HorzTurnBlkBridge`) read it without doing that. So they move
Mario sideways by the last value that another sprite wrote. The two codes patch
the same byte, so use only one of them.

**The star is the only thing affected this way.** `CODE_01C580` is the only code
in the ROM that sets `InvinsibilityTimer` to a non-zero value.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every winged Goomba is a Wiggler

**Codes:** `6663-0709`
**Raw form:** `0185ED:88` (orig `$8D`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:27:43

**Mechanism:** `CallSpriteMain` runs a sprite's behavior routine. It finds the
routine by looking up the sprite number in the `dw` table after
`JSL ExecutePtr`. Entry `N` is at `$0185CC + 2N`, so sprite `$10`, "Bouncing
Goomba with wings", is at `$0185EC`:

```
    dw WingedGoomba                           ; 10 - $018D2E, bytes 2E 8D
    ...
    dw Wiggler                                ; 86 - $01882E, bytes 2E 88
```

The two routines have the same low byte, `$2E`. If the high byte of entry `$10`
changes from `$8D` to `$88`, the entry points at `Wiggler`. So every winged
Goomba runs the Wiggler's main routine. `Wiggler` is a wrapper of two
instructions (`JSL WigglerMain` / `RTS`), so it works with the table's `JSR`
style of call.

The sprite now crawls along the ground at Wiggler speed with a flower on its
head. It turns at walls, and when Mario stomps it, it gets angry and moves
faster. It no longer hops or flies.

**Why it holds together:** The Wiggler routine does not look at the sprite
number. Its whole body in `bank_02.asm` (`WigglerMainRt` and its draw and
contact code) never reads `SpriteNumber`. That is important. A replacement
routine that checks the sprite number usually goes into the wrong branch, or
reads past the end of a table. Everything that the Wiggler keeps between frames
is in the misc tables `SpriteMisc151C` (angry flag), `SpriteMisc1534`,
`SpriteMisc1570`, `SpriteMisc157C` (direction), `SpriteMisc1540`,
`SpriteMisc154C` and `SpriteMisc15AC`. The sprite loader sets all of them to
zero, and `InitStandardSprite` sets the direction to face Mario. So starting from
zero gives a normal, calm Wiggler.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `2E 8D` at `$0185EC` (entry `$10`), and
`$01882E` is the address of `Wiggler` in `tools/linemap_U.tsv`. A read of the
rest of the body of `WigglerMain` found no read of `SpriteNumber`. The code
decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **The body starts in the wrong place.** The four body segments of a
Wiggler follow a trail of 128 bytes of earlier head positions. `WigglerInit`
fills that trail with the start position of the head. But the sprite is still
set up as a winged Goomba, so the trail is never filled. The segments are drawn
from whatever the trail held before, often from an earlier Wiggler, or zeros.
The trail moves by one position each frame, so the body catches up with the head
after about 64 frames.

**Only four trails exist.** `CODE_02F011` picks the trail from the sprite slot
`AND #$03`. So slots 0, 4 and 8 share one trail, and so on. The level designers
never place more Wigglers than that allows, but winged Goombas never had this
limit. If two fake Wigglers are in slots that share a trail, their bodies are
drawn along each other's path.

**The graphics may be wrong.** The Wiggler's tiles are only in the sprite
graphics set that its own levels load. Donut Plains 4 has 11 winged Goombas and
no Wigglers, so there the Wigglers are probably drawn with unrelated tiles.
Forest of Illusion 1 has one winged Goomba among 15 Wigglers, and the Special
World level `SP8` has two.

**The tweakers stay a winged Goomba's.** Clipping, palette and what kills it
come from the tweaker rows of sprite `$10`. A shell or a star kills it the way it
kills a winged Goomba. It does not get angry like a Wiggler, because the Wiggler
case in `HandleSprKilled` tests for sprite `$86`.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Yoshi's pink-berry egg hatches a fish that flops about on dry land

**Codes:** `8D6C-6D09`
**Raw form:** `0186A1:B0` (orig `$88`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:30:22

**Mechanism:** When Yoshi eats his second pink berry, `CODE_01F116` stores
sprite `$6A`, the coin game cloud, in `YoshiEggSpriteHatch`, and he lays an egg.
When the egg hatches, `CODE_01F83D` copies that number into `SpriteNumber,X`,
calls `InitSpriteTables`, and leaves the sprite in the normal status. After that,
`CallSpriteMain` runs the routine at entry `$6A` of its handler table, at
`$0185CC + 2 × $6A` = `$0186A0`:

```
    dw CoinCloud                              ; 6A - $018833, bytes 33 88
    ...
    dw Fish                                   ; 15 - $01B033, bytes 33 B0
```

The two routines have the same low byte, `$33`. If the high byte changes from
`$88` to `$B0`, entry `$6A` points at `Fish`, the routine for the horizontal and
vertical fish. No level's sprite data places the cloud (no `lvl/spr/*.bin` file
has sprite `$6A`). So the egg is the only place where you see this code.

`Fish` starts with `LDA SpriteInLiquid,X` / `BNE`. Out of water, it takes the
flopping branch. `SubUpdateSprPos` gives it gravity. Each time it lands, it picks
a random X speed from `DATA_01B029` and a random jump from `DATA_01B025`, and
sometimes turns upside down. So a cloud does not rise out of the egg. Instead a
fish drops out and bounces around at Yoshi's feet. Mario can kick it:
`CODE_01B12A` plays the kick sound, knocks it away in status `$02` and gives
points. If it flops into water, it swims.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `33 88` at `$0186A0` (entry `$6A`) and
`33 B0` at `$0185F6` (entry `$15`, `Fish`). `tools/linemap_U.tsv` puts
`CoinCloud` at `$018833` and `Fish` at `$01B033`. The body of `Fish` up to
`CODE_01B14E` does not read `SpriteNumber` itself. Sprite `$6A` has no init
routine (its entry in `CallSpriteInit` is `Return0185C2`), and the egg hatch skips
init anyway. So the swap loses nothing. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen
in play**.

**Caveats:** **The fish is drawn with the wrong tile.** `Fish` draws with
`SubSprGfx2Entry1`, which indexes `SprTilemapOffset` with the sprite number. That
table has 84 entries (`$00`-`$53`). So sprite `$6A` reads a byte past its end,
and the fish is drawn as some unrelated tile.

**The tweakers stay a coin cloud's.** `InitSpriteTables` loads the rows of sprite
`$6A` from `Sprite1656Vals` onward. They are different from the fish's rows in
every table except the first. Clipping, palette and what can kill it follow the
cloud's settings. The meanings of those bits are not written down in this
disassembly, so the exact interaction is not worked out here.

**No coin game cloud.** `CoinCloudMain` never runs, so the cloud and the coin
count that it keeps in `GameCloudCoinCount` never appear.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every sprite bubble is a piece of goal tape that bobs up and down forever

**Codes:** `AD6D-AFA9`
**Raw form:** `018707:C0` (orig `$87`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:32:04

**Mechanism:** `CallSpriteMain` runs a sprite's behavior routine from the `dw`
table after `JSL ExecutePtr`. Sprite `$9D`, "Bubble with sprite", is at
`$0185CC + 2 × $9D` = `$018706`:

```
    dw BubbleWithSprite                       ; 9D - $018798, bytes 98 87
    ...
    dw GoalTape                               ; 7B - $01C098, bytes 98 C0
```

The two routines have the same low byte, `$98`. If the high byte changes from
`$87` to `$C0`, every bubble runs `GoalTape`. The bubble is still set up as a
bubble, but it never runs `BubbleSpriteMain`. So it never floats, never pops and
never lets out the enemy inside it.

`GoalTape` draws the three tape tiles (`CODE_01C12D`, tiles `$D4`/`$D5`) and
moves the tape up and down. When `SpriteMisc1540` runs out, it sets it to `$7C`
again and increments `SpriteBlockedDirs,X`. Bit 0 of that byte picks a Y speed of
`$10` or `$F0` from `DATA_01C0A5`. So each bubble becomes a bar of goal tape that
goes up for 124 frames, goes down for 124 frames, and repeats. It moves one pixel
a frame in each direction.

**Why the level does not end:** `GoalTape` ends the level only when Mario is
inside a box that it reads from four misc fields. `InitGoalTape` normally fills
them: the left edge in `SpriteTableC2`/`SpriteMisc151C`, and the bottom in
`SpriteMisc1528`/`SpriteMisc1534`. A bubble runs `InitBubbleSpr` instead. That
leaves `SpriteTableC2` = 0-3 (the content index from `InitExplodingBlk`),
`SpriteMisc151C` = 0 and `SpriteMisc1528` = 0. So the left edge of the box is at
X `$0000`-`$0003`, the far left edge of the level, and not where the tape is
drawn. Going through the tape does nothing. `SpriteMisc187B` is also 0, so if
Mario ever did get into that box, it would count as the normal exit.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `98 87` at `$018706` (entry `$9D`) and
`98 C0` at `$0186C2` (entry `$7B`, `GoalTape`). `tools/linemap_U.tsv` puts
`BubbleWithSprite` at `$018798` and `GoalTape` at `$01C098`. `GoalTape` and
`CODE_01C12D` do not read `SpriteNumber`. Bubbles are placed in three levels:
`123_FoI3main` (31), `0C0_CI5sub` (12) and `0CE_CI2room3c` (11), counted from
`lvl/spr/*.bin`. The code decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`. The
effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **The tapes never despawn.** `GoalTape` never calls a
`SubOffscreen` routine, because the real goal tape must stay loaded. So each
bubble that scrolls into view uses a sprite slot forever. Forest of Illusion 3
has 31 bubbles. So the 12 slots fill up, and after that no other sprite can load.

**Graphics may be wrong.** The tape tiles come from the sprite graphics set, and
the bubble levels may not load the page that the goal tape uses.

**What was inside is gone.** The bubble never pops, so the sprite inside it is
never let out.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every enemy always thinks it is standing on solid ground

**Codes:** `DB6F-DD00`
**Raw form:** `018011:09` (orig `$29`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:36:49

Tags: `interesting` `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** Sprites do not test the ground themselves. The collision code
writes a contact byte for each sprite, `SpriteBlockedDirs` at `$7E1588` plus the
sprite index, and `IsOnGround` reads the floor bit back:

```
IsOnGround:                                   ; $01800E
    LDA.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X                 ; BD 88 15
    AND.B #$04                                ; 29 04   <- $29 is the patched byte
    RTS                                       ; 60
```

`IsOnGround` is called from 38 places, all in bank `$01`. Every call is a
`JSR IsOnGround` with a `BEQ` or `BNE` right after it. No caller looks at which
bits came back. They only look at zero or not zero.

If the opcode `$29` (`AND #`) changes to `$09` (`ORA #`), the routine becomes
`LDA SpriteBlockedDirs,X / ORA #$04 / RTS`. The result always has bit 2 set, so
it is never zero. So all 38 callers get "yes, on the ground" for every sprite,
all the time. This is the version of "Hold Select and every enemy in the level
thinks it is standing on solid ground" that is always on, with no button.

**What it does:** Koopas and Goombas walk straight off ledges and keep walking in
the air. Sprites that fall run their landing code on every frame. Shells,
Chargin' Chucks and Wigglers keep moving across empty space as if there were a
floor.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `BD 88 15 29 03 60 BD 88 15 29 04 60 BD
88 15 29 08 60` at `$018008`. This is `IsTouchingObjSide`, `IsOnGround` and
`IsTouchingCeiling` byte for byte, so the `AND` opcode is at `$018011`. Sprite
code runs with an 8-bit accumulator, so `$09` takes a one-byte immediate, the
same as `$29`. So the routine stays six bytes long and ends with its own `RTS`.
The code decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from
the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Falling becomes odd, not simply stopped.** `SubUpdateSprPos`
handles position and gravity, not this answer. But 13 of the 38 callers react to
"on the ground" by calling `SetSomeYSpeed__`, which sets the Y speed to `$00` (or
`$18` on a slope). The fall speed of those sprites is reset on every frame, so
gravity never builds up. They stay in the air, or drift down very slowly. The
exact result depends on whether each sprite checks the ground before or after it
moves.

**It is sprites only.** Mario's ground flag is `PlayerIsOnGround` `$7E13EF`,
which the player collision code in bank `$00` sets. Nothing here changes it.

**Do not combine it with the other `IsOnGround` cheats.** "Hold Select and every
enemy...", "Everything is permanently standing on solid ground, until you hold
Select" and "No enemy ever thinks it is standing on solid ground" all change the
same six bytes.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## No enemy ever thinks it is standing on solid ground

**Codes:** `DD6F-DD60`
**Raw form:** `018012:00` (orig `$04`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:36:50

Tags: `interesting` `demo-ready` `play-start`

**Mechanism:** `IsOnGround` is the routine that 38 places in bank `$01` call to
ask if a sprite is touching the floor:

```
IsOnGround:                                   ; $01800E
    LDA.W SpriteBlockedDirs,X                 ; BD 88 15
    AND.B #$04                                ; 29 04   <- $04 is the patched byte
    RTS                                       ; 60
```

`SpriteBlockedDirs` `$7E1588` is the contact byte for each sprite. The collision
code writes it, and bit 2 (`$04`) is the floor. Every caller is a
`JSR IsOnGround` with a `BEQ` or `BNE` after it, so only zero or not zero is
important.

If the mask changes from `$04` to `$00`, the instruction becomes `AND #$00`. The
result is always zero. So all 38 callers get "no, not on the ground" for every
sprite, all the time.

**What it does:** Everything that waits to land waits forever. Sprites that turn
around at a ledge only do so while they are on the ground, so they no longer
turn. Shells never bounce. Sprites that only walk, hop or attack while they stand
never start. No caller ever resets the Y speed on landing. So gravity keeps
adding speed up to the fall limit, while the block collision holds the sprite up.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `BD 88 15 29 04 60` at `$01800E`, so the mask
byte is at `$018012`. The 38 call sites were checked in pass 15: all are `BEQ` or
`BNE` right after the `JSR`. The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in
play**.

**Caveats:** **Sprites do not fall through the floor.** The contact bit is still
written, and the block collision still pushes sprites out of the ground. Only the
answer to the sprites' own code changes.

**It is sprites only.** Mario's `PlayerIsOnGround` `$7E13EF` is separate and does
not change.

**Do not combine it with the other `IsOnGround` cheats.** They change the same
six bytes.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Hold Select and every enemy in the game swims

**Codes:** `ADB9-0F60` + `EEB9-0FA0` + `C9EA-ADD5` + `F9EA-AD05` + `4BEA-AD65` +
`4DEA-ADA5` + `EDEA-AFD5` + `D7EA-AF05` + `0AEA-AF65` + `7CEA-AFA5` +
`B4EA-A4D5` + `0AEA-A405` + `FFEA-A465` + `B4EA-A4A5`

**Raw form:** (address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part
of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ADB9-0F60` | `019156:C0` | `$11` | `JSR $9211` becomes `JSR $FFC0` |
| `EEB9-0FA0` | `019157:FF` | `$92` | (high byte of the new target) |
| `C9EA-ADD5` | `01FFC0:A5` | `$FF` | `LDA $15` |
| `F9EA-AD05` | `01FFC1:15` | `$FF` | operand `$15`, `byetudlrHold` |
| `4BEA-AD65` | `01FFC2:29` | `$FF` | `AND #` |
| `4DEA-ADA5` | `01FFC3:20` | `$FF` | mask `$20`, Select |
| `EDEA-AFD5` | `01FFC4:F0` | `$FF` | `BEQ` |
| `D7EA-AF05` | `01FFC5:03` | `$FF` | branch `+3` |
| `0AEA-AF65` | `01FFC6:4C` | `$FF` | `JMP` |
| `7CEA-AFA5` | `01FFC7:3A` | `$FF` | target low byte |
| `B4EA-A4D5` | `01FFC8:92` | `$FF` | target high byte, `$01923A` |
| `0AEA-A405` | `01FFC9:4C` | `$FF` | `JMP` |
| `FFEA-A465` | `01FFCA:11` | `$FF` | target low byte |
| `B4EA-A4A5` | `01FFCB:92` | `$FF` | target high byte, `$019211` |

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 16:38:00

**Mechanism:** This is "All sprites use underwater physics" with a Select
button added. That cheat changes the first branch of the sprite liquid test,
`CODE_019211`, into `BRA CODE_01923A`, the path that sets bit 0 of
`SpriteInLiquid`. That routine has no space to test a button as well. So this
version does not change the routine, and puts a small new routine in front of it.

The block interaction routine `CODE_019140` clears `SpriteInLiquid,X`, and then
calls the liquid test:

```
CODE_019140:
    ...
    STZ.W SpriteInLiquid,X
    JSR CODE_019211                           ; $019155: 20 11 92
```

The first two codes change that call to `JSR $FFC0`. The other twelve write the
new routine into the unused `$FF` filler at the end of bank `$01`:

```
$01FFC0  A5 15      LDA $15                   ; buttons held this frame
$01FFC2  29 20      AND #$20                  ; Select
$01FFC4  F0 03      BEQ +                     ; not held -> the normal test
$01FFC6  4C 3A 92   JMP CODE_01923A           ; held -> "in liquid"
$01FFC9  4C 11 92 + JMP CODE_019211
```

**Select not held:** It jumps to `CODE_019211`. That routine runs exactly as in
the unmodified game, and ends with `RTS`. The `RTS` returns to `$019158`, where
the original `JSR` would have returned. Real water still works.

**Select held:** It jumps into `CODE_01923A` with `$20` in the accumulator:

```
CODE_01923A:
    TAY                                       ; Y = $20
    LDA.W SpriteInLiquid,X                    ; 0, cleared by the caller
    ORA.B #$01                                ; bit 0 = in liquid
    CPY.B #$04                                ; $20 is not $04, so not lava
    BNE CODE_019258
    ...
CODE_019258:
    STA.W SpriteInLiquid,X
CODE_01925B:
    ...                                       ; rest of the routine, then RTS
```

`$20` is never `$04`, so the lava path is never taken, and no sprite is killed.
After the store, the code continues into the rest of the routine, and its `RTS`
returns to `$019158` as before. Every sprite that runs block interaction gets
`SpriteInLiquid = $01` for that frame.

**What it does:** `SubUpdateSprPos` reads `SpriteInLiquid`, and uses the water
entries of its tables: gravity `$01` instead of `$03`, fall limit `$10` instead
of `$40`, X speed at three quarters, and upward speed limited to `$E8`. Sprites
with their own water code also read the byte. So Jumping Fish, Rip Van Fish,
Blurps and Porcu-Puffers swim on dry land. Hold Select, and for enemies the whole
level is under water. Let go, and on the next frame they use air physics again.

**Why only one call is patched:** `CODE_019140` calls the liquid test a second
time at `$01917D`. It only does this when `ScreenMode` bit 7 is set (levels with
layer-2 interaction), and with the sprite position moved by the layer-2 offset.
The liquid test only ever sets bits. So when the first call has set bit 0, the
second call cannot clear it. Not patching the second call saves two codes and
changes nothing.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `20 11 92` at `$019155`, and `$FF` from
`$01FFBF` to `$01FFFF` (`%insert_empty($3E,$41,…)` at the end of
`bank_01.asm`). `tools/linemap_U.tsv` puts the first `JSR CODE_019211` at
`$019155` and `CODE_01923A` at `$01923A`. `CODE_019211` has exactly two callers.
Both are `JSR`, and both are in `CODE_019140`. Every code decodes back correctly
with `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not
seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Splashes.** A splash is made when `SpriteInLiquid` is different
from the frame before (`$019248`, `EOR SpriteInterIndex`). So any sprite may
splash each time you press or let go of Select. Some sprites skip the splash
because of their tweaker bits.

**Lava does not kill sprites while Select is held.** The path for a held button
skips the tile test. So a sprite in lava is only marked "in liquid", not "in the
liquid that kills".

**Mario is not affected.** `PlayerInWater` is a separate byte with its own test
in bank `$00`.

**Fourteen codes is far more than real hardware takes.** A Game Genie cartridge
holds five, so this is a cheat for emulators.

**It can be combined with "Hold Select and sprites stop
dead".** That cheat uses `$01FFD8`-`$01FFE3` of the same filler, and this one
uses `$01FFC0`-`$01FFCB`, so they do not overlap. Do not combine it with "All
sprites use underwater physics", which is always on. That cheat skips the tile
test inside `CODE_019211` itself, so Select would make no difference.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every enemy takes the horizontal speed of the sprite in the previous slot

**Codes:** `89B9-D760`
**Raw form:** `01905E:B5` (orig `$B6`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 17:09:00

**Mechanism:** This is the other direction of *Every enemy steals the
horizontal speed of the sprite in the next slot* (`85B9-D760`). The two codes
patch the same byte, so use only one at a time.

`SpriteXSpeed` is a RAM table of 12 bytes at `$7E00B6`, one byte for each sprite
slot, read as direct page `$B6,X`. The X half of `SubUpdateSprPos` saves the
speed, moves the sprite, and then writes the speed back:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; $01905D  B5 B6  <- operand patched
    PHA                                       ; save it
    LDY.W SpriteInLiquid,X                    ; in water? halve the stored speed
    BEQ +
    ...
  + JSR SubSprXPosNoGrvty                     ; $019076  move by the table value
    PLA                                       ; $019079
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; $01907A  put the speed back
```

The patch changes the operand of the first load from `$B6` to `$B5`. So it reads
one byte back along the table: the X speed of the **next sprite slot down**. The
move still uses the sprite's own speed, because `SubSprXPosNoGrvty` reads the RAM
table and not the accumulator. What changes is the write at the end: the speed
that is written back to this sprite comes from the sprite in the slot below it.

The sprite loop counts **down** (`LDX #$0B ... DEX / BPL`, `bank_01.asm:132`).
So slot 11 runs first and slot 0 runs last. When a sprite takes the speed of the
slot below it, that sprite has not run yet in this frame. So the value it takes is
the value that the lower sprite had at the end of the previous frame. The
next-slot code moves a speed down all twelve slots in one frame. This code moves
each speed **up one slot per frame**. So a speed needs about twelve frames to
climb from slot 0 to slot 11. The sprites move in a wave: each one copies what the
sprite below it was doing one frame earlier.

Slot 0 has no previous slot. `$B5 + $00` is `$B5`, the last byte of
`SpriteYSpeed`. So the speed that goes into the bottom of the chain is **the
vertical speed of sprite slot 11**, and slot 11 has already run in this frame
when slot 0 reads it. A sprite in slot 11 that stands on the ground has a
vertical speed of `$00` or `$18` (`SetSomeYSpeed__`). So the chain often gets a
stop, or a slow drift to the right. When that sprite falls or jumps, the new
number moves up the slots.

**What it affects:** Enemies take the speed of the sprite next to them after a
short delay, not all at once. The speed of a kicked shell spreads to the sprites
in the slots above it, one frame for each slot.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `B5 B6 48` at `$01905D`, that is `LDA $B6,X /
PHA`. So the operand byte is at `$01905E`. `rammap.asm` gives `SpriteYSpeed` =
`$7E00AA` and `SpriteXSpeed` = `$7E00B6`. Each is twelve bytes, and they are next
to each other. This is why `$B5,X` reads the previous slot for slots 1-11, and
`SpriteYSpeed` slot 11 for slot 0. `SubUpdateSprPos` does the Y half before the X
half, so the vertical speed of slot 11 is already final when slot 0 reads it. The
mapping from line to address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`
(`bank_01.asm:2353` ->
`$01905D`). The code decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect
comes from the disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Sprites that set their speed every frame before they move are
unaffected.** If a sprite's main routine writes `SpriteXSpeed,X` before it calls
`SubUpdateSprPos`, it replaces the copied value before it is used.

**An empty slot breaks the chain.** Empty slots do not run `SubUpdateSprPos`, so
their speed byte never changes. The sprite in the slot just above an empty slot
keeps copying that old byte.

**Mario is not affected.** His movement code is in bank `$00`, and has its own
speed variables.

**Sprites that never call `SubUpdateSprPos` keep their own speed.** The routine
has 23 callers. They cover most of the sprites in the game, but not all.

**In water nothing else changes.** The liquid branch that halves the speed still
reads and writes the sprite's own slot. Only the copy that is saved and written
back comes from the sprite next to it.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Enemies in higher sprite slots fall faster, seeded by a sprite number

**Codes:** `CBB0-D460`
**Raw form:** `01904A:A9` (orig `$AA`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 17:10:00

**Mechanism:** This is the other direction of *How fast an enemy falls depends
on which sprite slot it is in* (`C8B0-D460`). The two codes patch the same
byte, so use only one at a time.

`SpriteYSpeed` is a RAM table of 12 bytes at `$7E00AA`, one byte for each sprite
slot, read as direct page `$AA,X`. The gravity step of `SubUpdateSprPos` reads
it, adds the gravity for this frame, writes it back, and limits the result to the
terminal fall speed:

```
  + LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $019049  B5 AA  <- operand patched
    CLC
    ADC.W DATA_019030,Y                       ; + gravity (3 in air, 1 in liquid)
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; back into THIS sprite's slot
    BMI +                                     ; rising? no cap
    CMP.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; \ falling: clamp to the
    BCC +                                     ; | terminal speed ($40 in air)
    LDA.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; /
```

The patch changes the operand of the load from `$AA` to `$A9`. So the speed that
gravity is added to is read from the **next sprite slot down**. The result is
still written to the sprite that is being processed.

The sprite loop counts down from slot 11 to slot 0 (`LDX #$0B ... DEX / BPL`,
`bank_01.asm:132`). So the sprite in the slot below has not run yet in this
frame. Each sprite's fall speed becomes *the speed of the slot below from the
previous frame, plus one gravity step*. Speeds climb up the slots at one frame
for each slot, and each slot adds 3 more. After a few frames, slot 0 falls at
*(seed + 3)*, slot 1 at *(seed + 6)*, and so on, limited to `$40`. **The higher
the slot number, the faster the sprite falls.** The next-slot code does the
opposite.

Slot 0 has no previous slot. `$A9 + $00` is `$A9`, the last byte of
`SpriteNumber`. So the seed at the bottom of the chain is **the sprite number of
whatever is in slot 11**, used as a speed.

- A low sprite number, such as a Koopa (`$00`-`$0C`), gives a slow start.
- A sprite number of `$3D` or more starts slot 0 at the terminal speed.
- A sprite number of `$7D` or more goes past `$7F` when gravity is added. The
  result is negative, which means going up, and the limit is skipped for
  negative values.

When slot 11 is empty, its sprite number byte still holds the last sprite that
used the slot.

**What it affects:** Everything that falls with `SubUpdateSprPos`. Two identical
enemies dropped next to each other fall at different speeds, because they are in
different slots. Nothing speeds up as it falls: each sprite falls at a constant
speed while the sprite in the slot below it keeps the same speed.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `B5 AA 18 79` at `$019049`, that is
`LDA $AA,X /
CLC / ADC abs,Y`. So the operand byte is at `$01904A`. `rammap.asm` gives
`SpriteNumber` = `$7E009E` and `SpriteYSpeed` = `$7E00AA`. Each is twelve bytes,
and they are next to each other. This is why `$A9,X` reads the previous slot for
slots 1-11, and `SpriteNumber` slot 11 for slot 0. The mapping from line to
address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (`bank_01.asm:2344` -> `$019049`). The
code decodes back correctly with `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:** **Enemies on the ground still look normal.** `SetSomeYSpeed__`
writes `$00` or `$18` into the sprite's own slot whenever it stands on something.
The block interaction at the end of the routine also stops a sprite that lands.
So a sprite in the slot just above a sprite on the ground falls slowly, at `$03`
or `$1B`.

**An empty slot breaks the chain.** Empty slots do not run `SubUpdateSprPos`, so
their speed byte never changes. The sprite in the slot just above an empty slot
falls at that old byte plus gravity.

**Mario is not affected.** He has his own gravity and fall limit in bank `$00`.

**The liquid rise clamp is untouched.** The other read of the table, which limits
how fast a sprite can go up in water (`$01903D`), still reads the sprite's own
slot.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Every sprite rises or falls at one fixed speed, always the same direction

There are four versions of this cheat. Each one replaces the gravity step with
one fixed vertical speed. This is different from "Every sprite rises or falls at
one fixed speed": here the sprite's own direction is ignored, and every sprite
gets the same speed and the same direction. Pick one. They patch the same bytes,
so you cannot combine them with each other or with that earlier cheat.

All four versions use the same two codes. Only the third code is different:

| Version | Codes | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| Always rising, slowly | `CBB0-D7D0` + `EEB0-D700` + `3CB0-D760` | -1, 1/16 pixel a frame up |
| Always falling, slowly | `CBB0-D7D0` + `DFB0-D700` + `3CB0-D760` | +1, 1/16 pixel a frame down |
| Always rising, 1 pixel a frame | `CBB0-D7D0` + `EDB0-D700` + `3CB0-D760` | -16 |
| Always falling, 1 pixel a frame | `CBB0-D7D0` + `FDB0-D700` + `3CB0-D760` | +16 |

**Raw form:** (address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part
of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)

| Code | Raw | Orig | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CBB0-D7D0` | `01904C:A9` | `$79` | `LDA #` |
| `EEB0-D700` | `01904D:FF` | `$30` | value `$FF`, -1 |
| `DFB0-D700` | `01904D:01` | `$30` | value `$01`, +1 |
| `EDB0-D700` | `01904D:F0` | `$30` | value `$F0`, -16 |
| `FDB0-D700` | `01904D:10` | `$30` | value `$10`, +16 |
| `3CB0-D760` | `01904E:EA` | `$90` | `NOP` |

**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 17:41:00

**Mechanism:** `SubUpdateSprPos` moves a sprite by its Y speed *first*, and then
updates that speed for the next frame:

```
SubUpdateSprPos:                              ; $019032
    JSR SubSprYPosNoGrvty                     ; move by the current Y speed
    ...                                       ; liquid rise cap
  + LDA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $019049  B5 AA
    CLC                                       ; $01904B  18
    ADC.W DATA_019030,Y                       ; $01904C  79 30 90   speed += gravity
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $01904F  95 AA
    BMI +                                     ; $019051  30 0A      rising? leave it alone
    CMP.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; $019053 \ falling: clamp to
    BCC +                                     ; $019056 | the terminal speed
    LDA.W DATA_01902E,Y                       ; $019058 |
    STA.B SpriteYSpeed,X                      ; $01905B /
  + LDA.B SpriteXSpeed,X                      ; $01905D
```

The value written into `SpriteYSpeed,X` here is what moves the sprite on the next
frame. The three codes change the three-byte `ADC` into a load of a constant and
a one-byte `NOP`:

```
$01904B  18      CLC                  <- original byte, unchanged, harmless
$01904C  A9 vv   LDA #vv              ; the fixed speed
$01904E  EA      NOP
$01904F  95 AA   STA SpriteYSpeed,X   <- original bytes, unchanged
$019051  30 0A   BMI +                <- original bytes, unchanged
```

`LDA #` sets the N flag from the constant, so the original `BMI` still works.

- For `-1` and `-16`, the branch is taken, and it jumps directly to `$01905D`,
  past the limit.
- For `+1` and `+16`, the code continues into the terminal speed limit, which
  does no harm. The terminal speed is `$40` in air and `$10` in liquid
  (`DATA_01902E`). `+1` is below both, so `BCC` skips the write. `+16` is below
  `$40`, and in liquid it is equal to `$10`, so the limit writes `$10` back.

That is why these four values need only three codes. The `NOP` is needed because
the byte after the constant is `$90`, a `BCC` opcode. The carry is clear there, so
if that byte stayed, the code would branch away.

**What the speeds mean.** `SubSprYPosNoGrvty` multiplies the speed by 16 and
adds it to the sub-pixel position. So a speed of 16 is one pixel a frame, and a
speed of 1 is 1/16 of a pixel, about four seconds for each pixel.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `B5 AA 18 79 30 90 95 AA 30 0A D9 2E 90
90 05 B9 2E 90 95 AA` at `$019049`. `$019049` is the target of all three
branches above it (`F0 0D` at `$01903A`, `10 08` at `$01903F`, `B0 04` at
`$019043`), and nothing branches into `$01904C`-`$01904E`. The `BMI` at `$019051`
branches `+$0A` from `$019053`, to `$01905D`. `DATA_01902E` is `db $40,$10`. The
mapping from line to address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`
(`bank_01.asm:2345` -> `$01904B`). All codes decode back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen
in play**.

**Caveats:** **There is no gravity left.** Sprites never speed up or slow down
vertically, and no path is curved.

**The rising versions send airborne sprites up and away.** Anything that leaves
the ground (a jumping enemy, a thrown shell, a stomped enemy, a falling platform)
drifts up and does not stop.

**Walking enemies still walk.** The sprite moves by its Y speed *before* this
code replaces it. `SetSomeYSpeed__` writes `$00` or `$18` into `SpriteYSpeed,X`
for a sprite that stands on something, so the move on the next frame still uses
that value. The block interaction at the end of `SubUpdateSprPos` also still
pushes a sprite out of the floor. So enemies on the ground stay on the ground in
all four versions.

**Mario is not affected.** He has his own gravity and his own movement code in
bank `$00`.

**Sprites that set their own Y speed are unaffected**: thwomps, sprites on a
fixed path and some bosses write `SpriteYSpeed,X` themselves on every frame.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## No music

**Codes:** `4A66-0F6D`
**Raw form:** `008186:2C` (orig `$8D`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-12 19:12:00

**Mechanism:** The game never sends music commands to the sound chip directly.
Code that wants a song stores the song number in `SPCIO2` (`$7E1DFB`). The NMI
routine then sends it to port 2 of the sound chip, `HW_APUIO2` (`$2142`), once
per frame:

```
I_NMI:
    ...
    LDA.W SPCIO2                              ; $008179  a new song requested?
    BNE +
    LDY.W HW_APUIO2                           ; $00817E  \ no: once the sound chip echoes
    CPY.W LastUsedMusic                       ;          | the last song, fall through
    BNE ++                                    ;          / and clear the port to 0
  + STA.W HW_APUIO2                           ; $008186  8D 42 21  <- opcode patched
    STA.W LastUsedMusic                       ; $008189  remember what was sent
    STZ.W SPCIO2                              ; $00818C  clear the request
 ++ LDA.W SPCIO0                              ; ports 0, 1 and 3: sound effects
    STA.W HW_APUIO0
    ...
```

The patch changes the `STA` opcode `$8D` to `$2C`, which is `BIT` with the same
absolute operand. `BIT $2142` only reads the port and sets flags. Reading an APU
port has no side effect. Nothing after it uses those flags, because the next
instruction is another `STA`. So the NMI still does all its other work:
`LastUsedMusic` still records the song, and the request in `SPCIO2` is still
cleared. But the song number never gets to the sound chip, so no song ever
starts.

**What it affects:** Every song and every music jingle. All 37 writes to
`SPCIO2` in the disassembly store a song number: a `!BGM_` constant, a saved
level song, or a line with the comment "Change music". These cover the title
screen, the map, level themes, the star and P-switch themes, course clear, death,
game over, boss themes and cutscenes. The music fade-out command uses the same
port, so it is also lost. But when nothing is playing, there is nothing to fade.

**Sound effects still play.** They use `SPCIO0`, `SPCIO1` and `SPCIO3`. The
three `STA`s that send those come after the `++` label, and do not change.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `AD FB 1D D0 08 AC 42 21 CC FF 1D D0 09 8D
42 21 8D FF 1D 9C FB 1D` at `$008179`, so the `STA HW_APUIO2` opcode is at
`$008186`. The only other writes to `HW_APUIO2` are in `SPC700UploadLoop`
(`bank_00.asm`). That loop sends upload addresses while it copies the sound
engine and music data. These are not song requests, and the loop only waits on
port 0. The only code that reads `HW_APUIO2` and `LastUsedMusic` is the NMI code
shown above. The mapping from line to address comes from `tools/linemap_U.tsv`
(`bank_00.asm:210` -> `$008186`). The code decodes back correctly with
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect comes from the disassembly and **was not seen
in play**.

**Caveats:** **Turn the code on before the title screen.** If a song is already
playing when you turn the code on, it keeps playing until the next song change,
and that change is lost. So the old song can keep playing.

**Provenance:** The addresses come from `tools/linemap_U.tsv` (fingerprint
`0589ebe7ef0f1639`), and were checked against a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` without its 512-byte copier header.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Mario throws fireballs while riding Yoshi, at any power-up

**Codes:** `DDAA-07A7`
**Raw form:** `00CDCF:00` (orig `$0C`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 18:21:49

**Mechanism:** Every frame Mario rides Yoshi, the player update jumps to
`CODE_00CDAD` (from `LDY PlayerRidingYoshi / BNE CODE_00CDAD`), which sets the
riding pose. It ends with a block of code the game never runs:

```
    LDA.W YoshiHasWingsEvt                    ; \ Check Yoshi wing ability address for #$01,
    CMP.B #$01                                ; / but this is an impossible value
    BNE Return00CDDC                          ; \ Unreachable/unused code
    BIT.B byetudlrFrame                       ; | Lets Mario (any power) shoot fireballs while on Yoshi
    BVC Return00CDDC                          ; |
    LDA.B #$08                                ; |
    STA.W Empty18DB                           ; |
    JSR ShootFireball                         ; /
Return00CDDC:
    RTS
```

`YoshiHasWingsEvt` is never `$01`, so the `BNE` always skips the block. The
patch sets the `BNE` displacement to `$00`. A branch of zero lands on the next
instruction, so both outcomes now fall into the block. Then `BIT byetudlrFrame`
copies bit 6 (Y or X newly pressed) into V, and on a press the block calls
`ShootFireball`, the same routine fire Mario uses on foot. The normal fire path
in `CODE_00D081` still refuses while riding Yoshi (`ORA PlayerRidingYoshi /
BNE`), so this block is the only way a fireball leaves Yoshi. `ShootFireball`
already has Yoshi rows: it steps its offset index on by two when
`PlayerRidingYoshi` is set and two more when `PlayerDuckingOnYoshi` is set, so
the fireball starts from Mario's hand at his height on Yoshi.

**Evidence:** the reference ROM holds `AD 1E 14 C9 01 D0 0C 24 16 50 08 A9 08 8D
DB 18 20 A8 FE 60` at `$00CDC9`, so the `BNE` is at `$00CDCE` and its operand
`$0C` (to `Return00CDDC`, `$00CDDC`) is at `$00CDCF`. `CODE_00CDAD` is at
`$00CDAD` in `SMW_U.sym`, and counting instruction sizes from there lands on the
same bytes. The code round-trips through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The block checks no power-up, so small, big, cape and fire Mario all throw
  fireballs on Yoshi.
- Y and X also make Yoshi stick out his tongue. One press does both.
- `ShootFireball` uses extended sprite slots 8 and 9 only, so at most two
  fireballs are on screen at once, the same as on foot.
- The wing check is gone too, so it also works while flying on a winged Yoshi.
- The block stores `$08` into `Empty18DB` (`$7E18DB`), which `rammap.asm` lists
  as unused and nothing reads.

**Provenance:** Address from `SMW_U.sym` (`CODE_00CDAD`) plus instruction
sizes, cross-checked against a direct read of `comparison_U.smc` minus its
512-byte copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was stale at the time and was not
used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## The auto-scroll sprite runs one of the unused scroll commands 04, 05 or 0A

Three separate cheats. Use only one at a time, because they patch the same
bytes.

| Version | Codes | Raw form (orig) |
|---|---|---|
| **05:** scroll right to the end, hide Layer 1, lift a solid Layer 2 | `8C8E-DDB5` + `8E8E-DD25` | `05BCF2:BA` (`$36`) + `05BCF3:BF` (`$BD`) |
| **04:** the screen scrolls vertically forever, jumping back 512 pixels each loop | `ED8E-DDB5` + `6786-D495` + `A486-D4B5` | `05BCF2:F0` (`$36`) + `05BC89:83` (`$4D`) + `05BC8A:C2` (`$C0`) |
| **0A:** the screen scrolls sideways forever, jumping back 6 screens each loop | `028E-DDB5` + `838E-DD25` + `4386-D495` + `A786-D4B5` | `05BCF2:4D` (`$36`) + `05BCF3:BE` (`$BD`) + `05BC89:2E` (`$4D`) + `05BC8A:C3` (`$C0`) |

(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 21:39:49

**Mechanism:** Scroll sprites are sprite numbers `$E7` and up in a level's
sprite data. When one scrolls into view, the sprite loader in `bank_02.asm`
stores `sprite number - $E7` in `Layer1ScrollCmd`, stores the sprite's first
data byte shifted right twice in `Layer1ScrollBits`, and calls `CODE_05BCD6`.
That runs a one-time setup routine for the command from the pointer table in
`CODE_05BCE9` (at `$05BCF0`). After that, `ProcScreenScrollCmds` runs a
per-frame routine for the command from the table in `CODE_05BC76` (at
`$05BC87`).

Commands 04, 05 and 0A (sprites `$EB`, `$EC`, `$F1`) have code behind both
tables, but no level places those sprites. All three cheats take over command
01, the auto-scroll sprite `$E8`: they point its setup entry (`$05BCF2`,
normally `CODE_05BD36`) and, where needed, its per-frame entry (`$05BC89`,
normally `CODE_05C04D`) at the unused routines.

**05** — setup `ADDR_05BFBA`, per-frame `ADDR_05C69E`. The setup writes `$0005`
to `Layer1ScrollCmd` itself, so only the setup entry needs changing.
- Setup: Layer 2 at X `$0000`, Y `$03C0`; clears `HorizLayer1Setting`,
  `Layer1ScrollBits` and every Layer 1 and Layer 2 scroll speed.
- Phase 0: raises `Layer1ScrollXSpeed` by 1 each frame up to `$0080` (half a
  pixel per frame to the right). When the camera's screen reaches
  `LastScreenHoriz - 1`, it sets `Layer1ScrollBits` to 1 and stops.
- Phase 1 (`ADDR_05C6CD`, the block marked `; \ Unreachable`): writes `$16` to
  `HW_TM` (BG2 + BG3 + sprites), so **Layer 1 disappears**. Then both layers
  scroll up, speeding up to half a pixel per frame, until `NextLayer2YPos` is 0.
- Every frame: Layer 2's X follows Layer 1's X, (`LastScreenHoriz` - 2) screens
  behind. When that is 0 or more, `ScreenMode` gets `ScrMode_EnableL2Int`, so
  Layer 2 becomes solid.

**04** — setup `ADDR_05BDF0`, per-frame `ADDR_05C283`. `ADDR_05BDF0` does not
set the command, so the per-frame entry for 01 is redirected too. (The table's
own entry 04 is `ADDR_05BDDD`, which picks a command from `DATA_05CA08` and then
falls into `ADDR_05BDF0`; for the bits these levels use it would give command 00
or put 04 on Layer 2, so it is skipped.)
- Setup: direction `Layer1ScrollType` from `DATA_05CA10` and a target Y
  `NextLayer1YPos ± DATA_05CA12` (stored in `Layer1ScrollXPosUpd`), both indexed
  by `Layer1ScrollBits`. Type 1 means down, anything else up.
- Per-frame: eases `Layer1ScrollYSpeed` toward `DATA_05CBE3,bits × 16` (±1 per
  frame) and moves the camera. When the camera gets within `DATA_05CBE3`
  pixels of the target, it adds `±$0200` (512 pixels) to `NextLayer1YPos`,
  opposite to the direction of travel. So it is an endless vertical loop.

**0A** — setup `ADDR_05BE4D`, per-frame `ADDR_05C32E`. Same shape as 04, but
sideways. (Entry 0A is `ADDR_05BE3A`, which picks commands 05 and 02 from
`DATA_05CA16` and never 0A, so it is skipped.)
- Setup: `Layer1ScrollType` from `DATA_05CA26,bits`; target X `$0F17` (screen
  15) for type 1, `-$0F17` otherwise (stored in `Layer1ScrollYPosUpd`).
- Per-frame: sets `Layer1ScrollDir`, eases `Layer1ScrollXSpeed` toward
  `DATA_05CBE5,bits × 16` (±4 per frame) and moves the camera. When it gets
  within `DATA_05CBE5` pixels of the target, it moves the camera back `$0600`
  (6 screens), sets `Layer1TileUp`/`Layer1TileDown` to force a tilemap reload,
  and does a 16-bit `STZ` of `$7E0095`-`$7E0096`: the high byte of
  `PlayerXPosNext` and the low byte of `PlayerYPosNext`. **Mario is moved back
  to screen 0 too.**

**Where you see it:** sprite `$E8` is placed in three levels' sprite data,
`009_DP2main`, `00C_BB1main` and `0C8_yoshiwingsdark` (names from `lvl/spr/`).
Their `Layer1ScrollBits` are 0, 3 and 4, which pick different table rows:

| Level file | bits | 04 | 0A |
|---|---|---|---|
| `009_DP2main` | 0 | up, 1.5 px/frame, loop at 320 px | right, 1.5 px/frame |
| `00C_BB1main` | 3 | down, 1.5 px/frame | right, 2 px/frame |
| `0C8_yoshiwingsdark` | 4 | up, 0.5 px/frame; type byte is `$E0`, so the loop distance comes from past the end of its table | left, 0.375 px/frame, target `-$0F17`, so it may never loop |

Rows 3 and 4 read past the end of some short tables (`DATA_05CA10`,
`DATA_05CA12`, `DATA_05CBE3`) into the next table. The numbers above come from
those neighbouring bytes.

**Evidence:** `CODE_05BCE9` (`$05BCE9`) reads `AD 3E 14 22 DF 86 00 36 BD 36 BD
...`: `LDA`, `JSL ExecutePtr`, then the table, so entry 01 is `$05BCF2` = `36
BD`. `CODE_05BC76` (`$05BC76`) reads `9C 56 14 AD 9D 00 D0 CB AD 3E 14 F0 C6 22
DF 86 00 4D C0 4D C0 ...`, so entry 01 is `$05BC89` = `4D C0`. Routine addresses
`ADDR_05BFBA`, `ADDR_05BDF0`, `ADDR_05BE4D`, `ADDR_05C283` and `ADDR_05C32E`
are from `SMW_U.sym`. Level sprite data was scanned with the 1-header-byte,
3-bytes-per-sprite, `$FF`-terminated format; no file holds `$E7`, `$EB`, `$EC`,
`$EE` or `$F1`. All codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effects
are derived from the disassembly and **have not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- Enter the level with the cheat already on. Setup runs once, when the sprite
  spawns.
- The levels lose their normal auto-scroll.
- 05: the levels were not built for Layer 2 at Y `$03C0`, so the background
  will probably look wrong. Nothing puts `HW_TM` back, so Layer 1 may stay
  hidden after the level.
- 04: the normal vertical camera code may fight the scroll. Moving the camera
  away from Mario probably kills him when he falls off the bottom of the screen.
- 0A: the jump back also clears the low byte of Mario's Y position, so he may
  drop or pop up to the top of the level.
- Setup entry 00 also points at `CODE_05BD36`, but no level places sprite `$E7`,
  so it is not changed.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym` plus direct reads of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was
stale at the time and was not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Every Wiggler is the unused winged cage instead

**Codes:** `1E66-6400` + `5C62-64D9`
**Raw form:** `018289:6F` (orig `$29`) + `0186D8:7A` (orig `$2E`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 21:47:01

**Mechanism:** Sprite `$88` is an unused "winged cage". Its setup and per-frame
code is still in the ROM, but no level places sprite `$88`. The sprite loader
runs a new sprite's setup routine from the pointer table in `CallSpriteInit`
(`$01817D`) and its per-frame routine from the table in `CallSpriteMain`
(`$0185CC`), both indexed by sprite number. Wiggler (sprite `$86`) points at
`InitWiggler` (`$018829`) and `Wiggler` (`$01882E`). The cage's routines,
`InitWingedCage` (`$01886F`) and `WingedCage` (`$01887A`), are in the same
256-byte page, so each redirect is one low byte.

What the cage does, from the code:

- `InitWingedCage` does nothing. It calls `Return02CBFD`, a bare `RTL`.
- `WingedCageMain` moves the sprite by `Layer1DXPos` and `Layer1DYPos` every
  frame, so **it stays at the same place on screen** while the camera moves.
- It draws four pairs of flapping wings as sprites (`ADDR_02CCB9`): tiles
  `$C6`/`$D6` and `$81`/`$D7`, 8x8, at X offsets `$00`, `$30`, `$60`, `$90`
  and Y offsets `$F8`, `$00`, `$F8`, `$00`. That is 16 OAM tiles.
- It does not draw a cage. `ADDR_00FF32` scrolls **Layer 3** so that Layer 3
  follows the sprite: `Layer3XPos = $30 - (sprite X on screen)` and
  `Layer3YPos = $100 - (sprite Y on screen)`. The cage itself was a Layer 3
  picture, and these levels have no such picture on Layer 3.
- It holds Mario in an invisible box, `$90` pixels wide, from its own X and Y
  (16-bit, level coordinates):
  - Mario moving right at 1 pixel/frame or more, and past X + `$90`: Mario is
    put at X + `$91` and his X speed is zeroed.
  - Otherwise (still or moving left), and Mario's X is at or left of the cage's
    X: Mario is put at the cage's X and his X speed is zeroed.
  - Mario moving up and above Y + `$20`: his Y speed is zeroed (a ceiling).
  - Otherwise, and Mario below Y + `$60`: Mario is put at Y + `$61`, his Y speed
    is zeroed, and `StandOnSolidSprite` and `StandingOnCage` are set (a floor).
- While `StandingOnCage` is set, `ADDR_00FF07` moves Mario with the camera, so
  he rides along.
- It skips the box while `PlayerAnimation` is 1 or more (dying, pipes, and so
  on).

**Where you see it:** Wiggler is placed 15 times in `11E_FoI1` and 10 times in
`126_SP7` (names from `lvl/spr/`).

**Evidence:** `CallSpriteInit` is at `$018172` in `SMW_U.sym`. `LDA #$08 / STA
abs,X / LDA dp,X / JSL ExecutePtr` is 11 bytes, so its table starts at
`$01817D`, and entry `$86` is `$01817D + $10C = $018289`. The ROM holds `29 88`
there (`InitWiggler`). `CallSpriteMain` is at `$0185C3`. `STZ abs / LDA dp,X /
JSL` is 9 bytes, so the table starts at `$0185CC`, and entry `$86` is
`$0186D8`, which holds `2E 88` (`Wiggler`). Both table starts were also found
by searching the ROM for the first six pointers of each table (one match each).
The ROM holds `8B A9 02 48 AB 22 FD CB 02 AB 60` at `$01886F` (`InitWingedCage`)
and `8B A9 02 48 AB 22 FE CB 02 AB 60` at `$01887A` (`WingedCage`). Level sprite
data was scanned with the 1-header-byte, 3-bytes-per-sprite, `$FF`-terminated
format. Both codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The box is built around a sprite that stays fixed on screen, but these levels
  let the camera follow Mario. Mario is usually to the left of the cage (it
  spawns near the right edge of the screen), so whenever he is not running
  right, the left-wall rule should yank him to the cage's X. Expect Mario to be
  dragged across the level. More than one cage on screen will fight over him.
- The floor rule pulls Mario up to Y + `$61` from anywhere below it.
- `HandleSprKilled` sends a killed Wiggler (status `$02`) back to
  `CallSpriteMain`, so a cage hit by a star or a shell keeps running.
- 16 wing tiles is more than a normal sprite slot's share of OAM, so other
  sprites may lose tiles or flicker.
- The wing tiles come from the sprite graphics the level loads; they may not
  look like wings.
- Moving Layer 3 shifts any Layer 3 background the level has.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym` plus direct reads of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was
stale at the time and was not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Clearing a level sends you to the Yoshi's Island submap, and the level stays unbeaten

**Codes:** `DDA2-0F64`
**Raw form:** `00C9D6:00` (orig `$06`) (address:new-byte — the original byte is
documentation, not part of the code; SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 21:52:56

**Mechanism:** When a level ends with the peace sign, `CODE_00C96B` goes to
`CODE_00C9AF`, and once the iris has closed (`SpotlightSize` = 0)
`CODE_00C9C2` decides which exit you took:

```
    LDA.W SecretGoalTape                      ; \ Branch if Goal Tape extra bits == #$02
    INC A                                     ; | (never happens)
    CMP.B #$03                                ; |
    BNE +                                     ; /
    LDA.B #$01                                ; \ Unreachable
    STA.W OWPlayerSubmap                      ; | Set submap to be Yoshi's Island
    LSR A                                     ; /
  + ...
CODE_00C9FE:
    STA.W OWLevelExitMode                     ; Store secret/normal exit info
```

The goal tape writes `SecretGoalTape` from its sprite's extra bits (`LSR`
twice of `SpriteMisc187B`, in `bank_01.asm`), so it is 0 for a normal tape and
1 for a secret one, and A reaches `OWLevelExitMode` as 1 (normal exit) or 2
(secret exit). A value of 2 was never used, so the block after the `BNE` never
runs. The patch sets the `BNE` displacement to `$00`. A branch of zero lands on
the next instruction, so the block now always runs: it writes
`!Submap_YoshisIsland` (1) to `OWPlayerSubmap`, and `LSR A` turns the 1 into
0, so `OWLevelExitMode` is 0. Exit mode 0 is the value for "no exit taken", so
the level is not marked beaten and no new path opens.

**Evidence:** `CODE_00C9C2` is at `$00C9C2` in `SMW_U.sym`. The ROM holds `20 44
CA A9 01 85 15 20 24 CD AD 33 14 D0 5F AD 1C 14 1A C9 03 D0 06 A9 01 8D 11 1F 4A
A0` there: `JSR`, `LDA #$01`, `STA $15`, `JSR`, `LDA $1433`, `BNE`, `LDA $141C`
(`SecretGoalTape`), `INC A`, `CMP #$03`, then `D0 06` at `$00C9D5`. Its operand
`$06` at `$00C9D6` skips exactly the 6 bytes `A9 01 8D 11 1F 4A`. The code
round-trips through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- It fires for every exit that reaches `CODE_00C9C2`: normal and secret goal
  tapes, and anything else that ends with the peace sign and the iris.
- `OWPlayerSubmap` is two bytes, one per player, but this is a plain
  `STA.W` to the first byte. When Luigi is playing, it changes Mario's submap
  instead of his.
- Only the submap changes. Mario's overworld position stays where the level
  was, so on the Yoshi's Island submap he may stand off the paths or on the
  wrong tile.
- The level stays unbeaten, so you cannot progress past it while this is on.
- The `BonusGameActivate` branch after the block still runs, so a level that
  ends in the bonus game keeps doing that.

**Provenance:** Address from `SMW_U.sym` (`CODE_00C9C2`) plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was
stale at the time and was not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Skidding leaves sparkles, a puff or a contact star instead of skid smoke

**Codes:**
- Sparkles (smoke type 05): `D9E5-6DA7`
- Puff of smoke (smoke type 01): `DFE5-6DA7`
- Contact star (smoke type 02): `D4E5-6DA7`

Use only one of these at a time. All three patch the same byte.

**Raw form:** `00FE73:05`, `00FE73:01` or `00FE73:02`. The original byte is
`$03`. SNES Game Genie has no compare byte, so the code writes the value
whatever is there.

**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 22:03:49

**Mechanism:** `CODE_00FE4A` makes the small dust clouds under Mario's feet.
Every fourth frame it looks for a free smoke sprite slot. `CODE_00FE72` then
fills that slot: `LDA #$03 / STA SmokeSpriteNumber,Y`, the position (Mario's X
plus 4, Y plus `$1A`, or plus `$2A` on Yoshi) and `SmokeSpriteTimer` = `$13`.
The immediate `$03` picks the smoke type, and `CODE_0296C0` runs the handler
for that type every frame:

- 01 `CODE_0296E3`: the 16x16 puff of smoke that enemies leave. It draws a
  tile from `DATA_0296D8` by timer / 4, so timer `$13` shows the last five
  frames of the puff animation.
- 02 `CODE_029797`: the 4-tile contact star (tiles `$7C`/`$7D`) seen when you
  stomp or kick something.
- 03 `CODE_029927`: the normal skid smoke.
- 05 `CODE_0298CA`: coin glitter. It draws nothing itself. When the timer is a
  multiple of 4, it spawns minor extended sprite 02 (a sparkle) at one of four
  offsets around the smoke position. Timer `$13` gives four sparkles for each
  smoke sprite.

All three handlers count the timer down and free the slot at 0, so each
sprite lasts `$13` frames, the same as the smoke.

**Evidence:** `CODE_00FE72` is at `$00FE72` in `SMW_U.sym`. The ROM holds `A9 03
99 C0 17 A5 94 69 04 99 C8 17 A5 96 69 1A DA AE 7A 18 F0 02 69 10 99 C4 17 FA A9
13 99 CC 17 60` there, which matches the source. The operand `$03` is at
`$00FE73`. The codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- `CODE_00FE4A` has three callers in `bank_00`: turning around at speed
  (skidding), sliding while ducking, and sliding down a slope. All three
  change.
- The skid smoke rises 1 pixel every 8 frames. The other types stay where
  they spawn.
- The puff and the contact star are 16x16, but the position is set for the
  8x8 skid smoke, so they appear a little low and right of Mario's feet.
- Sparkles use the minor extended sprite slots. If all 12 are busy, they
  overwrite the oldest one.
- Smoke type 03 is the normal value, so there is no "type 03" code.

**Provenance:** Address from `SMW_U.sym` (`CODE_00FE72`) plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was
stale at the time and was not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Mario always sparkles like he has a star, but is not invincible

**Codes:** `DD63-67AC`

**Raw form:** `028AEF:00`. The original byte is `$15`. SNES Game Genie has no
compare byte, so the code writes the value whatever is there.

**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 22:07:29

**Mechanism:** `RunSpriteSubsystems` runs once a frame in a level. When Mario has
a star (`InvinsibilityTimer` $08 or more), it masks `TrueFrame` with a value
from `DATA_028AA9` and draws a sparkle when the result is 0. Otherwise it goes
to `CODE_028AEB`:

```
CODE_028AEB:
    LDA.W PlayerSparkleTimer   ; AD D3 18
    BEQ +                      ; F0 15  -> skip the sparkle
    DEC.W PlayerSparkleTimer   ; CE D3 18
    AND.B #$01                 ; 29 01
CODE_028AF5:
    ORA PlayerXPosScrRel+1 / ORA PlayerYPosScrRel+1 / BNE +
    ... JSL CODE_02858F        ; spawn one sparkle near Mario
```

`PlayerSparkleTimer` is the short sparkle after a powerup. It is normally 0, so
the `BEQ` skips the sparkle. The code sets the branch displacement to 0, so the
`BEQ` does nothing. The timer then counts down every frame, wrapping from 0 to
`$FF`, and a sparkle spawns when its low bit is 0: every other frame. That is
the same rate as a new star (`DATA_028AA9` gives mask `$01` while the star
timer is `$60` or more). `CODE_02858F` places the sparkle at a random spot on
Mario as minor extended sprite 05. It does not change `InvinsibilityTimer`, so
enemies still hurt Mario and the star music does not play.

**Evidence:** `CODE_028AEB` is at `$028AEB` in `SMW_U.sym`. The ROM holds `AD D3
18 F0 15 CE D3 18 29 01` there, which matches the source. The `BEQ` operand
`$15` is at `$028AEF`. The code round-trips through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The
effect is derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- A real star still uses its own path, so it looks the same as before, slowing
  down as it runs out. When its timer drops below $08, the every-other-frame
  sparkle takes over again.
- No sparkle is drawn when Mario is off-screen or below screen row $D0.
- Sparkles use the 12 minor extended sprite slots. When all are busy, no new
  sparkle spawns, so other effects that use these slots (brick pieces, other
  sparkles) may be missing sometimes.

**Provenance:** Address from `SMW_U.sym` (`CODE_028AEB`) plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was
stale at the time and was not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Red Koopa Troopas sparkle like they have a star

**Codes:** `0366-ADD1` + `8F66-AD01` + `0C6E-DF01`

**Raw form:**
- `018B80:4E`, original `$98`
- `018B81:B1`, original `$88`
- `0188F5:4A`, original `$42`

SNES Game Genie has no compare byte, so the codes write the values whatever is
there. Use all three together.

**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 22:07:29

**Mechanism:** Sprites $00-$13 all run `Spr0to13Main`. What makes them different
is one byte each in `Spr0to13Prop`. When the sprite is on the ground, bit $08
makes it call `JumpOverShells` (only the yellow Koopas have it):

```
    PLA
    AND.B #$08                 ; 29 08
    BEQ +                      ; F0 03
    JSR JumpOverShells         ; 20 98 88  at $018B7F
  + BRA CODE_018BB0
```

- The first two codes change the call to `JSR CODE_01B14E`. `CODE_01B14E` is the
  sprite sparkle routine that Magikoopa's magic and three other sprites use.
  Every fourth frame, unless sprites are locked or the sprite is off-screen, it
  spawns minor extended sprite 05 (the same sparkle a star gives Mario) at a
  random spot on the sprite. It uses only Y and scratch RAM, and ends in `RTS`,
  and nothing after the call needs A or Y.
- The third code sets bit $08 in `Spr0to13Prop` entry $05 (the red Koopa
  Troopa): `$42` becomes `$4A`.

This only adds sparkles. The Koopa can still be stomped and still hurts Mario.

**Evidence:** `Spr0to13Main` is at `$018B0A` and `Spr0to13Prop` at `$0188F0` in
`SMW_U.sym`. The ROM holds `15 F0 05 A9 08 9D AC 15 68 29 08 F0 03 20 98 88`
from `$018B72`, so the `JSR JumpOverShells` ($018898) is at $018B7F. The table
reads `00 02 03 0D 40 42 43 45` from `$0188F0`, so entry $05 is `$42` at
`$0188F5`. `CODE_01B14E` starts `A5 13 29 03` (`LDA TrueFrame / AND #$03`). The
codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The yellow Koopas also have bit $08. Shell-less yellow Koopas ($03) and
  yellow winged Koopas ($0C) sparkle too, and no Koopa jumps over kicked
  shells any more.
- The sparkles only spawn while the Koopa walks on the ground. A falling Koopa,
  a Koopa in its shell, a shell-less red Koopa ($01) and red para-Koopas do
  not sparkle.
- The sparkle offsets were made for a 16x16 sprite, so they cover the lower
  half of the tall Koopa.
- With only the first two codes, the yellow Koopas sparkle and red Koopas do
  not. With only the third, red Koopas jump over kicked shells instead.
- Sparkles use the 12 minor extended sprite slots. Many Koopas on screen can
  fill them.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym` (`Spr0to13Main`, `Spr0to13Prop`,
`JumpOverShells`, `CODE_01B14E`) plus a direct read of `comparison_U.smc` minus
its 512-byte copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was stale at the time and was
not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Breaking the goal tape makes every sprite vanish instead of turning into coins

**Codes:** `FDA4-0400`

**Raw form:** `01C129:10`. The original byte is `$80`. SNES Game Genie has no
compare byte, so the code writes the value whatever is there.

**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 22:12:02

**Mechanism:** When Mario breaks the goal tape, the goal tape sprite sets the
level-clear music and `EndLevelTimer`, then calls `JSL TriggerGoalTape`
(`22 80 FA 00`). `TriggerGoalTape` (`$00FA80`) stops the P-balloon, sprite
respawn, the generator and silver coins. Then it loops over the 12 sprite
slots: a carried sprite gives Mario a powerup, and every on-screen sprite
(and the tape itself) turns into a coin.

A few bytes before it, at `$00FA10`, is a small routine that nothing calls:

```
    LDX.B #$0B            ; A2 0B
  - STZ.W SpriteStatus,X  ; 9E C8 14
    DEX                   ; CA
    BPL -                 ; 10 FA
    RTL                   ; 6B
```

It clears the status of all 12 sprite slots, which erases every sprite at
once with no puff or coin. The code changes the low byte of the `JSL`
operand from `$80` to `$10`, so breaking the tape calls this routine instead
of `TriggerGoalTape`. Both are in page `$00FA`, so one byte is enough. The
level still ends, because the music and `EndLevelTimer` were set before the
call.

**Evidence:** `Return01C12C` is at `$01C12C` in `SMW_U.sym`, so the 4-byte `JSL`
before it is at `$01C128`. The ROM holds `22 80 FA 00` there, and
`TriggerGoalTape` is at `$00FA80` in `SMW_U.sym`. The ROM holds `A2 0B 9E C8 14
CA 10 FA 6B` at `$00FA10`, after 8 `$FF` bytes of padding, and it matches the
source line marked "Unreachable". The code round-trips through
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the disassembly and **has not
been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The tape vanishes at once instead of turning into a coin, and enemies on
  screen give no coins.
- A sprite Mario carries past the tape vanishes, and he gets no powerup for
  it.
- The rest of `TriggerGoalTape` does not run. A P-balloon keeps Mario floating,
  a Bullet Bill or other generator keeps running (U release), and a sprite set
  to respawn can still come back during the walk to the right.
- Extended sprites (fireballs, hammers, smoke) stay on screen. Normally
  `TriggerGoalTape` clears all 8 of them.
- Only the goal tape uses this call. The goal sphere, keyholes and bosses end
  the level another way and are not changed.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym` (`Return01C12C`, `TriggerGoalTape`,
`CODE_00FA19`) plus a direct read of `comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte
copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was stale at the time and was not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Carrying an item past the goal tape gives a star instead of a powerup

**Codes:** `DDED-AF64`

**Raw form:** `00FB06:00`. The original byte is `$02`. SNES Game Genie has no
compare byte, so the code writes the value whatever is there.

**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 22:13:05

**Mechanism:** When the goal tape is broken, `TriggerGoalTape` calls
`LvlEndPowerUp` for each sprite Mario is carrying. It turns that sprite into
an item that pops up with status `$0C` (`HandleGoalPowerup`), and Mario can
walk into it. The item comes from `DATA_00FADF`, indexed by X:

```
LvlEndPowerUp:
    LDX.B Powerup             ; A6 19     0 small, 1 big, 2 cape, 3 fire
    LDA.W InvinsibilityTimer  ; AD 90 14
    BEQ +                     ; F0 02
    LDX.B #$04                ; A2 04     star row entry
  + LDA.W PlayerRidingYoshi   ; AD 7A 18
    BEQ +
    LDX.B #$05                ; on Yoshi
  + ... X += 7 for a springboard or P-switch, 14 for a key, 21 for Baby Yoshi
    LDA.L DATA_00FADF,X
```

`DATA_00FADF` is `74 74 77 75 76 E0 F0 / 74 74 77 75 76 E0 F1 / F0 F0 F0 F0 F1
E0 F2 / E0 E0 E0 E0 F1 E0 E4`. Entry 4 is `$76`, the star. The goal tape sprite
clears `InvinsibilityTimer` just before it calls `TriggerGoalTape`, so the
`LDX #$04` never runs and the star entry is never used. The code sets the
`BEQ` displacement to 0, so X is always 4 (or 5 on Yoshi).

| Carried sprite            | Normal item                      | With the code |
|---------------------------|----------------------------------|---------------|
| Shell, block, other       | mushroom, feather or fire flower | star          |
| Springboard or P-switch   | mushroom, feather or fire flower | star          |
| Key                       | 1-up                             | 1-up (`$F1`)  |
| Baby Yoshi                | 1-up                             | 1-up (`$F1`)  |

**Evidence:** `LvlEndPowerUp` is at `$00FB00` in `SMW_U.sym`. The ROM holds `A6
19 AD 90 14 F0 02 A2 04 AD 7A 18 F0 02 A2 05` there, which matches the source.
The `BEQ` operand `$02` is at `$00FB06`. The table bytes at `$00FADF` are as
above. The code round-trips through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- If Mario rides Yoshi, the code does nothing: X is 5 and he gets a 1-up as
  usual.
- If the star is already in the item box, the item becomes a 1-up instead
  (the same rule as other items).
- Getting the star increments `UnusedStarCounter`, which nothing reads.
- The level ends soon after the tape breaks, so the star has little use.
- For a key or Baby Yoshi the table entry changes from `$F0`/`$E0` to `$F1`.
  Both still make a 1-up; `$F1` stores 1 in `SpriteMisc1594` for it, and this
  has not been traced.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym` (`LvlEndPowerUp`, `DATA_00FADF`) plus a
direct read of `comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` was stale at the time and was not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Breaking the goal tape calls a loose Yoshi back, turns him green and keeps him for the next level

**Codes:** `47A4-0400` + `EAA4-0460`

**Raw form:**
- `01C129:23`, original `$80`
- `01C12A:FC`, original `$FA`

SNES Game Genie has no compare byte, so the codes write the values whatever is
there. Use both together.

**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 22:15:22

**Mechanism:** When Mario breaks the goal tape, the goal tape sprite sets the
level-clear music and `EndLevelTimer`, then calls `JSL TriggerGoalTape`
(`22 80 FA 00`, `$00FA80`). The codes change the call to `JSL $00FC23`. That is
an unused routine after `CODE_00FC1E` that nothing calls:

```
    LDY #$0B                      ; for each sprite slot, from $0B down
  - LDA SpriteStatus,Y / CMP #$08 / BNE next
    LDA SpriteNumber,Y / CMP #$35 / BNE next     ; a normal Yoshi?
    LDA #$01 / STA CarryYoshiThruLvls            ; keep Yoshi after the level
    STZ YoshiHasWingsEvt                         ; no wings
    LDA SpriteOBJAttribute,Y / AND #$F1 / ORA #$0A / STA SpriteOBJAttribute,Y
    LDA PlayerRidingYoshi / BNE done             ; ridden: stop here
    SpriteXPos = Layer1XPos - $10                ; left edge of the screen
    SpriteYPos = PlayerYPosNext                  ; Mario's height
    LDA #$03 / STA SpriteTableC2,Y               ; running state
    LDA #$00 / STA SpriteMisc157C,Y              ; face right
    LDA #$10 / STA SpriteXSpeed,Y                ; run right
  done: RTL
  next: DEY / BPL - / STZ CarryYoshiThruLvls / RTL
```

- `ORA #$0A` sets the sprite palette bits to 5. `YoshiAbilityIndex` maps
  palette 5 to colour class 0, green.
- A Yoshi state of 2 or more keeps its X speed on the ground
  (`CODE_01ECE1`), so Yoshi runs to the right behind Mario and he can jump on.
- `CarryYoshiThruLvls` = 1 is what makes the overworld save Yoshi for Mario.

**Evidence:** `CODE_00FC1E` is at `$00FC1E` in `SMW_U.sym`. The ROM holds `22 41 C6
01 60` there, then `A0 0B B9 C8 14 C9 08 D0 47 B9 9E 00 C9 35 D0 40 A9 01 8D C1
0D 9C 1E 14 B9 F6 15 29 F1 09 0A 99 F6 15 AD 7A 18 D0 28 ... A9 10 99 B6 00 6B
88 10 AF 9C C1 0D 6B` from `$00FC23` to `$00FC79`, which matches the source lines
marked "Unreachable instructions". `Return01C12C` is at `$01C12C`, so the
`JSL` is at `$01C128` and holds `22 80 FA 00`. The codes round-trip through
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the disassembly and **has not
been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- `TriggerGoalTape` no longer runs. Enemies on screen do not turn into coins,
  a carried item gives no powerup, the goal tape itself stays, a P-balloon
  keeps Mario floating, and extended sprites are not cleared.
- Enemies that stay on screen may still touch Mario during the walk to the
  right.
- If Mario is riding Yoshi, Yoshi only turns green. `YoshiColor`, which the
  overworld saves, was set when Mario got on, so he may come back in the old
  colour in the next level.
- If there is no Yoshi in the level, nothing visible happens.
- If Yoshi runs off the screen while no one rides him, the Yoshi sprite
  clears `CarryYoshiThruLvls` again, and he is lost as usual.
- Yoshi is placed `$10` pixels left of the screen edge, at Mario's Y. On uneven
  ground he may land in or fall through the ground.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym` (`CODE_00FC1E`, `ADDR_00FC25`,
`Return01C12C`, `TriggerGoalTape`) plus a direct read of `comparison_U.smc`
minus its 512-byte copier header. `tools/linemap_U.tsv` was stale at the time
and was not used.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Magikoopa waits longer before he raises his wand

**Codes:** `8DA4-DDA0`

**Raw form:** `01C023:B0`. The original byte is `$70`. SNES Game Genie has no
compare byte, so the code writes the value whatever is there.

**Recorded:** 2026-09-13 22:16:52

**Mechanism:** Magikoopa (sprite `$1F`) runs a four-phase cycle from
`SpriteTableC2`. When his fade-in ends, `CODE_01C004` starts phase 2 with
`LDA #$70 / STA SpriteMisc1540,X`. `SpriteMisc1540` counts down once a frame and
is the clock for all of phase 2 (`CODE_01BE6E`):

- He casts his magic on the frame the timer reads `$40`.
- His animation frame is `DATA_01BE69[timer >> 6]`, ORed with `(timer >> 3) & 1`.
  `DATA_01BE69` is `04 02 00`: frame `$02`/`$03` (wand up) for `$40`-`$7F`, and
  frame `$04`/`$05` (wand drawn out) below `$40`.
- The third entry, frame `$00`/`$01`, is for `$80`-`$BF`. The timer starts at
  `$70`, so this entry is never used. Frame `$00` is the pose he has while he
  fades in, and no wand tile is drawn for frames below `$04`.

The code starts the timer at `$B0`. For the first `$30` frames (0.8 seconds)
Magikoopa stands in his fade-in pose. Then the normal `$70` frames play: wand
up with sparkles, the cast at `$40`, and wand out until he fades away.

**Evidence:** `CODE_01C004` is at `$01C004` in `SMW_U.sym`. The ROM holds `BD 40 15
D0 55 A9 04 9D 40 15 FE 70 15 BD 70 15 C9 09 D0 04 A0 24 84 40 C9 09 D0 08 F6 C2
A9 70 9D 40 15 60` there, which matches the source. The `$70` is at `$01C023`.
`DATA_01BE69` at `$01BE69` holds `04 02 00`, followed by `DATA_01BE6C` (`10 F8`).
The code round-trips through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- He is visible and can be stomped or hit for `$30` more frames, so he is a
  little easier to beat.
- `CODE_01BE96` moves his first tile down 1 pixel in odd frames except `$03`.
  Frame `$01` passes that test too (`$01 - $02` wraps to `$FF`), so in the new
  band that tile bobs every 8 frames, as it does in frame `$05`.
- Do not use a value of `$C0` or more. Then `timer >> 6` is 3 and the frame is
  read from the byte after the table (`$10`), which is not a Magikoopa frame.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym` (`CODE_01C004`, `DATA_01BE69`) plus a
direct read of `comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.
`tools/linemap_U.tsv` was stale at the time and was not used.
