## Jump up through turn blocks and land on top of them

**Codes:** `723D-07D7` + `D5B6-D4A6` + `F165-DF6C`
**Raw form:** `00ED0C:3D` (orig `$2E`); `02908B:07` (orig `$01`);
`028876:16` (orig `$FF`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-29 17:29:25

**Mechanism:** Three things stop Mario from jumping up through a turn block:

1. **His rise is stopped.** When his head touches a block, `CODE_00ECFA`
   (`bank_00.asm`) processes the block, then checks for a turn block:
   `LDA Map16TileNumber / CMP #$1E / BEQ CODE_00ED3B`. `CODE_00ED3B` does
   `STZ PlayerYSpeed+1` and plays the bonk. `723D-07D7` changes the `BEQ`
   displacement from `$2E` to `$3D`, so a turn block now goes to
   `Normal_IP4` and skips both. Mario keeps his upward speed. (A turn block
   already skipped the position clip that other ceilings get.)
2. **The block stays solid while it bounces.** `TurnBlockSpr` (`bank_02.asm`)
   first puts an invisible solid tile (`InvisSldFromBncSpr`) where the block
   was. It changes it to the passable spinning tile (type `$05`) only when
   `BounceSpriteTimer` reaches 1, about 7 frames later. That is enough to stop
   Mario. `D5B6-D4A6` changes `CMP.B #$01` to `CMP.B #$07`. The timer starts
   at 8 and is decremented before `TurnBlockSpr` runs, so the first run sees
   7. The spinning tile now replaces the invisible solid on the same frame
   that it is made.
3. **The block spins for a long time.** `CODE_028752`'s bounce-sprite setup
   sets `TurnBlockSpinTimer` to `$FF` (about 4 seconds) for bounce sprite
   `$07`. When it runs out, `TurnBlockSpr` puts the solid turn block back.
   `F165-DF6C` sets it to `$16` (22 frames), so the block is solid again soon
   after Mario has gone through.

What that should look like:
- Mario jumps into a turn block from below. It starts to spin, and he goes up
  through it without a bonk. When he comes down, the block is solid again, and
  he lands on top of it.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `C9 1E F0 2E` at `$00ED09` (`$00ED0D + $2E =
$00ED3B`, `$00ED0D + $3D = $00ED4A` = `Normal_IP4`), `BD C5 16 F0 31 C9 01`
at `$029085`, and `C9 07 D0 05 A9 FF 99 CE 18` at `$028871`. All three codes
round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Alternatives:** The spin length is a guess. It depends on how fast Mario is
still rising when he hits the block. It must run out after his feet are above
the block, and before he falls back down to it. The spin timer starts on the
frame of the hit. Use the first two codes with one of these:

| Codes | Effect |
|---|---|
| `723D-07D7` + `D5B6-D4A6` + `FD65-DF6C` | shorter spin (16 frames), for a fast jump into a low block |
| `723D-07D7` + `D5B6-D4A6` + `4D65-DF6C` | longer spin (32 frames), for a high running jump |
| `723D-07D7` + `D5B6-D4A6` | pass up through turn blocks, but they spin for the normal 4 seconds, so Mario falls back through |

**Caveats:**
- If the spin runs out while Mario is still inside the block, the block goes
  solid around him. This happens when he hits it too slowly to get through,
  or when the timer is too short. Expect him to be pushed out of it, or to
  get stuck for a moment.
- If Mario hits the block near the top of his jump, he can't rise through
  it. He falls back down below it, as before but without the bonk.
- For 6 frames the bouncing block is drawn over the spinning tile, so both
  can be seen. The bounce sprite also moves in those frames. The final
  turn-block tile is still put back on the right tile: `TileFromBounceSpr1`
  rounds the position after the same number of moves as before.
- `D5B6-D4A6` and `F165-DF6C` change every turn block that is hit from
  below, including blocks hit by thrown shells.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Broken turn blocks rebuild themselves (spin-jump on one to bounce forever)

**Code:** `DA66-AD0B`
**Raw form:** `028781:0C` (orig `$02`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-29 17:31:45

**Mechanism:** When big Mario spin-jumps onto a turn block, `CODE_028752`
(`bank_02.asm`) gives 50 points, bounces Mario up (`LDA #$D0 / STA
PlayerYSpeed+1`), and throws out the four pieces with `ShatterBlock`. Then it
removes the block:

```
CODE_028780:
    LDA.B #$02                                ; \ Replace block with "nothing" tile
    STA.B Map16TileGenerate                   ; |
    JSL GenerateTile                          ; /
```

`Map16TileGenerate` picks the tile from `GeneratedTiles` (`bank_00.asm`), and
its values are listed under `Map16TileGenerate` in `rammap.asm`: `$02` is
`!Map16Gen_Empty`. The code changes it to `$0C`, `!Map16Gen_TurnBlock`. The
block breaks, with its pieces, sound and points, and a new turn block is put
in its place.

What that should look like:
- The block shatters but is still there. Mario bounces up and comes down on
  it, still spin-jumping, so it shatters again. He keeps bouncing on the
  same block and gets 50 points each time, until he moves off it or stops
  the spin jump.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A9 02 85 9C 22 B0 BE 00 6B` at `$028780`. The code
round-trips through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Alternatives:** Other `Map16TileGenerate` values that make a simple tile:

| Code | Effect |
|---|---|
| `D166-AD0B` (`$06`) | a broken turn block leaves a coin, which Mario usually collects at once |
| `D266-AD0B` (`$0D`) | a broken turn block leaves a used (brown) block, so Mario can't drill down |
| `D366-AD0B` (`$0E`) | a broken turn block leaves a note block, which bounces Mario on the next landing |
| `D866-AD0B` (`$0B`) | a broken turn block leaves a multiple-coin ? block |
| `D766-AD0B` (`$03`) | a broken turn block leaves a piece of vine that Mario can climb |
| `F766-AD0B` (`$13`) | a broken turn block leaves an ON/OFF switch block |

**Caveats:**
- Only the spin-jump shatter is changed. `ShatterBlock` calls from sprites
  (for example a charging Chargin' Chuck) remove their blocks with their own
  code, as before.
- With the "drills straight down" code (`6565-AF6B`), Mario does not bounce.
  So with the turn-block value here, he stands on a block that keeps
  breaking, and he gets points every frame that he is on it.
- The new tile is a plain Map16 tile. It is not saved in item memory, so it
  goes back to a turn block when the level is loaded again.
- `$0B` and `$13` make blocks that work when hit from below. The `$0E` note
  block is the one that bounces Mario when he lands on it.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Dust clouds puff out when Mario gets on Yoshi (restored dead code)

**Code:** `8B68-AFDC`
**Raw form:** `028BB4:B9` (orig `$B8`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-29 17:33:11

**Mechanism:** When Mario lands on Yoshi, the Yoshi code in `bank_01.asm`
plays the two mount sounds and then calls `JSL DisabledAddSmokeRt`. That
routine (`bank_02.asm`) does nothing:

```
DisabledAddSmokeRt:
    PHB                                       ; \ This routine does nothing at all
    PHK                                       ; | I believe it used to call the below
    PLB                                       ; | routine to add smoke when boarding
    JSR Return028BB8                          ; | Yoshi
    PLB                                       ; |
    RTL                                       ; /

Return028BB8:
    RTS

    STZ.B _0                                  ; \ Display smoke when getting on Yoshi
    JSR ADDR_028BC0                           ; |
    INC.B _0                                  ; |
ADDR_028BC0:
    ...
```

The `JSR` goes to a bare `RTS`, and the smoke code starts on the very next
byte, with no label. It looks like the `RTS` was put in front of it to switch
it off. The code changes the `JSR` operand's low byte from `$B8` to `$B9`, so
the `JSR` now calls the `STZ.B _0`.

That code runs `ADDR_028BC0` twice, with `_0` = 0 and then 1. Each run takes
a free minor extended sprite slot and makes it type `$0B`. It puts it at
Yoshi's feet (his Y + `$1C`), a little to one side of Mario (`DATA_028C0B`),
moving outward at `$40` or `$C0` (`DATA_028C09`). Type `$0B` is the last
entry in the minor extended sprite table, `ADDR_028C0F`, and nothing else in
the game makes it. It slows each mover by 8 each frame, so it stops after 8
frames. Every 4 frames, each mover leaves behind a still puff that lasts 16
frames and draws smoke tiles `$66`, `$66`, `$64`, `$62` from `DATA_028C6A`.

What that should look like:
- When Mario gets on Yoshi, two small trails of dust puff out to the left and
  right along the ground at Yoshi's feet, then fade.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `8B 4B AB 20 B8 8B AB 6B 60 64 00 20 C0 8B` at
`$028BB0`. That is `DisabledAddSmokeRt`, `Return028BB8`'s `RTS` (`$60`), and
then `STZ $00` (`64 00`) at `$028BB9`. The code round-trips through
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the disassembly and **has
not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The smoke code ends on `ADDR_028BC0`'s `RTS`, which returns to
  `DisabledAddSmokeRt`, and that ends with `PLB` and `RTL` as before. The
  routine sets the data bank to `$02` first, which `DATA_028C09` and the other
  tables need. `X` is still Yoshi's slot, which the code reads.
- The code writes `Y` and scratch `_0`, `_2` and `_3`, which it didn't write
  before. The Yoshi code after the `JSL` does not seem to need them, but this
  hasn't been checked in every path.
- Each trail uses minor extended sprite slots (up to 3 each). When all 12
  slots are in use, fewer puffs are made.
- The puffs are drawn from `BrokenBlock` as their OAM index, like the other
  minor extended sprites. They take palette and priority from
  `SpriteProperties`, so they could look different in some levels.
- Nothing in the game ever made a type-`$0B` sprite, so this code was never
  tested in the released game.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Hold R to freeze the level (SpriteLock while R is held)

**Codes:** `FDAD-6D07` + `B2AD-67D7` + `DDAD-6707`
**Raw form:** `00CE01:10` (orig `$30`); `00CE0C:9D` (orig `$01`);
`00CE0D:00` (orig `$14`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-29 21:59:05

**Mechanism:** `CODE_00CCBB` (`bank_00.asm`) runs every frame of Mario's
update. It calls `CODE_00CDDD`, then does `LDA SpriteLock / BNE Return00CCDF`.
So when `SpriteLock` is set, Mario's update is skipped as well as the sprites'.
`UpdateStatusBar` also stops the level timer when `SpriteLock` is set.

`CODE_00CDDD` is the L/R camera-shift handler. In any level with
`HorizLayer1Setting` set, it starts with `LDA CameraIsScrolling / STA
SpriteLock`, so it writes `SpriteLock` every frame. (This is why everything
stops while the camera shifts.) Then `CODE_00CDF6` checks for L or R held
alone:

```
CODE_00CDF6:
    LDA.B axlr0000Hold                        ; \ Branch if anything besides L/R being held
    AND.B #$CF                                ; |
    ORA.B byetudlrHold                        ; |
    BNE CODE_00CE49                           ; /
    LDA.B axlr0000Hold                        ; \ Branch if L/R not being held
    AND.B #$30                                ; |
    BEQ CODE_00CE49                           ; |
    CMP.B #$30                                ; |
    BEQ CODE_00CE49                           ; /
    LSR A
    LSR A
    LSR A
    INC.W CameraScrollTimer
```

The codes:
- `FDAD-6D07` changes `AND.B #$30` to `AND.B #$10`. In `axlr0000Hold`, `$10`
  is R and `$20` is L, so only R now passes.
- `B2AD-67D7` + `DDAD-6707` change the operand of `INC.W CameraScrollTimer`
  (`$1401`) to `$009D`, which is `SpriteLock`. Bank `$00` addresses below
  `$2000` are the low WRAM mirror.

On each frame that R is held, `CODE_00CDDD` first copies `CameraIsScrolling`
(0) to `SpriteLock`, and then the `INC` makes it 1. So the game is locked on
that frame. When R is released, the `INC` no longer runs, and the next frame's
copy clears `SpriteLock`.

What that should look like:
- While R is held (with no other button), Mario, every sprite and the level
  timer stop, as when the camera shifts. The music keeps playing. When R is
  released, everything goes on from where it stopped.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `AD FD 13 85 9D` at `$00CDE5` (`LDA
CameraIsScrolling / STA SpriteLock`), `A5 17 29 30` at `$00CDFE` and `EE 01
14` at `$00CE0B`. All codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The
effect is derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Codes | Effect |
|---|---|
| `FDAD-6D07` + `B2AD-67D7` + `DDAD-6707` + `DDAE-0707` | R freezes the level even with other buttons held (4 codes) |

`DDAE-0707` changes the `BNE CODE_00CE49` displacement at `$00CDFD` from `$4B`
to `$00`, so holding another button no longer cancels the check.

**Caveats:**
- **L and R no longer shift the camera.** `CameraScrollTimer` is never
  incremented, so it never reaches `$10`, and the camera shift never starts.
- R must be held **alone**. The `AND #$CF / ORA byetudlrHold` check still
  cancels it if any other button or the D-pad is held. The 4-code variant
  removes this.
- It works only in levels where `HorizLayer1Setting` is set. In other levels
  (vertical levels, for example), `CODE_00CDDD` returns at once, and R does
  nothing.
- `CODE_00CCBB` jumps away before `CODE_00CDDD` while `EndLevelTimer` is
  running, so R does nothing after the goal is reached.
- The lock goes into effect after `CODE_00CDDD` has run. Code that runs
  earlier in the frame is not stopped for that first frame.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## SpriteLock no longer freezes Mario (time stops for everything but him)

**Codes:** `DDAA-D407` + `DDAD-0DAF`
**Raw form:** `00CCC9:00` (orig `$15`); `00C503:00` (orig `$65`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-29 22:15:12

**Mechanism:** `SpriteLock` (`$7E009D`, "locks most animations and movements
when set") freezes the sprites, and two branches in `bank_00.asm` also make it
freeze Mario:

- `CODE_00CCBB`, the start of Mario's per-frame update, does `JSR CODE_00CDDD
  / LDA SpriteLock / BNE Return00CCDF`. When sprites are locked, the rest of
  Mario's update (movement, physics, block contact) is skipped.
  `DDAA-D407` changes the `BNE` displacement from `$15` to `$00`, so it goes
  to the next instruction either way.
- Earlier in the frame, `LDA SpriteLock / BNE CODE_00C569` skips `INC
  EffFrame` and the loop that counts down the 19 player timers after
  `ColorFadeTimer` (`PlayerAniTimer` through `EmptyTimer14A8`: invincibility
  frames, kicking, fireball pose, cape spin, takeoff, Yoshi's tongue, and so
  on). `DDAD-0DAF` changes that displacement from `$65` to `$00`. Without it,
  Mario could move, but any pose or action that waits on one of those timers
  would stay stuck until the lock ends.

The sprites still check `SpriteLock` in their own code, so they stay frozen.

In the normal game, `SpriteLock` is set mostly while the L/R camera shift runs
(`CODE_00CDDD` copies `CameraIsScrolling` into it every frame). On its own,
this cheat mainly lets Mario keep moving while the camera shifts. It is meant
to go with a cheat that sets `SpriteLock` on purpose, such as "Hold R to freeze
the level" above. The combined set is in the table below.

What that should look like:
- Whenever sprites are locked, Mario keeps running, jumping and flying while
  every enemy and item is frozen in place.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A5 9D D0 15` at `$00CCC6` (`$00CCCA + $15 =
$00CCDF`, `Return00CCDF`) and `A5 9D D0 65 E6 14` at `$00C500` (`$00C504 + $65
= $00C569`). Both codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Codes | Effect |
|---|---|
| `DDAA-D407` + `DDAD-0DAF` + `FDAD-6D07` + `B2AD-67D7` + `DDAD-6707` | time runs only while you press a button: hold R alone and the level stops; press any other button and everything runs again (5 codes). Observed in play: the earlier note here said Mario keeps moving while R is held, which was wrong, because any other button cancels the lock. See "Time moves only when you press a button" below for a 2-code version without R |
| `DDAA-D407` | Mario moves while sprites are locked, but his timers freeze, so poses such as the kick or the fireball throw can stay stuck |

**Caveats:**
- Frozen sprites skip their own code, and in most sprites that includes the
  contact check with Mario. Expect him to pass through frozen enemies without
  harm, to be unable to stomp them, and to fall through frozen platforms.
  A carried item may stay where it is while Mario walks away.
- The level timer still stops while `SpriteLock` is set (`UpdateStatusBar`
  checks it separately).
- With `DDAD-0DAF`, `EffFrame` and the P-switch timers in the same block
  also keep running while sprites are locked. In the normal game they stop.
- Mario is still frozen by other flags, such as `PlayerIsFrozen` (used with
  the keyhole), which this doesn't change.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Time moves only when you press a button (SuperHot mode)

**Codes:** `31AE-0767` + `B2AE-07A7`
**Raw form:** `00CDFE:E6` (orig `$A5`); `00CDFF:9D` (orig `$17`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-29 22:33:31

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `video-ready` `curated`

**Mechanism:** `CODE_00CDDD` (`bank_00.asm`) is the L/R camera-shift handler.
`CODE_00CCBB` calls it every frame before Mario's update, but only in levels
with `HorizLayer1Setting` set. It starts with `LDA CameraIsScrolling / STA
SpriteLock`, so it writes `SpriteLock` every frame. Then `CODE_00CDF6` tests
the controller:

```
CODE_00CDF6:
    LDA.B axlr0000Hold                        ; \ Branch if anything besides L/R being held
    AND.B #$CF                                ; |
    ORA.B byetudlrHold                        ; |
    BNE CODE_00CE49                           ; /
    LDA.B axlr0000Hold                        ; \ Branch if L/R not being held   <- patched
    AND.B #$30                                ; |
    BEQ CODE_00CE49                           ; |
```

The code only gets past the `BNE` when no button except L or R is held. The
two codes change the next instruction, `LDA.B axlr0000Hold` (`A5 17`), to
`INC.B SpriteLock` (`E6 9D`). Both are 2-byte instructions, so the rest of
the routine stays in step.

So on each frame with no button held, `SpriteLock` goes from 0 (the copy of
`CameraIsScrolling`) to 1. This happens before `CODE_00CCBB` tests
`SpriteLock`, so Mario, every sprite and the level timer stop on that same
frame. On a frame with any button held, the `BNE` skips the `INC`, and the
lock stays 0.

After the `INC`, A still holds 0 from the `ORA`. So `AND #$30` gives 0, and
`BEQ CODE_00CE49` is always taken. This means the camera shift can never
start.

This is the effect that the "Hold R" codes above gave when R was held. Any
other button cancels that lock, so the game ran only while a button was held.
This version needs no R, and it uses 2 codes instead of 5.

What that should look like:
- In a horizontal level, the moment you let go of every button, Mario, all
  enemies, items and the level timer stop dead. This includes Mario in
  mid-air. Press any button and everything runs again. The music keeps
  playing.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A5 17 29 30 F0 45` at `$00CDFE`, and `AD FD 13 85
9D` at `$00CDE5` (`LDA CameraIsScrolling / STA SpriteLock`). Both codes
round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**. The 5-code R version with
the same mechanism has been observed in play.

**Alternatives:**

| Codes | Effect |
|---|---|
| `31AE-0767` + `B2AE-07A7` + `DDAA-D407` | same, but Mario is not frozen: with no button held he keeps falling, sliding and being carried by momentum while everything else waits. His timers freeze, so a pose such as the kick or the fireball throw can stay stuck |
| `31AE-0767` + `B2AE-07A7` + `DDAA-D407` + `DDAD-0DAF` | as above, but Mario's timers also keep running (4 codes) |
| `31AE-0767` + `B2AE-07A7` + `DDAD-0DAF` | not useful: Mario stays frozen but his timers still run, so invincibility frames and star power wear off while you stand still |

**Alternate version with 3 codes:** `DDAD-6DA7` + `B2AD-67D7` + `DDAD-6707`
(recorded 2026-09-29 22:37:28). Raw form: `00CE03:00` (orig `$45`),
`00CE0C:9D` (orig `$01`), `00CE0D:00` (orig `$14`).

This version takes the "Hold R" cheat and removes its R check, instead of
changing the `LDA`:

```
    LDA.B axlr0000Hold                        ; \ Branch if L/R not being held
    AND.B #$30                                ; |
    BEQ CODE_00CE49                           ; |   <- DDAD-6DA7: displacement $45 -> $00
    CMP.B #$30                                ; |
    BEQ CODE_00CE49                           ; /
    LSR A
    LSR A
    LSR A
    INC.W CameraScrollTimer                   ;     <- B2AD-67D7 + DDAD-6707: operand $1401 -> $009D
```

- `DDAD-6DA7` sets the displacement of the first `BEQ` to 0, so it goes to
  the next instruction whether L/R is held or not.
- `B2AD-67D7` + `DDAD-6707` are the same two codes as in "Hold R". They
  change `INC.W CameraScrollTimer` to `INC.W $009D`, which is `SpriteLock`.

With no button held, A is 0 after `AND #$30`, which is not `$30`. So the second
`BEQ` is not taken, and the `INC` sets the lock. `CameraScrollTimer` is no
longer incremented, so it stays below `$10`, `BCC CODE_00CE4C` is always
taken, and the camera shift can never start.

How it differs from the 2-code version:
- Holding L and R together lets time run while Mario stands still (A is
  `$30`, so the second `BEQ` skips the `INC`). L or R alone keeps time
  stopped, as in the 2-code version.
- Everything else is the same, including the Mario variants in the table
  above (add `DDAA-D407`, and `DDAD-0DAF`, for the same effects; that is 4
  or 5 codes).

The 3 codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The ROM holds `F0 45` at
`$00CE02` and `EE 01 14` at `$00CE0B`. This version **has not been observed
in play**.

Other ways I considered:
- Tie the lock to Mario's speed ("time moves when Mario moves"). There is no
  single byte that is zero while Mario moves, so this needs more code than a
  Game Genie can give.

**Caveats:**
- It works only in levels with `HorizLayer1Setting` set, which means most
  horizontal levels. `CODE_00CDDD` returns at once in vertical levels and in
  levels without L/R scrolling, so there the game runs normally.
- L and R do not count as buttons. Holding them keeps time stopped, and the
  L/R camera shift is gone.
- Select and Start count as buttons. Hold Select, and time runs while Mario
  stands still (he does nothing while Select is held). Start still pauses.
- Pipes, doors, the goal and other cutscenes do not go through Mario's normal
  update, so they are not affected.
- While time is stopped, Mario does not flicker during invincibility frames.
  His draw code ORs `SpriteLock` into the blink test, so he is always drawn.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

## Blocks spawn the wrong sprites (SpriteInBlock read from a different offset)

**Code:** `BB67-04AC`
**Raw form:** `02893B:99` (orig `$A3`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-29 23:21:49

**Mechanism:** When Mario hits a block that holds an item, the block code in
bank `$00` puts an item index in `_5` (`CODE_00F1D0`: "_5 = powerup ID").
It is 1 = mushroom, 2 = fire flower, 3 = star, 4 = feather, 5 = 1-up. When
Mario has a powerup, a mushroom block gives its flower or feather, so the
index is already chosen at that point. The higher indices are the other items
in the table below. `GenSpriteFromBlk` (`bank_02.asm`) then spawns the sprite:

```
CODE_028922:
    STX.W TileGenerateTrackA
    LDY.B _5
    LDA.W StatusOfSprInBlk,Y                  ; \ Set sprite status
    STA.W SpriteStatus,X                      ; /
    LDA.W YoshiIsLoose
    BEQ +
    TYA
    CLC
    ADC.B #$11
    TAY
  + STY.W SpriteInterIndex
    LDA.W SpriteInBlock,Y                     ; \ Set sprite number   <- $02893A: B9 A3 88
    STA.B SpriteNumber,X                      ; /
```

`SpriteInBlock` (`$0288A3`) is two copies of the same 17-byte list of sprite
numbers. The second copy is used when `YoshiIsLoose` is set. This is the
only place that reads it.

`BB67-04AC` changes the low byte of the table address from `$A3` to `$99`,
so the game reads 10 bytes too early. Those bytes are the end of
`CODE_02887D` (`8D 6B 18 20 66 8A 6B`), then `DATA_0288A1` (`35 78`), then
the table itself. The sprite status still comes from `StatusOfSprInBlk` with
the correct index, so only the sprite number changes.

What that should look like:

| Block that would give | Now gives | ...when `YoshiIsLoose` is set |
|---|---|---|
| Mushroom (1) | `$8D` ghost house exit sign and door | `$79` growing vine |
| Fire flower (2) | `$6B` wall springboard | `$00` green Koopa, no shell |
| Star (3) | `$18` surface-jumping Cheep Cheep | `$3E` P-switch |
| Feather (4) | `$20` Magikoopa's magic | `$7D` P-balloon, which then becomes a key, red coin or balloon by block position |
| 1-up (5) | `$66` upside-down line-guided chainsaw | `$2C` Yoshi egg |
| Vine (8) | `$35` Yoshi | `$45` directional coins |
| P-switch (`$0A`) | `$00` green Koopa, no shell (spawned carryable) | same |
| P-balloon (`$0B`) | `$74` mushroom | same |
| Yoshi egg (`$0C`) | `$75` fire flower (spawned carryable) | same |
| Koopa shell (`$0D`) | `$76` star (spawned carryable) | same |
| Changing item (`$0E`) | `$77` feather | same |
| Directional coins (`$0F`) | `$78` 1-up | same |
| Key (`$10`) | `$00` green Koopa, no shell (spawned carryable) | same |

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A4 05 B9 C5 88 9D C8 14 AD E2 18 F0 05 98 18 69
11 A8 8C 95 16 B9 A3 88` at `$028925`. `$02889A`-`$0288A2` holds `8D 6B 18 20
66 8A 6B 35 78`, just before the table. (Index 1 is the first entry read.) The code round-trips through
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the disassembly and **has
not been observed in play**.

**Alternatives:**

These change the values as well as the offset. Both force the "Yoshi is
loose" branch and change the `LDA` to `ADC`:

- `DD67-0D0C` (`028931:00`, orig `$05`) sets the `BEQ +` displacement to 0.
  So `TYA / CLC / ADC #$11 / TAY` always runs, and A = Y = index + `$11`.
- `5B67-046C` (`02893A:79`, orig `$B9`) changes `LDA.W SpriteInBlock,Y` to
  `ADC.W SpriteInBlock,Y`. Carry is clear after `ADC #$11`, so the sprite
  number becomes the table value + index + `$11`.

The increase is not the same for every block: it is `$12` for the mushroom
block and `$21` for the key block.

| Codes | Effect |
|---|---|
| `DD67-0D0C` + `5B67-046C` | every value read from the table goes up: mushroom → `$86` Wiggler, fire flower → `$88` (unused sprite), star → `$8A` bird from Yoshi's house, feather → `$8C` side exit, 1-up → `$8E` invisible warp hole, vine → `$92` Splittin' Chuck, P-switch → `$59` turn block bridge, P-balloon → `$99` Volcano Lotus, Yoshi egg → `$49` growing/shrinking pipe end, shell → `$22` green net Koopa, changing item → `$A0` Bowser scene activator, directional coins → `$65` line-guided chainsaw, key → `$A1` Bowser's bowling ball |
| `BB67-04AC` + `DD67-0D0C` + `5B67-046C` | both: read 10 bytes early, then add index + `$11`. Mushroom → `$8B` puff of smoke from Yoshi's house, fire flower → `$13` Spiny, star → `$52` moving ledge hole (ghost house), feather → `$92` Splittin' Chuck, 1-up → `$42` dolphin, vine → `$5E` orange platform that goes on forever, P-switch → `$1B` bouncing football, P-balloon → `$90` large green gas bubble, Yoshi egg → `$92` Splittin' Chuck, shell → `$94` Whistlin' Chuck, changing item → `$96` (unused sprite), directional coins → `$98` Pitchin' Chuck, key → `$21` moving coin |

I picked the offset `$99` because every value it reads, in both halves, is a
valid sprite number (`$C8` or lower) and the mix is wide. Any low byte from
`$99` to `$BE` also keeps all values valid. For example, `$A4` shifts every
item by one (mushroom → fire flower, flower → star, and so on).

**Caveats:**
- The spawned sprite gets status `$08` or `$09` from `StatusOfSprInBlk`, so
  its own init routine never runs (`InitSpriteTables` only loads the tweaker
  bytes). Sprites that set themselves up in init, such as the Wiggler and the
  Chucks, may act or look wrong.
- Sprites whose graphics are not in the level's sprite tileset are drawn with
  the wrong tiles.
- Index 9 has status `$00` in `StatusOfSprInBlk`, so it spawns nothing in
  every version.
- Unused sprites (`$88`, `$96`), the Bowser scene activator (`$A0`) and the
  invisible warp hole (`$8E`) may glitch, lock up or warp Mario. Save a state
  first.
- Coin blocks (index 6 and 7) do not reach `GenSpriteFromBlk`, so they still
  give coins.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header. Sprite names come from
the standard SMW sprite list.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Level sprite lists end early (end-of-data marker changed from $FF to $51)

**Code:** `9FC7-DD0C`
**Raw form:** `02A831:51` (orig `$FF`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 17:43:52

**Mechanism:** Each level's sprite data in bank `$07` is a header byte, then
3-byte entries (`YYYYEEsy`, `XXXXSSSS`, sprite number), sorted by screen, and
then `$FF`. `LoadSprFromLevel` (`bank_02.asm`) runs every other frame. It
walks the list from the start each time:

```
LoadSpriteLoopStrt:
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr],Y                   ; Byte format: YYYYEEsy
    CMP.B #$FF                                ; \ Return when we encounter $FF, as it signals the end   <- patched
    BEQ Return02A84B                          ; /
    ...
    CMP.B _1                                  ; | If sprite screen (sSSSS) < adjusted screen boundary...
    BCS CODE_02A84C                           ; / ...skip the sprite
...
CODE_02A84C:
    BNE Return02A84B                          ; Return if sprite screen > adjusted screen boundary
```

This is the only place that checks for the end of the list. The code changes
the `CMP` operand from `$FF` to `$51`. Now the walk stops at the first entry
whose first byte is `$51`. That is a sprite placed on row `$15` (`YYYY` = 5,
`y` = 1) with no extra bits, on screens 0-`$0F`. That sprite and every sprite
after it in the list never load. Since the list is sorted by screen, the
level has its normal sprites up to that point and none after it.

When the list has no `$51` entry, almost nothing changes. The old `$FF` still
works as an end marker by accident: the walk already stops at the first
sprite on a screen past the camera. An `$FF` read as a first byte sets the
`s` bit, which puts that "sprite" on screen `$10` or higher. So in a level
shorter than about `$11` screens, the walk always stops at the `$FF` anyway.

I picked `$51` from a count over all 175 distinct sprite lists in the U ROM.
It ends 78 lists early, and in the middle of the list rather than at the
start: the median cut is 26% of the way through, and only 3 lists become
empty.

What that should look like:
- In about half of the levels, the enemies and items stop at some point.
  Past that point the level has no sprites at all. The other levels play
  normally.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `B7 CE C9 FF F0 17` at `$02A82E`. The level
counts come from parsing every list through the pointers at `Ptrs05EC00`
(`$05EC00`, 512 levels, 177 distinct pointers, 2876 sprites). The code
round-trips through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and the data, and **has not been observed in play**.

**Alternatives:** Every code here changes the same byte to a different value.

| Code | Value | Lists cut | Median cut point | Lists left empty | Goal tapes lost (of 46) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `9FC7-DD0C` | `$51` | 78 | 26% | 3 | 33 |
| `5FC7-DD0C` | `$71` (the most common first byte, row `$17`) | 92 | 6% | 31 | 37 |
| `3DC7-DD0C` | `$E0` | 54 | 36% | 4 | 17 |
| `D9C7-DD0C` | `$05` (never a first byte) | 0 | — | 0 | 0 |

With `$05` no list ends early. The walk can then go past the old `$FF` only
in a long level, once the camera is on screen `$10` or later and past the
last real sprite. The game then reads the next level's data in bank `$07`
as sprites, one byte out of step. A simulation over all horizontal levels
finds this in 17 levels, with a handful of stray sprites or scroll commands
near the end (for example level `$010` gets three `$41` dolphins). So this
value mostly shows that the end marker barely matters.

**Caveats:**
- A goal tape is a sprite (`$7B`), so a level cut before it has no tape. Use
  another exit, or leave with Start+Select on a level you have already
  beaten.
- Bosses, keys and other sprites the level needs can also be cut, which can
  make a level impossible to finish.
- In a level longer than about `$11` screens with no cut, reading past the
  end can spawn stray sprites or change the scroll (see `$05` above).

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## The level's early sprites keep re-loading at the screen edge

**Codes:** `6DC0-DFDC` + `FDC0-DF0C`
**Raw form:** `02A844:80` (orig `$B0`); `02A845:10` (orig `$06`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 17:45:34

Tags: `demo-ready` `interesting` `video-ready` `play-start`

**Mechanism:** `LoadSprFromLevel` (`bank_02.asm`) runs every other frame. It
works out an "adjusted screen boundary", which is the 16-pixel column just
off the edge of the screen in the direction the camera scrolls (screen in
`_1`, column in `_0`). Then it walks the level's sprite list:

```
    CMP.B _1                                  ; | If sprite screen (sSSSS) < adjusted screen boundary...
    BCS CODE_02A84C                           ; / ...skip the sprite   <- $02A844: B0 06
LoadNextSprite:
    INY                                       ; \ Move on to the next sprite
    INY                                       ; |
    INX                                       ; |
    BRA LoadSpriteLoopStrt                    ; /

Return02A84B:
    RTS

CODE_02A84C:
    BNE Return02A84B                          ; Return if sprite screen > adjusted screen boundary
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr],Y                   ; Byte format: XXXXSSSS
    AND.B #$F0                                ; \ Skip sprite if not right at the screen boundary
    CMP.B _0                                  ; |
    BNE LoadNextSprite                        ; /
    LDA.W SpriteLoadStatus,X                  ; \ This table has a flag for every sprite in the level (not just those onscreen)   <- $02A856
    BNE LoadNextSprite                        ; / Skip sprite if it's already been loaded/permanently killed
```

The codes change `BCS CODE_02A84C` to `BRA` (`$80`) and set its displacement
to `$10`, so it goes to `$02A856`. Every entry now skips all three boundary
tests (screen less than, screen greater than, column) and goes straight to
the `SpriteLoadStatus` test. Y still points at the `XXXXSSSS` byte, as it
does on the normal path.

So all the sprites in the list that are not loaded and not permanently
killed try to load at once. The walk no longer stops at the first sprite past
the camera, so it would go all the way to the `$FF`. But it stops as soon as
there is no free sprite slot: the slot search fails, `CODE_02A936` clears the
sprite's `SpriteLoadStatus` flag so it can load later, and the loader
returns. Level sprites get at most 10 of the 12 slots, and fewer in many
levels (the level's sprite memory setting picks the limit from
`SpriteSlotMax`). So the slots fill up with the first few sprites in the
list, and the walk gets no further.

Each walk starts again at the top of the list. A sprite that goes off the
screen is erased, and its flag is cleared, so on the next walk it is one of
the first to get the free slot again. The result is that the same early
sprites keep re-loading at the edge of the screen, and the sprites later in
the list rarely get a turn.

The loader does not use the sprite's own X position. It assumes the sprite
is at the boundary, and `CODE_02A95B` writes `_0`/`_1` as the X position.
The Y position still comes from the sprite data. So every sprite appears in
the same column, just off the screen, at its own height. In a vertical level
the axes are swapped: every sprite appears in the same row, at its own X.

What that should look like:
- At the start of a level, the level's sprites appear together in one
  column. The start-of-level load (`CODE_02ACA1`) uses a column `$60` pixels
  left of the normal boundary, so this column is on the screen. The first
  sprites in the list fill the free slots, and the rest wait.
- As sprites die or go off the screen, more come in at the edge of the screen
  every other frame. They are mostly the same early sprites again: a sprite
  that goes off the screen is not marked as killed, so it comes back from the
  edge. This gives an endless stream of the level's first few enemies and
  items.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `C5 01 B0 06 C8 C8 E8 80 E3 60 D0 FD B7 CE 29 F0
C5 00 D0 F0 BD 38 19 D0 EB` at `$02A842` (`$02A846 + $10 = $02A856`, the
`LDA SpriteLoadStatus,X`). Both codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`.
The effect is derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in
play**.

**Alternatives:**

| Codes | Effect |
|---|---|
| `FDC0-DF0C` | 1 code: only the displacement changes, so the `BCS` stays. Sprites on screens behind the boundary are still skipped. Sprites from the boundary screen to the end of the list try to load at the edge, up to the slot limit, but sprites behind the camera that went off the screen do not come back |
| `6DC0-DFDC` + `FDC0-DF0C` + `D9C7-DD0C` | adds the end-marker code that never matches (see "Level sprite lists end early"). Now every level reads past its own list, into the next level's data in bank `$07`, and loads it one byte out of step as sprites. The X index has no limit, so it can run past the 128 bytes of `SpriteLoadStatus` into `ExitTableLow`/`ExitTableHigh` and `ItemMemoryTable`. Expect wrong pipe and door exits, wrong coins and blocks, and crashes. Save a state first |

**Caveats:**
- The goal tape (`$7B`) is a sprite. It is usually near the end of the list,
  so it loads only if there is a free slot when the walk gets that far. If it
  does, it appears at the edge, and going past it may end the level at
  once. Levels without a tape (bosses, keyholes, sub-levels) are not affected
  in this way.
- Scroll commands (sprites `$E7` and up) all reach the loader at the start of
  the level. The first one that runs while no scroll is active wins, so
  auto-scroll and layer 2 scroll levels may scroll in the wrong way or not at
  all.
- Keys, P-switches, springboards and the like all appear in the same column,
  not where the level needs them.
- With the 2-code version, a sprite that goes off the screen comes back from
  the edge, so the stream never ends. Enemies that you can avoid only by
  running past them keep coming back.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## A chosen generator runs in every level from the start

**Code (Super Koopa generator):** `BF8D-DDD6`
**Raw form:** `02B000:91` (orig `$18`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 18:14:39

**Mechanism:** A level turns on a generator with a sprite `$CB`-`$D9` in its
sprite data. `CODE_02A8AC` (`bank_02.asm`) stores the type, 1-`$0F`, in
`CurrentGenerator` (`$18B9`). Each frame, `CallGenerator` reads it:

```
CallGenerator:
    LDA.W CurrentGenerator                    ;   $02AFFE: AD B9 18
    BEQ +
    LDY.B SpriteLock
    BNE +
    DEC A
    JSL ExecutePtr
    dw GenerateEerie                          ; 00 - Eerie, generator
    ...
```

The data bank here is `$02`, so `LDA.W $xxB9` with a high byte of `$80` or
more reads the ROM at `$02xxB9`. Each code changes the high byte of the
operand to a page where that ROM byte is the wanted generator type.
`CallGenerator` then sees that type on every frame of every level, whatever
`CurrentGenerator` holds. The level's own generators and the "turn off
generators" sprites are ignored.

Some generators read `CurrentGenerator` again with `LDY.W CurrentGenerator`
to pick a variant: para-enemies (`$02B340`), dolphins (`$02B272` and
`$02B2B4`) and the multi-bullet generators (`$02B0E4`). For those, each extra
read is pointed at the same ROM page, which costs one code per read. No page
holds `$06`, `$0D` or `$0E`, so those types use `LDA #imm` / `LDY #imm`
instead (`A9 xx 18` = `LDA #xx / CLC`; the `CLC` is harmless here).

| Generator | Codes | Raw form |
|---|---|---|
| Eerie (`$01`) | `C58D-DDD6` | `02B000:A7` |
| Para-Goomba (`$02`) | `698D-DDD6` + `6980-AD66` | `02B000:85`, `02B342:85` |
| Para-Bomb (`$03`) | `C18D-DDD6` + `C180-AD66` | `02B000:A6`, `02B342:A6` |
| Para-Bomb and Para-Goomba (`$04`) | `B68D-DDD6` + `B680-AD66` | `02B000:98`, `02B342:98` |
| Dolphin, left (`$05`) | `C28D-DDD6` + `C285-6FD6` + `C288-6F66` | `02B000:AD`, `02B274:AD`, `02B2B6:AD` |
| Jumping fish (`$07`) | `2C8D-DDD6` | `02B000:DA` |
| Super Koopa (`$09`) | `BF8D-DDD6` | `02B000:91` |
| Bubble with Goomba and Bob-omb (`$0A`) | `B28D-DDD6` | `02B000:9D` |
| Bullet Bill (`$0B`) | `E18D-DDD6` | `02B000:F6` |
| Bullet Bill surrounded (`$0C`) | `268D-DDD6` + `2683-DF66` | `02B000:D8`, `02B0E6:D8` |
| Bullet Bill diagonal (`$0D`) | `CBCE-A768` + `D2CE-A7A8` + `CD83-DFD6` + `D283-DF06` | `02AFFE:A9`, `02AFFF:0D`, `02B0E4:A0`, `02B0E5:0D` |
| Bowser statue fire breath (`$0E`) | `CBCE-A768` + `D3CE-A7A8` | `02AFFE:A9`, `02AFFF:0E` |

Dolphin, right (`$06`) is left out here: with no ROM page for `$06` it needs 6
codes. (A 4-code set was found later; see "Dolphin, right generator always
on, with every sprite swap".) Types `$08` and `$0F` turn generators off, so they are left out too.

The ROM pages are `$02A7B9` = `$01`, `$0285B9` = `$02`, `$02A6B9` = `$03`,
`$0298B9` = `$04`, `$02ADB9` = `$05`, `$02DAB9` = `$07`, `$0291B9` = `$09`,
`$029DB9` = `$0A`, `$02F6B9` = `$0B` and `$02D8B9` = `$0C`.

What that should look like:
- From the first frame of every level, the chosen generator runs as if the
  level had placed it. For example, Super Koopas fly in from the side every
  so often, in every level, and nothing in the level can turn them off.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `AD B9 18 F0 27 A4 9D D0 23 3A 22 DF 86 00` at
`$02AFFE`, and `AC B9 18` at `$02B0E4`, `$02B272`, `$02B2B4` and `$02B340`.
The ROM page bytes were found by a scan of `$0280B9`-`$02FFB9`. All codes
round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The generator also runs in the title screen demo, boss rooms, ghost
  houses, and so on.
- Generated sprites whose graphics are not in the level's sprite tileset are
  drawn with the wrong tiles. The Eerie, for example, looks right only in
  ghost houses.
- The generator stops while `SpriteLock` is set, as usual.
- Each code set fixes one type. Do not turn on two sets at once: they change
  the same byte.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## The jumping fish generator throws Bob-ombs

**Code:** `D281-0766`
**Raw form:** `02B16E:0D` (orig `$17`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 18:14:39

**Mechanism:** `GenerateFish` (`bank_02.asm`, generator `$07`) runs every 32
frames. It finds a slot, then does `LDA.B #$17 / STA.B SpriteNumber,X`
("Sprite = Flying Fish"), with status `$08`. It puts the sprite just below
the screen (`Layer1YPos + $C0`), at a random X near the edge, with Y speed
`$B8` (up) and a random X speed. This code changes the `#$17` to `#$0D`,
Bob-omb.

What that should look like:
- In a level with the jumping fish generator, Bob-ombs are thrown up from
  below the screen in an arc, instead of fish.
- CORRECTION (2026-09-30): with status `$08` the Bob-omb's fuse timer
  (`SpriteMisc1540`, set to `$FF` by `InitBomb`) is 0, so `Bobomb` makes it
  lit at once and it explodes about one second later. Add `DF81-0466`
  (`02B16A:01`, orig `$08`) to run its init, so it walks with a full fuse.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Sprite |
|---|---|
| `F781-0766` | `$13` Spiny |
| `DE81-0766` | `$0F` Goomba |
| `5081-0766` | `$74` mushroom |

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A9 08 9D C8 14 A9 17 95 9E` at `$02B168`. All
codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The sprite gets status `$08` directly, so its own init routine never runs.
- Only levels with the jumping fish generator use it. Add `2C8D-DDD6` (see
  "A chosen generator runs in every level from the start") to get it in every
  level.
- Sprites whose graphics are not in the level's sprite tileset are drawn with
  the wrong tiles.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## The Bullet Bill generator fires Bob-ombs

**Code:** `D28B-DFD6`
**Raw form:** `02B094:0D` (orig `$1C`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 18:14:39

**Mechanism:** `GenerateBullet` (`bank_02.asm`, generator `$0B`) runs every
128 frames. It plays the "kapow" sound, then does `LDA.B #$1C / STA.B
SpriteNumber,X` ("Sprite = Bullet Bill"), with status `$08`. It puts the
sprite at a random height, at the left or right edge of the screen, and
stores the side in `SpriteTableC2` for the Bullet Bill's direction. This
code changes the `#$1C` to `#$0D`, Bob-omb.

What that should look like:
- With the "kapow" sound, a Bob-omb appears at the left or right edge of the
  screen at a random height, then falls and walks.
- CORRECTION (2026-09-30): with status `$08` the Bob-omb's fuse timer
  (`SpriteMisc1540`, set to `$FF` by `InitBomb`) is 0, so `Bobomb` makes it
  lit at once and it explodes about one second later. Add `DF8B-DDD6`
  (`02B090:01`, orig `$08`) to run its init, so it walks with a full fuse.

**Alternatives:**

| Code | Sprite |
|---|---|
| `DE8B-DFD6` | `$0F` Goomba |
| `7E8B-DFD6` | `$3F` Para-Goomba |
| `568B-DFD6` | `$78` 1-up (a 1-up every 128 frames) |

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A9 08 9D C8 14 A9 1C 95 9E` at `$02B08E`. All
codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the

**Caveats:**
- Other sprites do not use `SpriteTableC2` for their direction the way the
  Bullet Bill does, so they may all face the same way.
- The sprite's own init routine never runs (status `$08`).
- Only levels with the Bullet Bill generator use it. Add `E18D-DDD6` (see

(Bullet Bill surrounded) and `$0D` (Bullet Bill diagonal). Every `$A0` timer

## Many level sprites turn on a generator instead

**Code:** `CCCC-D70C` + `4BC8-DF0C` + `D3C8-DF6C`
**Raw form:** `02A8AD:AA` (orig `$CB`), `02A8B5:29` (orig `$E9`),
`02A8B6:0E` (orig `$CB`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 18:21:21

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** `CODE_02A8AC` (`bank_02.asm`) runs when the sprite loader
reaches a sprite at the screen boundary. Sprites `$CB`-`$D9` are generators:

```
CODE_02A8AC:
    CMP.B #$CB                                ;   $02A8AC: C9 CB
    BCC CODE_02A8D4
    CMP.B #$DA
    BCS CODE_02A8C0
    SEC
    SBC.B #$CB                                ;   $02A8B5: E9 CB
    INC A
    STA.W CurrentGenerator
    STZ.W SpriteLoadStatus,X
```

Code 1 lowers the bound to `#$AA`, so sprites `$AA`-`$CA` also take this
path. That range holds many common sprites: Fishbone, Rex, Bowser statues,
Swooper, Mega Mole, Blurp, Porcu-Puffer, message boxes, the Bullet Bill
shooter, and so on. Codes 2 and 3 change `SBC #$CB` to `AND #$0E` so the
type is `(sprite number AND $0E) + 1`. The result is always `$01`, `$03`,
`$05`, `$07`, `$09`, `$0B`, `$0D` or `$0F`, which are all valid types. A
code that left the `SBC` alone would give types 0 and below for the new
range, which jump outside the generator table.

So when the screen scrolls to one of these sprites, the sprite does not
appear. A generator turns on instead, and its type depends on the sprite
number. Each level has its own sprite mix, so each level gets different
generators at different points.

Mapping (`(n AND $0E) + 1`):

| `n AND $0E` | Type | Generator |
|---|---|---|
| `$00` | `$01` | Eerie |
| `$02` | `$03` | Para-Bomb |
| `$04` | `$05` | Dolphin, left |
| `$06` | `$07` | Jumping fish |
| `$08` | `$09` | Super Koopa |
| `$0A` | `$0B` | Bullet Bill |
| `$0C` | `$0D` | Bullet Bill diagonal |
| `$0E` | `$0F` | Turns generators off |

For example, Rex (`$AB`) turns on Bullet Bills, a message box (`$B9`) turns
on Super Koopas, and a Mega Mole (`$BF`) turns generators off.

What that should look like:
- Partway through many levels, a generator starts up as the screen scrolls
  past where a sprite should have been. Later sprites can switch it to
  another type or off.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `C9 CB 90 24 C9 DA B0 0C 38 E9 CB 1A 8D B9 18` at
`$02A8AC`. All codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The sprites in `$AA`-`$CA` never appear. Some are needed: the Big Boo Boss
  (`$C5`), the light switch block (`$C8`) and message boxes (`$B9`). Boss
  rooms that need them cannot be finished.
- The real generators `$CB`-`$D9` are remapped by the same formula.
- The loader marks these sprites as not loaded, so a sprite turns its
  generator on again each time the screen boundary passes it.
- Generated sprites whose graphics are not in the level's sprite tileset are
  drawn with the wrong tiles.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Level sprites load with X and Y swapped

**Code:** `8DC0-0D0C`
**Raw form:** `02A941:B0` (orig `$90`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 18:21:21

**Mechanism:** When the loader places a sprite (`CODE_02A93C`,
`bank_02.asm`), it already has two versions of the position code. Horizontal
levels take the Y position from the sprite data and the X position from the
screen boundary (`_0`/`_1`). Vertical levels do the opposite:

```
CODE_02A93C:
    LDY.B _3
    LDA.B ScreenMode                          ; \ Branch if horizontal level
    LSR A                                     ; |
    BCC CODE_02A95B                           ; / $02A941: 90 18
    ...                                       ;   vertical: data -> X, boundary -> Y
CODE_02A95B:
    ...                                       ;   horizontal: data -> Y, boundary -> X
```

This code changes `BCC` to `BCS`, so each level type uses the other type's
code and the two coordinates swap.

What that should look like:
- Horizontal levels: a sprite's X becomes its data height (`$000`-`$1F0`,
  so the first two screens), and its Y becomes the screen boundary X. Near
  the start of a level, sprites appear near the left edge of the level at
  heights that follow the scroll position. Past the second screen the Y is
  below the level, so they are gone at once.
- Vertical levels: sprites get Y from their data X and X from the boundary
  Y, so they appear off to the side of the level.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A4 03 A5 5B 4A 90 18` at `$02A93C`. The code
round-trips through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- Most sprites end up far off screen and are erased at once. When a sprite
  is erased off screen it is marked as not loaded, so it can load again the
  next time the boundary passes it.
- The extra bits from the data (`EE`) are stored in the high byte of the
  new X (`AND #$0D`), so sprites that use extra bits go to an X screen of
  `$04`, `$08` or `$0C` and read their extra bits from the wrong place.
- Special loaders (5 Eeries, 3 platforms, shooters, scroll sprites) have
  their own position code and are not swapped.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Level sprites load 2 tiles higher

**Code:** `1BC9-076C` + `3DC9-07AC`
**Raw form:** `02A95E:69` (orig `$29`), `02A95F:E0` (orig `$F0`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 18:21:21

**Mechanism:** In horizontal levels the loader takes a sprite's Y position
from the first byte of its data (`YYYYEEsy`) in `CODE_02A95B`
(`bank_02.asm`):

```
CODE_02A95B:
    LDA.B [SpriteDataPtr],Y                   ; Byte format: YYYYEEsy
    PHA
    AND.B #$F0                                ;   $02A95E: 29 F0
    STA.B SpriteYPosLow,X
    PLA
    AND.B #$0D
    STA.W SpriteYPosHigh,X
```

The codes change `AND #$F0` to `ADC #$E0`. The carry is clear here: it comes
from the `LSR A` of `ScreenMode` just before, which branched here because
bit 0 was clear. So the low byte of Y becomes the data byte plus `$E0`,
which is 32 pixels higher. The high byte is still taken from the data, so
there is no carry into it.

What that should look like:
- Most sprites appear 2 tiles above their normal place. Walking enemies
  drop to the ground; flying and floating ones stay higher than usual.

**Alternatives** (change only the second code):

| Second code | Shift |
|---|---|
| `EDC9-07AC` (`$F0`) | 1 tile higher |
| `4DC9-07AC` (`$20`) | 2 tiles lower |
| `0DC9-07AC` (`$40`) | 4 tiles lower |

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `B7 CE 48 29 F0 95 D8` at `$02A95B`. All codes
round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The low byte wraps. With `$E0`, sprites in the top two rows of a
  256-pixel band (low byte `$00`-`$1F`) move 224 pixels down instead. Lower
  shifts wrap the bottom rows up in the same way.
- The low 4 bits of the data byte (`EEsy`) are no longer masked off, so
  they are added too: 1 pixel for sprites in the lower part of the level
  (`y`), 2 for screens `$10` and above (`s`), 4-12 for sprites that use
  extra bits.
- Only horizontal levels: in vertical levels Y comes from the screen
  boundary, and this code does not run.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Level sprites load one screen to the left

**Code:** `23C2-0FDC` + `3DC2-0F0C` + `F0C2-0F6C`
**Raw form:** `02A9D4:DE` (orig `$9D`), `02A9D5:E0` (orig `$E2`),
`02A9D6:14` (orig `$1F`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 18:21:21

**Mechanism:** In horizontal levels a sprite loads when the screen boundary
(`_0`/`_1`) reaches the sprite's column, and its X is set to that boundary.
The match must be exact, so a single-byte change to the boundary or to the
compare only changes *when* a sprite loads, not where. Instead, these codes
change an instruction near the end of the loader, after `InitSpriteTables`:

```
CODE_02A9C9:
    JSL InitSpriteTables
  + LDA.B #$01
    STA.W SpriteOffscreenX,X
    LDA.B #$04
    STA.W SpriteMisc1FE2,X                    ;   $02A9D4: 9D E2 1F
```

`STA $1FE2,X` becomes `DEC $14E0,X`, that is `DEC SpriteXPosHigh,X`. Every
level sprite's X position goes down by `$100`, one screen.

When Mario goes right, the boundary is `$120` past the left edge of the
screen (`DATA_02A7F6`/`DATA_02A7F9`, `!ScrollDir_RightDown`). One screen
less is `$20` past the left edge.

What that should look like:
- As Mario runs right, each sprite appears suddenly near the left edge of
  the screen, behind Mario, at its normal height, instead of coming in from
  the right.

**Alternatives:**

| Codes | Effect |
|---|---|
| `E3C2-0FDC` + `3DC2-0F0C` + `F0C2-0F6C` | `INC` instead: one screen to the right. Sprites start too far off screen and are erased at once, so most of them never appear |

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `22 D2 F7 07 A9 01 9D A0 15 A9 04 9D E2 1F` at
`$02A9C9`. All codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- When Mario goes left, the boundary is `$30` left of the screen; one
  screen less is far off screen, so those sprites are erased at once.
- At level start the loader runs with a boundary offset of 0 across the
  first screens, so the sprites there move a screen left too. Sprites on
  screen 0 go to X `$FF00`+ and are erased.
- `SpriteMisc1FE2` is no longer set to 4. `InitSpriteTables` clears it to 0,
  so sprites that use it as a short timer start with it at 0.
- In vertical levels the same `DEC` moves sprites one screen left as well,
  which is off the level.
- Special loaders (5 Eeries, 3 platforms, shooters, generators) do not run
  this code.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Every new sprite replaces the sprite in the first slot

**Code:** `6DCF-04AC` + `6DCD-6D0C`
**Raw form:** `02A91B:80` (orig `$F0`), `02AA01:80` (orig `$F0`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 18:21:21

**Mechanism:** Two slot searches pick a slot for a new sprite. Both start at
the highest slot and count down until they find one with status 0:

```
CODE_02A918:                                  ;   level sprite loader
    LDA.W SpriteStatus,X
    BEQ CODE_02A93C                           ;   $02A91B: F0 1F
    DEX
    ...
CODE_02A9FE:                                  ;   FindFreeSlotRt
    LDA.W SpriteStatus,Y
    BEQ Return02AA0A                          ;   $02AA01: F0 07
    DEY
    ...
```

Each code changes a `BEQ` to `BRA`, so the search takes the first slot it
checks, whether or not a sprite is in it. "First slot" here means the first
slot in search order, which is the highest one. For the usual sprite memory
setting that is slot 9 (`SpriteSlotMax`). `FindFreeSlotLowPri` leaves two
slots free, so its callers (most generators) get slot 7.

What that should look like:
- Each sprite that loads as the screen scrolls deletes the one before it,
  so at most one level sprite is around at a time, plus whatever was already
  in the lower slots.
- Items from blocks, sprites thrown out by other sprites and so on also
  replace whatever is in that slot.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `BD C8 14 F0 1F` at `$02A918` and
`B9 C8 14 F0 07` at `$02A9FE`. Both codes round-trip through
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the disassembly and **has
not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- A replaced level sprite stays marked as loaded, so it does not come back
  until the level is entered again.
- Many spawners have their own slot loop instead of `FindFreeSlotRt`; they
  are not affected.
- The sprite in that slot may be Yoshi, a carried shell, or a boss part;
  replacing those can leave Mario or the boss in a broken state.
- Sprite memory settings and reserved sprites (`SpriteSlotMax1`,
  `SpriteSlotMax2`) change which slot is first.
- Use only the first code for level sprites only, or only the second for
  everything else.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Level sprites load 4 tiles to the left (any X offset)

**Codes (12, emulator only):** `0AC1-046C` + `0BC1-04AC` + `CCC1-07DC` +
`1BC0-640C` + `ADC0-646C` + `B9C0-64AC` + `30C0-67DC` + `DFC0-676C` +
`EEC9-6DDC` + `0AC9-6D0C` + `13C9-6D6C` + `CBC9-6DAC`
**Raw form:**

| Address | New | Orig |
|---|---|---|
| `02A96A` | `4C` | `95` |
| `02A96B` | `49` | `E4` |
| `02A96C` | `AA` | `A5` |
| `02AA49` | `69` | `1E` |
| `02AA4A` | `C0` | `9D` |
| `02AA4B` | `95` | `4A` |
| `02AA4C` | `E4` | `0F` |
| `02AA4E` | `01` | `1B` |
| `02AA50` | `FF` | `00` |
| `02AA51` | `4C` | `9D` |
| `02AA52` | `6E` | `3E` |
| `02AA53` | `A9` | `1E` |

(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:11:31

**Mechanism:** In horizontal levels a sprite loads when the screen boundary
(`_0`/`_1`) reaches the sprite's column, and `CODE_02A95B` (`bank_02.asm`)
sets its X to that boundary. The match must be exact, so the offset has to
be added where X is stored. There is no room there for an `ADC`, so the
codes add a jump to a short routine:

```
CODE_02A95B:                                  ;   patched
    ...
    LDA.B _0                                  ;   $02A968: A5 00
    JMP $AA49                                 ;   $02A96A: 4C 49 AA (was STA.B SpriteXPosLow,X / LDA.B _1)
    db $01                                    ;   skipped
    STA.W SpriteXPosHigh,X                    ;   $02A96E: 9D E0 14
  + INY
    ...

$02AA49:                                      ;   new routine
    ADC.B #$C0                                ;   69 C0
    STA.B SpriteXPosLow,X                     ;   95 E4
    LDA.B _1                                  ;   A5 01 (already in the ROM)
    ADC.B #$FF                                ;   69 FF (69 already in the ROM)
    JMP $A96E                                 ;   4C 6E A9
```

So X = boundary + `$FFC0`, which is 64 pixels (4 tiles) left. The carry is
clear on entry: it comes from the `LSR A` of `ScreenMode` that branched to
`CODE_02A95B` because bit 0 was clear, and nothing in between changes it.

The routine goes over the middle of `CODE_02AA33`, the loader for cluster
sprite `$E4`. No level in the game uses sprite `$E4` (the disassembly marks
that routine unreachable). The routine is placed at `$02AA49` because the
bytes `A5`, `69` and `00` there already match, which saves codes.

When Mario goes right, the boundary is `$120` past the left edge of the
screen (`DATA_02A7F6`/`DATA_02A7F9`, `!ScrollDir_RightDown`). Sprites are
erased when they are more than `$130` past the left edge
(`SpriteOffScreen3`/`SpriteOffScreen4`). So the offset must be negative, or
at most `+$10`, for sprites to survive when they load on the right.

What that should look like:
- As Mario runs right, each sprite appears suddenly 32 pixels inside the
  right edge of the screen, instead of coming in from off screen.

**Alternatives** (change the 5th code; for `+$10`, also leave out the 9th):

| 5th code | Offset | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| `6DC0-646C` (`$80`) | `-$80` (8 tiles) | Sprites appear just right of the middle of the screen |
| `0DC0-646C` (`$40`) | `-$C0` (12 tiles) | Sprites appear about where Mario stands |
| `FDC0-646C` (`$10`) | `+$10` (1 tile) | Without `EEC9-6DDC`: sprites are one tile right of where they should be |

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A5 00 95 E4 A5 01 9D E0 14 C8` at `$02A968` and
`1E 9D 4A 0F A5 1B 69 00 9D 3E 1E` at `$02AA49`. With the codes applied,
those become `A5 00 4C 49 AA 01 9D E0 14 C8` and
`69 C0 95 E4 A5 01 69 FF 4C 6E A9`. All codes round-trip through
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the disassembly and **has
not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- 12 codes, so this is for emulators only.
- Partial sets are not safe. Without all of the routine codes, the jump runs
  into the rest of `CODE_02AA33` and the game will likely crash.
- When Mario goes left, the boundary is `$30` left of the screen. With a
  negative offset those sprites start past the left erase limit (`$40`), so
  they are erased at once. Positive offsets work the other way round.
- Only horizontal levels. Vertical levels take X from the sprite data in a
  different branch.
- Special loaders (5 Eeries, 3 platforms, shooters, generators) have their
  own position code and are not shifted.
- A ROM hack that uses sprite `$E4` would run into the new routine.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Always-on generators spawn Koopas (green, blue, yellow) or bouncing Paratroopas

**Example (Super Koopa generator spawns Green Koopas in every level):**
`BF8D-DDD6` + `D08A-07A6`
**Raw form:** `02B000:91` (orig `$18`), `02B1CF:04` (orig `$71`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:30:47 (blue and yellow added 2026-09-30 21:31:43)

Tags: `demo-ready`

**Mechanism:** Each code set is one of the sets from "A chosen generator
runs in every level from the start", plus codes that change the sprite
number the generator writes. Every generator except the para-enemy one has
a single `LDA.B #imm / STA.B SpriteNumber,X` (or `STA.W SpriteNumber,Y`):

| Generator | Routine | Sprite byte | Orig |
|---|---|---|---|
| Eerie | `GenerateEerie` | `$02B2E9` | `$38` Eerie |
| Dolphin, left | `CODE_02B288` | `$02B28E` | `$41` dolphin |
| Jumping fish | `GenerateFish` | `$02B16E` | `$17` flying Cheep Cheep |
| Super Koopa | `GenSuperKoopa` | `$02B1CF` | `$71` Super Koopa |
| Bubble | `GenerateBubble` | `$02B21A` | `$9D` bubble |
| Bullet Bill | `GenerateBullet` | `$02B094` | `$1C` Bullet Bill |
| Multi Bullet Bill (both) | `CODE_02B115` | `$02B11C` | `$1C` Bullet Bill |
| Bowser statue fire | `GenerateFire` | `$02B04E` | `$B3` statue fireball |

`GenParaEnemy` reads its sprite from `DATA_02B31F` (`$3F,$40,$3F,$3F,$40,
$40`), at index `CurrentGenerator - 2`, plus 3 at random. With the
Para-Goomba set, which reads `$02` from `$0285B9`, it uses entries 0 and 3
(`$02B31F` and `$02B322`), so both are changed. The Para-Bomb and mixed
sets would give the same result with their own two entries, so only the
Para-Goomba set is listed.

The new sprite is `$04` (Green Koopa), `$06` (Blue Koopa), `$07` (Yellow
Koopa) or `$09` (green bouncing Koopa, the Paratroopa that hops). Only the
first character of each sprite code changes: `D0` green, `D1` blue, `D5`
yellow, `DB` Paratroopa. The generators set status `$08` directly, so the
sprite's init routine (`InitStandardSprite`, or `InitGrnBounceKoopa`) never
runs. That init only picks a random value for `SpriteMisc1570`, faces Mario
and, for the bouncing Koopa, sets `SpriteMisc160E` from the Y position.

Use the base codes plus one column's codes. Every set is 5 codes or fewer,
so all of them fit real hardware.

What that should look like:
- In every level, Koopas arrive the way the generator's own sprite would:
  thrown up from below the screen (fish), dropped from above (para-enemy),
  from the screen edges at random heights (Super Koopa, bubble, Bullet
  Bill, statue fire), or in groups around the screen (multi Bullet Bill).
  Then they walk, or hop with the Paratroopa version.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A9 xx 95 9E` (or `A9 1C 99 9E` for the
multi-bullet routine) at each sprite byte minus 1, with the original values
in the table above, and `3F 40 3F 3F 40 40` at `$02B31F`. All codes
round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the
disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The level's own generators are ignored, as with the base sets.
- The generator's speeds and direction are made for its own sprite. A Koopa
  sets its own X speed from its direction (`SpriteMisc157C`), so the X speed
  is lost; the Y speed (fish, Super Koopa, dolphin) is kept until gravity
  takes over.
- Without the init, Koopas do not turn to face Mario. Generators that set
  `SpriteMisc157C` (Super Koopa, bubble, statue fire) make them face away
  from their side of the screen; the others leave it at 0, so those Koopas
  all face the same way.
- The statue fire and Bullet Bill generators spawn at the screen edge;
  Koopas that walk off screen are erased.
- Dolphin, right is left out, as in the base sets. (See "Dolphin, right
  generator always on, with every sprite swap", added later.)

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Always-on generators spawn Bullet Bills, Banzai Bills, Lakitus, Magikoopas or springboards

**Example (jumping fish generator throws springboards in every level):**
`2C8D-DDD6` + `4E81-0766`
**Raw form:** `02B000:DA` (orig `$18`), `02B16E:2F` (orig `$17`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:35:22

**Mechanism:** Same as "Always-on generators spawn Koopas (green, blue,
yellow) or bouncing Paratroopas": one always-on set, plus the code(s) that
change the generator's sprite number (sprite byte addresses are listed in
that entry). The first two characters of each sprite code pick the sprite:
`FA` Bullet Bill, `BE` Banzai Bill, `F3` Lakitu, `FE` Magikoopa, `4E`
portable springboard.

The generators write status `$08` (normal) directly, so the sprite's init
routine never runs. That is fine for the springboard (its init is
`Return0185C2`, an `RTS`), the Banzai Bill and the Magikoopa, but two of
these sprites need their init:
- `InitLakitu` creates the Lakitu's cloud (sprite `$87`). Without it the
  Lakitu never moves and is never erased off screen, so stuck Lakitus soon
  fill every slot.
- `InitBulletBill` sets the direction (`SpriteTableC2`) toward Mario.
  Without it most generators leave it at 0, so every Bullet Bill flies
  right.

For those two, one more code changes the generator's `LDA.B #$08` before
`STA.W SpriteStatus,X` to `#$01`, the status the level loader uses. The
init routine then runs on the sprite's first frame, after the generator has
set its position.

| Eerie | `$02B2E5` | `DF83-6F06` |
| Para-enemy | `$02B338` | `DF87-A4D6` |
| Dolphin, left | `$02B28A` | `DF86-6466` |
| Jumping fish | `$02B16A` | `DF81-0466` |
| Super Koopa | `$02B1CB` | `DF8A-04A6` |
| Bubble | `$02B216` | `DF8F-6F66` |
| Bullet Bill | `$02B090` | `DF8B-DDD6` |
| Multi Bullet Bill (both) | `$02B122` | `DF84-0D66` |
| Bowser statue fire | `$02B04A` | `DF80-D466` |

Sets of up to 5 codes fit real hardware; the 6-code sets are for emulators
only.

What that should look like:
- Bullet Bill: Bullet Bills arrive the way the generator's sprite would,
  then fly level toward the side Mario is on.
- Banzai Bill: giant Bullet Bills appear and fly left at a fixed speed.
- Lakitu: a Lakitu on a cloud appears, follows Mario and throws Spinies.
  `InitLakitu` erases a new Lakitu when one is already out, so there is one
  at a time.
- Magikoopa: several Magikoopas can be out at once, each teleporting and
  casting spells.
- Springboard: springboards fall in and land, and Mario can carry and use
  them.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A9 08 9D C8 14` (or `A9 08 99 C8 14` for the
multi-bullet routine) just before each status byte above, then the
`LDA #sprite` from the Koopa entry. `InitLakitu`, `InitBulletBill`,
`InitBanzai`, `InitMagikoopa` and `Return0185C2` are in `bank_01.asm`. All
codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from
the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The level's own generators are ignored, as with the base sets.
- Banzai Bills always fly left (`CODE_02D587` sets X speed `$E8`). Ones
  that spawn at the left edge leave the screen at once. Their init, which
  would erase a Banzai Bill with Mario to its right and play the "kapow"
  sound, is skipped.
- `InitMagikoopa` would allow only one Magikoopa; skipping it allows many.
  Magikoopa magic and graphics are made for one, so several at once may
  draw wrongly.
- Lakitu, Magikoopa, Banzai Bill and springboard graphics are not in every
  sprite tileset, so in many levels they are drawn with the wrong tiles.
- Dolphin, right is left out, as in the base sets. (See "Dolphin, right
  generator always on, with every sprite swap", added later.)

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.


## Always-on generators spawn POW switches

**Example (Super Koopa generator spawns P-switches in every level):**
`BF8D-DDD6` + `738A-07A6` + `DF8A-04A6`
**Raw form:** `02B000:91` (orig `$18`), `02B1CF:3E` (orig `$71`),
`02B1CB:01` (orig `$08`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:36:22

**Mechanism:** Same as "Always-on generators spawn Bullet Bills, Banzai
Bills, Lakitus, Magikoopas or springboards": an always-on set, a code that
changes the sprite number to `$3E` (POW, the P-switch; sprite codes start
with `73`), and a code that changes the status from `$08` to `$01` so the
init routine runs.

The init is needed. `InitPSwitch` (`bank_01.asm`) picks blue or silver from
bit 4 of the X position (`SpriteMisc151C`), sets the palette to match, and
sets status `$09` (carryable). The generators place sprites at random or
varying X positions, so both colors show up. A blue P-switch turns coins
and blocks into each other; a silver one turns enemies into silver coins.

only.

What that should look like:
- In every level, blue and silver P-switches arrive the way the generator's
  sprite would and land. Mario can carry them, throw them and step on them.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A9 08 9D C8 14` (or `A9 08 99 C8 14`) before
each status byte and the `LDA #sprite` bytes listed in the Koopa entry. All
codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from
the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The level's own generators are ignored, as with the base sets.
- Pressed P-switches start the P-switch timer and music each time, so the
  level can stay in P-switch mode most of the time.

  P-switches out, generated enemies may stop because no slot is free.

## Always-on generators spawn pipe Lakitus, exploding blocks, throw blocks or coin game clouds

**Example (Super Koopa generator spawns exploding blocks in every level):**
`BF8D-DDD6` + `0A8A-07A6` + `DF8A-04A6`
**Raw form:** `02B000:91` (orig `$18`), `02B1CF:4C` (orig `$71`),
`02B1CB:01` (orig `$08`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:39:01

**Mechanism:** Same as "Always-on generators spawn Bullet Bills, Banzai
Bills, Lakitus, Magikoopas or springboards": an always-on set, a code that
changes the generator's sprite number, and for some sprites a code that
changes the status the generator writes (`$08`). The sprite code's first two
characters pick the sprite: `08` pipe Lakitu, `0A` exploding block, `97`
throw block, `1C` coin game cloud. The status codes use the same addresses
as that entry: `DF..` codes write `$01` (run init), `DB..` codes write `$09`
(carryable).

- **Pipe-dwelling Lakitu (`$4B`):** its init is `InitPiranha`, which only
  moves it 8 pixels right and 1 up, so it is skipped. `PipeLakituMain`
  never applies gravity, so it stays where it spawns, rises and sinks
  through its states and throws Spinies.
- **Exploding block (`$4C`):** `InitExplodingBlk` picks what comes out from
  bit 4-5 of the X position (`ExplodingBlkSpr`: `$15` fish, `$0F` Goomba,
  `$00` shell-less Koopa, `$04` Koopa) and stores it in `SpriteTableC2`. So
  the status is changed to `$01` to run it. Without it most generators leave
  `SpriteTableC2` at 0 and every block holds a shell-less Koopa.
  `ExplodingBlkMain` shakes the block in place and, when Mario is within
  `$60` pixels and it is on screen, turns it into that sprite (`CODE_02E463`).
- **Throw block (`$53`):** both its init and its normal-status main are
  `Return0185C2` (`RTS`), so in status `$08` it would be invisible, never
  erased, and fill the slots. The status is changed to `$09`, carryable, as
  for a stunned shell. A throw block from a block gets a vanish timer
  (`SpriteMisc1540` = `$FF`, `CODE_02862F`); here the timer is 0, and
  `CODE_01969C` returns while the timer is 0, so the block never vanishes.
  `StunThrowBlock` cycles its palette while the timer is below `$40`, so it
  flashes the whole time.
- **Coin game cloud (`$6A`):** init is `Return0185C2`. `ADDR_02EEB5` moves
  it right at speed `$08`, drifts its Y toward `$110`, and drops a coin
  every `$80` frames, 11 in all. Only after the 11th coin does it call the
  off-screen check, so each cloud stays for about 23 seconds.
