only.

What that should look like:
- Pipe Lakitu: Lakitus with no pipe hang in the air where they spawn, and
  throw Spinies.
- Exploding block: shaking blocks hang in the air and burst into a fish,
  Goomba or Koopa as Mario gets close.
- Throw block: flashing blocks land. Mario can carry and throw them, and
  they break when thrown into a wall.

**Evidence:** The routines named above are in `bank_01.asm` and
`bank_02.asm`. The ROM bytes are the same as in the earlier generator
entries. All codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The level's own generators are ignored, as with the base sets.
- A coin cloud resets the coin game count (`GameCloudCoinCount`) when it
  starts, if its `SpriteTableC2` is 0. Clouds stay for about 23 seconds and
  are not erased off screen, so they can fill the generator's slots.
- The bubble, Bullet Bill and diagonal generators set `SpriteTableC2`. Pipe
  Lakitus from those start in a later state, and coin clouds from them do
  not reset the coin count.
- Many of these sprites are not in every sprite tileset, so in some levels
  they are drawn with the wrong tiles.
- Dolphin, right is left out, as in the base sets. (See "Dolphin, right
  generator always on, with every sprite swap", added later.)

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.


## Always-on generators spawn stars, 1-ups, fireworks, P-balloons, Lakitu clouds or Chargin' Chucks

**Example (Super Koopa generator spawns stars in every level):**
`BF8D-DDD6` + `518A-07A6`
**Raw form:** `02B000:91` (orig `$18`), `02B1CF:76` (orig `$71`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:42:07

**Mechanism:** Same as "Always-on generators spawn Koopas (green, blue,
yellow) or bouncing Paratroopas": an always-on set plus a code that changes
the generator's sprite number. The first two characters of the sprite code
pick the sprite: `51` star, `56` 1-up, `5C` firework, `52` P-balloon, `65`
Lakitu's cloud, `BF` Chargin' Chuck.

None of these needs its init routine, so the generator's status `$08` is
kept:
- Star and 1-up: `InitPowerUp` only does `INC SpriteTableC2`. In
  `PowerUpRt` a nonzero `SpriteTableC2` makes the item rise until it hits a
  block side; at 0 it just moves normally, which is fine here.
- Firework, P-balloon, Lakitu's cloud and Chargin' Chuck: the init is an
  `RTS` (`Return018583`, `Return0185C2`, `Return018869`).

Notes on the less usual ones:
- **Firework (`$7A`):** `Firework` (`bank_03.asm`) is the ending's
  firework. State 0 sets an upward speed and plays a sound, then it rises,
  bursts with more sounds, fades, and clears its own status. It also sets
  `SpriteMisc1564+9`, a timer in sprite slot 9.
- **Lakitu's cloud (`$87`):** `LakituCloud` (`bank_01.asm`) first looks for
  a Lakitu (`$1E`, status `$08`) and carries it if there is one. With none,
  it is the empty cloud: with `SpriteTableC2` = 0 it waits until Mario lands
  on it, then he rides it (`PlayerInCloud`) until he jumps off.
- **Chargin' Chuck (`$91`):** `ChucksMain` runs its states from
  `SpriteTableC2`.

All of these sets fit real hardware (5 codes or fewer).

What that should look like:
- Star: a stream of stars, so Mario can stay invincible nearly all the time.
- 1-Up: a stream of extra lives.
- Firework: fireworks shoot up and burst with their sounds.
- P-balloon: balloons drift across; one touch inflates Mario.
- Lakitu's cloud: empty clouds hang in the air for Mario to ride.
- Chargin' Chuck: Chucks arrive and charge. (The Bullet Bill version has its
  own entry, "Bullet Bill generator always on, spawns Chargin' Chucks".)

**Evidence:** The routines named above are in `bank_01.asm`,
`bank_02.asm` and `bank_03.asm`. The ROM bytes are the same as in the
earlier generator entries. All codes round-trip through
`tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from the disassembly and **has
not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The level's own generators are ignored, as with the base sets.
- The bubble, Bullet Bill and diagonal generators set `SpriteTableC2` after
  the sprite is made. For the cloud, a nonzero value means "being ridden",
  so those clouds snap to Mario at once and he is in a cloud. Stars and
  1-ups from them start in the rising state, and Chucks from them start in
  a later state.
- `LakituCloud` never calls an off-screen check, so clouds are not erased
  and soon fill the generator's slots.
- Firework graphics come from the ending and are drawn to fixed OAM slots
  (`CODE_03C96D`), so in a level they will likely look wrong and may clash
  with other sprites.
- Many of these sprites are not in every sprite tileset, so in some levels
  they are drawn with the wrong tiles.
- Dolphin, right is left out, as in the base sets. (See "Dolphin, right
  generator always on, with every sprite swap", added later.)

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.


## Bullet Bill generator always on, spawns Chargin' Chucks

**Codes:** `E18D-DDD6` + `BF8B-DFD6`
**Raw form:** `02B000:F6` (orig `$18`), `02B094:91` (orig `$1C`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:42:07

Tags: `bullet-bill-generator-collection` `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated` `challenge`

**Mechanism:** This is the Bullet Bill row of the Chargin' Chuck column in
"Always-on generators spawn stars, 1-ups, fireworks, P-balloons, Lakitu clouds
or Chargin' Chucks".

`E18D-DDD6` turns the plain Bullet Bill generator on in every level. It moves the
`LDA.W CurrentGenerator` in `CallGenerator` to the ROM byte at `$02F6B9`, which
is `$0B`. See "A chosen generator runs in every level from the start".

`BF8B-DFD6` changes the sprite that `GenerateBullet` makes. The operand of
`LDA.B #$1C` ("Sprite = Bullet Bill") becomes `$91`, a Chargin' Chuck. Every 128
frames, a Chuck appears just off the left or right edge of the screen at a random
height, with the Bullet Bill sound, and then charges.

The generator sets status `$08`, so the sprite's init routine never runs. For a
Chuck the init is only an `RTS`, so nothing is lost.

**Evidence:** The ROM has `A9 1C 95 9E` at `$02B093`, and `$02F6B9` holds
`$0B`. Both codes decode back to the raw form above. The effect comes from the
disassembly and **was not seen in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The level's own generators are ignored.
- `GenerateBullet` sets `SpriteTableC2` to the edge it picked (0 or 1) after
  the sprite is made, and Chucks use that byte as their state. So the Chucks
  from one of the two edges start in state 1, not state 0.
- Chucks are not in every sprite tileset, so in some levels they are drawn with
  the wrong tiles.

The addresses were checked for the U release. The other four releases have not
been checked.

## Always-on generators spawn Hammer Bro flying blocks

**Example (Super Koopa generator spawns flying blocks in every level):**
`BF8D-DDD6` + `BA8A-07A6`
**Raw form:** `02B000:91` (orig `$18`), `02B1CF:9C` (orig `$71`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:42:51

**Mechanism:** Same as "Always-on generators spawn Koopas (green, blue,
yellow) or bouncing Paratroopas": an always-on set plus a code that changes
the generator's sprite number, here to `$9C` ("Flying blocks for Hammer
Brother"; sprite codes start with `BA`). Its init is `Return0185C2`
(`RTS`), so the generator's status `$08` is kept.

`CODE_02DB5C` (`FlyingPlatformMain`, `bank_02.asm`) draws the two blocks,
then looks through slots 0-9 for a Hammer Brother (`$9B`, status `$08`). If
it finds one, it moves that Hammer Brother onto itself. Then it calls
`SubOffscreen1Bnk2` and swings its X and Y speeds back and forth
(`DATA_02DB54`-`DATA_02DB5A`), so it flies in a loop. Mario can stand on
it.

| Bowser statue fire | `CBCE-A768` + `D3CE-A7A8` + `BA80-D766` |

All of these sets fit real hardware (5 codes or fewer).

What that should look like:
- In every level, pairs of flying blocks arrive the way the generator's
  sprite would, then loop around in the air. Mario can ride them.

**Evidence:** The ROM bytes are the same as in the earlier generator
entries. All codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is
derived from the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The level's own generators are ignored, as with the base sets.
- In a level with a Hammer Brother, every flying block moves the same
  (first-found) Hammer Brother onto itself each frame, so he jumps between
  platforms and is drawn on more than one.
- The flying block graphics are not in every sprite tileset, so in some
  levels they are drawn with the wrong tiles.
- Dolphin, right is left out, as in the base sets. (See "Dolphin, right
  generator always on, with every sprite swap", added later.)

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## Always-on generators spawn Hammer Brothers

**Example (Super Koopa generator spawns Hammer Brothers in every level):**
`BF8D-DDD6` + `B88A-07A6`
**Raw form:** `02B000:91` (orig `$18`), `02B1CF:9B` (orig `$71`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:44:29

**Mechanism:** Same as "Always-on generators spawn Koopas (green, blue,
yellow) or bouncing Paratroopas": an always-on set plus a code that changes
the generator's sprite number, here to `$9B` ("Hammer Brother"; sprite
codes start with `B8`). Its init is `InitHammerBrother`, which does
nothing, so the generator's status `$08` is kept.

`CODE_02DA5A` (`HammerBrotherMain`, `bank_02.asm`) checks contact with
Mario, calls `SubOffscreen1Bnk2`, and throws a hammer on a timer
(`HammerFreq`). It never applies its speeds to its position and has no
gravity. So a Hammer Brother stays at the point where the generator puts
it, and only moves when a flying block (`$9C`) carries it.

## Level sprites load 4 tiles higher

**Code:** `1BC9-076C` + `ADC9-07AC`
**Raw form:** `02A95E:69` (orig `$29`), `02A95F:C0` (orig `$F0`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-09-30 21:49:57

**Mechanism:** Same as "Level sprites load 2 tiles higher". The first code
changes `AND #$F0` in `CODE_02A95B` (`bank_02.asm`) to `ADC`. The
carry is clear here. The second code sets the operand to `$C0`. So the low
byte of a sprite's Y position becomes the data byte plus `$C0`, which is
64 pixels (4 tiles) higher. The high byte is still taken from the data.

What that should look like:
- Most sprites appear 4 tiles above their normal place. Walking enemies
  drop to the ground; flying and floating ones stay higher than usual.

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `B7 CE 48 29 F0 95 D8` at `$02A95B`. Both
codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from
the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The low byte wraps. Sprites in the top four rows of a 256-pixel band (low
  byte `$00`-`$3F`) move 192 pixels down instead.
- The low 4 bits of the data byte (`EEsy`) are no longer masked off, so
  they are added too: 1 pixel for sprites in the lower part of the level
  (`y`), 2 for screens `$10` and above (`s`), 4-12 for sprites that use
  extra bits.
- Only horizontal levels: in vertical levels Y comes from the screen
  boundary, and this code does not run.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

init runs. `InitBomb` (`bank_01.asm`) sets its fuse timer
`SpriteMisc1540` to `$FF`. Without it the timer is 0, and `Bobomb` at
once makes it stunned (lit) with `$40` frames left, so it explodes about
one second after it appears. The 3-code set `CBCE-A768` + `D3CE-A7A8` +
`D280-D766` gives these lit Bob-ombs.

The other sprites keep status `$08`. Their own generators also skip their
init routines, and `InitStandardSprite` (Goomba, Spiny) only sets the facing
direction, which `GenerateFire` already sets.

What that should look like:
- Goombas, Spinies, Bob-ombs and mushrooms appear at the right edge and walk.
- Para-Goombas and Para-Bombs float down from where they appear.
- Bubbles float with a Goomba inside (`SpriteTableC2` is left at 0).

**Evidence:** The ROM holds `A9 08 9D C8 14 A9 B3 95` at `$02B048`. All
codes round-trip through `tools/gg_encode.py`. The effect is derived from
the disassembly and **has not been observed in play**.

**Caveats:**
- The level's own generators are ignored, as with the base set.
- The Eerie, Dolphin, jumping fish and Super Koopa generators give their
  sprite a starting speed. `GenerateFire` does not, so these start with
  speed 0 and may move differently: a jumping fish just falls.
- Sprites whose graphics are not in the level's sprite tileset are drawn
  with the wrong tiles.

**Provenance:** Addresses from `SMW_U.sym`, plus a direct read of
`comparison_U.smc` minus its 512-byte copier header.

Addresses verified for the U release; the other four releases have not been
checked.

## A new game skips the intro message and starts on the map

**Code:** `DDB8-DD07`

**Raw form:** `$009CB1 ← $00 (originally $E9)`

**Recorded:** 2026-10-01 17:41:20

Tags: `fast-load-collection`

**Mechanism:** When a new game starts, the game first loads the intro
level (level `$C5`, the "Welcome! This is Dinosaur Land" message). It
does this through `OverworldOverride`. When that byte is not zero, the
overworld load goes to that level instead of the map. `EnterFileSelect`
sets it to the intro level each time the file select screen opens:

```
EnterFileSelect:
    LDA.B #!MainMapLvls+!IntroCutsceneLevel   ;\ Upon entering file select,  <- $009CB1, operand $E9
    STA.W OverworldOverride                   ;| Set overworld override to intro cutscene
    JSR InitSaveData                          ;/ And initialize save data for new game
```

`GM08FileSelect` clears `OverworldOverride` only when the chosen file is
valid (`STZ.W OverworldOverride ; Don't to go intro cutscene`). An empty
file goes to `.NotValid` and keeps the value. The code changes the
immediate from `$E9` (`36 + $C5`) to `$00`. Now a new file keeps
`OverworldOverride` = 0, the same as a loaded file. `GM0CLoadOverworld`
then loads the map, not the intro level. Mario starts on Yoshi's House
at the position from `InitPlayerOverworldData` (`!InitOWPosX`,
`!InitOWPosY` = `$68`, `$78`), which `InitSaveData` copies in.

**Evidence:** The ROM at `$009CB1` has `A9 E9 8D 09 01`: `LDA #$E9` /
`STA $0109`. This matches the source. `EnterFileSelect`,
`OverworldOverride` and `!IntroCutsceneLevel` are all named, and the
`.NotValid` path is commented in `bank_00.asm`. A headless Mesen run
(fresh SRAM, Start pressed until file 1 / 1 player) logged `GameMode` and
`OverworldOverride` per frame. Without the code: `$0C` → `$10`–`$14` with
`OverworldOverride` = `$E9` (the intro level), then the map. With the code
(added through Mesen's own `snesGameGenie` cheat type): `$0C` → `$0D` →
`$0E` with `OverworldOverride` = `$00`, so no level loads. Not played by
hand.

**Caveats:**

- **Works on any empty file.** `EnterFileSelect` sets the byte for all
  three files, and `GM08FileSelect` treats every empty file the same way.
  A second headless run that picked file 2 (`SaveFile` = 1) also went
  straight to the map. A file that already has a save never plays the
  intro, with or without the code.
- **Turn the code on before file select opens.** The byte is read only
  when `EnterFileSelect` runs, as the file select screen comes up. If the
  code is turned on at file select, or a save state from after that point
  is loaded, `OverworldOverride` is already `$E9` and the intro still
  plays. Turn the code on and then reset, or go back to the title
  screen. Pressing X or Y on the player select screen also works, since
  `BackToFileSelect` runs `EnterFileSelect` again.
- **No walk-in.** At the end of the intro, `CODE_05B15B` puts Mario at
  Y = `$8E`, below Yoshi's House. `CODE_048EF1` sees that exact position
  and plays the short walk up into the house. With the code, Mario is
  already on the house, so this walk does not happen.
- `EnterFileSelect` is the only place that sets the intro level. It
  runs from both `PrepareFileSelect` and `BackToFileSelect`, so the code
  covers every way to reach file select.
- The value `$E9` is also compared in `UploadLevelMusic` and
  `GM11LoadLevel` to pick the intro music. Those checks read
  `OverworldOverride`, not this byte, so they just never match.
- The code is for the U version. The other versions have the same
  `A9 E9 8D 09 01` at their own `EnterFileSelect` (read from each
  `SMW_*.smc`, address from each `SMW_*.sym`):

  | Version | Raw form | Code |
  |---|---|---|
  | J | `$009C43 ← $00 (originally $E9)` | `DDB0-DDA7` |
  | E0 | `$009CB6 ← $00 (originally $E9)` | `DDB8-DF67` |
  | E1 | `$009CB8 ← $00 (originally $E9)` | `DDB8-D4D7` |
  | SS | `$009BC2 ← $00 (originally $E9)` | `DDBA-AD64` |

  In SS, `GM08FileSelect` already clears `OverworldOverride` when a zone
  other than zone 1 is picked. With the code, zone 1 skips the intro too.

**Provenance:** The address comes from `SMW_U.sym` (`EnterFileSelect` =
`$009CB0`, plus 1 for the operand). The byte was read from
`comparison_U.smc` at file offset `0x1EB0` (LoROM `0x1CB0` plus the
`0x200` copier header). The code decodes back to `$009CB1:$00` with a
scratchpad encoder that also decodes `2DB4-DD0F` and `DDB4-A467`
correctly.

## Smart basic enemies

**Codes:** `DD6F-A401` + `DD61-ADD1` + `DD65-A761` + `DD6B-A401`

**Raw form:**
- `018B19:00`, original `$02` (fast)
- `018B60:00`, original `$19` (face Mario)
- `018B7E:00`, original `$03` (jump over kicked shells)
- `018B99:00`, original `$16` (turn round at ledges)

SNES Game Genie has no compare byte, so the codes write the values whatever is
there. Use all four together.

**Recorded:** 2026-10-01 20:48:13

Tags: `basic-enemies` `play-start` `interesting` `video-ready` `challenge`

**Mechanism:** Every Goomba, Koopa (with or without a shell, and the yellow
winged one), Bob-omb, Buzzy Beetle and Spiny walks with `Spr0to13Main` in
`bank_01.asm`. Each sprite has one byte of flags in `Spr0to13Prop`, and four of
the bits are:

```
$01  fast (use the second pair of Spr0to13SpeedX entries)
$02  turn round at a ledge
$04  face Mario
$08  jump over a kicked shell
```

`Spr0to13Main` reads the table in four separate places, one for each bit, so
no single byte turns on all four for every sprite. Each code changes the
branch that tests one bit. The new displacement is `$00`, so the branch goes
to the next instruction whether it is taken or not, and the code for that bit
always runs:

```
    LDA.W Spr0to13Prop,Y      ; $018B11
    LSR A
    LDY.W SpriteMisc157C,X
    BCC +                     ; $018B19: $02 -> $00, so INY INY always runs
    INY
    INY
  + LDA.W Spr0to13SpeedX,Y    ; $0C/$F4 (fast), not $08/$F8
    ...
    LDA.W Spr0to13Prop,Y      ; $018B59
    PHA
    AND.B #$04
    BEQ +                     ; $018B60: $19 -> $00, so face Mario always runs
    ...
  + PLA
    AND.B #$08
    BEQ +                     ; $018B7E: $03 -> $00
    JSR JumpOverShells        ;           so this always runs
    ...
SpriteInAir:
    ...
  + LDA.W Spr0to13Prop,Y      ; $018B93
    AND.B #$02
    BEQ CODE_018BB0           ; $018B99: $16 -> $00, so the ledge turn always runs
```

The branches no longer read the table at all, so this also works for the
sprites whose byte is `$00` (the green Koopa without a shell, the Buzzy Beetle
and the Spiny). The "AND #$FF" codes in "Every Goomba, Koopa and Buzzy Beetle
turns round and comes after you" do not reach those sprites.

**One byte for one enemy type:** if you only want one kind of enemy to be
smart, set the low four bits of its `Spr0to13Prop` entry (`OR $0F`). This is
one code, and it changes only that sprite:

| Sprite | Code | Raw (original) |
|---|---|---|
| `$00` Green Koopa, no shell | `DE6E-DDD1` | `0188F0:0F` (`$00`) |
| `$01` Red Koopa, no shell | `DE6E-DD01` | `0188F1:0F` (`$02`) |
| `$02` Blue Koopa, no shell | `DE6E-DD61` | `0188F2:0F` (`$03`) |
| `$03` Yellow Koopa, no shell | `DE6E-DDA1` | `0188F3:0F` (`$0D`) |
| `$04` Green Koopa | `0E6E-DFD1` | `0188F4:4F` (`$40`) |
| `$05` Red Koopa | `0E6E-DF01` | `0188F5:4F` (`$42`) |
| `$06` Blue Koopa | `0E6E-DF61` | `0188F6:4F` (`$43`) |
| `$07` Yellow Koopa | `0E6E-DFA1` | `0188F7:4F` (`$45`) |
| `$0C` Yellow Koopa with wings | `2E6E-D7D1` | `0188FC:DF` (`$DD`) |
| `$0D` Bob-omb | `DE6E-D701` | `0188FD:0F` (`$05`) |
| `$0F` Goomba | `4E6E-D7A1` | `0188FF:2F` (`$20`) |
| `$11` Buzzy Beetle | `DE6D-0D01` | `018901:0F` (`$00`) |
| `$13` Spiny | `DE6D-0DA1` | `018903:0F` (`$00`) |

The other bits of each byte (two tiles tall, flutter) are kept. The Bob-omb
code is the same as `DE6E-D701` in "Every Goomba, Koopa and Buzzy Beetle turns
round and comes after you", because the Bob-omb already had bits `$01` and
`$04`.

**Evidence:** The ROM reads `b9 f0 88 4a bc 7c 15 90 02 c8 c8` from `$018B11`,
`b9 f0 88 48 29 04 f0 19` from `$018B59`, `29 08 f0 03 20 98 88` from
`$018B7B` and `b9 f0 88 29 02 f0 16` from `$018B93`. These are the four reads
of `Spr0to13Prop` (`$0188F0`) and their branches, as in the source. The table
reads `00 02 03 0D 40 42 43 45 50 50 50 5C DD 05 00 20 20 00 00 00`. The codes
round-trip through a scratchpad encoder that also decodes the existing
`DE6E-D701` to `0188FD:0F`.

A headless Mesen run on a new file entered Yoshi's Island 2 with the four
codes on. The red Koopas there walked at X speed `+12`/`-12`, not `+8`/`-8`,
and the level ran for 900 frames with no crash. The face-Mario, shell jump and
ledge parts are derived from the disassembly and **have not been observed in
play**.

**Caveats:**
- "Fast" is the faster walk speed from `Spr0to13SpeedX`, `$0C` instead of
  `$08`, so 1.5 times as fast.
- Every sprite in the group changes, including Bob-ombs, Buzzy Beetles and
  Spinies. The para-Koopas, the winged Goomba and the keyhole have their own
  handlers and do not change.
- The ledge turn runs on the first frame a sprite is in the air, and
  `JumpOverShells` puts it in the air. So after a sprite jumps over a shell,
  it probably turns round in the air and lands going back the way it came. The
  ledge turn does not happen if the sprite's turning timer is still set.
- The face-Mario turn still runs only once every `$80` animation frames.
- Shell-less Koopas also use `Spr0to13Main`, but only between their own
  actions (sliding into a shell, kicking it), so the new behaviour shows only
  while they walk.

## R turns Mario's gravity off and on

**Codes:** `F6CF-67DD` + `E7C7-6FDD` + `E7C7-640D` (all three needed)

**Raw form:**
- `00A21C:18`, original `$16`
- `00A234:F3`, original `$D4`
- `00A239:F3`, original `$D4`

SNES Game Genie has no compare byte, so the codes write the values whatever is
there.

**Recorded:** 2026-10-01 21:01:07

**Mechanism:** This is "Select inflates and deflates Mario like a P balloon,
at any time" with R instead of Select. The pause toggle (`CODE_00A21B`) reads
a new press of a button and switches a flag between 0 and 1:

```
CODE_00A21B:
    LDA.B byetudlrFrame       ; <- $00A21C, operand $16
    AND.B #$10                ; bit 4 = Start
    BEQ CODE_00A242
    ...
    LDA.W PauseFlag           ; <- $00A234, operand $D4
    EOR.B #$01
    STA.W PauseFlag           ; <- $00A239, operand $D4
```

- `F6CF-67DD` changes the `LDA` operand from `byetudlrFrame` (`$16`) to
  `axlr0000Frame` (`$18`). Bit 4 of that byte is R, so the `AND #$10` now
  tests a new press of R, not Start.
- `E7C7-6FDD` + `E7C7-640D` point the toggle at `PBalloonInflating`
  (`$13F3`) instead of `PauseFlag` (`$13D4`), as in the Select entry.

When `PBalloonInflating` is set, `CODE_00CD39` skips all of Mario's speed
code: gravity, the fall speed limit, friction and the input reads. The position
update `CODE_00DC2D` runs before that test, so Mario keeps moving at the speed
he had when you pressed R, in a straight line. Press R while standing, and he
stays where he is. Press R in a jump, and he keeps rising at the same speed.
Press R again, and gravity starts again.

**Evidence:** The ROM reads `A5 16 29 10 F0 21` at `$00A21B` and `D4` at
`$00A234` and `$00A239`. `axlr0000Frame` is `$18` in `rammap.asm`, and
the "Hold R to freeze the level" entry gives R as bit `$10` of the axlr bytes.
The codes round-trip through a scratchpad encoder.

A headless Mesen run on a new file entered Yoshi's Island 2, jumped, and pressed
R 10 frames into the jump. Without the codes, Mario's Y speed went from `-44`
to `+70` and he landed. With the codes, his Y speed stayed at `-44` and he rose
22 pixels every 8 frames until R was pressed again 100 frames later. Then he
fell as normal.

**Caveats:**
- **This switches off all of Mario's physics, not only gravity.** You cannot
  steer, run or jump while it is on. Mario drifts at a fixed speed until you
  press R again.
- **The game can no longer be paused.** Start does nothing in a level, and the
  Start+Select level skip is gone, because it needs the pause.
- R still shifts the camera when it is held alone, as normal.
- Each press starts the 60-frame pause lockout (`PauseTimer`), so you can
  switch it at most once a second. It also plays the pause and unpause sounds.
- Only a ceiling stops him. He drifts through floors and walls in every other
  direction (see the Select entry).
- The goal tape and a real P-balloon clear `PBalloonInflating`, so they turn
  gravity back on.
- Do not use this with the Select P-balloon cheat. They patch the same bytes.

## Chargin' Chuck charges at 3x speed, both directions

**Code:** `06AC-6D0B` + `86AC-6D6B` (apply both together)
**Raw form:** `02C6A1:48` (orig `$18`) + `02C6A2:B8` (orig `$E8`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-01 23:01:27

Tags: `demo-ready` `enemy-movement-collection` `play-start` `curated` `challenge`

**Mechanism:** A Chuck's walk and charge both run in state `1` of his state
machine, `CODE_02C6A7` (`bank_02.asm`). On every frame that he is on the
ground, it loads his X speed from a table with 4 entries. The index is his
facing direction (`SpriteMisc157C`), plus 2 while he is charging
(`SpriteMisc187B != 0`):

```
DATA_02C69F:
    db $10,$F0,$18,$E8

    ...
    LDA.W SpriteMisc187B,X
    BEQ CODE_02C70E
    ...
  + INY
    INY
CODE_02C70E:
    LDA.W DATA_02C69F,Y
    STA.B SpriteXSpeed,X
```

Indices `0`/`1` (`$10`/`$F0`, one pixel per frame) are the patrol speed.
Indices `2`/`3` (`$18`/`$E8`, 1.5 pixels per frame) are the charge speed.
The two codes make the charge entries three times as large, `$48` (`+72`)
and `$B8` (`-72`). That is 4.5 pixels per frame, so a charging Chuck runs
three times as fast whichever way he faces. The patrol speed does not
change.

**Evidence:** This patches `$02C6A1`/`$02C6A2`, the last two bytes of
`DATA_02C69F`, read by `LDA.W DATA_02C69F,Y` with `Y` = 2 or 3. The reference
ROM has `10 F0 18 E8` at `$02C69F`-`$02C6A2`, as the source says. Both codes
decode back to these addresses and bytes with `ggpatch`.

**Caveats:**

- This was first listed as a row in the "Chargin' Chuck splits when
  stomped" Alternatives table. It has its own entry now. The row is still
  there.
- `$48` is still below `$80`, so the sign is right in both directions. A
  larger value such as `$90` would wrap to a negative speed and make him
  charge backwards.
- Every Chuck that walks and charges through this state is faster, not only
  Chargin' Chucks. Add `0DAB-67AB` (from the same table) to make the patrol
  speed faster too.
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## The cape hits every sprite on the screen

**Code:** `DBB3-A466`
**Raw form:** `0293EA:09` (orig `$03`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 21:14:15

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** While Mario's cape swings, `CapeInteracts` is set, and on every
other frame `CODE_0294F5` runs `QuakeCapeHitSprites` (`bank_02.asm`). The same
loop also handles quake sprites (a block bumped from below), so it builds one
of two hitboxes and then runs one shared contact test:

```
    LDA.B _E                  ; _E = CapeInteracts, or 0 for a quake sprite
    BEQ CODE_0293EB
    JSR CODE_029696           ; cape hitbox
    BRA +                     ; <- $0293E9, operand $03 at $0293EA
CODE_0293EB:
    JSR CODE_029663           ; quake sprite hitbox
  + JSL CheckForContact       ; $0293EE
    BCC CODE_0293F7           ; no contact: next sprite
    JSR CODE_029404           ; $0293F4: hit the sprite
```

The code changes the cape path's `BRA` from `+3` to `+9`. It now jumps past
`JSL CheckForContact` and the `BCC`, straight to `JSR CODE_029404`. So every
sprite that passes the loop's other checks is hit by the cape, wherever it is.
`CODE_029404` is the normal cape hit: most enemies are knocked off the screen
for points, and Koopas and other stompable sprites are flipped over. The quake
path does not change, so bumping a block still only hits the sprites on top of
it.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `20 96 96 80 03 20 63 96 22 2B B7 03 90 03
20 04 94` at `$0293E6`, as in the source. The `BRA` operand is at `$0293EA`.
`$0293EB + 9 = $0293F4`, the `JSR CODE_029404`. The code decodes back to
`$0293EA:$09` with `tools/gg_encode.py`.

**Caveats:**

- The loop still skips sprites that the cape can never hurt (`SpriteTweakerC`
  bit 5), sprites on Yoshi's tongue, carried sprites, sprites in their short
  no-hit time after a hit (`SpriteMisc154C`), and sprites on the other side of
  a climbing net.
- "Every sprite" means every loaded sprite slot, so sprites just off the
  screen are hit too.
- The cape only counts while it swings: a cape spin, or the other moves that
  set `CapeInteracts`.
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## One fireball kills a Chuck

**Code:** `DFCD-0DA6`
**Raw form:** `02A103:01` (orig `$05`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 21:36:09

**Mechanism:** When a fireball touches a sprite, `ProcessFireball`
(`bank_02.asm`) checks `SpriteTweakerF` bit 3. Most sprites do not have it
and turn into a coin at once (`TurnSpriteToCoin`). A sprite that has it goes
to a hit counter instead:

```
    LDA.W SpriteTweakerF,X    ; $02A0F5
    AND.B #$08
    BEQ TurnSpriteToCoin
    INC.W SpriteMisc1528,X
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1528,X
    CMP.B #$05                ; <- operand at $02A103
    BCC FireRtNextSprite
    ...                       ; kill: splat sound, knock off the screen, points
```

The code changes the `CMP` operand from `$05` to `$01`. The counter is at
least 1 after the `INC`, so the first hit kills the sprite. It dies the
same way it does after the fifth hit in the normal game.

Only Chucks have `SpriteTweakerF` bit 3: sprite `$46` (Diggin' Chuck) and
`$91`-`$98` (the other Chucks). Sprite `$C6` also has it, but it is immune to
fire, so it never reaches this check. So this code changes only Chucks.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `BD 0F 19 29 08 F0 28 FE 28 15 BD 28 15
C9 05 90 3D` at `$02A0F5`, as in the source. The `CMP` operand is at
`$02A103`. The bit 3 list comes from `Sprite190FVals` (`$07F659`), the table
that `LoadTweakerBytes` copies into `SpriteTweakerF`. The code decodes back to
`$02A103:$01` with `tools/gg_encode.py`.

**Caveats:**

- `SpriteMisc1528` is also the Chuck's stomp counter. In the normal game, 2
  stomps mean the Chuck then needs 3 fireballs. With this code, it always
  needs only 1.
- Bosses do not use this check, so this code does not change them.
- Works with "Fireball-killed Chuck knockback", which patches the same kill
  code at `$02A151`.
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## One fireball kills Morton, Roy or Ludwig

**Code:** `DF2E-A7A0`
**Raw form:** `01D3FF:01` (orig `$0C`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 21:37:20

**Mechanism:** Morton, Roy and Ludwig (the three Mode 7 Koopa Kids) run
`WallKoopaKids` (`bank_01.asm`). On every frame of the fight it calls
`CODE_01D3B1`, which checks Mario's fireballs (extended sprite `$05`) against
the boss. A fireball that touches the boss becomes a puff of smoke and adds
one to the hit counter:

```
    INC.W SpriteMisc1626,X
    LDA.W SpriteMisc1626,X
    CMP.B #$0C                ; <- operand at $01D3FF
    BCC +
    JSR CODE_01CFD0           ; boss dies
```

The code changes the `CMP` operand from `$0C` (12 fireballs) to `$01`. The
counter is at least 1 after the `INC`, so the first fireball kills the boss.
`CODE_01CFD0` is the same death code that the third stomp runs: the boss-dead
sound, the death spin and the level clear.

No other boss counts fireballs. Iggy and Larry (`CODE_01FD0A`) turn a fireball
into smoke and count nothing. Lemmy, Wendy, Reznor, Bowser and the Big Boo
boss do not check Mario's fireballs at all. Chucks are not bosses. They are
covered by "One fireball kills a Chuck".

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `FE 26 16 BD 26 16 C9 0C 90 03 20 D0 CF` at
`$01D3F9`, as in the source. The `CMP` operand is at `$01D3FF`. The code
decodes back to `$01D3FF:$01` with `tools/gg_encode.py`.

**Caveats:**

- Stomps and fireballs share `SpriteMisc1626`. So this `CMP` is a second test
  of the counter, besides the stomp test at `$01CFCD` that "Morton, Roy and
  Ludwig die in one stomp" patches. It can be used together with those codes.
- `CODE_01D3B1` does nothing while the boss is stomped or dying
  (`SpriteMisc151C` 3 or more).
- Only Mario fireballs (`$05`) count. With "Mario throws Yoshi's fireballs"
  (`smw_game_genie_big_codes.md`), Mario's fireballs are `$11` and do not
  hurt these bosses.
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## A charging Chuck smashes any wall

**Code:** `DDAC-6F06`
**Raw form:** `02C2A5:00` (orig `$3E`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 21:38:14

Tags: `interesting` `play-start` `video-ready`

**Mechanism:** All Chucks run `ChucksMain` → `CODE_02C22C` (`bank_02.asm`).
When a charging Chuck (`SpriteMisc187B` set) runs into something from the
side, on the screen and on layer 1, it checks which tile it hit:

```
    LDA.W Map16TileDestroy
    CMP.B #$2E
    BEQ CODE_02C2A6
    CMP.B #$1E
    BNE CODE_02C2E4           ; <- operand $3E at $02C2A5
CODE_02C2A6:
    ...                       ; shatter the tile and the one above it
```

`Map16TileDestroy` is the low byte of the last page-1 tile that a sprite hit
from the side, so only tiles `$11E` (turn block) and `$12E` (throw block)
break. The code changes the `BNE` operand to `$00`, so the branch goes to the
next instruction whether it is taken or not. Every side hit then reaches
`CODE_02C2A6`. It runs `ShatterBlock` and then `GenerateTile` with tile `$02`
(empty) on the tile the Chuck touched, and does the same for the tile above
it.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `AD A7 18 C9 2E F0 04 C9 1E D0 3E` at
`$02C29B`, as in the source. The `BNE` operand is at `$02C2A5`, and
`$02C2A6 + $3E = $02C2E4`. The code decodes back to `$02C2A5:$00` with
`tools/gg_encode.py`.

**Caveats:**

- "Any wall" includes ground, pipes, cement blocks and question blocks. A
  question block is broken without giving its item.
- `CODE_02C2A6` checks that the Chuck is on the ground, so a Chuck in the air
  breaks nothing. A charging Chuck on the ground can dig a tunnel two tiles
  high through a wall.
- Walls on layer 2 still do not break.
- The check runs only while a Chuck charges, so in practice this is the
  Chargin' Chuck (and other Chucks only if they charge).
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## Stomping an enemy knocks Mario off to the side

**Codes:** `DDC0-0761` `3CC9-07D1`
**Raw form:** `01A94E:00` (orig `$0E`); `01A95C:EA` (orig `$60`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 21:39:18

Tags: `interesting` `play-start` `stomp-collection` `video-ready` `challenge`

**Mechanism:** `CODE_01A947` (`bank_01.asm`) is the normal stomp, when Mario
lands on an enemy without a spin jump or Yoshi:

```
CODE_01A947:
    JSR CODE_01A8D8           ; splat sound, bounce Mario up
    LDA.W SpriteMisc187B,X
    BEQ CODE_01A95D           ; <- operand $0E at $01A94E
    JSR SubHorizPos
    LDA.B #$18
    CPY.B #$00
    BEQ +
    LDA.B #$E8
  + STA.B PlayerXSpeed+1      ; push Mario away from the sprite
    RTS                       ; <- $01A95C
CODE_01A95D:
    ...                       ; hurt or kill the stomped sprite
```

In the normal game only a sprite with `SpriteMisc187B` set, such as the disco
shell, takes the middle path: Mario is pushed sideways and the sprite is not
hurt. That is the same knock-back a Chuck gives (`CODE_02C79D` sets
`PlayerXSpeed+1` to `$20` or `$E0` after a stomp).

The first code changes the `BEQ` operand to `$00`, so every stomp runs the
push. The second code changes the `RTS` to `NOP`, so the code then falls into
`CODE_01A95D` and the sprite is hurt as usual. Mario bounces up, is pushed
`$18` away from the enemy, and the enemy is still stomped.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `20 D8 A8 BD 7B 18 F0 0E 20 30 AD A9 18
C0 00 F0 02 A9 E8 85 7B 60 20` at `$01A947`, as in the source.
`$01A94F + $0E = $01A95D`. The codes decode back to `$01A94E:$00` and
`$01A95C:$EA` with `tools/gg_encode.py`.

**Caveats:**

- Enemies still die from one stomp. Only the bounce changes. Use the first
  code alone and stomps push Mario away but never hurt anything.
- The disco shell is no longer safe to land on: the stomp now goes on to
  `CODE_01A95D` for it too.
- Spin jumps and stomps from Yoshi use a different path, so they do not
  change. Chucks use their own stomp code, so they do not change either.
- Do not use this with "Stomps don't hurt enemies". That code puts an `RTS`
  at `$01A94A`, before these bytes.
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## Berries leave a note block behind

**Codes:** `D38D-ADAC` `D32D-64D6`
**Raw form:** `02BB03:0E` (orig `$04`); `02D208:0E` (orig `$04`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 21:41:31

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `curated`

**Mechanism:** When Yoshi eats a berry, the game replaces the berry tile with
`GenerateTile`, using tile `$04` ("tree background, for berries" in
`GeneratedTiles`, `bank_00.asm`). There are two paths, one for each way
of eating a berry (`bank_02.asm`):
- Yoshi's tongue: `CODE_02BA92` finds the berry and `CODE_02BAC0` puts
  the tile where the berry was (`LDA.B #$04` at `$02BB02`).
- Yoshi walks into the berry: `CODE_01F00F` calls `SetTreeTile`, which puts
  the tile at `YoshiXPos`/`YoshiYPos` (`LDA.B #$04` at `$02D207`).

Both codes change the `$04` to `$0E`, the music block entry in the same table.
It draws Map16 tile `$113` from `TileToGeneratePg1`, the plain note block. So
each eaten berry turns into a note block, which bounces Mario when he lands
on it. `$0E` is also what an ordinary note block puts back after it is hit
(`IntBlk_BlockToGenerate`).

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `A9 04 85 9C 22 B0 BE 00` (`LDA #$04 /
STA Map16TileGenerate / JSL GenerateTile`) at both `$02BB02` and `$02D207`, as
in the source. The codes decode back to `$02BB03:$0E` and `$02D208:$0E` with
`tools/gg_encode.py`.

**Caveats:**

- Use both codes. With only one, berries eaten the other way still leave the
  tree tile.
- The note block is solid. When Yoshi walks into a berry, the block appears at
  Yoshi's own position, so Yoshi and Mario may end up inside it or be pushed
  out of it.
- The berry still counts as eaten, so the berry counters, the eggs and the
  green berry time bonus work as before.
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## Mario can pick up almost any solid block

**Code:** `DDE1-646D`
**Raw form:** `00F26A:00` (orig `$20`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 21:42:28

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `video-ready` `curated`

**Mechanism:** Mario picks up a throw block in `CODE_00F267` (`bank_00.asm`):

```
CODE_00F267:
    CPY.B #$2E                ; Map16 tile $12E, the throw block
    BNE Return00F28B          ; <- operand $20 at $00F26A
    BIT.B byetudlrFrame
    BVC Return00F28B          ; Y/X not just pressed
    LDA.W IsCarryingItem
    ORA.W PlayerRidingYoshi
    BNE Return00F28B
    ...
    JSL CODE_02862F           ; new throw block sprite, carried by Mario
    ...                       ; tile becomes empty (GenerateTile $02)
```

It has two callers, and both call it only for the solid page-1 tiles
`$111`-`$16D`, with the low byte of the tile in Y:
- `CODE_00EC4E`: Mario touches the tile from the side while facing it.
- `CODE_00EE57`: Mario stands on the tile.

The code changes the `BNE` operand to `$00`, so the branch goes to the next
instruction whether it is taken or not. Every tile in that range then passes
the test. When Mario presses Y or X next to such a block, or standing on it,
the block disappears and Mario holds a throw block. He can carry it and throw
it like a normal throw block.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `C0 2E D0 20 24 16 50 1C` at `$00F267`, as
in the source. `$00F26B + $20 = $00F28B`, the `RTS`. The code decodes back to
`$00F26A:$00` with `tools/gg_encode.py`.

**Caveats:**

- Whatever the block was, Mario always gets a throw block. Items inside
  question blocks are lost.
- The `$111`-`$16D` range includes turn blocks, question blocks, used blocks,
  cement blocks and pipes. Some levels also use tiles in that range for
  ground, so Mario can dig into it by pressing Y or X.
- Pressing Y or X to start running while standing on such a tile picks it up.
- Tiles outside the range (most ground, ledges, coins) cannot be picked up.
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## Yoshi's pink-berry egg hatches a Chargin' Chuck

**Code:** `BFE4-0FD0`
**Raw form:** `01F124:91` (orig `$6A`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 21:43:24

**Mechanism:** When Yoshi eats his second pink berry, `CODE_01F116`
(`bank_01.asm`) chooses the sprite that his egg will hatch:

```
CODE_01F116:
    INC.W PinkBerriesEaten
    LDA.W PinkBerriesEaten
    CMP.B #$02
    BNE Return01F12D
    STZ.W PinkBerriesEaten
    LDA.B #$6A                ; <- operand at $01F124 (coin game cloud)
CODE_01F125:
    STA.W YoshiEggSpriteHatch
```

The code changes `$6A` to `$91`, the Chargin' Chuck. The egg copies
`YoshiEggSpriteHatch` into `SpriteMisc151C`. When it hatches, `CODE_01F83D`
writes that into `SpriteNumber,X` and calls `InitSpriteTables`, so a Chargin'
Chuck comes out of the egg instead of the cloud.

The hatch never runs a sprite's init routine. That loses nothing here,
because the Chargin' Chuck's entry in `CallSpriteInit` is `Return018869`,
which does nothing.

Only the pink berry path loads this `$6A`. The other berry path jumps to
`CODE_01F125` with its own sprite number, so it does not change.

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `EE D5 18 AD D5 18 C9 02 D0 0D 9C D5 18 A9
6A 8D DA 18` at `$01F116`, as in the source. The `LDA` operand is at
`$01F124`. The code decodes back to `$01F124:$91` with `tools/gg_encode.py`.

**Caveats:**

- The Chuck uses whatever sprite graphics the level loaded. In a level without
  the Chuck graphics, it is drawn with the wrong tiles.
- No coin game cloud appears.
- With "Yoshi's pink-berry egg hatches a fish that flops about on dry land",
  this code wins: the egg holds a Chuck, so the cloud's handler never runs.
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

## Mario throws Yoshi fireballs

**Codes:** `FFEA-6DD7` `DDEA-6F07` `E4EA-6707` `D5EC-6407` `D9E8-6D07`
**Raw form:** `00FEC0:11` (orig `$05`); `00FEC5:00` (orig `$30`);
`00FECD:F2` (orig `$FE`); `00FEA9:07` (orig `$09`); `00FEB1:05` (orig `$07`)
(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
SNES Game Genie has no compare byte)
**Recorded:** 2026-10-04 22:07:59

Tags: `demo-ready` `play-start` `video-ready` `curated`

**Mechanism:** This is a 5-code version of "Mario throws Yoshi's fireballs" in
`smw_game_genie_big_codes.md`. `ShootFireball` (`$00FEA8`, `bank_00.asm`)
spawns extended sprite `$11` (`YoshiFireball`) instead of `$05`, with no Y
speed, in slot 7 or 6 instead of 9 or 8. `YoshiFireball` gets its OAM index
from `DATA_02A153`, which has entries only for slots 0-7.

The 6-code version writes new X speeds into both bytes of `DATA_00FE94`. This
one saves a code by changing only the high byte of the table's address in
`LDA.W DATA_00FE94,Y` (`B9 94 FE` at `$00FECB`). It reads `$00F294,Y`
instead. Those two bytes are code in `RunPage0Blocks`, `CD 21`. As speeds,
that is `$CD` (-3.2 px per frame) facing left and `$21` (+2.1 px per frame)
facing right. `YoshiFireball` moves in 1/16 px units, and Yoshi's own speed
is `$28` (2.5 px per frame).

**Evidence:** The reference ROM has `A9 30 9D 3D 17 A4 76 B9 94 FE` at
`$00FEC4`, and `CD 21` at `$00F294`. The codes decode back to their raw forms
with `tools/gg_encode.py`. The other four codes are the ones in the
`smw_game_genie_big_codes.md` entry.

**Caveats:**

- Fireballs thrown left move about 50% faster than fireballs thrown right.
- The other caveats of the `smw_game_genie_big_codes.md` entry apply: slots
  6-7 are shared, and a fireball can hit the same Chuck more than once.
- Do not use this with the codes that patch `$00FEC0`, `$00FEC5` or
  `$00FEB1` ("Mario throws hammers instead of fireballs", "Fireball launch Y
  speed", "Mario gets four fireballs at once").
- Not tested in play. The effect comes from the disassembly.

(address:new-byte — the original byte is documentation, not part of the code;
